response:
The house of Mr. Henry Lomax stood upon a quiet street in the town of Belford, at that point where the thoroughfare, having passed the last of the brick stores and the Methodist church, relaxed into a leisurely succession of picket fences, magnolia trees, and modest frame dwellings, each with its front porch and its strip of lawn. It was not the largest house in the neighborhood, nor the most pretentious; but it was among the neatest, and those who knew the family were wont to say that it reflected very fairly the character of its owners, who were persons of moderate means, quiet tastes, and a rigid, if somewhat anxious, respectability. Mr. Lomax kept a drug store on Market Street, where he compounded prescriptions with a precision that had won the confidence of several physicians of both races, and sold patent medicines, toilet articles, and soda water to a clientele which, if not large, was at least loyal. His wife, who had been a school-teacher before her marriage, presided over the household with a firm and gracious hand, and was esteemed by the colored society of Belford, which had its grades and distinctions no less rigorously observed than those of its white neighbors, as a woman of refinement and good judgment.

It was upon an evening in early October, some years ago, that Mr. Lomax returned from a journey to the North, whither he had gone, as his friends understood, upon business connected with the purchase of supplies. He came up the walk with a step somewhat slower than his wont, and his wife, who had been watching for him from the parlor window, observed that he paused at the gate and looked at the house for a moment, as a man might look at a picture which he admired but did not intend to buy. She went to the door to meet him, and he kissed her with his customary affection; but there was something in his manner, an abstraction, a certain avoidance of her eyes, which did not escape her.

"You are tired, Henry," she said, taking his valise from him and setting it down in the hall. "Supper has been waiting this half-hour. Dicey has kept the chicken warm, and there is a peach cobbler, which I made myself, because I knew you would be hungry for something that was not cooked in a hotel."

"You are very good, Clarissa," he replied. "I am not so hungry as I ought to be; but I shall do justice to the cobbler, if only for your sake. Where is the boy?"

"He is asleep. He tried his best to stay awake for you, but the sandman was too strong for him. You may go up and look at him after supper, if you will promise not to wake him."

They sat down to the table, which was spread with a white cloth and furnished with silver and china that had been wedding presents, and which Mrs. Lomax brought out only upon occasions. The old woman who served them, a stout, black, motherly person who had been in Mrs. Lomax's family since before the war, set the dishes before them with many expressions of satisfaction at the master's return.

"Lawd, Mist' Henry," she said, "I sho' is glad ter see you back home. Miss Clarissy ain' been fittin' ter live wid sence you be'n gone. She be'n a-walkin' de flo' an' a-lookin' out'n de winder 'tel I tol' her she gwine wear a hole in de cyarpet. An' de little man, he be'n axin' eve'y day w'en his pa comin' home. I reckon dem Yankees didn' feed you nothin' fitten, nuther; you looks peaked."

"They fed me well enough, Aunt Dicey," said Mr. Lomax with a smile; "but they did not feed me so well as you will, I am sure."

When the meal was ended, and the old woman had cleared the table and withdrawn to her own quarters in the rear of the lot, Mrs. Lomax took up her sewing and seated herself in her accustomed chair beside the lamp in the sitting-room, while her husband, having gone upstairs to look at his sleeping son, came down again and stood for some time before the fireplace, in which a small fire of pine knots had been kindled against the chill of the autumn evening. He was a man of perhaps five-and-thirty, of medium height and good figure, with straight brown hair, gray eyes, and a complexion which, though a shade darker than that of the average Anglo-Saxon, would have attracted no remark in any company where his antecedents were unknown. His wife was of a warmer hue, a soft brown, like the color of a ripe chestnut; her hair, which she wore smoothly parted, had a slight wave in it, and her features, though regular and pleasing, bore unmistakably the impress of that race from which, in the eyes of the law and of society, both she and her husband derived their status. It was a difference which had never, in the eight years of their married life, been spoken of between them; and if Mr. Lomax had ever reflected upon it, he had kept his reflections to himself.

"Clarissa," he said at length, without turning from the fire, "I have something to tell you."

She did not look up from her sewing, but her needle paused for an instant before it resumed its course.

"I thought as much," she answered quietly. "You have been carrying it about with you ever since you came in at the gate. I saw you stop and look at the house."

He turned and regarded her with some surprise. "You are very observant," he said.

"A wife learns to be, Henry. What is it? You have not lost money, I hope?"

"No, I have not lost money. On the contrary, I have been offered a great deal of it—more, I dare say, than I could hope to make in twenty years behind the counter on Market Street." He drew a letter from his pocket and held it in his hand, but did not offer it to her. "You know that I went to Philadelphia to see the Messrs. Hargrove, the wholesale chemists, about a line of goods. I saw the senior partner, Mr. Josiah Hargrove, an old gentleman of great wealth and, I should judge, of great kindness. We fell to talking of pharmacy, and of chemistry in general, and he found that I knew something of the subject—more, perhaps, than he had expected to find in a country druggist from the South. He asked me to dine with him at his house. I went. He showed me through his laboratories the next day, and put some questions to me which I was fortunate enough to answer to his satisfaction. And on the morning that I left, he called me into his private office and offered me the position of assistant to the superintendent of his works, at a salary of three thousand dollars a year, with the promise of advancement."

Mrs. Lomax laid down her sewing and looked at her husband with eyes in which surprise and pleasure were for the moment mingled.

"Three thousand dollars!" she exclaimed. "Why, Henry, that is splendid! I always knew that you were wasted here. I am proud of you—very proud. But why do you look so grave about it? One would think you had been offered a position in the penitentiary rather than in a great house like that."

He did not answer at once, and in the silence the pine knots crackled in the grate, and the clock upon the mantel ticked off the seconds with an insistence that seemed, to the woman at least, unnaturally loud.

"Did you tell him," she asked slowly, "who you are?"

He met her gaze, and then looked away.

"He did not ask me," he said.

There are moments in human intercourse when a few words convey more than volumes could express, and when the speaker, having uttered them, would gladly give a year of his life to recall them. Mr. Lomax felt, as soon as he had spoken, that he had said too much and yet not enough; and his wife, who understood him better than he understood himself, perceived in that brief reply the whole history of his temptation.

"I see," she said. "He did not ask you; and you did not tell him. And he dined you at his house, with his wife and daughters, I suppose, and showed you his laboratories, and offered you a place among his white workmen and his white clerks, believing you to be what you seemed. And now you have come home to tell me about it."

"Clarissa," he said, with some warmth, "you are unjust. I did nothing dishonorable. I made no false statement. I was asked my name, and I gave it. I was asked where I had studied, and I told him. I was asked my business, and I described it truthfully. If he chose to draw conclusions which the facts did not warrant, was it my duty to correct him? Does any white man, when he applies for a position, think it necessary to announce that his grandfather was an Englishman or an Irishman or a Dutchman? Why should I be held to a stricter accountability than other men?"

"Because," she answered, "the world holds you so. You know it as well as I. You may call it unjust—it is unjust—but it is the fact; and a man does not escape a fact by refusing to mention it."

"A man may escape it," he said, "by going where it is not known."

She looked at him steadily. "And have you accepted?"

He hesitated. "I have not refused," he said. "I asked for a fortnight in which to consider the matter, and to arrange my affairs. Mr. Hargrove was good enough to grant it. This letter is his formal offer, which he handed me as I was leaving."

He laid the letter upon the table beside her, and she glanced at it without touching it, as one might glance at a serpent whose fangs had not yet been drawn.

"And what of us, Henry?" she asked, in a voice that was very low but quite steady. "What of the boy and me?"

It was the question he had foreseen, and for which he had been preparing an answer through all the long hours of the journey southward; yet now that it had come, the answer, which had seemed so reasonable in the railway carriage, seemed suddenly to have lost its plausibility.

"I have thought of that," he said, "and I have thought of nothing else. It would not be possible, at first, for you to come with me. You must see that. I should have to establish myself, to make my position secure, to win the confidence of my employer. In a year, or two years at most, I should be in a position to do as I pleased. Then we might go elsewhere—to the West, perhaps, where no one would know us, and where—"

"Where no one would look at me," she interrupted, "and wonder what a man like you was doing with a wife of my complexion. Go on, Henry. I am listening."

"You are making it very hard for me, Clarissa."

"I do not think it is I who am making it hard," she replied. "Did you think that I had never looked in a glass? Did you think that I did not know, when I married you, that you might have married otherwise, had you chosen to forget where you were born? I have known it for eight years. I have seen white men in the cars speak to you civilly until they saw me beside you, and then turn away. I have seen the clerks in the stores look from your face to mine with a question in their eyes. I have never spoken of it, because I thought you did not care. I thought that you had made your choice, once for all, when you made me your wife, and that you were content with it."

"I was content," he said. "I am content. Do you think that I love you less because of this? Good God, Clarissa, it is for you that I would do it, for you and the boy. What is there for him here? What is there for any of us? I have worked for fifteen years, and I have saved a little money, and I have the good will of a few doctors who send me their prescriptions because I fill them accurately and charge them fairly. But I may not sit in the front of the theatre; I may not ride in the same car with men whose fathers sold my grandmother; I may not vote, save at the peril of my business and perhaps of my life. And our son—what will he be? A druggist like his father, if he is fortunate; a porter or a waiter, if he is not. He has my complexion, Clarissa. He has a better mind than mine. Up there, the world would be open to him. Here, it is shut, and barred, and the key thrown away."

The woman was silent for a long time. The fire had burned low, and the shadows had crept in from the corners of the room, so that the lamp seemed to burn in a little island of light, in which the two figures sat facing each other across the table where the letter lay.

"You speak of the boy," she said at length. "Have you thought what you would teach him? Would you tell him, when he is old enough to understand, that his mother is a servant in his father's house, or a poor relation whom it is not convenient to acknowledge? Or would you tell him that she is dead? Would you take him from me, Henry, and bring him up to be ashamed of me, and to despise the people from whom I came, and from whom you came, too, however you may try to forget it?"

"You put it cruelly," he said.

"I put it truly. It is the truth that is cruel, not I. You talk of going West, after a year or two. But you know, and I know, that it would not end there. A man who has once begun to hide does not stop hiding. There would always be someone who might recognize you, some old acquaintance from Belford who might meet you on the street, some letter that might fall into the wrong hands. You would live in fear of every stranger. And I should be the thing you feared most, because I should be the proof. You would not mean to hate me, Henry. You are too good a man for that. But in the end you would come to wish that I had never been born."

He rose from his chair and went again to the fireplace, where he stood with his back to her, his hands clasped behind him. It was a long time before he spoke, and when he did, his voice was hoarse.

"And if I stay," he said, "what then? Shall I not come, in the end, to hate the life that I have chosen, and perhaps to hate the cause of it? Is not that a danger also?"

"It is," she answered simply. "I do not pretend that it is not. I cannot promise you that you will be happy here. I can only promise you that you will be honest, and that you will not be alone. If that is not enough, then go. I shall not hold you. I shall tell the neighbors that you have gone North on business, and they may think what they please. You may send money for the boy, if you like; and when he is old enough to choose, he may choose for himself. But I will not go with you as a lie, Henry. I have been a great many things that the world did not respect, but I have never yet been that."

It is related of a certain ancient philosopher that, being offered his liberty upon condition that he would deny the truth of his teaching, he chose rather to drink the hemlock; and the world has ever since applauded his choice, though it has seldom been disposed to imitate it. It would be pleasant to record that Mr. Lomax, confronted thus with the alternative of fortune and freedom on the one hand and duty and affection on the other, chose instantly and without regret the nobler course. But the historian, who is bound by the facts, must confess that he stood for a long while before the dying fire, and that the struggle which went on within him was neither brief nor easy. For the prize which he was asked to renounce was not merely money, nor even position, but that thing which every man desires and which he had never possessed—the right to be judged by what he was rather than by what his ancestors had been. And it is not to be wondered at if, for a time, the scales hung even.

The clock struck ten. Somewhere upstairs the child stirred in his sleep and murmured a word or two, and was still again. The woman by the lamp had taken up her sewing once more, and her needle went in and out with a steadiness which might have deceived a casual observer, but which did not deceive her husband, who, turning at last, saw that her hands were trembling and that her eyes were wet.

He crossed the room and stood beside her. He took the letter from the table, read it through once more by the light of the lamp, and then, without a word, folded it and dropped it into the embers of the fire. It caught, and flared up for a moment, illuminating the room with a sudden brightness in which the two faces, the fair and the dark, were seen side by side; and then it fell into ashes, and the shadows came back.

"I shall write to Mr. Hargrove in the morning," he said, "and tell him that my affairs here will not permit me to leave them. It will be the truth."

She put down her sewing and took his hand and held it against her cheek, and for some time neither of them spoke.

"You will not be sorry, Henry?" she asked at last.

"I do not know," he answered honestly. "I may be, sometimes. But I think I should be sorrier the other way."

It was perhaps not the answer of a hero of romance; but Mrs. Lomax, who was a sensible woman and had no great opinion of heroes of romance, was quite content with it, and said so.

The Messrs. Hargrove, it may be added, found no difficulty in filling the vacancy. They engaged, within the month, a young man from Baltimore whose credentials were excellent and whose complexion was beyond reproach, and who rose in time to be superintendent of the works, and married the younger Miss Hargrove, and was much respected in Philadelphia. It was whispered, many years afterward, by an old woman who had known his people in Maryland, that his grandmother had been born in a cabin on the Eastern Shore and had been sold at auction in Annapolis. But the old woman was known to be garrulous and not altogether reliable; the firm never heard of the rumor; and it is therefore, in the eyes of the world, of no consequence whatever.

response:
It was in the latter part of September, when the cotton fields about Clarendon had begun to whiten, and the long, languid summer of the Carolina lowlands was yielding, with characteristic reluctance, to the first faint coolness of autumn, that Mr. Edward Lacy alighted from the northbound train at the little brick station which had served the town since before the war. He was a man of perhaps thirty-five, of medium height and well-knit figure, dressed with that sober correctness which marks the professional man of the Northern cities, and which, in a town like Clarendon, was apt to excite rather more curiosity than admiration. His complexion was of so light a shade that a stranger, seeing him for the first time, might have hesitated before assigning him to either of the two great divisions into which Southern society was then, and is yet, so sharply separated. But Clarendon was not a town of strangers, and there were those upon the platform who, after a second glance, nudged one another and remarked that this must be "old Mis' Lacy's boy Edward, that went off up No'th to school and never come back."

The truth of this observation was not to be disputed. Edward Lacy had left Clarendon at the age of seventeen, with a carpetbag, a letter of introduction from the Northern missionary who had conducted the colored school, and a sum of money, laboriously saved by his widowed mother from the proceeds of her needle, which would scarcely have paid a white boy's fare to the state capital. He had worked his way through a Western college, had read law in the office of a liberal-minded attorney in the city of Lakeport, upon the shores of one of the Great Lakes, and had there attained a modest practice and a position of some consideration among the colored people of that community, who were, as he had found, by no means without their own distinctions of rank and refinement. His mother had died some years before, and he had come down for the funeral, remaining but a single day; and since that time no tie had drawn him back to the town of his birth, until a letter from a local attorney informed him that a small parcel of land, the last remnant of his grandfather's estate, required his signature before it could be sold.

He had written, in advance of his coming, to his cousin Calvin, the son of his mother's elder sister, with whom he had passed the greater part of his childhood, and who, as he understood from the infrequent correspondence that had passed between them, was now established as a wheelwright and blacksmith upon the edge of town. He had half expected to find Calvin at the station, and was conscious of a slight disappointment, mingled with a certain relief, when no familiar face presented itself. He engaged an elderly hackman, whose vehicle bore marks of having seen service under the old régime, and gave the direction.

"Calvin Lacy's shop? Yas, suh, I knows de place," said the driver, eyeing his fare with frank interest. "You's kin to Calvin, I reckon?"

"His cousin," replied Edward.

"Den you mus' be de lawyer. Calvin been talkin' 'bout you all de week. He 'lowed you'd be comin' on de fo'-o'clock train, but a man fum out in de country brung in a buggy wid a broke axle, an' he couldn' leave it. Calvin's a mighty good workman, suh. White folks an' black folks bofe fetches deir wuk to him."

The road led through the main street of the town, past the market-house with its arched openings and its belfry, past the courthouse in its grove of oaks, and out along a sandy lane bordered by modest dwellings, some of them whitewashed, some of them innocent of paint, and all of them surrounded by gardens in which late okra and collards contested the ground with sunflowers and the hardier sorts of roses. Edward observed, with the eye of a returning native, how little and how much the place had changed. The market-house was the same, though a new clock had been set in its tower; the courthouse was the same, though a granite soldier, in the uniform of a cause which Edward had been taught to regard with very different sentiments from those which had erected him, now stood guard before its portico. There was a cotton mill by the river, which had not been there before, and from its tall chimney a thin column of smoke ascended into the still air, the visible sign of what the local newspapers were fond of calling the New South.

Calvin's shop stood at the corner of the lane and the county road, a low, wide structure of weathered boards, with a forge glowing in its dim interior and a litter of wheels, tires, and shafts about its door. Behind it, at a little distance, stood a neat cottage of four rooms, painted white, with green blinds and a porch shaded by a scuppernong vine. As the hack drew up, a tall, broad-shouldered man, with a skin of a rich brown and a leather apron about his waist, laid down his hammer and came forward, wiping his hands upon a piece of sacking.

The two cousins regarded each other for a moment in silence. Each, perhaps, was measuring the other against a recollection eighteen years old; and each, perhaps, found that the measure did not quite fit. Edward saw before him a man whose features he knew, but whose bearing had acquired a gravity and a quiet assurance which the boy he remembered had not possessed. Calvin saw a gentleman, as the word was understood in Clarendon,—a man of fine linen and soft hands, whose speech, when he opened his mouth, had lost every trace of the soft local accent, and who carried himself with an air of reserve which might have been either pride or shyness.

"Well, Edward," said Calvin at length, holding out his hand, and then, with a sudden recollection, glancing at its condition and withdrawing it, "I'd shake han's wid you, but I'm afeard I'd spile yo' gloves."

Edward stripped off his glove and seized the hard, blackened hand in his own.

"Confound the gloves, Calvin," he said, with a warmth that surprised himself. "It's been a long time."

"It sho' has," said Calvin, and his face broke into the wide, slow smile that Edward remembered from their boyhood. "Come on up to de house. Ma'y Jane's been cookin' since sun-up, an' de chillen's been washed till dey shines. You'll have to 'scuse me a minute while I put up dis axle. Dat man fum Rockfish Creek's gwine want his buggy fo' night."

Calvin's wife received her husband's cousin with a mixture of hospitality and awe, which manifested itself chiefly in an excessive solicitude for his comfort, and in frequent apologies for the plainness of a table which would have done credit to a much more pretentious household. There was fried chicken, and ham of Calvin's own curing, and sweet potatoes, and hot biscuits, and a dish of field peas cooked with bacon, and a pie made from the scuppernongs that hung in purple clusters over the porch. The children, three in number, ranging in age from four to eleven, sat in a row upon a bench and regarded the visitor with round eyes, until the eldest, a sturdy boy named for his grandfather, was emboldened to ask whether it was true that in the North there were houses ten stories high, and whether the cousin had ever been up in one of them.

"I have an office in one," said Edward, smiling, "on the seventh floor. I go up and down in an elevator,—a little room that moves on ropes."

The boy's eyes grew rounder still, and his mother bade him not to be asking so many questions; but Edward observed that the question had been not unwelcome to the parents, and that Calvin, in particular, regarded him with a pride in which there was no trace of envy.

When the meal was finished and the children had been put to bed, the two men went out upon the porch, where the evening air, heavy with the scent of the ripening grapes, had grown pleasantly cool. Calvin produced a pair of clay pipes and a pouch of tobacco, and Edward, who in Lakeport smoked only cigars, and those rarely, accepted a pipe without hesitation. For a while they smoked in silence, watching the moon rise over the pine woods beyond the county road.

"Do you remember," said Edward presently, "the time we took old Major Dancy's skiff and went down the river to the Narrows, and couldn't get back against the current, and had to walk home through the swamp?"

Calvin laughed softly. "Does I remember? I got de wust whippin' I ever had in my life fo' dat. Yo' ma didn' whip you, though. She jes' cried, an' dat was wuss fo' you dan any whippin'. You always was tender-hearted dat way."

"I'd forgotten that," said Edward.

"An' de Major," continued Calvin, "he come ridin' 'roun' next day, cussin' an' swearin' he gwine have us bofe sent to de chain-gang. But when he seen de skiff wa'n't hurt none, he cooled off, an' 'fo' he lef' he give us each a dime an' tol' us we was a couple o' young rascals. He's daid now. Died de year after yo' ma did. Dey say he lef' his money to a home fo' ole Confederate soldiers, an' his niece what kep' house fo' him twenty years didn' git a cent."

The conversation thus begun flowed on, as such conversations will, from one recollection to another, and from the dead to the living. Edward learned that Aunt Hagar, who had nursed half the colored children of the town through the measles and the whooping-cough, still lived, though nearly blind, and still dispensed her remedies of horehound and catnip to such as would take them. He learned that the Northern missionary who had taught them their letters had gone back to Massachusetts and died there, and that the school had been taken over by the county, which had cut its term from eight months to four. He learned that Sam Gatling, who had been the best scholar in the school and the despair of his teacher's efforts to make him behave, was now a preacher of great power in the African Methodist connection; and that Lucy Maybin, a pretty mulatto girl for whose favor the two cousins had once been rivals, had married a white man in another state, where no one knew her, and had never been heard from since.

"Her folks don' never speak of her," said Calvin. "It's de same as ef she was daid. Mo' so, maybe. Folks speaks o' de daid."

Edward was silent for a moment. The moonlight, falling through the vine, made a tracery of light and shadow upon his face, and Calvin, glancing at him, could not read its expression.

"I don't know that I blame her," said Edward at length.

"I didn' say I blamed her," replied Calvin. "I jes' said her folks don' speak of her."

There was another pause, which Edward was the first to break.

"You've done well, Calvin," he said, with a gesture which included the cottage, the shop, and the garden. "Better than I expected,—I don't mean that unkindly. I mean that when I left, there didn't seem to be much chance for anybody here."

"I've done tol'able," said Calvin modestly. "I owns de house an' de shop, an' two acres o' groun' back yonder, an' dey ain' no mortgage on none of it. I does mo' wuk dan any smith in de county, 'cause I does it right an' charges fair. Some o' de white folks calls me 'Uncle Calvin,' dough I ain' but thirty-six, an' some of 'em calls me Lacy, an' one or two of 'em calls me Mister when dey ain' nobody else 'roun' to hear 'em. I keeps my mouf shet 'bout politics, an' I don' go to town on Sat'day nights, an' I minds my own business. Dat's de way a colored man gits along in Clarendon."

He said this without bitterness, as a man might describe the conditions of the weather or the soil; but Edward, who had acquired in the North the habit of examining such conditions with a more critical eye, felt the words strike upon him with a peculiar force.

"And you can bear it?" he asked.

Calvin took his pipe from his mouth and looked at it reflectively.

"Edward," he said, "I'm gwine tell you somethin' I ain' never tol' nobody but Ma'y Jane. 'Bout two years after you lef', dat same missionary lady wrote to me fum Massachusetts. She say she done foun' a place fo' me in a school up dere, where I could learn to be a machinist, an' she'd pay my way. I had de letter in my pocket fo' a month. I used to take it out an' read it when nobody was lookin'. But my ma had de rheumatism so bad she couldn' git out o' bed half de time, an' dey wa'n't nobody else to look after her, an' after a while I wrote back an' tol' de lady I couldn' come. Ma lived eleven years after dat. I ain' never been sorry, an' I ain' never stopped wonderin', bofe at de same time. I reckon dat soun's foolish."

"It doesn't sound foolish," said Edward slowly. "It sounds very human."

"An' as fo' bearin' it," Calvin went on, "a man kin bear mos' anything ef he has to. Las' spring dey come mighty nigh lynchin' a colored boy here fo' somethin' it tu'ned out a white man done. Dey had de rope 'roun' his neck down by de river bridge, an' it was ole Judge Spencer, what was in de war an' hates de colored folks in a gen'al way, dat rode down dere an' talked 'em out of it. Dey's all kinds o' white folks, same as dey's all kinds o' colored folks. But I ain' gwine tell you dat it's easy. Dey passed a law two years ago dat a man has to read an' 'splain de Constitution 'fo' he kin vote, an' de registrar ax me what de Constitution say 'bout de writ o' habeas corpus, an' when I tol' him, he say I didn' 'splain it right. De same day he registered Bill Pruitt, what can't write his own name. Dat's de law, an' dat's de way dey 'splains it."

Edward laughed, though not with much mirth.

"You understand the Constitution better than half the lawyers in Lakeport," he said.

"Maybe so," said Calvin. "But tell me 'bout yo'self. You ain' said a word 'bout how things is wid you up yonder. I reckon a colored man's as good as anybody up No'th."

Edward did not answer at once. He was conscious, as he had often been in the course of his career, of a certain inward reluctance to speak of matters which, when he contemplated them in the solitude of his own thoughts, did not always present themselves in the most flattering light.

"In law," he said at length, "a colored man is as good as anybody in Lakeport. He can vote, and his vote is counted. He can ride in any car and sit in any seat. His children go to the same schools as white children. I have white clients,—not many, but some,—and I have won cases before white juries. In those respects it is a different world from this."

"Dat's what I always heared," said Calvin, with satisfaction.

"But there are other respects," continued Edward, as if he had not heard. "There are hotels where I could not get a room, though there is no law that forbids it, and restaurants where I should be served so slowly and so badly that I should not care to go back. There are clubs and societies that a man of my profession would naturally belong to, and to which I shall never be asked. There are white lawyers who meet me in court with perfect civility and would not know me on the street. And there is another thing, Calvin, which I have never told anyone."

Calvin waited.

"There are many places in Lakeport," said Edward, with a certain effort, "where I am not known, and where I am taken for a white man. I have never told anyone that I was white. But I have not always told them that I was not. When a man at a lunch counter or a theatre or a railway station speaks to me as one white man speaks to another, I do not correct him. I have told myself it is no one's business but my own, and I suppose that is true. But I have sometimes wondered, on such occasions, what I should do if one of my own people,—if you, for instance,—were to come up and speak to me by name."

The moon had risen above the vine, and its light fell full upon the two men,—upon the one face, dark and grave, and upon the other, pale and troubled. Calvin was silent for so long that Edward began to regret his confidence. When at last Calvin spoke, his voice was gentle.

"I reckon," he said, "dat you'd speak to me. You was always tender-hearted."

Edward did not reply; but he reached over in the darkness and laid his hand for a moment upon his cousin's shoulder.

The talk drifted thereafter to lighter matters, and it was nearly midnight when they parted. Edward slept in the best room of the cottage, upon a feather bed of formidable depth, beneath a quilt which Calvin's mother had pieced in the year of the surrender; and if he lay awake longer than the fatigue of his journey would have warranted, it was not because the bed was uncomfortable.

The business of the land was concluded on the following morning, in the office of a white attorney who addressed Edward with scrupulous courtesy as "Lacy," and contrived, with an ingenuity which Edward could not but admire, to avoid any form of address whatever when the need for one arose. In the afternoon the cousins visited Aunt Hagar, who passed her withered hands over Edward's face and declared that she would have known him anywhere, and the little cemetery behind the colored Baptist church, where Edward stood for a long while before two plain headstones, while Calvin, with a delicacy which the most polished society might have envied, busied himself at the other end of the enclosure pulling weeds from his own mother's grave.

On the third day Edward took the train for the North. Calvin drove him to the station in a light wagon of his own construction, and the two stood together upon the platform until the train drew in. It was made up, after the custom of the state, of a single car for colored passengers, placed next to the baggage car, and several cars for white passengers behind it. The conductor, a portly man with a gray moustache, came down the platform, glanced at Edward, and with a wave of his hand directed him toward the rear.

"Plenty of room back yonder, sir," he said.

Edward hesitated for a fraction of a second. He was aware of Calvin standing beside him, of the black faces at the windows of the forward car, and of the conductor's eye, which had not yet perceived anything to arrest it. Then he picked up his bag.

"Good-by, Calvin," he said, and gripped his cousin's hand. "Write to me. And send the boy up to me when he's old enough. I'll see that he gets his chance."

"I'll do it," said Calvin.

Edward turned and walked, not toward the rear of the train, but toward the forward car. The conductor stared, opened his mouth as if to speak, then shrugged his shoulders, as a man will in the presence of a phenomenon which it is not his business to explain, and called out his signal to the engineer.

Calvin stood upon the platform until the train had rounded the curve beyond the cotton mill, and the last trailing smoke had faded into the blue September sky. Then he climbed into his wagon and drove slowly back toward the shop, where, as he reminded himself, a man from Rockfish Creek would be calling in the morning for a set of new tires. But he drove with a lighter heart than he had known for many a day; for he had learned that the world beyond Clarendon, of which he had dreamed so long, was not so very different from the world within it, and that the best things a man carries with him, he carries wherever he goes.

Mr. Lucius Hammond, principal of the colored graded school at Clarendon, was accounted by those who knew him, and by a good many who knew him only by report, as a man of singular equanimity. He had been born a slave, but had been too young at the time of the surrender to retain any very vivid recollection of that condition; and the years which had since elapsed had been spent, first at a mission school founded by Northern benevolence, and afterwards at a normal institute in a neighboring State, where he had acquired, along with a fair knowledge of Latin and a smattering of Greek, that habit of self-restraint which the circumstances of his race had made a prime necessity of its more ambitious members. It was his settled conviction that the colored people of the South would rise, if they rose at all, by the slow accretion of character, and that no single quality would serve them better in that ascent than the ability to keep their tempers under provocation. He had preached this doctrine from the platform, he had practiced it in the street, and he had instilled it, with varying success, into some hundreds of the youth of Clarendon. He was therefore not a little disconcerted, upon a certain afternoon in early October, to find himself standing in his own front yard, with his hat still upon his head and his books still under his arm, and a degree of anger in his breast which he had not felt for many years.

The occasion of this disturbance was a small boy of seven, who stood at that moment on the bottom step of the porch, with his hands behind him and his eyes fixed upon a point somewhere in the neighborhood of his father's watch-chain. Philip Hammond was a well-grown child for his age, with his mother's straight nose and his mother's complexion, which was of that clear olive tint that in more southern latitudes might have passed for the effect of a Spanish or Italian ancestry, but which in Clarendon was perfectly well understood to signify something else. He had been the object of a good deal of fond attention from both his parents, and of somewhat more than was good for him from his mother's relations, who were people of some little property and of a certain standing among those of their own color, and who had not failed to remark, in his hearing, upon the fineness of his hair and the fairness of his skin.

Mr. Hammond had come upon the scene by the merest accident. He had been detained at the school-house beyond his usual hour by a conference with one of his assistant teachers, and had chosen, upon setting out for home, to go by way of the lane behind the cotton warehouse instead of by the main street, for no better reason than that the afternoon was fine and the lane was shaded. At the corner where the lane debouched upon Pine Street there stood a vacant lot, overgrown with jimson-weed and dog-fennel, which served the children of the neighborhood, white and colored indiscriminately, as a common playground; for while the line was drawn with tolerable strictness among their elders, it was not always so carefully observed by those whose years had not yet taught them its importance. Across this lot, as Mr. Hammond approached, there was slowly making his way an old black man, bent nearly double under a bundle of fat-pine kindling which he carried upon his back by means of a rope passed across his shoulders. This was old Isom Pettigrew, who had been a slave of the Pettigrews before the war, and who had since supported himself, after a fashion, by cutting wood and selling lightwood knots to such of the townspeople as had not yet learned to depend upon the coal dealer. He was very black, very old, and very poor; and these three facts, which in a more enlightened community might have commended him to compassion, had in Clarendon rendered him a fit subject for the diversion of the idle.

There were four or five boys in the lot, and Mr. Hammond, before he had fairly turned the corner, heard their voices raised in a chorus whose words he could not at first distinguish. As he drew nearer, however, the words became plain enough. They were not new to him; he had heard them, or their like, a thousand times, in the mouths of white boys and white men, and had learned to pass them by with that outward composure which was the badge of his philosophy. But he had not before heard them, as he heard them now, in the clear treble of his own son, who stood a little apart from the others, with a clod of red clay in his hand, and who was calling out, with every appearance of enjoyment, "Old black crow! Old black crow! Look at the old black crow!"

The old man had stopped and turned, so far as his burden would permit, and was regarding his tormentors with a look in which there was more of weariness than of resentment.

"Go 'long, chillun," he said mildly. "Go 'long an' lemme be. I ain' done nuffin ter none er you-all."

Whereupon Philip, emboldened, it would seem, by the applause of his companions, two of whom were white, drew back his arm and let fly the clod, which struck the bundle of kindling squarely and scattered a little shower of red dust over the old man's shoulders.

Mr. Hammond did not run, for a man in his position could not afford to be seen running in the public streets; but he crossed the lot with a celerity which caused the white boys to disappear over the back fence as if by magic, and the two or three colored urchins to scatter in as many directions. Philip alone, who had not seen his father until that moment, remained rooted to the spot, his mouth open and his face, in spite of its natural pallor, grown visibly paler.

Mr. Hammond did not speak to his son. He went directly to the old man, and, setting down his books upon the grass, assisted him to ease his burden to the ground.

"I am very sorry, Uncle Isom," he said. "I am more sorry than I can tell you."

The old man straightened himself by degrees, with a hand upon the small of his back, and peered at the schoolmaster out of eyes which age had dimmed and filmed.

"Dat you, Mistah Hammon'? Lawd, suh, don' you fret yo'se'f 'bout dat. Chillun is chillun, suh. Dey don' mean no harm. I been called wuss'n crow in my time, an' by bigger folks dan dem."

"That may be true," returned Mr. Hammond, "but it is no excuse for my boy. He shall make you amends."

"He ain' got ter do nuffin, suh. 'Tain' no 'casion fer dat."

"There is every occasion," said Mr. Hammond, and with that he helped the old man to readjust his burden, and watched him go on his slow way down Pine Street, before he turned to his son, who had not moved, and said, in a voice whose very quietness was more alarming to the child than any outburst could have been, "Go home, Philip, and wait for me on the porch."

It was thus that the two had arrived at their present position; and Mr. Hammond, having walked the three blocks behind his son in a silence which he did not trust himself to break, now stood regarding the boy with feelings which he found it difficult to analyze. He was conscious of anger, certainly, and of a sense of personal humiliation; for there could be no doubt that the incident would be talked about, and that there would be persons, both white and colored, who would take a malicious pleasure in the spectacle of the apostle of self-control unable to govern his own household. But beneath these feelings there lay another, deeper and more painful, which he did not at once permit himself to name.

"Philip," he said at length, "look at me."

The boy raised his eyes with evident reluctance.

"Do you know what you have done?"

"I—I threw a clod, papa."

"You threw a clod at an old man who had done you no injury, who was carrying a heavy load, and who could neither run after you nor defend himself. That is one thing that you did. What else did you do?"

Philip was silent.

"You called him a name. What was the name you called him?"

The child's lips trembled. "I called him—old black crow."

"And why did you call him that?"

"The other boys were saying it, papa. Tom Ransom said it first, and Willie Mabry, and they said—they said I could play with them if I said it too."

"Tom Ransom and Willie Mabry," repeated Mr. Hammond slowly. He knew the boys; they were the sons of a white druggist and a white lawyer respectively, and it had not before occurred to him that they ever condescended to play with his son. "And did it not occur to you, Philip, that you ought not to do a wrong thing merely because other boys were doing it?"

"They're white boys, papa," said Philip, as though that settled the matter.

Mr. Hammond was a man who did not readily lose his self-possession, but he was conscious at this moment of a sensation very like that of a sudden blow. He sat down upon the top step of the porch, laid his books beside him, and removed his hat, which he held for some moments upon his knee, turning it slowly round and round by the brim.

"Come here, Philip," he said, "and sit beside me."

The boy obeyed, with the wary air of one who suspects that the softening of the parental voice may portend a severer punishment than he has yet anticipated.

"You say they are white boys," Mr. Hammond went on. "That is true. And what are you?"

The child looked up at him in some perplexity. "I'm—I'm not black, papa," he said. "Not like Uncle Isom. Aunt Sophronia says I'm almost white. She says I'm whiter than lots of white folks."

There was a pause, during which Mr. Hammond looked out across the little yard, with its bed of late zinnias and its single crape-myrtle tree, toward the street, where the long shadows of the afternoon were beginning to stretch across the sand. He had suspected something of the sort; he had more than once overheard remarks in his wife's family which had grated upon him, and he had more than once resolved to speak of the matter, and had put it off, as men do put off unpleasant things, in the hope that it might somehow mend itself. It was borne in upon him now, with a force which was the more painful because he could not wholly acquit himself of responsibility, that the thing had not mended itself, but had grown, as such things will, in the warm soil of a child's vanity, until it had borne this bitter fruit.

"Philip," he said, "your Aunt Sophronia is a good woman, and she loves you very much; but she has said a foolish thing, and I want you to forget it. Will you listen to me while I tell you something?"

"Yes, papa."

"You may be whiter than some white people. I do not know; I have never troubled myself to make the comparison. But I will tell you this: if Tom Ransom and Willie Mabry should go home to-night and tell their fathers that you had thrown a clod at Uncle Isom, their fathers would laugh, and say that one nigger had been chunking another. That is the word they would use, Philip. They would not say that a white boy had thrown at a black man, nor that an almost white boy had done so. They would put you and Uncle Isom in the same class, and they would think no more about it. And if, when you are grown, you should go into a court of law, or into a railroad car, or into a hotel, or into any of the places where men are sorted and labeled, you will find that you are labeled with Uncle Isom, and not with Tom Ransom; and all the fairness of your skin will not avail to change the label."

The boy's face clouded, and his lip began once more to tremble. It was evident that this was a new and not altogether welcome revelation.

"But that is not the worst of it," Mr. Hammond continued, and his voice, though still low, took on a graver note. "If it were only a question of what other people think of us, we might bear it, as we have borne a great deal. What troubles me is what you have shown me that you think of yourself, and of your own people. You called Uncle Isom a crow because he is black. Your grandmother, my mother, was as black as Uncle Isom. Did you know that?"

Philip shook his head.

"She died before you were born. She was a slave, and she worked in the fields from the time she was eight years old until the day the Yankees came, and after that she worked at the wash-tub, so that I might go to school and learn the things that I now teach to you and to other children. Her hands were so hard that she could scarcely bend her fingers, and her back was bent almost as Uncle Isom's is bent; and if she were alive to-day, and were walking across the lot by Pine Street with a bundle on her shoulders, I suppose you would call her a crow, too, and throw clods at her, to please Tom Ransom and Willie Mabry."

"No, papa! No, I wouldn't!" cried the boy, and burst into tears.

Mr. Hammond let him cry for a little while. He was not a hard man, and the sight of his son's distress was painful to him; but he had observed, in the course of his professional experience, that the tears of children are frequently more efficacious than any argument, and that a lesson which has been wept over is less apt to be forgotten than one which has been merely heard. Moreover, he was conscious that his own emotions were not altogether under control, and he was not unwilling to take a moment in which to compose them.

From within the house there came presently the sound of a light step, and Mrs. Hammond appeared in the doorway. She was a comely woman of some thirty years, with an air of gentle dignity which became her well, and she regarded the scene upon the porch with an expression of mild alarm.

"Why, Lucius," she exclaimed, "whatever is the matter? Has Philip been hurt?"

"Philip has not been hurt, Caroline," replied her husband, "but he has hurt some one else, and we are discussing the matter."

Mrs. Hammond, who knew her husband well enough to understand from his tone that the matter was serious, and who had besides a wholesome respect for his judgment in the government of the household, withdrew without further question; but not before she had cast upon her son a look in which reproach and tenderness were about equally mingled, and which did nothing to diminish the child's contrition.

When the boy's sobs had somewhat subsided, Mr. Hammond spoke again.

"I do not intend to whip you, Philip," he said. "I have thought about it, and I have concluded that a whipping would be too easy for you. You would cry for a few minutes, and then you would forget all about it, and the next time Tom Ransom asked you to throw a clod at an old man you would very likely do it. I want you to remember this, and so I am going to give you something harder to do than to take a whipping."

The child looked up, his wet face full of apprehension.

"To-morrow is Saturday, and there is no school. In the morning, after breakfast, you and I are going to Uncle Isom's cabin, down by the branch, and you are going to tell him that you are sorry for what you did and for what you said. You are going to tell him yourself, in your own words; I shall not tell you what to say. And then you are going to stay and help him to split his kindling and tie it into bundles, until he tells you that you may go. If he keeps you there all day, you shall stay all day."

Philip's face, at this sentence, underwent a remarkable series of changes. It was plain that the prospect of a public humiliation, for so he conceived it, was more dreadful to him than any amount of corporal punishment; and Mr. Hammond, observing this, felt more strongly than before that he had chosen rightly.

"But, papa," the boy faltered, "suppose—suppose Tom Ransom sees me?"

"If Tom Ransom sees you," replied his father, "you may tell him that you are helping an old man who is one of your own people. And if he laughs at you, you may consider that his laughter is the price of being a gentleman, and that a gentleman of any color must sometimes pay it."

It is perhaps worth while to record, for the benefit of those who take an interest in such matters, that the sentence was duly executed. Mr. Hammond and his son presented themselves at the door of old Isom's cabin at a little after eight o'clock on Saturday morning, and Philip, after several false starts and a good deal of swallowing, made his apology in a form which, though it would not have passed muster in his father's school as an example of English composition, was accepted by the old man with every appearance of satisfaction.

"Dat's all right, honey," said Uncle Isom, laying a gnarled hand upon the child's head. "Dat's all right. I knowed you didn' mean no harm. Yo' gran'mammy, she wuz a good 'oman, an' her chillun wuz good chillun, an' I 'lows her gran'chillun gwine be good chillun too, w'en dey gits growed. Now you come 'long here an' I'll show you how ter split lightwood so it won' fly up an' put yo' eye out."

He kept the boy until the middle of the afternoon, not, as Mr. Hammond afterwards learned, because there was so much kindling to be split, but because he had a great many stories to tell about the old times, and had not for many years enjoyed so attentive an auditor. And it may be set down as one of those small ironies with which the world abounds, that Philip, who had gone to the cabin in fear and trembling, came home at four o'clock with blistered hands and a smudged face, and announced at the supper-table, to the scandal of his Aunt Sophronia, who happened to be visiting, that he meant to be a woodcutter when he grew up, like Uncle Isom, and live in a cabin by the branch, and know all about conjure and hants and the days before the war.

Mrs. Hammond's sister received this declaration with a look of pained astonishment, and remarked that she did not see what the child could be thinking of, with his advantages; to which Mr. Hammond, helping himself to another biscuit, replied with perfect gravity that he thought the boy might do a great deal worse, and that he, for one, would be well content if his son should grow up to have half the patience and good temper of the old man whom he had so lately chosen to call a crow.

Whether Philip ever again played with Tom Ransom and Willie Mabry this narrative does not record. It is known, however, that the lot at the corner of Pine Street was shortly afterwards fenced in by its owner, a white man of some means, who had grown weary of the noise; and that the children of Clarendon, white and colored, were thereafter obliged to seek their diversion in separate places, as their elders had long since done. It is likewise known that old Isom Pettigrew, during the two winters that remained to him, never wanted for a boy to help him tie his bundles, and that when he died, there walked behind his coffin, among the handful of mourners, a slender lad with a clear olive skin, who wept as sincerely as any there, and who did not seem to care in the least who saw him.

Carteret fished from the depths of the waste-basket and handed to the general an eighteen by twenty-four sheet, poorly printed on cheap paper, with a "patent" inside, a number of advertisements of proprietary medicines, quack doctors, and fortune-tellers, and two or three columns of editorial and local news. Candor compels the admission that it was not an impressive sheet in any respect, except when regarded as the first local effort of a struggling people to make public expression of their life and aspirations. From this point of view it did not speak at all badly for a class to whom, a generation before, newspapers, books, and learning had been forbidden fruit.

"It's an elegant specimen of journalism, isn't it?" laughed the general, airily. "Listen to this 'ad':— "'Kinky, curly hair made straight by one application of our specific. Our face bleach will turn the skin of a black or brown person four or five shades lighter, and of a mulatto perfectly white. When you get the color you wish, stop using the preparation.' "Just look at those heads!—'Before using' and 'After using.' We'd better hurry, or there'll be no negroes to disfranchise! If they don't stop till they get the color they desire, and the stuff works according to contract, they'll all be white. Ah! what have we here? This looks as though it might be serious." Opening the sheet the general read aloud an editorial article, to which Carteret listened intently, his indignation increasing in strength from the first word to the last, while McBane's face grew darkly purple with anger. The article was a frank and somewhat bold discussion of lynching and its causes. It denied that most lynchings were for the offense most generally charged as their justification, and declared that, even of those seemingly traced to this cause, many were not for crimes at all, but for voluntary acts which might naturally be expected to follow from the miscegenation laws by which it was sought, in all the Southern States, to destroy liberty of contract, and, for the purpose of maintaining a fanciful purity of race, to make crimes of marriages to which neither nature nor religion nor the laws of other states interposed any insurmountable barrier. Such an article in a Northern newspaper would have attracted no special attention, and might merely have furnished food to an occasional reader for serious thought upon a subject not exactly agreeable; but coming from a colored man, in a Southern city, it was an indictment of the laws and social system of the South that could not fail of creating a profound sensation.

"Infamous—infamous!" exclaimed Carteret, his voice trembling with emotion. "The paper should be suppressed immediately."

"The impudent nigger ought to be horsewhipped and run out of town," growled McBane.

"Gentlemen," said the general soothingly, after the first burst of indignation had subsided, "I believe we can find a more effective use for this article, which, by the way, will not bear too close analysis,—there's some truth in it, at least there's an argument." "That is not the point," interrupted Carteret.

"No," interjected McBane with an oath, "that ain't at all the point. Truth or not, no damn nigger has any right to say it."

"This article," said Carteret, "violates an unwritten law of the South. If we are to tolerate this race of weaklings among us, until they are eliminated by the stress of competition, it must be upon terms which we lay down. One of our conditions is violated by this article, in which our wisdom is assailed, and our women made the subject of offensive comment. We must make known our disapproval."

"I say lynch the nigger, break up the press, and burn down the newspaper office," McBane responded promptly.

"Gentlemen," interposed the general, "would you mind suspending the discussion for a moment, while I mind Jerry across the street? I think I can then suggest a better plan." Carteret rang the bell for Jerry, who answered promptly. He had been expecting such a call ever since the gentlemen had gone in.

"Jerry," said the general, "step across to Brown's and tell him to send me three Calhoun cocktails. Wait for them,—here's the money."

"Yas, suh," replied Jerry, taking the proffered coin.

"And make has'e, charcoal," added McBane, "for we're gettin' damn dry." A momentary cloud of annoyance darkened Carteret's brow. McBane had always grated upon his aristocratic susceptibilities. The captain was an upstart, a product of the democratic idea operating upon the poor white man, the descendant of the indentured bondservant and the socially unfit. He had wealth and energy, however, and it was necessary to make use of him; but the example of such men was a strong incentive to Carteret in his campaign against the negro. It was distasteful enough to rub elbows with an illiterate and vulgar white man of no ancestry,—the risk of similar contact with negroes was to be avoided at any cost. He could hardly expect McBane to be a gentleman, but when among men of that class he might at least try to imitate their manners. A gentleman did not order his own servants around offensively, to say nothing of another's. The general had observed Carteret's annoyance, and remarked pleasantly while they waited for the servant's return:— "Jerry, now, is a very good negro. He's not one of your new negroes, who think themselves as good as white men, and want to run the government. Jerry knows his place,—he is respectful, humble, obedient, and content with the face and place assigned to him by nature."

"Yes, he's one of the best of 'em," sneered McBane. "He'll call any man 'master' for a quarter, or 'God' for half a dollar; for a dollar he'll grovel at your feet, and for a cast-off coat you can buy an option on his immortal soul,—if he has one! I've handled niggers for ten years, and I know 'em from the ground up. They're all alike,—they're a scrub race, an affliction to the country, and the quicker we're rid of 'em all the better." Carteret had nothing to say by way of dissent. McBane's sentiments, in their last analysis, were much the same as his, though he would have expressed them less brutally. "The negro," observed the general, daintily flicking the ash from his cigar, "is all right in his place and very useful to the community. We lived on his labor for quite a long time, and lived very well. Nevertheless we are better off without slavery, for we can get more out of the free negro, and with less responsibility. I really do not see how we could get along without the negroes. If they were all like Jerry, we'd have no trouble with them." Having procured the drinks, Jerry, the momentary subject of the race discussion which goes on eternally in the South, was making his way back across the street, somewhat disturbed in mind.

"O Lawd!" he groaned, "I never troubles trouble till trouble troubles me; but w'en I got dem drinks befo', Gin'l Belmont gimme half a dollar an' tol' me ter keep de change. Dis time he didn' say nothin' 'bout de change. I s'pose he jes' fergot erbout it, but w'at is a po' nigger gwine ter do w'en he has ter conten' wid w'ite folks's fergitfulniss? I don' see no way but ter do some fergittin' myse'f. I'll jes' stan' outside de do' here till dey gits so wrop' up in deir talk dat dey won' 'member nothin' e'se, an' den at de right minute I'll ban' de glasses 'roun, an' moa' lackly de gin'l 'll fergit all 'bout de change." While Jerry stood outside, the conversation within was plainly audible, and some inkling of its purport filtered through his mind.

"Now, gentlemen," the general was saying, "here's my plan. That editorial in the negro newspaper is good campaign matter, but we should reserve it until it will be most effective. Suppose we just stick it in a pigeon-hole, and let the editor,—what's his name?"

"The nigger's name is Barber," replied McBane. "I'd like to have him under me for a month or two; he'd write no more editorials."

"Let Barber have all the rope he wants," resumed the general, "and he'll be sure to hang himself. In the mean time we will continue to work up public opinion,—we can use this letter privately for that purpose,—and when the state campaign opens we'll print the editorial, with suitable comment, scatter it broadcast throughout the state, fire the Southern heart, organize the white people on the color line, have a little demonstration with red shirts and shotguns, scare the negroes into fits, win the state for white supremacy, and teach our colored fellow citizens that we are tired of negro domination and have put an end to it forever. The Afro-American Banner will doubtless die about the same time."

"And so will the editor!" exclaimed McBane ferociously; "I'll see to that. But I wonder where that nigger is with them cocktails? I'm so thirsty I could swallow blue blazes."

"Here's yo' drinks, gin'l," announced Jerry, entering with the glasses on a tray. The gentlemen exchanged compliments and imbibed—McBane at a gulp, Carteret with more deliberation, leaving about half the contents of his glass. The general drank slowly, with every sign of appreciation.
