The lamp had been lit in the sitting-room of the Dunmore house for perhaps an hour before Henrietta Dunmore heard her husband's step upon the gravel walk. It was a heavier step than usual, and slower. She had learned, in eleven years of marriage, to read the moods of Isaac Dunmore from the sound of his coming home very much as an old sailor reads the weather from the color of the sky. The step that evening foretold a storm, or, what was worse, a calm of that oppressive kind which precedes one.

The house stood at the upper end of Mulberry Street, in that quarter of the town of Clarendon where the more prosperous colored people had, since the war, built their homes. It was a story and a half in height, painted white, with green blinds, a deep porch, and a small flower-garden in front, enclosed by a picket fence which Dunmore had made with his own hands. He was a carpenter and builder by trade. Beginning as a journeyman with no capital but a chest of tools and an unusually steady character, he had risen, by industry and thrift, to be the employer of a dozen men and the owner of several houses which he rented to tenants of his own race. Some of the finest residences on Front Street had been built under his direction. The white people who lived in them were accustomed to speak of him as "a very decent sort of negro," which, in the vocabulary of Clarendon, was praise of a high and somewhat condescending order. It implied that he did good work at a fair price, kept his place, and gave no trouble, and these were the virtues which the community most esteemed in a man of his complexion.

Mrs. Dunmore laid down the paper she had been reading and rose to meet him at the door. She was a slender woman of thirty, a shade or two lighter than her husband, with a quiet face, a pair of fine dark eyes, and that air of gentle reserve which a good education and a sensitive nature, placed amid surroundings not always kind, are apt to produce. She had been for some years a teacher in the colored graded school, before her marriage, and still retained something of the precision of speech and manner which that calling had given her.

"You are late, Isaac," she said, taking his hat. "Supper has been waiting this half-hour. Is anything the matter?"

"Nothing that won't keep till after supper," he replied, and kissed her, but absently, as a man might sign a paper whose contents he had not troubled to read.

The meal passed almost in silence. The two children, a boy of nine and a girl of seven, chattered of their lessons and their games, and Dunmore answered them kindly, but with a manner so abstracted that the little girl presently asked him whether he had the toothache. Old Aunt Milly, who did the cooking and had been in the family since before the children were born, observed him from the kitchen door with a shrewd and anxious eye.

"Somep'n done gone wrong wid Mist' Isaac," she muttered to herself as she scraped the plates. "He ain' eat 'nough ter keep a jaybird 'live, an' he lookin' lak he done seed a ha'nt. W'en a man lak him quits his vittles, dey's trouble comin', sho's you bawn."

When the children had been sent to bed, and the old woman had gone to her own cabin at the back of the lot, Dunmore sat for some time looking into the fire, which had been kindled against the chill of the early spring evening. His wife took up her sewing and waited. She had learned that much patience, if no more.

"Henrietta," he said at length, without lifting his eyes from the coals, "you have heard about the fire at Mr. Hollister's warehouse?"

"Everybody has heard of it. The whole town was out to see it. They say the loss is very great."

"Twenty thousand dollars, so they claim. And you have heard that they have arrested Sam Tolliver for setting it?"

"Yes," she answered, and her needle paused for the fraction of a second. "Mrs. Bryant told me this afternoon. She said there was a good deal of ugly talk on the street. I am sorry for Sam's mother. He was always a wild boy, but I would not have believed him capable of such a thing."

"He isn't capable of it," said Dunmore. "He didn't do it."

She looked up quickly. There was something in his tone that made her lay down her work altogether.

"How can you know that, Isaac?"

He was silent a moment, and when he spoke again it was slowly, as though each word cost him an effort.

"Because I know who did. I was coming home Tuesday night from the Hargis place, out on the Wilmington road, where I'd been to look at the new wing they want built. It was late,—past eleven,—for Mr. Hargis kept me talking. I came in by the back way, along the river, past the rear of Hollister's warehouse. There was no moon, but there was a light in the window of the little office at the back, and I saw a man come out of the door, lock it behind him, and go off up the alley in a great hurry. He passed within ten feet of me. I was in the shadow of the lumber-shed, and he didn't see me. But I saw him, as plain as I see you. Not twenty minutes afterwards, before I'd got to the corner of Second Street, the fire-bell rang."

"And who was the man?"

"It was Mr. Gilbert Hollister," said Dunmore. "The old man's son."

There was a long pause. The fire crackled upon the hearth, and the clock upon the mantel, a wedding-gift from the congregation of the church to which they belonged, ticked with a loudness that seemed suddenly unnatural.

"You must be mistaken," said Mrs. Dunmore at last, in a low voice.

"I am not mistaken. I've built two houses for the Hollisters. I've known Mr. Gilbert since he was a boy in knee-breeches. I'd know his walk, and that long gray coat he wears, if I saw him in the dark at the other end of the world. And there's more. It's known among business men—I heard it from Mr. Hargis's own lips, not a week ago—that Hollister and Son are in deep water; that the young man has been speculating in cotton and has lost heavily, and that the warehouse was insured for more than twice what was in it. They have arrested Sam because he was discharged from the place a month ago and was heard to say, when he was drunk, that he'd like to see old Hollister's warehouse burn. That is all the evidence they have against him, and it is enough to hang him,—or worse."

Mrs. Dunmore had grown very pale. She knew, as every colored woman in the South knew, what was meant by the word "worse."

"Isaac," she said, "what do you mean to do?"

"I mean to go to the solicitor in the morning and tell him what I saw."

She rose from her chair and came and stood beside him, and laid her hand upon his shoulder. He could feel that it trembled.

"You must not do it," she said.

He looked up at her for the first time since he had begun to speak.

"Must not? Henrietta, a man's life is at stake."

"So is yours," she answered quickly, "and mine, and the children's. Isaac, think what you are saying! You would go to the solicitor,—a white man, a friend of the Hollisters, who dines at their table and whose wife sits beside Mrs. Hollister in church,—and accuse the son of one of the first families in Clarendon of arson, upon your bare word, the word of a colored man, against his? Who would believe you?"

"The truth is the truth, whoever tells it."

"In heaven, perhaps," she said, with a bitterness he had never heard in her voice before, "but not in Clarendon. You know it as well as I. You have lived here all your life."

It may be remarked, by way of digression, that the sentiment which Mrs. Dunmore expressed was not a novel one, nor was it confined to the colored people of Clarendon. It had been held, in substance, by a long line of persons, black and white, in many lands and ages, who had learned from experience that the scales of justice, though fashioned by the gods, are commonly held by men, and that men are prone to weigh the testimony of their equals with one set of weights and that of their inferiors with another. It is a melancholy reflection, and not a new one; but it is precisely such reflections which, being old, are most easily forgotten by those whom they do not inconvenience.

"I have lived here all my life," said Dunmore, "and I have kept my mouth shut a good many times when I ought to have opened it. I have taken off my hat to men I despised, and said 'yes, sir,' when I meant 'no.' I have done it for business, and for peace, and for you and the children. But there is a point beyond which a man cannot go and still call himself a man. If Sam Tolliver is taken out of that jail some night and hanged to a tree, and I have held my tongue, his blood will be on my hands as surely as if I had tied the rope."

"And if you speak," she said, "do you think it will save him? They will not believe you, and they will not let Sam go. They will only say that the negroes are banding together to protect each other, and to slander a white gentleman. It will make the feeling worse, not better. And then they will turn on you."

"Let them turn."

"Isaac!" She drew back from him and stood with her hands clasped before her. "You do not know what you are saying. You have worked twenty years to build up what we have,—this house, your business, the houses you rent, the good-will of the people you work for. Do you suppose Mr. Hargis will give you his new wing to build, when you have called his friend's son a criminal? Do you suppose any white man in Clarendon will employ you again? They will not need to lay a hand on you; they will simply let you starve. And if they do lay hands on you,—"

She stopped. Her voice had broken, and she turned away toward the window, where the lamp-light lay in a pale square upon the drawn shade.

Dunmore rose and stood looking at her back. He was a large man, broad of shoulder and slow of movement, and the struggle that was going on within him showed itself only in the working of his jaw and the clenching and unclenching of his heavy hands.

"Henrietta," he said, more gently, "do you think I haven't thought of all that? I have thought of nothing else since Tuesday night. I have lain awake two nights going over it. I have told myself that it was none of my business; that Sam was a worthless fellow anyhow, who drank and gambled and would likely come to a bad end sooner or later; that I had a wife and children to think of; that one more poor negro more or less would not make any great difference in the world. I have said all the things you are saying, and a good many more. But this afternoon I passed the jail, and Sam's mother was sitting on the steps of the jail-yard, with her apron over her head, rocking back and forth, and I could not look at her. I crossed the street rather than pass her by. And then I knew that I could not keep still."

Mrs. Dunmore turned around. Her eyes were wet, but her face was set and resolute.

"Then go to her," she said. "Give her money for a lawyer. Get Mr. Trent, from Fayetteville; he is a fair man, and he has defended colored men before. Let him find out the truth some other way,—from the insurance people, from the bank, from the men who work in the warehouse. There are other ways, Isaac, without putting your own head into the noose."

"And if there are no other ways? If the lawyer finds nothing, and the trial comes on, and the jury,—twelve white men, every one of whom has made up his mind already,—brings in a verdict of guilty? Am I to sit in the court-room with what I know locked up in my breast, and see Sam sent to the gallows, or to the penitentiary for life? Or am I to wait until the night when they don't trouble to wait for a trial?"

She made no answer. The question admitted of none.

"You were a teacher, Henrietta," he went on. "You used to tell the children in your school that they must always speak the truth, no matter what it cost them. I've heard you say it. You told me once that it was the first thing you tried to teach them, because without that there was no use in teaching them anything else. Were you lying to them?"

The color rose painfully in her face.

"That is not fair, Isaac."

"Maybe not. But it is the question."

"I taught them what I believed," she said slowly. "I believe it still. But I did not know, then, what it was to be a wife and mother. I did not know what it was to lie awake listening for footsteps in the road, and to wonder, every time you are late, whether some white man has taken offense at a word or a look. You do not know, Isaac,—you cannot know,—what a woman suffers who loves a colored man in this country. The truth is a fine thing to teach children. But I would rather have a living husband who held his tongue than a dead one who told the truth."

He turned away from her and walked to the fireplace, where he stood with one hand upon the mantel, looking down into the dying fire. For some moments neither spoke.

There are situations in life wherein neither party to a dispute is wholly in the right nor wholly in the wrong, and wherein the bitterness of the conflict arises precisely from the fact that each perceives, with painful clearness, the force of the other's argument. Isaac Dunmore knew that his wife spoke from love and from a terror which the history of his people had made only too reasonable. Henrietta Dunmore knew that her husband spoke from a sense of duty which she herself had helped to nourish, and which she would have despised him for lacking. It was the curse of their condition that a plain duty, which in any other community would have been discharged as a matter of course, and with no greater sacrifice than the loss of a morning's work, should here have become an act of something very like martyrdom. For it was not the law, but the temper of the people who administered the law, that made the difference; and against that temper the law itself, as written in the statute-books and declared in the Constitution, was as helpless as a paper wall against a freshet.

"Henrietta," said Dunmore at length, without turning around, "do you remember the night we were married, and old Elder Price asked me, before the whole congregation, whether I would cherish and protect you?"

"Yes," she said faintly.

"I said I would. I meant it. I mean it still. But I have been thinking that a man protects his wife and children in more ways than one. I want our boy to grow up a man. I want him to be able to look a white man in the face and tell him the truth, if need be. How is he ever to do it if his own father, when the time came, turned his back and walked across the street? Children learn more from what we do than from what we say. You taught me that, too."

She came slowly across the room and stood beside him at the hearth. For a long moment she looked at him, at the strong, plain face, lined now with care and sleeplessness, at the gray which had begun to show at his temples, at the hands which had built so much and asked so little. And it may be that in that moment she saw him, not as the husband she feared to lose, but as the man she had chosen; and that the woman in her, which had pleaded for safety, gave way a little before something older and sterner, which had come down to her, perhaps, from forebears who had borne worse things than this, and borne them in silence.

"If you go," she said, very low, "you will not go alone to the solicitor. You will go first to Mr. Trent, and let him go with you. Promise me that."

He looked down at her, and for the first time that evening his face softened.

"I promise."

"And you will write down tonight, before you sleep, all that you saw, and the hour, and the place, and sign it, and give it to me to keep. So that if,—if anything should happen,—it will not be lost."

"I will do it now," he said.

She went to the little writing-desk in the corner, which had come with her from her father's house, and brought out paper and pen and ink, and set them on the table under the lamp. Then she sat down again in her chair by the fire and took up her sewing. But her needle did not move, and when Dunmore, bending over the table, glanced up once from his slow and laborious writing, he saw that her eyes were closed and her lips were moving, and he knew that she was praying.

The clock ticked on. Outside, a dog barked in the distance, and was answered by another, and then the night was still again. Somewhere, a few streets away, in a brick building with barred windows, a frightened young black man lay upon a pallet of straw and wondered whether he would live to see the morning; and somewhere, in a handsome house upon Front Street, a young white gentleman of excellent family lay upon a feather bed and wondered, perhaps, whether anyone had seen him go up the alley on Tuesday night. Neither knew that his fate was being written down, line by line, in a cramped and careful hand, by a colored carpenter at a table in a little white house on Mulberry Street, while a woman sat by the fire and prayed that the truth might, for once, prove stronger than the hands that held it.

The train from the north, which was due at Clarendon at half-past four, arrived, according to its custom, something less than an hour behind its schedule, and discharged upon the platform of the little station a handful of passengers, a crate of chickens, and a gentleman of perhaps five-and-thirty, whose dress and bearing at once distinguished him from the remainder of the company. He wore a suit of gray cloth, cut in the latest mode of a city where the latest mode was a matter of some consequence. His hat was of the soft felt then affected by men of business who wished to appear at ease, and he carried in one hand a leather valise and in the other a cane with a silver head. The hackmen who lounged about the station, observing these signs of prosperity, made a simultaneous rush in his direction, and the foremost of them, a lank white man with a tobacco-stained beard, seized upon the valise with the proprietary air of one who has already earned his fee.

"Hotel, suh? The Clarendon House is the onliest place fit for a gentleman. Two dollars a day, an' the best table in the county."

The stranger hesitated, and in that moment of hesitation a curious expression crossed his face. It was not exactly embarrassment, nor yet amusement, but partook somewhat of both. He reclaimed his valise with a courteous firmness.

"Thank you, I shall not need a carriage," he said. "I am going but a short distance, and I prefer to walk."

The hackman shrugged his shoulders and retired, remarking to his fellows that drummers were getting stingier every year, and that this one, if he was any judge, was a Yankee who had come down to sell patent churns to the farmers. It may be observed in passing that the hackman was, as hackmen go, a fair judge of men, and that his error was a pardonable one; for the color line, which in the South is held to be as plain as the meridian of noonday, has a curious way of blurring at the edges, and many a man has crossed it, in one direction or the other, without the lynx-eyed guardians of caste perceiving that any boundary had been passed.

The stranger, having thus disposed of his would-be patrons, set off down the main street of the town at a leisurely pace. He looked about him with the eyes of one who sees a familiar scene after long absence, and who notes with a kind of melancholy interest the changes which time has wrought. The courthouse stood where it had always stood, at the head of the square, its white columns a trifle grayer and its cupola sadly in need of paint. The market-house had been rebuilt in brick. The old Confederate monument, which he remembered as a project much discussed and long deferred, now rose in the center of the square, a granite soldier leaning upon his musket and gazing northward with an expression of stony reproach. Upon the steps of the post-office a group of idle men were discussing, with the earnestness which such men bring to matters wholly beyond their control, the latest news from the state capital.

Passing beyond the square, the stranger turned into a street which ran down toward the river, and here the aspect of things underwent a gradual transformation. The houses grew smaller and the yards less trim; the brick sidewalk gave place to a path of trodden earth; and the faces which he met, instead of being white, were of every shade from the tawny yellow of old ivory to the deep and lustrous black of polished ebony. Several of these persons regarded him with that frank curiosity which a well-dressed white man excites in a colored neighborhood,—a curiosity not wholly unmixed with apprehension, for experience had taught them that such visitors seldom came on errands of benevolence. One old woman, who was sweeping her doorstep, paused to stare at him, and then, as though some faint recollection stirred within her, stared harder still; but he passed on before the recollection could ripen into recognition.

At length he stopped before a small frame cottage, which stood a little back from the street in a yard enclosed by a whitewashed paling fence. The house was plainly built, but it had about it an air of thrift and self-respect that distinguished it from its neighbors. The porch was swept clean; a row of flowerpots, in which geraniums and touch-me-nots were blooming, lined the railing; and a well-kept vegetable garden, in which the cabbages stood up in orderly ranks like soldiers on parade, occupied the space at one side. Upon the porch, in a split-bottomed chair tilted back against the wall, sat a man of middle age, broad-shouldered and stout of frame, whose complexion was of a rich brown, and whose grizzled hair was beginning to recede from a forehead of no inconsiderable breadth. He was reading a newspaper, holding it at arm's length in the manner of one whose eyes have begun to fail him, and he did not look up until the gate creaked upon its hinges.

"Evenin', suh," he said, rising, with the instinctive courtesy which his race had learned in a hard school. "Is you lookin' fer somebody?"

The visitor came up the walk and stopped at the foot of the steps. For a moment he did not speak, and the man upon the porch, peering at him over the top of his newspaper, began to show signs of uneasiness.

"Ben," said the stranger at last, in a voice that was not altogether steady, "don't you know me?"

The newspaper fell to the floor. The brown man took a step forward, then another, and leaned over the railing, staring into the visitor's face with an intensity that seemed to search out every line and feature.

"Fo' de Lawd!" he exclaimed. "It ain' never—it can't be—Johnny! Johnny Merriwether! Is it you, sho' 'nuff?"

"It is I, Ben, or what is left of me."

Benjamin Tolliver came down the steps two at a time, with an agility surprising in a man of his years and bulk, and seized his cousin by both hands. Then, as though a handshake were an inadequate expression of his feelings, he threw his arms about him and embraced him heartily, to the manifest detriment of the gray suit.

"Phoebe!" he called over his shoulder, when he had sufficiently recovered his breath. "Phoebe! Come out here, quick! Here's Cousin Johnny come home, after all dese yeahs! Fifteen yeahs, an' never a word, an' here he is a-standin' in de yard like he dropped out'n de sky!"

A comely woman, somewhat younger than her husband and several shades lighter, appeared in the doorway, wiping her hands upon her apron. She had never seen John Merriwether, having married into the family after his departure, but she had heard of him often enough, and she received him with a warmth that was none the less genuine for being tempered by a certain shyness in the presence of so fine a gentleman.

"Come in, come in," she said. "Ben's talked about you so much I feel like I knowed you all my life. You'll stay to supper, of co'se. I'll kill a chicken."

"Kill two," said Ben. "Johnny allus did have a appetite, when he was a boy. I reckon dey ain' starved it out'n him up No'th."

Within the house all was neat and orderly. The front room, which served as parlor upon state occasions, was furnished with a horsehair sofa, a center-table bearing a family Bible and a stereoscope, and an organ, upon which a hymn-book lay open at "Shall We Gather at the River." Upon the walls hung several chromos, a framed certificate of membership in a benevolent society, and an enlarged crayon portrait of an old woman in a white head-handkerchief, whose shrewd black eyes seemed to follow the visitor about the room. John Merriwether stopped before this portrait and stood for some time regarding it in silence.

"Dat's Granny," said Ben softly, coming up beside him. "I had it made f'm a little tintype de summer befo' she died. De man charged me eight dollars, but I never begrudged a cent of it. It favors her mighty well, don't it?"

"It is very like her," said John. "I should have known it anywhere. When did she die, Ben?"

"Fo' yeahs ago dis comin' Feb'uary. She was ninety-one, or close to it,—she never did know her age exac'ly, bein' bawn in slavery times, when dey didn' keep no account er sich things fer colored folks, 'cep'n' in de ledger wid de mules an' de cattle. She talked about you to de las', Johnny. She used to say, 'Dat boy'll come back some day. He's got too much er my blood in him to stay away fer good.' I wrote you when she died,—I sent de letter to dat place in Ohio whar you wrote f'm de onliest time you ever did write,—but I reckon you never got it."

"No," said John slowly; "I never got it. I had moved from there long before."

He did not add, what was nevertheless the truth, that he had moved from there for the express purpose of leaving no address behind him; nor that, for ten years past, he had been at some pains to sever every thread that might lead back from his present life to the cottage in which he now stood. But something in his tone, or perhaps in his silence, conveyed to his cousin more than his words, and Ben, who was a man of considerable natural penetration, forbore to press the subject.

Supper, when it was at length announced, more than justified Phoebe's reputation as a cook, a reputation which, as Ben took occasion to inform his guest, extended throughout the colored community and even into certain white households, where her services were in demand for weddings and christenings. There was fried chicken, crisp and golden; there were hot biscuits and sweet potatoes, and collard greens cooked with a piece of side meat, and a dish of fresh butter, and a pitcher of buttermilk, and a blackberry cobbler swimming in its own rich juice. John Merriwether, who had dined in the best hotels of three or four cities, ate as he had not eaten in years, and Phoebe, observing his appetite with housewifely satisfaction, kept his plate replenished until he was obliged to beg for quarter.

The conversation at table turned, as such conversations will, upon the fortunes of the family and of the neighbors whom John had known in his youth. Ben was a willing chronicler, and the record which he unfolded was, like most human records, a mingled tale of joy and sorrow, of success and failure, of birth and marriage and death.

"Cousin Sally married dat yaller man f'm Wilmin'ton,—you 'member him, de one dat played de fiddle at all de parties. Folks said he wouldn' never 'mount to nothin', but he settled down an' learned de barberin' trade, an' now he's got a shop wid three chairs, an' Sally rides to chu'ch in her own buggy. Uncle Peter's dead,—he was kicked by a mule de same winter as Granny. Little Jim Mangum, dat you used to fight wid behin' de schoolhouse, is a preacher now, an' a mighty powerful one, too; when he gits to talkin' 'bout de Judgment Day, de sisters shouts so you kin hear 'em clean to de river. An' ole Mis' Pettigrew—you 'member de white lady dat used to give us cakes at Christmas?—she's gone, too, an' her son's in de Legislature, an' he's one er de leadin'est men in dis new movement to take de vote away f'm de colored folks."

"Is there such a movement here?" asked John.

"Is dey?" Ben laughed, but there was little mirth in his laughter. "Dey ain' talkin' 'bout nothin' else, f'm de courthouse to de cross-roads sto'. Dey say de colored man ain' fitten to vote, 'caze he can't read an' write. But I kin read an' write, an' I owns dis house an' de lot it stan's on, an' I pays my taxes reg'lar as de seasons, an' I reckon dey'll fin' some way to say I ain' fitten, neither. Dey's got a new thing dey calls de grandfather clause, which says a man kin vote if his gran'daddy could vote; an' seein' as how none er our gran'daddies could vote, bein' slaves, dat leaves us out, smart as you please. It's a mighty cu'ious law, Johnny, dat makes a man's right to vote depen' on whether his gran'daddy was bought an' sold. But I reckon dey knows what dey's doin'. Dey gener'ly does."

John Merriwether said nothing, but his face grew grave, and he toyed absently with his fork. It is one of the ironies of a complex civilization that a man may escape from a burden without escaping from the knowledge of it; and the knowledge, in such a case, is apt to weigh the more heavily for being borne in secret.

"But tell us about yo'se'f, Johnny," said Ben, when the cobbler had been disposed of and Phoebe had retired to the kitchen to wash the dishes, leaving the cousins alone with the lamp and the remains of the feast. "You looks like you'd done mighty well. What is you doin' up dere in de No'th?"

"I am in the real-estate business," replied John, "in Cleveland. I buy and sell property, and manage buildings for other people. I have been fairly fortunate. I have a house of my own, and an office downtown, with two clerks."

"Two clerks!" Ben repeated the words with evident pride. "Well, well! Granny allus did say you'd be somebody. An' is you married?"

"Yes. I have a wife, and a little girl of six."

"Is dat so? Why didn' you bring 'em along? Phoebe would 'a' been tickled to death to see 'em, an' I'd 'a' liked to see de chile. Does she favor you?"

John hesitated, and in that hesitation, which was longer than the question seemed to warrant, Ben read the answer to a question which he had not asked. He looked at his cousin long and searchingly across the table, and when he spoke again it was in a lower tone.

"Johnny," he said, "does dey know? Up dere, I mean. Does yo' wife know?"

The lamp flickered, and a moth, which had been circling about the chimney, fell scorched upon the tablecloth. John Merriwether watched its feeble struggles for a moment before he replied.

"No, Ben," he said at length. "She does not know. Nobody knows. When I went North, I had no thought of anything of the kind. I worked at whatever I could find,—I was a porter, a waiter, a clerk in a store. People took me for what I seemed to be, and I did not undeceive them. It was not, at first, a deliberate choice; it was simply that no one asked, and I did not volunteer. And then, by the time I might have spoken, it was too late. My employer had taken me into his confidence; I had friends, prospects, a position. I met the woman who is now my wife. To have told the truth then would have been to throw away everything,—and for what? For a principle that the world does not respect, and a kinship that the world does not acknowledge. I do not defend myself, Ben. I merely tell you how it was."

Ben was silent for some time. He took out his pipe, filled it slowly from a tin box upon the mantel, and lighted it with a splinter from the fire.

"I ain' blamin' you, Johnny," he said at last, between puffs. "Dey's plenty folks would blame you, but I ain' one of 'em. De Lawd made you de color you is, an' if de w'ite folks can't tell de diff'ence, I don' see dat it's yo' place to learn 'em. It's dey own law dat says one drop er black blood makes a man a nigger; an' it 'pears to me dat if a man kin git roun' a law like dat, he's got as much right to do it as dey had to make it. But I'll tell you one thing, Johnny, an' den I won' say no mo'. It mus' be a mighty lonesome thing, to have to keep yo' own gran'mammy a secret."

The words were simply spoken, without reproach, but they struck home; and John Merriwether, who had built up, through fifteen years, an elaborate structure of reasons and justifications, felt it tremble beneath this single blow. He rose and went to the window, and stood looking out into the darkness, where the frogs were singing in the marsh beyond the river.

"That is why I came, Ben," he said, without turning around. "I had a dream about her, a month ago,—I dreamed that she was standing at the foot of my bed, in that same white head-handkerchief, looking at me as she used to look when I had been in mischief. I could not get it out of my mind. I told my wife I had business in the South, which was true enough, in a way. I wanted to see her grave. I wanted to see you. I suppose I wanted to remember, for a day or two, who I really am."

"Well," said Ben, rising and laying a broad hand upon his cousin's shoulder, "you's welcome here, Johnny, fer a day or two, er fer as long as you wants to stay. An' in de mawnin', fust thing, we'll go out to de buryin'-groun'."

They went out early, before the dew was off the grass, to the colored cemetery, which lay upon a slope beyond the edge of the town, separated from the white cemetery by a road and a barbed-wire fence,—for the dead of the two races, though they must needs lie in the same earth, were not permitted, in Clarendon, to lie in the same enclosure. The graves were marked for the most part by wooden headboards, upon which the names and dates had been painted by unskilled hands, and which the weather had already begun to obliterate; but here and there a modest stone bore witness to the greater prosperity or the more enduring affection of the survivors. Upon one of these, a plain slab of white marble, John Merriwether read the inscription:

"DICEY TOLLIVER. Born a Slave. Died Free. She Done What She Could."

"I had de stone cut in Wilmin'ton," said Ben. "It cost a heap er money, but I figgered she'd earned it. I put de part 'bout bein' bawn a slave 'caze she was proud of it,—not of bein' a slave, you understan', but of comin' th'oo it de way she did. She used to say she'd outlived ole Marse an' ole Mis' an' all dey chillun, an' she reckoned de Lawd was tryin' to tell somebody somethin'."

John Merriwether stood bareheaded beside the grave, and if his eyes were moist, the morning breeze, which was sharp for the season, may perhaps be held accountable. Ben, with the delicacy of true feeling, withdrew a little distance and occupied himself with pulling the weeds from around an adjoining headboard.

When they had returned to the house, and John was preparing to take the afternoon train, he drew from his pocket a roll of banknotes and pressed it into his cousin's hand.

"I want you to take this, Ben," he said. "It is very little, compared with what I owe. Use it for anything you like,—for the house, or for Phoebe, or for yourself."

Ben looked at the money, and then at his cousin, and slowly shook his head.

"I don' need it, Johnny," he said. "I got my trade, an' I makes a good livin', an' I don' owe nobody nothin'. But I'll tell you what I'll do. Dey's a school out here fer de colored chillun, an' dey ain' got but one teacher fer sixty chillun, an' de county won' give 'em no mo', 'caze dey says eddication spiles a nigger. I'll give dis to de school, an' tell 'em it come f'm a frien' er Granny's. Dat's what she'd 'a' wanted. She never could read a word herse'f, but she set a heap er sto' by learnin'."

And so it was arranged. Ben accompanied his cousin to the station, but stopped at the corner of the square, by mutual and unspoken consent, and watched him walk on alone to the platform, where the same hackman who had greeted him upon his arrival touched his hat respectfully to the departing gentleman. When the train had pulled out, and the last puff of smoke had dissolved against the blue of the afternoon sky, Ben Tolliver turned and walked slowly homeward, past the courthouse and the Confederate monument and the idlers upon the post-office steps, down the street that ran toward the river.

He was a man of few books, but of considerable reflection; and it occurred to him, as he walked, that of the two cousins who had parted that afternoon, the one who rode away upon the train had gained the world and all its privileges, while the one who walked home in the dust had kept only his name, his house, and the right to stand openly beside his grandmother's grave. Which of them had made the better bargain, Ben did not undertake to decide. It is a question which the laws of the land have rendered peculiarly difficult of solution, and which, it may be ventured, will continue to perplex the conscience of the nation until the nation shall have resolved that a man's worth is not to be measured by the shade of his skin, nor his rights by the condition of his grandfather.

The note had come by the hand of old Peter, the Fairleighs' coachman, a little after four o'clock in the afternoon, and Mrs. Merriwether had laid it upon the mantel in the front room, where it remained, unopened and accusing, until her husband should return from his work. It was addressed in a fine, sloping, feminine hand to "Elias Merriwether," without any prefix whatever. This omission was so customary in communications of that sort, and from that quarter, that Mrs. Merriwether would scarcely have observed it but for the circumstance that the envelope bore, in the upper corner, a little embossed crest of gilt, which seemed to emphasize, by its very elegance, the bareness of the name beneath.

"Mis' Fairleigh say she'd thank yo' ole man ter read dat de minute he gits home," Peter had said, standing at the gate with his hat in his hand and his eyes discreetly averted from the house. "An' she say tell him she 'spects he'll know w'at ter do. I's sorry ter be de one ter fetch it, Mis' Lucindy, 'deed I is; but w'en de w'ite folks sen's, a nigger has ter go, an' dat's all dey is to it."

"I know it, Uncle Peter," Mrs. Merriwether had replied, with a sigh. "Is the little boy much hurt?"

"Hurt?" said the old man, with a chuckle which he promptly suppressed, glancing over his shoulder as though the very hedges might report it. "Well, ma'am, I wouldn' say he wuz hurt, ez you mought say hurt; but his feelin's is mighty bad tore up, an' his nose is a little swole. He hollered so loud you'd 'a' thought de Yankees wuz comin' back. I 'spec' de ole jedge'll hear 'bout it w'en he gits in fum de co'thouse, an' den dey'll be some mo' hollerin'. Good-evenin', ma'am. Tell de little man ole Peter say he better be good fer a w'ile."

It may be well, before proceeding further, to explain the position of the Merriwether family, for it had a material bearing upon the events of the evening. Elias Merriwether was a carpenter and builder, who had learned his trade in slavery and practiced it in freedom, and who had prospered, by industry and thrift, to a point where he owned the neat cottage in which he lived, with a garden behind it and a row of rose-bushes before. He employed, in the busy season, as many as six workmen, two of whom were white men; and it was perhaps the most delicate of his many daily problems so to direct these two that they should never be made to feel that they were directed at all. He had a little learning, acquired by night and by stealth, and a great deal of common sense, acquired by the harder method of experience. He was respected by the colored people as a man of substance, and tolerated by the white people as one who knew his place,—a phrase which, in that town and in that day, signified a place assigned without consultation and to be kept without complaint. Whether he knew his place in the sense intended may be doubted; that he knew precisely where it was supposed to be, and could find it in the dark, admits of no question at all.

His son Benjamin, called Benny by everyone except his father in moments of gravity, was eight years old, small for his age, bright of eye and quick of tongue, and possessed of a certain directness of character which his mother attributed to her own family and his father attributed, with less confidence, to the Almighty. He attended the colored public school, where he stood at the head of his class, and spent his afternoons in such pursuits as boys of eight have followed since the foundation of the world, among which the spinning of tops held, at this particular season, the place of first importance.

Benny had come home that afternoon with his jacket torn at the shoulder, a scratch upon his cheek, and his knuckles skinned, but with a countenance in which apprehension struggled with a certain unmistakable satisfaction. To his mother's questions he had returned evasive answers, and had then retired to the woodshed, whence he had not emerged even for his supper, though a plate had been carried out to him by his grandmother, old Mrs. Hagar Wilkins, who lived with the family and who regarded herself as the boy's natural protector against all comers, his parents included.

Mr. Merriwether came home at six. He washed his hands at the bench by the kitchen door, kissed his wife, observed her face, and asked what was the matter. She handed him the note without a word. He read it standing, and then read it again, sitting down, and then folded it and laid it upon the table, and looked for some moments out of the window at the rose-bushes, which were just coming into bloom.

The letter, which need not be given in full, informed him that his son had that afternoon, without provocation, assaulted Master Archibald Fairleigh, grandson of Judge Fairleigh, in the public road before the Fairleigh gate; that the child had been struck in the face and his nose made to bleed; that Mrs. Fairleigh had hitherto believed the Merriwethers to be a respectable family and was distressed to find herself mistaken; that she was unwilling, out of consideration for that respectability, to lay the matter before the judge, who would doubtless know how to deal with it; and that she trusted Elias would administer such correction as would insure that nothing of the sort should ever happen again. It was signed "Mrs. Cornelia Fairleigh," and there was a postscript which stated that she remembered with kindness the excellent work Elias had done upon the judge's back piazza.

"Where is the boy?" asked Mr. Merriwether.

"In the woodshed. Mother's with him."

"Tell him to come to me in the front room."

He went into the front room, which was used only on Sundays and on occasions of ceremony, and seated himself in the horsehair armchair beside the center-table, upon which lay the family Bible, a photograph album, and a volume of the speeches of Frederick Douglass. He was not a man given to dramatic effect, but he was aware that the front room had a certain solemnity which the kitchen lacked, and he had chosen it deliberately. A man who must perform a disagreeable duty may be pardoned for seeking whatever assistance the furniture can lend him.

Benny came in presently, propelled by his mother and followed by his grandmother, who seated herself in the corner by the door with the air of one who has no intention of interfering, but who will remain within easy reach of the proceedings. The boy stood before his father with his hands behind him and his eyes upon the carpet, the pattern of which, a design of improbable roses upon a ground of impossible green, he seemed to find of absorbing interest.

"Benjamin," said his father, "look at me."

The boy raised his eyes. They were his mother's eyes, large and dark and very clear, and Mr. Merriwether found them, at that moment, less easy to meet than he had expected.

"Did you strike Archie Fairleigh this afternoon?"

"Yes, sir."

"Why?"

Benny hesitated. It was evident that the answer was ready enough, but that he doubted whether it would be received in the spirit in which it was offered.

"He took my top, papa. The new one,—the red one you brought me from Wilmington. I was spinning it by the side of the road, not in front of his gate at all, but down by the big oak, and he came out and picked it up, and said a nigger hadn't any business with a top like that, and he reckoned I'd stolen it. And I said I hadn't, that my papa bought it for me. And he said my papa was a stuck-up nigger that thought he was as good as white folks, and that his grandpa said so, and that somebody ought to take him down a peg. And then he put my top in his pocket and started to go in the gate, and—and I hit him."

"Where did you hit him?"

"On the nose, papa," said Benny, with a candor which did him credit, and with a faint accent of pride which did not escape his father's ear.

"And then?"

"Then he hollered, and dropped the top, and I picked it up, and he tore my jacket, and scratched me, and Uncle Peter came out and pulled us apart and told me to run home quick. And I ran."

There was a silence in the room. Mrs. Merriwether, standing behind her son's chair, laid her hand upon his shoulder, and then, at a glance from her husband, removed it. In the corner, old Mrs. Wilkins was heard to murmur something which sounded like "Bless de chile," but which she converted, upon reflection, into a cough.

Mr. Merriwether was, as has been said, a man of common sense, and he perceived with entire clearness the nature of the dilemma in which he found himself. Had his son been white, and had the same thing happened between two white boys, he would have heard the story with a smile, cautioned the child against fighting, and perhaps privately rewarded him with a nickel for the defense of his property and his father's name. Had the Fairleigh boy been colored, the matter would have been settled between the two families in a quarter of an hour, with mutual apologies and a division of the blame. But the case presented no such simplicity. It is one of the peculiar burdens of the colored parent in the South,—a burden which the white parent, whatever his own perplexities, has never been called upon to bear,—that he must teach his child two lessons which flatly contradict each other, and must teach them both at once. He must teach him that he is a man, with a man's rights and a man's dignity, the equal in the sight of God of any creature that walks the earth; and he must teach him, in the same breath, that he must never by any act or word assert that equality in the presence of those who deny it. He must make him brave, and then make him careful of his bravery. He must give him self-respect, and then show him how to hide it. If he fails in the first lesson, the child grows up a slave in spirit, though the law has made him free; if he fails in the second, the child may not grow up at all.

"Benjamin," said Mr. Merriwether at length, "do you know what you have done?"

"I got my top back, papa."

"You struck a white boy."

"He struck me too, papa. He scratched me,—see?"

"That is not the point," said his father, and was conscious, as he said it, of an unpleasant sense that he was saying what other men, in other rooms, had said with less excuse. "The point is that you struck him first, and that he is a white boy, and that he is Judge Fairleigh's grandson."

"But he took my top, papa. It was mine. You said a man has a right to what's his."

Mr. Merriwether had, in fact, said exactly that, upon more than one occasion, with reference to the title to the very cottage in which they sat, which he had defended through two lawsuits brought by a white man who had coveted the lot. He had said it to his wife, and to his friends, and to the boy himself, with a certain honest pride. He had not anticipated that it would be returned to him, in this form, across his own center-table.

"A man has a right to what is his," he said slowly. "That is true, and you must never forget it. But a man must also know when and how to claim it. There are some rights, Benjamin, that a colored man must ask for in the courts, and not take with his fists. When a white man wrongs you, you must remember that the law is on his side before it is on yours, and that he has friends where you have none, and that what would be called spirit in his boy is called impudence in you, and what would be called a boys' quarrel between two white children will be called an outrage when one of them is black. You did not hurt Archie Fairleigh very much. You may have hurt your father a great deal."

"How, papa?" asked the boy, with genuine alarm.

Mr. Merriwether did not immediately reply. He might have told the boy that the judge's back piazza was not the only work he had done for white people, nor the last he hoped to do; that his living, and therefore the boy's own bread and schooling, depended upon the good will of a community which could withdraw that good will at a word; that a colored man who was known as "stuck-up" might find his contracts going to other hands, his notes called at the bank, his lumber delayed at the mill, and his white workmen suddenly unwilling to take orders from him; and that a colored boy who was known to have struck a white one might find, as he grew older, that the incident had been remembered against him by persons whose memories were long and whose methods were not always confined to the law. He might have told him of a colored boy in a neighboring county, not much older than Benny, whose fate need not be described here. But there are things which a father cannot say to a child of eight, even when the child must be made to feel them; and the strong man in the armchair looked at the small one before him and found that his lesson must be given in a language less exact than the truth.

"Never mind how," he said. "You will understand some day. Now listen to me. Tomorrow morning, before school, you will go with me to Judge Fairleigh's house, and you will go to the back door, and you will ask for Mrs. Fairleigh, and when she comes you will tell her that you are sorry you struck her grandson."

"But I'm not sorry, papa," said Benny, whose truthfulness had been carefully cultivated in that household, and who chose this inconvenient moment to display its fruits.

His mother made a little movement. His grandmother, in the corner, coughed again, with considerable violence.

"You will be sorry," said Mr. Merriwether, "that you made trouble for your father and mother. You can say that much, and say it honestly. You need not say what you do not feel; but you will say that, and you will say it politely, and you will take off your cap when you say it. And you will not take your top with you, and you will not spin it again for two weeks."

The boy's lip trembled. The loss of the top was a heavier blow than the apology, which he did not, at his age, fully comprehend; but he had been taught not to cry before his father, and he did not cry. He only said, in a small voice, "Yes, sir," and stood looking at the carpet again.

It was at this point that old Mrs. Wilkins, who had sat through the proceedings with exemplary restraint, found herself unable to maintain her neutrality any longer.

"'Lias," she said, rising from her chair, "I ain't got no call ter meddle 'twix' a man an' his own chile, an' I ain't gwine ter meddle; but I wants ter say one thing, an' den I'll hol' my peace. I wuz bawn in slavery, an' raise' in it, an' I seen my own mammy whup' fer sassin' de overseer's chile, an' I 'members how I cried, 'cause she didn' do nothin' but tell dat chile ter take its han's off'n her apron. An' I s'posed w'en freedom come dat my gran'chillun wouldn' have ter go th'oo nothin' lack dat. Now I ain't sayin' you's wrong, 'Lias. Mebbe you's right. De Lawd knows dese w'ite folks is sca'ier now dan dey wuz befo' de wah, 'cause den dey owned us an' didn' have ter wuk so ha'd ter keep us down. But I does say dat dis chile ain't stole nothin', an' ain't tol' no lie, an' ain't done nothin' but stan' up fer his daddy's name; an' ef he got ter go 'pologize fer dat, I hopes de good Lawd 'll 'pologize ter him some day fer de kind er worl' he wuz bawn inter. Dat's all. Come 'long, honey, an' let gran'mammy wash dat scratch."

She took the boy by the hand and led him out, and Mr. Merriwether did not prevent her. The door closed behind them, and he and his wife were left alone in the front room, with the Bible and the album and the speeches of Frederick Douglass.

For some moments neither spoke. Mrs. Merriwether went to the window and stood looking out at the roses, as her husband had done an hour before.

"Was I too hard on him, Lucinda?" he asked at length.

"No," she said, without turning. "You were not hard enough on Archie Fairleigh, but that was not in your power."

"I had to do it."

"I know you did."

"If it had been any other boy in town,—if it had been one of the Buxtons, or the Hallidays,—I'd have let it go with a talking-to. But the judge sits on the bench. He'll sit on it again when my suit for the Pender job comes up, if it ever does. And there's talk, Lucinda. There's been talk all spring, at the mill and on the street. They say the colored people are getting too independent. They say there are too many of us owning property. I heard a man say on the courthouse steps, last week, that the colored people in this town needed a lesson, and that it wouldn't be long before they got one. I don't want my boy to be the text for that lesson."

"I know," she said again.

He was silent a little while longer, and then, with a sound that was half a laugh and half something else, he said:—

"He hit him square on the nose, Lucinda. Did you hear him say it? 'On the nose, papa,'—as proud as a little bantam rooster. And he got his top back, too."

His wife turned from the window, and there were tears in her eyes, but she was smiling.

"You were proud of him," she said.

"God help me, I was," said Elias Merriwether. "And I had to punish him for the very thing I was proud of. What kind of a country is it, Lucinda, where a man must whip the manhood out of his own son to keep somebody else from killing it?"

To this question, which was not the first time it had been asked in that region, nor by any means the last, his wife made no answer, for there was none to make. It has been asked since by many fathers, in many front rooms, with Bibles on the table and the speeches of great men beside them; and the answer, if there is one, has not yet been written into the statutes of the states, nor into the hearts of those who make them.

The next morning, at half past seven o'clock, a colored man and a small colored boy might have been seen standing at the back door of Judge Fairleigh's handsome residence on Front Street. The boy took off his cap, and said something to a lady in a morning wrapper, who received it with a gracious inclination of the head, and remarked to her husband at breakfast that Elias was really a very sensible negro, and that it was a pity there were not more like him. The judge, who had heard the whole story from his grandson the evening before, and who had formed his own opinion of its merits, grunted, and observed that the boy seemed to have a good deal of spirit for a darky, and that spirit in a darky was a thing to be watched.

Whether it was watched, and with what consequences, is a matter which belongs to a later chapter of the history of that town. It is enough to record here that the red top lay for two weeks upon the shelf above the kitchen mantel, where Benny could see it every morning and every night; and that on the fifteenth day his father took it down, without a word, and put it into his hand; and that the boy, who had learned something in the interval, though not perhaps all that his father had intended, carried it thereafter to the far end of the lane behind the house, where no white children ever came, and spun it there alone.
