The rain had been falling upon the town since noon, and by night it had become a thing of weight and malice. It beat upon the roof of the little house at the end of Ferry Street as if it held a grievance, and it ran from the eaves in gray ropes that swung and twisted in the wind. Beyond the window the river was invisible, but it could be heard, a vast and sullen muttering, like an army that had been told to wait.

Within, the lamp upon the table made a small yellow kingdom. Its light fell upon a red cloth, upon a sugar bowl with a broken handle, upon two plates from which the supper had long departed. At the edges of this kingdom the shadows crouched, black and patient. The stove in the corner glowered through its seams. Now and then it gave a little click of iron, as though it had remembered something and decided not to speak of it.

The man sat at one side of the table and the woman sat at the other. Between them lay a letter. It was a soiled envelope, and it had been opened with a thumb, so that its edge was torn into a ragged grin.

The man's name was Weller, and he was thirty-one years old. He had a mustache of which he was secretly proud, and a pair of large hands that he did not know what to do with in a room. They lay now upon the cloth like two animals that had been beaten into submission. He kept his eyes upon the lamp. The flame stood up straight and still, and it seemed to him that it regarded him with a cold and impartial interest.

The woman's name was Hattie. She had been pretty in the way that girls in river towns are pretty, briefly and with great industry, and some of it remained to her about the mouth. Her hair was drawn back so tightly that it appeared to be in pain. She held a dish towel in her lap and folded it, and unfolded it, and folded it again.

"Well," she said at last.

The word fell into the silence like a stone into a well. The man waited to hear it strike bottom, but it did not.

"Well," he answered.

The stove clicked.

"You might as well say it," said the woman. "You been sittin' there with it in your mouth all through supper. You et like a man that's chewin' on a speech."

He moved one of his hands. It crept a little way toward the letter and stopped, as if it had seen a sentry.

"It's from Dan Fitch," he said.

"I know who it's from. I seen the post-mark. I ain't blind, Ed."

"He says there's work out there. Real work. He says a man with two good arms can make more in a month than he can make here in a year at the mill. He says—"

"I know what he says." She folded the towel. "Dan Fitch has been sayin' things since he was nine years old. He said he'd marry Lottie Barnes, and he run off to St. Louis. He said he'd pay back your father the forty dollars, and your father died waitin'. Dan Fitch could talk the bark off a sycamore."

The man's face grew red. The color began at his collar and mounted slowly, like water in a cistern, until it reached the roots of his hair. He felt it climbing and was ashamed of it, and the shame made it climb faster.

"This is different," he said.

"It's always different."

"He sent the fare, Hattie. Half of it. It's in there. He wouldn't send money if it wasn't true."

She looked at the envelope then. Her eyes rested upon it with a curious flatness, as one might regard a snake that had been killed but might not know it yet.

"How much?"

"Thirty-two dollars."

The rain made a sudden rush against the window, and the glass shuddered in its frame. Somewhere out in the dark a loose shutter began to bang, slowly and stupidly, like a drunkard knocking at the wrong door.

"Thirty-two dollars," she repeated. She said it as though she were weighing it in her palm. Then she laughed, and the laugh was a small dry thing that seemed to have no connection with her face. "That's what you're worth to Dan Fitch. Thirty-two dollars. He's buyin' you, Ed, like a mule at the county fair."

"He ain't buyin' nobody."

"Then what's he want you for?"

The man could not answer this. He had not thought of it. He had read the letter four times in the alley behind the mill, standing in the rain with his collar turned up, and each time it had seemed to him a gleaming and splendid thing, a door flung open upon a country of sunlight. He had seen himself walking down a street in a far-off town, a street of raw new lumber, with money in his pocket and men turning to look at him. He had seen himself coming home in a year, two years, with a gold watch chain across his vest, and the people of Ferry Street standing in their doorways to watch him pass. He had seen Hattie running to meet him.

Now, in the yellow light, with the stove clicking and the shutter banging, the vision had grown thin. He could see the wall through it.

"He wants a partner," he said doggedly. "Somebody he can trust."

"He wants somebody to do the diggin'," said the woman.

The man brought his fist down upon the table. It was not a great blow, but the sugar bowl leaped, and a spoon slid from a plate and fell to the floor with a thin, foolish clatter. Both of them looked at the spoon. It lay upon the boards and gleamed. It seemed to the man that it was mocking him, and he hated it.

The woman did not pick it up. Neither did he.

"I'm sick of it," he said. His voice was low and hoarse. "I'm sick of the mill. I'm sick of Hennessey standin' over me with his watch in his hand like I was a hog he was fixin' to weigh. I'm sick of this house. I'm sick of the river. Eleven years I been in that mill, Hattie. Eleven years. And what've I got?"

He waved his hand at the room. The gesture took in the stove and the red cloth and the broken sugar bowl and the calendar upon the wall, which displayed a picture of a fat child holding a kitten and the name of a feed store in Quincy. The shadows in the corners seemed to draw back a little, as if offended.

"You got me," said the woman.

It was spoken very quietly. The man heard it and did not wish to hear it. He looked away from her, at the window, where the rain ran down in crooked lines and the lamp made a second, ghostly lamp upon the glass. In the black pane he could see his own face, yellow and drawn, the mustache drooping like a wet flag.

"That ain't what I meant," he said.

"I know what you meant."

"I meant—" He struggled. Words were not his trade. He had a feeling that there was a great truth somewhere within him, a fine and shining truth that would explain everything, but when he reached for it his fingers closed upon nothing. "A man's got to do somethin'. A man can't just sit. He's got to go out and—and make his mark."

"Make his mark," said the woman. She seemed to taste the words and find them sour. "You been readin' the papers again."

This was true, and it stung him. For a month he had been reading the papers, in the evenings, under this same lamp. He had read of men who went into the far places and came back with fortunes. He had read of strikes and claims and nuggets the size of a hen's egg. The papers had said that the world belonged to the bold. He had believed the papers. They were printed, and printed things had a kind of iron authority, like the voice of a preacher or a judge.

"There ain't nothin' wrong with the papers," he muttered.

"No," she agreed. "There ain't nothin' wrong with the papers. They don't have to go nowhere."

The stove clicked twice, rapidly, and was silent. The man fixed his gaze upon it. It was a squat black thing with a nickel rail and a door like a mouth, and through the cracks about the door the fire showed red, red as a wound. It seemed to him that the stove had sat in this corner since the beginning of the world, watching him, waiting for him to grow old. He thought of all the winters it had seen him come in from the mill with his hands frozen and his back aching, and he thought of all the winters to come, and a great dull fear rose up in him like water in the hold of a sinking boat.

"I'm goin'," he said.

He said it loudly. It came out of him with a kind of explosion, and when it was out he was astonished at it. It rang in the little room. It seemed to bounce from the walls and come back to him, louder than he had spoken it. He felt suddenly very tall and very brave, and at the same time somewhat sick.

The woman did not move. Her hands had ceased folding the towel. They lay still in her lap.

"When?" she asked.

"Monday. There's a boat to Keokuk Monday, and I can get the cars from there."

"Monday," she said.

"Yes."

"That's four days."

"Yes."

She looked at him then, fully, for the first time since supper. Her eyes were gray, and in the lamplight they had a strange depth, like the river on a still morning when you cannot tell whether you are seeing the bottom or the sky. He met them for a moment and then found that he could not, and his glance went sliding away to the spoon upon the floor.

"And what am I to do?" she said. "While you're makin' your mark."

"I'll send money."

"When?"

"Soon as I get some."

"And till then?"

"There's the twelve dollars in the coffee can."

"There's nine," she said. "I paid Mr. Kessler on Saturday."

The man had not known this. It was a small thing, three dollars, but it seemed to him in that moment like a vast and terrible accusation. Three dollars to Kessler for flour and lard and coffee, and she had paid it without a word, and he had not known. He felt as though he had been walking in the dark and had put his foot down upon nothing.

"Nine, then," he said.

"Nine dollars," said the woman. "And the rent's due the first."

"Your brother—"

"I ain't goin' to Will."

"He'd help."

"I ain't goin' to Will," she said again, and something in her voice made him stop. It was not anger. It was harder than anger. It was the voice of a person who has stood a long time at a gate and has decided, finally, that the gate will not open.

The shutter banged. The rain roared. Out on the river a steamboat whistle sounded, far off and mournful, a long low cry that seemed to come from the bottom of the night. They both listened to it. It rose and hung in the air and died, and when it had died the silence was worse than before.

"That'll be the Molly Gray," said the man, from habit. "She's late."

"Everything's late," said the woman.

She got up then. She rose slowly, as though her body were a burden she had been asked to carry and had not agreed to. She went to the stove and opened the door, and the red light leaped out at her and painted her face, so that for a moment she looked like a figure in a burning house. She put in a stick of wood. The fire seized it with a little hiss of greed. She closed the door, and the room went back to yellow.

She did not return to her chair. She stood by the stove with her back to him, and he looked at her back and the knot of her hair and the thin strings of her apron, and he could not tell what she was thinking. It was as though a wall had come up out of the floor between them, a wall of glass, through which he could see her plainly and could not reach her at all.

"Hattie," he said.

She did not answer.

"Hattie, it ain't that I want to leave you."

"Then don't."

"It's that I got to."

"Nobody's got to." She turned around. Her face was white, and two spots of color burned in her cheeks, as if she had been slapped. "Nobody in this world has got to do anything, Ed Weller. You want to. That's all. You want to go off and be somebody in a story, and you want me to sit here and be the woman in the window that waits. Well, I read the papers, too. I know how those stories go. The man comes back rich or he don't come back at all, and either way the woman in the window don't get but one line."

The man stared at her. He had not known she could speak like this. In seven years of marriage he had heard her talk of the price of eggs, of the neighbor's children, of the weather and the church social and the leak in the roof. He had thought that was all there was. Now it seemed to him that he had been living beside a stranger, and he was frightened.

"That ain't fair," he said weakly.

"No," she said. "It ain't."

They looked at each other across the yellow table. The lamp burned between them, steady and indifferent. It had lit a thousand suppers in this room and would light a thousand more, and it did not care in the least whether one of them was missing.

The man looked down at his hands. They were large and scarred and brown, with black crescents of machine grease under the nails that no soap would move. He thought of them holding a pick in some far mountain. He thought of them holding a gold nugget. Then, without wishing to, he thought of them holding nothing, lying open upon a strange bed in a strange town, with no one to see. He closed them slowly into fists.

"Dan says it's a sure thing," he said, but his voice had lost its iron.

"Dan's been sure before."

"He sent the money."

"He sent half."

The man picked up the envelope. He held it between his fingers and looked at it. It was a poor, dirty thing, creased and stained, and the address was written in a sprawling hand that ran uphill. In the alley behind the mill it had seemed to him like a golden key. Now it looked like what it was: a piece of paper that had come a long way and had grown tired on the journey.

He did not put it down. Neither did he tear it. He sat holding it, and the woman stood watching him hold it, and the rain beat upon the roof.

After a time she came back to the table. She bent and picked up the spoon from the floor and wiped it upon her apron and laid it carefully beside his plate. Then she sat down in her chair and took up the dish towel and began again to fold it.

"Your coffee's cold," she said. "You want I should heat it?"

The man did not answer at once. He was looking at the spoon. It lay beside the plate, clean and bright, as though nothing had happened to it. It occurred to him dimly that this was the way of things. A spoon fell and was picked up, and the world did not mark it.

"No," he said. "I don't want it."

"There's pie."

"No."

She folded the towel. The stove clicked. Somewhere in the dark the shutter gave one last bang and then was quiet, as if it had at last found the right door and been let in.

"I'll write to Dan tomorrow," said the man.

The woman's hands paused upon the towel.

"What'll you tell him?"

"I don't know," said the man. "I'll tell him somethin'."

He sat with the envelope between his fingers. He did not know himself what he would tell Dan Fitch. He knew only that the splendid country of sunlight had receded somewhere beyond the rain, and that it might come back in the morning, gleaming, when he stood again in the alley behind the mill with Hennessey's watch ticking at him through the wall. Or it might not. He could not tell. He felt as though he were a man standing upon a riverbank in a fog, hearing the water and unable to see it, uncertain whether the next step would carry him onto solid ground or into the current.

The woman watched him. Her face had grown quiet again, and the color had gone out of her cheeks, but her eyes did not leave him. There was in them neither triumph nor forgiveness. There was only a long, patient wariness, like that of a person who has seen a dog go mad once and has learned to watch its mouth.

The lamp burned. The flame stood up straight and yellow, and it regarded them both with the same cold attention it would have given to two chairs. Outside, the river went on muttering in the dark, rolling down toward the Gulf as it had rolled for ten thousand years, bearing away upon its back the drift of a thousand little towns and a thousand little kitchens, and it did not know that there was anyone named Weller in the world at all.

prompt:
Write a 2,500–3,000-word prose narrative in the exact literary style and voice of Stephen Crane, depicting the following scene: Cousins catching up after a long time apart.
Write in third-person perspective. Match their diction, syntax, tone and voice as closely as you can.  Do not paraphrase or reuse any of the author's content. Output only the piece itself with no title, preamble, or commentary.
response:
I

The train came out of the west at dusk. It had the appearance of a great black beast that had run very far and was angry at the end of it. It howled at the crossing below the tannery, and the howl went up among the hills and returned, diminished and plaintive, as if the hills did not care to keep it.

Upon the platform of the Hollisville station stood a young man in a new derby hat. The hat was very stiff and very black, and it sat upon his head with an air of formidable dignity, as though it knew itself to be the chief thing about him. He had bought it that afternoon. He had paid two dollars for it, and the transaction had caused him some private anguish, for he was a clerk in Simpson's feed store and he had a wife and a child of eleven months and a parlor organ upon which there remained four payments.

But his cousin was coming home, and it was a thing that demanded a hat.

The clerk had not seen his cousin in eight years. In his mind there was a picture of a lank boy with red wrists and a voice that cracked upon important words, a boy who had once flung him, the clerk, headlong into the mill-race behind Thompson's and then stood upon the bank and laughed with a laughter that seemed to the clerk, gasping in the brown water, the most cruel sound in all creation. Afterward the boy had pulled him out. This had been worse. The clerk had hated him with great purity for a week.

Then the cousin had gone West. Letters had come at long intervals, and each letter had been a kind of thunderclap in the family. There had been Kansas, and then Colorado, and then a long silence that the clerk's mother had filled with tears and dark prophecies, and then a letter from a place called Leadville, which the clerk had read seven times. It spoke of mines and of men with revolvers, and the clerk had carried it about in his coat until the folds wore through.

Now the train shrieked again and came grinding into the station, and the clerk's heart performed a curious leap. He had rehearsed. He had resolved to be calm and a little careless, to say "Hello, Jack," in the manner of a man who had seen a great deal of the world himself and was not to be overcome by any returning wanderer. He had practised it before the glass that morning while his wife watched him from the bed with an expression he had not liked.

The cars stopped. A drummer got down with his sample cases. A fat woman got down, assisted by the brakeman, and stood upon the platform blinking at the lamps as if they had insulted her. Then a man appeared upon the steps of the second coach.

He was thin. His face was the color of an old saddle, and upon his lip there was a mustache of some magnitude. He wore a broad gray hat with a crease in the crown, and his coat had been good once. He carried a valise that was strapped with a piece of rope. He stood a moment upon the step and looked at the station, the platform, the lamps, the clerk, and the hills beyond, and in his eyes there was an expression that the clerk could not read.

"Well," said the clerk. His voice had a sudden treachery in it. "Well, Jack."

The man from the West came down the steps. "Well, Ed," he said.

They shook hands. Afterward they stood regarding each other with the grave suspicion of two dogs who meet in a road. Each was searching for the boy he had known, and each was finding instead a stranger who had stolen the boy's features and rearranged them with indifferent skill.

"You've got fat," said the man from the West at last.

The clerk was wounded. He had not considered himself fat. He had considered himself substantial. "I'm married," he said, as if this explained it.

"So Aunt Mary wrote me." The man from the West surveyed the derby. "That's a mighty fine hat."

The clerk's soul expanded again like a sail. "Oh, this?" he said. "Well, I don't know. It's a pretty good hat, I guess."

II

They walked up Main Street in the blue evening. The lamps were being lit in the windows, and each yellow square seemed to the clerk to contain an eye. He walked very straight. He wished the whole town to see him beside this lean, brown man with the broad hat, and in a measure the town obliged him. Old Hasbrouck, sitting on the step of the harness shop, took his pipe from his mouth and stared with his jaw sagging. Two small boys left off throwing a ball against the side of the bank and followed at a distance of twenty paces, stealthily, like Indians in a book.

The man from the West was looking about him with that same unreadable expression.

"It's got smaller," he said.

"What has?"

"The town. Everything. The bank used to look like a church to me. It ain't much bigger'n a woodshed."

The clerk felt that the bank had been in some fashion insulted, and that he himself, as a citizen, was obliged to resent it. But he did not know how, so he said nothing. Presently he said: "They put in a new brick front on Waller's last spring."

"Did they?" said the man from the West.

There followed a silence in which they walked. The clerk began to recite the dead. It was the principal news of Hollisville, and he felt it his duty. Old man Peabody had died. Mrs. Corliss had died, very sudden, at the church supper, with a plate of oysters before her. The younger Breen boy had been killed by a horse. Lucy Wheaton had married a man from Albany and gone away, and it was said that he drank.

The man from the West received each of these tidings with a nod. When the clerk named Lucy Wheaton, however, the nod was somewhat delayed, and the clerk, who had forgotten until that instant that there had once been something between Lucy Wheaton and his cousin, a matter of a sleigh ride and a mitten, felt his face grow hot. He hurried on to the Breen boy's funeral, which had been well attended.

At the corner of Elm Street the clerk could endure it no longer.

"Say, Jack," he said, "was it like what you wrote? Out there?"

The man from the West took a little time. "How do you mean?"

"Why, the mines, and the—the shooting, and all that."

The man from the West looked down at the clerk. Then he looked at the two small boys, who had crept nearer and now stood behind a hitching post with their mouths open, as though they waited to be fed.

"Well," he said slowly, "I saw a man shot once."

The clerk drew in his breath. The small boys drew in theirs.

"It was in a place in Leadville called the Silver Moon. Feller come in and had words with another feller about a mule, and they went at it. I was right near. The ball went through the window behind me." He paused. "Busted a lamp in the street."

"Was he killed? The man that got shot?"

"No. Got him in the arm. He was round again in a week."

The clerk was a little disappointed that the man had not been killed, but he was also filled with a great, glowing respect. His cousin had stood within a few feet of a flying bullet. The bullet had gone singing past his very head, and here he was, walking along Elm Street in the dusk as calm as a deacon. The clerk himself had never been nearer to violence than the afternoon a load of oats had fallen off a wagon in front of the feed store.

What the man from the West did not relate was that he had been standing near the window of the Silver Moon because he was employed to wash its glasses, and that he had dropped a tray of them when the shot was fired, and that the proprietor had afterward stopped the cost of the glasses out of his wages, so that the bullet, which had in no way touched him, had nevertheless cost him a dollar and sixty cents. These details did not seem to him to belong to the story. A story, he had found, is a thing that improves with pruning, like a fruit tree.

The small boys ran off to spread the news through Hollisville that Ed Worden's cousin had been shot at in a saloon, and by nine o'clock it was generally understood that he had killed a man.

III

The clerk's house stood at the end of Pell Street. It was a narrow white house with a narrow porch, and it had a look of having been squeezed between its neighbors. In the window of the parlor there was a lamp with a pink shade, and the clerk regarded this lamp as his cousin approached it, and felt a pride that was very nearly holy.

His wife met them in the hall. She was a small woman with a sharp chin, and she had put on her brown silk. She looked at the man from the West in the way a woman looks at a dog that her husband has brought home without consulting her.

"How do you do, Mr. Marsh," she said.

"How do, ma'am," said the man from the West. He took off the broad gray hat, and the clerk saw with a kind of shock that his hair had receded from his temples, so that he looked suddenly older, and almost weary.

There was supper. There was cold ham and hot biscuit and a pickle dish of pressed glass that had been a wedding present. The man from the West ate with great attention and very little speech. The clerk's wife watched him across the table. She was waiting for him to commit some barbarity with his knife. He did not, and this seemed in a manner to offend her further, as if he had cheated her out of something.

Midway through the ham the baby set up a howl in the next room. It was a sudden and appalling noise, the noise of a small creature that has awakened and found the universe empty. The clerk's wife rose and went out, and presently returned with the baby, which was red and furious and had its fists clenched in a posture of defiance against the whole world.

"This is Edward," said the clerk with a terrible bashfulness.

The man from the West put down his fork. He regarded the baby. The baby regarded him. It ceased howling and fixed upon the stranger a stare of enormous and unwinking gravity, a stare like that of a judge who has heard all the evidence and is about to pronounce.

"Well," said the man from the West. He seemed to be at a loss. "Well, he's a fine big boy." He put out one brown finger, and the baby seized it and held it with a grip of iron and continued to stare.

The man from the West sat very still. Something passed across his face that the clerk did not see, because he was looking at his son with the fatuous adoration of a young father, but which the clerk's wife did see. It caused her chin to lose a little of its edge.

After supper the clerk led his cousin into the parlor. This was the clerk's great moment, and he had been approaching it all evening as a pilgrim approaches a shrine. There was a Brussels carpet with roses upon it as large as cabbages. There was a horsehair sofa that glittered under the pink lamp. There was a chromo of a stag at bay, and the stag wore an expression of profound and noble despair. And there, against the wall, stood the parlor organ, with its fretwork and its little mirrors and its rows of white knobs.

"Well," said the clerk. He made a gesture that included the whole room. He could not say more. It seemed to him that the room spoke for itself.

The man from the West stood in the doorway. For a time he said nothing at all. He was thinking of a room on Harrison Avenue in Leadville, eight feet by ten, with a cot and a box and a nail upon which to hang his coat, and of the nights he had lain upon the cot listening to the wind come down off the mountains and pluck at the tar paper of the walls, as if it were trying to get in and find him. He was thinking that he was twenty-seven years old, and that he owned a valise strapped with rope and a gray hat and eleven dollars, and that the eleven dollars had been fourteen when he left Denver.

"That's a mighty handsome organ, Ed," he said, and his voice was very careful.

The clerk was satisfied. He sat down upon the horsehair sofa, which received him with a slight shriek, and began to explain the system of payments.

IV

Later, when the clerk's wife had gone up with the baby, the two cousins sat upon the narrow porch and smoked cigars. The clerk had bought the cigars also. They were five cents each, and he smoked his with the air of a man who smokes five-cent cigars every evening of his life.

The night had come down over Hollisville like a soft black cloth. The houses across the street were dim shapes, each with its single eye of lamplight, and one by one the eyes were closing. Somewhere a dog was barking at nothing with great conviction. The stars stood over the town in their old cold rows. They had looked down upon Hollisville for a long time, and they did not appear to think much of it.

"Jack," said the clerk after a while.

"What?"

"I had a notion to go too, once. Out there. Did you know that?"

The man from the West turned his head. The end of his cigar glowed and faded. "No," he said. "I didn't know that."

"It was the year after you went. I had it all planned. I had twenty-two dollars saved. I was going to go to Kansas City first and then on." The clerk stopped. He was surprised to find that his throat had grown tight. He had not thought of this in years, and here it was, rising up in him out of the darkness like a ghost out of a cellar. "Then Pa took sick, and somebody had to stay, and old Simpson offered me the place at the store. And then there was Lottie." He laughed, and the laugh did not come out well. "So I stayed."

The man from the West said nothing.

"I used to read your letters," said the clerk, "and I'd think: there's Jack, out there with the mines and all. And here's me weighing out bran." He pulled at his cigar. "I don't know. I guess I used to hate you some, Jack."

A wind came up the street and stirred the leaves of the maple in front of the house, and they whispered together for a moment in the manner of old women at a funeral, and were quiet.

The man from the West sat looking out into the dark. He was aware that a moment had arrived. He could tell his cousin now. He could tell him about the glasses at the Silver Moon, and the room on Harrison Avenue, and the claim that had turned out to be nothing but a hole in a hill, and the winter he had shovelled snow off the roofs of Denver for fifty cents a roof, and the night he had stood on the bridge over Cherry Creek and looked down at the black water for a long time. He could say: "Ed, you didn't miss anything. You got the best of it. You got the organ and the baby and the pink lamp, and I got a busted valise." The words were all there, ranged in his mind like soldiers.

But his cousin was sitting beside him in the dark in a new derby hat, and his cousin had hated him a little for eight years, and had loved him a little too, and had built upon him a whole small cathedral of envy and wonder. It is a dreadful thing to pull down a man's cathedral, even when it is built of nothing.

"Well," said the man from the West, "it was pretty rough out there, Ed. You were a sight better off to stay."

He said it in the voice of a man who has passed through fire and does not care to talk about it. The clerk heard that voice and was abashed. He felt that his cousin was being generous, as heroes are generous, and he loved him for it.

"I guess maybe that's so," he said humbly.

V

After a time the clerk rose and said, "Let's walk down to the mill-race."

They went down Pell Street and across the Corliss pasture in the starlight. The grass was wet, and it soaked the clerk's good shoes, and he did not care. They came to the old mill, which had burned four years before and was now a black skeleton against the sky, and below it the race ran in its stone channel.

The clerk stood upon the bank. He had expected a torrent. In his memory it was a brown and roaring thing that had seized him like a hand and dragged him down into a place of cold and terror. Before him now there flowed a little stream perhaps three feet deep, choked with weeds, murmuring over the stones with a sound like a child talking in its sleep.

"Why," said the clerk, "it ain't nothing."

The man from the West laughed. It was the same laugh. The clerk heard it come across eight years and a thousand miles, and he turned with a sudden heat in him, and then the heat went out, because his cousin's face in the starlight was not cruel at all. It was only tired.

"No," said the man from the West. "It ain't nothing. I guess none of it was."

He stooped and picked up a stone and flung it into the water. It made a small sound. A frog, somewhere in the weeds, expressed its opinion of the matter in a deep and insolent voice, and then the night closed over the place where the stone had been as though there had never been any stone.

They stood together for a while. Neither spoke. The clerk was thinking that his cousin was a great man who had done great things and was too proud to boast of them. The man from the West was thinking that his cousin was a fortunate fool, and that he would have given his gray hat and his eleven dollars and the whole of Colorado to be such a fool. Each pitied the other a little. Each was wrong, and each was right, and the frog in the weeds knew nothing of either and continued to sing.

Presently they turned and went back across the wet pasture toward the town. The clerk's wife had left the pink lamp burning in the parlor, and it shone out over Pell Street, small and rosy and very brave against the immense indifferent dark. The clerk saw it from a long way off and walked faster. The man from the West saw it too, and for a moment he stood still in the middle of the pasture with his hands in his pockets, looking at it, as a man might look at a ship's light from the deck of another ship that is going the other way.

Then he followed his cousin up the street.

The sun lay upon the back lot like a great sheet of hot brass, and the weeds, standing in their ranks along the fence, hung their heads in the manner of soldiers who have marched a long way and have no particular expectation of glory at the end of it. A hen moved among them with a fussy and important air. She paused, cocked one eye at the sky as if she suspected it of some treachery, and went on.

In the shade of the woodshed sat Willie Haggard, aged seven years. He held to his mouth a small tin harmonica, and from it he drew a sound which resembled the protest of a gate that has not been oiled since the war. He was enraptured. His eyes were half closed. His cheeks swelled and collapsed with the regularity of a bellows. He conceived himself to be a performer of the most exalted kind, and he was certain that if the people of the town could but hear him they would come running in the road, crying out to one another, and presently he would be taken away to the city in a carriage drawn by four white horses, and there would be a band.

The harmonica had cost him dearly. He did not, at the moment, dwell upon the price. A man in the full flush of a fine possession does not stop to examine the bill. It had belonged formerly to the Ferris boy, who lived beyond the lumber-yard, and who was a person of large and loose dealings. The Ferris boy had been willing to part with it for a consideration, and the consideration had been a small silver thimble with a band of little roses running about the rim. Willie had obtained the thimble from his mother's work-basket that morning, in a moment when the kitchen was empty and the basket sat upon the window-ledge in a ray of sun, glinting, as if it wished to be taken.

He had felt, in the instant of taking it, a strange cold thrill along the spine, which was not unpleasant. Afterward, walking down the yellow road toward the lumber-yard with the thimble burning in his fist, he had experienced a sense of tremendous adventure. The trees along the way had seemed to lean and whisper. A dog had looked at him with an expression of the darkest suspicion. But the trade had been made swiftly, in the manner of men of business, and now the harmonica was his, and the thimble was gone into the deep and inscrutable pockets of the Ferris boy, and the world was a fine place in which to blow upon a tin instrument.

He blew again. The hen, startled, ran a short distance, her wings held out from her sides like the arms of a fat woman who has been surprised at a pump. Willie took this as a tribute.

---

In the kitchen, Mrs. Haggard had finished with the bread. She stood a moment with her hands resting upon the edge of the table, and her shoulders sagged. The kitchen was hot. The stove sat in its corner like a black idol, satisfied with its sacrifices, ticking a little as it cooled. Upon the shelf the clock chopped the afternoon into small pieces with a dry and indifferent sound. She was a thin woman, with a face that had once been pretty and was now merely patient, and her hair was drawn back so tightly that it seemed to pull her eyes into an expression of perpetual mild surprise.

She went to the window for her mending. She took up the basket and sat down with it in her lap, and her fingers went into it as a hand goes into a familiar pocket in the dark. They searched. They searched again. Presently she tipped the basket and looked into it, and then she turned it out entirely upon the oilcloth, and spools and buttons and a paper of needles went rolling and scattering in a small riot.

The thimble was not there.

She looked under the table. She looked upon the window-ledge, and in the crack between the ledge and the wall, and behind the flour-crock. She stood in the middle of the floor with her hands at her sides. A curious stillness had come upon her face. The thimble had been her mother's, and her mother's mother's before that, and it had come over from somewhere across the water in a time so far away that it was like a story. It was the only thing of silver in the house.

Her mind, moving slowly and then with a sudden terrible swiftness, arrived at the woodshed.

Out of the back lot there came at that moment a long, quavering, triumphant blast, as if some small demon were celebrating a victory.

---

The voice of the mother went across the back lot like a cavalry charge. "Willie! You Willie Haggard! You come here to me!"

At the first syllable the boy's soul had leaped up and away from the harmonica as a bird leaps from a branch at the crack of a rifle. He sat frozen. The instrument was still at his lips. Then, with a movement which he had not decided upon, his hand closed over it and thrust it deep into his pocket, and he rose and slid along the wall of the woodshed toward the lilac bush.

The lilac bush was an ancient and trusted ally. It had sheltered him from many pursuits. He crept into its green heart and crouched there, and the leaves shut behind him, and the light came through them in little shifting coins of gold that lay upon his hands and knees. His heart was beating in great slow thuds, like a drum at a funeral.

He knew. He had known, in a vague way, all day. It is the misfortune of sinners that their sin goes with them about the world, keeping pace at their elbow, and can be dropped behind for an hour, but no longer. Now it stood up before him in the gloom of the lilac bush and regarded him with a face of brass.

"Willie!"

The voice was nearer. He could see, through a gap in the leaves, a portion of his mother's skirt, of a faded blue calico, moving across the yard with an awful deliberation. It paused by the woodshed. It turned. It came toward the lilac bush.

He began to compose in his mind an elaborate account. A stranger had come by, a tall man with a black beard, and had leaped the fence, and had gone into the kitchen, and had come out again, running, with something shining in his hand, and Willie had pursued him valiantly as far as the lumber-yard, where the villain had escaped upon a fast horse. It was a good tale. It had color. He felt that it would bear examination.

The skirt stopped before the bush. There was a silence in which the hen could be heard, very far off, expressing doubt.

"I can see your shoes," said his mother.

He looked down at his shoes. They were indeed outside the bush, in the full light, two small brown boots with the toes scuffed white, and they appeared to him at that moment to be the most traitorous objects in the whole of creation.

"Come out of there."

He came out. He came out slowly, backward, with leaves in his hair, and stood before her with his hands clasped behind him and his eyes fixed upon a point somewhere near her apron-string. He felt very small. The yard had grown suddenly enormous, and the sky above it was a vast blue judgment.

---

In the kitchen she sat him upon the chair by the table, the hard chair, and she stood over him. The clock went on chopping. The cat, which had been asleep upon the rag rug, opened one green eye, looked at the two of them, and closed it again with an air of great worldly contempt. It had seen these things before.

"Where is my thimble?"

He opened his mouth, and the tall man with the black beard rose up in his throat, and then, unaccountably, sank back again and was lost. He found that he could not say anything at all. He shut his mouth.

"Willie, where is my thimble?"

"I dunno," he said.

She regarded him. Her eyes were gray and very steady, and it seemed to him that they went into him like nails, and that they could see the harmonica lying in his pocket as plainly as if his trousers had been made of window-glass.

"Turn out your pockets."

He was overwhelmed by the injustice of it. A man's pockets were his own; they were his fortress and his treasury; they were the last citadel of a free soul. He felt that he was about to be stripped of everything. Slowly, with an expression of the deepest tragedy, he drew forth a piece of string, a broken knife with one blade, three marbles, a dead beetle of a fine green sheen, a lump of something which had once been candy, and the harmonica.

The harmonica lay upon the oilcloth among the spools and buttons and glittered there with a bold and impudent air, as if it did not know what it had done.

"Where did you get that?"

"Fella give it to me."

"What fella?"

"Ferris."

"The Ferris boy don't give anybody anything," said his mother, "and you know it." She took up the harmonica and turned it in her fingers. It was a cheap thing, battered, with a dent upon one side, and some of the paint gone. She looked at it for a long time. "What did you give him for it?"

There was no help anywhere. The cat slept. The clock chopped. The stove ticked. He looked at the floor, and the boards of the floor ran away from him in long parallel lines that converged, very far off, at the door, and there was no escape there either.

"The thimble," he said.

It came out of him very small, scarcely a sound at all. Yet it seemed to him that it went up and filled the whole kitchen and pressed against the walls, and that the windows would presently burst outward with it.

His mother did not say anything for a moment. She set the harmonica down upon the table very gently, as if it were made of eggshell. Then she sat down in the other chair, and put her hands in her lap, and looked at them.

He had been prepared for thunder. He had braced his small frame against a storm of words, against the old familiar trumpet-blasts of wrath, and this silence undid him. It was a far more dreadful thing. It was like the silence in a church when the minister has stopped in the middle of a sentence and everyone waits.

"That was your grandma's thimble," she said at last. "And her mother's. It come across the ocean. Did you know that?"

He had known it. He had heard it a hundred times. But it had never seemed to him a matter of the least consequence. The ocean was a word in a book. His grandmother was a picture in an oval frame upon the parlor wall, a stern old woman in black with her hands folded, who looked as though she had never in her life desired a harmonica. Now, abruptly, the ocean and the grandmother and the thimble swam together in his mind into a single great accusing shape, and he felt that he had committed a crime of enormous dimensions, a crime against generations, against continents.

"You stole it," said his mother.

The word fell upon him like a stone. He had not thought of it as stealing. He had thought of it as a kind of borrowing, or a trade, or simply as a thing which had happened in a ray of sunshine. But now the word stood up naked in the kitchen, and he saw that it was the true name of the deed, and he was filled with horror.

"I never—" he began.

"You took a thing that wasn't yours, without asking, and you give it away. What do you call that?"

He did not answer. His lower lip had begun to perform certain motions over which he had no command. He set his teeth upon it fiercely. He was resolved that he would not cry. To cry would be to surrender the last of his honor. He thought of the Indian chiefs in the books, who could be burned at the stake and would only sing.

"Go out and cut me a switch," said his mother.

---

He went out into the brass afternoon. The peach tree stood at the corner of the garden, and it seemed to him that it had been waiting there all his life for exactly this moment, holding its slender limbs out to him with a kind of horrible courtesy.

It was the custom of the house that the condemned should select his own instrument. Willie approached the tree as a man approaches a scaffold. He walked around it once. He examined its branches with the eye of a connoisseur. There was a stout one, too stout; she would send him back. There was a thin one, a whip of a thing, that would sting like a hornet. He stood a long time in contemplation. The sun beat upon his neck. Somewhere beyond the fence a man was driving a wagon along the road, and the wheels made a dry, grinding sound, and the man was whistling, and Willie hated him with a deep and sudden hatred because he was free and whistling and did not know.

At last he chose a branch of a middle sort and broke it off and stripped it of its leaves, very slowly, one leaf at a time, prolonging the ceremony as long as it could decently be prolonged. The leaves fell about his feet. He reflected that perhaps his mother would die before he returned, or that the house would take fire, or that the end of the world would arrive, as the minister frequently promised, in a single blaze of glory. None of these things occurred. The house sat placidly in the sun with smoke rising thinly from the kitchen chimney.

He went back inside and held out the switch.

His mother took it and looked at it. She flexed it once between her hands. He watched her face, and he saw that it was very tired, and that the line between her eyes had grown deep, and he did not understand any of this. He only knew that the moment had come.

"Hold out your legs," she said.

He stood before her and she struck him three times across the backs of his calves, below the trousers. It was swift and sharp. Each blow was like the touch of a hot wire. At the first he jumped; at the second he set his jaw; at the third the Indian chiefs deserted him entirely, and a great sob broke up out of his chest, and he wept.

He wept with his whole body. He wept as if his heart had been rent asunder. The tears ran down his cheeks and into the corners of his mouth and tasted of salt. He was ashamed, and the shame made him weep harder, and through the blur of his weeping he saw the kitchen swim and waver, and the black stove, and the cat, which had risen and stretched and was walking away toward the door with its tail in the air as if it would have no part in such a spectacle.

"Go up to your room," said his mother. "And stay there till supper."

---

His room was under the roof, and it was very hot, and a wasp was crawling upon the window-pane with an air of having important business elsewhere. Willie flung himself upon the bed and lay face downward with his arms over his head.

He wept a while longer, and then, finding that no one came to hear it, he stopped. He turned upon his back and looked at the ceiling. There was a water-stain there in the shape of a lion, or of a country upon a map, depending upon the hour. Now it looked like a lion.

A tremendous resolve was forming in him. He would run away. He would go that night, when the house was asleep, and he would go down to the river and follow it to the sea, and there he would ship upon a vessel as a cabin-boy, and he would sail to the far countries, and he would become a captain, and fight pirates, and grow a beard, and after many years he would return to the town in a fine coat with gold upon the sleeves. His mother would be old then. She would be sitting upon the porch in a rocking-chair. And he would come up the yellow road with a sack upon his shoulder, and in the sack would be a thousand thimbles of pure gold, and he would empty them out at her feet, in a heap that glittered in the sun, and he would say nothing at all, but would turn and walk away again, and she would cry out after him, too late, too late.

This picture gave him the profoundest satisfaction. He played it over several times, improving it. He added a parrot. He added a scar upon his cheek. At the end of each performance his mother wept more bitterly, and the townspeople came running down the road to gaze upon him, and the Ferris boy stood among them, abashed and small, with his hands empty.

His legs smarted. He drew up his trousers and examined the three red welts with interest and some pride. They were very fine welts. He felt that they would be greatly admired.

The wasp found the crack at the top of the window and went out into the afternoon. Willie watched it go. The room was quiet. Gradually the lion upon the ceiling became a country upon a map, and the sea receded, and the gold coat grew dim, and he slept.

---

Downstairs, Mrs. Haggard sat at the kitchen table with the switch lying before her among the spools. She did not move for a long time. The clock went on. Her hands lay in her lap, and she looked at them as though they belonged to someone else, some stranger who had come into the house and done a thing and gone away again.

Presently she rose and put on her bonnet. She took the harmonica from the table and put it in the pocket of her apron, and she went out by the front door and down the yellow road in the direction of the lumber-yard. The dust rose about her skirts in small pale clouds. A dog came out from under a porch to look at her, and decided she was of no account, and went back.

She was gone nearly an hour.

---

When Willie came down to supper, his eyes were swollen and his hair stood up in a crest at the back, and he walked with the stiff dignity of a man who has suffered greatly and intends that the world shall know it. His father was already at the table, a large silent man who smelled of the feed-store and who looked at his son once over the top of his newspaper and said nothing, which was his custom in all things.

Willie took his place. He looked at the plate before him. Beside it, upon the oilcloth, lay the silver thimble with its band of little roses, shining in the lamplight.

He looked at it for a long moment. Then he looked at his mother. She was setting down the dish of potatoes, and her face showed nothing, nothing at all. She sat down and folded her hands for the blessing.

The harmonica was nowhere to be seen. He understood, dimly, that it had gone back across the lumber-yard into the deep and inscrutable pockets of the Ferris boy, and that the world had been, in some mysterious fashion, set right again, and that he had been left out of the arrangement entirely.

His father said the blessing in a low rumble, like a wagon going over a bridge.

At the end of the meal, his mother cut the pie. She cut it in the ordinary way, in six pieces. But when she put Willie's piece upon his plate it was, beyond any question, the largest of the six. It was perhaps a third again as large as the others. He perceived this at once with the eye of a man of business. He looked up at her quickly, but she was not looking at him; she was looking at the lamp, and her face in the yellow light was soft and tired and very far away.

He ate the pie slowly. It was cherry. A strange feeling had come into his chest, which he did not understand and could not name, and which made the pie difficult to swallow. It was something like the feeling of the cold thrill along his spine in the morning, and yet it was altogether different. He did not like it. He wished that she had struck him again instead.

---

The next day, in the hollow behind the schoolhouse, he showed the welts to an assembly of four boys. They examined them gravely, bending down, and one of them touched a welt with a grimy forefinger, and drew back.

"Did you holler?" asked the largest boy.

Willie looked at him with an expression of lofty scorn. He looked past him, at the trees, which stood in their green ranks against the sky, and at the sky itself, which was blue and empty and did not care.

"No," he said.

The boys were silent, considering this. Then they went away to throw stones at a tin can upon a post, and he went with them, and after a while he had forgotten everything, the thimble and the harmonica and the peach tree and the pie, everything except the can, which rang like a bell when it was struck, and the stones, and the brass light of the sun, which lay upon all of them alike and made no distinctions.

In the darkness he saw visions of a thousand-tongued fear that would babble at his back and cause him to flee, while others were going coolly about their country’s business. And as he sweated with the pain of these thoughts, he could hear low, serene sentences. “I’ll bid five.” “Make it six.” “Seven.” “Seven goes.” He stared at the red, shivering reflection of a fire on the white wall of his tent until, exhausted and ill from the monotony of his suffering, he fell asleep.

The man came up the stairs slowly, as if each step were a separate argument which he must win. At the landing he paused. Beneath the door of his room there lay a thin yellow line of lamplight, and he regarded it for some moments with the air of one who sees, far off, the camp fires of a hostile people. Behind him, in the well of the stairway, the dark was full of the smells of cabbage and wet wool. Somewhere below a child was crying with a steady, mechanical persistence, like a pump.

He had resolved upon a manner during the walk from the mill. It was to be a manner of great calm. He would enter, he would hang his cap upon the nail, and he would say, in a voice of iron indifference, that he was done with Haskell and Haskell's furnaces. He had rehearsed it along three streets. At each corner it had grown more noble. By the time he passed the saloon of the one-eyed Dutchman, he had become a figure of tranquil defiance, a man who had flung down his tools before a tyrant and walked out into the bright air of his own will. But now, upon the landing, the figure shrank. It was as if the yellow line beneath the door had the power to measure him.

He opened the door. His wife was at the stove. She turned her head, and he saw at once that she knew something. It was in the set of her shoulders. Women, he reflected bitterly, had a way of knowing things through walls.

"You're early," she said.

"Yes," said the man. He hung his cap upon the nail. The calm voice did not come. He had to search for it, as for a coin dropped in the dark.

The room was small, and the stove made it smaller. It squatted in the corner like a black beast, its single red eye glaring through a crack in the door. Upon the table was a plate with a cloth over it, and beside the plate a cup with a broken handle. The lamp threw upon the ceiling a round, pale shape that trembled when anyone moved. The window gave upon a wall of brick, and the brick was wet and shone like the hide of some great sleeping animal.

The woman wiped her hands upon her apron. She did this deliberately, finger by finger. "Mis' Callahan was up," she said. "She says her Mike seen you go out the gate at three o'clock."

The man sat down in the chair by the table. He lifted the cloth from the plate and looked at the potatoes beneath it as if they were a strange and interesting country. "Did she?" he said.

"She did."

"Well, Mike Callahan has got good eyes, then. That's all I got to say about it."

The woman came a step nearer. She was a small woman, with a face that had once been round and pink and had since been worn down, as a step is worn, by the feet of many days. Her hair was drawn back tightly, and the tightness gave to her brow a look of perpetual endurance. Her eyes now were very bright.

"Tom," she said, "what happened?"

He had intended to tell it grandly. He had intended to make of it a tale in which Haskell's foreman, a large man named Bracken with a voice like a falling wall, stood humbled and confused while he, Tom, delivered certain sentences which would be repeated in the mill for many weeks. But now, under the fixed gaze of his wife, the tale seemed to wither in his throat. He perceived that it would not survive the light of this lamp.

"I quit," he said.

There was a silence. The child below had stopped crying. The stove ticked. A drop of water ran down the windowpane, hesitated, and then went on, as if it had been given orders.

"You quit," said the woman.

"Yes."

"You was put out."

"I quit, I tell yeh!" He struck the table with the flat of his hand, and the cup with the broken handle jumped and rattled. "D'yeh think I'd stand there an' let a man like Bracken call me names in front of the whole gang? I ain't no dog. I told him what he was, an' I come away. That's what I done."

He looked up at her, expecting—he did not know what he expected. Perhaps some light of admiration. Perhaps, at the least, an acknowledgment that he had been grievously wronged. In his own mind the injury had become enormous. It had swelled during the walk home until it filled the whole sky of his thought. Bracken had said that he was slow. Bracken had said it loudly, with his hands upon his hips, and three men had laughed. The man had heard the laughter as a sort of thunder, and he could still hear it, rolling about in the back of his skull.

But the woman's face showed nothing of this. It had become very still, and she was looking past him at the wall.

"What did he call yeh?" she said at last.

"Never mind what he called me."

"I'd like to know what it was worth."

The man stared. The words had come out of her quietly, almost gently, but he felt them strike him as a stone strikes a window. He was outraged. It seemed to him that the universe had conspired to place him in a position where even his wife could look upon him with this cold eye of calculation. He had expected the world to be against him. He had braced himself for Bracken, for Haskell, for the whole black machinery of the mill. He had not expected to be ambushed in his own room.

"What's it worth!" he cried. "It's worth a man's pride, that's what it's worth! I s'pose you'd have me stand there an' grin like a monkey while he—"

"I'd have yeh think about the rent," said the woman.

He rose from the chair. His shadow leaped up upon the wall, a great black giant with flailing arms, and for an instant he was a little comforted by the size of it. He began to walk about the room. There was not much room to walk in. Three strides took him to the window and three strides brought him back to the stove, and so he went to and fro like a creature in a cage, while his shadow followed him, now swelling, now dwindling, upon the yellow wall.

"The rent," he said. "Always the rent. A man can't do nothin' in this world without somebody comes along an' says, 'What about the rent?' I'm sick of it. I'm sick of the whole business."

The woman sat down in the chair he had left. She folded her hands upon the table. She did not look at him as he walked. She looked at her hands.

"There's four dollars in the tin," she said, "an' it's due Saturday."

"I know when it's due."

"An' there's the grocer."

"I know about the grocer!"

He stopped by the window and looked out at the wet brick. It gleamed dully. Somewhere above, a gutter was pouring water in a thin, unending stream, and the sound of it was like a voice repeating the same small word over and over. He had a sudden and violent wish that he were anywhere else—on a ship, in the West, in a war. He thought of the men in the papers who went out to the gold country and came back with their pockets full. He thought of them with a kind of anguish. They had escaped. They had walked out of rooms like this one, out of cities like this one, and the great free distances had swallowed them up. He felt that he too had been made for such distances, and that it was only a cruel accident of the world that kept him here, pacing between a stove and a window.

"Jim Reardon's cousin," he said, without turning, "says they're takin' on men at Pittsburg. Good wages. Better'n Haskell's."

"Jim Reardon's cousin," said the woman, "says a good many things."

"He knows what he's talkin' about."

"Did he give yeh the fare?"

The man wheeled about. "There's the four dollars," he said.

He had not meant to say it. The words had come out of some dark place in him, and once they were spoken they hung in the air of the little room like smoke. The woman lifted her head slowly. Her face had gone white, so that the two spots of red which the stove had painted on her cheeks stood out upon it like marks of fever. She looked at him for a long time. He found that he could not meet her eyes. He looked instead at the stove, and the red eye of the stove looked back at him, steady and contemptuous.

"That's the rent money," she said.

"I'd send it back. I'd send back twice that. Inside a month."

"An' where'd I live, inside a month?"

"You could go to your mother's."

The woman laughed. It was a short laugh, without any mirth in it, and it frightened him more than any cry would have done. "My mother's," she said. "My mother's got six in two rooms an' a man that drinks. You've seen it. You've been there. You said yourself it was like a rat's nest."

"Well, it'd only be a little while—"

"You said it was like a rat's nest, Tom."

He was silent. He had, indeed, said it. He remembered the occasion. It had been a Sunday, and he had worn his good collar, and he had looked about him at the crowded, steaming kitchen of her mother's place with the lofty disdain of a man who rents his own room and owes nothing to anybody. He had felt, that day, enormously superior. Now the memory came back to him and sat down beside him, grinning.

The woman rose and went to the shelf above the stove. She took down the tin. It was a small tin that had once held tea, and it had a picture upon it of a Chinaman in a blue coat standing beneath a pink tree. She held it in both hands against her breast, and she stood so, facing him, as a soldier might stand before a gate.

"This here," she said, "is four dollars an' eleven cents. I put the eleven cents in myself. I took it out of the egg money. I went without the eggs."

"I never asked yeh to go without no eggs."

"No," she said. "Yeh never asked."

He felt a great wave of self-pity rise in him. It came up from his boots and filled him to the eyes. It seemed to him a terrible thing that a man should be thus driven into a corner by circumstance. He had done nothing, he told himself, but defend his honor as any man would. And for this he was to be punished—he was to be made to stand in a small room and be looked at by a small woman holding a tea tin, as if he were a thief. He thought that if anyone could see into his heart they would perceive that he was, at bottom, a fine fellow, generous and brave, who had been crushed by a world too mean to understand him. He wished that she could see into his heart. He was almost certain that if she could, she would put down the tin and weep and ask his pardon.

"Mary," he said, and his voice shook a little, in a way that he rather admired, "yeh don't understand. A man's got to be a man. He can't be lettin' people walk on him. Yeh wouldn't want a husband that let people walk on him."

"I'd want a husband," said the woman, "that come home Saturday with his pay."

He flung out his arms. His shadow flung out its arms upon the wall, vast and despairing. "There it is!" he cried. "Money! That's all a man is to a woman—so much money of a Saturday! I might as well be a horse. I might as well be a mule in a mine. Yeh don't care nothin' about me. Yeh care about the rent an' the grocer an' your blamed eggs!"

The woman did not answer this. She stood with the tin held against her, and he saw that her lips were pressed together very hard, and that her chin was trembling. The trembling of her chin angered him strangely. It seemed to him an unfair weapon. He felt that she was using it against him on purpose, as a general might bring up a hidden battery.

"Don't go to cryin'," he said harshly.

"I ain't cryin'."

"Yeh are."

"I ain't!"

She turned her back to him and set the tin upon the shelf again, and stood with her hands upon the shelf and her head bowed. Her shoulders were very narrow. He looked at them. The apron strings were tied in a small, neat bow at the back of her waist, and for some reason he could not take his eyes from this bow. It seemed to him a pitiful thing. He did not know why. It was only a bow of cotton string, a little frayed at the ends, and yet it struck at him somewhere beneath the ribs.

The room was very quiet. The gutter outside went on with its small, monotonous word. Below, a door banged, and a man's voice was raised in a sudden roar of profanity, and then a woman's voice answered, shrill as a fife. The voices rose and fell. They wrangled up through the floor like two cats in a cellar. The man listened to them. He had heard them many times before, upon many nights, and he had always lain in bed and laughed at them with a fine contempt. "Callahans goin' at it again," he would say, and turn over, and sleep. Now, for the first time, it seemed to him that the voices were not so very far away. It seemed to him that the floor between was thin.

He sat down again in the chair. He took up the fork and pushed one of the potatoes about the plate. It was cold. A skin had formed upon it. He put the fork down.

"Bracken," he said, after a while, to the table, "said I was slow."

The woman did not turn.

"He said it before Dolan an' them. He said I was the slowest man on the floor. He said he'd seen better work out of a cripple." He paused. The words, now that he said them aloud in this small room, sounded strangely little. In the mill they had been great and terrible, like the roaring of the furnaces. Here they were only words, and rather foolish ones. "An' they laughed," he said.

The woman's hands moved upon the shelf. She said nothing.

"I wasn't slow," said the man. "I was as quick as any of 'em." He considered this. A small, honest voice somewhere within him observed that he had, perhaps, been somewhat slow that day, and the day before, owing to a pain in his back and a certain disinclination to labor. He silenced this voice with indignation. "I was as quick as any of 'em," he repeated loudly.

"I know yeh was," said the woman.

He looked up, startled. She had turned around. Her face was wet, but she was not crying now. She was looking at him with an expression he could not read. It was not admiration. It was not anger. It was something older and wearier than either, and it made him uneasy, as a man is uneasy who finds that he has been seen through a window when he thought himself alone.

"Yeh'll go back in the mornin'," she said.

"I won't."

"Yeh'll go to Haskell himself. Not Bracken. Haskell. An' yeh'll say yeh lost your temper an' yeh're sorry for it."

The man rose halfway from his chair. "I'll see him in—" He stopped. "I won't do it. I won't crawl."

"Yeh'll do it," said the woman, "because it's Thursday."

There was something in the simplicity of this that defeated him utterly. He sat down again. He looked at the stove. The red eye glowered at him through the crack in the door. It seemed to him that it had been watching the whole affair with a sardonic satisfaction, as if it had known from the beginning how it would end.

He thought of Pittsburg. He thought of the great free distances and the men with their pockets full of gold. They receded from him now, swiftly, like the lights of a train going away in the night, and he watched them go with a dull pain. He thought of Haskell's office, with its brass rail and its smell of ink and cigars, and of himself standing before the rail with his cap in his hands. He thought of Bracken's face when he came back upon the floor. He thought of Dolan grinning. The vision was intolerable. He shut his eyes against it, but it remained, painted upon the inside of his lids.

"They'll laugh," he said.

"Let 'em."

"It's easy for you to say. You don't have to hear 'em."

The woman came and stood beside him. She did not touch him. She stood with her hands folded under her apron and looked down at the top of his head, and he felt her looking, and he hated it, and he did not want her to go away.

"Tom," she said, "I hear plenty."

He did not answer. He sat with his elbows upon the table and his chin in his hands, and he stared at the cold potatoes. He felt that he was a martyr. He felt that he was being led out to some public place to be made a show of, and that the whole world would gather to watch, and that no one in all that crowd would understand the greatness of his sacrifice. He composed, silently, several speeches in which he described his sufferings to some sympathetic listener. In these speeches he was very noble and the woman was very hard. But even as he composed them they grew thin and unconvincing, and presently he let them go.

The woman went back to the stove. She opened the door, and the red light leaped out and painted her face and her arms and the front of her apron, so that for a moment she seemed to be standing in a fire. She put a stick of wood upon the coals. Then she shut the door, and the light went back into its iron cave, and the room was yellow again.

"I'll warm them potatoes," she said.

"I ain't hungry."

"Yeh'll be hungry in the mornin'."

She took the plate from before him. He let her take it. He watched her as she moved about the small space, scraping the potatoes into the pan, setting the pan upon the stove. Her movements were quick and certain. They seemed to him to belong to some world of plain, small, necessary things in which he had no part—a world of tins and pans and eleven cents—and he felt, watching her, at once very lofty and very lost.

Below, the Callahans had ceased their wrangling. The gutter outside continued. The lamp burned with a small, steady hiss, and the round pale shape upon the ceiling no longer trembled, for no one in the room was moving very much now.

After a time the potatoes began to sizzle in the pan. The smell of them rose and filled the room, and the man, to his own vast disgust, found that he was hungry after all.
