The youth felt, however, that his problem was in no wise lifted from him. There was, on the contrary, an irritating prolongation. The tale had created in him a great concern for himself. Now, with the newborn question in his mind, he was compelled to sink back into his old place as part of a blue demonstration. For days he made ceaseless calculations, but they were all wondrously unsatisfactory. He found that he could establish nothing. He finally concluded that the only way to prove himself was to go into the blaze, and then figuratively to watch his legs to discover their merits and faults. He reluctantly admitted that he could not sit still and with a mental slate and pencil derive an answer. To gain it, he must have blaze, blood, and danger, even as a chemist requires this, that, and the other. So he fretted for an opportunity. Meanwhile, he continually tried to measure himself by his comrades. The tall soldier, for one, gave him some assurance. This man’s serene unconcern dealt him a measure of confidence, for he had known him since childhood, and from his intimate knowledge he did not see how he could be capable of anything that was beyond him, the youth. Still, he thought that his comrade might be mistaken about himself. Or, on the other hand, he might be a man heretofore doomed to peace and obscurity, but, in reality, made to shine in war. The youth would have liked to have discovered another who suspected himself. A sympathetic comparison of mental notes would have been a joy to him. He occasionally tried to fathom a comrade with seductive sentences. He looked about to find men in the proper mood. All attempts failed to bring forth any statement which looked in any way like a confession to those doubts which he privately acknowledged in himself. He was afraid to make an open declaration of his concern, because he dreaded to place some unscrupulous confidant upon the high plane of the unconfessed from which elevation he could be derided. In regard to his companions his mind wavered between two opinions, according to his mood. Sometimes he inclined to believing them all heroes. In fact, he usually admired in secret the superior development of the higher qualities in others. He could conceive of men going very insignificantly about the world bearing a load of courage unseen, and although he had known many of his comrades through boyhood, he began to fear that his judgment of them had been blind. Then, in other moments, he flouted these theories, and assured him that his fellows were all privately wondering and quaking. His emotions made him feel strange in the presence of men who talked excitedly of a prospective battle as of a drama they were about to witness, with nothing but eagerness and curiosity apparent in their faces. It was often that he suspected them to be liars. He did not pass such thoughts without severe condemnation of himself. He dinned reproaches at times. He was convicted by himself of many shameful crimes against the gods of traditions. In his great anxiety his heart was continually clamoring at what he considered the intolerable slowness of the generals. They seemed content to perch tranquilly on the river bank, and leave him bowed down by the weight of a great problem. He wanted it settled forthwith. He could not long bear such a load, he said. Sometimes his anger at the commanders reached an acute stage, and he grumbled about the camp like a veteran. One morning, however, he found himself in the ranks of his prepared regiment. The men were whispering speculations and recounting the old rumors. In the gloom before the break of the day their uniforms glowed a deep purple hue. From across the river the red eyes were still peering. In the eastern sky there was a yellow patch like a rug laid for the feet of the coming sun; and against it, black and patternlike, loomed the gigantic figure of the colonel on a gigantic horse. From off in the darkness came the trampling of feet. The youth could occasionally see dark shadows that moved like monsters. The regiment stood at rest for what seemed a long time. The youth grew impatient. It was unendurable the way these affairs were managed. He wondered how long they were to be kept waiting. As he looked all about him and pondered upon the mystic gloom, he began to believe that at any moment the ominous distance might be aflare, and the rolling crashes of an engagement come to his ears. Staring once at the red eyes across the river, he conceived them to be growing larger, as the orbs of a row of dragons advancing. He turned toward the colonel and saw him lift his gigantic arm and calmly stroke his mustache. At last he heard from along the road at the foot of the hill the clatter of a horse’s galloping hoofs. It must be the coming of orders. He bent forward, scarce breathing. The exciting clickety-click, as it grew louder and louder, seemed to be beating upon his soul. Presently a horseman with jangling equipment drew rein before the colonel of the regiment. The two held a short, sharp-worded conversation. The men in the foremost ranks craned their necks. As the horseman wheeled his animal and galloped away he turned to shout over his shoulder, “Don’t forget that box of cigars!” The colonel mumbled in reply. The youth wondered what a box of cigars had to do with war. A moment later the regiment went swinging off into the darkness. It was now like one of those moving monsters wending with many feet. The air was heavy, and cold with dew. A mass of wet grass, marched upon, rustled like silk. There was an occasional flash and glimmer of steel from the backs of all these huge crawling reptiles. From the road came creakings and grumblings as some surly guns were dragged away. The men stumbled along still muttering speculations. There was a subdued debate. Once a man fell down, and as he reached for his rifle a comrade, unseeing, trod upon his hand. He of the injured fingers swore bitterly, and aloud. A low, tittering laugh went among his fellows. Presently they passed into a roadway and marched forward with easy strides. A dark regiment moved before them, and from behind also came the tinkle of equipments on the bodies of marching men. The rushing yellow of the developing day went on behind their backs. When the sunrays at last struck full and mellowingly upon the earth, the youth saw that the landscape was streaked with two long, thin, black columns which disappeared on the brow of a hill in front and rearward vanished in a wood. They were like two serpents crawling from the cavern of the night. The river was not in view. The tall soldier burst into praises of what he thought to be his powers of perception. Some of the tall one’s companions cried with emphasis that they, too, had evolved the same thing, and they congratulated themselves upon it. But there were others who said that the tall one’s plan was not the true one at all. They persisted with other theories. There was a vigorous discussion. The youth took no part in them. As he walked along in careless line he was engaged with his own eternal debate. He could not hinder himself from dwelling upon it. He was despondent and sullen, and threw shifting glances about him. He looked ahead, often expecting to hear from the advance the rattle of firing. But the long serpents crawled slowly from hill to hill without bluster of smoke. A dun-colored cloud of dust floated away to the right. The sky overhead was of a fairy blue. The youth studied the faces of his companions, ever on the watch to detect kindred emotions. He suffered disappointment. Some ardor of the air which was causing the veteran commands to move with glee—almost with song—had infected the new regiment. The men began to speak of victory as of a thing they knew. Also, the tall soldier received his vindication. They were certainly going to come around in behind the enemy. They expressed commiseration for that part of the army which had been left upon the river bank, felicitating themselves upon being a part of a blasting host. The youth, considering himself as separated from the others, was saddened by the blithe and merry speeches that went from rank to rank. The company wags all made their best endeavors. The regiment tramped to the tune of laughter. The blatant soldier often convulsed whole files by his biting sarcasms aimed at the tall one. And it was not long before all the men seemed to forget their mission. Whole brigades grinned in unison, and regiments laughed. A rather fat soldier attempted to pilfer a horse from a dooryard. He planned to load his knapsack upon it. He was escaping with his prize when a young girl rushed from the house and grabbed the animal’s mane. There followed a wrangle. The young girl, with pink cheeks and shining eyes, stood like a dauntless statue. The observant regiment, standing at rest in the roadway, whooped at once, and entered whole-souled upon the side of the maiden. The men became so engrossed in this affair that they entirely ceased to remember their own large war. They jeered the piratical private, and called attention to various defects in his personal appearance; and they were wildly enthusiastic in support of the young girl. To her, from some distance, came bold advice. “Hit him with a stick.” There were crows and catcalls showered upon him when he retreated without the horse. The regiment rejoiced at his downfall. Loud and vociferous congratulations were showered upon the maiden, who stood panting and regarding the troops with defiance. At nightfall the column broke into regimental pieces, and the fragments went into the fields to camp. Tents sprang up like strange plants. Camp fires, like red, peculiar blossoms, dotted the night. The youth kept from intercourse with his companions as much as circumstances would allow him. In the evening he wandered a few paces into the gloom. From this little distance the many fires, with the black forms of men passing to and fro before the crimson rays, made weird and satanic effects. He lay down in the grass. The blades pressed tenderly against his cheek. The moon had been lighted and was hung in a treetop. The liquid stillness of the night enveloping him made him feel vast pity for himself. There was a caress in the soft winds; and the whole mood of the darkness, he thought, was one of sympathy for himself in his distress. He wished, without reserve, that he was at home again making the endless rounds from the house to the barn, from the barn to the fields, from the fields to the barn, from the barn to the house. He remembered he had so often cursed the brindle cow and her mates, and had sometimes flung milking stools. But, from his present point of view, there was a halo of happiness about each of their heads, and he would have sacrificed all the brass buttons on the continent to have been enabled to return to them. He told himself that he was not formed for a soldier. And he mused seriously upon the radical differences between himself and those men who were dodging implike around the fires. As he mused thus he heard the rustle of grass, and, upon turning his head, discovered the loud soldier. He called out, “Oh, Wilson!” The latter approached and looked down. “Why, hello, Henry; is it you? What are you doing here?”

“Oh, thinking,” said the youth. The other sat down and carefully lighted his pipe. “You’re getting blue my boy. You’re looking thundering peek-ed. What the dickens is wrong with you?”

“Oh, nothing,” said the youth. The loud soldier launched then into the subject of the anticipated fight. “Oh, we’ve got ’em now!” As he spoke his boyish face was wreathed in a gleeful smile, and his voice had an exultant ring. “We’ve got ’em now. At last, by the eternal thunders, we’ll lick ’em good!”

“If the truth was known,” he added, more soberly, “they’ve licked us about every clip up to now; but this time—this time—we’ll lick ’em good!”

“I thought you was objecting to this march a little while ago,” said the youth coldly.

“Oh, it wasn’t that,” explained the other. “I don’t mind marching, if there’s going to be fighting at the end of it. What I hate is this getting moved here and moved there, with no good coming of it, as far as I can see, excepting sore feet and damned short rations.”

“Well, Jim Conklin says we’ll get plenty of fighting this time.”

“He’s right for once, I guess, though I can’t see how it come. This time we’re in for a big battle, and we’ve got the best end of it, certain sure. Gee rod! how we will thump ’em!” He arose and began to pace to and fro excitedly. The thrill of his enthusiasm made him walk with an elastic step. He was sprightly, vigorous, fiery in his belief in success. He looked into the future with clear proud eye, and he swore with the air of an old soldier. The youth watched him for a moment in silence. When he finally spoke his voice was as bitter as dregs. “Oh, you’re going to do great things, I s’pose!” The loud soldier blew a thoughtful cloud of smoke from his pipe. “Oh, I don’t know,” he remarked with dignity; “I don’t know. I s’pose I’ll do as well as the rest. I’m going to try like thunder.” He evidently complimented himself upon the modesty of this statement.

“How do you know you won’t run when the time comes?” asked the youth.

“Run?” said the loud one; “run?—of course not!” He laughed.

“Well,” continued the youth, “lots of good-a-’nough men have thought they was going to do great things before the fight, but when the time come they skedaddled.”

“Oh, that’s all true, I s’pose,” replied the other; “but I’m not going to skedaddle. The man that bets on my running will lose his money, that’s all.” He nodded confidently.

“Oh, shucks!” said the youth. “You ain’t the bravest man in the world, are you?”

The train drew up to the little station with a long, shuddering sigh, as if it had come a great distance to deliver a grievance. A man in a brakeman's cap swung down and stood upon the platform with an air of having been personally insulted by the country. Behind him, carefully, descended a young man in a derby hat.

The young man in the derby had been rehearsing this descent for forty miles. He had arranged in his mind the precise angle of his chin, the manner in which his valise should hang from his hand, and the faint, tolerant smile with which he would regard the village. He had worn the hat for eleven months in the city, where it was one hat among ten thousand. Here, he perceived at once, it was the only hat of its kind in the county. It sat upon his head like a crown. He felt that the very cows in the field beyond the depot paused in their cud to observe it.

The platform was empty save for a dog of no particular color that lay with its nose upon its paws and regarded the derby with profound suspicion. Beyond, in the road, stood a wagon. A bony horse drooped in the shafts. Upon the seat sat a large young man in a brown coat, with his elbows on his knees and the reins slack in his hands. He was looking at the train with the patient vacancy of one who has waited for many trains.

The young man in the derby hesitated. He had expected a little crowd, or at least a hand waving. He had pictured his cousin running forward. Instead, the figure on the wagon seat merely straightened slowly, as a tree might straighten after a wind, and then climbed down.

"Hello, George," said the large young man.

"Why, hello, Pete."

They shook hands. It was a brief and gingerly business. Each seemed to fear that the other might hold on too long. The cousin's hand was immense and hard, and the city man felt his own fingers, which had for a year known nothing more violent than a pen and a ledger, crumple within it like paper. He withdrew them hastily and placed them in his pocket.

"Train's late," observed the cousin.

"Yes," said George. "They always are, out here. In the city they run them to the minute."

He was immediately sorry he had said it, and then immediately glad. The cousin made no reply. He took the valise and swung it into the back of the wagon, where it fell among some sacks with a dull sound, like a dignitary tumbled into a ditch. George winced. The valise had cost him two dollars and a half.

They climbed to the seat. The horse, after a period of deliberation, consented to move. The wagon lurched forward and began to creak along the road with a sound like an old man complaining of his joints.

The country lay about them in the long light of the afternoon. The fields were of a fat green, and the fences ran across them in crooked gray lines like the writing of a child. Far off, a wood stood dark and still, and above it a single hawk turned and turned upon the air as if it were winding up some invisible thread. The road was of a red clay, and the wheels cut into it and lifted it in wet ribbons.

George sat very erect. He was conscious of his collar, which was high and stiff and new. He was conscious of his cuffs. He resolved to say nothing of the city unless asked. He would be modest. He would let these things speak for themselves. He arranged his face into an expression of easy worldliness and waited to be asked.

The cousin said nothing. He clucked once to the horse. The horse ignored him.

A long silence fell upon them. It grew, and spread, and filled the wagon like water filling a trough. George felt it rise to his chin. He began to suspect that his cousin was regarding him with contempt. Then he began to suspect that his cousin was not regarding him at all, which was worse.

"Well," he said at last, "how's everything?"

"Oh, about the same."

"Crops good?"

"Fair. Corn's late. Too much rain in May."

"Is that so," said George. He did not know whether corn ought to be early or late. He had known once. He had hoed it, as a boy, with this same cousin, in this same red earth, and had cursed it with the vivid and inventive profanity of the very young. But the city had washed this knowledge from him, and he found that he could not now recall whether a wet May was a calamity or a blessing. He nodded gravely, as one who receives news of a distant war.

"How's the city?" asked the cousin.

George had been waiting for this. He had prepared, over many evenings in his narrow room above the cobbler's, a number of phrases. Now, however, they would not come in the proper order. They rushed upon him all together, like a herd at a gate.

"Oh, fine," he said. "It's—well, it's fine. It's big, Pete. You wouldn't believe it. There's more people on one street than in this whole county. And the noise! At first I couldn't sleep for it. Now I couldn't sleep without it."

He was pleased with this last sentence. It seemed to him to have the ring of a man who has passed through fire.

"That so," said the cousin.

"I'm with Hopper and Lyle now. Dry goods. It's one of the biggest houses on Grand Street."

"What do you do?"

George paused. In truth he copied invoices in a back room lit by a single gas jet that sang all day a thin, mean song. He sat upon a high stool beside an old man with a cough, who had copied invoices for twenty-two years and who would, George sometimes feared in the night, copy them for twenty-two more and then die upon the stool, still coughing. But the question had come so plainly, without any guile, that it threw him into confusion.

"Oh, I'm in the office," he said. "Accounts, mostly. They think pretty well of me."

He looked sidelong at his cousin to see how this was received. The large young man was watching the horse's ears. His face, which the sun had burned to the color of a saddle, showed nothing at all. George felt as though he had thrown a stone into a deep well and heard no splash.

The road dipped down toward a creek. A little wooden bridge spanned it, gray and swaybacked, and beneath it the water ran brown and quick over the stones. George looked down as they crossed, and something turned over in his breast.

"That's the old place," he said. "Where we used to swim."

"Yes."

"Remember when you held me under? I thought I was going to drown. I came up yelling murder."

"I remember," said the cousin. For the first time something moved in his face. It was not quite a smile; it was the ghost of a smile, a thing that came and went like a fish rising in dark water. "You hit me with a rock after. Right here." He touched a place above his eye.

"I did not!"

"You did. Bled like a stuck pig. Aunt Mattie thought you'd killed me."

George was silent. He had no recollection of the rock. He remembered only the water closing over him, green and roaring, and the long terror of it, and his own wild shrieking when he came up. In his memory he had been entirely the victim. He had told the story twice in the city, to young men at the boarding house, and in each telling his cousin had grown larger and more brutal, and he himself smaller and more piteous. Now it appeared there had been a rock. He felt vaguely cheated, as if a man had come forward to dispute his title to a piece of land.

"Well," he said, "I guess I had cause."

"I guess you did," said the cousin peaceably.

This peaceableness annoyed George more than any contradiction. He had wished to argue. He had wished, in some obscure way, to win something. But the large young man merely sat there, slack upon the seat, as immovable as the hills, and George's small sallies broke against him and fell back.

They climbed out of the creek bottom. The sun was lowering now, and it laid long yellow bars across the road, and the shadows of the fence posts reached out like the fingers of a hand. A meadowlark flung up from the grass and went whistling away over the field. In a pasture a group of cattle stood in a row, all facing one way, solemn as deacons.

"I got married," said the cousin suddenly.

George turned on the seat. "You what?"

"Got married. Last fall. Ma wrote you, I think."

"She never," said George. Then he paused. There had been a letter, in the winter, which he had put aside to read later and had never read, because it had come in a week when he was low and had not wished to be reminded of home. He felt his ears grow hot. "Well—well, I'll be switched. Who to?"

"Ellen Dodd."

"Ellen Dodd!"

He had a sudden picture of a thin girl with yellow braids who had sat in the front row at the schoolhouse and recited "The Burial of Sir John Moore" in a voice like a cricket. He had once put a toad in her dinner pail. She had wept, and he had been whipped, and he had considered it, on the whole, a fair exchange.

"Ellen Dodd," he said again, wonderingly.

"She's filled out some," said the cousin, as if in apology.

George sat back. The news had struck him in an odd place. He could not have said why. His cousin was married; his cousin had a wife and a house and a bed of his own, and a table at which he was master. And he, George, with his derby and his high collar, went home at night to a room nine feet by seven, where a woman named Mrs. Gorman brought him a hard egg in the mornings and regarded him as a species of lodger insect. He saw abruptly that his cousin had passed him upon some road that he had not known they were traveling. The large young man had gone around a bend and out of sight, and George was left standing in the dust with his hat.

He was seized with a desire to retrieve his position.

"There's a girl in the city," he began.

"That so?"

"Yes. A fine girl. Works in a millinery shop. We go walking Sundays, in the park. There's a band on Sundays."

This was very nearly true. There was a girl in a millinery shop, and there was a band on Sundays, and George had walked in the park. It was merely that he had not yet, in eleven months, found the occasion to walk with the girl. He had passed the shop window many times. Once she had looked up. He had carried that glance about with him for a week like a coin in his pocket, taking it out to look at it.

"What's her name?" asked the cousin.

"Her name," said George, "is Miss Kitty Flynn."

He had read the name on a parcel. He felt it was a fine name. It seemed to him to have a city swing to it, a kind of jaunty ring, like the bell on a streetcar. He watched his cousin's face for envy.

"Irish?" said the cousin.

"Well—yes."

"Huh," said the cousin, and fell to studying the horse again.

George could not tell what this "huh" contained. It might have been admiration. It might have been disapproval. It might have been nothing more than the noise a man makes when he has run out of other noises. He turned it over and over in his mind for a mile and could make nothing of it. It lay in him like a stone in a shoe.

At a place where the road bent sharply around a wood, the wagon came abruptly to a halt. The horse had stopped. It stood with its head down and its feet planted, in the attitude of a creature that has reached a philosophical conclusion.

"What's the matter with him?"

"He does this," said the cousin. He climbed down without haste. "Wheel's in the soft. You'll have to get down and push, George, or we'll be here till Christmas."

George looked down. The road at this place had turned to a dark, glistening mire. It shone wetly in the yellow light. He looked at his shoes. They were new shoes, with narrow toes, and they had been blacked that morning by a boy at the depot in the city who had whistled the while and called him "Cap." He had paid the boy a nickel and felt, for a moment, like a millionaire.

"Can't you just—" he began.

"Nope," said the cousin. He was already at the back of the wagon, his great shoulders set against the boards.

George climbed down. The mud received his feet with a soft and greedy sound, like a mouth. It came up over the narrow toes and over the laces and stopped somewhere about the ankle. He stood a moment in silent horror. Then he set his shoulder beside his cousin's and pushed.

The wagon did not move. The horse turned its head and regarded them with mild interest.

"Hup!" roared the cousin suddenly, in a voice that shook the wood. The horse, startled out of its philosophy, lunged forward. The wagon gave a heave and a groan and rolled free. George, who had been pushing with all his strength against a thing that was no longer there, pitched forward upon his hands into the mire.

He knelt there. The mud was cool and smelled of leaves. His derby had remained upon his head by a miracle, but it was knocked over one eye, and he regarded the world through a single aperture, like a man looking out of a cave.

He heard a sound above him. He looked up. The large young man was standing over him, and his shoulders were shaking, and his face, which had been as blank all afternoon as a barn wall, was split from ear to ear.

For a moment George was filled with a white rage. He thought of rocks. He thought of the creek. He thought of saying some cold and crushing thing in the manner of the city, a thing that would wither this great grinning oaf where he stood. And then, unaccountably, he felt his own face begin to give way. Something rose in him from a great depth, from beneath the collar and the cuffs and the eleven months of the singing gas jet, and broke out of him in a loud, foolish bray. He sat back in the mud and laughed until his sides hurt. The cousin laughed with him, roaring, slapping his knee. The horse waited. The hawk, very high, went on winding its thread.

When at last they climbed again upon the seat, the silence that came between them was of a different stuff. It no longer rose like water. It lay easily about them, like an old coat.

"Your shoes are done for," observed the cousin.

"I s'pose they are."

"I got a pair you can wear. They'll be big on you."

"I s'pose they will."

The cousin chuckled again, low in his throat. "You looked like a hog in a wallow, George. A hog in a hat."

"Shut up," said George, without any heat at all.

The farmhouse came into view as the sun touched the hills. It was smaller than George remembered. Everything was smaller. The barn, which had once loomed over his childhood like a cathedral, was a plain gray building with a sag in its ridgepole. The well sweep stood up against the sky like a thin arm raised in warning. A light was burning in the kitchen window, and against it moved a figure.

The figure came out upon the porch as the wagon drew up. It was a young woman, broad and fair, with her sleeves rolled to the elbow and a dish cloth in her hand. She looked at George, and at the mud upon him, and at the derby, and her eyes widened.

"Pete Carver," she said, "what have you done to him?"

"Nothing," said the cousin. "He done it to himself."

George climbed down. He took off the derby. He had intended, in this moment, to bow a little, after a manner he had observed in a young man who sold gloves at Hopper and Lyle. Instead he stood holding the hat in his muddy hands, with his muddy knees, and his ears grew hot again, and he could think of nothing whatever to say.

"Hello, Ellen," he said finally.

"Hello, George," said she. And then, after a moment, with the faintest smile, "Still got the toad?"

He gaped at her. Behind him he heard his cousin begin again to laugh.

They ate supper at the kitchen table under a lamp that hissed faintly and threw a round yellow pool upon the cloth. There were potatoes and side meat and biscuits and a pie of dried apples. George ate enormously. He had not eaten so in eleven months. He found, to his astonishment, that he did not wish to speak of the city at all. When Ellen asked him of it he said that it was large, and noisy, and that the streetcars went very fast, and then he could think of nothing else and asked for more pie.

Afterward the two cousins sat upon the back step in the dark. The cousin smoked a pipe. George, who had learned in the city to smoke cigarettes, did not take one out. The night came down over the fields soft and enormous. The frogs in the creek bottom had begun their chorus, a high, shrill, endless song, as of a thousand small creatures all protesting at once. Fireflies drifted above the grass, kindling and going out, kindling and going out, like the thoughts of a sleepy man.

"George," said the cousin presently.

"Yes."

"You like it there? Truly?"

George was silent. He looked out at the dark. He thought of the back room and the old man with the cough. He thought of the girl in the millinery window, who did not know his name. He thought of Mrs. Gorman's egg. And he thought of the noise, the great roaring, ceaseless noise of the city, which he had said he could not now sleep without, and he wondered suddenly whether it had been true.

He opened his mouth to tell his cousin all of it. It rose up in him, the whole tale, and stood ready at his lips.

"Sure," he said. "Sure, I like it fine. It's the place for a man to get on."

"I s'pose so," said the cousin.

He drew upon his pipe, and the little coal glowed red and faded. He did not ask anything further. Perhaps he knew. Perhaps he did not care to know. Perhaps, George thought later, lying awake in the narrow spare bed under the eaves, with the frogs still shrilling and his ruined shoes standing in the corner like two drowned animals, his cousin had his own tale standing ready at his lips, and had, in the same moment, swallowed it.

The moon came up late, lopsided and orange, and hung above the barn. It looked down upon the farm with an expression of vast and weary indulgence, as upon a thing it had seen many times before and expected to see again.

“No, I ain’t,” exclaimed the loud soldier indignantly; “and I didn’t say I was the bravest man in the world, neither. I said I was going to do my share of fighting—that’s what I said. And I am, too. The little boy came up the road at a slow pace. He had been running for some time, but as the white house loomed before him his legs had grown suddenly thoughtful, and they now carried him with the deliberation of an old man going to a funeral. He kept one hand pressed against the seat of his trousers. Under this hand there was a rent, an enormous rent, a rent that seemed to him to let in all the winds of the world.

The sun was going down behind the Trescotts' barn. It hung there, a great orange ball, and it peered at him over the ridgepole with an air of having seen everything. The maples along the road were full of a yellow light. In the grass a cricket made a little dry noise, like a clock that has been wound too tight.

He had been in the Fanhalls' orchard. This was a crime in itself, for old Mrs. Fanhall had a voice like a rusty pump-handle, and she had said many times at the gate that she would have the law on the next boy. He had gone over the fence in company with Jimmie Trescott and the two Margate boys, and for a space of time they had been bandits. They had dealt out a great slaughter among the green apples. Then Mrs. Fanhall had come out upon the back porch and raised her pump-handle, and the bandit army had fled in four directions. The little boy had gone over the fence at its highest part, and a nail had reached out and taken hold of him. He had heard the sound of tearing. It had been the most terrible sound he had ever heard.

When he dropped into the road on the other side, his comrades had disappeared. Afar off he saw the back of the eldest Margate boy, going very fast toward the creek. No one had waited. He had felt then a great bitterness against the treachery of men.

Now, as he came near the gate, he began to make calculations. It might be that his mother was in the kitchen. If she were in the kitchen, he could go around by the woodshed and up the back stairs and change into his old pair, and the new ones could be put somewhere—in the bottom of the chest, perhaps, under the winter things—and it might be months before anyone thought of them. By that time the matter would have become ancient. Nobody would care about a pair of trousers that had been torn in some far-off and forgotten age.

But it might be that his father was home. He looked toward the barn. The buggy was there. The wheels were splashed with the mud of the river road, and the horse was standing in the yard with the harness yet upon him, eating at a tuft of grass with an air of philosophic calm. The little boy halted. He felt his heart go down within him like a stone dropped into a well.

He considered flight. He might go to the creek and join the eldest Margate boy. He might go and live among the willows, and eat fish, and never come home again; and then they would be sorry; then they would walk the roads at night with lanterns, calling his name. This picture gave him a moment's comfort. He saw his mother weeping, and his father standing with bowed head, and Mrs. Fanhall overcome with remorse. But it was growing dark, and the willows at night were full of noises. He remembered that he had had no supper.

He went in at the gate.

He crept along the side of the house with great caution. He was a scout in the enemy's country. Each window was an eye. The kitchen door stood open and a broad bar of yellow lamplight fell out upon the step, and across this bar, as he watched, passed the shadow of his mother, large and swift, carrying something. He waited until it had passed. Then he stole forward. He had his foot upon the step of the woodshed when a voice spoke from the dusk of the porch.

"Willie."

It was his father. The little boy stood perfectly still. It seemed to him that if he did not move, perhaps he might not be there; perhaps the voice would conclude that it had been mistaken and would go back into the house. But the voice spoke again.

"Willie. Come here."

He went. His feet moved over the boards of the porch as if they had been taken from him and given to someone else. In the gloom he could see the long figure of his father in the rocking-chair, and the red spark of his cigar, which glowed and faded, glowed and faded, like a slow, deliberate pulse. The little boy stood before it. He kept his hand behind him.

"Where have you been?"

"Oh, nowhere," said the little boy.

"Nowhere?"

"Just down the road."

The cigar glowed. There was a long silence. A moth came and beat itself against the lamp in the window, and the sound of its wings was the only thing in the world. The little boy felt that his father was looking at him, looking through him, looking into all the secret corners of his soul where the apples were and the fence and the nail. It was intolerable. He shifted his feet.

"Mrs. Fanhall was by here," said his father.

The little boy said nothing. There was nothing to say. Mrs. Fanhall had been by. This was a calamity of such dimensions that it took away his breath. He had not thought that she would come so far. He had pictured her as fixed forever upon her own back porch, a sort of dragon chained to its cave. Now it appeared that she could travel. She could come down the road in her black bonnet with the jet beads upon it, and she could open the gate, and she could sit in his own parlor and say things. He was filled with a great sense of injustice.

"She said there was some boys in her orchard this afternoon."

"I never," said the little boy.

The cigar glowed very bright.

"Turn around," said his father.

The little boy did not turn around. He stood with his hand clamped behind him, and his face grew hot, and he looked at the floor. He knew that the game was lost. Yet some stubborn creature within him refused to surrender the hand. It seemed to him that while the hand remained there, the rent did not altogether exist. It was a matter between himself and the hand.

His father rose from the rocking-chair. He was very tall. The little boy had always known that his father was tall, but now he was enormous; he went up into the shadows of the porch roof like a tree. He took hold of the little boy's shoulder, not roughly, and turned him about. The hand fell away. There was a pause.

"Well," said his father.

It was only one word, but it was the most dreadful word the little boy had ever heard. It had in it a world of meanings. It said that the trousers were new; that they had been bought at Stickney's store not two weeks gone; that they had cost a sum of money that was very great; that his mother had stood a whole morning at the ironing-board over them; that he had been told, and told again, and told yet a third time. All these things were in the word. The little boy felt them descend upon him one after another, like stones.

"Come into the house," said his father.

They went into the kitchen. His mother turned from the stove. She had a long spoon in her hand, and her face was red from the heat, and when she saw them her mouth went into a straight line. The little boy looked at her quickly, seeking some sign. In other campaigns she had been his ally. She had often stood between him and the great wrath. But now her eyes went to the trousers, and he saw in them a cold, hard light, and he knew that he was alone.

"Willie Bradley," she said. "Willie Bradley, look at you."

He did not need to look at himself. He knew too well what he would see.

His small sister was at the table, upon the high chair, with a bowl of bread and milk before her. She had been beating her spoon upon the board. Now she ceased. She gazed upon him with round, bright, interested eyes, as a spectator gazes upon a man being led to the gallows. The little boy hated her. He hated the bread and milk. He hated the spoon. He resolved that when he was grown he would go away to some far country and become a great man, and he would never send her anything.

"Sit down," said his father.

He sat down upon the wooden chair by the woodbox. His legs did not reach the floor, and they hung there, helpless and foolish. His father stood before him. His mother stood a little behind, holding the spoon. The lamp on the table threw their shadows up the wall, and the shadows were huge and black and bent at the ceiling, and they leaned over him like the shadows of giants. He looked at them and then he looked away.

"Now," said his father, "I want the truth."

The little boy considered. The truth was a vast and complicated thing. It had in it the Margate boys, and Jimmie Trescott, and the green apples, and the glory of the charge, and the shameful retreat, and the nail. He could not see how any of these could be laid out on a kitchen floor so that a grown man could understand them. Besides, there was the matter of Jimmie Trescott. To tell of Jimmie would be to betray a comrade, and he had a vague, shining idea that this was the worst thing a person could do—worse, even, than tearing trousers. It is true that Jimmie had run away. But the little boy felt that two crimes do not make a virtue.

"I was in the orchard," he said at last, in a small voice.

"Who else?"

"Nobody."

"Willie."

"Some fellers," he admitted.

"Which fellers?"

The little boy looked at the woodbox. A piece of bark was there, curled up like a little brown boat. He studied it with great attention.

"I ain't going to tell," he said.

There was a silence in the kitchen. His mother made a sound, a quick sound, as if she were about to speak; but she did not speak. The kettle on the stove began to mutter. His father looked at him a long time. The little boy could not see his father's face, for the lamp was behind it, and there was only a dark shape with the light making a ragged gold line around the edges of the hair. He waited for the thunder to fall. He had made his declaration, and now the heavens would open.

"All right," said his father slowly. "You needn't tell."

The little boy was astonished. He had braced himself for the blow, and the blow had not come, and he felt as a man feels who leans with all his strength upon a door that suddenly swings open. He looked up. He could not make anything of it.

"But you'll tell me this," continued his father. "Did Mrs. Fanhall say you could go in her orchard?"

"No, sir."

"Did she say you couldn't?"

"Yes, sir," said the little boy. "But she says it all the time. She says it to everybody. She says it to the Margates. She—"

He stopped. He had said "the Margates." It had slipped from him as a fish slips from the hand. He felt his face go scarlet. He looked at his father in an agony. But his father's dark shape did not move. It was as if it had not heard. Yet the little boy was certain that it had heard; that it had heard everything; that it had always heard everything, from the beginning of the world.

"It don't matter how many times she says it," said his father. "It's her orchard. It ain't yours. It ain't the Margates'. Those are her apples. She raised them. If a man came in here and took what's ours, what would you think of him?"

The little boy did not know what he would think. He tried to imagine a man coming into the kitchen and taking things. He saw a large, bearded person with a sack, putting the kettle and the lamp and the high chair into it. He saw the person taking his small sister. On the whole he did not think this would be so very bad. But he understood that he was not expected to say so.

"I'd think he was mean," he said.

"Well," said his father.

Again there was that word. The little boy felt it settle upon him. It was a heavy word, a word with a great deal of iron in it. He began to perceive that he was a thief. He had not known it before. In the orchard he had been a bandit, and a bandit is a gallant person who rides about on a black horse and is admired. But now the black horse had gone, and the gallant person had gone, and there remained only a small boy with green apples in his stomach and a hole in his trousers, sitting by a woodbox. The transformation was terrible. He had a sudden vision of himself in the county jail, behind bars, with a striped suit. His lip began to tremble. He set his teeth upon it, but it would not stop.

His mother came forward then. She put down the spoon on the table with a little click.

"And your new trousers," she said. "Your brand-new trousers that your father paid two dollars and a half for. Two dollars and a half, Willie! And I told you this morning. Didn't I tell you this morning? Didn't I stand in that very door and tell you?"

"Yes'm," said the little boy.

"And what did I say?"

"You said—you said don't go climbing in 'em."

"And what did you do?"

He was silent. The question did not appear to need an answer. It seemed to him a cruel thing to make a person say aloud what everybody already knew. He felt the tears coming up behind his eyes, and he fought them, for he believed that tears were a disgrace, and that Jimmie Trescott would never cry, and that the Margate boys would laugh themselves into fits if they could see him. Yet the tears came on, regardless of Jimmie Trescott. They gathered in great hot drops and swam before him so that the lamp became a blazing star with long golden spokes.

His small sister began to beat upon the board with her spoon. She seemed to consider that some festival was in progress.

"Hush, Annie," said his mother.

Annie did not hush. She beat with greater vigor. She crowed. Her face shone with joy. The little boy, through his tears, regarded her with a deep and silent fury. Here was he, at the bottom of the pit, and here was she, making merry upon the brink of it. It was the way of the world. He thought darkly that nobody cared what happened to him. He thought that if he were to die there, upon the wooden chair by the woodbox, they would only step over him and go on with supper.

His father took the spoon away from Annie. Annie considered this for a moment, and then she opened her mouth and let out a great wail. The kitchen was filled with it. His mother went to her, and lifted her, and walked up and down with her, saying, "There, there," and the shadows on the wall swayed and bowed like the shadows of trees in a gale.

In the midst of this the little boy sat alone. For a space he had been the center of the world, and now, it appeared, the world had turned away from him to attend to Annie. He was not sure whether he was glad of it. There was relief in it, certainly. But there was also a kind of insult. He felt that a crime as large as his ought not to be interrupted by a baby who had lost a spoon.

His father turned back to him. He bent down. For the first time the little boy could see his face, for the lamp now fell upon the side of it, and he saw that it was not the face of a giant, but only his father's face, with the lines at the corners of the eyes and the brown mustache with the grey hairs in it. It was a tired face. It did not look angry. It looked as if it had been a long way that day, over the river road, and had come home wanting its supper.

"Willie," said his father, "you're going to go over to Mrs. Fanhall's in the morning."

The little boy's heart stopped. He stared.

"You're going to go up to the door and knock, and when she comes you're going to tell her you were in her orchard and that you're sorry."

The little boy could not speak. The horror of it was too vast. To go up that path, between those rows of hollyhocks, to that door, with its brass knocker in the shape of a lion's head—to stand there, alone, while the door opened and Mrs. Fanhall came forth in her black bonnet with the jet beads—it was not to be thought of. He would rather go to the county jail. He would rather go to the willows by the creek and live on fish. He saw her face, with its long chin, bending over him; he heard the rusty pump-handle of her voice. He shivered.

"I can't," he whispered.

"Yes, you can."

"She'll—she'll—"

"She won't eat you," said his father. Something moved at the corner of his mustache. It might have been a smile, but it passed before the little boy could make certain of it. "And you'll take her a quarter out of your bank, for the apples."

This was a second blow, falling upon the first. The bank was an iron dog, and it sat upon the shelf over his bed, and inside it there were forty-five cents, which represented the hoarded fortune of a lifetime. He had been saving them for a jack-knife with two blades and a corkscrew. Now a quarter of it, more than half of it, was to go to Mrs. Fanhall, who did not need it, who had a whole orchard. He felt that the universe was arranged entirely against small boys.

But he said nothing. He looked at the woodbox. The little brown boat of bark lay there, upon its sea of chips, untroubled.

"Now go up and change," said his father, "and come down to supper."

The little boy got off the chair. He went toward the stairs. As he passed his mother she looked at him over Annie's head, and he saw that the cold light had gone out of her eyes. He did not understand where it had gone. He was still a thief, and his trousers were still torn, and Mrs. Fanhall was still waiting at the end of the night like a dragon at the end of a road; and yet his mother looked at him as she looked at him when he was sick with the croup. It was very confusing. He went up the stairs slowly, one at a time.

In his room it was nearly dark. Through the window he could see the last red streak of the sun lying along the top of the Fanhalls' woods, and above it one star, very small and white. He took off the trousers. He held them up and looked at the rent. It was not so large as he had thought. In the dark it was hardly to be seen at all. He was almost disappointed. He had carried it home like a mortal wound, and now it was only a hole in some cloth.

He put on his old pair. Then he went to the shelf and took down the iron dog and shook it. The pennies and the nickels inside made a sad little music. He sat on the edge of the bed with the dog upon his knees and thought about the morning.

Gradually a change came over his thoughts. He began to see himself going up the path between the hollyhocks. He saw himself lift the lion's head knocker, a small, lonely, but resolute figure. He saw Mrs. Fanhall open the door. He saw himself hold out the quarter and speak, in a clear and manly voice, and he saw her face soften with astonishment and respect. Perhaps she would give him a cooky. Perhaps she would tell everybody in the village that Willie Bradley was the only honest boy in the whole lot of them. He thought of Jimmie Trescott, who had run away, and of the Margate boys, who had run away, and he felt a slow, warm glow begin to spread within him. They had fled. He alone would face the dragon. It was clear to him now that he was a person of remarkable courage, and that it had only wanted a proper occasion to reveal it.

From below came the voice of his mother calling him to supper, and the smell of fried potatoes rose up the stairwell like an incense. He set the iron dog carefully upon the shelf. He went down to the kitchen with his chin held high, and he ate three helpings, and when Annie threw her bread and milk upon the floor, he regarded her with the large, mild tolerance of a man who has been through great things.

"Hully gee! Dey makes me tired," he said. "Mos' e'ry day some farmer comes in an' tries teh run deh shop. See? But dey gits t'rowed right out! I jolt dem right out in deh street before dey knows where dey is! See?"

"Sure," said Jimmie.

'Git deh hell outa here an' don' make no trouble'; like dat. 'Git deh hell outa here,' I says. See?" Jimmie nodded understandingly. Over his features played an eager desire to state the amount of his valor in a similar crisis, but the narrator proceeded.

Like dat! 'Deh hell,' I says. See? 'Don' make no trouble,' I says. Like dat. 'Don' make no trouble.' See? 'Oh, gee,' I says, 'oh, gee, go teh hell and git off deh eart',' I says, like dat. See? 'Go teh hell an' git off deh eart',' like dat. Den deh blokie he got wild. He says I was a contempt'ble scoun'el, er somet'ing like dat, an' he says I was doom' teh everlastin' pe'dition an' all like dat. 'Gee,' I says, 'gee! Deh hell I am,' I says.
