The train came in at four o'clock and Walt was waiting on the platform. He was standing by the baggage truck with his hat pushed back and his hands in the pockets of his canvas coat. He was bigger than Tom remembered. He had been big before, but now he was big the way a man gets who works outside all year, thick in the neck and the shoulders, and his face was brown and lined at the corners of the eyes.

Tom stepped down with his bag. The conductor handed down the rod case after him.

"Hello, Walt," he said.

"Hello, Tommy."

They shook hands. Walt's hand was hard and dry. He took the bag and Tom kept the rod case, and they walked out past the station house to where the truck was parked in the shade of a cottonwood. The truck was old and green and there was a dog in the back of it. The dog stood up and wagged and watched them.

"That's not Duke," Tom said.

"Duke's dead. That's his pup. That's Sam."

"Hello, Sam."

The dog put his head down and Tom rubbed behind his ears. Walt put the bag in the back and they got in. The cab smelled of oil and tobacco and old hay. Walt started the truck and they drove out of town on the gravel road with the dust coming up behind them.

"You look thin," Walt said.

"I've been sick."

"Ellen said you'd been sick. Your mother wrote her."

"It wasn't anything. It's all right now."

"Good," Walt said.

They drove along the road. The wheat was up on both sides and it was green and moving in the wind. Beyond the wheat were the hills, and beyond the hills the mountains, and there was still snow on the mountains. Tom looked at the snow. It had been a long time since he had seen it.

"The wheat looks good," he said.

"It's all right. We had rain in May. We'll see."

"Is it all yours now?"

"The north half and the bottom land. I sold the section by the Hansen place. I had to."

"I didn't know that."

"No," Walt said. "There wasn't any way you'd know it."

They did not say anything for a while. The truck went over the bridge at the creek and Tom looked down and saw the water. It was high and fast and the color of tea. Walt saw him look.

"It'll clear in a week," Walt said. "It's still running off the snow. But there's a pool below the old dam that's fishing. I was down there Sunday."

"Any good?"

"I got four. Nothing big. But they were fat."

"I brought the rod."

"I saw you did."

---

The house was the same. It was white and square with the porch on two sides and the big elm in the yard, and the windmill behind it was turning slowly in the wind. Ellen came out on the porch when the truck stopped. She was drying her hands on her apron. She came down the steps and Tom got out and she put her arms around him and held him.

"Look at you," she said. "Look how thin you are."

"Walt already told me."

"Well, it's true. Come in. Come in and wash. Supper's nearly ready."

He went into the house. It smelled of bread and coffee and the oilcloth on the kitchen table. There were two children in the kitchen, a boy and a girl, and they looked at him and did not say anything.

"This is your cousin Tom," Ellen said. "Say hello."

"Hello," the boy said. The girl said nothing. She was very small.

"The last time I saw you," Tom said to the boy, "you were in a basket."

The boy looked at him. He did not believe it.

Tom washed at the sink and they ate supper. There was fried chicken and new potatoes and bread and butter and a dish of pickled beets, and there was coffee and afterward there was pie. Tom ate a great deal. He had not been hungry for a long time and now he was hungry and the food was good. Ellen watched him eat and was pleased.

"You'll stay a while," she said.

"A week. Maybe a little longer."

"You'll stay as long as you want."

"Thank you, Ellen."

Walt did not say anything. He ate his pie and drank his coffee and then he pushed his chair back.

"I've got to look at the heifer," he said. "You want to come?"

"All right."

---

They went out to the barn. It was getting dark now and the air was cool. The swallows were going in and out of the high door of the barn. Inside it was dark and smelled of manure and straw and the heifer was in the box stall at the end. She was lying down and she turned her head and looked at them.

Walt went in and squatted beside her and put his hand on her flank. He stayed there a long time.

"Tonight?" Tom said.

"Maybe. Maybe tomorrow. It's her first."

"You want me to stay out with you?"

"No. I'll come out and look at her at midnight. There's nothing to do yet."

He came out of the stall and latched it. They stood in the door of the barn and looked out at the yard. The kitchen window was yellow with the lamp and they could see Ellen moving in it.

Walt took a bottle out from behind a feed bin. It was a pint bottle and it was half full. He uncorked it and handed it to Tom.

"Ellen doesn't care," he said. "But I keep it out here anyway."

Tom drank. It was rough whiskey and it burned going down and then it was warm. He handed the bottle back. Walt drank and put the cork back in and held the bottle in his hand.

"She looks well," Tom said. "Ellen."

"She's fine."

"And the kids."

"They're fine. The boy's going to be smart. Smarter than me."

"That's not hard."

"No," Walt said. "It isn't."

He uncorked the bottle again and handed it over. Tom drank and gave it back.

"I got your letter," Walt said. "About your father's watch."

"I wanted you to have it."

"I know you did. I didn't write back."

"That's all right."

"No, it isn't. I meant to write back. I sat down to do it twice."

"It's all right, Walt."

Walt looked at the bottle. Then he drank from it.

"I wear it Sundays," he said. "It still keeps good time."

"He always kept it wound."

"I keep it wound too."

They stood there. It was dark now and the stars were out over the windmill. The windmill had stopped turning. There was no wind at all.

"We'll fish in the morning," Walt said. "Early. Before it gets hot."

"I'd like that."

"I'll get you up."

---

Walt got him up before it was light. He knocked on the door and Tom woke and did not know where he was. Then he heard the rooster and knew. He got up and dressed in the dark and went down to the kitchen. Walt had the stove going and there was coffee and he was frying eggs.

"How's the heifer?"

"She had it at three. A bull calf. They're both fine."

"You didn't wake me."

"There wasn't any need to."

They ate the eggs with bread and drank the coffee. Then they went out to the truck. Walt had put the rods in the back and a can of worms and a canvas bag with sandwiches in it, and the bottle. The dog got in the back. It was getting light in the east now and it was cold, and they drove with the windows up.

They drove out along the creek road and then turned off on a track that went down through the pasture. Walt stopped the truck by a gate and they got out and went through the gate and walked down toward the creek. The grass was wet and soon their trousers were wet to the knee. The dog went ahead of them through the grass and they could see where he had gone by the dark line he left in it.

The old dam was made of logs and rocks and most of it had washed out. The water came through the break in it and dropped into a long pool. The pool was deep and green at the head and the water was clearer here than at the bridge. At the tail of the pool there was a riffle and then the creek went on around a bend under the willows.

Tom put his rod together. His hands were cold and he was slow with it. He tied on a hook and put on a worm and then he walked up to the head of the pool and dropped the worm in where the water came over the logs. He let it go down with the current. He could feel it bumping along the bottom. Then it stopped and he felt the line go tight and he struck and the rod bent and the fish was on.

It was not a big fish but it fought well. It went down deep and then came up and jumped, and he saw it in the air, bright and spotted, and then it was down again. He kept the rod up and let it run and then brought it in. Walt came with the net and netted it for him.

"That's a good fish," Walt said.

"It's a nice fish."

He killed it and put it in the creel on the wet grass. Then he baited again. Walt had gone down to the tail of the pool and was fishing the riffle. Tom watched him. Walt fished the way he did everything, carefully and without hurry, and Tom saw him take a fish and then another. The sun was coming up over the hills and it was on the water now and it was warm on Tom's back.

They fished until the sun was high. Tom caught five and Walt caught seven. Then they sat on the grass under a cottonwood above the pool and ate the sandwiches. The sandwiches were cold meat and mustard and bread and they were very good. Walt took the bottle out of the bag and went down to the creek and filled a tin cup with water and came back. He poured whiskey in the cup with the water and handed it to Tom.

"That's the way to drink it," he said. "With creek water."

Tom drank and gave it back. The water was cold and the whiskey was warm in it. Walt drank and filled the cup again.

"This is fine," Tom said. "This is a fine place."

"It's the best place on the creek. Dad used to bring us here. You remember."

"I remember."

"You caught that big one. The summer you were twelve."

"You netted it and it got off."

"It didn't get off. You never brought it in close enough. I couldn't reach it."

"It got off in the net."

"That's not the way it happened."

"That's the way I remember it."

Walt laughed. "All right," he said. "That's the way it happened."

They drank. A kingfisher came down the creek and went past them, low over the water, and they heard it chattering after it was gone around the bend. The dog was lying in the shade with his head on his paws and he was asleep.

"How was it over there?" Walt said.

"It was all right."

"Ellen said you were in the hospital a long time."

"A while."

"Was it bad?"

"It was bad for a while. Then it was better."

"What was it?"

"It was a fever. Then it was something in the blood. They didn't know what it was for a while. Then they found out."

"But you're all right now."

"I'm all right now."

Walt looked at the creek. "I thought about going," he said. "When it started. I thought about it a lot."

"You had the place."

"I had the place and I had Ellen and the boy. And Dad was sick then. I didn't know how sick."

"You did right."

"I don't know if I did right. I didn't go. That's all."

"You did right, Walt."

Walt poured more whiskey in the cup and went down and put water in it and came back. He sat down and drank and handed it over. Tom drank. The whiskey was making him feel good and easy and he lay back on the grass and looked up through the leaves of the cottonwood. The leaves were moving a little now. There was a little wind coming up the creek.

"I should have come back," Tom said. "When he died."

Walt did not say anything.

"I got the cable. I couldn't get out. There wasn't any ship for three weeks. Then I was sick."

"I know it."

"I wanted to come."

"I know you did," Walt said. "It doesn't matter."

"It matters."

"It doesn't matter now. It was a long time ago. There wasn't anything you could have done."

"I could have been here."

"Yes," Walt said. "You could have been here."

They lay there. Tom looked up at the leaves. He did not want to look at Walt. He heard Walt drink and then he heard him put the cup down on the grass.

"He asked for you," Walt said. "At the end. He thought you were coming. He thought you were in the next room."

Tom did not say anything.

"I told him you were. I told him you were out in the kitchen with Ellen. He was all right after that. He went to sleep."

"Thank you."

"There wasn't anything else to tell him."

"I know. Thank you, Walt."

"Don't thank me."

The wind was moving the leaves and the light came down through them and moved on the grass. Tom shut his eyes. He could hear the creek going over the logs of the old dam. It made a steady sound. He lay and listened to it and after a while he opened his eyes and sat up.

"He was good to me," he said. "After my father."

"He liked you better than me."

"That's not true."

"It's true. You were quick. You read books. He used to say you were going to be something."

"I'm not anything."

"You're something. You went over there. You saw all that."

"It isn't anything to see. It's just a lot of places."

"It's more than I've seen."

"You've got this," Tom said. "You've got the place and Ellen and the kids. You've got the creek."

"I've got the mortgage on the place."

"You've still got it."

"Yes," Walt said. "I've still got it."

He picked up the cup and looked at it and then he threw the rest of the water and whiskey out onto the grass. He put the cup in the bag and corked the bottle and put it in too.

"We'll have some tonight," he said. "After supper. There's more in the barn."

"That's good."

"Let's fish down around the bend. There's a hole under the willows. Dad never fished it. He said it was too hard to get to. But there's fish in it."

"All right."

They got up. The dog woke and stood and stretched and looked at them. They picked up the rods and the creel and walked down along the creek. The grass was dry now and the sun was hot. At the bend the willows grew thick and they had to go down into the water to get past them. The water was cold on Tom's legs through his trousers. It was so cold it hurt and then it did not hurt.

Under the willows the water was deep and dark and it went slowly. There was a log in it. Walt pointed at the log.

"Under there," he said. "You go first."

"No, you go."

"Go on. You're the company."

Tom baited the hook. He swung the worm out and let it drop above the log and the current took it down and under. He waited. He did not feel anything. The wheat was on both sides and it was moving in the wind and there was still snow on the mountains.

In the afternoon the wind came up out of the northwest. The man stopped splitting wood and stood and looked at the lake. It had been flat all morning, and now it was dark where the wind touched it, and you could see the wind moving across the water toward the point. The birches along the shore turned the pale undersides of their leaves up. He set the axe in the block and wiped his hands on his trousers and walked down through the long grass to the dock.

The boat was gone.

He stood on the dock and looked for it. The boards were gray and warm under his feet, and the water slapped against the pilings. He looked first toward the big rock where the boy was allowed to go, and the boat was not there. He looked toward the point, and then out toward the island, and then he saw it. It was very small and far out, past where the bottom dropped away. It was not moving the way a boat moves when someone is rowing it. It was turning slowly, sideways to the wind. He could see the boy sitting in the stern, and he could see one oar.

He did not shout. It was too far to shout, and the wind was wrong for it.

The canoe was on the rack under the cedars. He lifted it down and turned it over and carried it to the water and put it in. He went back for the paddle, and then he went back again for the coil of line that hung on the nail by the woodshed door. He knelt in the canoe a little behind the center and pushed off from the dock with the paddle and turned the bow out toward the island.

Inside the cove the water was not bad. When he came out past the point the wind took the bow and pushed it around, and he had to paddle hard on the one side to bring it back. The waves were short and steep and the color of slate, and the tops of them were beginning to break white. Spray came over the bow and wet his shirt. It was cold. The lake was always cold out past the drop, even in August. He knew that, and he did not think about it. He paddled and kept his eyes on the boat.

He paddled for a long time. His shoulders began to burn, and then they stopped burning and only ached, and then he did not notice them. He counted the strokes for a while and then stopped counting. The boat got larger. Once he lost it behind a wave and felt something go tight in his stomach, and then the canoe rose and he saw it again, closer now, still turning. The boy was sitting very still. He was holding the gunwales with both hands.

When he was close he eased off and let the canoe come up alongside. The boat was pitching, and he was careful not to let the two hulls knock. The boy looked at him. The boy's face was white, and there were marks on it where he had been crying, but he was not crying now.

"Where's the other oar?" the man said.

"It went over."

"Where?"

The boy pointed. Far off toward the north shore there was something small and yellow on the water, and then it was gone, and then it was there again.

"All right," the man said. "Hand me the painter. The rope at the front. Don't stand up. Crawl."

The boy crawled forward along the bottom of the boat with the water sloshing around his knees and found the painter and held it out. The man took it and tied it to the thwart behind him with two half hitches and pulled them tight.

"Now get back in the stern and sit down in the bottom. Not on the seat. In the bottom."

"What about the oar?"

"Leave the oar in the boat."

"I mean the other one."

"Sit down," the man said.

The boy sat down in the bottom of the boat.

Going back was harder. The wind was behind them, and that should have been easier, but the boat was heavy and yawed on the line, and the waves came up under the stern of the canoe and tried to turn it. He had to watch each one. He had to feel each one before it came. He did not look back at the boy, because he could not look back and keep the canoe straight, and he did not speak because there was nothing to say that needed saying out there. He paddled. The line went tight and slack and tight again. When they came around the point into the cove the water lay down all at once, and the noise of the wind went up into the tops of the cedars, and he could hear his own breathing.

He ran the canoe up on the sand beside the dock and got out into the shallow water and pulled the boat in by the painter until it grounded. The boy started to climb out.

"Stay there," the man said.

He pulled the canoe higher on the sand and turned it over. He coiled the line. He pulled the boat up and untied the painter and took the one oar out and laid it on the dock. He tipped the boat on its side and let the water run out of it, and set it down again. Then he sat down on the end of the dock with his feet hanging over the water. His shirt was wet through, and the wind was cold on it. His hands were shaking a little, and he put them between his knees.

"Come here," he said.

The boy got out of the boat and came up onto the dock. He stood a little way off.

"Sit down."

"Are you going to whip me?"

"I don't know yet," the man said. "Sit down."

The boy sat down on the dock. He sat with his legs crossed under him, not hanging over the water, and he looked at the boards.

"Who said you could take the boat?"

"Nobody."

"Did I say you could take the boat?"

"No, sir."

"What did I tell you about the boat?"

"You said I could take it to the big rock."

"That's right. And what else?"

"You said I had to ask first."

"Did you ask?"

"You were splitting wood."

"Did you ask?"

"No," the boy said.

"Where were you when I found you?"

The boy did not answer.

"Where were you?"

"Past the rock."

"How far past it?"

The boy picked at a splinter in the board with his fingernail. He did not answer.

"How far past it?"

"A long way."

"That's right," the man said. "A long way."

They sat there. Out on the lake the whitecaps were running all the way across now, and the island looked dark and close the way it did before rain. A gull came over low and turned and went back out.

"Look at me," the man said.

The boy looked at him.

"Why did you go out there?"

"I don't know."

"Yes, you do."

"I wanted to see the loons."

"There are loons in the cove. You can see loons from the porch."

"Not the young ones. The young ones are by the island."

"That's not why."

The boy looked down again. "I wanted to fish," he said. "Where you fish. Off the island where the bottom comes up. Where you got the big one."

The man did not say anything for a while.

"I brought the worms," the boy said. "They're in the can. They went in the water when the oar went."

"How did the oar go?"

"I was trying to turn around. When the wind came. It was in the lock and then it wasn't."

"You tried to reach for it."

"Yes."

"Did you stand up?"

The boy didn't answer.

"Did you stand up in the boat?"

"A little."

The man looked out at the water. He was quiet for a long time, and the boy watched him and then stopped watching him.

"Do you know how deep it is out there?" the man said.

"No."

"Neither do I. Nobody knows. They tried to sound it once with a line and the line wasn't long enough." He said it flatly, the way he would say what time it was. "It's cold down there. It's cold even now, at the end of the summer. You put your hand in it out there and it hurts your hand."

"I can swim."

"You can swim to the rock."

"I can swim farther than the rock."

"You can swim to the rock in the cove on a flat day in July with me standing on the dock. You can't swim in that." He moved his chin toward the lake. "Nobody can swim very long in that. Not grown men. Not strong ones."

The boy was quiet.

"If you had gone over out there," the man said, "I would not have found you. Do you understand that? I would have come out in the canoe and there would have been the boat and nobody in it. I would have looked and looked and there would have been nothing to find."

The boy began to cry. He did not make much noise. His face went tight and red, and the tears came, and he wiped at them with the back of his wrist.

"Don't cry," the man said.

The boy kept crying.

"All right," the man said. "Cry if you want to."

He waited. The wind moved the tops of the cedars, and down along the shore a loose board on the boathouse knocked and knocked. After a while the boy stopped crying and sat with his shoulders going up and down, and then they stopped going up and down.

"You're not to take the boat again this summer," the man said.

The boy looked up quickly.

"Not to the rock. Not anywhere."

"The whole summer?"

"The whole summer."

"But there's three weeks."

"That's right. There's three weeks."

"That's not fair."

"No," the man said. "It isn't fair. It's what it is."

"You didn't say that before. You didn't say if I went past the rock I couldn't have it."

"I didn't think I had to say it."

"You should have said it."

"Maybe I should have," the man said. "I'm saying it now."

The boy looked at the boat lying on its side on the sand. The water had run out of it and the bottom was dark and wet.

"Are you still going to whip me?"

The man looked at his hands. They had stopped shaking. He opened them and closed them.

"No," he said.

"Why not?"

"Because I don't want to."

"You whipped me when I broke the window."

"That was different."

"How?"

"It was a window," the man said. "Go on up to the house and get out of those wet things. Put on your dry trousers and the wool shirt. Then come back down and help me put the canoe away."

The boy got up. He stood for a moment as though he were going to say something, and then he did not say it, and he turned and went up the path through the grass toward the house. The man watched him go. He was very thin, and his wet shirt stuck to his back, and he walked carefully, the way you walk when you are trying not to run.

When the boy was in the house the man sat on the dock for a while longer. He looked out toward the north shore for the oar, but he could not see it now. It was too far, or the waves were too high, or it had gone in among the rocks. It was a good oar. He had shaped it himself two winters ago out of a piece of ash, and it had taken him a long time to get the blade right. It did not matter.

He had been on bad water before. There had been a river once, a long time ago, and a night on it, and men in it who had not come out. He had not thought about that river in a long time and he did not want to think about it now. He sat and looked at the lake and did not think about it. The wind was dropping. You could see it dropping. The whitecaps did not run so far now before they broke, and over toward the west the clouds had come apart and there was light behind them.

The boy came back down in his dry clothes, and they carried the canoe up together and put it on the rack. The boy took the stern end, and it was too heavy for him, and he did not say anything about it. The man took the paddle and the line up to the woodshed and hung them on their nails. Then he went in and made supper.

He fried potatoes in the iron pan with onions and some bacon fat, and when they were brown he broke four eggs into the pan beside them. He cut bread. He poured milk for the boy and opened a bottle of beer for himself and set the bottle on the table by his plate. They ate at the table by the window, where they could see the lake. Neither of them said much. The boy ate everything on his plate, and the man gave him the other egg, and he ate that too.

"Are you going to tell Mother?" the boy said.

"Yes."

"Do you have to?"

"Yes."

"When she comes Saturday?"

"When she comes Saturday."

The boy pushed a piece of bread around the plate in the yellow of the egg.

"She'll be sore."

"She'll be scared," the man said. "It's the same thing, mostly."

"Were you scared?"

The man drank from the bottle and set it down.

"Eat your bread," he said.

After supper the boy dried the dishes while the man washed them. Then the boy read for a while by the lamp in a book about a dog in the Klondike, and then he went to bed. The man went in after a time to put out the lamp. The boy was lying on his back with the blanket pulled up to his chin, and his eyes were open.

"Are you still sore at me?" the boy said.

"No."

"Honest?"

"Honest."

"I'm sorry about the oar."

"It's only an oar."

"You said it was a good oar."

"It was a good oar," the man said. "Go to sleep."

"Can we look for it tomorrow?"

"Maybe. If it's flat."

"In the canoe?"

"In the canoe."

"Can I paddle?"

"Go to sleep," the man said.

He put out the lamp and went out onto the porch. It was dark now, and the wind was gone. The lake was flat and black, and there was a moon coming up behind the island, and the moon made a road on the water all the way to the dock. A loon called out there somewhere, and then another one answered it from farther off. It was very quiet. He could hear the water moving a little against the pilings.

He sat down in the chair and lit a cigarette and smoked it. He looked out at the lake where the boat had been. It was hard to believe now that it had been the way it was. It looked like a lake you could walk on. It always looked that way at night, and it was never true.

In the morning, he thought, if it was flat, they would go out and look for the oar. They would go along the north shore among the rocks where the wind would have carried it, and the boy would sit in the bow and watch the water. Maybe he would let the boy paddle a little. Not far. In the cove, where it was shallow and you could see the bottom.

He had said the whole summer. He knew he would not keep it the whole summer. He knew that, and he did not mind knowing it. He sat on the porch and smoked and watched the moon come up clear of the island, and after a while the loons stopped calling, and he went in.

I wore one when we went up to the posts and carried an English gas mask. We were just beginning to get some of them. They were a real mask. Also we were required to wear an automatic pistol; even doctors and sanitary officers. I felt it against the back of the chair. You were liable to arrest if you did not have one worn in plain sight. Rinaldi carried a holster stuffed with toilet paper. I wore a real one and felt like a gunman until I practised firing it. It was an Astra 7.65 caliber with a short barrel and it jumped so sharply when you let it off that there was no question of hitting anything. I practised with it, holding below the target and trying to master the jerk of the ridiculous short barrel until I could hit within a yard of where I aimed at twenty paces and then the ridiculousness of carrying a pistol at all came over me and I soon forgot it and carried it flopping against the small of my back with no feeling at all except a vague sort of shame when I met English-speaking people. "No."

"I'm sorry."

"You didn't tell me."

"No."

"I don't know. There wasn't any good time."

"Don't think about it."

"How do you not think about it?"

"You just don't."

"Yes."

"Sometimes."

"Sometimes," she said. "That's very fine. Sometimes."

"Darling, I'm counting already."

"What do you want?" he said. "Tell me what you want and I'll do it if I can."

"You won't do it."

"Tell me."

"I want you to write Martin and say no. I want you to say that you're through. I want us to go back to Paris and have the winter and not have anybody's war in it. I want you to sleep with the light off. That's what I want." She stopped. "There. Now I've said it. Now you know."

"All right."

"Will you do it?"

"No," he said.

"No," she said. "I didn't think you would."

"I'm sorry, Ellen."

"Don't be sorry. Please don't be sorry. I can't stand it if you're sorry."

"All right. I'm not sorry."

"Do you want me to come up?"

"It's best in the evening."

"Maybe."

"I hope you do," she said. "I really do. I hope you catch him."

"It isn't cold."

"She thinks it is."

"No," Jim said. "That's not a bad way."

"She's high," he said.

In the morning it was clear and Jim was already up. The heifer had calved in the night. It was a bull calf and it was standing up on its legs and sucking when they went out to see it.

"He's all right. We'll see."

"You kept it," Paul said.

"Sure I kept it. It was yours."

"I thought it'd be gone."

"Where would it go?"

The grass was wet and their boots were soaked through before they got halfway. The river was still high but it was clearer than the day before and you could see down into it a little way along the edges.

It was a brown trout and it weighed two pounds and four ounces on Jim's father's scale and they had cooked it that night and eaten it and it was the best thing he had ever eaten.

"That's a good one," Jim said.

"He's all right."

"Keep him out of the roots."

"I know."

It lay there and flopped and was very bright in the sun.

"That's a good fish," Jim said. "That's two pounds."

"Maybe."

"That's as good as the first one you got here."

"That one was bigger."

"No, it wasn't. You only think it was bigger."

They sat down on the bank in the sun. Jim got out his tobacco and rolled a cigarette and offered the sack to Paul and Paul rolled one too. They smoked and looked at the river.

"I'm going to sell it," Jim said.

Paul did not say anything for a moment.

"The farm?"

"The farm. Halvorsen's boy wants it. He wants the bottom land and the pasture. He'll give a fair price."

"I didn't know you were thinking about it."

"I been thinking about it since Christmas."

"Is it the money?"

"Some. It's not good. It hasn't been good for three years. But that's not it altogether."

"Are you going to Eau Claire?"

Jim looked at the cigarette.

"I don't know," he said. "Maybe. I wrote her. She hasn't written back yet."

"She might."

"She might. And she might not." He drew on the cigarette. "Either way I'm going to sell it. I can't stay here by myself. I thought I could. It's no good by yourself."

"No," Paul said. "It isn't any good."

"I wanted you to come up before I did it," Jim said. "I wanted you to see it again."

"I'm glad you did."

"You don't have to say anything about it."

"I wasn't going to."

"Well," Jim said. "Good."

"You want to fish some more?" he said.

"Sure."

"There's another one under there. There's always another one under there."

"There was always another one."

"That's right," Jim said. He stood up and picked up his rod. "There always was."

"There'll be one," the father said. "There always is."

A warm wind came with daylight and he could hear the snow melting in the trees and the heavy sound of its falling. It was a late spring morning. He knew with the first breath he drew that the snow had been only a freak storm in the mountains and it would be gone by noon. Then he heard a horse coming, the hoofs balled with the wet snow thumping dully as the horseman trotted. He heard the noise of a carbine scabbard slapping loosely and the creak of leather.

“Maria,” he said, and shook the girl’s shoulder to waken her. “Keep thyself under the robe,” and he buttoned his shirt with one hand and held the automatic pistol in the other, loosening the safety catch with his thumb. He saw the girl’s cropped head disappear with a jerk under the robe and then he saw the horseman coming through the trees. He crouched now in the robe and holding the pistol in both hands aimed it at the man as he rode toward him. He had never seen this man before. The horseman was almost opposite him now. He was riding a big gray gelding and he wore a khaki beret, a blanket cape like a poncho, and heavy black boots. From the scabbard on the right of his saddle projected the stock and the long oblong clip of a short automatic rifle. He had a young, hard face and at this moment he saw Robert Jordan. He reached his hand down toward the scabbard and as he swung low, turning and jerking at the scabbard, Robert Jordan saw the scarlet of the formalized device he wore on the left breast of his khaki blanket cape. Aiming at the center of his chest, a little lower than the device, Robert Jordan fired. The pistol roared in the snowy woods. The horse plunged as though he had been spurred and the young man, still tugging at the scabbard, slid over toward the ground, his right foot caught in the stirrup. The horse broke off through the trees dragging him, bumping, face downward, and Robert Jordan stood up holding the pistol now in one hand. The big gray horse was galloping through the pines. There was a broad swath in the snow where the man dragged with a scarlet streak along one side of it. People were coming out of the mouth of the cave. Robert Jordan reached down and unrolled his trousers from the pillow and began to put them on.

“Get thee dressed,” he said to Maria. Overhead he heard the noise of a plane flying very high. Through the trees he saw where the gray horse had stopped and was standing, his rider still hanging face down from the stirrup.

“Go catch that horse,” he called to Primitivo who had started over toward him. Then, “Who was on guard at the top?”

“Rafael,” Pilar said from the cave. She stood there, her hair still down her back in two braids.

“There’s cavalry out,” Robert Jordan said. “Get your damned gun up there.” He heard Pilar call, “Agustín,” into the cave. Then she went into the cave and then two men came running out, one with the automatic rifle with its tripod swung on his shoulder; the other with a sackful of the pans.

“Get up there with them,” Robert Jordan said to Anselmo. “You lie beside the gun and hold the legs still,” he said. The three of them went up the trail through the woods at a run. The sun had not yet come up over the tops of the mountains and Robert Jordan stood straight buttoning his trousers and tightening his belt, the big pistol hanging from the lanyard on his wrist. He put the pistol in its holster on his belt and slipped the knot down on the lanyard and passed the loop over his head.

Excerpt 2: Anselmo was crouched in the lee of the trunk of a big tree and the snow blew past on either side. He was pressed close against the tree and his hands were inside of the sleeves of his jacket, each hand shoved up into the opposite sleeve, and his head was pulled as far down into the jacket as it would go. If I stay here much longer I will freeze, he thought, and that will be of no value. The Inglés told me to stay until I was relieved but he did not know then about this storm. There has been no abnormal movement on the road and I know the dispositions and the habits of this post at the sawmill across the road. I should go now to the camp. Anybody with sense would be expecting me to return to the camp. I will stay a little longer, he thought, and then go to the camp. It is the fault of the orders, which are too rigid. There is no allowance for a change in circumstance. He rubbed his feet together and then took his hands out of the jacket sleeves and bent over and rubbed his legs with them and patted his feet together to keep the circulation going. It was less cold there, out of the wind in the shelter of the tree, but he would have to start walking shortly. As he crouched, rubbing his feet, he heard a motorcar on the road. It had on chains and one link of chain was slapping and, as he watched, it came up the snow-covered road, green and brown painted, in broken patches of daubed color, the windows blued over so that you could not see in, with only a half circle left clear in the blue for the occupants to look out through. It was a two-year-old Rolls Royce town car camouflaged for the use of the General Staff but Anselmo did not know that. He could not see into the car where three officers sat wrapped in their capes. Two were on the back seat and one sat on the folding chair. The officer on the folding chair was looking out of the slit in the blue of the window as the car passed but Anselmo did not know this. Neither of them saw the other. The car passed in the snow directly below him. Anselmo saw the chauffeur, red-faced and steel-helmeted, his face and helmet projecting out of the blanket cape he wore and he saw the forward jut of the automatic rifle the orderly who sat beside the chauffeur carried. Then the car was gone up the road and Anselmo reached into the inside of his jacket and took out from his shirt pocket the two sheets torn from Robert Jordan’s notebook and made a mark after the drawing of a motorcar. It was the tenth car up for the day. Six had come down. Four were still up. It was not an unusual amount of cars to move upon that road but Anselmo did not distinguish between the Fords, Fiats, Opels, Renaults, and Citroens of the staff of the Division that held the passes and the line of the mountain and the Rolls-Royces, Lancias, Mercedes, and Isottas of the General Staff. This was the sort of distinction that Robert Jordan should have made and, if he had been there instead of the old man, he would have appreciated the significance of these cars which had gone up. But he was not there and the old man simply made a mark for a motorcar going up the road, on the sheet of note paper. Anselmo was now so cold that he decided he had best go to camp before it was dark. He had no fear of missing the way, but he thought it was useless to stay longer and the wind was blowing colder all the time and there was no lessening of the snow. But when he stood up and stamped his feet and looked through the driving snow at the road he did not start off up the hillside but stayed leaning against the sheltered side of the pine tree. The Inglés told me to stay, he thought. Even now he may be on the way here and, if I leave this place, he may lose himself in the snow searching for me. All through this war we have suffered from a lack of discipline and from the disobeying of orders and I will wait a while still for the Inglés. But if he does not come soon I must go in spite of all orders for I have a report to make now, and I have much to do in these days, and to freeze here is an exaggeration and without utility. Across the road at the sawmill smoke was coming out of the chimney and Anselmo could smell it blown toward him through the snow. The fascists are warm, he thought, and they are comfortable, and tomorrow night we will kill them. It is a strange thing and I do not like to think of it. I have watched them all day and they are the same men that we are. I believe that I could walk up to the mill and knock on the door and I would be welcome except that they have orders to challenge all travellers and ask to see their papers. It is only orders that come between us. Those men are not fascists. I call them so, but they are not. They are poor men as we are. They should never be fighting against us and I do not like to think of the killing. These at this post are Gallegos. I know that from hearing them talk this afternoon. They cannot desert because if they do their families will be shot. Gallegos are either very intelligent or very dumb and brutal. I have known both kinds. Lister is a Gallego from the same town as Franco. I wonder what these Gallegos think of this snow now at this time of year. They have no high mountains such as these and in their country it always rains and it is always green. A light showed in the window of the sawmill and Anselmo shivered and thought, damn that Inglés! There are the Gallegos warm and in a house here in our country, and I am freezing behind a tree and we live in a hole in the rocks like beasts in the mountain. But tomorrow, he thought, the beasts will come out of their hole and these that are now so comfortable will die warm in their blankets. As those died in the night when we raided Otero, he thought. He did not like to remember Otero. In Otero, that night, was when he first killed and he hoped he would not have to kill in this of the suppressing of these posts. It was in Otero that Pablo knifed the sentry when Anselmo pulled the blanket over his head and the sentry caught Anselmo’s foot and held it, smothered as he was in the blanket, and made a crying noise in the blanket and Anselmo had to feel in the blanket and knife him until he let go of the foot and was still. He had his knee across the man’s throat to keep him silent and he was knifing into the bundle when Pablo tossed the bomb through the window into the room where the men of the post were all sleeping. And when the flash came it was as though the whole world burst red and yellow before your eyes and two more bombs were in already. Pablo had pulled the pins and tossed them quickly through the window, and those who were not killed in their beds were killed as they rose from bed when the second bomb exploded. That was in the great days of Pablo when he scourged the country like a tartar and no fascist post was safe at night. And now, he is as finished and as ended as a boar that has been altered, Anselmo thought, and, when the altering has been accomplished and the squealing is over you cast the two stones away and the boar, that is a boar no longer, goes snouting and rooting up to them and eats them. No, he is not that bad, Anselmo grinned, one can think too badly even of Pablo. But he is ugly enough and changed enough. It is too cold, he thought. That the Inglés should come and that I should not have to kill in this of the posts. These four Gallegos and their corporal are for those who like the killing. The Inglés said that. I will do it if it is my duty but the Inglés said that I would be with him at the bridge and that this would be left to others. At the bridge there will be a battle and, if I am able to endure the battle, then I will have done all that an old man may do in this war. But let the Inglés come now, for I am cold and to see the light in the mill where I know that the Gallegos are warm makes me colder still. I wish that I were in my own house again and that this war were over. But you have no house now, he thought. We must win this war before you can ever return to your house. Inside the sawmill one of the soldiers was sitting on his bunk and greasing his boots. Another lay in his bunk sleeping. The third was cooking and the corporal was reading a paper. Their helmets hung on nails driven into the wall and their rifles leaned against the plank wall.

“What kind of country is this where it snows when it is almost June?” the soldier who was sitting on the bunk said.

“It is a phenomenon,” the corporal said.

“We are in the moon of May,” the soldier who was cooking said. “The moon of May has not yet terminated.”

“What kind of a country is it where it snows in May?” the soldier on the bunk insisted.

“In May snow is no rarity in these mountains,” the corporal said. “I have been colder in Madrid in the month of May than in any other month.”

“And hotter, too,” the soldier who was cooking said.

“May is a month of great contrasts in temperature,” the corporal said. “Here, in Castile, May is a month of great heat but it can have much cold.”

“Or rain,” the soldier on the bunk said. “In this past May it rained almost every day.”

“It did not,” the soldier who was cooking said. “And anyway this past May was the moon of April.”

“One could go crazy listening to thee and thy moons,” the corporal said. “Leave this of the moons alone.”

“Any one who lives either by the sea or by the land knows that it is the moon and not the month which counts,” the soldier who was cooking said. “Now for example, we have just started the moon of May. Yet it is coming on June.”

“Why then do we not get definitely behind in the seasons?” the corporal said. “The whole proposition gives me a headache.”

“You are from a town,” the soldier who was cooking said. “You are from Lugo. What would you know of the sea or of the land?”

“One learns more in a town than you analfabetos learn in thy sea or thy land.”

“In this moon the first of the big schools of sardines come,” the soldier who was cooking said. “In this moon the sardine boats will be outfitting and the mackerel will have gone north.”

“Why are you not in the navy if you come from Noya?” the corporal asked.

“Because I am not inscribed from Noya but from Negreira, where I was born. And from Negreira, which is up the river Tambre, they take you for the army.”

“Worse luck,” said the corporal.

“Do not think the navy is without peril,” the soldier who was sitting on the bunk said. “Even without the possibility of combat that is a dangerous coast in the winter.”

“Nothing can be worse than the army,” the corporal said.

“And you a corporal,” the soldier who was cooking said. “What a way of speaking is that?”

“Nay,” the corporal said. “I mean for dangers. I mean the endurance of bombardments, the necessity to attack, the life of the parapet.”

“Here we have little of that,” the soldier on the bunk said.

“By the Grace of God,” the corporal said. “But who knows when we will be subject to it again? Certainly we will not have something as easy as this forever!”

“How much longer do you think we will have this detail?”

“I don’t know,” the corporal said. “But I wish we could have it for all of the war.”

“Six hours is too long to be on guard,” the soldier who was cooking said.

“We will have three-hour watches as long as this storm holds,” the corporal said. “That is only normal.”

“What about all those staff cars?” the soldier on the bunk asked. “I did not like the look of all those staff cars.”

“Nor I,” the corporal said. “All such things are of evil omen.”

“And aviation,” the soldier who was cooking said. “Aviation is another bad sign.”

“But we have formidable aviation,” the corporal said. “The reds have no aviation such as we have. Those planes this morning were something to make any man happy.”

“I have seen the red planes when they were something serious,” the soldier on the bunk said. “I have seen those two motor bombers when they were a horror to endure.”

“Yes. But they are not as formidable as our aviation,” the corporal said. “We have an aviation that is insuperable.” This was how they were talking in the sawmill while Anselmo waited in the snow watching the road and the light in the sawmill window. I hope I am not for the killing, Anselmo was thinking. I think that after the war there will have to be some great penance done for the killing. If we no longer have religion after the war then I think there must be some form of civic penance organized that all may be cleansed from the killing or else we will never have a true and human basis for living. The killing is necessary, I know, but still the doing of it is very bad for a man and I think that, after all this is over and we have won the war, there must be a penance of some kind for the cleansing of us all. Anselmo was a very good man and whenever he was alone for long, and he was alone much of the time, this problem of the killing returned to him. I wonder about the Inglés, he thought. He told me that he did not mind it. Yet he seems to be both sensitive and kind. It may be that in the younger people it does not have an importance. It may be that in foreigners, or in those who have not had our religion, there is not the same attitude. But I think any one doing it will be brutalized in time and I think that even though necessary, it is a great sin and that afterwards we must do something very strong to atone for it. It was dark now and he looked at the light across the road and shook his arms against his chest to warm them. Now, he thought, he would certainly leave for the camp; but something kept him there beside the tree above the road. It was snowing harder and Anselmo thought: if only we could blow the bridge tonight. On a night like this it would be nothing to take the posts and blow the bridge and it would be all over and done with. On a night like this you could do anything. Then he stood there against the tree stamping his feet softly and he did not think any more about the bridge. The coming of the dark always made him feel lonely and tonight he felt so lonely that there was a hollowness in him as of hunger. In the old days he could help this loneliness by saying of prayers and often coming home from hunting he would repeat a great number of the same prayer and it made him feel better. But he had not prayed once since the movement. He missed the prayers but he thought it would be unfair and hypocritical to say them and he did not wish to ask any favors or for any different treatment than all the men were receiving.

Excerpt 3: So now everything had been done that there was to do that night. All orders had been given. Every one knew exactly what he was to do in the morning. Andrés had been gone three hours. Either it would come now with the coming of the daylight or it would not come. I believe that it will come, Robert Jordan told himself, walking back down from the upper post where he had gone to speak to Primitivo. Golz makes the attack but he has not the power to cancel it. Permission to cancel it will have to come from Madrid. The chances are they won’t be able to wake anybody up there and if they do wake up they will be too sleepy to think. I should have gotten word to Golz sooner of the preparations they have made to meet the attack, but how could I send word about something until it happened? They did not move up that stuff until just at dark. They did not want to have any movement on the road spotted by planes. But what about all their planes? What about those fascist planes? Surely our people must have been warned by them. But perhaps the fascists were faking for another offensive down through Guadalajara with them. There were supposed to be Italian troops concentrated in Soria, and at Siguenza again besides those operating in the North. They haven’t enough troops or material to run two major offensives at the same time though. That is impossible; so it must be just a bluff. But we know how many troops the Italians have landed all last month and the month before at Cádiz. It is always possible they will try again at Guadalajara, not stupidly as before, but with three main fingers coming down to broaden it out and carry it along the railway to the west of the plateau. There was a way that they could do it all right. Hans had shown him. They made many mistakes the first time. The whole conception was unsound. They had not used any of the same troops in the Arganda offensive against the Madrid-Valencia road that they used at Guadalajara. Why had they not made those same drives simultaneously? Why? Why? When would we know why? Yet we had stopped them both times with the very same troops. We never could have stopped them if they had pulled both drives at once. Don’t worry, he told himself. Look at the miracles that have happened before this. Either you will have to blow that bridge in the morning or you will not have to. But do not start deceiving yourself into thinking you won’t have to blow it. You will blow it one day or you will blow it another. Or if it is not this bridge it will be some other bridge. It is not you who decides what shall be done. You follow orders. Follow them and do not try to think beyond them. The orders on this are very clear. Too very clear. But you must not worry nor must you be frightened. For if you allow yourself the luxury of normal fear that fear will infect those who must work with you. But that heads business was quite a thing all the same, he told himself. And the old man running onto them on the hilltop alone. How would you have liked to run onto them like that? That impressed you, didn’t it? Yes, that impressed you, Jordan. You have been quite impressed more than once today. But you have behaved O.K. So far you have behaved all right. You do very well for an instructor in Spanish at the University of Montana, he joked at himself. You do all right for that. But do not start to thinking that you are anything very special. You haven’t gotten very far in this business. Just remember Durán, who never had any military training and who was a composer and lad about town before the movement and is now a damned good general commanding a brigade. It was all as simple and easy to learn and understand to Durán as chess to a child chess prodigy. You had read on and studied the art of war ever since you were a boy and your grandfather had started you on the American Civil War. Except that Grandfather always called it the War of the Rebellion. But compared with Durán you were like a good sound chess player against a boy prodigy. Old Durán. It would be good to see Durán again. He would see him at Gaylord’s after this was over. Yes. After this was over. See how well he was behaving? I’ll see him at Gaylord’s, he said to himself again, after this is over. Don’t kid yourself, he said. You do it all perfectly O.K. Cold. Without kidding yourself. You aren’t going to see Durán any more and it is of no importance. Don’t be that way either, he told himself. Don’t go in for any of those luxuries. Nor for heroic resignation either. We do not want any citizens full of heroic resignation in these hills. Your grandfather fought four years in our Civil War and you are just finishing your first year in this war. You have a long time to go yet and you are very well fitted for the work. And now you have Maria, too. Why, you’ve got everything. You shouldn’t worry. What is a little brush between a guerilla band and a squadron of cavalry? That isn’t anything. What if they took the heads? Does that make any difference? None at all. The Indians always took the scalps when Grandfather was at Fort Kearny after the war. Do you remember the cabinet in your father’s office with the arrowheads spread out on a shelf, and the eagle feathers of the war bonnets that hung on the wall, their plumes slanting, the smoked buckskin smell of the leggings and the shirts and the feel of the beaded moccasins? Do you remember the great stave of the buffalo bow that leaned in a corner of the cabinet and the two quivers of hunting and war arrows, and how the bundle of shafts felt when you closed your hand around them? Remember something like that. Remember something concrete and practical. Remember Grandfather’s saber, bright and well oiled in its dented scabbard and Grandfather showed you how the blade had beer thinned from the many times it had been to the grinder’s. Remember Grandfather’s Smith and Wesson. It was a single action, officer’s model .32 caliber and there was no trigger guard. It had the softest, sweetest trigger pull you had ever felt and it was always well oiled and the bore was clean although the finish was all worn off and the brown metal of the barrel and the cylinder was worn smooth from the leather of the holster. It was kept in the holster with a U. S. on the flap in a drawer in the cabinet with its cleaning equipment and two hundred rounds of cartridges. Their cardboard boxes were wrapped and tied neatly with waxed twine. You could take the pistol out of the drawer and hold it. “Handle it freely,” was Grandfather’s expression. But you could not play with it because it was “a serious weapon.” You asked Grandfather once if he had ever killed any one with it and he said, “Yes.” Then you said, “When, Grandfather?” and he said, “In the War of the Rebellion and afterwards.” You said, “Will you tell me about it, Grandfather?” And he said, “I do not care to speak about it, Robert.” Then after your father had shot himself with this pistol, and you had come home from school and they’d had the funeral, the coroner had returned it after the inquest saying, “Bob, I guess you might want to keep the gun. I’m supposed to hold it, but I know your dad set a lot of store by it because his dad packed it all through the War, besides out here when he first came out with the Cavalry, and it’s still a hell of a good gun. I had her out trying her this afternoon. She don’t throw much of a slug but you can hit things with her.” He had put the gun back in the drawer in the cabinet where it belonged, but the next day he took it out and he had ridden up to the top of the high country above Red Lodge, with Chub, where they had built the road to Cooke City now over the pass and across the Bear Tooth plateau, and up there where the wind was thin and there was snow all summer on the hills they had stopped by the lake which was supposed to be eight hundred feet deep and was a deep green color, and Chub held the two horses and he climbed out on a rock and leaned over and saw his face in the still water, and saw himself holding the gun, and then he dropped it, holding it by the muzzle, and saw it go down making bubbles until it was just as big as a watch charm in that clear water, and then it was out of sight. Then he came back off the rock and when he swung up into the saddle he gave old Bess such a clout with the spurs she started to buck like an old rocking horse. He bucked her out along the shore of the lake and as soon as she was reasonable they went on back along the trail.

“I know why you did that with the old gun, Bob,” Chub said.

“Well, then we don’t have to talk about it,” he had said. They never talked about it and that was the end of Grandfather’s side arms except for the saber. He still had the saber in his trunk with the rest of his things at Missoula. I wonder what Grandfather would think of this situation, he thought. Grandfather was a hell of a good soldier, everybody said. They said if he had been with Custer that day he never would have let him be sucked in that way. How could he ever not have seen the smoke nor the dust of all those lodges down there in the draw along the Little Big Horn unless there must have been a heavy morning mist? But there wasn’t any mist. I wish Grandfather were here instead of me. Well, maybe we will all be together by tomorrow night. If there should be any such damn fool business as a hereafter, and I’m sure there isn’t, he thought, I would certainly like to talk to him. Because there are a lot of things I would like to know. I have a right to ask him now because I have had to do the same sort of things myself. I don’t think he’d mind my asking now. I had no right to ask before. I understand him not telling me because he didn’t know me. But now I think that we would get along all right. I’d like to be able to talk to him now and get his advice. Hell, if I didn’t get advice I’d just like to talk to him. It’s a shame there is such a jump in time between ones like us. Then, as he thought, he realized that if there was any such thing as ever meeting, both he and his grandfather would be acutely embarrassed by the presence of his father. Any one has a right to do it, he thought. But it isn’t a good thing to do. I understand it, but I do not approve of it. Lache was the word. But you do understand it? Sure, I understand it but. Yes, but. You have to be awfully occupied with yourself to do a thing like that. Aw hell, I wish Grandfather was here, he thought. For about an hour anyway. Maybe he sent me what little I have through that other one that misused the gun. Maybe that is the only communication that we have. But, damn it. Truly damn it, but I wish the time-lag wasn’t so long so that I could have learned from him what the other one never had to teach me. But suppose the fear he had to go through and dominate and just get rid of finally in four years of that and then in the Indian fighting, although in that, mostly, there couldn’t have been so much fear, had made a cobarde out of the other one the way second generation bullfighters almost always are? Suppose that? And maybe the good juice only came through straight again after passing through that one? I’ll never forget how sick it made me the first time I knew he was a cobarde. Go on, say it in English. Coward. It’s easier when you have it said and there is never any point in referring to a son of a bitch by some foreign term. He wasn’t any son of a bitch, though. He was just a coward and that was the worst luck any man could have. Because if he wasn’t a coward he would have stood up to that woman and not let her bully him. I wonder what I would have been like if he had married a different woman? That’s something you’ll never know, he thought, and grinned. Maybe the bully in her helped to supply what was missing in the other. And you. Take it a little easy. Don’t get to referring to the good juice and such other things until you are through tomorrow. Don’t be snotty too soon. And then don’t be snotty at all. We’ll see what sort of juice you have tomorrow. But he started thinking about Grandfather again.

“George Custer was not an intelligent leader of cavalry, Robert,” his grandfather had said. “He was not even an intelligent man.” He remembered that when his grandfather said that he felt resentment that any one should speak against that figure in the buckskin shirt, the yellow curls blowing, that stood on that hill holding a service revolver as the Sioux closed in around him in the old Anheuser-Busch lithograph that hung on the poolroom wall in Red Lodge.

“He just had great ability to get himself in and out of trouble,” his grandfather went on, “and on the Little Big Horn he got into it but he couldn’t get out.

“Now Phil Sheridan was an intelligent man and so was Jeb Stuart. But John Mosby was the finest cavalry leader that ever lived.” He had a letter in his things in the trunk at Missoula from General Phil Sheridan to old Killy-the-Horse Kilpatrick that said his grandfather was a finer leader of irregular cavalry than John Mosby. I ought to tell Golz about my grandfather, he thought. He wouldn’t ever have heard of him though. He probably never even heard of John Mosby. The British all had heard of them though because they had to study our Civil War much more than people did on the Continent. Karkov said after this was over I could go to the Lenin Institute in Moscow if I wanted to. He said I could go to the military academy of the Red Army if I wanted to do that. I wonder what Grandfather would think of that? Grandfather, who never knowingly sat at table with a Democrat in his life. Well, I don’t want to be a soldier, he thought. I know that. So that’s out. I just want us to win this war. I guess really good soldiers are really good at very little else, he thought. That’s obviously untrue. Look at Napoleon and Wellington. You’re very stupid this evening, he thought. Usually his mind was very good company and tonight it had been when he thought about his grandfather. Then thinking of his father had thrown him off. He understood his father and he forgave him every thing and he pitied him but he was ashamed of him. You better not think at all, he told himself. Soon you will be with Maria and you won’t have to think. That’s the best way now that everything is worked out. When you have been concentrating so hard on something you can’t stop and your brain gets to racing like a flywheel with the weight gone. You better just not think. But just suppose, he thought. "There are six," he said. "Two of them are good ones."

"That's nice."

"I got the two big ones below the log jam where the river bends. Late. After the rain stopped."

"I heard the rain stop," she said. "I sat here and heard it stop."

He opened the creel and took the trout out and laid them on the oilcloth of the table on the wet ferns he had packed them in. They were cold and firm, and their backs were dark with the spots on them, and their sides were bright where the light from the lamp came on them. The two big ones were as long as his forearm.

"Look at them," he said.

"They're very beautiful."

"You didn't look at them."

"I looked at them, Peter. They're very beautiful trout."

The water was very cold and his hands ached from it. He threw the guts out into the dark for whatever would come for them. Then he brought the trout in and laid them on a clean board and dried his hands on the towel by the stove.

"Is there coffee?" he asked.

"The water's hot. I didn't make it."

"I'll make it."

He made the coffee and it boiled up and he took it off the stove and poured a little cold water in to settle the grounds. He poured two cups and put one on the sill by her. She did not pick it up. She had her hands in the pockets of her coat.

"It's warm in here," he said. "You don't need the coat."

"I know."

"You might as well take it off."

"I'd rather keep it on."

"All right," he said. He sat at the table with his cup. The coffee was hot and good and he held the cup in both hands to get the ache out of them. I will not ask about the bag, he thought. If you do not ask about it then it is only a bag by the door. A bag by the door is nothing. People put bags by doors.

"Mr. Haskell came up with the truck," she said. "About four o'clock. While it was still raining."

"What did he want?"

"That was nice of him."

"I asked him to come back," she said. "He said he would come by at seven."

"Yes. That's what the bag is."

"All right."

It was high from the rain and it made a steady sound. It had been a good day on the river. "There was a letter," she said.

"From who?"

"You know from who. It's on the table. Under the lamp."

"Yes."

"She'll be there. Yes."

"I know you will."

"No," she said. "It doesn't matter what you do with the trout."

He took his hand off her shoulder. He went back to the table and sat down and looked at the letter. He thought he might read it now. Then he thought, no, there is nothing in it you do not know. You know exactly what is in it. You knew what would be in it when you wrote the other one.

"Would you have gone?" he asked.

"Gone where?"

"To Africa. If I had told you. If I'd asked Charles if you could come."

"He didn't ask me."

"I could have asked him."

"You didn't, though."

"No."

"Why didn't you?"

He thought about it. It was not a thing he wanted to think about, but she had asked him, and he thought about it truly, the way you have to think about it when you know the answer will not help anything. Because you wanted to go alone, he thought. Not alone from her, Margaret. Not that. Alone from everything. "I don't know," he said.

"Yes, you do."

"All right. I do."

"Then tell me."

"I wanted to go by myself," he said. "Not by myself. You know what I mean. Without anybody of my own."

"Without me."

"Without anybody."

"I'm the only anybody you've got," she said. "That's the same thing."

"I suppose it is."

"That's the first true thing," she said. "Thank you for that."

"It isn't anything to thank anybody for."

"It's something," she said. "It's more than the trout."

The wind had come up a little outside and he could hear it in the tops of the birches, and under it the river. The river was the same as it had been. It would be good tomorrow, he thought. It would be clearing with the high water dropping and the fish would be on the feed in the morning. You said so yourself. Now you have it. Now you have it four weeks early and no one is paying you for it.

"What will you do?" he asked.

"Go to my sister's. In Cleveland."

"For how long?"

"I don't know. Until I know something."

"Will you write to me?"

"I don't know that either."

"Maybe," she said. "If I know anything by then."

"And if you don't know anything?"

"I don't want it to mean that."

"You wrote the letter, Peter," she said. "You wanted it to mean something. Everything you do means something. You only don't like it when it means the thing it means."

Then he got up and found the frying pan and put it on the stove and cut some bacon into it. When the bacon had cooked he took it out and put it on a plate and rolled two of the smaller trout in the corn meal and laid them in the fat. They made a fine noise and the smell was good in the cabin. She sat with her coat on and watched him.

"You don't need to cook," she said.

"I'm hungry."

"You're cooking two."

"In case you want one."

"I won't want one."

"Then I'll eat two."

He turned the trout carefully with the fork. The skins were crisp and brown and curled at the edges. He took them out and put them on the plate with the bacon and cut a piece of bread and sat down and ate. They were very good. They were as good as any trout he had ever eaten and he was ashamed that they were so good and he ate them anyway. She watched him eat.

"Is it good?" she asked.

"It's fine."

"It always is," she said. "That's the worst of it. It always is."

Then they heard the truck. It was coming up the track from the road below, slowly in the mud, and they could hear it laboring in low gear and then the lights came swinging up through the birches and across the window, white, and the birch trunks stood out very sharp in them and then the lights stopped and held. The motor ran on and he heard a door open and shut.

She stood up. She buttoned the top button of the coat, which had been the only button open, and went to the door and picked up the bag.

"I'll carry it," he said.

"I can carry it."

"Let me carry it out to the truck."

"No," she said. "Haskell will carry it."

She stood in the door with the bag. The cold air came in around her. He could see Haskell's shape against the lights of the truck, standing by the fender, waiting, not coming any closer. "Helen," he said.

"Yes."

He did not know what he had meant to say. He stood there by the table with the plate and the fish bones on it and he did not know.

"Good-bye, Peter," she said. "The trout were beautiful. Truly. I did look at them."

He sat down at the table. After a while he picked up the letter and took it out of the envelope and unfolded it and read it under the lamp. It said everything she had said it said. Very glad. It was underlined twice. He folded it and put it back in the envelope and put the envelope under the lamp where it had been.

Then he got up and wrapped the four trout that were left in a clean towel and put them out in the cold box on the back porch for the morning. He stood out there a while on the porch in the cold and looked at the stars, which were very bright now that the sky had cleared. The river would be dropping by morning. It would be clearing and dropping and the fish would be on the feed. It will be good tomorrow, he thought. It will be a fine day on the river.
