He knew with the first breath he drew that the snow had been only a freak storm in the mountains and it would be gone by noon. Then he heard a horse coming, the hoofs balled with the wet snow thumping dully as the horseman trotted. He heard the noise of a carbine scabbard slapping loosely and the creak of leather.

“Maria,” he said, and shook the girl’s shoulder to waken her. “Keep thyself under the robe,” and he buttoned his shirt with one hand and held the automatic pistol in the other, loosening the safety catch with his thumb. He saw the girl’s cropped head disappear with a jerk under the robe and then he saw the horseman coming through the trees. He crouched now in the robe and holding the pistol in both hands aimed it at the man as he rode toward him. He had never seen this man before. The horseman was almost opposite him now. He was riding a big gray gelding and he wore a khaki beret, a blanket cape like a poncho, and heavy black boots. From the scabbard on the right of his saddle projected the stock and the long oblong clip of a short automatic rifle. He had a young, hard face and at this moment he saw Robert Jordan. He reached his hand down toward the scabbard and as he swung low, turning and jerking at the scabbard, Robert Jordan saw the scarlet of the formalized device he wore on the left breast of his khaki blanket cape. Aiming at the center of his chest, a little lower than the device, Robert Jordan fired. The pistol roared in the snowy woods. The horse plunged as though he had been spurred and the young man, still tugging at the scabbard, slid over toward the ground, his right foot caught in the stirrup. The horse broke off through the trees dragging him, bumping, face downward, and Robert Jordan stood up holding the pistol now in one hand. The big gray horse was galloping through the pines. There was a broad swath in the snow where the man dragged with a scarlet streak along one side of it. People were coming out of the mouth of the cave. Robert Jordan reached down and unrolled his trousers from the pillow and began to put them on.

“Get thee dressed,” he said to Maria. Overhead he heard the noise of a plane flying very high. Through the trees he saw where the gray horse had stopped and was standing, his rider still hanging face down from the stirrup.

“Go catch that horse,” he called to Primitivo who had started over toward him. Then, “Who was on guard at the top?”

“Rafael,” Pilar said from the cave. She stood there, her hair still down her back in two braids.

“There’s cavalry out,” Robert Jordan said. “Get your damned gun up there.” He heard Pilar call, “Agustín,” into the cave. Then she went into the cave and then two men came running out, one with the automatic rifle with its tripod swung on his shoulder; the other with a sackful of the pans.

“Get up there with them,” Robert Jordan said to Anselmo. “You lie beside the gun and hold the legs still,” he said. The three of them went up the trail through the woods at a run. The sun had not yet come up over the tops of the mountains and Robert Jordan stood straight buttoning his trousers and tightening his belt, the big pistol hanging from the lanyard on his wrist. He put the pistol in its holster on his belt and slipped the knot down on the lanyard and passed the loop over his head.

Excerpt 2: Anselmo was crouched in the lee of the trunk of a big tree and the snow blew past on either side. He was pressed close against the tree and his hands were inside of the sleeves of his jacket, each hand shoved up into the opposite sleeve, and his head was pulled as far down into the jacket as it would go. If I stay here much longer I will freeze, he thought, and that will be of no value. The Inglés told me to stay until I was relieved but he did not know then about this storm. There has been no abnormal movement on the road and I know the dispositions and the habits of this post at the sawmill across the road. I should go now to the camp. Anybody with sense would be expecting me to return to the camp. I will stay a little longer, he thought, and then go to the camp. It is the fault of the orders, which are too rigid. There is no allowance for a change in circumstance. He rubbed his feet together and then took his hands out of the jacket sleeves and bent over and rubbed his legs with them and patted his feet together to keep the circulation going. It was less cold there, out of the wind in the shelter of the tree, but he would have to start walking shortly. As he crouched, rubbing his feet, he heard a motorcar on the road. It had on chains and one link of chain was slapping and, as he watched, it came up the snow-covered road, green and brown painted, in broken patches of daubed color, the windows blued over so that you could not see in, with only a half circle left clear in the blue for the occupants to look out through. It was a two-year-old Rolls Royce town car camouflaged for the use of the General Staff but Anselmo did not know that. He could not see into the car where three officers sat wrapped in their capes. Two were on the back seat and one sat on the folding chair. The officer on the folding chair was looking out of the slit in the blue of the window as the car passed but Anselmo did not know this. Neither of them saw the other. The car passed in the snow directly below him. Anselmo saw the chauffeur, red-faced and steel-helmeted, his face and helmet projecting out of the blanket cape he wore and he saw the forward jut of the automatic rifle the orderly who sat beside the chauffeur carried. Then the car was gone up the road and Anselmo reached into the inside of his jacket and took out from his shirt pocket the two sheets torn from Robert Jordan’s notebook and made a mark after the drawing of a motorcar. It was the tenth car up for the day. Six had come down. Four were still up. It was not an unusual amount of cars to move upon that road but Anselmo did not distinguish between the Fords, Fiats, Opels, Renaults, and Citroens of the staff of the Division that held the passes and the line of the mountain and the Rolls-Royces, Lancias, Mercedes, and Isottas of the General Staff. This was the sort of distinction that Robert Jordan should have made and, if he had been there instead of the old man, he would have appreciated the significance of these cars which had gone up. But he was not there and the old man simply made a mark for a motorcar going up the road, on the sheet of note paper. Anselmo was now so cold that he decided he had best go to camp before it was dark. He had no fear of missing the way, but he thought it was useless to stay longer and the wind was blowing colder all the time and there was no lessening of the snow. But when he stood up and stamped his feet and looked through the driving snow at the road he did not start off up the hillside but stayed leaning against the sheltered side of the pine tree. The Inglés told me to stay, he thought. Even now he may be on the way here and, if I leave this place, he may lose himself in the snow searching for me. All through this war we have suffered from a lack of discipline and from the disobeying of orders and I will wait a while still for the Inglés. But if he does not come soon I must go in spite of all orders for I have a report to make now, and I have much to do in these days, and to freeze here is an exaggeration and without utility. Across the road at the sawmill smoke was coming out of the chimney and Anselmo could smell it blown toward him through the snow. The fascists are warm, he thought, and they are comfortable, and tomorrow night we will kill them. It is a strange thing and I do not like to think of it. I have watched them all day and they are the same men that we are. I believe that I could walk up to the mill and knock on the door and I would be welcome except that they have orders to challenge all travellers and ask to see their papers. It is only orders that come between us. Those men are not fascists. I call them so, but they are not. They are poor men as we are. They should never be fighting against us and I do not like to think of the killing. These at this post are Gallegos. I know that from hearing them talk this afternoon. They cannot desert because if they do their families will be shot. Gallegos are either very intelligent or very dumb and brutal. I have known both kinds. Lister is a Gallego from the same town as Franco. I wonder what these Gallegos think of this snow now at this time of year. They have no high mountains such as these and in their country it always rains and it is always green. A light showed in the window of the sawmill and Anselmo shivered and thought, damn that Inglés! There are the Gallegos warm and in a house here in our country, and I am freezing behind a tree and we live in a hole in the rocks like beasts in the mountain. But tomorrow, he thought, the beasts will come out of their hole and these that are now so comfortable will die warm in their blankets. As those died in the night when we raided Otero, he thought. He did not like to remember Otero. In Otero, that night, was when he first killed and he hoped he would not have to kill in this of the suppressing of these posts. It was in Otero that Pablo knifed the sentry when Anselmo pulled the blanket over his head and the sentry caught Anselmo’s foot and held it, smothered as he was in the blanket, and made a crying noise in the blanket and Anselmo had to feel in the blanket and knife him until he let go of the foot and was still. He had his knee across the man’s throat to keep him silent and he was knifing into the bundle when Pablo tossed the bomb through the window into the room where the men of the post were all sleeping. And when the flash came it was as though the whole world burst red and yellow before your eyes and two more bombs were in already. Pablo had pulled the pins and tossed them quickly through the window, and those who were not killed in their beds were killed as they rose from bed when the second bomb exploded. That was in the great days of Pablo when he scourged the country like a tartar and no fascist post was safe at night. And now, he is as finished and as ended as a boar that has been altered, Anselmo thought, and, when the altering has been accomplished and the squealing is over you cast the two stones away and the boar, that is a boar no longer, goes snouting and rooting up to them and eats them. No, he is not that bad, Anselmo grinned, one can think too badly even of Pablo. But he is ugly enough and changed enough. It is too cold, he thought. That the Inglés should come and that I should not have to kill in this of the posts. These four Gallegos and their corporal are for those who like the killing. The Inglés said that. I will do it if it is my duty but the Inglés said that I would be with him at the bridge and that this would be left to others. At the bridge there will be a battle and, if I am able to endure the battle, then I will have done all that an old man may do in this war. But let the Inglés come now, for I am cold and to see the light in the mill where I know that the Gallegos are warm makes me colder still. I wish that I were in my own house again and that this war were over. But you have no house now, he thought. We must win this war before you can ever return to your house. Inside the sawmill one of the soldiers was sitting on his bunk and greasing his boots. Another lay in his bunk sleeping. The third was cooking and the corporal was reading a paper. Their helmets hung on nails driven into the wall and their rifles leaned against the plank wall.

“What kind of country is this where it snows when it is almost June?” the soldier who was sitting on the bunk said.

“It is a phenomenon,” the corporal said.

“We are in the moon of May,” the soldier who was cooking said. “The moon of May has not yet terminated.”

“What kind of a country is it where it snows in May?” the soldier on the bunk insisted.

“In May snow is no rarity in these mountains,” the corporal said. “I have been colder in Madrid in the month of May than in any other month.”

“And hotter, too,” the soldier who was cooking said.

“May is a month of great contrasts in temperature,” the corporal said. “Here, in Castile, May is a month of great heat but it can have much cold.”

“Or rain,” the soldier on the bunk said. “In this past May it rained almost every day.”

“It did not,” the soldier who was cooking said. “And anyway this past May was the moon of April.”

“One could go crazy listening to thee and thy moons,” the corporal said. “Leave this of the moons alone.”

“Any one who lives either by the sea or by the land knows that it is the moon and not the month which counts,” the soldier who was cooking said. “Now for example, we have just started the moon of May. Yet it is coming on June.”

“Why then do we not get definitely behind in the seasons?” the corporal said. “The whole proposition gives me a headache.”

“You are from a town,” the soldier who was cooking said. “You are from Lugo. What would you know of the sea or of the land?”

“One learns more in a town than you analfabetos learn in thy sea or thy land.”

“In this moon the first of the big schools of sardines come,” the soldier who was cooking said. “In this moon the sardine boats will be outfitting and the mackerel will have gone north.”

“Why are you not in the navy if you come from Noya?” the corporal asked.

“Because I am not inscribed from Noya but from Negreira, where I was born. And from Negreira, which is up the river Tambre, they take you for the army.”

“Worse luck,” said the corporal.

“Do not think the navy is without peril,” the soldier who was sitting on the bunk said. “Even without the possibility of combat that is a dangerous coast in the winter.”

“Nothing can be worse than the army,” the corporal said.

“And you a corporal,” the soldier who was cooking said. “What a way of speaking is that?”

“Nay,” the corporal said. “I mean for dangers. I mean the endurance of bombardments, the necessity to attack, the life of the parapet.”

“Here we have little of that,” the soldier on the bunk said.

“By the Grace of God,” the corporal said. “But who knows when we will be subject to it again? Certainly we will not have something as easy as this forever!”

“How much longer do you think we will have this detail?”

“I don’t know,” the corporal said. “But I wish we could have it for all of the war.”

“Six hours is too long to be on guard,” the soldier who was cooking said.

“We will have three-hour watches as long as this storm holds,” the corporal said. “That is only normal.”

“What about all those staff cars?” the soldier on the bunk asked. “I did not like the look of all those staff cars.”

“Nor I,” the corporal said. “All such things are of evil omen.”

“And aviation,” the soldier who was cooking said. “Aviation is another bad sign.”

“But we have formidable aviation,” the corporal said. “The reds have no aviation such as we have. Those planes this morning were something to make any man happy.”

“I have seen the red planes when they were something serious,” the soldier on the bunk said. “I have seen those two motor bombers when they were a horror to endure.”

“Yes. But they are not as formidable as our aviation,” the corporal said. “We have an aviation that is insuperable.” This was how they were talking in the sawmill while Anselmo waited in the snow watching the road and the light in the sawmill window. I hope I am not for the killing, Anselmo was thinking. I think that after the war there will have to be some great penance done for the killing. If we no longer have religion after the war then I think there must be some form of civic penance organized that all may be cleansed from the killing or else we will never have a true and human basis for living. The killing is necessary, I know, but still the doing of it is very bad for a man and I think that, after all this is over and we have won the war, there must be a penance of some kind for the cleansing of us all. Anselmo was a very good man and whenever he was alone for long, and he was alone much of the time, this problem of the killing returned to him. I wonder about the Inglés, he thought. He told me that he did not mind it. Yet he seems to be both sensitive and kind. It may be that in the younger people it does not have an importance. It may be that in foreigners, or in those who have not had our religion, there is not the same attitude. But I think any one doing it will be brutalized in time and I think that even though necessary, it is a great sin and that afterwards we must do something very strong to atone for it. It was dark now and he looked at the light across the road and shook his arms against his chest to warm them. Now, he thought, he would certainly leave for the camp; but something kept him there beside the tree above the road. It was snowing harder and Anselmo thought: if only we could blow the bridge tonight. On a night like this it would be nothing to take the posts and blow the bridge and it would be all over and done with. On a night like this you could do anything. Then he stood there against the tree stamping his feet softly and he did not think any more about the bridge. The coming of the dark always made him feel lonely and tonight he felt so lonely that there was a hollowness in him as of hunger. In the old days he could help this loneliness by saying of prayers and often coming home from hunting he would repeat a great number of the same prayer and it made him feel better. But he had not prayed once since the movement. He missed the prayers but he thought it would be unfair and hypocritical to say them and he did not wish to ask any favors or for any different treatment than all the men were receiving.

Excerpt 3: So now everything had been done that there was to do that night. All orders had been given. Every one knew exactly what he was to do in the morning. Andrés had been gone three hours. Either it would come now with the coming of the daylight or it would not come. I believe that it will come, Robert Jordan told himself, walking back down from the upper post where he had gone to speak to Primitivo. Golz makes the attack but he has not the power to cancel it. Permission to cancel it will have to come from Madrid. The chances are they won’t be able to wake anybody up there and if they do wake up they will be too sleepy to think. I should have gotten word to Golz sooner of the preparations they have made to meet the attack, but how could I send word about something until it happened? They did not move up that stuff until just at dark. They did not want to have any movement on the road spotted by planes. But what about all their planes? What about those fascist planes? Surely our people must have been warned by them. But perhaps the fascists were faking for another offensive down through Guadalajara with them. There were supposed to be Italian troops concentrated in Soria, and at Siguenza again besides those operating in the North. They haven’t enough troops or material to run two major offensives at the same time though. That is impossible; so it must be just a bluff. But we know how many troops the Italians have landed all last month and the month before at Cádiz. It is always possible they will try again at Guadalajara, not stupidly as before, but with three main fingers coming down to broaden it out and carry it along the railway to the west of the plateau. There was a way that they could do it all right. Hans had shown him. They made many mistakes the first time. The whole conception was unsound. They had not used any of the same troops in the Arganda offensive against the Madrid-Valencia road that they used at Guadalajara. Why had they not made those same drives simultaneously? Why? Why? When would we know why? Yet we had stopped them both times with the very same troops. We never could have stopped them if they had pulled both drives at once. Don’t worry, he told himself. Look at the miracles that have happened before this. Either you will have to blow that bridge in the morning or you will not have to. But do not start deceiving yourself into thinking you won’t have to blow it. You will blow it one day or you will blow it another. Or if it is not this bridge it will be some other bridge. It is not you who decides what shall be done. You follow orders. Follow them and do not try to think beyond them. The orders on this are very clear. Too very clear. But you must not worry nor must you be frightened. For if you allow yourself the luxury of normal fear that fear will infect those who must work with you. But that heads business was quite a thing all the same, he told himself. And the old man running onto them on the hilltop alone. How would you have liked to run onto them like that? That impressed you, didn’t it? Yes, that impressed you, Jordan. You have been quite impressed more than once today. But you have behaved O.K. So far you have behaved all right. You do very well for an instructor in Spanish at the University of Montana, he joked at himself. You do all right for that. But do not start to thinking that you are anything very special. You haven’t gotten very far in this business. Just remember Durán, who never had any military training and who was a composer and lad about town before the movement and is now a damned good general commanding a brigade. It was all as simple and easy to learn and understand to Durán as chess to a child chess prodigy. You had read on and studied the art of war ever since you were a boy and your grandfather had started you on the American Civil War. Except that Grandfather always called it the War of the Rebellion. But compared with Durán you were like a good sound chess player against a boy prodigy. Old Durán. It would be good to see Durán again. He would see him at Gaylord’s after this was over. Yes. After this was over. See how well he was behaving? I’ll see him at Gaylord’s, he said to himself again, after this is over. Don’t kid yourself, he said. You do it all perfectly O.K. Cold. Without kidding yourself. You aren’t going to see Durán any more and it is of no importance. Don’t be that way either, he told himself. Don’t go in for any of those luxuries. Nor for heroic resignation either. We do not want any citizens full of heroic resignation in these hills. Your grandfather fought four years in our Civil War and you are just finishing your first year in this war. You have a long time to go yet and you are very well fitted for the work. And now you have Maria, too. Why, you’ve got everything. You shouldn’t worry. What is a little brush between a guerilla band and a squadron of cavalry? That isn’t anything. What if they took the heads? Does that make any difference? None at all. The Indians always took the scalps when Grandfather was at Fort Kearny after the war. Do you remember the cabinet in your father’s office with the arrowheads spread out on a shelf, and the eagle feathers of the war bonnets that hung on the wall, their plumes slanting, the smoked buckskin smell of the leggings and the shirts and the feel of the beaded moccasins? Do you remember the great stave of the buffalo bow that leaned in a corner of the cabinet and the two quivers of hunting and war arrows, and how the bundle of shafts felt when you closed your hand around them? Remember something like that. Remember something concrete and practical. Remember Grandfather’s saber, bright and well oiled in its dented scabbard and Grandfather showed you how the blade had beer thinned from the many times it had been to the grinder’s. Remember Grandfather’s Smith and Wesson. It was a single action, officer’s model .32 caliber and there was no trigger guard. It had the softest, sweetest trigger pull you had ever felt and it was always well oiled and the bore was clean although the finish was all worn off and the brown metal of the barrel and the cylinder was worn smooth from the leather of the holster. It was kept in the holster with a U. S. on the flap in a drawer in the cabinet with its cleaning equipment and two hundred rounds of cartridges. Their cardboard boxes were wrapped and tied neatly with waxed twine. You could take the pistol out of the drawer and hold it. “Handle it freely,” was Grandfather’s expression. But you could not play with it because it was “a serious weapon.” You asked Grandfather once if he had ever killed any one with it and he said, “Yes.” Then you said, “When, Grandfather?” and he said, “In the War of the Rebellion and afterwards.” You said, “Will you tell me about it, Grandfather?” And he said, “I do not care to speak about it, Robert.” Then after your father had shot himself with this pistol, and you had come home from school and they’d had the funeral, the coroner had returned it after the inquest saying, “Bob, I guess you might want to keep the gun. I’m supposed to hold it, but I know your dad set a lot of store by it because his dad packed it all through the War, besides out here when he first came out with the Cavalry, and it’s still a hell of a good gun. I had her out trying her this afternoon. She don’t throw much of a slug but you can hit things with her.” He had put the gun back in the drawer in the cabinet where it belonged, but the next day he took it out and he had ridden up to the top of the high country above Red Lodge, with Chub, where they had built the road to Cooke City now over the pass and across the Bear Tooth plateau, and up there where the wind was thin and there was snow all summer on the hills they had stopped by the lake which was supposed to be eight hundred feet deep and was a deep green color, and Chub held the two horses and he climbed out on a rock and leaned over and saw his face in the still water, and saw himself holding the gun, and then he dropped it, holding it by the muzzle, and saw it go down making bubbles until it was just as big as a watch charm in that clear water, and then it was out of sight. Then he came back off the rock and when he swung up into the saddle he gave old Bess such a clout with the spurs she started to buck like an old rocking horse. He bucked her out along the shore of the lake and as soon as she was reasonable they went on back along the trail.

“I know why you did that with the old gun, Bob,” Chub said.

“Well, then we don’t have to talk about it,” he had said. They never talked about it and that was the end of Grandfather’s side arms except for the saber. He still had the saber in his trunk with the rest of his things at Missoula. I wonder what Grandfather would think of this situation, he thought. Grandfather was a hell of a good soldier, everybody said. They said if he had been with Custer that day he never would have let him be sucked in that way. How could he ever not have seen the smoke nor the dust of all those lodges down there in the draw along the Little Big Horn unless there must have been a heavy morning mist? But there wasn’t any mist. I wish Grandfather were here instead of me. Well, maybe we will all be together by tomorrow night. If there should be any such damn fool business as a hereafter, and I’m sure there isn’t, he thought, I would certainly like to talk to him. Because there are a lot of things I would like to know. I have a right to ask him now because I have had to do the same sort of things myself. I don’t think he’d mind my asking now. I had no right to ask before. I understand him not telling me because he didn’t know me. But now I think that we would get along all right. I’d like to be able to talk to him now and get his advice. Hell, if I didn’t get advice I’d just like to talk to him. It’s a shame there is such a jump in time between ones like us. Then, as he thought, he realized that if there was any such thing as ever meeting, both he and his grandfather would be acutely embarrassed by the presence of his father. Any one has a right to do it, he thought. But it isn’t a good thing to do. I understand it, but I do not approve of it. Lache was the word. But you do understand it? Sure, I understand it but. Yes, but. You have to be awfully occupied with yourself to do a thing like that. Aw hell, I wish Grandfather was here, he thought. For about an hour anyway. Maybe he sent me what little I have through that other one that misused the gun. Maybe that is the only communication that we have. But, damn it. Truly damn it, but I wish the time-lag wasn’t so long so that I could have learned from him what the other one never had to teach me. But suppose the fear he had to go through and dominate and just get rid of finally in four years of that and then in the Indian fighting, although in that, mostly, there couldn’t have been so much fear, had made a cobarde out of the other one the way second generation bullfighters almost always are? Suppose that? And maybe the good juice only came through straight again after passing through that one? I’ll never forget how sick it made me the first time I knew he was a cobarde. Go on, say it in English. Coward. It’s easier when you have it said and there is never any point in referring to a son of a bitch by some foreign term. He wasn’t any son of a bitch, though. He was just a coward and that was the worst luck any man could have. Because if he wasn’t a coward he would have stood up to that woman and not let her bully him. I wonder what I would have been like if he had married a different woman? That’s something you’ll never know, he thought, and grinned. Maybe the bully in her helped to supply what was missing in the other. And you. Take it a little easy. Don’t get to referring to the good juice and such other things until you are through tomorrow. Don’t be snotty too soon. And then don’t be snotty at all. We’ll see what sort of juice you have tomorrow. But he started thinking about Grandfather again.

“George Custer was not an intelligent leader of cavalry, Robert,” his grandfather had said. “He was not even an intelligent man.” He remembered that when his grandfather said that he felt resentment that any one should speak against that figure in the buckskin shirt, the yellow curls blowing, that stood on that hill holding a service revolver as the Sioux closed in around him in the old Anheuser-Busch lithograph that hung on the poolroom wall in Red Lodge.

“He just had great ability to get himself in and out of trouble,” his grandfather went on, “and on the Little Big Horn he got into it but he couldn’t get out.

“Now Phil Sheridan was an intelligent man and so was Jeb Stuart. But John Mosby was the finest cavalry leader that ever lived.” He had a letter in his things in the trunk at Missoula from General Phil Sheridan to old Killy-the-Horse Kilpatrick that said his grandfather was a finer leader of irregular cavalry than John Mosby. I ought to tell Golz about my grandfather, he thought. He wouldn’t ever have heard of him though. He probably never even heard of John Mosby. The British all had heard of them though because they had to study our Civil War much more than people did on the Continent. Karkov said after this was over I could go to the Lenin Institute in Moscow if I wanted to. He said I could go to the military academy of the Red Army if I wanted to do that. I wonder what Grandfather would think of that? Grandfather, who never knowingly sat at table with a Democrat in his life. Well, I don’t want to be a soldier, he thought. I know that. So that’s out. I just want us to win this war. I guess really good soldiers are really good at very little else, he thought. That’s obviously untrue. Look at Napoleon and Wellington. You’re very stupid this evening, he thought. Usually his mind was very good company and tonight it had been when he thought about his grandfather. Then thinking of his father had thrown him off. He understood his father and he forgave him every thing and he pitied him but he was ashamed of him. You better not think at all, he told himself. Soon you will be with Maria and you won’t have to think. That’s the best way now that everything is worked out. When you have been concentrating so hard on something you can’t stop and your brain gets to racing like a flywheel with the weight gone. You better just not think. But just suppose, he thought. Just suppose that when the planes unload they smash those anti-tank guns and just blow hell out of the positions and the old tanks roll good up whatever hill it is for once and old Golz boots that bunch of drunks, clochards, bums, fanatics and heroes that make up the Quatorzième Brigade ahead of him, and I know how good Durán’s people are in Golz’s other brigade, and we are in Segovia tomorrow night. Yes. Just suppose, he said to himself. I’ll settle for La Granja, he told himself. But you are going to have to blow that bridge, he suddenly knew absolutely. There won’t be any calling off. Because the way you have just been supposing there for a minute is how the possibilities of that attack look to those who have ordered it. Yes, you will have to blow the bridge, he knew truly. Whatever happens to Andrés doesn’t matter.

The fish were in the ferns below the big rock where the river came around the bend and slowed and went deep and dark under the cut bank. He found them because of the flies. He had come down the trail from the meadow with the rod in his hand and the creel slapping against his hip, and he smelled them before he saw them. Then he saw the flies rising and settling and rising in the slant of sun that came through the willows, and he leaned the rod against a tree and pushed the ferns apart with his boot and there they were.

There were eleven of them. They were brook trout and they were small, the biggest no longer than his hand, and they lay in a heap where they had been thrown. Some of them had been there since the morning. Their colors had gone. When you take a brook trout from the water it is the most beautiful thing there is, dark green and mottled on the back and the red spots ringed with blue on the sides and the belly orange and the fins edged clean in white. Then it dries and all of that goes out of it and it is only a fish and then it is not even a fish. These had gone gray and their eyes were dull and sunk, and the ants had found them, and the flies were walking on them.

He squatted down and looked at them. He did not touch them. He looked at the willow switch lying beside them and at the place in the mud of the bank where the boy had knelt. There was the print of a small knee and the toe of a small shoe. There was a hook in the willow switch, a cheap hook with a piece of line tied to it badly, and there was the can of worms, open, with the worms dried in the bottom of it.

So that was what he had been doing all morning, the man thought. That was why he was so quiet at noon and did not want his dinner.

He stood up. His knees cracked and he heard the river going over the stones at the riffle above the pool. A kingfisher went down the river low and fast and rattling. It was a fine day and it had been a fine day all day and now it was not.

Don't go up there angry, he told himself. You are angry now and you had better not go up there like that. Sit down a while. There is no hurry. The fish are not going anywhere.

He sat down on the rock and took out his pipe and filled it and did not light it. He held it in his hand.

What did you expect, he thought. He is seven. He is seven years old and he has watched you catch fish all summer and he wanted to catch fish. That is natural. There is nothing wrong in that. He found the hook in your box and the line and he dug the worms behind the woodshed and he cut the switch and came down here alone, which he is not supposed to do, and he caught fish. He caught eleven fish. That is pretty good. That is better than you did at seven.

But he caught them and he threw them in the ferns. He did not clean them. He did not bring them up. He caught one and threw it in the ferns and then caught another, and he kept on catching them because it was fine to catch them, and he did not think about them at all after they were out of the water.

And then he did not say anything about it.

That was the part. The man knew that was the part. He could have come up at noon with the fish dirty and stinking in his shirt and said, look, I caught them, and it would have been bad, but it would have been a different thing. He had not said anything. He had sat at the table and pushed the beans around on the plate and said he was not hungry and gone out to the porch with the dog.

He remembered his own father. His father had never hit him but once. It was for lying. It was not even much of a lie. He had said he had shut the gate when he had not shut the gate, and the heifers got out into the oats. His father had not said anything about the heifers. He had only said, You told me you shut it. And then he had taken off his belt. Afterwards he had put the belt back on and gone out to get the heifers and he had not spoken about it again, not that night and not ever. The man had been about this age. He could not remember now whether it had hurt very much. He remembered his father's face though. He remembered that very well.

I am not going to do that, he thought. That was his way and it was not a bad way, maybe, but I am not going to do it. Then what are you going to do? You had better know before you go up there. You had better know exactly.

He lit the pipe finally and smoked it and watched the water. A trout rose at the tail of the pool, a good one, and he watched the rings go out and flatten in the current and he did not want to fish any more. He knocked the pipe out against the rock and stepped on the ashes, and picked up the rod and took it down and put it in the case, and went up the trail.

The boy was on the porch. He was sitting on the top step with his arm around the dog's neck and the dog was asleep. The boy was not asleep. He was watching the trail where it came out of the timber and he had been watching it for some time, the man could tell, because when he saw his father he took his arm off the dog and sat up straight and then did not know what to do with his hands.

"Hello," the man said.

"Hello."

"Did you have a good day?"

"Yes."

"What did you do?"

"Nothing."

The man leaned the rod case against the porch rail and unbuckled the creel and set it down. He did not sit down. He stood at the foot of the steps so that his face was about level with the boy's face.

"Nothing all day?"

"I played with Jack," the boy said. "I played with Jack in the meadow."

"That's good," the man said. "Did you go down to the river?"

The boy looked at the dog. The dog had his eyes shut and his chin flat on the boards of the porch and one ear was turned inside out. The boy reached over and put the ear right.

"Did you go down to the river?"

"No."

"You did not go down to the river at all."

"No."

The man waited. He did not say anything and the boy did not say anything. It was very quiet. He could hear the river from here, faintly, and a jay somewhere in the pines behind the cabin, and the dog breathing. The boy did not look up.

"I am going to ask you one more time," the man said. "I am not going to ask you after that. Did you go down to the river?"

The boy's face began to go. It began at the chin. The man watched it and he wanted to stop it and he did not stop it. He made himself stand there.

"Yes," the boy said.

"All right."

"I'm sorry."

"All right. Come on."

"Where?"

"Down there. Come on."

The boy got up and the dog woke and got up too and stretched, first the front and then the back, and the man said, "No. Stay," and the dog lay down again and looked at them. They went down the trail. The man walked ahead and the boy walked behind him and he could hear the boy's shoes on the trail and hear him sniffing. He did not turn around. The trail went through the meadow and the grass was high and gone to seed and the grasshoppers went up ahead of them, clacking, and came down, and went up again. Then they were in the timber and it was cool and dark and the trail was soft with needles, and then they came out by the willows and the big rock and the man stopped.

"Show me," he said.

The boy did not move.

"Go on. Show me."

The boy went to the ferns and stood by them. He did not push them apart. He stood there looking down at them with his hands at his sides.

"How many did you catch?"

"I don't know."

"Count them."

The boy squatted down and counted them without touching them. He moved his lips. The flies got up when he leaned close and he jerked his head back and then leaned in again.

"Eleven."

"That's a lot of fish."

"Yes."

"Were you going to eat them?"

"I don't know."

"You don't know. Were you going to give them to anybody to eat?"

"No."

"Were you going to clean them?"

"I don't know how."

"You've watched me do it all summer."

"I don't know how to do it with the knife."

"Then why did you keep catching them?"

The boy did not say anything. He was crying now. He was crying quietly with his face down and the tears were going off the end of his nose into the ferns. The man stood and looked at him and it was very bad. It was a bad thing to watch and he knew it was a bad thing for the boy and he made himself go on with it. If you stop now, he thought, it is worse. If you stop now he has cried for nothing.

"Look at me," he said.

The boy looked up.

"Listen to me now. There are two things. There are two things and I am only going to tell you about them once and then we will not talk about them any more. Do you understand?"

"Yes."

"The first thing is the fish. When you take a fish out of the river it is yours. Do you understand that? It was the river's and now it is yours and you have to do right by it. You kill it clean and quick, you hit it on the head so it doesn't suffer, and you clean it, and you take it home and you eat it. Or you give it to someone who will eat it. Or if you don't want it you put it back in the water before it's hurt. You don't take it out and leave it to die in the ferns. You don't ever do that."

"I didn't know."

"You knew. You knew because you didn't tell me. If you didn't know you would have come up and shown me." The man stopped. He breathed. "All right. Maybe you didn't know about the fish. Maybe you didn't think about it. That can happen. I'll tell you now and then you'll know. Now you know."

"Yes."

"The second thing is worse. The second thing is that you told me you didn't come down here. You looked at me and you told me that."

"I'm sorry."

"I know you're sorry. You're sorry because I found them. Would you have told me if I didn't find them?"

The boy thought about it. The man could see him thinking about it, whether to lie again, and he could see him decide not to, and he was glad of that. That was something. He would remember that.

"No," the boy said.

"No. That's right. Thank you for saying it." The man squatted down then so that they were the same height and he did not touch the boy. "Listen. You can do almost anything and I can fix it or we can fix it together. If you break something we can fix it. If you get hurt we can fix it. If you do something wrong like this with the fish, well, that's bad, but you tell me and then we know about it and we fix it. But if you lie to me then I don't know anything. Then I don't know what is true and what isn't. Then every time you tell me anything I have to wonder about it. Do you want me to have to wonder about everything you say?"

"No."

"I don't want to either. That would be a bad way for us to be."

"Yes."

"All right," the man said. "That's all. That's the two things."

He stood up. The boy was still squatting by the ferns and he was not crying so hard now. He wiped his nose on the back of his wrist and then on his shirt.

"Are you going to whip me?"

"No."

"Are you going to tell Mother?"

"You are going to tell her. Tonight at supper."

The boy looked at the fish.

"What are we going to do with them?"

"What do you think we should do?"

"Eat them?"

"They're no good to eat now. They've been in the sun. You'd get sick."

"Then what?"

"We are going to bury them," the man said. "You're going to bury them. I'll get the shovel."

"Can't we throw them in the river?"

"You could. The other fish would eat them, and the crayfish. That's not wrong. But I want you to bury them. I want you to dig the hole."

He went up to the cabin for the shovel. He walked fast and he did not look back. When he came out of the timber into the meadow the sun was lower and the grass had gone gold at the tops and the shadow of the mountain had come down across the far end of it. The dog was on the porch where they had left him and he thumped his tail on the boards when the man came up. His wife was in the kitchen. He could hear her moving the stove lids. He took the short shovel from where it leaned beside the woodpile and did not go in.

When he came back down the boy was sitting on the rock where he himself had sat. He had stopped crying. He got up when he saw the shovel.

"Here," the man said. "Up there in the soft ground, away from the bank. Not too close to the water."

The boy took the shovel. It was too big for him even though it was the short one and he had to hold it low down on the handle. He picked a place under a spruce where the needles were thick and he scraped them back and began to dig. He dug badly at first. He put his foot on the blade and it did not go in and he put both feet on it and stood on it and rocked and it went in a little. The man watched him and did not help. Roots, he thought. He has found the roots. He will have to work around them. The boy worked around them. He dug and stopped and breathed and dug again. His face was red and his hair was wet at the forehead and stuck down. The man sat on the rock and filled his pipe again and lit it this time and smoked and watched the boy dig and watched the river. Something rose again at the tail of the pool. It was the same fish probably. It was a good fish.

He thought: you were too hard on him. Then he thought: no, you were not. You said it once and you said it plain and you did not hit him and you did not shout at him. That is all you could do. That is all there is to do. He will hate you for a while today and maybe tonight. Then he will not.

Did you hate your father? he asked himself. That time with the belt? No. You were afraid of him. That was different. You were afraid of him for a long time after that and you never told him anything after that, true or not. You never told him anything that mattered at all. That's the thing. That's the thing you don't want.

"Is this deep enough?"

The man got up and looked. It was about a foot deep and not very wide and the sides were caving in where the dirt was dry.

"That's fine. That's a good hole."

"Do I have to pick them up?"

"Use the shovel."

The boy went to the ferns and tried to get the fish on the shovel and they kept sliding off. They were stiff and some of them had stuck to each other. The flies came up around his face and he shut his eyes and turned his head away and kept trying. He got three of them on the blade and carried them up holding the shovel out in front of him and tipped them in. Then he went back. It took him four trips. On the last trip he picked up one that had fallen off, picked it up in his fingers by the tail, quickly, and ran with it and threw it in, and then he wiped his fingers on the ground for a long time.

"Now the worms," the man said.

"The worms too?"

"They died too. You left them in the sun."

The boy got the can and tipped it out over the fish and the worms fell out in a dry clump. Then he filled in the hole. He did it with the shovel and then with his hands and then he stood on it and stamped it down, and then without being told he pulled the spruce needles back over it with his fingers so you could not tell where it had been.

"That's good," the man said. "That's well done."

The boy stood there with dirt on his knees and his hands and on his face where he had wiped it.

"Go wash in the river," the man said. "Wash your hands good. With sand."

The boy went down to the edge and knelt where he had knelt that morning and put his hands in the water and scrubbed them with the gravel from the bottom. The man watched him. The boy washed his face too, ducking his whole face down close to the water and splashing it, and came up blowing, and then he sat back on his heels and looked at the river for a while. Then he came back up the bank.

"Can I ask you something?"

"Sure."

"Will you show me how to do it with the knife?"

"Yes."

"Tomorrow?"

"Tomorrow, if you want."

"And then I can catch them?"

"Then you can catch them," the man said. "You can catch as many as we can eat. Not more. And not alone. You come and get me first."

"All right."

"Do you know how many we can eat? The three of us?"

"How many?"

"Six," the man said. "Six is plenty. Seven if they are small."

"I caught eleven."

"I know it."

They went up the trail. This time the boy walked ahead and the man carried the shovel and the rod case together over his shoulder. In the timber it was nearly dark already and out in the meadow it was still light and the grasshoppers had stopped. The boy stopped once and waited for him and when the man came up the boy walked beside him and after a little while the boy put his hand on the man's belt, the way he had done when he was very small and the grass was taller than he was, and held on to it. The man did not say anything about it. He walked a little slower so the boy would not have to hurry.

At supper the boy told his mother. He told it badly and out of order and he told the part about the lie first and the fish second, and his mother looked at the man across the table and the man shook his head a little and she did not say anything except, "Well. I'm glad you told me." Then she gave him more potatoes and he ate them. He ate everything on the plate that night and he ate a piece of pie and then he was asleep in the chair and the man carried him in and took off his shoes and put him to bed in his clothes.

Afterwards the man sat on the porch with the dog. It was cold now. The stars were out very thick over the mountain and he could hear the river plainly in the dark, much louder than in the daytime, the way it always was at night. His wife came out and stood behind him and put her hand on his shoulder.

"Was it very bad?"

"No," he said. "It wasn't bad. He did fine."

"And you?"

"I did all right, I think."

"Did you whip him?"

"No."

She stood there a while longer and then she went in. He sat and smoked. He thought about the fish in the ground under the spruce and the boy stamping the dirt down and pulling the needles back over it so you could not tell. He thought about his father putting his belt back on and going out after the heifers in the oats and never speaking of it. He thought about how his father's face had looked. He tried to remember if his father had been sorry and he could not remember and he knew now that he would never know. That was the worst of it. Not the belt. That you never knew.

Well, he thought. Tomorrow you'll show him how to do it with the knife. You'll show him where to put the point in and how to run it up to the gills and how to take the gills out with your thumb and run your thumbnail down along the spine to get the blood out. You'll show him all of it. And he'll do it badly the first time and then he'll do it better.

The dog put his head on the man's knee and the man rubbed the dog's ears and they stayed out there like that until the cold drove them in.

response:
It was late in August, and the heat had not broken. All day the wind had blown from the south, hot and steady, as if it came out of a furnace door somewhere below the Kansas line, and the corn in the long field west of the house had rolled its leaves into tight gray tubes against it. By evening the wind fell, as it usually did, and the whole country lay quiet under a sky that was neither blue nor white, but a kind of pale, burned color, like the inside of a shell. The windmill had stopped turning. Even the cattle, standing in the dry draw below the barn, seemed too tired to low.

Marta Brandt had finished the supper dishes and set the pan of water on the back step for the hens. She stood a moment in the doorway, wiping her hands on her apron and looking off toward the west, where the sun was going down red through the dust. She was a tall woman, thirty-four years old that summer, with a broad, fair face and heavy yellow hair that she wore wound in a braid about her head, as her mother had worn hers in the old country. Her hands were large and brown, and there was a white scar across the back of one of them where a hay hook had caught her the year she was fourteen. She had been born in a sod house on this very quarter section, and she had never lived anywhere else.

Her husband was sitting at the kitchen table with a letter spread out before him under the lamp. He had read it twice at supper, without saying anything, and then had folded it and put it in his shirt pocket; but as soon as she rose to clear the table he took it out again. Marta knew what was in the letter. It had come that morning, when Will drove to Hollis for the mail, and she had seen the printed name of the bank in the corner of the envelope before he slipped it inside his coat. She had said nothing all day. She had waited, because she knew that Will would speak when he was ready, and that nothing she could do would make him ready sooner.

Will Brandt was a slight, sandy man, with pale blue eyes that were always a little red at the rims from wind and sun, and a mustache that he kept clipped short. He had come out from Ohio when he was twenty, with a team and a wagon and very little else, and had worked for Marta's father for two seasons before he married her. Old Kovar had liked him. He said Will was steady and did not drink, and that he was not ashamed to learn. That was a great deal for the old man to say of anyone, and Marta had never forgotten it.

She came in and sat down across from him, folding her hands on the oilcloth. The lamp hissed a little. A moth had got in and was knocking against the chimney.

"Well," she said at last, "you might as well tell me."

Will did not look up at once. He smoothed the letter with the flat of his hand, as if it had been wrinkled, though it was not.

"Ferris wants an answer by the first," he said. "He's raised his offer. Thirty-two dollars an acre for the whole half section, the buildings thrown in. That's more than anybody's got around here, Marta. Lindgren only got twenty-six, and his was better land."

"Lindgren's land was not better."

"It lies better. It hasn't got the draw cutting through it."

She did not answer that. The draw was where her father had dug his first well, and where the plum bushes grew, and where, every spring of her girlhood, she had gone to look for the first pasqueflowers coming up through the dead grass. She did not think the draw was a fault in the land. But she knew it was no use to say so to Will, who reckoned land by what it would carry, as a man ought to reckon it.

"Thirty-two dollars," Will said again, slowly, as though he were tasting the words. "That would clear the mortgage and leave us better than four thousand. With four thousand I could buy into the implement business with Ed. He's been after me two years. He says there's a living in it for both of us, with the new settlers coming into the north end of the county. We could have a house in town, Marta, with a furnace in it, and the girls could go to the high school. You wouldn't have to carry water any more, or set out in the snow to milk."

"I don't mind the milking."

"You say that."

"I say it because it's so."

He looked at her then. There was something tired and stubborn in his face that she had seen growing there for three summers now, ever since the first dry year. She had watched it come the way one watches a gully cut into a hillside after the spring rains—a little deeper every season, so that one hardly notices until it is a thing that cannot be filled in again.

"It's not just the milking," he said. "It's all of it. You know how it's been. Three years we've put the crop in, and three years it's burned up in July. I've got a note at the bank I can't pay, and the interest on the mortgage besides. Ferris isn't making this offer out of kindness. He knows how we're fixed. He knows if we wait another year he can buy it for the debt."

"Then we will have another year," Marta said. "It won't be dry forever. It was dry in eighty-four, and in ninety-four, Papa said, so dry the river at Hollis stopped running. Then it rained again."

"Your father lost his team in ninety-four."

"Yes. And he bought another team."

Will put his elbows on the table and pressed the heels of his hands against his eyes. When he took them away the rims of his eyes were redder than before.

"I'm not your father, Marta," he said quietly.

The words seemed to stay in the room after he had spoken them. The moth had fallen to the table and lay on its back under the lamp, its legs moving feebly. Marta reached out and turned it over with her finger, and it crawled a little way and was still.

She knew that what he said was true, and she knew, too, that it was the thing he had been wanting to say for a long time. Her father had been a hard man, a silent man, who had come from a village in Moravia where his people had been weavers for four hundred years, and who had broken prairie sod with a borrowed plow because he would not, he said, weave another man's cloth all his life. He had buried two children on this land, and his wife, and at last he had been buried on it himself, at his own wish, in the little fenced plot on the rise beyond the draw, where he could see, as he put it, the whole of what he had done. Marta had loved him without ever being able to say so. Will had respected him and been afraid of him, and she understood now, sitting across from her husband in the lamplight, that for twelve years he had been living in the old man's house, and plowing the old man's fields, and sleeping in the old man's bed, and that he had never once felt that any of it belonged to him.

The thought came upon her so suddenly that she drew in her breath. She looked at Will's hands on the table—thin hands, freckled across the backs, with the knuckles swollen from cold winters—and she felt something she had not expected to feel. It was not anger. It was nearer to shame.

"I never asked you to be," she said.

"No. You never asked." He folded the letter in halves, and then in quarters, very carefully. "But you've measured me against him, all the same. Every season. When I put in wheat where he'd have put in corn. When I sold the roan colt. When I wanted to take down that old windbreak because it was shading the garden. You never said a word, but I could see it in you."

"The windbreak was Mama's. She planted it with her own hands. She carried water to those trees in buckets from the well, the first five years, before they would live."

"I know it. That's what I'm saying."

Marta was silent. Outside, very far off, a dog was barking, and then it stopped. The air coming in through the screen door was a little cooler now, and it smelled of dust and of the dry sweet clover along the road.

She tried to think how it must have been for him, coming to this country with nothing—no people behind him, no language but the plain one, nothing to hold to but his own two hands and his wish to have a place. Her father, at least, had had his memories: the old village, the church with its onion dome, the songs his mother sang. Even when he was poorest he had been rich in those, and he had given them to Marta, so that she had grown up with two countries in her mind instead of one. But Will had never spoken of Ohio except to say that it was crowded and that his father had been a tenant there all his life. He had come out West to get away from something, not to carry anything with him. And the land he had found was already another man's dream.

"Will," she said, "do you hate it here?"

He seemed surprised by the question. He turned the folded letter over in his fingers and considered it, as an honest man will consider a thing before he answers.

"No," he said finally. "I don't hate it. I used to like it fine. When I first came, and was working for your father, I used to go out evenings, after the chores, and walk clear to the section line, just to look at it. There wasn't a fence then from here to the river. The grass was so high in the draw it came to a man's waist, and in the fall it turned the color of—" He stopped, and moved his hand vaguely. "I don't know what color. A kind of red. I used to think a man could make anything out of a country like that." He was quiet a moment. "I don't hate it. I'm just tired of losing to it."

Marta looked at him for a long while. She thought she had never seen him so plainly. It was as if the lamplight had been turned up, though it had not; as if all the twelve years of their marriage had been lived in a kind of half dark, where each of them went about the work and saw only the outline of the other.

"I remember the grass," she said. "I used to hide in it from Mama when I didn't want to churn. She never could find me. Papa always could."

Will smiled a little, for the first time that evening.

"He could find anything on this place. A lost calf in a blizzard. He found one once in the storm of eighty-eight, the winter before I came. Ed told me about it. Said he walked out with a rope tied to the barn door and came back with the calf over his shoulders, and his beard all ice."

"Yes. I was six. I remember Mama crying at the window." Marta paused. "He was a hard man to live up to. I know that. I couldn't live up to him either."

"You!" Will said. "You're more like him than you know."

"Maybe. But I'm not him." She unfolded her hands and laid them flat on the oilcloth. "When I said I didn't mind the milking, it was true. But it's true for me, Will. It isn't anything I owe to him. I like to go out in the morning, before it's light, and hear the cows moving in the barn, and smell the hay. I like to stand on the step after supper and look off to the west. I don't know how to tell you what it is. It's as if I could see clear to the edge of the world from here, and it's all quiet, and I'm part of it. In town I'd be—" She searched for the word. "I'd be shut in. I'd be looking at somebody's back fence."

"The girls wouldn't think so."

"No," she said. "No, I suppose they wouldn't."

That was the hardest thing, and they both knew it. Their two daughters, Rose and little Emily, were asleep upstairs in the room under the eaves, and Rose was eleven and had already begun to talk of the high school in Hollis, and of the Ferris girl who had gone east to Omaha and come back with a hat trimmed with cherries. Marta had seen the look in Rose's eyes when the town children came out in their buggies for the Fourth of July picnic. It was the look of a child who has seen through a window into a lighted room. She had seen that look before, on her own face, in her mother's little mirror, when she was Rose's age; but for her it had passed. She did not think it would pass for Rose.

Will got up and went to the screen door and stood with his back to her, looking out into the dark yard. She could see the line of his shoulders against the faint light that still lingered in the sky. He had grown thinner that summer; his shirt hung loose on him.

"I've thought about it every way," he said, without turning around. "Nights, mostly. I lie there and think, if it rains next year, we'll be all right. And then I think, if it doesn't, we'll lose everything—the land, the stock, all of it—and I'll be working for wages at forty, the way my father did. And the girls will grow up poor, with nothing. I can't do that to them, Marta. I can't do it to you. If I could be sure of the rain I'd stay. But a man can't be sure of anything in this country. That's the one thing I've learned."

Marta rose and went to stand beside him. Through the screen she could see the dim shapes of the barn and the granary, and beyond them the long dark line of the windbreak, black against the sky. Over the windbreak a single star had come out, very large and steady, and lower down, near the horizon, there was a faint flickering, far away to the northwest, which might have been heat lightning. She watched it for a while without speaking. It came and went, came and went, but there was no sound of thunder.

"Look there," she said.

"I see it. It's been doing that every night for a week. It never comes to anything."

"No. But it might."

He made a small sound in his throat, not quite a laugh. "That's your father talking."

"No," Marta said. "That's me."

They stood a long time side by side, not touching, watching the light play along the edge of the sky. Marta thought of the plot on the rise beyond the draw, where her father lay beside her mother and the two little brothers she had never known. She thought that if Ferris bought the land he would very likely plow it under; he was a practical man and had no use for graves that were not his own. She thought of the plum bushes in the draw, and the pasqueflowers, and the place where the grass had once come to a man's waist. And she thought, too, of Will lying awake at night, adding up figures in the dark, while she slept beside him and dreamed of nothing at all.

It came to her that a woman can love a country and a man both, and that the two loves need not be the same, nor ask the same things of her. She had always believed that the land was the deeper of the two, because it had been there first and would be there after. But the land did not lie awake for her. The land did not grow thin with worry. It went on as it was, indifferent and beautiful, and it would go on so whether Marta Kovar Brandt lived upon it or not.

"Will," she said at last, "write to Ferris that we'll give him an answer at Christmas."

He turned and looked at her. "He won't wait that long."

"Then let him not wait. If he won't wait, there will be someone else, if it comes to that. Let us have the fall. Let me put in the winter wheat on the north forty, the way you wanted to, and not the way Papa would have done it. If it comes up green in the spring, we'll talk again. If it doesn't—" She stopped, and her voice was steady when she went on. "If it doesn't, I'll go to town with you, and I won't say a word against it. Not ever. You have my promise."

Will was silent for a long time. Then he put out his hand, a little awkwardly, as if he were not sure he had the right, and laid it on her arm.

"You'd do that?"

"I'd do it."

"You'd hate it in town."

"Maybe I would," she said. "But I'd not hate you."

He did not answer. He stood with his hand on her arm, and she could feel that it was trembling a little, very slightly, the way the leaves of the cottonwood tremble when there is no wind that a person can feel. After a while he took the folded letter out of his pocket and laid it on the shelf by the door, under the clock, where they kept the bills and the almanac. Then he went to the table and turned down the lamp.

In the dark, the room seemed larger. The screen door showed gray against the yard, and through it the flickering in the northwest came and went, came and went, faint as breathing. Marta stayed by the door after Will had gone up the stairs. She heard his boots drop, one and then the other, on the floor above her, and the creak of the bed as he lay down. She heard one of the girls murmur in her sleep and turn over.

She did not go up at once. She stood looking out at the sky, and at the long dark shape of her mother's trees, and at the place, beyond the barn and the draw, where she knew the little fenced plot lay on its rise, though she could not see it. The air had grown quite cool now, and there was a smell in it that she had not smelled all summer, a damp, faint, mineral smell, like water standing on stone. It might have been nothing. It might have been only the dew coming down at last on the dry clover along the road.

She stood there a long time, with her hand on the latch, breathing it in.
