The train was nearly an hour late, and by the time it drew into Hallett the sun had dropped behind the grain elevator and the whole town lay in its long blue shadow. Ellen Moberg stood on the platform of the day coach with her valise in her hand and looked out at the board station, the water tank, the single row of brick and frame buildings along the main street, and felt that she had never been away at all. Nothing was changed, except that everything was smaller. The elevator, which in her childhood had seemed to her as tall as a church, was only a gray box against the sky.

There were not many people at the station. A drayman was backing his team toward the baggage car, and two farmer boys in clean shirts sat on a truck, swinging their legs and staring at the passengers. At the far end of the platform a woman in a brown dress and a wide straw hat was standing beside a spring wagon, one hand on the bridle of a sorrel horse. She did not wave. She simply stood and watched the coaches come to rest, and when Ellen stepped down she came forward slowly, as if she wished to be sure.

"Ellen," she said. "It is you. I thought it was, and then I thought, no, she is too thin."

"Signe!"

They took each other's hands and stood so for a moment, laughing a little, not knowing whether to kiss. Then Signe put her arms around her cousin and held her, and Ellen smelled the familiar smell of starch and wood smoke and something like dried clover, the smell of farm kitchens, which she had not known she remembered.

"Twelve years," Signe said, holding her off and looking at her. "Twelve years in October. You went away the fall Mother died."

"I know. I have counted too."

Signe took the valise from her and swung it into the back of the wagon, where there was a horse blanket and a sack of flour and a box of groceries. She handled the heavy bag as if it were nothing. She was a large woman now, broad in the shoulders and deep in the bosom, and her arms, where the sleeves were pushed up, were brown and strong. Her face had grown square and weather-colored, and there were fine lines about her eyes from looking into the wind. But the eyes themselves were the same, a clear, light gray, very steady, and when she smiled her whole face opened as it had when she was a girl of fifteen.

"Get up," she said. "Nils wanted to come, but the threshers are at Pedersen's tomorrow and he has to be there early with the team. The children are wild to see you. I told them you were a fine lady from Chicago and they must wash behind their ears."

"I am not a fine lady."

"You look like one," said Signe, and clucked to the horse.

They drove out of town by the road that ran north between the stubble fields. The wheat had been cut, and the shocks stood in long rows across the land, gold where the light struck them and violet on their shadowed sides. Beyond the wheat the corn was still green, and beyond the corn the country rolled away in long, low swells to the edge of the world, where the sky came down to meet it in a band of pale, burning yellow. There was no tree anywhere except the cottonwoods along the creek bottoms, and a windbreak here and there around a farmhouse, dark and compact as a bunch of grapes. The air was very still. A meadowlark sang from a fence post as they passed, and then another, farther on, and the road ran straight ahead of them, red and dusty, until it was lost in the light.

Ellen sat with her hands in her lap and said nothing for a long while. She had thought about this country many times in the city, in her room at the boarding house on Ohio Street, in the draughting office where she worked among the long tables and the green-shaded lamps. She had remembered it as one remembers a face, the general expression rather than the features. Now that she was here, she found that she had forgotten how wide it was, and how the sky took up so much of everything, and how the land seemed to breathe slowly under it, like a sleeping animal.

"It is just the same," she said at last.

"Oh, no. It's very much changed. There are four new houses between here and our place, and the Lutheran church has a steeple now. And the road is graded. When you were here, you remember, it went wherever the wagons went."

"I mean that it looks the same. It feels the same."

Signe glanced at her. "Does it? I suppose it would, to you. When you see a thing every day you only notice what's different."

They passed a farmhouse set back from the road, a white house with a red barn and a windmill turning lazily, though there was hardly any wind. A woman was taking clothes off a line in the yard, and she straightened and shaded her eyes to look at them.

"That's Hilda Engstrom," said Signe. "She was Hilda Rask. You went to school with her."

"Hilda Rask! The one with the braids that came down to her knees?"

"She has six children now and her hair is all cut off. She had typhoid two winters ago and nearly died. She'll be over to see you, I expect. Everyone will. You don't know what it means here, someone coming back."

Ellen laughed. "They'll be disappointed. I have nothing to tell."

"You have Chicago to tell. That's enough for most of them."

The sun was down now, and the yellow band along the horizon was turning to rose and then to a deep, smoky red. The shocks in the fields had lost their gold and stood up gray and solemn, like figures waiting. A little wind came up from the south and moved the tops of the corn, and the sound it made was like a long sigh, rising and falling. Ellen took off her hat and let the wind blow through her hair.

"Do you remember," she said, "the summer we were going to run away to the Black Hills and dig for gold?"

Signe laughed aloud, a deep, warm laugh that seemed to come up out of the earth itself. "We got as far as the Dvorak place. And old Mrs. Dvorak gave us kolaches and sent her boy to fetch Father, and he whipped us both, though you were not his child."

"He said Uncle Anders would never know the difference."

"And he was right. Father was always right about such things." Signe was quiet a moment. "He's been gone six years now. Did you know that?"

"Mother wrote me. I meant to come. I was ill that spring."

"It didn't matter. He wouldn't have known you. He didn't know any of us at the last." She flicked the reins over the sorrel's back. "He talked about Sweden, mostly. About a lake there, and some boat he had when he was a boy. We never heard of the boat before. Nils said it was strange how a man could carry a thing around in his head for seventy years and never speak of it."

Ellen thought about that. She thought of her uncle as she remembered him, a tall, stooped man with a yellow beard and enormous hands, who could lift a calf in his arms and who said almost nothing from one week's end to the next. She thought of him lying in the dark at the end of his life, rowing on a lake she would never see, among people who had been dead half a century.

"I suppose we all carry such things," she said.

"I suppose we do."

It was dusk when they turned in at the gate. The farmhouse stood on a little rise, with the windbreak of box elders and ash behind it and the barn and the sheds below. It was a two-story house, painted white, with a porch along the front; but Ellen saw at once, at the back, the low, grassed-over hump of the old sod house where she and Signe had been born, in the same room, eleven months apart. It was used for a cave now, Signe said, for potatoes and crocks of butter.

The children came running out of the house before the wagon stopped, four of them, all towheaded and barefoot, and stood in a row at the edge of the porch looking at Ellen with the frank, solemn curiosity of country children. The oldest was a girl of perhaps eleven, tall and thin, with Signe's gray eyes. She held a baby on her hip.

"This is Karin," said Signe, "and this is Anders, after Father, and Olaf, and Lena, and the baby is Ellen."

Ellen looked at her cousin. Signe was busy with the harness and did not turn around.

"You never wrote me that."

"Didn't I? I thought I had. Well, she's only seven months. There hasn't been much time for writing." She lifted the valise down. "Karin, take your cousin in and show her where she's to sleep. Anders, put the horse away and give him his oats, and mind you rub him down. I'll start supper."

They ate in the kitchen, at a long table covered with oilcloth, under a hanging lamp that drew moths through the screen door. Nils came in from the field when the meal was half over, a lean, quiet man with sandy hair going thin on top and a slow, pleasant smile. He shook hands with Ellen gravely, washed himself at the basin by the door, and sat down to eat without much talk. The children watched Ellen all through supper. When she asked them questions, they answered in single words and looked at their plates, and when she turned away they began to stare again. Only the baby, who sat on Signe's lap and was fed bits of potato from her mother's fork, seemed perfectly at ease. She looked at Ellen with round, unblinking blue eyes and once, when Ellen smiled at her, she smiled back and reached out a fat hand.

"She likes you," said Signe. "She doesn't take to everybody."

After supper Nils went out to see to the stock, and the children were sent up to bed, protesting. Ellen helped with the dishes, though Signe said she should not. They worked side by side at the dry sink, Signe washing and Ellen drying, as they had done in the sod house when they were small and their mothers had stood behind them, speaking Swedish to each other over their heads.

"Do you remember any Swedish?" Signe asked, as if she had been thinking the same thing.

"Hardly a word. A few songs. Nobody speaks it in the city."

"We speak it in the church still, on the first Sunday. But the children don't care for it. Karin says it sounds like old people." She handed Ellen a plate. "I suppose that's what it is now."

When the dishes were done they went out on the porch. The night had come down completely, and the sky was full of stars, so many of them and so bright that Ellen caught her breath. In the city she had forgotten that there were so many. The Milky Way lay across the heavens like a drift of smoke, and low in the east the moon was coming up, enormous and the color of a ripe apricot, out of the black edge of the land. The wind had gone down. The only sounds were the crickets in the grass and, from somewhere far off, a dog barking, and then another answering it from a different farm, so that one could tell where the houses were, scattered out across the darkness.

They sat on the porch step, as they used to sit on the doorsill of the sod house. Signe had brought out a shawl and she put it around Ellen's shoulders without asking.

"You're not used to the nights here anymore," she said. "It gets cold after the sun goes."

For a while neither of them spoke. The moon climbed and grew smaller and paler, and its light came across the stubble fields and touched the tops of the shocks with silver. Ellen could see the line of the creek now, where the cottonwoods grew, and beyond it the long rise of the land toward the north, where the Hagstrom place had been.

"Is the Hagstrom house still standing?" she asked.

"No. It burned the winter after you left. They went to Oregon." Signe paused. "You know Peter Hagstrom is married. He has a fruit farm out there, and a wife from Portland. His mother wrote my mother before she died."

"I didn't know." Ellen was silent a moment. "I'm glad. He was always good."

"You might have married him."

"I might have. I thought so, once." She drew the shawl closer. "But I wanted to go away, and he wanted to stay. And then he didn't stay, after all. It's strange, isn't it, how things come out."

Signe did not answer. She was looking out over the fields, her hands clasped around her knees. In the moonlight her face looked younger, the lines smoothed away, and Ellen saw in it suddenly the girl she had been, the big, fair, slow-moving girl who had always seemed to know exactly what she wanted and to be in no hurry to get it.

"Are you happy there, Ellen?" Signe asked at last. "In Chicago?"

Ellen considered. It was not a question people asked in the city. "I think so," she said. "I like my work. I draw plans for buildings, you know, warehouses mostly, and sometimes a school. There are three women in the office, and the men are decent to us. I have a room on the third floor with a window that looks over the lake, and on Sundays I go to the Art Institute, or to hear the orchestra if I have the money. I have friends." She stopped. "It's a good life. It's the life I wanted."

"But?"

"I didn't say but."

"You were going to."

Ellen laughed softly. "You always could tell. Well, then. Sometimes in the winter, when the wind comes off the lake and the streets are full of dirty snow, and I come home in the dark and climb all those stairs, I think about this. About the light here. I remember the way the snow used to lie on the prairie, so clean, all blue in the evening, and the smoke going straight up out of the chimney. And I wonder if I ought to have stayed. Then in the morning I go to the office and I forget." She turned to look at her cousin. "And you, Signe? Are you happy?"

Signe took her time. A night bird called from the windbreak, two low notes, and was still.

"I don't think about it much," she said. "There isn't time, mostly. In the spring there's the planting and the garden and the little chickens, and in summer there's harvest and canning, and in the fall butchering, and in the winter somebody is always sick. The years go by so fast. Karin was a baby just the other day, and now she can make bread as good as mine." She smiled a little. "Nils is a good man. He doesn't drink, and he's never once raised his hand to me or the children. We own this place clear now, all three quarters. Father would be proud of that. He came here with nothing, you know, nothing but a plow and a team of oxen, and he lived in a hole in the ground."

"I remember the hole in the ground," said Ellen. "I was born in it."

"So was I." Signe laughed. Then she grew serious again. "Sometimes I think I have done what Father and Mother came here for. That this is what they meant, when they left the old country and came across the ocean and all that way in the wagon. They wanted a house like this and children going to school and land that belonged to them. And I have it. I have it all. And sometimes, when I'm out in the garden in the evening and the light is going, I feel such a happiness, Ellen, I can't tell you. Just to stand there with my hands in the dirt and look at the fields. As if everything was right and I was where I belonged." She paused. "And other times I'm so tired I could lie down in the furrow and never get up."

Ellen put her hand over her cousin's hand. It was rough and warm and very strong.

"I'm glad you named her Ellen," she said.

"I wanted to. You were always the one who was going to do something. I used to think, when we were girls, that you would go out into the world and do all the things I never would, and that would be almost as good as doing them myself." She turned her hand over and held Ellen's fingers. "And you have. You have done them."

"I draw warehouses."

"You draw buildings that people will stand in long after we're gone. That's something."

The moon was high now, small and white and very clear, and the whole country lay open under it, silver and gray and black, without a sound. Ellen looked out at it and felt something in her loosen that had been held tight for a long time. It seemed to her that the land had not changed at all, that it had only been waiting, the way it had waited for her grandparents when they came across it in their wagon, the way it would wait for the children asleep upstairs, and for their children. The people came and went upon it like the shadows of clouds. They broke the sod and built their houses and quarreled and loved and died, and the land took them back and kept their secrets. An old man rowed on a lake in Sweden in his dying dreams; a boy she had once loved was picking apples in Oregon; and here she sat on the doorstep with her cousin, as they had sat when they were children and the whole of life was before them, unknown and shining, like the country itself at sunrise.

"Do you know," she said, "I think this is the place where we were happiest. You and I. Before anything had happened to us."

Signe was quiet for so long that Ellen thought she had not heard. Then she said, "No. I think we're happy now. We just don't know it yet. We'll know it in twenty years, when we look back."

Ellen laughed, and the sound went out across the yard and was lost in the great silence. Somewhere in the house the baby woke and began to cry, a thin, small, insistent sound, and Signe rose at once, heavily, with a hand on the porch post.

"That's my namesake," she said. "Your namesake, I mean. Come in when you're ready. The lamp is lit in your room."

She went inside, and Ellen heard her footsteps on the stairs and then her low voice, crooning in Swedish, words that Ellen did not know she remembered until she heard them. She sat on alone a long while, with the shawl around her shoulders, watching the moon go over, until the cold drove her in.

The October sun was already low when Nils Ekstrom came up out of the draw, and he came slowly, though there was nothing to hinder him. The red grass stood to his knees on either side of the cattle path. It had the colour of wine held up to a lamp, and when the wind ran over it, the whole slope seemed to shift and settle again, like the hide of a great animal stirring in its sleep. Ahead of him, on the rise, stood his father's house. It was frame, painted white two summers ago, and it was the only painted house between the creek and the county road. Behind it were the sod stable, the windmill, and the long, low cornfield, already stripped and rattling. A thread of smoke went straight up from the kitchen chimney into the still air and then, at a certain height, bent eastward all at once, as if it had been told to.

Nils was seven years old. He had a round, sunburned face, and his hair, which his mother cut over a bowl, was so pale that in summer it was nearly white. He wore a red knitted cap that his grandmother had sent from Värmland in a box with a Bible and a pound of coffee, and he was proud of it, because no other boy in the district had one like it. Now, as he came near the house, he pulled it off and pushed it inside his jacket. He did not know why he did this. It was an instinct, like the instinct of a rabbit that flattens itself in the furrow when a hawk's shadow goes over.

His mother was at the stove when he came in. She was a tall woman, with a broad forehead and grey eyes set far apart, and she moved about her kitchen with a kind of large deliberation, as if every object in it had been put there by her own hand and she meant it to stay. She looked at him once, and then she looked back into the kettle.

"Wash," she said. "Your father is seeing to the horses."

He washed at the bench by the door, in the tin basin, and dried his face on the roller towel. The water was cold and smelled of the iron in the well. He took a long time over it, and when he had finished, he stood with his hands hanging and did not know what to do with himself. His little sister, Signe, was sitting on the floor by the woodbox, dressing a corncob in a scrap of calico. She held it up for him to admire. He did not look at it.

"Set the plates," said his mother.

He set them. There were four tin plates and one that was china, white with a blue rim, which had come all the way from Sweden and was used only by his father. Nils put it at the head of the table, as he did every night, and he put it down so carefully that it made no sound at all.

Jens Ekstrom came in when the light outside had gone from gold to a deep, clear rose. He was not a large man, but he was thick through the shoulders and he stooped a little, the way men stoop who have walked many years behind a plough. His beard was brown and grizzled at the corners of the mouth. He hung his hat on its peg and washed in the basin his son had used, and he did not speak to anyone. That in itself was nothing remarkable; he was often silent. But Nils, who was watching him from the corner of his eye, saw that he dried his hands for a long time, longer than there was any need, and then folded the towel back over the roller, smoothing it with his palm, as though he were thinking of something far away.

They ate their supper. There was fried mush and side-meat, and a dish of plums Mrs. Ekstrom had put up in August, and coffee for the grown people. Signe chattered about her corncob, which she had named Fru Lind after a woman at church, and her mother answered her quietly. Jens ate as he always ate, steadily and without hurry, wiping his plate at the end with a piece of bread. Once he looked across at his son, and Nils felt the look as one feels a draught from a door left open. He put a plum in his mouth and could not swallow it, and held it there, sour and slippery, until his father looked away.

When the meal was over, Jens pushed back his chair. "Nils," he said, "come out with me to the barn. I want you to hold the lantern."

There was no need of a lantern. The moon was rising, full, behind the cottonwoods along the creek, and the whole yard was white with it. But Nils got the lantern down from its nail and lit it with a splinter from the stove, his fingers not quite steady, and followed his father out of the door. Behind him he heard his mother say something low to Signe, and then the door shut, and he was alone in the great cold night with his father.

The barn was warm and dark and smelled of horses and hay and the sweetish dust of the oats bin. The two big greys, Kalle and Prins, turned their heads in the stalls and blew softly through their noses. Jens took the lantern from the boy's hand and hung it on a hook, so that a small circle of yellow light fell on the floor, and the rest of the barn went off into shadows that seemed to have no end. Then he sat down on an upturned feed box and put his hands on his knees.

"Now," he said. "Tell me what you did today."

Nils stood in the circle of light. He looked at the toes of his boots, which were scuffed white at the ends, and at the straw around them. He had thought, all the way up the draw, of what he would say if he were asked; he had made up several things, and some of them were very good. But now they were all gone out of his head, the way water goes out of a broken crock, and there was nothing left.

"I was with Frank and Joe Kovar," he said at last.

"Yes. And where were you with Frank and Joe Kovar?"

"Down by the creek."

"Where by the creek?"

The boy did not answer. One of the horses stamped, and the sound was very loud.

"I came home by the lower road this afternoon," said Jens, "with the load of cobs from Peterson's. I came past the place where old Hrubek lives. I saw three boys run off into the plum thicket, and one of them had a red cap."

Nils's face grew hot, and then it grew cold, and he felt the tears coming up behind his eyes, though he did not want them. He bit the inside of his cheek, hard.

"I stopped the team," his father went on, in the same even voice. "Hrubek was standing in his door. His window was broken, the one window that he has, and there were clods all over the step, and some of them had gone inside. He was picking the glass out of the frame with his fingers. I asked him who had done it. He said he did not know. He said it was the wind." Jens was silent a moment. "There was no wind today, Nils. You know that. All day it has been as still as a church."

"Frank threw first," the boy burst out. "Frank threw the first one, and Joe—"

"I did not ask you about Frank. Frank has his own father." Jens leaned forward a little, and the lantern light caught in his beard and in the deep lines around his eyes. "Did you throw?"

There was a long silence. Somewhere out in the night a coyote began, far off, and then another answered it, and their thin crying went up and up and broke into pieces against the sky.

"Yes," said Nils.

"Did you break the window?"

"I don't know. I think—maybe. We all threw. He came out and shook his stick, and we—" He stopped. He could not tell his father the rest of it: that they had laughed at the old man, at his long coat that came nearly to his heels and was green with age at the shoulders, at the way he talked, half in his own tongue and half in broken English, at the way his hands shook. Joe Kovar had called him a crazy old Bohunk, though Joe's own people were Bohemians and came from the same country, and Nils had laughed loudest of all, because it was the first time he had ever heard a boy say such a thing about his own kind, and it had seemed to him very bold and very funny.

His father seemed to know all of this without being told. He looked at his son for a long while, and Nils, who had been waiting for the strap and had almost wished for it, began to understand that there would be no strap, and that whatever was coming would be harder.

"Sit down," said Jens.

Nils sat down on the edge of the oats bin. His legs did not quite reach the floor.

"I will tell you something about Hrubek," said his father. "You do not know it, because you are young, and because he does not talk about himself, and nobody asks him. When I first came into this country, eleven years ago, before you were born, before your mother came out to me, Hrubek already had his place down there on the creek. He had a house then, a real house, of logs, and a wife. She was a little woman with black hair. She used to sing when she hung out the washing. You could hear her from the road."

The boy said nothing. He was watching his father's hands. They were brown and cracked across the knuckles, and there was a white scar along the side of one thumb where a corn knife had slipped.

"In the old country," Jens went on, "Hrubek played the violin. Not as the Kovars' uncle plays, at the dances, for beer. He played in a great theatre in Prague, in an orchestra, with sixty other men. He played before the Emperor. Fru Kovar told me this once; she had it from people at home. He came here because he had a brother in Omaha who wrote letters about land, about how a man could have as much land as he could see, if he would only work. He paused and looked down at the floor, at the round, yellow pool of light, as if he could see something there.

They found her in the spring, in the draw, not two hundred steps from the door. After that his house burned. I do not know how; maybe he let the stove go red, maybe he did not care. And so he dug the hole in the bank where he lives now, and he has lived there ever since, by himself, with his chickens and his one cow, and he does not ask anything from anybody. Do you understand me, Nils?"

"Yes, Father," said Nils, though he was not sure that he did. He only knew that something was happening in his chest, a slow, heavy aching, as though a stone had been laid there.

"Now I will tell you something about myself," said Jens. "When I came to this country I was nineteen years old. I came on the ship to New York, and on the train to Omaha, and I had on a coat my mother had made me, of grey wadmal, with horn buttons. In Omaha I went into a store to buy a pair of boots, and there were some young men standing there, American boys, about the age Olof Peterson is now. They looked at my coat, and they laughed. One of them said something, I did not know the words, and then he took me by the sleeve and pretended to be a sheep, and said 'baa, baa,' and they all laughed again. I did not buy the boots. I went out into the street, and I stood there a long time, and I thought I would go home to Sweden on the next ship, if I had to walk back to New York to get it."

Nils looked up, astonished. He had never thought of his father as being young, or as being laughed at, or as being anything but what he was: strong, and silent, and always right. It was as if the barn wall had opened and shown him another country behind it.

"I did not go home," said Jens. "I came out here and took up this land, and I have made something of it. But I have never forgotten those young men. I have forgotten a great deal—I have forgotten the name of the ship, and the names of the men who worked with me on the railroad that first summer. But I remember their faces, and I remember how it was to stand in that street. I am forty years old, and I remember it still." He leaned forward and put one of his heavy hands on the boy's knee. "Old Hrubek will remember you, Nils. When he is sitting in his hole in the bank this winter, with the snow over the door and the wind blowing, he will remember three boys running into the plum thicket, and one of them in a red cap. He will remember it when he is dying. That is a thing you have done today. You cannot take it back."

Then the tears came, and Nils could not stop them. He put his face in the crook of his arm and cried, with great, tearing sobs that shook his whole body, and the horses shifted uneasily in their stalls and looked around at him with their mild, dark eyes. His father did not move to comfort him. He sat on the feed box with his hands on his knees and waited, and his face in the lantern light was grave and patient and very tired.

When the worst of it was over, Jens said, "That is enough now. Crying is all right, but it does not mend windows. Look at me."

Nils lifted his face. It was swollen and wet, and his nose was running, and he wiped it on his sleeve.

"How much money have you got in the baking-powder tin?"

The boy swallowed. "Sixty-two cents." It was the bounty on gophers, a penny a tail, that he had been saving since spring for a pocket knife with a bone handle, which he had seen in the window of Lindquist's store in town.

"A pane of glass that size costs forty cents," said his father. "Saturday we go to town for flour. You will take your forty cents and you will go into the store yourself, and you will buy the glass, and you will carry it home on your knees in the wagon so that it does not break. Sunday after church you and I will go down to Hrubek's, and I will show you how to set it with putty. And you will tell him what you did. Not that you are sorry—anybody can say he is sorry. You will tell him what you did, in plain words, and then you will ask him if there is work you can do for him, carrying water or splitting kindling, until the snow comes. Whatever he says, you will do it."

Nils looked down at the floor again. The thought of standing before the old man, before that long green coat and those trembling hands and that face he had laughed at, was more terrible to him than anything else in the world. He felt that he would rather be whipped every day for a year.

"Do you understand?" said Jens.

"Yes, Father."

"Good." Jens stood up, and his knees cracked as he did so. He took the lantern down from its hook and looked at it a moment, and then he blew it out. At once the barn filled with moonlight, which came in through the cracks between the boards in long, pale bars and lay across the straw and across the backs of the horses, and the boy saw that it had been there all the time, only the lantern had kept him from seeing it. His father put out his hand, and Nils took it, and they went out together into the yard.

The night was enormous. The moon had cleared the cottonwoods and swung up into the open sky, and the whole prairie lay under it, silver and grey and silent, rolling away and away on every side until it met the stars. The windmill stood up black against it. Far down along the creek, Nils could see a single small point of yellow light, low to the ground, steady and alone, and he knew that it was Hrubek's lamp, shining through the hole where the window had been.

His father saw it too. He stood still a moment, holding the boy's hand, and looked at it. Then he said, more to himself than to his son, "He will be cold tonight," and they went in.

His mother had put Signe to bed and was sitting by the stove, mending a stocking over a darning egg. She did not ask anything. She only looked at Nils's face, and then she got up and wet a cloth in the warm water from the reservoir and washed his eyes and his nose, gently, as she had not done since he was very small. Then she took him into the little room off the kitchen, where he slept, and helped him with his buttons, and heard his prayer. When he had finished it, she stood a moment beside the bed with her hand on his hair.

"Your father was not angry," she said, in Swedish. "You must not think he was angry."

"I know," said Nils. But he did not know, and he lay awake a long time after she had gone, looking at the square of the window where the moonlight came through, and listening to the low sound of his parents' voices in the kitchen, and thinking about the little woman with black hair who used to sing when she hung out the washing.

Many years afterward, when Nils Ekstrom was a man past fifty, and owned three sections of land and a brick house in town, and had sat in the state legislature for two terms, he used to say that his father had never once laid a hand on him. This was not strictly true. There had been the usual whippings, for the usual things: for letting the calves into the corn, for fighting at school. But he had forgotten all of those. What he remembered was the barn, and the circle of lantern light on the straw, and his father's cracked hands lying quiet on his knees; and the way the moonlight had been waiting there all along, when the lantern was put out; and that one small yellow light, far down along the creek, burning by itself in the great white silence of the plains.

Bergson had spent his first five years on the Divide getting into debt, and the last six getting out. He had paid off his mortgages and had ended pretty much where he began, with the land. He owned exactly six hundred and forty acres of what stretched outside his door; his own original homestead and timber claim, making three hundred and twenty acres, and the half-section adjoining, the homestead of a younger brother who had given up the fight, gone back to Chicago to work in a fancy bakery and distinguish himself in a Swedish athletic club. So far John had not attempted to cultivate the second half-section, but used it for pasture land, and one of his sons rode herd there in open weather. John Bergson had the Old-World belief that land, in itself, is desirable. But this land was an enigma. It was like a horse that no one knows how to break to harness, that runs wild and kicks things to pieces. He had an idea that no one understood how to farm it properly, and this he often discussed with Alexandra. Their neighbors, certainly, knew even less about farming than he did. Many of them had never worked on a farm until they took up their homesteads. They had been handwerkers at home; tailors, locksmiths, joiners, cigar-makers, etc. Bergson himself had worked in a shipyard. For weeks, John Bergson had been thinking about these things. His bed stood in the sitting-room, next to the kitchen. Through the day, while the baking and washing and ironing were going on, the father lay and looked up at the roof beams that he himself had hewn, or out at the cattle in the corral. He counted the cattle over and over. It diverted him to speculate as to how much weight each of the steers would probably put on by spring. He often called his daughter in to talk to her about this. Before Alexandra was twelve years old she had begun to be a help to him, and as she grew older he had come to depend more and more upon her resourcefulness and good judgment. His boys were willing enough to work, but when he talked with them they usually irritated him. It was Alexandra who read the papers and followed the markets, and who learned by the mistakes of their neighbors. It was Alexandra who could always tell about what it had cost to fatten each steer, and who could guess the weight of a hog before it went on the scales closer than John Bergson himself. Lou and Oscar were industrious, but he could never teach them to use their heads about their work. Alexandra, her father often said to himself, was like her grandfather; which was his way of saying that she was intelligent. John Bergson’s father had been a shipbuilder, a man of considerable force and of some fortune. Late in life he married a second time, a Stockholm woman of questionable character, much younger than he, who goaded him into every sort of extravagance. On the shipbuilder’s part, this marriage was an infatuation, the despairing folly of a powerful man who cannot bear to grow old. In a few years his unprincipled wife warped the probity of a lifetime. He speculated, lost his own fortune and funds entrusted to him by poor seafaring men, and died disgraced, leaving his children nothing. But when all was said, he had come up from the sea himself, had built up a proud little business with no capital but his own skill and foresight, and had proved himself a man. In his daughter, John Bergson recognized the strength of will, and the simple direct way of thinking things out, that had characterized his father in his better days. He would much rather, of course, have seen this likeness in one of his sons, but it was not a question of choice. As he lay there day after day he had to accept the situation as it was, and to be thankful that there was one among his children to whom he could entrust the future of his family and the possibilities of his hard-won land. The winter twilight was fading. The sick man heard his wife strike a match in the kitchen, and the light of a lamp glimmered through the cracks of the door. It seemed like a light shining far away. He turned painfully in his bed and looked at his white hands, with all the work gone out of them. He was ready to give up, he felt. He did not know how it had come about, but he was quite willing to go deep under his fields and rest, where the plow could not find him. He was tired of making mistakes. He was content to leave the tangle to other hands; he thought of his Alexandra’s strong ones.

“Dotter,” he called feebly, “dotter!” He heard her quick step and saw her tall figure appear in the doorway, with the light of the lamp behind her. He felt her youth and strength, how easily she moved and stooped and lifted. But he would not have had it again if he could, not he! He knew the end too well to wish to begin again. He knew where it all went to, what it all became. His daughter came and lifted him up on his pillows. She called him by an old Swedish name that she used to call him when she was little and took his dinner to him in the shipyard.

“Tell the boys to come here, daughter. I want to speak to them.”

“They are feeding the horses, father. They have just come back from the Blue. Shall I call them?” He sighed. “No, no. Wait until they come in. Alexandra, you will have to do the best you can for your brothers. Everything will come on you.”

“I will do all I can, father.”

“Don’t let them get discouraged and go off like Uncle Otto. I want them to keep the land.”

“We will, father. We will never lose the land.” There was a sound of heavy feet in the kitchen. Alexandra went to the door and beckoned to her brothers, two strapping boys of seventeen and nineteen. They came in and stood at the foot of the bed. Their father looked at them searchingly, though it was too dark to see their faces; they were just the same boys, he told himself, he had not been mistaken in them. The square head and heavy shoulders belonged to Oscar, the elder. The younger boy was quicker, but vacillating.

“Boys,” said the father wearily, “I want you to keep the land together and to be guided by your sister. I have talked to her since I have been sick, and she knows all my wishes. I want no quarrels among my children, and so long as there is one house there must be one head. Alexandra is the oldest, and she knows my wishes. She will do the best she can. If she makes mistakes, she will not make so many as I have made. When you marry, and want a house of your own, the land will be divided fairly, according to the courts. But for the next few years you will have it hard, and you must all keep together. Alexandra will manage the best she can.” Oscar, who was usually the last to speak, replied because he was the older, “Yes, father. It would be so anyway, without your speaking. We will all work the place together.”

“And you will be guided by your sister, boys, and be good brothers to her, and good sons to your mother? That is good. And Alexandra must not work in the fields any more. There is no necessity now. Hire a man when you need help. She can make much more with her eggs and butter than the wages of a man. It was one of my mistakes that I did not find that out sooner. Try to break a little more land every year; sod corn is good for fodder. Keep turning the land, and always put up more hay than you need. Don’t grudge your mother a little time for plowing her garden and setting out fruit trees, even if it comes in a busy season. She has been a good mother to you, and she has always missed the old country.” When they went back to the kitchen the boys sat down silently at the table. Throughout the meal they looked down at their plates and did not lift their red eyes. They did not eat much, although they had been working in the cold all day, and there was a rabbit stewed in gravy for supper, and prune pies. John Bergson had married beneath him, but he had married a good housewife. Mrs. Bergson was a fair-skinned, corpulent woman, heavy and placid like her son, Oscar, but there was something comfortable about her; perhaps it was her own love of comfort. For eleven years she had worthily striven to maintain some semblance of household order amid conditions that made order very difficult. Habit was very strong with Mrs. Bergson, and her unremitting efforts to repeat the routine of her old life among new surroundings had done a great deal to keep the family from disintegrating morally and getting careless in their ways. The Bergsons had a log house, for instance, only because Mrs. Bergson would not live in a sod house. She missed the fish diet of her own country, and twice every summer she sent the boys to the river, twenty miles to the southward, to fish for channel cat. When the children were little she used to load them all into the wagon, the baby in its crib, and go fishing herself. Alexandra often said that if her mother were cast upon a desert island, she would thank God for her deliverance, make a garden, and find something to preserve. Preserving was almost a mania with Mrs. Bergson. Stout as she was, she roamed the scrubby banks of Norway Creek looking for fox grapes and goose plums, like a wild creature in search of prey. She made a yellow jam of the insipid ground-cherries that grew on the prairie, flavoring it with lemon peel; and she made a sticky dark conserve of garden tomatoes. She had experimented even with the rank buffalo-pea, and she could not see a fine bronze cluster of them without shaking her head and murmuring, “What a pity!” When there was nothing more to preserve, she began to pickle. The amount of sugar she used in these processes was sometimes a serious drain upon the family resources. She was a good mother, but she was glad when her children were old enough not to be in her way in the kitchen. She had never quite forgiven John Bergson for bringing her to the end of the earth; but, now that she was there, she wanted to be let alone to reconstruct her old life in so far as that was possible. She could still take some comfort in the world if she had bacon in the cave, glass jars on the shelves, and sheets in the press. She disapproved of all her neighbors because of their slovenly housekeeping, and the women thought her very proud. Once when Mrs. Bergson, on her way to Norway Creek, stopped to see old Mrs. Lee, the old woman hid in the haymow “for fear Mis’ Bergson would catch her barefoot.”

One Sunday afternoon in July, six months after John Bergson’s death, Carl was sitting in the doorway of the Linstrum kitchen, dreaming over an illustrated paper, when he heard the rattle of a wagon along the hill road. Looking up he recognized the Bergsons’ team, with two seats in the wagon, which meant they were off for a pleasure excursion. Oscar and Lou, on the front seat, wore their cloth hats and coats, never worn except on Sundays, and Emil, on the second seat with Alexandra, sat proudly in his new trousers, made from a pair of his father’s, and a pink-striped shirt, with a wide ruffled collar. “Want to go with us?” Lou called. “We’re going to Crazy Ivar’s to buy a hammock.”

“Sure.” Carl ran up panting, and clambering over the wheel sat down beside Emil. “I’ve always wanted to see Ivar’s pond. They say it’s the biggest in all the country. He might want it and take it right off your back.” Emil grinned. “I’d be awful scared to go,” he admitted, “if you big boys weren’t along to take care of me. Did you ever hear him howl, Carl? “No, I’d be too scared to run,” Emil admitted mournfully, twisting his fingers. “I guess I’d sit right down on the ground and say my prayers.” The big boys laughed, and Oscar brandished his whip over the broad backs of the horses.

The dry summer of that year began early, in the latter part of May, and by the first of July there was no one on the Divide who did not know what was coming. The wheat had headed out short and thin, and the corn, which had promised well in June, stood rolled up in the fields like so many green cigars, rattling when the wind blew through it. Every morning the sky was a hard, bright blue, and every afternoon a few white clouds came up in the west, piled themselves high and handsome over the river bluffs, and then melted away before sundown without having done anything at all. The farmers had stopped watching them. They went about their work with their heads down, and when two of them met on the road they talked about prices in Chicago, or about the new Methodist preacher, or about anything except the weather.

Peter Moravec had been nine years on his quarter-section, which lay along the north fork of Plum Creek, six miles from the town of Hollis. He had come over from Bohemia when he was nineteen, and had worked for four years in a lumberyard in Chicago, stacking boards in the rain and snow and saving his money in a tin box under the floor of his boarding-house. There he had met Klara Hruby, the daughter of a weaver from Pilsen, who sewed buttons in a coat factory and went to the same church. They were married in the spring of the year he turned twenty-four, and in the fall they came west on the emigrant train, with a cookstove, a featherbed, two chairs, and a little money sewed into the lining of Klara's petticoat. Peter had wanted land; that was all he had ever wanted. In the old country his father had been a tenant on a nobleman's estate, and Peter had grown up with the idea that a man who owned the ground under his feet could not be made to take his hat off to anybody.

The first years had been hard, as they were for everyone. Their house was a dugout in the side of a draw, and Klara had cooked and washed and borne her first child in it. Later Peter built a frame house of three rooms, with a porch on the south side, and Klara planted morning-glories along the porch and a row of cottonwoods to the west for a windbreak. They had three children: two girls, Marie and Bozena, who were now eight and six, and a boy, Tomas, who had died of diphtheria in his third winter. He was buried at the corner of the place, where the land rose a little toward the road, and Klara had planted a mulberry tree at the head of the grave. It was the only mulberry for miles around, and she carried water to it every evening in the summer, even in years when there was little enough water for the stock.

Klara was a small woman, dark and quick, with a firm mouth and large brown eyes that seemed always to be measuring something. She did not talk much, and the neighbor women thought her a little stiff; but she kept a clean house and a good garden, and when there was sickness on the creek it was Klara Moravec who came with her basket and sat up through the night. Peter was a tall, loose-jointed man, fair-haired, with a long face and a soft, rather boyish voice. He was a good worker and a kind husband, but he was given to sudden hopes and sudden discouragements, and his wife had learned, over the years, to wait out both of them as one waits out a hailstorm, without saying very much.

On the second Saturday in July, Peter drove into Hollis with a load of oats he could not afford to sell, and came home late in the afternoon with a sack of flour, a pound of coffee, and a folded paper in the breast pocket of his coat. He did not speak of the paper at supper. He ate his potatoes and side-meat in silence, and when the little girls asked him what he had seen in town, he told them about a dog that rode on the seat of the ice-wagon, and a lady at the hotel who had a green parrot in a cage. After supper he went out and sat on the edge of the porch, with his elbows on his knees, and looked off across the burned pasture toward the creek.

Klara put the girls to bed, washed the dishes, and swept the kitchen floor. Then she took off her apron, hung it on its nail behind the door, and came out and stood beside him. The sun had gone down, and the whole west was the color of a ripe apricot. The windmill turned slowly in the last of the wind, creaking at every turn, and the tank below it gave back the sky in a flat, bright sheet. Somewhere down the creek a cow was lowing for her calf.

"You saw Hobart," she said. It was not a question.

Peter did not look up. "How do you know I saw Hobart?"

"You have been sitting on that paper all through supper like a hen on an egg. I am not blind, Petr."

He laughed a little, without much pleasure, and took the paper out of his pocket and turned it over in his hands. "Well, then, yes. I saw him. He came into Lindquist's store while I was waiting for my flour. He asked me to step over to the bank with him."

"And you went."

"Why shouldn't I go? It does no harm to listen to a man." He unfolded the paper and smoothed it on his knee, though it was too dark now to read it. "He made an offer for the place, Klara. Fourteen hundred dollars, and he takes the mortgage. Fourteen hundred dollars, clear."

Klara said nothing. She sat down on the step beside him, not close, and folded her hands in her lap. Her face, in the fading light, was perfectly still.

"That is more than anybody will give next year," Peter went on, a little faster. "You know it, and I know it. If this corn is gone, and it is gone, then we will have to borrow again to get through the winter, and there will be the interest, and then the interest on that. Hobart says the company will not carry many more of us. He says there are men down on the Republican who have walked off and left everything, the house, the furniture, the chickens in the yard, and gone back east with nothing but what they could put in a wagon. He says in another year they will be buying land for nothing, and the people who held on will have nothing to show for it but their trouble."

"Hobart says," Klara repeated quietly. "Hobart is a loan agent. He says what is good for Hobart."

"He is not a bad fellow. He has been fair with me."

"He is fair with you because he wants something from you. When he does not want anything, you will see how fair he is."

Peter folded the paper again and put it away. He was silent for a while. The apricot color had gone out of the sky, and the first stars were coming out over the creek, very large and soft, as they are on the high prairie in summer. A nighthawk dropped out of the dusk with a sound like tearing cloth, and swept up again.

"I have had a letter from Vaclav," he said at last.

"I know. It came a week ago. You have read it every night since, when you thought I was asleep."

He turned and looked at her then, and she met his eyes without flinching. Peter had always been a little afraid of his wife's eyes. They saw so much more than he wished them to see, and they never seemed to be surprised by any of it.

"He says there is work in Omaha," Peter said. "In the packing houses, and on the railroad. He is a foreman now, in the car shops. He says he can get me on in a week, and the pay is a dollar and a half a day, every day, rain or shine, drought or no drought. A dollar and a half, Klara! Think of it. No more watching the sky. No more lying awake listening for the wind to change. A man works his ten hours, and then he goes home, and the money is in his pocket, and nobody can take it away from him. There are schools for the girls, good schools, and a Bohemian church, and Bohemian people all around. You would not be alone all day with nobody to talk to but the hens."

"I am not alone," said Klara.

"You know what I mean."

"I know what you mean. You mean that you are tired." She spoke without any harshness, but very distinctly, as if she were explaining something to one of the children. "You have been tired since May, and now Hobart has given you a paper and Vaclav has written you a letter, and you think that if you put the two of them together you will not be tired any more. But you will be tired in Omaha too, Petr. You will be tired in the car shops. Only there you will be tired for somebody else."

Peter got up and walked a few steps out into the yard, and stood with his back to her. When he spoke again his voice had risen, and there was a roughness in it she had seldom heard.

A mortgage, and a house that the wind goes through in winter, and a team that is getting too old to pull. "In Omaha we would have a little yard behind a house that belonged to somebody else, and the smoke from the packing houses would come over it, and nothing would grow." She shook her head. "And there is Tomas."

"Tomas is dead," he said. "He has been dead four years. He does not know whether we are here or in Omaha or in the old country. It is foolishness, Klara, to stay on a place and starve because there is a grave on it. The priest would tell you the same."

The moment he had spoken he would have given a great deal to have the words back. Klara did not move or cry out. She only sat looking at him, and in the starlight he saw that her face had gone white and set, as it had been on the morning they buried the boy, when she had stood by the grave in the snow and would not let anyone take her arm.

"Yes," she said. "The priest would tell me the same. And you would tell me the same. And Hobart would tell me the same, and Vaclav, and everybody. Everybody is very wise about what the dead know." She stood up. "I know that I carried water to that tree every night for four summers, and it is alive. It is the only thing on this place that is alive this year. You can go and look at it."

She went down the steps and past him, across the yard, and out along the path that led through the dry pasture toward the corner of the place. She did not hurry. Peter watched her small, straight figure grow dim against the gray grass until he could hardly tell it from the shadows of the fence posts. Then he heard the windmill pump begin to clank, and he knew that she had stopped at the tank to fill her bucket.

He sat down again on the porch step, heavily, like an old man. The night had grown quite still. The wind had dropped, and the windmill had stopped turning, and the air smelled of dust and dry grass and the faint sweetness of the morning-glories that had closed along the porch. Far off to the south, along the river, there was a little heat lightning, flickering pink and silent at the edge of the world, promising nothing.

Peter took the paper out of his pocket again and held it in his two hands. He thought of the car shops in Omaha, which he had never seen, and tried to imagine himself walking home through lighted streets in the evening with a dollar and a half in his pocket. He tried to imagine Klara at a window in a narrow brick house, looking out at other brick houses. But the picture would not stay; it kept slipping away from him, and in its place he saw only the things before his eyes: the dark shape of the barn he had built, the line of cottonwoods against the stars, the pale ribbon of the road going over the hill toward Hollis. He had dug the well himself, the first summer, and had nearly been killed when the curbing gave way. He had broken every acre of that pasture with a team of borrowed oxen, walking behind the plow from daylight to dark, with the sod turning over in long, shining strips, and the smell of the torn roots so strong and sweet that it made him a little drunk. He remembered how he used to stand at the end of a furrow, in those first years, and look back at what he had done, and feel that he could take the whole country in his two hands and shape it like clay.

He did not feel that way now. He knew the country better. It was not clay; it was something older and harder and more indifferent than anything he had known in the old world, and it did not care whether he stayed or went. That was what he had wanted to say to Klara, and what he had not been able to say. It was not that he was tired, though he was tired. It was that he had begun to be afraid of the land, as a man is afraid of a horse that has thrown him once, and he did not want her to know it.

After a long time he got up and went out along the path himself. The grass crackled under his boots. When he came to the little rise at the corner of the place he saw her sitting on the ground beside the grave, with the empty bucket beside her and her hands clasped around her knees. The mulberry was not much taller than she was, but it had leafed out thick and dark, and in the starlight it looked very green against all that burned and colorless country, as if it had been painted there.

He stood a little way off, not knowing what to say. Klara did not look up.

"I should not have said that about the boy," he said at last.

"No," she agreed. "You should not."

"I did not mean it the way it sounded."

"I know how you meant it." She was silent a moment. "You meant that you would like to be free of everything, and that he is one of the things. Well, he is. I am one of the things too, Petr, and the girls. You cannot sell us to Hobart."

Peter sat down on the ground beside her, with his long legs drawn up, and looked at the little tree. He reached out and touched one of the leaves, and it was cool and a little damp from the water she had just poured.

"What will we do, then," he said, "if the corn is gone?"

"We will do what we did the year of the grasshoppers. You will go and work on the railroad for the winter, if you want to, and I will stay here with the girls and the stock. We will kill the old sow and the steer, and we will eat potatoes and cabbage, and I will make the girls' dresses over again. In the spring we will plant. It is not the first bad year, and it will not be the last."

"And if next year is bad too?"

"Then we will talk about it next year." She turned and looked at him for the first time since she had left the porch. "I am not saying never, Petr. I am not a fool. I am saying not now, not because Hobart came into Lindquist's store on a hot Saturday when you were feeling sorry for yourself."

Peter did not answer. He felt in his pocket for the paper and found it there, folded small, the edges soft from handling. He did not take it out. Down along the creek the frogs had begun, in the little pools that were left, and their voices came up thin and shrill through the warm dark. The heat lightning still flickered in the south, very faint now, as if it were very far away, in some other country where it might be raining.

They sat there until the dew began to fall, which it did even in the driest years, so lightly that one felt it only as a coolness on the hands. Then Klara got up and took her bucket, and Peter got up and followed her back across the pasture toward the house, where the lamp she had left burning in the kitchen window made a small yellow square in the darkness. Neither of them spoke on the way. When they reached the porch she went in ahead of him, and he heard her moving about softly in the bedroom, so as not to wake the girls.

Peter stood for a while on the step. Then he went into the kitchen, took the paper out of his pocket, and put it behind the clock on the shelf over the stove, where they kept the tax receipts and the children's baptismal certificates and the letter from the old country telling them that his mother was dead. He did not burn it; he was not a man for such gestures, and in any case he was not sure. He only put it there, among the other papers that belonged to the house, and blew out the lamp, and went to bed.

Bergson had spent his first five years on the Divide getting into debt, and the last six getting out. He had paid off his mortgages and had ended pretty much where he began, with the land. He owned exactly six hundred and forty acres of what stretched outside his door; his own original homestead and timber claim, making three hundred and twenty acres, and the half-section adjoining, the homestead of a younger brother who had given up the fight, gone back to Chicago to work in a fancy bakery and distinguish himself in a Swedish athletic club. So far John had not attempted to cultivate the second half-section, but used it for pasture land, and one of his sons rode herd there in open weather. John Bergson had the Old-World belief that land, in itself, is desirable. But this land was an enigma. It was like a horse that no one knows how to break to harness, that runs wild and kicks things to pieces. He had an idea that no one understood how to farm it properly, and this he often discussed with Alexandra. Their neighbors, certainly, knew even less about farming than he did. Many of them had never worked on a farm until they took up their homesteads. They had been handwerkers at home; tailors, locksmiths, joiners, cigar-makers, etc. Bergson himself had worked in a shipyard. For weeks, John Bergson had been thinking about these things. His bed stood in the sitting-room, next to the kitchen. Through the day, while the baking and washing and ironing were going on, the father lay and looked up at the roof beams that he himself had hewn, or out at the cattle in the corral. He counted the cattle over and over. It diverted him to speculate as to how much weight each of the steers would probably put on by spring. He often called his daughter in to talk to her about this. Before Alexandra was twelve years old she had begun to be a help to him, and as she grew older he had come to depend more and more upon her resourcefulness and good judgment. His boys were willing enough to work, but when he talked with them they usually irritated him. It was Alexandra who read the papers and followed the markets, and who learned by the mistakes of their neighbors. It was Alexandra who could always tell about what it had cost to fatten each steer, and who could guess the weight of a hog before it went on the scales closer than John Bergson himself. Lou and Oscar were industrious, but he could never teach them to use their heads about their work. Alexandra, her father often said to himself, was like her grandfather; which was his way of saying that she was intelligent. John Bergson’s father had been a shipbuilder, a man of considerable force and of some fortune. Late in life he married a second time, a Stockholm woman of questionable character, much younger than he, who goaded him into every sort of extravagance. On the shipbuilder’s part, this marriage was an infatuation, the despairing folly of a powerful man who cannot bear to grow old. In a few years his unprincipled wife warped the probity of a lifetime. He speculated, lost his own fortune and funds entrusted to him by poor seafaring men, and died disgraced, leaving his children nothing. But when all was said, he had come up from the sea himself, had built up a proud little business with no capital but his own skill and foresight, and had proved himself a man. In his daughter, John Bergson recognized the strength of will, and the simple direct way of thinking things out, that had characterized his father in his better days. He would much rather, of course, have seen this likeness in one of his sons, but it was not a question of choice. As he lay there day after day he had to accept the situation as it was, and to be thankful that there was one among his children to whom he could entrust the future of his family and the possibilities of his hard-won land. The winter twilight was fading. The sick man heard his wife strike a match in the kitchen, and the light of a lamp glimmered through the cracks of the door. It seemed like a light shining far away. He turned painfully in his bed and looked at his white hands, with all the work gone out of them. He was ready to give up, he felt. He did not know how it had come about, but he was quite willing to go deep under his fields and rest, where the plow could not find him. He was tired of making mistakes. He was content to leave the tangle to other hands; he thought of his Alexandra’s strong ones.

“Dotter,” he called feebly, “dotter!” He heard her quick step and saw her tall figure appear in the doorway, with the light of the lamp behind her. He felt her youth and strength, how easily she moved and stooped and lifted. But he would not have had it again if he could, not he! He knew the end too well to wish to begin again. He knew where it all went to, what it all became. His daughter came and lifted him up on his pillows. She called him by an old Swedish name that she used to call him when she was little and took his dinner to him in the shipyard.

“Tell the boys to come here, daughter. I want to speak to them.”

“They are feeding the horses, father. They have just come back from the Blue. Shall I call them?” He sighed. “No, no. Wait until they come in. Alexandra, you will have to do the best you can for your brothers. Everything will come on you.”

“I will do all I can, father.”

“Don’t let them get discouraged and go off like Uncle Otto. I want them to keep the land.”

“We will, father. We will never lose the land.” There was a sound of heavy feet in the kitchen. Alexandra went to the door and beckoned to her brothers, two strapping boys of seventeen and nineteen. They came in and stood at the foot of the bed. Their father looked at them searchingly, though it was too dark to see their faces; they were just the same boys, he told himself, he had not been mistaken in them. The square head and heavy shoulders belonged to Oscar, the elder. The younger boy was quicker, but vacillating.

“Boys,” said the father wearily, “I want you to keep the land together and to be guided by your sister. I have talked to her since I have been sick, and she knows all my wishes. I want no quarrels among my children, and so long as there is one house there must be one head. Alexandra is the oldest, and she knows my wishes. She will do the best she can. If she makes mistakes, she will not make so many as I have made. When you marry, and want a house of your own, the land will be divided fairly, according to the courts. But for the next few years you will have it hard, and you must all keep together. Alexandra will manage the best she can.” Oscar, who was usually the last to speak, replied because he was the older, “Yes, father. It would be so anyway, without your speaking. We will all work the place together.”

“And you will be guided by your sister, boys, and be good brothers to her, and good sons to your mother? That is good. And Alexandra must not work in the fields any more. There is no necessity now. Hire a man when you need help. She can make much more with her eggs and butter than the wages of a man. It was one of my mistakes that I did not find that out sooner. Try to break a little more land every year; sod corn is good for fodder. Keep turning the land, and always put up more hay than you need. Don’t grudge your mother a little time for plowing her garden and setting out fruit trees, even if it comes in a busy season. She has been a good mother to you, and she has always missed the old country.” When they went back to the kitchen the boys sat down silently at the table. Throughout the meal they looked down at their plates and did not lift their red eyes. They did not eat much, although they had been working in the cold all day, and there was a rabbit stewed in gravy for supper, and prune pies. John Bergson had married beneath him, but he had married a good housewife. Mrs. Bergson was a fair-skinned, corpulent woman, heavy and placid like her son, Oscar, but there was something comfortable about her; perhaps it was her own love of comfort. For eleven years she had worthily striven to maintain some semblance of household order amid conditions that made order very difficult. Habit was very strong with Mrs. Bergson, and her unremitting efforts to repeat the routine of her old life among new surroundings had done a great deal to keep the family from disintegrating morally and getting careless in their ways. The Bergsons had a log house, for instance, only because Mrs. Bergson would not live in a sod house. She missed the fish diet of her own country, and twice every summer she sent the boys to the river, twenty miles to the southward, to fish for channel cat. When the children were little she used to load them all into the wagon, the baby in its crib, and go fishing herself. Alexandra often said that if her mother were cast upon a desert island, she would thank God for her deliverance, make a garden, and find something to preserve. Preserving was almost a mania with Mrs. Bergson. Stout as she was, she roamed the scrubby banks of Norway Creek looking for fox grapes and goose plums, like a wild creature in search of prey. She made a yellow jam of the insipid ground-cherries that grew on the prairie, flavoring it with lemon peel; and she made a sticky dark conserve of garden tomatoes. She had experimented even with the rank buffalo-pea, and she could not see a fine bronze cluster of them without shaking her head and murmuring, “What a pity!” When there was nothing more to preserve, she began to pickle. The amount of sugar she used in these processes was sometimes a serious drain upon the family resources. She was a good mother, but she was glad when her children were old enough not to be in her way in the kitchen. She had never quite forgiven John Bergson for bringing her to the end of the earth; but, now that she was there, she wanted to be let alone to reconstruct her old life in so far as that was possible. She could still take some comfort in the world if she had bacon in the cave, glass jars on the shelves, and sheets in the press. She disapproved of all her neighbors because of their slovenly housekeeping, and the women thought her very proud. Once when Mrs. Bergson, on her way to Norway Creek, stopped to see old Mrs. Lee, the old woman hid in the haymow “for fear Mis’ Bergson would catch her barefoot.”

One Sunday afternoon in July, six months after John Bergson’s death, Carl was sitting in the doorway of the Linstrum kitchen, dreaming over an illustrated paper, when he heard the rattle of a wagon along the hill road. Looking up he recognized the Bergsons’ team, with two seats in the wagon, which meant they were off for a pleasure excursion. Oscar and Lou, on the front seat, wore their cloth hats and coats, never worn except on Sundays, and Emil, on the second seat with Alexandra, sat proudly in his new trousers, made from a pair of his father’s, and a pink-striped shirt, with a wide ruffled collar. Oscar stopped the horses and waved to Carl, who caught up his hat and ran through the melon patch to join them.

“Want to go with us?” Lou called. “We’re going to Crazy Ivar’s to buy a hammock.”

“Sure.” Carl ran up panting, and clambering over the wheel sat down beside Emil. “I’ve always wanted to see Ivar’s pond. They say it’s the biggest in all the country. Aren’t you afraid to go to Ivar’s in that new shirt, Emil? He might want it and take it right off your back.” Emil grinned. “I’d be awful scared to go,” he admitted, “if you big boys weren’t along to take care of me. Did you ever hear him howl, Carl? “But suppose there wasn’t any badger-hole,” Lou persisted. “Would you run?”

“No, I’d be too scared to run,” Emil admitted mournfully, twisting his fingers. “I guess I’d sit right down on the ground and say my prayers.” The big boys laughed, and Oscar brandished his whip over the broad backs of the horses.

“He wouldn’t hurt you, Emil,” said Carl persuasively. “He came to doctor our mare when she ate green corn and swelled up most as big as the water-tank. He petted her just like you do your cats. I couldn’t understand much he said, for he don’t talk any English, but he kept patting her and groaning as if he had the pain himself, and saying, ‘There now, sister, that’s easier, that’s better!’” Lou and Oscar laughed, and Emil giggled delightedly and looked up at his sister.

“I don’t think he knows anything at all about doctoring,” said Oscar scornfully. “They say when horses have distemper he takes the medicine himself, and then prays over the horses.” Alexandra spoke up. “That’s what the Crows said, but he cured their horses, all the same.
