The hot winds had blown for nine days, and on the tenth they stopped. Nils Hovland came home from town in the late afternoon, driving slowly, letting the team pick their own way along the section line. The corn on either side of the road stood white and papery, the leaves curled tight as cigarettes, and when a little puff of air went over them they made a dry, scratching sound, like mice in a wall. He did not look at the corn. He had looked at it enough. He kept his eyes on the horses' ears and on the long, pale road that ran straight west into the sun, and he did not lift them until he saw his own windmill turning lazily against the sky.

Marta was in the garden when he drove into the yard. She had a tin pail on her arm and was picking the last of the beans, such as they were, for the vines had dried on the poles and the pods were small and twisted. She straightened up and shaded her eyes with her hand. She was a tall woman, broad in the shoulders, and her hair, which had been very yellow when she was a girl, had faded to the color of oat straw. She watched him unhitch, and she knew from the way he stood beside the wagon, with his hand on the wheel, that something had happened in town. She went into the house without calling to him and began to get supper.

They had lived on that place fourteen years. When they first came out from Wisconsin, there had been nothing on the quarter but a dugout cut into the side of the draw, and a few rods of breaking that the former owner had abandoned. Marta had cried every night that first winter. She had not let Nils see it; she cried in the morning, before he was awake, standing at the little window where the light came in gray and low, and she thought she would die of the bigness of the country and the emptiness of it, and of the wind, which never stopped and seemed to have something to say to her that she could not understand. In the spring she had planted morning-glories about the door of the dugout, and when they came up she stopped crying. People said afterward that Marta Hovland was the steadiest woman in the township. They did not know about that first winter. Nobody knew but Marta herself.

Now there was a frame house, painted white, with a porch on the south side, and a row of cottonwoods along the lane that Nils had set out with his own hands, carrying water to them in buckets the first two summers. There was a good barn and a granary, and a chicken house, and a cave for vegetables. There was a plum thicket on the rise behind the windbreak, and under the plum thicket there was a small grave with a white wooden cross and a little picket fence about it, which Nils painted every spring.

Supper was on the table when he came in. He washed at the bench by the door, drying his face and his thick, sunburned neck on the roller towel, and sat down. Marta poured his coffee. Neither of them spoke while she set out the fried potatoes and the cold pork and the plate of rye bread. The kitchen was very hot, for she had had the fire going all afternoon, and the flies walked about on the oilcloth and on the rim of the sugar bowl. Outside, the light had turned coppery, and the windows were full of it.

"I saw Fenton," Nils said at last.

Marta did not answer at once. She cut a slice of bread and buttered it carefully, all the way to the edges, the way she had always done for the children when they were little. Then she laid it on his plate.

"Fenton the land man?"

"Yes. He came over to me at the bank. He has a man from Iowa who wants a farm out this way. A man with money. He is looking at the Kruger place and at ours."

"The Kruger place is no good," said Marta. "The west forty is all gumbo."

"That is what Fenton says. He says the man likes our place better."

Marta got up and went to the stove for the coffeepot, although both cups were still full. She stood there with her back to him, her hand on the hot handle, and looked down into the fire box, where the cobs had burned to a red shimmer.

"You told him it was not for sale," she said.

Nils was silent. He turned his cup slowly round and round in its saucer. He was a slow man, slow to speak and slow to anger, and he had a way of looking at a thing a long time before he said what he thought of it. His neighbors trusted him for that. They used to say that when Nils Hovland made up his mind, the matter was settled, and it was no use arguing.

"I did not tell him that," he said.

She came back and sat down. Her face was quite calm; only her hands, lying in her lap on the blue apron, were held very tightly together.

"What did you tell him?"

"I told him I would talk to my wife."

"Well," said Marta, "now you have talked to her."

He looked up at her then, and for a moment they regarded each other across the table, across the plate of bread and the brown crockery pitcher, as if they were two strangers who had sat down at the same table in a railway eating house. It was a curious thing, Marta thought afterward, how a face one has looked at for twenty years can suddenly become a face one has never seen. She saw that the lines about his eyes had grown very deep, and that there was gray in his mustache, and that his hands, lying on either side of his plate, were cracked across the knuckles. She thought he looked like an old man. She had not thought it before.

"Marta," he said, "it is the third year."

"I know what year it is."

"The third year. In 'ninety-two we got half a crop, and we said, next year. Last year the grasshoppers came, and we said, next year. Now this. I went out this morning before I hitched up and pulled an ear in the north field. There is nothing on it, Marta. Not a kernel. It is like a cob a pig has been at." He spread out his hands. "We have the mortgage on the stock already. In November there is the interest. I do not know where I am to get it."

"We will get it somehow. We always have."

"We always had something to sell."

"There are the hogs."

"The hogs will not bring enough. Nobody has corn to feed them. Everybody is selling hogs. You cannot give a hog away in Cedar Bend this fall."

She did not answer. The light was going out of the windows now, and the kitchen grew dim. She got up and lit the lamp and set it in the middle of the table, and the flame jumped and steadied, and their two shadows came out large and black upon the wall behind them. Outside a mourning dove began to call from the cottonwoods, over and over, with that soft, foolish insistence which seems so sorrowful to human ears and probably means nothing at all to the dove.

"And where would we go?" Marta asked. "Back to Wisconsin, to live with your brother and be poor relations?"

"Not to Wisconsin." He reached into the pocket of his shirt and brought out a letter, much folded, and laid it on the oilcloth beside the lamp. She knew the handwriting. It was from his cousin Anders, who had gone out to the State of Washington six years before. "Anders writes again. He has forty acres in apples now. He says it rains there. He says it rains all winter, soft, like in the old country, and in summer the river comes down from the mountains, and they lead it out into ditches, and nobody looks at the sky. He says there is land to be had near him, already cleared, with young trees on it. He says a man can make a living on twenty acres there."

Marta did not touch the letter. She looked at it as if it were something that might bite.

"Anders always wrote fine letters," she said. "When he was in Dakota he wrote fine letters too."

"That is not fair, Marta."

"Maybe not." She pressed her lips together. "You have been thinking about this a long time."

"Since spring," he admitted. "Since the winds in May, when the wheat went."

"And you said nothing to me."

"I did not want to say anything until I was sure."

"And now you are sure."

He did not answer. He pushed his plate a little away from him, though he had eaten almost nothing, and sat looking at the lamp. The wick needed trimming; one corner of the flame was higher than the other, and a thin thread of smoke went up from it and blackened the chimney. Marta saw it and did not get up to fix it. It was the first time in fourteen years, perhaps, that she had seen a lamp smoke in her kitchen and let it be.

"Nils," she said, in a different voice, low and quite steady, "do you remember the first spring? When you broke the sod on the south eighty, and I walked behind the plow and threw out the roots?"

"I remember."

"You said then that we would never move again. You said you were done with moving. Your father moved, and your grandfather, and you said the Hovlands had been going from one place to another for a hundred years, and it was time one of them stayed put and let his bones lie where he planted them. You said that. You stood out there with the lines around your neck and said it."

"I was young," Nils said. "I did not know the country."

"You knew it well enough. You knew it was dry. Everybody told us it was dry. Old Mrs. Lindgren told us, the first week, that it was a country for the strong and the patient and nobody else. And you laughed and said we were both."

He moved his shoulders heavily. "Being patient does not make it rain."

"No. But being in Washington does not make the children come back."

She had not meant to say it. She saw him flinch, as a horse flinches when a fly bites it, a quick shudder that went over him and was gone. He did not look at her. He looked down at his cracked hands, and for a long while there was no sound in the kitchen but the dove in the cottonwoods and the tick of the clock on the shelf. Their two older girls were married and gone, one to Omaha and one to a farm in the next county; the youngest boy, Peter, was working out for a neighbor that summer and slept there. And Erik, who had come between the girls and Peter, lay under the plum thicket on the rise. He had died in the third winter, when he was six years old, of the diphtheria. It had been a winter of deep snow, and Nils had tried to go for the doctor and had been lost in the storm all night and had come home in the morning with his feet frozen, and the boy had died while he was gone. Marta had been alone with him. She had held him in her arms by the stove, and he had choked and fought for his breath, and toward morning he had stopped fighting. She had never told Nils exactly how it was, and he had never asked her.

"That is not why," Nils said at last, very low.

"No. I know it is not why." She put her hand over her eyes for a moment. "I should not have said it."

"You can say what you like."

"I should not have said it," she repeated stubbornly.

He got up and went to the door and stood looking out through the screen. The sun had gone down, and the sky in the west was a clear, cold green, like the inside of a glass bottle, with one long bar of red cloud lying across it. The windmill had stopped turning. Beyond the barn the dead cornfields stretched away, gray now, without any color at all, and over them the first star had come out, very bright and alone. The whole country had a look of waiting, of holding its breath. It was always so in the evenings of a dry year. One felt that something must happen, that the land could not lie so still under the sky without some answer coming. And nothing happened. Night came, and morning, and the sky was as hard and empty as before.

"I am fifty-one years old, Marta," he said, without turning. "Fourteen years I have put into this place. Every year I have said, next year. I do not have so many more years to say it in. If I am going to begin again somewhere, I must begin now. In ten years I will not be able to."

"Nobody asks you to begin again."

"The bank asks me. Wick—" he stopped himself; he had been going to say the banker's name, and he did not like to say it in the house. "The bank will ask me in November. And if I have nothing, they will take the stock, and then what? Then we stay on the land with no horses to work it. Then I hire out to Fenton's man from Iowa, and plow my own fields for him, at a dollar a day." His voice had risen, and he heard it, and brought it down again. "I would rather sell now, while there is something to sell. While a man still wants it."

Marta sat at the table with her hands folded. The lamplight fell on her face, and on her faded hair, and on the strong, worn hands. She looked, Nils thought, turning at last to her, exactly as her mother had looked, in the little house by the lake in Wisconsin, the evening he had come to ask for her. Her mother had sat just so, very upright, listening to him, and had said nothing at all for a long time, and then had said, "Marta is not a girl who changes her mind. You had better be sure of yours." He had been sure. He had been twenty-nine years old, and sure of everything.

"I will tell you something," Marta said. "When we came here, I hated it. I hated it so that I could not breathe. The first winter I used to stand at that window in the dugout every morning and wish that I was dead. I thought the wind would drive me crazy. I thought the country was trying to kill us. I never told you."

He stared at her. "You never told me."

"No. I did not want you to think you had brought me to a bad place. And then the spring came, and I planted the morning-glories, and I thought, well, I can stand it until fall. And in the fall I thought, I can stand it until spring. And after a while I did not have to stand it any more. I do not know when it happened. It was not all at once. But one day I was out by the haystacks, and the sun was going down, and all the grass was red, and I thought, this is mine. This is my country. I am not a stranger here any more." She looked up at him. "It took me so long, Nils. I do not think I could do it again. I am too old to learn a new country. I would be a stranger there until I died."

He came back slowly and sat down across from her. He put out his hand, after a moment, and laid it on the table near hers, not touching it.

"You would not be a stranger. You would have me."

"I have you here."

"Here we will starve."

"Then we will starve here," said Marta.

She said it quite simply, without any heat, as she might have said that it would be a cold winter. And Nils, looking at her, saw that she meant it, and that she would always mean it, and that nothing he could say would change it. It was heat lightning, so far off that they could hear no thunder. They had seen it every night for a month.

"It might be rain," Nils said.

"It might," said Marta.

Neither of them believed it. But they watched it for a long time, side by side, until the stars began to go pale in the east and the dove woke again in the cottonwoods below.

Of all the strange, uprooted people among the first settlers, those two men were the strangest and the most aloof. Their last names were unpronounceable, so they were called Pavel and Peter. They went about making signs to people, and until the Shimerdas came they had no friends. Krajiek could understand them a little, but he had cheated them in a trade, so they avoided him. Pavel, the tall one, was said to be an anarchist; since he had no means of imparting his opinions, probably his wild gesticulations and his generally excited and rebellious manner gave rise to this supposition. He must once have been a very strong man, but now his great frame, with big, knotty joints, had a wasted look, and the skin was drawn tight over his high cheek-bones. His breathing was hoarse, and he always had a cough. Peter, his companion, was a very different sort of fellow; short, bow-legged, and as fat as butter. He always seemed pleased when he met people on the road, smiled and took off his cap to every one, men as well as women. At a distance, on his wagon, he looked like an old man; his hair and beard were of such a pale flaxen color that they seemed white in the sun. They were as thick and curly as carded wool. His rosy face, with its snub nose, set in this fleece, was like a melon among its leaves. He was usually called “Curly Peter,” or “Rooshian Peter.” The two Russians made good farmhands, and in summer they worked out together. I had heard our neighbors laughing when they told how Peter always had to go home at night to milk his cow. Other bachelor homesteaders used canned milk, to save trouble. Sometimes Peter came to church at the sod schoolhouse. It was there I first saw him, sitting on a low bench by the door, his plush cap in his hands, his bare feet tucked apologetically under the seat. After Mr. Shimerda discovered the Russians, he went to see them almost every evening, and sometimes took Ántonia with him. She said they came from a part of Russia where the language was not very different from Bohemian, and if I wanted to go to their place, she could talk to them for me. As we rode up the draw we skirted a big melon patch, and a garden where squashes and yellow cucumbers lay about on the sod. We found Peter out behind his kitchen, bending over a washtub. He was working so hard that he did not hear us coming. His whole body moved up and down as he rubbed, and he was a funny sight from the rear, with his shaggy head and bandy legs. When he straightened himself up to greet us, drops of perspiration were rolling from his thick nose down on to his curly beard. Peter dried his hands and seemed glad to leave his washing. He took us down to see his chickens, and his cow that was grazing on the hillside. He told Ántonia that in his country only rich people had cows, but here any man could have one who would take care of her. The milk was good for Pavel, who was often sick, and he could make butter by beating sour cream with a wooden spoon. Peter was very fond of his cow. He patted her flanks and talked to her in Russian while he pulled up her lariat pin and set it in a new place. There were no screens or window-blinds in the house, and all the doors and windows stood wide open, letting in flies and sunshine alike. Peter put the melons in a row on the oilcloth-covered table and stood over them, brandishing a butcher knife. Before the blade got fairly into them, they split of their own ripeness, with a delicious sound. He gave us knives, but no plates, and the top of the table was soon swimming with juice and seeds. I had never seen any one eat so many melons as Peter ate. He assured us that they were good for one—better than medicine; in his country people lived on them at this time of year. He was very hospitable and jolly. Once, while he was looking at Ántonia, he sighed and told us that if he had stayed at home in Russia perhaps by this time he would have had a pretty daughter of his own to cook and keep house for him. He said he had left his country because of a “great trouble.” When we got up to go, Peter looked about in perplexity for something that would entertain us. He ran into the storeroom and brought out a gaudily painted harmonica, sat down on a bench, and spreading his fat legs apart began to play like a whole band. The tunes were either very lively or very doleful, and he sang words to some of them. Before we left, Peter put ripe cucumbers into a sack for Mrs. Shimerda and gave us a lard-pail full of milk to cook them in. I had never heard of cooking cucumbers, but Ántonia assured me they were very good. We had to walk the pony all the way home to keep from spilling the milk.

One afternoon we were having our reading lesson on the warm, grassy bank where the badger lived. It was a day of amber sunlight, but there was a shiver of coming winter in the air. I had seen ice on the little horse-pond that morning, and as we went through the garden we found the tall asparagus, with its red berries, lying on the ground, a mass of slimy green. Tony was barefooted, and she shivered in her cotton dress and was comfortable only when we were tucked down on the baked earth, in the full blaze of the sun. She could talk to me about almost anything by this time. That afternoon she was telling me how highly esteemed our friend the badger was in her part of the world, and how men kept a special kind of dog, with very short legs, to hunt him. Those dogs, she said, went down into the hole after the badger and killed him there in a terrific struggle underground; you could hear the barks and yelps outside. Then the dog dragged himself back, covered with bites and scratches, to be rewarded and petted by his master. She knew a dog who had a star on his collar for every badger he had killed. The rabbits were unusually spry that afternoon. They kept starting up all about us, and dashing off down the draw as if they were playing a game of some kind. But the little buzzing things that lived in the grass were all dead—all but one. While we were lying there against the warm bank, a little insect of the palest, frailest green hopped painfully out of the buffalo grass and tried to leap into a bunch of bluestem. He missed it, fell back, and sat with his head sunk between his long legs, his antennæ quivering, as if he were waiting for something to come and finish him. Tony made a warm nest for him in her hands; talked to him gayly and indulgently in Bohemian. Presently he began to sing for us—a thin, rusty little chirp. She held him close to her ear and laughed, but a moment afterward I saw there were tears in her eyes. She told me that in her village at home there was an old beggar woman who went about selling herbs and roots she had dug up in the forest. If you took her in and gave her a warm place by the fire, she sang old songs to the children in a cracked voice, like this. Old Hata, she was called, and the children loved to see her coming and saved their cakes and sweets for her. When the bank on the other side of the draw began to throw a narrow shelf of shadow, we knew we ought to be starting homeward; the chill came on quickly when the sun got low, and Ántonia’s dress was thin. What were we to do with the frail little creature we had lured back to life by false pretenses? I offered my pockets, but Tony shook her head and carefully put the green insect in her hair, tying her big handkerchief down loosely over her curls. I said I would go with her until we could see Squaw Creek, and then turn and run home. We drifted along lazily, very happy, through the magical light of the late afternoon. All those fall afternoons were the same, but I never got used to them. As far as we could see, the miles of copper-red grass were drenched in sunlight that was stronger and fiercer than at any other time of the day. The blond cornfields were red gold, the haystacks turned rosy and threw long shadows. The whole prairie was like the bush that burned with fire and was not consumed. That hour always had the exultation of victory, of triumphant ending, like a hero’s death—heroes who died young and gloriously. It was a sudden transfiguration, a lifting-up of day. How many an afternoon Ántonia and I have trailed along the prairie under that magnificence! And always two long black shadows flitted before us or followed after, dark spots on the ruddy grass. We had been silent a long time, and the edge of the sun sank nearer and nearer the prairie floor, when we saw a figure moving on the edge of the upland, a gun over his shoulder. He was walking slowly, dragging his feet along as if he had no purpose. We broke into a run to overtake him.

“My papa sick all the time,” Tony panted as we flew. “He not look good, Jim.” As we neared Mr. Shimerda she shouted, and he lifted his head and peered about. Tony ran up to him, caught his hand and pressed it against her cheek. She was the only one of his family who could rouse the old man from the torpor in which he seemed to live. He took the bag from his belt and showed us three rabbits he had shot, looked at Ántonia with a wintry flicker of a smile and began to tell her something. She turned to me.

“My tatinek make me little hat with the skins, little hat for win-ter!” she exclaimed joyfully. “Meat for eat, skin for hat,”—she told off these benefits on her fingers. Her father put his hand on her hair, but she caught his wrist and lifted it carefully away, talking to him rapidly. I heard the name of old Hata. He untied the handkerchief, separated her hair with his fingers, and stood looking down at the green insect. When it began to chirp faintly, he listened as if it were a beautiful sound. I picked up the gun he had dropped; a queer piece from the old country, short and heavy, with a stag’s head on the cock. When he saw me examining it, he turned to me with his far-away look that always made me feel as if I were down at the bottom of a well. He spoke kindly and gravely, and Ántonia translated:— “My tatinek say when you are big boy, he give you his gun. Very fine, from Bohemie. It was belong to a great man, very rich, like what you not got here; many fields, many forests, many big house. My papa play for his wedding, and he give my papa fine gun, and my papa give you.”

I was glad that this project was one of futurity. There never were such people as the Shimerdas for wanting to give away everything they had. Even the mother was always offering me things, though I knew she expected substantial presents in return. We stood there in friendly silence, while the feeble minstrel sheltered in Ántonia’s hair went on with its scratchy chirp. The old man’s smile, as he listened, was so full of sadness, of pity for things, that I never afterward forgot it. As the sun sank there came a sudden coolness and the strong smell of earth and drying grass. Ántonia and her father went off hand in hand, and I buttoned up my jacket and raced my shadow home.

The train was an hour late, and Hilda Forslund had been waiting on the station platform since half-past three. She had come in early because the roads were dry and the horses fresh, and because she had not been able to settle to anything at home after dinner. She had put on her brown merino and taken it off again, then put it on a second time, scolding herself in Swedish while she did up the hooks. Now she stood in the lee of the freight-house, out of the wind, with her hands folded inside her coat-sleeves, and watched the long line of the railroad running east until it narrowed to a needle and was lost in the shimmer over the stubble fields.

It was the last week in October. The country lay bare and open, the corn shocked and the wheat land already disked for the fall sowing. Along the creek the cottonwoods held a few yellow leaves, very high up, that trembled and flashed whenever the wind caught them. Everything else was the color of a lion's hide. Hilda had lived in that country all her life, except for the two years when she was a baby on the ocean and in a cold house in Illinois that she did not remember, and she had never been able to say whether she thought it beautiful. It was simply there, as her own hands were there. But today, because she knew her cousin would be looking at it through the car window, she found herself looking at it, too, as if for the first time, and she was a little ashamed of it; of its flatness and its plainness, and the way the town sat down in the middle of it with no trees to speak of, like a man who has come into a strange house and does not know where to put his hat.

When the train came at last it came quickly, with a great deal of noise, and only one passenger got down. Hilda knew her at once, and yet for a moment she did not go forward. The woman on the step was slender and wore a gray traveling dress and a small hat with a dark wing on it, and she stood looking up and down the platform with an expression at once eager and uncertain. The station agent handed down her bag. Then she saw Hilda and her face changed, and she came across the boards with both hands out.

"Hilda! Oh, Hilda, it's you. I was afraid nobody would be here."

"Where else would I be?" said Hilda. She took her cousin's hands and held them, and then, because there seemed nothing else to do, she put her arms around her. Kristina was thinner than she had been. Under the good cloth of the jacket Hilda could feel the shoulder-blades, light and sharp as a bird's. She smelled faintly of violets and of the coal smoke of the cars.

"Twelve years," Kristina said, standing back. "Twelve years in March. I counted on the train. I kept counting, and every time I came out the same."

"It's long enough," Hilda said. "Come, the team is behind the elevator. Is this all you brought, this one bag?"

"The trunk is coming tomorrow, they told me. I don't need it. I don't need anything. Let me look at you."

But Hilda had already picked up the bag and was walking toward the wagon, and Kristina had to follow her.

The horses were a pair of bays, heavy and quiet, and Hilda drove them herself. She had always driven well. Kristina sat beside her on the spring seat with her gloved hands in her lap and turned her head constantly from side to side, as a child does on its first journey. They went out of town past the lumber-yard and the Methodist church, which had a new steeple since Kristina's time, and over the iron bridge, and then the road went straight south between the section lines and there was nothing ahead of them but the long, tawny swells of the land, one behind another, going away toward the Kansas line.

"It's just the same," Kristina said softly. "I thought it would be different. I thought I had made it bigger in my mind. But it is just as big."

"There are more fences," said Hilda. "And the Peterson boys have put in alfalfa where the old pasture was. You'll see it when we come to the corner."

"And the sky. I had forgotten the sky. In Chicago you never see it, except in pieces between the buildings, like something cut out of a magazine."

Hilda glanced at her sidewise. Her cousin's face, in the strong afternoon light, showed what the station platform had not. There were fine lines about the eyes, and the skin had that look of being too much indoors, too much under gaslight; but the eyes themselves were what they had always been, gray and very clear and quick to fill with feeling, so that one never quite knew whether she was going to laugh or cry. When they were girls together, Kristina had cried at everything—at a dead meadow-lark, at a song in church, at the sight of a train going away in the dusk. Hilda had been the one who did not cry. She had stood by, red-faced and stubborn, and waited for it to be over.

"You have a little gray," Kristina said suddenly. "Just here, over your ear. Oh, I don't mind. It becomes you. And you are so brown, Hilda, and so strong-looking. You look like Grandmother."

"I am as heavy as Grandmother, anyhow," said Hilda, and laughed. It was the first time she had laughed, and with it something in her chest seemed to loosen and give way, as ice gives way on a creek in March, all at once, with a little sound.

They talked then, as people talk who have a great deal to say and do not know where to begin; about the journey, and the price of wheat, and Kristina's position in the music store on Wabash Avenue, where she sold sheet music and pianos and gave lessons in a little room at the back to the daughters of men who had made money in hides and lumber. Kristina told it lightly, with a good many funny touches. She described the proprietor, who was a German and wore a velvet cap and believed that nobody could play Schubert who had not been born within sight of the Danube; and a pupil of hers, a fat girl of fourteen who wept over her scales and ate chocolate creams between them; and her landlady, who kept seven canaries and named them all after Presidents. Hilda listened and smiled, and asked a question now and then. But she noticed that Kristina said nothing at all about the man she had written of, three years ago, in the only long letter she ever sent; and Hilda did not ask.

The sun was low when they came over the last rise and saw the Forslund place below them, set down in a shallow fold of the land with its windbreak of box-elders and its tall windmill, and the red barn that Gustav had built the year their second boy was born. Smoke was going up straight from the kitchen chimney. Kristina drew a long breath.

"You have trees," she said. "Real trees."

"Gustav planted every one of them. He carried water to them in buckets the first three summers. The neighbors laughed at him. They don't laugh now."

The children had been watching from the gate, and they came running down the lane before the wagon reached it; three boys, tow-headed and barefooted in spite of the cold, and a little girl in a red flannel dress who stopped short when she saw the strange lady and put her finger in her mouth. Gustav came out of the barn, wiping his hands on a sack. He was a big, slow, fair man, very shy with women, and he shook Kristina's hand without looking at her and said that he hoped she had a good trip, and then took the horses and went away again with an air of great relief.

That evening, after supper was over and the children had been put to bed in the loft, the two women sat in the kitchen with the lamp between them. Gustav had gone out to see to a sick calf. The kitchen was warm and smelled of coffee and of the apples Hilda had been drying on the warming-oven, and in the south window three geraniums, planted in lard-pails, still carried a few scarlet flowers. Kristina had taken off her jacket and her little winged hat, and in her white shirtwaist, with her hair loosened a little from the journey, she looked younger, more as she used to look. She sat with her elbows on the oilcloth and her chin in her hands.

"I keep thinking," she said, "of the night we ran away to the river. Do you remember? We were going to walk to Omaha and go on the stage."

"I remember that I was ten and you were eleven, and that you were going to sing and I was going to sell the tickets," said Hilda. "And that Uncle Lars came after us with the lantern and found us under the bridge, eating the bread and cheese we had taken, before we had gone two miles."

"And he didn't whip us. He only stood there with the lantern, and looked at us, and said, 'Well, girls, it is a long way to Omaha.' And then he carried you home on his back because you had lost a shoe in the mud."

"I had not lost it. You had thrown it in the river to make it seem more like a real adventure."

Kristina put back her head and laughed until the tears came. "Did I? Oh, Hilda, did I really? I had forgotten that. I am sure it is true. I was a dreadful child."

"You were not dreadful. You were only always going somewhere."

Kristina stopped laughing. She looked down at the oilcloth, at the pattern of little blue windmills on it, and traced one with her finger. "Well," she said, "I went."

The wind had risen with the dark, and it came now in long breaths against the north side of the house and went sighing off through the box-elders. Somewhere out on the prairie a dog was barking, very far away; the sound came and went with the wind, so that sometimes it seemed close by and sometimes not to be there at all. Hilda got up and put another stick in the stove, and the firelight leaped out through the cracks around the lids and played over the ceiling.

"Tell me about Grandmother," Kristina said. "At the last. You wrote, but you didn't say very much. I have wanted to know."

Hilda sat down again. For a while she did not speak. She was not a woman to whom words came easily, and she wanted to tell this rightly.

"She was not sick long," she said at last. "It was in the haying, the second summer after you went away. She had been out in the garden all morning, cutting pieplant, and she came in and sat down in her chair by the window and said she was tired. That was all. She never said she was tired, you know. Not once in her life. So I knew. I sent Gustav for the doctor, but she would not have him in the room. She said she had lived seventy-nine years without a doctor and she did not mean to begin with one now."

Kristina smiled, but her eyes were bright.

"She talked a good deal, that last night. Mostly about the old country. About the farm by the lake where she was a girl, and the birch woods, and how they used to row across to church on Sundays in summer and drive across on the ice in winter. She talked about her mother. I had never heard her speak of her mother before. And she asked for you." Hilda paused. "She wanted to know whether you were singing yet. I told her you were. I did not know whether it was so, but I told her."

Kristina did not answer. She had turned her face toward the dark window, where the lamp was reflected, and the geraniums, and her own face, pale against the black glass.

"I was not," she said presently, very low. "Not then. I had a cold all that winter, and I was working in a laundry on the West Side. I did not write you about the laundry. I could not bear to." She turned back from the window. "I did sing afterward. For a while. In a church choir, and once with an orchestra at a summer garden, by the lake. People clapped. There was a notice in one of the papers—only a few lines, but it said I had a voice of uncommon warmth. I cut it out and carried it in my purse until it fell apart. But it did not come to anything, Hilda. You must have known it would not come to anything. I suppose everybody knew but me."

"I did not know it," said Hilda. "I thought you would be famous. I used to look in the Omaha paper for your name."

"Did you? Did you truly?" Kristina reached across the table and caught her cousin's hand, the big, rough, capable hand, and held it against her cheek, as she used to do when they were little and slept together in the trundle-bed under Grandmother's eaves, and Hilda was afraid of the wind. "And here I have been, all these years, thinking you must pity me. Thinking of you here with your husband and your children and your trees, and of what a poor thing I had made of it."

Hilda drew her hand away, not unkindly, and smoothed the oilcloth in front of her. "Pity you?" she said. "No. Not that." She was silent a moment, and her broad face worked a little. "I will tell you something I never told anybody. The spring you went away, I used to go up on the hill behind the old place, where you could see the train go by in the evening, far off, with the smoke lying back over it. And I would stand there until it was gone. I did that every night for a month. Gustav was courting me then, and he would come over after supper and find me gone, and Mother would tell him I was out after the cows. I was not out after the cows. I was watching that train, and wishing I were on it, and hating you because you were brave enough and I was not."

Kristina stared at her. "Hilda! You never wanted to go away. You always said this country was good enough for anybody."

"I said it," Hilda answered. "I said it because you were saying the other thing. Somebody had to say it." She gave a short laugh. "And then I married Gustav, and the babies came, and there was the drought, and the year the hail took everything, and there was no more time for watching trains. And now I would not change. That is the truth, too. But I have thought about that hill a good many times."

The door opened, and Gustav came in with the cold about him, stamping his feet and blowing on his hands. He said the calf was better. He looked from one woman to the other, as if he felt that something had happened in the room while he was away; then he poured himself a cup of coffee from the pot on the back of the stove, drank it standing, said good night, and went up the narrow stairs. They heard his boots drop, one and then the other, on the floor overhead.

"He is a good man," Kristina said.

"Yes," said Hilda simply. "He is good."

In the morning the wind had gone down and the day came up clear and very still, with a hard white frost on everything. The windmill stood motionless, every blade outlined with rime, and the box-elders were feathered with it to their last twigs, so that when the sun struck them the whole windbreak seemed to be made of spun glass. Kristina came down early, in an old coat of Hilda's that hung on her like a sack, and said that she wanted to go out to the old place, where their grandparents had homesteaded, before the frost was gone.

It was a mile and a half across the fields. They went on foot, cutting through the corn stubble and over a pasture where a few red cattle lifted their heads to watch them pass, their breath hanging in clouds about their muzzles. The ground was hard and rang under their shoes. Neither of them said much. When they came to the draw where the old sod house had been, there was nothing left of it but a low, grass-grown mound, and a depression where the cave cellar had fallen in. Somebody had pastured horses over it. But the plum thicket was still there, along the side of the draw, gray and thorny, with a few shriveled plums still clinging to the branches; and the big cottonwood that their grandfather had set out as a switch, the first year, had grown into a tree that could be seen for miles.

Kristina stood a long while looking at the mound. Then she went over and knelt on it, in the frosty grass, careless of Hilda's old coat, and put her hand flat on the ground.

"The door was here," she said. "Facing south. And Grandmother's chair was just inside, where she could see out. And the bed was against that wall, and the stove—no, the stove was here, and the shelf with the coffee-mill and the clock." She looked up. "Do you remember the clock? It had a ship painted on the door, a ship with three masts, and when it struck, Grandmother always stopped whatever she was doing and counted the strokes, as if she did not quite trust it."

"Gustav's brother has it," said Hilda. "In Lincoln. It still keeps time."

"I used to think that ship was carrying me somewhere. Every night, when the clock struck, I went a little farther." Kristina got to her feet and brushed off her skirt. Her cheeks were red with the cold, and her eyes were shining. "It is strange, Hilda. I have been homesick for twelve years, and I never knew what for. I thought it was for you, and for Grandmother, and the singing in the church at Christmas. But I believe it was for this. For this draw, and that ugly old tree, and the way the frost looks on the plum bushes. Isn't it foolish? There is nothing here at all."

Hilda looked around her, at the bare draw and the gray thicket and the great pale sky arching over everything, and the long swells of the stubble going away on every side until they met it. The sun was higher now, and the frost was beginning to go; the grass under their feet was turning from white to silver and from silver to its own tawny color, and here and there a drop of water caught the light and burned like a spark. Far off on the section road a wagon was moving, so small and slow that it seemed not to move at all.

"No," she said. "It is not foolish. I think it is the only thing there is."

They stood together for a time without speaking. Then a meadow-lark, one of the last of the year, rose out of the grass near the plum thicket and lit on a fence post and sang, a few clear notes, very sweet and rather cracked, as if the cold had got into his throat. Kristina caught her breath. She turned to her cousin, and Hilda saw that she was crying, as she had always cried, easily and without shame, the way the sky in that country sometimes rains in sunlight.

Hilda did not cry. She put her arm through her cousin's, and after a little while they turned and went back across the fields toward the windmill and the box-elders and the thin blue smoke going up from Gustav's chimney, walking slowly, matching their steps as they had done when they were children and went together to school in the mornings, with their dinner-pails knocking against their knees.
