response:
The stage from the railroad comes up the valley with the wind behind it in the afternoons, so that the dust it raises travels faster than the horses and arrives first at every station, a kind of yellow herald announcing to whoever cares to look that somebody is coming. At Pinyon Wells nobody cares very much, as a rule, for the people who come by stage are mostly drummers or mining men with leather cases, and they go on again by the same road. But on the afternoon of which this is told, Saranna Ware had been watching the dust since it first lifted over the shoulder of the black mesa south of town, and she stood at her gate with one hand shading her eyes long after it was plain that the stage had stopped at Cantrell's store, and that the woman getting down from it in a gray traveling dress was her cousin Hester Breen.

It had been nineteen years. That is a long time anywhere, but in a country like this one it is longer than elsewhere, for the land keeps no calendar a woman can use. The sage blooms and goes to seed, the cottonwoods along the ditch put out their leaves and lose them, the snow comes down on the high peaks to the west and draws back again into the cañons, and all this happens so exactly the same, year upon year, that one might suppose nothing had happened at all, if it were not for the children growing up and the graves in the little fenced yard back of the Methodist church. Saranna had both to count by. She had counted, standing there at the gate, and knew to the month how long it had been since Hester went out by the same road in a spring wagon, with her trunk tied on behind and her face set toward the railroad as if she had been looking at it all her life.

The cousins met in the road halfway between the gate and the store. It is worth saying that they did not run, either of them, for they were women in their middle years and the afternoon was hot, but they walked a little faster than was needful, and when they came together they stood a moment looking before they kissed. There is a way women have of reading one another at such a time, quick and entire, as a sheepherder reads the sky at morning; and what each of them read is not to be set down here, except that Hester had grown handsomer than anyone in Pinyon Wells would have predicted, and Saranna had grown browner and leaner and quieter, as people do who live where the sun has the last word about everything.

"You've kept your hair," said Hester, which was the first thing either of them said, and Saranna laughed and put up her hand to it, for it was true. It was the one vanity she had brought through. 

They went in at the gate together, and Cantrell's boy came behind with the valise.

Saranna's house stood at the upper end of the town where the ditch comes out from among the willows, so that she had water when other people had only the hope of it. Her husband had been shrewd about that, and about little else, and he had been dead now six years of a pneumonia he took riding after strays in a March norther. The house was adobe, low and thick-walled, with a porch on the east side where the cottonwood shade lay in the afternoons. There was a bench there, and two chairs with rawhide seats, and an olla hanging from the beam with a wet sack about it, sweating cool water into the dry air. Hester sat down in one of the chairs as if she had been sitting in it all her life, and drank from the dipper Saranna handed her, and looked out across the valley.

It is a view that people who have lived with it do not speak of. From the porch the land goes down by long tilted benches to the river, which is only a line of willows at that distance, and then rises beyond in the same long benches, gray-green with sage and rabbit-brush, to the foot of the eastern range, which is red and bare and seamed with dry gullies like the palm of an old hand. Over all lies the light, which is not like light elsewhere, but has a body to it, so that the far ranges seem near and the near ones seem made of something finer than rock. Hester looked a long time. Saranna, watching her, saw her throat move once, but she said nothing about it then, nor afterward.

"I'd forgot it was so big," said Hester at last. "You'd think a person couldn't forget a thing like that."

"You can forget anything, give it time," said Saranna. "That's what time's for, I reckon."

Then, because it was the hour for it, and because there are some things women can only say to each other with their hands busy, Saranna brought out a pan of beans for stringing, and Hester took half of them into her lap without being asked, in her gray traveling dress, and they began.

They began, as kinswomen always do, with the dead. That is the proper order, and neither of them would have thought of any other. Hester had known of her uncle's going, Saranna's father, for there had been letters in those first years, but she had not known of Aunt Lucretia, nor of Will Pettibone who had been sweet on them both one summer and had died in the Silver Peak country with a mine shaft caved in on him; nor of the Lacey twins, nor old Mrs. Drum who kept the post office and steamed open everybody's letters and was never once known to repeat what she found in them. Saranna told these over as she strung the beans, one after another, not dwelling on any, as a woman tells the beads of a rosary she has said so often that the words have worn smooth. Hester listened and said, "Oh," and, "I never knew," and once, at the name of Will Pettibone, she stopped her hands altogether and sat looking at the eastern range.

"He was a good boy," she said.

"He was a fool about mines," said Saranna. "But he was good." 

Then they came to the children, and here it was Saranna who went slowly. There had been five. Two were in the little yard back of the Methodist church, taken the same week by a throat sickness that went through the valley the winter of the big snow, when the roads were shut and the doctor could not get up from the railroad. One was married and lived on a cattle ranch over toward the Nevada line, and had two of her own. One was a boy, Edwin, eighteen now, who had gone down to the oil country to work on the rigs and wrote home once a month on ruled paper. And the youngest, a girl named Lucy, was at that very moment somewhere out on the mesa with a neighbor's children looking for chuckwalla lizards, and would be home at dark, burnt and scratched and quite unrepentant.

"You named her for Mother," said Hester.

"I named her for your mother," said Saranna. "I always liked Aunt Lucy better than my own. I expect you knew that."

Hester did not answer, but she reached over and laid her hand a moment on Saranna's wrist, and then took it back and went on stringing beans.

There is this to be said of women who have lived long in a dry country, that they learn to wait for things to come to them. The land teaches it. A man may go out and dig for water, but a woman learns early that the rain comes when it comes and not otherwise, and that the best one can do is to have the barrels ready. So Saranna waited, and did not ask. It was Hester, after a long time, who began to tell of herself; and she told it badly, as people do who are not used to being listened to without interruption.

She had gone first to San Francisco, as everyone knew, and taught in a school there for two years, and then had married a man named Ormsby who dealt in insurance. They had gone East together, to Philadelphia, where his people were; and there she had lived in a brick house on a street of brick houses, every one alike, with a little square of grass before each, and an iron fence about the grass. There had been no children. Mr. Ormsby had been a kind man, she said, and saying it she looked down at her hands, and Saranna understood that he had been kind in the way of men who do not know there is any other way to be. He had died two years since, of his heart, very suddenly, at his desk, and had left her well provided for. She had stayed on in the brick house. She had belonged to a club where ladies read papers to one another on the poets and on the condition of the poor. She had gone to concerts. She had had her portrait painted once, in a blue dress, by a young man who afterward became quite well known.

"And then one morning," said Hester, "I was standing at the window, and there was a little wind came up the street, the way it does in the spring there, and it blew a piece of paper along the pavement, and it went turning over and over, and I thought of the tumbleweeds going down the wash below Father's place. And I sat right down and cried. Like a child. I hadn't thought of the tumbleweeds in fifteen years." She laughed, not very steadily. "That's a foolish reason to come three thousand miles."

"There's no such thing as a foolish reason for coming home," said Saranna. "There's only foolish reasons for leaving."

She had not meant it unkindly, and Hester did not take it so; but it lay between them a moment like a stone dropped into still water, and they both watched the rings go out from it.

The shadows of the cottonwoods had crept clear across the yard by this, and lay now on the ditch bank, where the water went by quick and bright, talking to itself. A pair of mourning doves came down to drink at the edge of it, and a roadrunner went across the far end of the yard with his tail up, in that great hurry roadrunners are always in, which never seems to bring them anywhere in particular. Out on the benches the sage had begun to turn from gray to violet, as it does in the hour before sundown, and the red range across the valley stood up with every gully in it filled to the brim with blue shadow, so that it looked like a thing cut out of colored paper and pasted on the sky.

It was Hester who spoke again, and she spoke looking at the range, not at her cousin.

"You might have come too, Sairy. I asked you. You remember I asked you."

"I remember."

"You'd have done well. You were always quicker than me at books. You'd have been a better teacher than I ever was." She turned then. "Were you ever sorry? You can tell me. There's nobody else to hear."

Saranna did not answer at once. She took up the last handful of beans and strung them carefully, one by one, and dropped them into the pan, and set the pan on the bench beside her. Then she wiped her hands on her apron and folded them in her lap, and it was a long time before she said anything at all.

It should be understood that there is a kind of knowledge which the desert puts into those who stay in it, which is not to be got any other way, and which does not go well into words. It is something like the knowledge an old Paiute has of where the water lies under the sand in a dry wash, which he cannot explain to you but can show you, if he likes you, by digging. People who have it are not always happy, and they are seldom rich, but they are very rarely surprised by anything. Saranna had it. It was in the way she sat, and in her hands, and in the long look she sent out across the valley now, as if she were consulting something out there before she spoke.

"Sorry's a town word," she said at last. "I don't know as it means much out here. You might as well ask the greasewood is it sorry it didn't grow up a pine tree. It grows where the seed fell, and it puts down roots as far as it can reach, and it takes what water there is. It doesn't spend itself thinking about the mountains." She was quiet a moment. "There was a while, after the children went, the two of them, that I'd have given anything to be somewhere else. Anywhere. I used to stand out there by the gate and look at the road. But you can't leave a grave, Hester. I don't know how other folks do it. And after a while the looking wore off, the way it does, and I found I'd got roots after all. Deeper than I'd thought."

"I used to think of you," said Hester, "standing at that gate."

"I used to think of you," said Saranna, "in a city with lights in it. All the lights. I'd lie awake and try to make a picture of it in my head." She smiled. "I never could get it right. I'd never seen more than the lights at the railroad, and they don't amount to much."

"They don't amount to much in the city, either," said Hester. "Not after the first year."

Then they both laughed, and the thing that had been lying between them was gone, or had settled into its place, which in a long kinship is much the same thing.

The sun went down behind the western range while they sat there, not slowly, as it goes in wet countries, with a great deal of fuss among the clouds, but all at once, like a lamp turned out; and immediately the whole valley filled up with a clear cool light that seemed to come from nowhere, from the air itself, and the red range across the river went first to rose and then to a color there is no name for, and then to gray. A little wind came down out of the cañons smelling of snow and pine, though there was neither within twenty miles, and the cottonwood leaves began to talk overhead. Somewhere out on the mesa a coyote set up his evening complaint, and was answered from somewhere else, and the two of them went on for a while, back and forth, as if they also had a great deal of news to exchange after a long separation.

"I'd forgot that, too," said Hester softly. "The way they sing."

"They'll sing you to sleep tonight," said Saranna. "You'll lie awake an hour, being glad of it, and then you'll sleep like you haven't slept since you were a girl. That's the way it takes people."

Presently there were voices down the road, and a child's high laughing, and Lucy came in at the gate with her skirt torn and her sunbonnet hanging by its strings down her back, carrying something alive in both her hands. She stopped short at the sight of the lady in the gray dress, and stood looking with her mother's eyes, a little wary, a little bold, in the way of children who have grown up where there are more lizards than people.

"This is your Aunt Hester," said Saranna. "Come and show her what you've got."

The child came slowly up the steps and opened her hands, and there lay a horned toad, flat and spiny and the exact color of the dust, blinking its little gold-ringed eyes at the three of them. Hester bent over it a long moment. Then she put out one finger, gloveless now, and stroked the creature down its back, against the grain of its small horns, as a person does who has done it many times before and has only been waiting to remember how.

"When your mother and I were your age," she said, "we kept one of these in a box for a whole summer. We called him the Governor."

Lucy looked at her mother, astonished that she should ever have been anybody's age but her own, and Saranna nodded. "That's so. He got away in September. We cried a week."

They went in to supper after that, the three of them, and lit the lamp. But late that night, when the child was asleep and the coyotes had gone off somewhere about their own business, the two women came out again and stood together at the gate in their wrappers, looking down the long pale road toward the railroad, which ran away under the stars until it was lost among the dark benches. They did not say much. There was not, after all, so very much more to say; and in a country like this one it is understood that some things are better left out under the sky, where there is room enough for them.

"It hasn't changed," said Hester.

"It doesn't," said Saranna. "That's the comfort of it. It's only us that change, and it lets us, and waits."

They stood a while longer, two women who had gone different roads and come by them, as roads in the desert do, very nearly back to the same place. Then the wind came cold off the high snow, and they went in.

response:
The spring at the mouth of Pahranat Canyon comes up under a ledge of rust-colored rock, so quietly that a stranger might pass within a stone's throw and know nothing of it but a greener tint to the sage and a smell, very faint, of wet earth in a country where nothing else is wet. It fills a basin no larger than a bread trough, spills over a lip worn smooth by the drinking of a thousand years of creatures, and runs perhaps forty paces down the wash before the sand drinks it. In those forty paces it raises a strip of wire grass, a clump of willows that never get above a man's shoulder, and one ragged cottonwood whose roots must go down a great way. Beyond that the desert takes up again as if there had been no interruption, and the land runs out flat and colorless to the foot of the next range.

There are springs enough in that country that the Shoshones know and the white men do not, but there are none that the Shoshones hold in greater esteem than this. Every trail in the district bends toward it at last. The coyotes come down at dusk with a careless air, as if they happened that way. The quail come in the early morning in a running, bobbing procession, the cock first, stopping every little while with his topknot cocked to listen. Rabbits come, and the small gray foxes, and once in a dry year a bighorn ewe came down out of the rocks with her lamb and drank and stared and went away again. All these respect the spring after their fashion, which is to drink and go and leave the water no worse than they found it. It is the custom of the country; whatever is born there learns it before it learns to fear the hawk.

At the time I speak of there were six wickiups pitched on the bench above the spring, which made a campoodie of perhaps twenty souls, and of these the smallest that could walk was a boy called Tavu, who was the son of a woman named Neuma and of a man who was away that season shearing at the big sheep camps on the Kern. Tavu was in his sixth summer, round-bellied, sturdy, and as brown as the tufa he played on, with hair cut straight across his eyebrows in the fashion of the campoodie, and a pair of black eyes that were never still. He was not a bad child as children go, but he had more of what the Shoshones call coyote-heart than was convenient: an inquisitiveness that ran ahead of his judgment, and a way of doing a thing first and considering it afterward, if at all.

Neuma was a basket-maker of some repute, a broad, quiet woman with a scar across the back of one hand where a rattlesnake had struck her in her girlhood. She had been married young, had lost two children to the coughing sickness that came up from the towns one winter, and was the more careful with Tavu on that account. But the care of a Shoshone mother is not the care of a white mother. She does not hover. She lets the child go where it will within the circle of her eye, and sometimes a little beyond it, and trusts the land to teach it the greater part of what it needs to know; for the land is a stern teacher and repeats no lesson twice. What the land does not teach, the mother teaches, and in her own time.

It was a day in the latter part of August, which in that country is the hardest part of the year. The sky had the look of hot brass, and there was no wind except a little sullen stirring at noon that lifted the sand in spirals and set it down again a few rods off. The women of the campoodie had gone up the canyon at daybreak to beat the seed out of the late grasses, and Neuma with them, leaving Tavu with an old grandmother who sat in the shade of the brush shelter and dozed over a half-finished basket. The old woman's eyes were not what they had been, and her ears were worse, and toward the middle of the morning she was asleep in good earnest with her chin upon her breast.

Tavu went down to the spring.

He had been forbidden to go there alone, and he knew it; but forbidding is a thin fence to a child of six when the day is long and the shade is short. He went down the trail with his hands behind him, as he had seen the old men walk, and looked about him with an air of great unconcern. The willows were full of small birds that rose up at his coming and settled again. A lizard on the ledge above the spring did push-ups at him, which is the lizard's way of saying that he holds the ground and means to keep it. Tavu threw a pebble at the lizard and missed, and the lizard did not so much as change color.

Then Tavu looked at the water, and the water looked back at him, very clear and cool, with the sky in it and the shape of his own round head against the sky, and little threads of sand dancing up from the bottom where the spring breathed. It is a thing that children in that country seldom see, a body of water that will hold a person's shape. He put in one finger and drew it out. He put in his hand. And then, being a child, and the morning hot, and the old woman asleep, and the lizard looking on with what seemed to him a challenge, he sat down upon the worn lip of the basin and put in both his feet.

It was very pleasant. The water was colder than he had expected and took his breath a little, and he laughed aloud at the feel of it. He worked his toes in the sand of the bottom and watched the clouds of it rise up and spread and turn the clear water yellow. He found that by stamping he could make the clouds rise faster, and that by pushing the water with his heels he could make it slop over the lip in little waves and run down to the willows. He made a great many waves. Before long he had got down into the basin altogether, up to his middle, and was digging in the bottom with both hands to see where the water came from, and the spring that had been as clear as air was as thick and brown as a puddle in a cattle wallow.

So his mother found him.

She had come down early because the seed was poor that year and the work went slowly, and she had thought to fill the water basket at the spring before going up to the wickiup. She came round the ledge with the basket on her back and the tump-line across her forehead, and she stopped.

It is a thing worth observing that a Shoshone woman, when she is most angry, is most still. A white woman under the same provocation would have cried out, would have run forward, would very likely have snatched the child up and shaken him, or slapped him soundly and dragged him home by one arm, scolding as she went. Neuma did none of these things. She stood where she was with the empty basket hanging at her back, and looked at her son, and at the water, and at the wet sand where the waves he had made had run down and been lost, and for the space of perhaps ten breaths she said nothing at all.

Tavu, looking up from his digging, saw her standing so, and the laughter went out of his face as the color goes out of a stone when it is lifted out of the stream. There was something in her stillness he had not met before. He had been scolded often enough, for the coyote-heart in him made him a frequent offender, but he had always been scolded quickly and briskly and forgotten as quickly. This was different. It was as if the whole of the hot, silent land had drawn itself up behind his mother and was looking at him through her eyes.

"Come out," said Neuma.

He came out. He stood on the lip of the basin with the muddy water running off him, very small and very naked, and dripping in the dust.

"Sit," said Neuma, and pointed to a flat rock a little way off, in the full sun.

He sat. The rock was hot enough that he moved uneasily upon it, but he did not dare to get up. Neuma let down her basket and set it carefully against the ledge, and then she sat down too, not near him but across the spring from him, so that the ruined water lay between them; and she folded her hands in her lap and looked at it.

The Shoshones have a saying that it is a waste of breath to speak to a child whose ears are still full of his own noise, and Neuma waited until her son's ears were empty. She waited while the mud began to settle in the basin and the first thin clearness showed at the top of it like the light that comes before the sun. She waited while a pair of quail came down the wash, saw that something was amiss, and went back again. She waited until Tavu had stopped fidgeting on the hot rock and had begun to be afraid of the silence itself. Then she spoke, and her voice was low and level and without any heat in it at all, which was worse to him than any heat could have been.

"What is this place?" she said.

Tavu did not answer. He was not sure what answer was wanted.

"I asked you a question. What is this place?"

"The spring," said Tavu in a very small voice.

"Whose spring?"

He considered this. "Ours," he said.

"No," said his mother. "Not ours. Look there." She lifted one hand and pointed to the lip of the basin, where the rock was worn into a soft hollow like the inside of a bowl. "Who wore that?"

He did not know.

"Coyote wore it," said Neuma. "And Rabbit, and Quail, and Fox, and the Old People who were here before we were, and the people before them, back to the beginning. It was made by drinking. Every one that ever drank here took away a little of the rock with his mouth. That is how long they have been coming. And in all that time, did any one of them ever do what you have done?"

Tavu looked at the hollow in the rock and said nothing.

"Coyote is a thief," his mother went on. "He steals from the traps. He steals from the hen-roosts at the ranches. He tells lies, and he laughs at everything, and there is no shame in him. But Coyote drinks at this spring and goes away and leaves it clean. Even Coyote knows that much. And you, a man-child of the People, who will be a hunter one day, and sit in the council, and have children of your own to teach, you come down here when the old one is asleep and do a thing that Coyote would be ashamed to do."

This was very bitter to Tavu, for he had been brought up, like all the children of the campoodie, on stories of Coyote and his foolishness, and to be set beneath Coyote was the worst thing that he could think of. His lip began to tremble. But Neuma had not finished.

"Now I will tell you what you have done," she said, "and you will listen, and afterward you will not forget it. In the wickiups up there are twenty people. There is your grandmother, who is old and cannot walk to the next water. There is Tuhuna's baby, who is sick with the summer sickness and must have water often. There are the women who will come down out of the canyon tonight with their mouths full of dust from the seed-beating. All of them must drink from this. And the next water is half a day's walk across the flat, and the sun is hot, and the old one cannot go so far, and the baby cannot be carried so far in this heat. So until this water is clear again, they will be thirsty. You did that."

She paused, and let him look at the water.

"And it is not only the People," she said. "When the sun goes down, Quail will bring her young ones here, and they are very small, and they have been all day in the brush without water. Quail will come and look at this and go away again, because Quail will not drink from a dirty place. And some of her little ones will not live till morning. Fox will come, and Rabbit, and they will smell what you have done and go away. And the willows there, that live by the water running over the edge: you have thrown the water out on the sand faster than the spring can make it, and if you had kept on, the willows would have been thirsty too. Everything that lives within a day's walk of here lives by this. You thought it was a thing to play in. It is not a thing to play in. It is a thing to live by."

Tavu was crying now, though quietly, for it is not good manners among the Shoshones for a boy to cry loudly, and he knew that much. The tears made pale tracks in the mud on his cheeks. His mother watched him cry and did not go to him. There is a time for comforting, and she knew to a hair's breadth when it would be, and it was not yet.

"I am sorry," said Tavu.

"Sorry is a word," said his mother. "A jay can say words. I want to see what you are."

She rose then and went to the spring and knelt beside it and looked down into the water. It was clearing somewhat. The heavy sand had gone down, and only the fine yellow silt still hung in it, turning slowly. In an hour, perhaps less, it would be clear; but in that country an hour is a long time to be thirsty, and the old woman was already awake up at the wickiup and calling for her grandson in a thin, quavering voice that carried down the slope.

"Come here," said Neuma.

Tavu came and knelt beside her.

"Do not touch it. Only look."

He looked. And as he looked, his mother put out one hand, very slowly, and laid it flat upon the surface of the water without breaking it, so lightly that the skin of the water only dimpled under her palm.

"This is how you touch water," she said. "This is how the Old People touched it. Like a sleeping child. Like a bird's nest with the eggs in it. You do not put your feet in what you drink. You do not dig in it. You do not throw it out on the ground to see it run. You take what you need, in your hands or in a basket, and you take it gently, and you go away. When I was a little girl, younger than you, my grandmother brought me here and taught me this, and her grandmother taught her, and now I am teaching you. When you are a man, you will teach your children. That is how the water stays clean."

Then, because she was a just woman and a punishment that is all words goes in at one ear and out at the other, she gave him his sentence.

"You will not drink," she said, "until the sun is on that rock." She pointed across the wash to a tall black boulder, a quarter of the way down the sky toward the west. "The old one is thirsty because of you; you will be thirsty with her. And every morning until the pine nuts are ripe, you will come down here with me before anyone else is awake, and carry out the leaves that fall into the water, and the dead bees, and whatever else is in it, with your hands, gently, the way I showed you. That is your work now. The spring has been taking care of you since before you were born. Now you will take care of the spring."

Tavu nodded. He did not trust his voice.

They went up the slope together, the woman with the empty basket and the child walking a little behind her, and the old grandmother, who had waked and missed him and been frightened, scolded him shrilly in the way of old women and was not listened to; for after his mother, she was as a wren chattering after a hawk has gone over. The afternoon wore on in heat and silence. The women came down out of the canyon, dusty and tired, and heard the story and looked at Tavu and said nothing to him, which is the hardest kind of rebuke there is among the People, and went down to the spring, which by then was clear again, and drank and filled their baskets. Tuhuna's baby had water and slept. The shadow of the black boulder crept round, very slowly, as shadows do in the desert, where time is measured in that fashion and in no other.

Tavu sat in the door of the wickiup with his chin on his knees and watched the shadow and was more thirsty than he had ever been in his life. His tongue felt like a piece of rawhide. He watched the women going up and down with the water baskets, and the dark wet stains on the baskets where the water seeped through the pitch, and he thought about the quail and her little ones going to bed thirsty in the brush. It is likely that he thought more in that one afternoon than in all the six summers that had gone before.

When the sun touched the black rock, his mother came out of the wickiup with a small basket of water and held it out to him without a word. He took it in both hands, as carefully as if it had been a bird's egg, and drank, not greedily, though he wanted to, but in small sips, looking at her over the edge of the basket to see if he was doing it right. She watched him drink, and when he had done she took the basket from him and set it down, and then at last she put her hand on his head, on the straight-cut hair, and let it rest there.

"So," she said. That was all. But it was enough, and Tavu leaned his head against her knee and was forgiven.

That evening, at the hour when the light goes long and yellow across the flats and every bush throws a shadow ten times its own length, the quail came down the wash to the spring. The cock came first, as is the custom, stopping every little while to listen, with his topknot cocked over one eye; and behind him came the hen, and behind her a dozen little ones no bigger than walnuts, running so fast on their small legs that they seemed to be rolled along the ground. They went down to the lip of the basin, to the place that had been worn smooth by a thousand years of drinking, and dipped their beaks, and lifted their heads to let the water run down, and dipped again. And on the bench above, in the door of the wickiup, a small brown boy with his chin on his knees watched them drink, and did not throw a pebble, and did not move, and hardly breathed until they had gone.

It is said in that country that a lesson the land teaches is never forgotten, because the land does not trouble to teach it gently. It may be so. But there are some lessons the land leaves to the mothers, and these, if the mothers know their business, are not forgotten either. Long after, when Tavu was a grown man with a voice in the council and children of his own, he was known among the People for one peculiarity which the young men laughed at a little behind his back: that he would go out of his way, when he came to any water whatever, a spring, a seep, a tinaja in the rocks with a hand's breadth of rain in it, to kneel down and take the dead leaves out of it with his fingers before he drank. And if anyone asked him why, he would only say that the water had been taking care of him a long while, and it was time somebody took care of the water.

"I see you are greatly excited about something!"

"What is it I don't see, Eunice?"

The slight act of doing something for her restored him for the moment to reality; he bent over her. "I've never wanted to hurry you, dearest—— It shall be when you say." She put up her hands suddenly with a shivering movement.

"Oh, never, never at all; never to you!" Peter could feel that working its track of desolation inward, but the first instinctive movement of his surface was to close over the wound. He took it as he knew he could only take it: as the explosive crisis of the virginal resistance which he remembered he had heard came to girls when marriage loomed upon them. He took a turn down the room to steady himself, praying dumbly for the right word.

"It isn't as if I didn't respect you"—she was eager in explanation, hurried and stumbling—"as if I didn't know how good you are ... it is only, because we are so different."

"Oh ... older, I suppose." She grew quieter; it appeared on the whole they were getting on. "I care for so many things, you know—dancing—and bridge—young things—and you are always reading and reading. Oh! I couldn't stand it." So it was out now. She was jealous of his books, a little. "Oh," she seemed to have found a suffocating quality in his gentleness, against which she struck out with drowning gestures, "if you could only understand what it would mean to me never to have anybody I liked to talk to about things,—anybody I liked to be with all the time!" She was choked and aghast at the enormity of it.

"But I thought...." Peter was not able to go on with that. "Isn't there anybody you like to be with, Eunice?"

"Yes," said Eunice. "Burton Henderson." Mutinous and bright she looked at him out of the chair with a hand on either arm of it poised for flight or defence. After an interval Peter heard his own voice out of a fog rising to the conventional utterance.

"From the very beginning," she said, "but he had so little money, and mother ... I promised you, I know, but it's not as if I ever said I loved you." She should have spared him that! She found at last the barbedest. The sharp edge of her young sufficiency had lopped off the right limb of his manhood. Never, even in his dreams, if life had allowed him to dream again, should he be able to see himself in any other guise than the meagre, austere front which his obligation to his mother and Ellen had obliged him to present to destiny. She had beggared him of all those aptitudes for passionate relations, by the faith in which he had kept himself inwardly alive. Anna Westerby had known for three days that he would have to tell her, and the knowledge had settled on the house like the thick yellow light which at that season rose off the alkali flats and leaned against the windows all afternoon, so that every object in the room seemed to hold it a little after the sun had gone. She had sat so, with the lamp unlit and her sewing gone slack upon her knee, while the long shadow of the cottonwood crept across the dooryard and touched the step. It was the hour at which he commonly came, and she had found it, through all the seven years of their being married, an hour of such pleasant expectancy that she could not now get rid of the habit of it. The mere sound of the gate latch was enough to set her pulses forward. They went forward now, and then came back upon her with a dull recoil as she remembered what it was she waited for.

She had had it, in the beginning, from Mrs. Pardee at the post office. That lady, with her bright, inquisitive eye and the air she had of handing out the town's affairs with the mail, had let it fall that the Company's notes had gone to protest in San Francisco. She plainly supposed Mrs. Westerby knew. It had been necessary, Anna saw, to appear to know, and the effort of keeping her face had carried her the whole length of the dusty street before she felt her knees shake under her. It was not the money. She told herself that it was not the money, and believed it, so far as she was able to believe anything in that first numb astonishment. It was that he should have let her go on, all those weeks, planning the new room on the north side and the cistern, and talking at the table about the peach orchard that was to come out of the Company's water, without once letting her see that the ground was going from under them.

He came in at last with the dust of the road on him, and she saw at once, by the way he stood his hat on the rack, carefully, as though it might break, that he knew she knew. There was a kind of shrinking in his large frame, the look of a man who has carried a weight so long that he goes on stooping after it is set down.

"You haven't lit the lamp, Anna."

"I didn't want it." She heard her own voice, very level, and wondered at it. "I wanted to see you first without it."

He made no answer to that, but crossed over and struck a match, as if the small business of lifting the chimney and adjusting the wick were a refuge he could not deny himself. The light flared up between them and steadied, and in it she saw how gray he had grown at the temples since spring, how the lines had cut themselves down from the corners of his mouth. It touched her with a pang which she put away from her deliberately, for she felt that if she gave way to pity now she would never get to the bottom of the thing at all.

"Mrs. Pardee told me," she said, "on Tuesday."

"I supposed somebody would." He sat down heavily across from her, his hands hanging between his knees. "I meant to tell you myself. I meant to tell you every day."

"Every day for how long, Gilbert?"

"Since—oh, since the first of June, I suppose. Since Carmody went East."

It was out now, and she had the curious sensation of having expected it to strike harder. It seemed instead to spread out slowly in her, like water poured on dry ground, finding its way down into all the small hollows of the summer just gone: the evening he had brought home the plans for the north room and spread them on this very table; the Sunday they had driven out to look at the headgate and he had stood a long time on the bank with his back to her, so long that she had called to him, laughing, to ask whether he meant to grow there. She saw now what he had been looking at. She saw it with such a sick clearness that for the moment she could not speak.

"I thought," he went on, encouraged perhaps by her silence, "that it would come right. Carmody wrote that there were people in New York who would take up the whole issue if we could hold on through the summer. There was no use in troubling you until it was certain one way or the other."

"No use in troubling me." She turned it over, as though it were some strange coin he had put into her hand. "And the house, Gilbert? Was there no use in troubling me about the house?"

He looked up at her quickly then, and she knew by the start of his eyes that he had hoped she had not heard that part of it. It was the thing which, of all the rest, she had found it hardest to carry home from the post office. Mrs. Pardee had said it with a little sidelong sympathy, as one woman to another, that it was a mercy at least the house had been put in Mrs. Westerby's name, and Anna, who had never signed anything but the letters she wrote her sister in Ohio, had felt the street tilt under her.

"I had to have something to show them," he said. "It was only a form. Lassiter at the bank knew it was a form. Nobody thought, Anna, that it would ever come to anything."

"But you signed my name."

"I signed it as your husband. I had a right——" He broke off, seeing, perhaps, how the word fell between them. "That is, I thought I had. I thought you would want me to do whatever would save it for us."

She got up then, because she could not bear any longer to be sitting so near him with the lamp throwing their two shadows together on the wall, and went and stood at the window. The flats beyond the town had gone a deep violet, and the long line of the Company's ditch, which she had watched them dig with such a lift of hope two winters ago, lay across them like a scar drawn with a pencil. There was no water in it. There had been no water in it since July, and she had heard him say, a dozen times, that it was only the late snows in the Sierra, that the head would come down in the fall. She had believed him, because it had never occurred to her to do anything else. It occurred to her now, standing with her back to him and her fingers pressed hard upon the sill, that what she was suffering from was not so much the loss of the house as the loss of that unquestioning habit of belief, which had been, she began dimly to perceive, the very ground on which she had built her notion of being married.

"You might have asked me," she said, without turning.

"I know it."

"You might have let me be a partner in it, Gilbert, instead of a—a kind of child that has to be kept from knowing there is a fire in the house until the roof falls in."

"I didn't think of it so." He had risen, too, and she could feel him standing behind her, uncertain, not daring to come nearer. "I thought of it as sparing you. A man doesn't want his wife to have to carry his mistakes."

"His mistakes!" She swung around upon him with a suddenness that surprised them both. "Is it only your mistake? Wasn't I to have had the orchard too, and the north room, and the cistern, and all the rest of it? Didn't I lie awake nights planning where the roses were to go when we had water enough to waste on roses? It was mine as much as yours, Gilbert—the hope of it was mine. And you let me go on hoping after you knew. That's what I can't get past. You let me go on making a fool of myself, setting out slips in the window there for a garden that was never going to be."

She saw him wince, and was aware of a fierce small satisfaction in it, which she was immediately ashamed of, and which nevertheless she could not quite let go. It was as if, having been shut out of his trouble all those months, she must now at any cost make herself felt in it, must thrust her way into the very middle of it, even if she had to hurt him to get there. He stood under it with a kind of patience that was more than she could endure.

"Don't look like that," she cried. "Say something. Tell me I'm unjust if you think it. Tell me anything, only don't stand there as though I were a—a dust storm you had to wait out."

"What is there to say, Anna? You are right. I ought to have told you."

"That isn't what I want."

"What is it, then?" He was honestly at a loss; she could see him casting about in his mind for the thing she needed, as he might have cast about for a tool he had mislaid. "If it's the house—Lassiter will give us till spring, I think. I can go back to surveying. Hollister wrote me only last month that there's work on the railroad line north of Mojave. It isn't as if we would starve."

"Oh, the house!" She made a gesture as though she brushed it from her. "Do you think I care so much about the house?" And yet even as she said it she knew that she did care, that the thought of the bare boards being carried out of these rooms where she had learned to be a wife lay at the bottom of everything, a dumb ache under the sharper pain. But it was not what she meant, and she struggled to find words for what she did mean, standing there with her hands locked before her and the lamp shining full on her troubled face.

"It's that I thought we were—together," she said at last. "I thought, whatever came, we'd be in it side by side. When we came out here, and everybody at home said I'd never stand it, the heat and the wind and being so far from any one—I didn't mind any of it, because it was ours, you and I against the country. I used to think of us that way, Gilbert, like two people walking into a wind, holding on to each other. And all this summer you've been walking into it alone, and leaving me behind in the house with the curtains drawn, thinking it was a fine day."

She had not meant to cry, and she did not quite cry, but her voice broke on the last of it, and she turned away again to the window so that he should not see her face working. There was a long silence in the room. A moth had come in at the open door and was beating itself against the lamp chimney with a small soft persistent sound, and she found herself listening to it with a strained attention, as though the whole issue between them hung upon whether it would find its way into the flame.

"I was ashamed," he said behind her, very low.

She did not move.

"You don't know what it is," he went on, with a kind of difficulty, as if each word had to be pried loose, "to have talked big to a woman. To have told her, the way I told you, that I'd make something out of this country for her—that she'd have a better house than her sister's in Columbus, and a garden, and all the rest. I'd been telling you that for six years, Anna. Every time I came home from the ditch I'd tell you. And then to have to come in and say it was all gone, that I'd been a fool, that Carmody had pulled out and left the rest of us holding his paper.... I couldn't do it. I'd get as far as the gate, and see you at the window, and I couldn't."

She turned slowly and looked at him, and saw him, for the first time that evening, not as the man who had wronged her but as he stood: big and gray and dusty, with his hands hanging helplessly, and his eyes, which had always been so steady, gone shy and wavering before her. It came to her, with the shock of a discovery made too late, that she had never in all their years together seen him ashamed before, and that she did not in the least know what to do with it. She had been prepared for anger, for justification, even for that masculine patience which she had found so galling; she had braced herself against them all. But against this she had no defence, and the very ground of her grievance seemed to slip away from under her, leaving her with nothing to stand on but the bare fact of his need.

"So it was your pride," she said, but gently now, almost as if she were feeling her way.

"I suppose it was."

"And you thought I'd love you less for having failed?"

He did not answer that, and the not answering said more to her than anything he could have put into words. She saw then how the whole fabric of their life together had been woven on a pattern which he had set and she had accepted without ever turning it over to look at the wrong side: he the provider, she the provided for; he the one who went out into the wind and the alkali, she the one who kept the lamp. She had liked it so. She had been proud of being taken care of, as a woman of her bringing up was taught to be proud of it. And all the while it had been laying upon him a burden which he could not share without seeming to himself to have failed in the one thing that made him worth her keeping. The perception went through her with a kind of anguish, not for herself now, but for both of them, for the long blindness in which they had walked side by side, each believing they held the other's hand.

"Gilbert," she said, "come here."

He came, slowly, and stood before her, and she put up her hands and took hold of the lapels of his dusty coat as she had used to do in the first year of their marriage, when it had been a little game between them that she should make him stoop to be kissed. He did not stoop now. He stood looking down at her with that wavering look still in his eyes, as if he did not dare yet to believe the change in her.

"I'm not going to say it doesn't matter," she began, "because it does. It matters dreadfully. I don't know that I shall ever quite get over your having signed my name like that without asking me—not because of the house, but because it was my name, and you used it as if I weren't there to own it. You'll have to let me be angry about that for a while, Gilbert. I can't help it."

"I know."

"But the rest of it——" She stopped, because she found that her throat had closed on the words, and she had to wait a moment before she could go on. "The rest of it, the failing—did you really think I married you because I was sure you'd succeed? Did you think I came all this way out of my father's house and left everybody I knew because you'd promised me a better parlour than Lucy's?"

A faint flush went up over his weather-beaten face. "I didn't know what you'd come for," he said simply. "I never knew. It seemed too much to ask, that you should come at all."

She laughed then, a little unsteadily, and shook him by the coat lapels she held. "Oh, you great blind thing! And all these years you've been trying to pay me for it, as if I were a hired girl you'd brought out on wages."

He did stoop then, all at once, and put his face down against her hair, and she felt the whole weight of his tiredness come against her, so that she had to brace herself to bear it. She bore it, standing very still in the lamplight with her arms about him, and the moth, which had found its way at last into the flame, fell blackened on the table between the lamp and her forgotten sewing. Neither of them saw it. She was thinking, with a strange lucid detachment that seemed to stand a little apart from the tumult of her feelings, that this was what she had wanted all along: not his apology, nor the house saved, nor even the truth told, but just this—that he should let her take the weight of him, once, as he had taken hers so many times without her knowing.

It was not over. She knew well enough, even as she held him, that it was not over; that there would be days when she would wake in the gray of the morning and remember the forged signature and turn cold toward him all over again; that there would be the dreadful business of Lassiter and the bank, and the packing, and the going north to some railroad camp among the greasewood where there would be no window to set slips in. She knew that he would forget, in a week or a month, what he had learned tonight, and would come home again with his trouble shut up behind his face, and she would have to break it open again, and perhaps again, before he understood that she meant it. All that lay before them, and she saw it with the clear, unflattering vision which seemed to have been given her along with the pain of the last three days. But she saw also, and it was this that made her lift her face at last and draw his down to it, that they had come through something, the two of them, which they would not have to come through in that way again; that whatever wind they walked into after this, they would know at least where each other's hands were.

"We'll manage, Gilbert," she said against his cheek. "We'll manage somehow. Only you're never to keep me out again. Promise me that."

"I promise," he said, and she believed him, not because she thought he would keep it, but because she saw that he wished to, and because she had learned, in the course of that one hard evening, that believing was a thing one did with one's eyes open, or it was not worth doing at all.

It had been, he recalled on some one of those occasions of social approval by which it appeared engagements in the Best Society proceeded, that he had sat thus, waiting until the clock ticked on the moment when he might properly join her, sat so full of the sense of her that for the instant he accepted her unannounced appearance at the darkened doorway as the mere extension of his white-heated fancy. The next moment as she charged into the circle of the lamp he saw that the umbra of some strange electrical excitement hung about her. It fairly crackled between them as he rose hurriedly to his feet.

"You have come, Eunice! You have come——" But he saw well enough what she had come for. She laid the case on the table, but as she tugged impatiently at her glove, the fringe of her wrap caught the clasp of it and scattered the jewels on the cloth. She tried then to put the ring beside them, but her hand shook so that it fell and rolled upon the floor behind them. Peter picked it up quietly, but he did not offer it to her hand again.

"I have come," said Eunice, "to say what in my mother's house I was afraid of being interrupted in saying; what you must see, what my mother won't see."

"I see you are greatly excited about something!"

"I'm not, I'm not.... That is ... I am, but not in the way you think," she was sharp with insistence; "that is what you and mother always say, that I'm nervous or excited, and all the time you don't see."

"What is it I don't see, Eunice?"

"That I can't stand it, that I can't go on with it, that it is dreadful to me,—dreadful!"

"What is dreadful?"

"Everything, being engaged—being married and giving up...." It was fairly racked out of her by some inward torture to which he had not the key.

"Of course, Eunice, if you don't wish to be married so soon——" Peter was all at sea. He brought a chair for her, and perceiving that he would go on standing as long as she did, she sat upon the edge of it but kept both the arms as a measure of defence. The slight act of doing something for her restored him for the moment to reality; he bent over her. "I've never wanted to hurry you, dearest—— It shall be when you say." She put up her hands suddenly with a shivering movement.

"Oh, never, never at all; never to you!" Peter could feel that working its track of desolation inward, but the first instinctive movement of his surface was to close over the wound. He took it as he knew he could only take it: as the explosive crisis of the virginal resistance which he remembered he had heard came to girls when marriage loomed upon them. He took a turn down the room to steady himself, praying dumbly for the right word.

"It isn't as if I didn't respect you"—she was eager in explanation, hurried and stumbling—"as if I didn't know how good you are ... it is only, because we are so different."

"How different, Eunice?"

"Oh ... older, I suppose." She grew quieter; it appeared on the whole they were getting on. "I care for so many things, you know—dancing—and bridge—young things—and you are always reading and reading. Oh! I couldn't stand it." So it was out now. She was jealous of his books, a little. Well, he had been self-absorbed. It occurred to him dimly that the thing to have done if he had known a little more about women, had practised with them, was to have provoked her at this point to the tears which should have sealed the renewal of his claim to her. What he said was, very quietly: "Of course I never meant, Eunice, that you shouldn't have everything you want."

"Oh," she seemed to have found a suffocating quality in his gentleness, against which she struck out with drowning gestures, "if you could only understand what it would mean to me never to have anybody I liked to talk to about things,—anybody I liked to be with all the time!" She was choked and aghast at the enormity of it.

"But I thought...." Peter was not able to go on with that. "Isn't there anybody you like to be with, Eunice?"

"Yes," said Eunice. "Burton Henderson." Mutinous and bright she looked at him out of the chair with a hand on either arm of it poised for flight or defence. After an interval Peter heard his own voice out of a fog rising to the conventional utterance.

"Of course, if you have learned to love him——" "I've loved him all the time." She was so bent on making this clear to him that she was careless what went down before her. "From the very beginning," she said, "but he had so little money, and mother ... I promised you, I know, but it's not as if I ever said I loved you." She should have spared him that! He had not put out a hand to hold her that he should be so pierced through with needless cruelty. But she was bent on clearing her skirts of him.

"Do you think," she expostulated to his stricken silence, "that if I'd cared in the least I'd have made it so easy for you? Can't you see that it was all arranged, that we jumped at you?" All the time she sat opposite him, thrusting swift and hard, there was no diminution of her appealing beauty, the flaming rose of her cheeks and the soft, dark flare of her hair. As if she felt how it belied at every turn the quality of her unyielding intention, her voice railed against him feverishly. "I suppose you think I'm mercenary, and I thought I was, too. You don't know how people like us need money sometimes. All the things we like cost so—all the real things. And poor mamma, she needed things; she'd never had them, and I thought that I could stand being married to you if I could get them that way.... Maybe I could, you know, if you'd been different, more like us I mean. But there was such a lot you didn't understand ... things you hadn't even heard about. I found that out as soon as we were engaged. There wasn't a thing between us; not a thing." It poured scalding hot on Peter's sensitive surfaces: made sensitive by the way in which even in this hour her beauty moved him. He felt tears starting in his heart and prayed they might not come to his face. "So you see as we hadn't anything in common it would be better for us not to go on with it even"—she broke a little at this—"even if there hadn't been anybody else. You see that, don't you?" She dared him to deny it rather than begged the concession of him as she gathered herself for departure.

"I see that."

"You never really belonged to our set, you know——" She rose now and he rose blindly with her; he hoped that she was done, but there was something still. "It hasn't been easy to go through with it.... Mother isn't going to make it any easier. It's natural for her to want me to have everything that money would mean, and I thought that if you would just keep away from her ... you owe something to Burton and me for what we've been through, I think ... just leave it to me to manage in my own way...."

"I shall never trouble you, Eunice." He came close to her then to open the door, seeing that she was to leave him, and he saw too that she had suffered, was at the very ebb and stony bottom of emotion as she hung for the moment in the doorway searching for some winged shaft of separation that should cut her off from the remotest implication of the situation. She found at last the barbedest. All the succeeding time after he closed the door on her was marked for Peter, not by the ticked moments but by successive waves of anguish as that poisoned arrow worked its way to his secret places.

"It isn't as if I had ever loved you; I owe it to Mr. Henderson to remind you that I never said I did.... You know I never liked to have you kiss me." He had in the months that succeeded to that last sight of Eunice Goodward, moments of unbearably wanting to go to her to try for a little to ease his torment in a more tender recognition of it—days when he would have taken from her, gratefully even if she had fooled him and he had seen her do it, whatever would have saved him from the certainty that never even in those first exquisite moments had she been his. The sharp edge of her young sufficiency had lopped off the right limb of his manhood. Never, even in his dreams, if life had allowed him to dream again, should he be able to see himself in any other guise than the meagre, austere front which his obligation to his mother and Ellen had obliged him to present to destiny. She had beggared him of all those aptitudes for passionate relations, by the faith in which he had kept himself inwardly alive. The capacity for loving died in him with the knowledge of not being able to be loved. Out of the anæsthesia of exhaustion from which Italy had revived him, it rolled back upon him that by just the walled imperviousness that shut Eunice Goodward from the appreciation of his passion, he was prevented now from Savilla Dassonville.

It was odd, then, having come to this conclusion in the middle of the night, that when he joined the ladies in the morning he should have experienced a sinking pang in not being able any longer to be sure what Miss Dassonville thought of him. There was in her manner, as she thanked him for the flowers, nothing to ruffle the surface of the bright, impersonal companionship which she had afforded him for weeks past. The occasion which brought them together was an agreement entered into some days earlier, to go and look at palaces, and as they turned past the Saluti to the Grand Canal, he found himself wondering if there had not been a touch of fatuity in his reading of the incident of the morning before. He had gone so far in the night as to think even of leaving Venice, and saw himself now forlornly wishing for some renewal of yesterday's mood to excuse him from the caddishness that such a flight implied. It came out a little later, perhaps, when after traversing many high and resounding marble halls, with a great many rooms opening into one another in a way that suggested rather the avoidance of privacy than its security, they found themselves in one of those gardens of shut delight of which the exteriors of Venetian houses give so little intimation. As she went about from bough to bough of the neglected roses, turned all inward as if they took their florescence from that still lighted human passion which had found its release and centre there, her face glowed for the moment with the colour of her quick sympathies. She turned it on him with an unconscious, tender confidence, which not to meet seemed to Peter, in that gentle enclosure full of warmth and fragrance, to assume the proportions of a betrayal. He did meet it there as she came back to him for the last look from the marble balustrade by which they had descended, covering her hand, there resting, lingeringly with his own. He was awakened only to the implication of this movement by the discovery that she had deeply and exquisitely blushed. It was a further singularity in view of the conviction with which Peter had come through the night, that the mood of protectingness which the girl provoked in him should have multiplied itself in pointing out to him how many ways, if he had not made up his mind not to marry her at all, such a marriage could be made to serve its primal uses. She had turned up her cuff to trail her hand overside as they slid through the lucent water, and the pretty feminine curve of it had brought to mind what the Princess had told him of the shirt-waists she made herself. He decided that she made them very well. But she was too thin for their severity—and if he married her he would have insisted on her wearing them now and then as a tender way to prevent her suspecting that it was on their account he had thought of not marrying her. The revealed whiteness of her wrist, the intimacy of her relaxed posture, for though her mind had played into his as freely as a child in a meadow, she had been always, as regards her person, a little prim with him, had lent to their errand of house visiting a personal note in which it was absurdly apt for them to have run across Captain Dunham of the Merrythought at the door of the Consulate. Mr. Weatheral had some papers which Lessing had sent him to acknowledge there, and it was a piece of the morning's performance, when he had come back from that business, to find that the meeting had taken on—from some mutual discovery of the captain's and Mrs. Merrithew's of a cousin's wife's sister who had married one of the Applegates who was a Dunham on the mother's side—quite the aspect of a family party. It came in the end to the four of them going off at Peter's invitation to have lunch together in a café overhanging the calle. He told himself afterward that he would not have done it if he had recalled in time the friendly seaman's romantic appreciation of the situation between himself and Miss Dassonville. He saw himself so intrigued by it that, by the time lunch was over, he felt himself in a position which to his own sensitiveness, demanded that he must immediately leave Venice or propose to Miss Dassonville. To see the way he was going and to go on in it, had for him the fascination of the abyss. He caught himself in the act even of trying to fix Miss Dassonville's eye to include her by complicity in the beguilement of the captain, a business which she seemed to have undertaken on her own account on quite other grounds. He perceived with a kind of pride for her that she had the ways of elderly sea-going gentlemen by heart. It was something even if she had failed to charm Peter, that she shouldn't be found quite wanting in it by other men. "When are you coming to lunch with me?" demanded the captain.

It was characteristic of the way in which Hallam Brede had been accustomed for twelve years to take his surprises, singly and in the open, that he should have found the most disconcerting feature of his return to be that his cousin Lydia had grown, in his absence, so exactly into the likeness of her house. He had been prepared for the house. He had carried it about with him through all the dust and glare of the Inyo country as one carries a picture turned face inward in the bottom of a trunk, knowing it to be there and not needing to look. He had expected the brass knocker, worn thin on the striking side, and the fanlight, and the faint, persistent odour of beeswax and sweet-fern that met him in the hall as if it had been waiting there all this while on the chance of his coming back. What he had not expected was that Lydia, coming down the stair to him with one hand on the rail in the old way, should seem to have taken her colour from the walls, to have been rubbed, like the knocker, to a certain thinness on the side that had borne the strokes.

"Hallam! You've come.... I'd begun to think the train had carried you on to Boston." She gave him both her hands, and he saw that she had meant to kiss him and had thought better of it at the last step, so that her face, lifted for the instant, went past his shoulder and recovered itself in a little laugh. "You're browner than I thought you'd be. I don't know why I thought you wouldn't be brown."

"You're not, at any rate," said Hallam, and was immediately sorry for it, because it seemed to touch upon something.

It was not until they had got themselves into the back parlour, where the fire had been lit against the October damp and the late sun came through the ailanthus leaves in a kind of yellow sediment, that he was able to sort out for himself what it was. He had left her a girl of twenty, all gestures, with a way of flinging her opinions at you from across a room and then running after them to see where they had struck; and he found her now a woman who sat very still in a straight chair, with her hands laid one upon the other in her lap, and who seemed to have learned somewhere in the interval the art, which he had always associated with their grandmother, of waiting for things to come to her. It was not that she had faded. Her hair kept its warm, uncertain brown, and her eyes, when she turned them on him, had the old trick of lighting suddenly from within as a lamp is turned up behind a curtain. But the light, when it came, came from farther back.

"Well," she said, "you must tell me everything. I've had your letters, of course—four of them, Hallam, in twelve years, and one of those was about the Dorrance mortgage—but I mean everything. Was it as dreadful as Aunt Sophia always said? She used to read your letters aloud at Thanksgiving, the few there were, and stop at the places where you said you'd slept on the ground, as if it were something that ought to be prayed over."

"It wasn't dreadful at all." He considered how he could make it plain to her, and found that he could not, that the whole of that country lay in him like a language that had no equivalents in this one. "It was—large. You get used to the size of things there. You get so that a mountain forty miles off is a neighbour, and you speak of it by name, and notice when it changes colour. I used to watch one peak in particular, from the cabin door at Coso, every evening.... It went the colour of a peach about six o'clock, and then blue, and then nothing. I don't know that I could tell you why it mattered."

"I think I know," said Lydia; and he looked at her quickly, because it was the thing their grandmother would have said, and their grandmother had never known anything of the sort.

But it appeared, as they went on, that she did know, or knew something near enough to it to make him feel that he had not altogether wasted his breath. She asked him the right questions: not whether he had made money, which he had, though not so much as the family supposed, nor whether he had been lonely, which was a thing he did not intend to be asked; but what the Indians had been like, and whether the desert flowers came all at once, and how the water tasted that had been brought for miles in a canvas bag. She listened with her head a little on one side, and he perceived that she was listening not so much to what he said as to the places where his voice changed in saying it; and it gave him a curious, half-uneasy pleasure, as of being handled by somebody who knew, without having been told, where the bones were sore.

It was only when he had talked himself out, and had sat for a moment looking into the fire with the sense, familiar to him from long evenings by himself, that the room had grown larger and very quiet around him, that it occurred to him he had been there the better part of an hour and had not asked her a single thing.

"And you, Lydia?" He turned on her with an awkwardness that was half penitence. "Here I've been talking about mountains.... What has happened to you?"

"To me?" She made a little movement of her hands, unfolding them and folding them again the other way. "Nothing has happened to me. That's the whole of it, you see. Grandmother died—you knew that—and Aunt Sophia came to live here for a while, and then she went back to Hartford, and there was the question of the house, and nobody wanted it but me...." She stopped, and he waited, and she went on in a lighter key, as if she had been caught going down a road she had meant to avoid. "I have the Ladies' Library on Tuesdays, and a class at Saint Michael's, and I keep the books for the Dorcas Society, which is a great deal more exciting than you'd suppose; you've no idea how the members contrive to get into debt over flannel petticoats. And I read. I've read everything, Hallam. I've read all the books you used to say I'd never get through, and some you'd never heard of."

"I don't doubt it."

"You needn't say it as if it were something to be sorry for."

"I wasn't sorry," said Hallam; but he was, and she saw it. It lay between them for a moment, a small, clean, irrefutable fact, like a pebble on a table, and neither of them put out a hand to move it.

He remembered now, with the suddenness with which such things will come back upon a man in the very room where they first had their existence, the last evening he had spent in it before he went West. It had been spring then, with the windows open on the lilacs and the frogs making a shrill, continuous fringe of sound to everything that was said; and Lydia had sat on the hassock by the fire, which had not been lighted, with her chin in her hands, and told him that he was a fool to go. He had not been able, then, to make her understand why he must, that he had come to the end of something in himself which the town, the family, the very furniture of the house conspired to keep him from getting beyond. She had been angry with him; she had said things which he had carried off with him to Coso and turned over, on nights when the wind came down off the Sierra and rattled the stovepipe, until they were worn smooth and he could no longer tell whether they had been cruel or only young. He had a notion that she had not meant him to go at all, that she had taken it for granted, as the whole family had taken it for granted, that he would read law with Judge Pellew and marry, if not her, then someone like her, and grow by degrees into one of those solid, quiet, slightly melancholy men who sat on the vestry and spoke at town meetings about the drains. And he had a notion, too, though he had never permitted it to come quite to the surface of his mind, that it was for precisely this reason he had gone.

"Do you remember," he began, and then thought better of it; but she had caught him up.

"The lilacs? Yes, I remember. I was horrid to you."

"You were perfectly right, from where you stood."

"Oh, from where I stood...." She laughed, and the light came up behind her eyes and went down again. "That's just it, isn't it? I've been standing in the same place ever since. People took things for granted, and then it was easier to go on with them than to explain why they hadn't happened. I let them take it for granted as long as it was any use to anybody. "It wasn't any use to you."

"It was a great deal of use," said Lydia. "It let me alone."

He sat looking at her, and she at him, across the small, bright circle of the lamp; and it was borne in upon him, with a kind of slow astonishment, that she was not in the least asking to be pitied—that she had, in fact, a quality which he could only describe to himself as a sort of proud spareness, like a tree that has been pruned back hard and has come to an understanding with the knife. He had thought of her, when he thought of her at all in those years, as something he had left behind in a sheltered place, as one leaves a plant on a window-ledge, and he had taken it for granted, very much as the town had taken Fred Haverly for granted, that she would be found on his return either flourishing a little stupidly in the sun or gone quite dry for want of tending. It had not occurred to him that she might have put down roots of her own into the cracks of that narrow ledge, and drawn up out of it a nourishment which he, with all his mountains, had never so much as guessed at.
