It was the custom in Westover, when a child had to be corrected, to proceed less by inquiry into the nature of the offence than by a reckoning of what it had cost the family in the opinion of the neighbours; and Clara Pryor, who had been brought up in Westover and had never lived anywhere else, would not have known how to go about it otherwise. She had besides a natural timidity, the sort that in women bred to the narrow round of house and church does duty for principle. She would have suffered anything rather than be talked about, and it was the bitterest feature of the afternoon that what had been said of her had been said kindly. Mrs. Gedney had laid a hand on her arm at the Ladies' Aid, between the cutting out of the flannel petticoats for the Indian mission and the passing of the seed cakes, and had told her in a lowered voice that she had never known, not in all these years, and that she did think it beautiful, the way Clara kept it up.

"Kept what up?" Clara had asked, with a horrid prescience of something gone wrong at home.

"Why, the flowers, dear. On the little grave under the snowball bush. Your Lucy told me. She said you go out with the lantern every night, after Mr. Pryor is asleep."

There was nothing to be said to it. Clara had sat through the rest of the afternoon with her needle going in and out of the flannel, and the faces of the Westover ladies, none of whom had been near enough to overhear, swimming before her as though every one of them had. She had not told Mrs. Gedney there was no grave, because that would have been to tell her that Lucy lied. She had not let her believe there was one, either, for she had only said, "Lucy is a very strange child," and Mrs. Gedney had pressed her arm again and said she supposed they all were, at that age, where there had been a sorrow in the house. Clara knew that by Sunday it would have gone the length of the church, and that nothing she could do afterward would quite get it back.

She walked home by the plank sidewalk under the maples with her black kid gloves buttoned tight over her wrists, and her reticule held before her as if it were the evidence in the case. It was the end of May; the lilacs were done, and the snowball bush by the woodshed corner had come into its full white pomp. She did not look at it as she came up the side path. Ever after, I think, she disliked it a little.

Lucy was in the woodshed. She had been there most of the afternoon, with an apron full of clothespins and a cigar box lined with a scrap of turkey red, conducting the obsequies of a clothespin doll with all the grief and ceremony the occasion seemed to her to demand. She was seven that spring, a thin child with a great deal of straight brown hair which would not stay plaited, and eyes so dark in her pale face that people who did not like her called them sly, and people who did called them old-fashioned. Westover had no other word for that look of a child who is attending to something you cannot see. She had lit, with matches she had no business to have, a stub of candle at the head of the cigar box, and she was singing over it, very low, a hymn of which she knew only the tune and had supplied the words herself. The words were about a little lamb that had gone to sleep in the snow, and had to do, in a way she would not have been able to explain, with the white petals coming down outside the shed door.

"Lucy Ellen," said her mother from the doorway, "you come in the house."

Lucy got up at once, not because she apprehended anything, but because that tone was the one in which she had always been called in, and she had never been able to tell from it whether she was wanted to set the table or to be whipped. She blew out the candle, an act which by its very promptness seemed to her mother an admission of guilt, and followed into the kitchen with the cigar box held carefully level in both hands.

"Put that down."

Lucy put it on the end of the wood box, and stood beside it with her hands behind her.

Clara Pryor took off her gloves finger by finger, and then her hat, which she laid upon the kitchen table, where it looked oddly ceremonious against the oilcloth. She did these things slowly, because she had not yet made up her mind how to begin, and because it was a part of the Westover tradition of reprimand that there should be a pause beforehand in which the culprit might be supposed to search her own heart. Lucy employed it in noticing that her mother's best collar was pinned a little crooked, and in wondering whether it would be polite to say so.

"Lucy," said her mother at last, "did you tell Mrs. Gedney there was a grave in our yard?"

"Yes, ma'am."

It was the readiness of the admission that disconcerted her. Clara had been prepared for a denial, and had armed herself against it with the full weight of Mrs. Gedney's testimony; she had foreseen tears and was ready to be unmoved by them; but she had not foreseen that Lucy would simply stand there and say yes, as though she had been asked whether she had swept the back porch.

"And you told her," Clara went on, getting her breath, "that I go out at night with a lantern and put flowers on it?"

"Yes, ma'am. Bleeding hearts," Lucy added, with the air of furnishing a detail that had been inadvertently omitted. "And sometimes the white violets from under the pump."

"Lucy Ellen Pryor!"

The child flinched at that, not so much because she understood what was coming as because the use of her whole name had always been the signal of an approaching calamity, like the bell at the depot that rang before the train came in. But she did not see what she had done. That was the dreadful part of it, and the part which Clara Pryor, for all her conscientious searching afterward, was never able to grasp; for there was in Lucy's mind no line at all between the things that were so and the things she said, but only between the things that were well said and the things that were not. She had told Mrs. Gedney about the grave because Mrs. Gedney had stopped her at the gate, and asked in that voice grown people used for asking children questions which do not expect an answer, whether she was a good girl and helped her mother. And Lucy, who did not feel that she was particularly a good girl and could not think of anything else to say, had looked past Mrs. Gedney's bonnet at the snowball bush, white and heavy in the sun, and had felt rise up in her, as she often felt it, the shape of something that wanted saying. She had said it, and Mrs. Gedney had wiped her eyes; and Lucy had gone back into the yard with that warm, tingling sense about the back of her neck which she had come to look for whenever she had told a thing so that people believed it.

"Do you know what that is," said her mother, "to say a thing that isn't so?"

Lucy considered.

"It's a story," she offered.

"It's a lie." Clara pronounced the word as though it burned her. In Westover it was hardly ever pronounced at all; children told fibs, and grown people were mistaken, and only the very wicked lied, so that to bring it out in her own kitchen was almost like taking down from the top shelf of the cupboard the bottle marked poison. "It's a wicked lie, and what is more you've told it on your own mother, and made her a laughing-stock before all the Ladies' Aid. Do you know what Mrs. Gedney thinks of me now? She thinks I go creeping about the yard at night like a—" She could not, on the spur of the moment, think what she was like, and fell back on the ultimate authority. "What do you suppose your father will say?"

Lucy did not know. Her father, who kept the feed store on Main Street and came home smelling of bran and harness oil, did not as a rule say anything about her at all, except at the table, where he asked her to pass the bread. But she had begun to understand, by the way her mother's mouth worked, that the thing was serious; and with this understanding came, not contrition, for she could not feel sorry for what still seemed to her a good and pleasant thing, but a confused and enlarging fear. She put her hand out toward the cigar box on the wood box, as if for comfort, and her mother saw it.

"And what's that? What have you got in there?"

"It's Mehitabel," said Lucy faintly. "She died."

Clara Pryor took the lid off the cigar box and looked at the clothespin doll lying in its turkey red with a sprig of snowball blossom on its breast. I suppose there had never been, in the whole course of her life, any occasion on which she had been brought so near to the thing in her daughter that was afterward to set Lucy apart from all the Westover she had come of; and I suppose there was never a woman less able to recognize it. What she saw was a waste of good turkey red and a burnt-out candle end, and behind them a disposition she did not have the least idea how to deal with, except that, by the light of everything she had ever been taught, it was very much better done away with.

"Playing funerals," she said, and her voice went up in spite of her. "Playing funerals in the woodshed and burning candles, and then going out to the gate and telling the neighbours there's a grave in the yard! I don't know what's to become of you. I declare I don't. I don't know where you get it from; it isn't from my side."

That was the one thing she was sure of. On her side there had been Merriams and Holcombs, all solid people who had cleared their farms and joined the church and been buried in the Westover cemetery under stones that said exactly who they were and when they had died, and nothing more. If there had been anything strange among them, it had been kept, as such things were kept in Westover, so far out of sight that the family had honestly forgotten it.

"Now you listen to me," she said, and sat down in the kitchen rocker so that she might have the child before her, a little below the level of her eyes, where a child ought to be. "To-morrow morning you are going straight over to Mrs. Gedney's, and you are going to say you told her a lie, and you are sorry. And you are going to bed this minute without any supper, and you are to ask God to forgive you. And if I ever hear of you telling such a thing again, I'll cut a switch off that peach tree, and you know I mean it."

It was the formula; it was what had been said to Clara herself, and to her mother before her, and it had the virtue of all such formulas, that it could be gone through without thinking. But there must have been something in the very completeness with which it disposed of the matter that worked in Lucy as a provocation; for as she stood there, with her hands knotted in her apron and her lip beginning to go, the sense of injustice, of having had a thing of hers taken and broken and given back to her as an ugliness, rose up in her and overflowed in the only defence she had.

"It isn't all a lie," she cried. "Grandma said. Grandma said there was one before me that didn't stay. She told Aunt Hattie. She said it was a little boy and he was buried—" She stopped, because she had come to the end of what she had overheard, and had only the snowball bush to finish it with.

Clara Pryor did not say anything at all.

She sat quite still in the rocker, with her hands lying on the black silk of her lap, and her face, which had been flushed with the walk home and the heat of her indignation, went slowly to the colour of the flannel she had been cutting all afternoon. It had been eight years. There had been a child, born too soon in the hard February before Lucy came, and it had lived a day and a night, and her husband had carried it out to the Holcomb lot in the cemetery in a box not very much larger than the one on the wood box, while she lay upstairs and heard the sleigh bells go and come again. Nobody in Westover had spoken of it since, not because they did not know, but because it was not the sort of thing that was spoken of; and Clara herself had accepted the silence so wholly that she had come to think of it as a kindness. She had not known that her mother-in-law talked of it in the sitting room with the door ajar. She had certainly not known that it had been all this while lying in the mind of her daughter, putting out pale shoots like a potato in a cellar, and coming up at last in the form of bleeding hearts and white violets and a lantern carried across the grass at night.

The worst of it was, and she felt it even then without being able to put it to herself, that she had wanted to. There had been nights that first spring when she had lain awake beside Amos and thought of getting up and going out somewhere with flowers, and had not, because there was nowhere in the yard to go, and because it would have looked so queer if anybody had seen her. Lucy had not invented anything. She had only finished what her mother had not dared to begin.

"Don't you ever," said Clara at last, and her voice was so altered that Lucy, who had been bracing herself for the peach tree, looked up in a kind of terror; "don't you ever say that again. To anybody. Do you hear me?"

"Yes, ma'am."

"It isn't a thing to tell."

"But if it's so—"

"It doesn't matter if it's so." It was the nearest Clara Pryor ever came, in all her life, to the statement of her philosophy, and she did not know that she had made it. "There are things you don't tell, whether they are so or not. Nice people don't. You'll understand when you're older."

But Lucy did not understand, and when she was older she understood still less; and it is certain that if Clara Pryor had been able to see where that afternoon's lesson was to carry her daughter, by what devious roads and in what unforeseen company, she would have cut the switch from the peach tree after all, as being the lesser evil.

She did not, however. She got up from the rocker and put her hat away in the hall closet and came back and tied on her kitchen apron over the black silk, all without looking at the child, and then, because something had to be done, she took the cigar box off the wood box and held it out.

"Take that out of the house."

Lucy took it, and stood holding it.

"Where shall I put it?"

There was a pause in which the clock over the shelf, with its painted glass picture of a lake and a castle such as neither of them had ever seen, ticked off what seemed to the child a very long time. Then Clara turned to the stove and began rattling the lids.

"Put it where you like," she said. "And then go up to bed."

It was so that Amos Pryor found them a little after six, coming in at the back door with his hat on and the evening paper under his arm, and finding no supper on the table, which had not happened, so far as he could recollect, since the winter his wife had the quinsy. He stood in the doorway taking in the cold stove and his wife standing over it with the stove lifter in her hand, as though she had forgotten what it was for, and the absence of his daughter, about whom he did not ordinarily think at all until he missed her.

"Anything the matter?"

"Lucy's been telling stories," said his wife without turning round.

"Well, well," said Amos. He hung his hat on the nail by the door, and sat down to take off his boots, which was a thing he never did until after supper, and which he did now, I think, to give himself something to occupy him while the matter was explained. But it was not explained. It was one of the conditions of married life in Westover that a man should not be troubled with the bringing up of girls, and Amos would have been as much embarrassed to be asked to take a hand in it as to be asked to trim a bonnet. He only inquired, after a while, whether Clara wanted him to go up and speak to her, and on being told that it had been attended to, he unfolded his paper with a relief which he was too honest to conceal.

Lucy, meanwhile, had gone out by the side door with the cigar box, and had stood for some time in the yard, in the long yellow light that comes up the Westover streets at the end of a spring day, uncertain what she was permitted to do. She did not go to the snowball bush. She had a feeling, which she was not able to have accounted for, that the snowball bush now belonged to her mother in a way it had not before, and that she had no right there. In the end she buried Mehitabel under the rhubarb by the back fence, with no hymn and no candle, and smoothed the earth over very carefully, so that nobody would know. Then she went up the back stairs to the little slant-roofed room over the kitchen, and undressed in the dusk, and said her prayers as she had been told, asking God to forgive her for the lie, and adding, after a moment's reflection, a request that He would also take care of the little boy, wherever he was, since nobody else seemed to think about him.

She lay awake a long time listening to the sounds that came up through the stovepipe hole, the scrape of a skillet, the creak of her father's chair, the click of plates. They did not talk, though once she heard her mother say "Amos—" and then nothing more, as if she had thought better of it. And presently, just as the last of the light was going out of the window, she heard the kitchen door open softly and close again, and footsteps go down the path on the grass beside it, where they would make no sound on the boards.

She got up on her knees and looked out. Her mother was standing by the snowball bush in the half dark with her apron on, not doing anything, only standing, with her hands folded under the apron as if she were cold. She did not have a lantern. After a while she reached up and broke off one of the great white clusters and stood holding it, and then, as if she had been caught at something, she looked quickly up and down the empty street and went back into the house with it hidden in her apron.

Lucy did not go to Mrs. Gedney's in the morning. Nobody spoke of it, and she was wise enough, for once, not to ask. But it is from that evening that she always dated, when she came to look back upon her childhood with the clearer eyes of a woman who had made her way in the world by the very faculty Westover had tried so hard to punish out of her, the knowledge that there were two kinds of truth, the kind you might tell and the kind you might only live; and that her mother, who had whipped her more than once for lesser things, had never again been able to whip her for anything at all.

On the evening when the matter was at last to be spoken of, Mr. Henry Cottrell came home a little later than usual, and he came up the brick walk between the two iron urns with the air of a man who has rehearsed something in a streetcar and is no longer entirely satisfied with it. The urns had been placed there by his wife's father in the year of the great Exposition, when urns were thought to give a house distinction, and they had held geraniums every summer since. They held geraniums now, though somewhat sooty ones, for the town had grown up around the old Wainwright place as a river rises around a stump, and the smoke that was the town's pride and its breath came down upon Pennsylvania Street with an impartiality no geranium could withstand.

Mr. Cottrell paused upon the porch, wiped his feet with more care than the mat required, and looked for a moment at the house across the street. It had been the Hollister house once; it was now a "rooming house," and a printed card in the parlor window said as much. Beyond it, where the Pettigrews' lawn had sloped down to a picket fence, there rose the red bulk of the new Belvedere Apartments, five stories of pressed brick with a canopy over the door and a negro in a green uniform standing beneath it. Mr. Cottrell looked at the Belvedere as a man looks at an argument he means to use, and then he went indoors.

His wife was in the sitting room. She had been sitting there, as it happened, for the better part of an hour, with a piece of embroidery in her lap upon which she had not taken three stitches; but when she heard his key she bent her head over it with an industry so apparent that a more observant husband might have taken warning. Mr. Cottrell was not, in the ordinary course of things, a very observant husband, which is perhaps only to say that he had been married twenty-two years.

"Well, Mattie," he said, and kissed her upon the part of her forehead she presented to him.

"You're late, Henry."

"Kept at the office. Fellow came in just as I was getting my hat." He sat down in the Morris chair, which creaked in a manner familiar to them both, and unfolded the evening paper. Then he folded it again, which was not like him. "Where's Florence?"

"Upstairs. She's dressing. The Lowery boy is taking her to the Assembly."

"The Assembly? On a Tuesday?"

"It's Thursday, Henry."

"So it is," he said. "So it is." And he laughed in a way that was meant to be comfortable and was not.

Mrs. Cottrell drew her needle through the linen and held it up at the full length of the thread, examining it as though the needle were a new and curious thing. "Mrs. Bascom was here this afternoon," she said.

There was a pause in the room. Somewhere above them Florence was opening and shutting bureau drawers with the energy of eighteen preparing for an Assembly, and out upon the street a trolley car went grinding by, its bell clanging at the corner of Walnut as it had clanged ten thousand times before. Mr. Cottrell found that he had unfolded his paper once more.

"Was she?" he said. "That's nice. How's Bascom's rheumatism?"

"We didn't speak of Mr. Bascom's rheumatism." Mrs. Cottrell laid down the embroidery. "We spoke of Mr. Kessler."

Now, Mr. Theodore Kessler was a person of whom it would have been impossible, a decade earlier, for anyone on Pennsylvania Street to have spoken at all, because a decade earlier no one on Pennsylvania Street had heard of him. He had come out of somewhere to the south, with a patent for a vulcanizing process and a manner of shaking hands that left the recipient feeling he had been agreed with; and the vulcanizing process had turned out to be precisely the thing that the age of the automobile was waiting for. He now owned a great part of the north side of the river and was said to be "going in heavily for real estate," a phrase which, in the mouths of the older residents, had very much the sound that "going in heavily for drink" had had in the mouths of their parents.

"Kessler?" said Mr. Cottrell. "What about him?"

"Henry," said his wife, "don't."

"Don't what?"

"Don't sit there and say 'Kessler?' to me as if you'd never heard the name. Mrs. Bascom says her husband says that you have had two meetings with Mr. Kessler at the Commercial Club, and that you lunched with him on Monday, and that the whole of downtown knows he wants this property for a garage." She brought out the last word as though it were something she had found in the cistern. "A garage, Henry! For automobiles!"

"Well," said Mr. Cottrell, with an attempt at humor, "you'd hardly keep cows in it."

Mrs. Cottrell did not smile. She was a handsome woman still, in the full and somewhat stately manner that had been admired in the town when she was the youngest Wainwright girl and the town had been small enough to admire anyone it liked; and when she did not smile, her face took on a look of her father's portrait over the mantel, the look of the old Judge listening to a lawyer whose case he has already decided against. Mr. Cottrell, who had been afraid of the Judge for six years and of the portrait for sixteen, glanced up at it now and then hurriedly away.

"I meant to tell you, Mattie," he said. "I meant to tell you this very evening. I've been turning it over."

"Turning it over! Turning it over with Mr. Kessler at the Commercial Club, and with the Bascoms, and with heaven knows who else, before you ever said one word to me! Do you know what it was like to sit in my own parlor and hear it from Effie Bascom? Effie Bascom, Henry, who was asking me if it was true, with her mouth all pursed up as though she were sorry for me, and all the time just dying to get home and telephone it to the Merriweathers?"

"Now, Mattie—"

"I said I didn't know what she meant. I said I supposed people would always talk. And then she said, 'Oh, my dear, then he hasn't told you?' and I had to sit there—" Mrs. Cottrell's voice, which had been mounting, broke off at this point, and she picked up her embroidery again and held it very still.

Mr. Cottrell rose from the Morris chair and walked to the window, where he stood with his hands behind him, looking out at the canopy of the Belvedere. He was a man of medium height, of medium prosperity, and of medium years; he had been for a long while the junior partner of a firm of wholesale druggists that had never quite done as well as it ought, and the town, which classified everyone, had long since classified him as "a nice fellow—married one of the Wainwright girls." It is not the most stimulating description a man can carry about with him, and it may be that Mr. Cottrell had grown a little tired of it.

"I'm sorry about Effie Bascom," he said to the window. "I'm sorry she got hold of it first. That's Bascom's fault; I told him in confidence. But I'm not sorry about the rest, Mattie, and I may as well say so."

"You mean you've done it?"

"No, I haven't done it. I couldn't do it without you. You know that. The property's in your name."

"Yes," said Mrs. Cottrell. "It is."

He turned around. "Now listen to me a minute. Just listen. You haven't any idea what Kessler's offering."

"I don't care what he's offering."

"Forty-two thousand dollars," said Mr. Cottrell.

The figure fell into the room with a certain weight. Even Mrs. Cottrell, who did not care what Mr. Kessler was offering, was for an instant silent before it; for the Wainwright place, when the Judge had built it, had cost eleven thousand, and that had been thought a great deal of money for a house, even a house with a cupola and a carriage block and a stained-glass window on the landing showing a young woman in a nightgown releasing a dove.

"Forty-two thousand," Mr. Cottrell repeated, encouraged. "Cash. And you know as well as I do what this property would bring on the open market if we tried to sell it as a residence. Who wants to live on Pennsylvania Street any more? Who's left? The Bascoms and ourselves and old Mrs. Tulley, and Mrs. Tulley's selling in the spring—her son told me so. Look out that window, Mattie. Look at it! Rooming houses and flats and a Chinese laundry down at the corner where the Gilberts lived. The whole neighborhood's gone. It went five years ago and we've just been too stubborn to notice."

"I noticed," said Mrs. Cottrell.

"Then what on earth—"

"I noticed," she said, "and I didn't think it was any reason to go and help it along."

Mr. Cottrell made a gesture of large despair, the gesture of a man appealing to an invisible jury. "Help it along! Mattie, it's going along whether we help it or not. That's what I'm trying to make you see. This town's growing. It's growing every minute. There's going to be a business district out here inside of ten years, clear to Fourteenth Street, and the people that see it coming are the people that are going to come out of it with something. Kessler sees it. He's no fool. And here we are, sitting on the best corner on the street, and he comes to me—comes to me, mind you—and makes us an offer like that, and you want to turn it down because of what Effie Bascom thinks?"

"I don't care what Effie Bascom thinks!"

"Then what do you care about?"

It was, as he perceived the instant it was out, a question he ought not to have asked; for Mrs. Cottrell's eyes went, quite without her meaning them to, to the portrait above the mantel, and Mr. Cottrell's went there after them, and for a moment the Judge looked down upon the two of them with the air of having been consulted at last.

"Papa built this house," said Mrs. Cottrell, in a low voice. "He built it for Mamma. I was born upstairs in the front room. Ellen was married in that bay window—you were there, Henry; you were an usher. You stood right where you're standing now and dropped the ring box and Papa had to get down on his knees and hunt for it under the piano. And Mamma died here, and Papa died here, and Florence was born here, and Teddy—" She stopped.

Teddy was the little boy who had lived to be four. Mr. Cottrell did not move from the window.

"I know, Mattie," he said, after a while, more gently. "I know all that. Don't you suppose I know it?"

"Then how can you want to sell it to a man who'll tear it down and put up a—a shed for automobiles, with gasoline smelling all over everything, and men in overalls spitting on the sidewalk where the carriage block was? How can you?"

"Because," said Mr. Cottrell, and now his own voice had begun to rise, "because I'm fifty-one years old, and I'd like to have something before I'm sixty! Because I've worked for Hammond and Fitch for twenty-four years, and they've never paid me what I'm worth, and they never will! Because Florence is going to want to be married one of these days, and I'd like to give her something better than a set of fish forks! Because I'm tired, Mattie—I'm tired of being the man that married one of the Wainwright girls and lives in the old Wainwright place. I'd like to be the man that did something, just once!"

The bureau drawers upstairs had fallen silent. Neither of them noticed it.

Mrs. Cottrell looked at her husband with an expression that had in it, along with a great deal of indignation, a certain surprise; for it is one of the curiosities of marriage that two people may live side by side for twenty-two years and yet one of them may never have heard the other say that he was tired. She had heard Henry say that he was hungry, and that the furnace was smoking, and that the Democrats would ruin the country; but she had not heard him say this, and it disconcerted her.

"I never knew you felt like that," she said.

"Well, I do."

"You never said."

"What was there to say? A man doesn't go around complaining." Mr. Cottrell came away from the window and sat down again in the Morris chair, which creaked; and he looked, sitting there, a good deal older than he had looked when he came in. "I didn't mean to go at it this way. I meant to put it to you sensibly. I had it all worked out. Kessler wants to put up a first-class establishment—not a shed, Mattie; it's going to be a fine big building with plate-glass windows, and a showroom in front. He's taking the agency for the Pierce-Arrow. And he said—" Mr. Cottrell hesitated, and then went on rather fast, as a man goes on over thin ice. "He said that if we sold to him, he'd want somebody he could trust to take charge of the business end of it. Somebody who knew the town and had a head for figures. He said he'd want me."

"You?" said Mrs. Cottrell. "In the automobile business?"

"Why not me? It's the coming thing. Everybody says so. A man can't stay in drugs forever."

"Henry Cottrell, you don't know the first thing about automobiles. You've never even ridden in one except the time Mr. Lowery took us to the Fair Grounds, and you held on to your hat the whole way and said it was a menace."

"I don't have to know about automobiles to keep books on 'em," said Mr. Cottrell, with some heat. "Kessler doesn't know about automobiles either. He knows about rubber. And money."

"Yes," said his wife. "He seems to know about money."

There was a quality in this that Mr. Cottrell did not like. "Now, what do you mean by that?"

"I mean," said Mrs. Cottrell, laying aside the embroidery altogether, "that I think it's very curious that Mr. Kessler should suddenly discover he can't get on without you, Henry, at the very same time he wants to buy our house. I think it's very curious indeed. Did he say how much he'd pay you?"

"We didn't go into details."

"Did he put anything in writing?"

"It isn't the kind of thing you put in writing. It's an understanding between gentlemen."

"Between gentlemen," said Mrs. Cottrell, and something in the way she said it made Mr. Cottrell feel, for the first time that evening, that he was in the wrong; though he could not, in the confusion of the moment, have said precisely how. He knew only that he had walked up the brick walk with a strong case and that it had somehow, in the last quarter of an hour, become a case with a hole in it, and that the hole was exactly the size and shape of Mr. Kessler's hand as it closed warmly about his own at the Commercial Club.

"You think he's making a fool of me," he said.

"I didn't say that."

"You think it, though."

Mrs. Cottrell was silent, and her silence was a kind of answer. Then, unexpectedly, she rose from her chair and came across to where he sat, and stood beside him, and after a moment put her hand upon his shoulder. It was a thing she had not done in a long while, and they were both a little embarrassed by it.

"Henry," she said, "I don't think he's making a fool of you. I think he's using you, which isn't the same thing. He knows I'd never sell to him—he must know it; everybody in town knows how I feel about this place. So he goes to you. And he says nice things to you, and he talks about the coming thing, and the plate glass, and the business end, and he makes you feel—" She stopped, because she had been about to say "important," and she perceived that it would be unkind.

But Mr. Cottrell had heard the word as clearly as if she had spoken it. He sat very still under her hand.

"Maybe so," he said at last. "Maybe that's so. But the forty-two thousand's real enough, Mattie. Whatever Kessler is, that money's real."

"I know it is."

"And the neighborhood's real. And the smoke. And the Chinese laundry. You can't stop it by sitting in here with the shades pulled down."

"I know that too," she said, and her voice was not quite steady. "Don't you think I know it? Every morning I look out at that dreadful Belvedere and that colored man in the green coat, and I think, 'Papa wouldn't know the street.' But it's all I've got left of him, Henry. It's all I've got of any of them. When it's gone, there won't be anything to show they were ever here at all. Nobody'll remember. Florence won't remember—not really. She was too little when Papa died. And Florence's children won't even know where it stood."

"They'll know if we tell 'em."

"It isn't the same."

"No," said Mr. Cottrell slowly. "No, I suppose it isn't."

They remained so for some moments, the man seated and the woman standing beside him, and the Judge looking down upon them from over the mantel; and if there was any expression upon the painted face, it was perhaps a kind of grim satisfaction, as of a man who has lived long enough to see that his son-in-law was, after all, no match for his daughter. But it may be that this is only a fancy. Portraits are like the dead: they mean whatever we bring to them.

Footsteps sounded upon the stair, and Florence came down into the hall, all white tulle and a blue sash and a little gilt fan, looking as Mattie Wainwright had looked on the night she first danced with Henry Cottrell, though neither of her parents happened to think of it just then. She paused in the doorway of the sitting room and regarded them with the curious, half-anxious brightness of a young person who has been listening at a register and does not intend to say so.

"Is anything the matter?" she asked.

"Nothing at all, dear," said her mother, taking her hand from Mr. Cottrell's shoulder. "Your father and I were talking about business."

"Oh," said Florence. She looked from one to the other. "Is Harvey Lowery's car outside? I thought I heard it."

Mr. Cottrell rose and went to the window. A long gray touring car, very new and very brassy, had drawn up at the curb beneath the sooty urns, and a young man in a duster and goggles was climbing down from it with the grave self-importance of one who controls forty horses. Its engine continued to throb in a manner that rattled the stained-glass dove upon the landing.

"Yes," said Mr. Cottrell. "That's him."

Florence kissed them both, hastily and impartially, and was gone; they heard her laugh in the hall, and the front door open and close, and the Lowery boy's voice saying something about the roads; and then the car went away up Pennsylvania Street with a great blatting and a cloud of blue smoke that hung for a while in the light of the street lamp and slowly dissolved into the larger smoke of the town.

Mr. Cottrell stood looking after it.

"There it goes," he said, without explaining what he meant; and his wife, who had come to stand beside him at the window, did not ask him. Perhaps she knew. Perhaps there was nothing that needed explaining—only the street, and the lamp, and the canopy of the Belvedere, and the long, faint, unending grind of the trolley cars carrying the new people to their new houses on the other side of town.

"I'll tell Kessler no," said Mr. Cottrell presently. "I'll tell him in the morning."

Mrs. Cottrell did not answer at once. When she did, it was in a voice so low that he was not perfectly sure he had heard her.

"Not yet, Henry," she said. "Don't tell him anything yet. Let me—let me think about it."

He turned and looked at her in astonishment; but her face was toward the window, and he could see only the line of her cheek, which was the line of her father's cheek, and of the cheek of the girl he had danced with long ago in the old Assembly rooms over Pfeiffer's hardware store, when the town was small and everybody knew everybody, and nobody had heard of vulcanizing. He thought he had never understood her in his life, and that he understood her now; and in both of these opinions he was, very probably, mistaken. But it was a comfortable thing to think, at the end of such an evening, and he went back to the Morris chair and unfolded his paper and read the same paragraph about the tariff four times over, while across the room his wife took up her embroidery again and set, at last, a few small and careful stitches, as if there were all the time in the world.

Of all the conditions to which the human male is liable, none is more difficult to carry off with dignity than the age of sixteen years and two months. At sixteen and two months a boy has put away childish things, and has not yet found anything to put in their place except a manner, and the manner is apt to slip. It slips at the dinner table, it slips upon stairways, it slips most fatally in the presence of relatives, who remember everything and forgive nothing. Thus it was with a sensation not far removed from dread that Mr. Wilbur Dennison Speer learned, upon a warm Saturday in June, that his cousin Eugenia Hollister was coming from Cincinnati to spend a fortnight in the house.

"Eugenia?" he said, setting down his fork with the air of a man who has been informed of a death in the family, though not, perhaps, of a near one. "You mean the one that bit me?"

"Wilbur!" said his mother. "That was seven years ago. You were both children."

"I was not a child," said Wilbur. "I was nine. And she drew blood. I got the mark yet." He extended his left wrist across the tablecloth, but his mother declined to examine it, and his father, who was reading the produce quotations folded beside his plate, merely said "Hm," in a tone that conveyed nothing except that a man has a right to his breakfast.

"She was a dear little thing," Mrs. Speer went on placidly, "and I expect she's grown into a lovely girl. Aunt Clara writes that she's very much admired. You'll be nice to her, Wilbur. You'll take her about and show her things."

"What things?" Wilbur asked, with genuine bewilderment; for it seemed to him that there was nothing in the town worth showing to anybody, and especially not to a person from Cincinnati, which he understood to be a place of great size and corruption.

"Why, the new library, and the park, and—and there's the band concert Thursday evening. And you might take her canoeing on the river."

Wilbur gave a short laugh, of the kind he had lately been practising, and which he believed to be bitter. "Canoeing," he said. "With Eugenia."

"I'm sure I don't see why not."

He did not explain. It was not a thing that could be explained to a mother. He folded his napkin with elaborate care, as one who must leave the table on business of the gravest character, and went out upon the side porch, where he sat down upon the railing and gazed at the lilac bushes with an expression that would have suited a deposed monarch looking upon the scene of his former splendours. His dog, a person of mixed ancestry named Duke, came and leaned against his leg, and was ignored.

The truth was that Wilbur's recollections of his cousin were not all of them recollections of the wrist. There had been a summer, the summer of the bite, when the Hollisters had stayed a month at old Grandfather Dennison's big house on Meridian Street, and Wilbur had been sent over every day to play. He remembered a tall, square, brick house with a cupola on top and an iron deer upon the lawn; he remembered a grape arbour at the back, and a cistern with a wooden lid that they had been forbidden to lift and had lifted daily; and he remembered a thin, freckled, fierce little girl with two braids the colour of a new penny, who could climb higher in the walnut tree than he could, and said so, and who had once made him eat a dandelion to prove that he was not afraid of being poisoned. He had eaten it. He had then waited, for the greater part of an afternoon, to die, and Eugenia had sat beside him in the grape arbour, very solemn, holding his hand and promising to put flowers on his grave every Sunday. He had been, if he were honest, slightly disappointed when he did not die.

These were not memories a man of sixteen and two months could take pride in. He had since then become acquainted with the world; he had smoked a cigarette, though not all of it; he had a pair of white flannel trousers and a straw hat with a striped band; he had written, though not sent, a letter of eleven pages to Miss Mae Belle Purcell, in which the word "soul" occurred fourteen times. And it was intolerable that his cousin should arrive, as she undoubtedly would, with the dandelion fresh in her mind.

He resolved, therefore, to be distant. He would be courteous, as befitted a host; he would be grave, even a little weary; he would allow it to be gathered that he had passed through experiences which had aged him beyond his years, and of which it was better not to speak. He spent the remainder of the morning before the mirror in his bedroom, practising an expression suitable to these purposes, and arrived at one which consisted chiefly in lowering the eyelids and drawing down the corners of the mouth. Seen by his small sister Ethel, who happened to pass the door, it caused her to inquire whether he had a stomach-ache, and the question was answered in a manner that brought Mrs. Speer up the stairs.

Eugenia arrived upon the four-fifteen.

Wilbur had been sent to meet her, and he went, wearing the white flannels and the straw hat, and carrying a light cane which belonged to his father and had not been asked for. He stood upon the station platform with the cane under his arm, in a posture he had observed in an illustration of an English gentleman awaiting a train at a country halt, and he did not look at the approaching locomotive at all, but at a point somewhat above the roof of the freight shed, as if the arrival of trains were a matter long since beneath his notice. In consequence he did not see his cousin descend, and was first made aware of her by a voice at his elbow.

"Why, it's Wilbur! Aren't you Wilbur? You must be. You've got the same ears."

He turned, and the cane fell from under his arm and rolled off the edge of the platform onto the track.

It is not easy to set down what Wilbur saw, because what he saw and what was there were, at that moment, two different things, and only the first concerns this history. What was there was a girl of sixteen, of moderate height, in a blue travelling suit and a hat with a good deal of white about it, who had a few freckles still, though not so many as formerly, and whose hair, done up now and not in braids, was rather more the colour of an old penny than a new one. What Wilbur saw was something considerably more radiant, against which the station, the freight shed, the baggage truck, and the agent, Mr. Foltz, who was spitting meditatively upon the rails, all faded into a kind of golden haze.

"Your cane," said Eugenia, looking down at the track.

"It's—it don't matter," said Wilbur. "I mean, it doesn't matter. It's an old one."

"But you'll want it, won't you?"

"Oh, I have dozens," said Wilbur, and lowered his eyelids and drew down the corners of his mouth.

She looked at him with interest. "Have you got a toothache?"

"No," said Wilbur, recovering his features hastily. "No, I—the sun's in my eyes." And he climbed down after the cane, while Mr. Foltz observed that the five-ten freight was liable to be along most any time and he wouldn't fool around down there if he was some folks. Wilbur came up again with a streak of cinders across the knee of the white flannels, and a sense that the afternoon had not begun according to the plan.

They walked home, a boy carrying her bag, for the Speers lived but four squares from the station; and Wilbur, labouring to restore his position, spoke of the weather in a deep voice, and of the town as one who has outgrown it.

"It's a pretty dead place," he said. "Nothing much ever happens here. I expect you'll find it pretty slow, after Cincinnati."

"Oh, I don't know," said Eugenia. "I like it. I always remembered it. Is Grandfather's house still there? The one with the deer?"

Wilbur hesitated. "No," he said. "They tore it down. Two years ago, after Aunt Mattie sold it. There's flats there now. The Dennison Arms, they call it."

She stopped on the sidewalk. "Not the grape arbour too?"

"Well, they had to," said Wilbur. "They put the flats right over it. And the walnut tree. They cut that down the first thing."

Eugenia said nothing for a moment, and then, "Oh," in a small voice; and they went on. Wilbur, glancing sideways, saw with consternation that she was looking straight ahead and blinking, and he was seized with a powerful and novel desire to have the Dennison Arms immediately destroyed, together with its builder, its owners, its tenants, and the City Council which had permitted it. He did not say so. What he said, after some thought, was, "The deer's still there. They moved it. Old man Schwab bought it. He's got it in his side yard over on Pennsylvania Street."

"Has he?" said Eugenia, turning toward him. "Truly?"

"I'll show you," said Wilbur, and for an instant forgot entirely to be distant.

He remembered it again at supper, however, and was distant all through the cold ham and the potato salad, and all through the strawberry shortcake, though this last was a great trial to him. His father, who had looked up from his plate long enough to say that Eugenia had grown a good deal, and to ask after her father's lumber business, relapsed afterward into silence; but Mrs. Speer talked for everybody, and Ethel, who was eleven, stared at the visitor with frank and unwinking admiration, and asked her whether all the girls in Cincinnati wore their hair like that, and whether she had a beau.

"Ethel!" said Mrs. Speer.

"Well, I only asked," said Ethel. "Wilbur's got one. I mean, he's got a girl. Mae Belle Purcell. He wrote her a letter and it's in his bureau drawer under the—"

The rest was lost in the confusion of Wilbur's chair being pushed back, and of Mrs. Speer saying "Children!" in the voice she used for emergencies; and when order had been restored, Wilbur was very red, and Ethel was very injured, and Eugenia was looking at her shortcake with a gravity so profound and so sustained that it could not possibly have been natural.

After supper the cousins sat upon the front steps, the elder Speers having withdrawn to the porch swing at the far end, where Mr. Speer could read the evening paper by the last of the daylight and Mrs. Speer could keep an eye on things without appearing to. It was the hour when the sprinklers go round on all the lawns of a Middle Western town in June, and the smell of wet grass rises up, and somewhere a screen door slams, and somewhere a piano is being practised upon, rather badly, and a mother calls a boy in, and the boy does not come. The sky over the Methodist church had turned the colour of a peach, and the first lightning bugs were blinking down along the hedge.

Wilbur, who had been silent for some minutes, cleared his throat. "I expect," he said, in the deep voice, "you've been going around a good deal. In society, I mean."

"Oh, some," said Eugenia.

"Dances and all that."

"Some."

"I don't go in for that much any more," said Wilbur. "I used to. I guess a person gets tired of it." He let a pause fall, heavy with meaning. "A person's interests change," he said.

"What are your interests now, Wilbur?"

He had not expected to be asked, and he looked at the lightning bugs. "Oh—things," he said. "Life, and that. Thinking about things."

"Mae Belle Purcell?" said Eugenia.

He turned upon her, and found that she was not laughing—or, at least, that she was not laughing with her mouth; but there was something at the corners of her eyes which he recognized. He had seen it in a grape arbour, seven years before, just after he had eaten the dandelion; and he had then been too young to know what it meant, but he knew now. It was the look of a person who is very sorry for you and enjoying herself enormously at the same time.

"That's all over," he said with dignity. "That was a long time ago."

"How long?"

"Since—well, since about Wednesday," said Wilbur, and then, to his own great surprise, he laughed, not the bitter laugh but quite another kind, and Eugenia laughed too, so that Mrs. Speer, at the end of the porch, looked up and smiled and nudged her husband, who said "Hm," and turned to the editorial page.

"Wilbur," said Eugenia, when they had finished, "do you remember the dandelion?"

"I knew you would," said Wilbur. "I knew it the minute I heard you were coming. I said to myself, 'She'll bring up that dandelion.'"

"I didn't mean to be horrid," she said. "Truly, I didn't. I've thought about it lots of times. You were so brave. You just sat there and waited to die, and you never cried at all, and you gave me your agate shooter to remember you by. I've got it yet."

"You have not."

"I have so. It's in my handkerchief box at home. I'll show it to you when you come to visit."

Wilbur looked at her a long moment in the dusk, and was silent, because there was nothing in the whole of his experience of life, wide as he had lately believed it to be, that had prepared him for the information that a girl from Cincinnati had kept his agate shooter for seven years in a handkerchief box.

"I've still got the mark where you bit me," he said at last, because something had to be said.

"Let me see."

Then he went in to explain about the cane.

Upon a certain sultry evening in August, at about the hour when the shadows of the maples along Sycamore Street had grown long enough to reach across the brick sidewalks and lay themselves, with a kind of tired benevolence, upon the lawns opposite, Willis Pettibone, aged ten years and some months, sat upon the bottom step of the back porch of his father's house and contemplated the grievous instability of human affairs.

It is a truth not sufficiently recognized by those who write books upon the training of the young that a boy of ten possesses, in a degree unknown to his elders, the faculty of foreseeing calamity. He may not foresee it far in advance; indeed, he commonly foresees it only after the event that will produce it is irrevocably accomplished; but within these limits his prophetic powers are terrible and exact. Willis did not know precisely what was going to happen to him. He knew only that something was, and that it would happen soon, and that it would be connected in some manner with his father, with an old-clothes man named Mr. Kupfer, and with forty cents, of which twenty-two remained in his pocket and eighteen had passed, by way of Schlotzhauer's Confectionery, into the interior of himself and Clifford Mapes.

The house behind him was quiet, but it was not the quiet of peace. It was the quiet that precedes a summons. Some twenty minutes earlier Mr. Pettibone had come home, not by way of the front walk, which was his habit, but by way of the alley, which was not; and he had come through the back gate with a large bundle under his arm and an expression upon his face that Willis, peering from behind the rain barrel, had recognized at once as belonging to the category of expressions upon which it is not well to intrude. Mr. Pettibone had passed within six feet of the rain barrel without looking at it, which was in itself ominous, and had gone into the house, where he could be heard addressing Mrs. Pettibone in a voice of singular restraint. Then a door had closed, and the voices had become a murmur, and the murmur had become, from time to time, an exclamation in a feminine register, followed by what sounded remarkably like a laugh, instantly suppressed.

This laugh troubled Willis more than anything else. A father's anger he understood; it was a natural phenomenon, like the weather, and could be endured. But a laugh, suppressed, from his mother, at such a time, suggested that the matter had taken on some new and unforeseeable dimension, and that he was to be confronted not merely with justice but with irony, a thing he dreaded above all punishments, as boys do, because it cannot be cried at.

Jupe, the Pettibones' dog, a person of mingled ancestry and unmingled devotion, came and sat beside him on the step, and leaned against him, and looked up into his face with the anxious sympathy of one who has himself been summoned to judgment, on matters of slippers and of the Wilkinsons' chickens, more often than he could remember. Willis placed an arm about him.

"Well, I don't care," Willis said, addressing Jupe in a low voice. "How'd I know? It was all up in the attic. Things that are up in the attic, nobody wants 'em. That's why they're up in the attic."

Jupe, who held no opinion on the attic, wagged his tail feebly in agreement.

"Anyways," Willis went on, his voice growing firmer as he heard the strength of his own case, "it was Clifford thought of it. I wouldn't of thought of it. I never would of thought of it in a hundred years."

He paused, and a certain honesty, which was one of the more inconvenient features of his character, compelled him to add, "Well, I would of thought of it, maybe. But he thought of it first."

The back door opened. It opened slowly, and Willis, without turning his head, knew from the very sound of the hinge that it was opened by his mother, and that she had been sent.

"Willis," said Mrs. Pettibone.

He did not answer. There is a period, in such crises, during which a boy will pretend not to have heard, though he knows perfectly that the pretense deceives nobody; it is a kind of ceremonial delay, like the reading of the indictment, and he would feel himself defrauded without it.

"Willis," said his mother again. "Your father wants to see you in the library."

"What for?" said Willis.

"I think you know what for."

"I don't either," said Willis. "I don't know what for. I haven't done anything. I been right here the whole time."

"Willis," said Mrs. Pettibone, and there was in her voice a quality which he could not identify, but which seemed to him, even in his extremity, oddly unsteady, "your father has been to some trouble this afternoon on your account. I think you had better come in and not make it any worse."

Willis rose. He rose with the air of one who is innocent, but who is willing, out of mere generosity of spirit, to humor the eccentricities of others. Jupe rose with him, and the two of them crossed the porch together; but at the door Mrs. Pettibone gently excluded the dog, who sat down outside with an expression of the deepest foreboding and remained there.

The Pettibone library was a room so called because it contained a bookcase, a globe, a steel engraving of Daniel Webster, and a leather chair in which Mr. Pettibone was accustomed to read the evening paper and sometimes, toward nine o'clock, to fall into a doze from which he would afterward deny having fallen. In this chair Mr. Pettibone was now seated, but he was not reading the paper. Upon the table at his elbow lay the bundle Willis had seen him carry through the gate; and from one end of it there protruded, unmistakably, a portion of a fur collar.

Willis looked at the collar, and then at the steel engraving of Daniel Webster, and then at the carpet, which had a pattern of red and brown scrolls, and which he began to study with absorbing interest.

"Close the door, Willis," said Mr. Pettibone.

Willis closed the door. His mother had remained on the other side of it, and he was sorry, for though she was not to be relied upon as an ally, she was at least a witness, and the presence of a witness had been known to moderate the severity of sentences.

"Come here," said Mr. Pettibone.

Willis came a little way. He came to a point about halfway between the door and the chair, where the scrolls in the carpet formed a particularly interesting knot, and there he stopped, and examined the knot.

Mr. Pettibone regarded him for some moments in silence. He was a man of forty-four, of moderate stature and a moderate mustache, who dealt in fire insurance and was a deacon of the Second Presbyterian Church and a past officer of the Royal Order of Moose; and he was, in most of the relations of life, a reasonable man and a mild one. But he had passed that afternoon through an experience which no reasonable man is ever wholly prepared for, and he was resolved that his son should understand the full nature of it.

"Willis," he said at last, "do you know where I was at half-past four o'clock this afternoon?"

"No, sir," said Willis.

"I was at the corner of Washington Street and Fourth," said Mr. Pettibone, "waiting for the streetcar. I was standing there with Mr. Hendricks, of the Second National Bank, and with Mr. and Mrs. Theodore Coffin, and with a number of other persons, whose names I need not trouble you with, but who know me, and know my appearance, and who are, in general, observant. And do you know what came down Washington Street, while I was standing there, in plain view of all these persons?"

Willis did not answer. He knew. He had known, in a general and prophetic way, since the moment his father came through the back gate; but he had not until this instant pictured the scene with any particularity, and now that it presented itself to his imagination it seemed to him so dreadful, and at the same time so entirely glorious, that he was obliged to clench every muscle of his face to keep it from betraying him.

"I will tell you," said Mr. Pettibone. "There came down Washington Street a wagon drawn by a horse, which I should judge to be approximately thirty years of age; and upon the seat of that wagon, in the heat of a day which the Weather Bureau has since informed the evening paper was the hottest of the summer, there sat a man. And that man, Willis, was wearing an overcoat."

He paused. The silence in the library became so profound that the ticking of the clock upon the mantel seemed to grow louder, as if it, too, were waiting.

"It was a black overcoat," Mr. Pettibone went on, in a voice that was very quiet and very distinct, "of a quality somewhat superior to anything commonly seen upon the seat of a junk wagon. It had a collar of sealskin. And it had, upon the lining of the inside pocket, which the man had turned out, in order, I suppose, to display it to the populace, my name, Willis. My name, embroidered in silk, by your Aunt Hattie, at Christmas, three years ago."

Willis made a sound. It was a small sound, of no very definite character, and he converted it immediately into a cough.

"The man," continued Mr. Pettibone, "recognized me. I do not know how. I had never seen him before in my life. But he recognized me, and he stopped his horse, and he called out to me, in a voice that could have been heard, I believe, in the courthouse, 'Hey, Mister Pettibone! How you like it? Fits me pretty good, hah?' And Mr. Hendricks, of the Second National Bank, asked me whether I had gone into a new line of business; and Mrs. Theodore Coffin laughed until she had to sit down on the steps of the Odd Fellows' Building."

Here a curious thing happened. From the other side of the closed door there came a sound that Willis could have sworn was a smothered exclamation, followed by footsteps retreating hastily in the direction of the kitchen. Mr. Pettibone's mustache moved slightly; whether in anger or in some other emotion it was impossible to say. He cleared his throat.

"I was obliged," he said, "to purchase my own overcoat back from that man, on the public street, in the presence of witnesses, for the sum of three dollars and a half. He said he had paid a high price for it, and that it had sentimental associations for him. Now, Willis, I want you to tell me, in your own words, how that man came to be in possession of my overcoat."

It is at this point, in all such interviews, that the accused is invited to make his defense; and it is also at this point that he discovers, invariably, that his defense, which seemed so strong upon the back step, has somehow shrunk and dwindled in the interval, and become a poor, thin, unconvincing thing that he is ashamed to bring out into the light. Nevertheless, Willis brought it out. He had nothing else.

"Well," he said, "it was up in the attic."

"It was in the cedar chest in the attic," said Mr. Pettibone. "Where it is kept every summer. Where it has been kept every summer since you were born."

"Well, how'd I know?" said Willis. "Nobody told me. I thought it was just old things up there. I thought everything up there was just old things nobody wanted. Mr. Kupfer, he came down the alley yelling 'Rags, old iron,' and Clifford said—"

He stopped. Even in his extremity a certain code forbade him to proceed further along that line.

"Clifford said what?" said Mr. Pettibone.

"Nothing," said Willis.

"Clifford Mapes said something. What did Clifford Mapes say?"

"Well," said Willis, unhappily, "he said his mother sold Mr. Kupfer a whole bunch of things out of their attic last week, and got a dollar and ten cents, and he said we could get money for things out of our attic, too, and buy the seven-shot air rifle at Gruber's Hardware, and go halves on it. And so we went up there, and there was just this old coat with mothballs on it, and some old shoes, and a lamp that's busted. And Mr. Kupfer, he wouldn't take the lamp."

"I see," said Mr. Pettibone. "And how much did Mr. Kupfer give you for my overcoat?"

Willis hesitated. "Forty cents," he said, in a low voice.

Mr. Pettibone closed his eyes. He kept them closed for some little time, and when he opened them he looked not at his son but at the steel engraving of Daniel Webster, as though seeking from that great orator some assistance in a situation for which his own eloquence was insufficient.

"Forty cents," he repeated. "Willis, that overcoat cost me forty-five dollars."

The figure struck Willis with something like awe. It was a sum so enormous that it passed entirely out of the realm of money as he understood it and entered the realm of astronomy, where numbers are merely large and have no practical application. He could not feel guilty about forty-five dollars; it was too big; one might as well feel guilty about the distance to the moon. But he could feel, and did feel, a slow and sinking certainty that the seven-shot air rifle at Gruber's Hardware had receded into a future so remote as to be practically indistinguishable from never.

"Where is the forty cents?" said Mr. Pettibone.

Willis put his hand into his pocket and brought out its contents, which consisted of two dimes, two pennies, a marble of the variety known as a "glassie," a piece of string, a broken watch-key, and a substance which may once have been licorice. He separated the coins from the rest with great care and held them out.

"There's only twenty-two cents," said Mr. Pettibone.

"Yes, sir."

"What became of the other eighteen?"

Willis studied the carpet. "Schlotzhauer's," he said.

Mr. Pettibone took the coins and laid them on the table beside the overcoat. Then he leaned back in his chair and folded his hands across his waistcoat, and assumed that expression which, in fathers, signifies that the facts of the case having been established, the moral is now to be drawn.

"Willis," he said, "I want you to understand something. I am not going to whip you."

Willis looked up, startled. It was the first thing that had been said in the interview that he had not foreseen, and it disconcerted him exceedingly, for he had already composed his spirit for a whipping and had even taken a certain dark comfort in the prospect, as being definite, and soon over, and something that could afterward be described to Clifford Mapes in terms that would do him credit.

"I am not going to whip you," Mr. Pettibone repeated, "because I do not believe that you intended to do wrong. I believe you are simply a boy who does not think. And I want you to think now. I want you to think about what it means to take something that does not belong to you, even when you suppose it to be of no value, and to sell it, without asking. Do you understand what I am saying?"

"Yes, sir," said Willis. He did not, in fact, understand it in the least, but he recognized the tone as one that required this answer, and he had been long enough in the world to know that the answer was not truly a statement of fact, but a kind of response in a liturgy.

"Suppose," said Mr. Pettibone, warming to his argument, "suppose I were to go up to your room and take your—" he searched his memory for some object of value in his son's possession— "your baseball glove, and sell it to Mr. Kupfer for forty cents. How would you feel?"

Willis considered this seriously. It was the first part of the lecture that had touched upon anything real, and he gave it his whole attention.

"Mr. Kupfer wouldn't give you forty cents for it," he said at last. "It's got a hole in it. You'd be lucky to get a nickel."

Mr. Pettibone's mustache moved again, more violently this time. He coughed into his hand and was some moments recovering.

"That," he said, with some severity, "is not the point."

"No, sir," said Willis.

"The point is that you would not like it. And the point is that you must not take other people's things. And in order that you may remember the point, Willis, you are to remain in this house, and in this yard, for the rest of the week. You are not to go over to Clifford Mapes's, and Clifford Mapes is not to come over here. And on Saturday, when the Hagenbeck and Wallace Circus comes to town, you will not go to it."

The words fell upon Willis like the stroke of doom. For a moment he could not breathe. The circus! The circus, which had been the light and object of his existence since the first lithographs of it had appeared, three weeks before, upon the side of Gruber's warehouse; the circus with its four elephants and its Royal Bengal tiger and its lady who was shot from a cannon, twice daily, rain or shine; the circus that he and Clifford had planned, down to the last detail and the last peanut, through long afternoons in the hayloft! A vision rose before him of Saturday afternoon: the whole town gone to the fairgrounds, the streets empty, the very dogs departed, and himself alone in the back yard, a solitary and forsaken figure, staring at the distant tents across the rooftops while the faint music of the calliope drifted to him on the wind.

He saw, further, that he would very probably sicken and die in consequence of this deprivation, perhaps within the week; and he saw the scene at his bedside, his father bowed with remorse, his mother weeping, the doctor shaking his head and saying, "If only he had been allowed to go to the circus, I might have saved him." These visions were so affecting that his eyes filled, and his chin began to tremble, and he turned his face away so that his father should not have the satisfaction of witnessing his grief.

"You may go now," said Mr. Pettibone.

Willis went. He went slowly, and with dignity, and he closed the door behind him with a gentleness that was meant to be more reproachful than any slam. He passed through the hall, and through the kitchen, where his mother stood at the stove with her back to him and her shoulders shaking in a manner he did not stop to investigate, and out the back door onto the porch.

Jupe rose to meet him, his whole body expressing sympathy and inquiry. Willis sat down heavily upon the step and laid his cheek against the dog's head.

"I'm not goin' to the circus," he said brokenly. "I'm never goin' to anything ever again."

Jupe licked his ear.

They sat thus for some time, in the deepening dusk, a picture of desolation complete enough to have melted any heart but a father's. The katydids began their argument in the maples. Down the street someone was playing a phonograph, and the faint, tinny strains of "In the Good Old Summertime" came floating over the fences in mockery of all his woe.

Over the top of the back fence there appeared, by slow degrees, a cap, a shock of tow-colored hair, and the round, freckled, and somewhat apprehensive face of Clifford Mapes.

"Hey, Willis," said Clifford, in a hoarse whisper. "Did you get it?"

"I got it," said Willis, in a voice of tragic depth. "I can't go to the circus."

Clifford absorbed this in silence. Then his face, by a gradual process, assumed an expression of the deepest gloom, which was succeeded, after a moment, by a look of dawning and unholy interest.

"Hey, Willis," he whispered, "listen. Mr. Kupfer was by our place again just now. He says he's got a lady's hat with a whole bird on it, a real one, stuffed, that he'll trade for anything. And he says your pa's coat was the best thing he got all summer, and you got any more like it, he'll give fifty cents."

Willis sat very still. Within him, the vision of his own funeral grew dim, and wavered, and dissolved, as such visions will, like mist upon a pond at morning. He thought of the bird. He thought, for some reason, of the bundle of his father's old Moose regalia, which lay, as he happened to know, in a pasteboard box beneath the eaves, behind the busted lamp.

Then, with an effort that did him honor, he shook his head.

"Can't," he said. "I got to stay in the yard all week."

"Well," said Clifford reasonably, "Mr. Kupfer comes down the alley. The alley's right next to the yard."

Willis looked at the alley. It lay there in the dusk, innocent and inviting, exactly one fence-board's width beyond the boundaries of his sentence.

From several letters from my mother, and one from Aunt Fanny, I hear you are seeing a good deal of the family since I left. I hope sometimes you think of the member who is absent. I got a silver frame for your photograph in New York, and I keep it on my desk. When I look at your photograph, I say to myself, “At last, at last here is one that will not prove shallow.” My faithful briar has gone out. I will have to rise and fill it, then once more in the fragrance of My Lady Nicotine, I will sit and dream the old dreams over, and think, too, of the true friend at home awaiting my return in June for the summer vacation. Friend, this is from your friend, G.A.M. George’s anticipations were not disappointed. But the Major, declining to hear him out, interrupted querulously, saying that he had enough to bother him without any advice from George; and retired to his library, going so far as to lock the door audibly.

“Second childhood!” George muttered, shaking his head; and he thought sadly that the Major had not long to live. However, this surmise depressed him for only a moment or so. Of course, people couldn’t be expected to live forever, and it would be a good thing to have someone in charge of the Estate who wouldn’t let it get to looking so rusty that riffraff dared to make fun of it. For George had lately undergone the annoyance of calling upon the Morgans, in the rather stuffy red velours and gilt parlour of their apartment at the hotel, one evening when Mr. Frederick Kinney also was a caller, and Mr. Kinney had not been tactful. In fact, though he adopted a humorous tone of voice, in expressing his sympathy for people who, through the city’s poverty in hotels, were obliged to stay at the Amberson, Mr. Kinney’s intention was interpreted by the other visitor as not at all humorous, but, on the contrary, personal and offensive. George rose abruptly, his face the colour of wrath. “Good-night, Miss Morgan. Good-night, Mr. Morgan,” he said. “I shall take pleasure in calling at some other time when a more courteous sort of people may be present.”

“Look here!” the hot-headed Fred burst out. “Don’t you try to make me out a boor, George Minafer! I wasn’t hinting anything at you; I simply forgot all about your grandfather owning this old building. Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor! I won’t—” But George walked out in the very course of this vehement protest, and it was necessarily left unfinished. Mr. Kinney remained only a few moments after George’s departure; and as the door closed upon him, the distressed Lucy turned to her father. She was plaintively surprised to find him in a condition of immoderate laughter.

“I didn’t—I didn’t think I could hold out!” he gasped, and, after choking until tears came to his eyes, felt blindly for the chair from which he had risen to wish Mr. Kinney an indistinct good-night. His hand found the arm of the chair; he collapsed feebly, and sat uttering incoherent sounds.

“Papa!”

“It brings things back so!” he managed to explain, “This very Fred Kinney’s father and young George’s father, Wilbur Minafer, used to do just such things when they were at that age—and, for that matter, so did George Amberson and I, and all the rest of us!” And, in spite of his exhaustion, he began to imitate: “Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor!” “I shall take pleasure in calling at some time when a more courteous sort of people—” He was unable to go on. There is a mirth for every age, and Lucy failed to comprehend her father’s, but tolerated it a little ruefully.

“Papa, I think they were shocking. Weren’t they awful!”

“Just—just boys!” he moaned, wiping his eyes. But Lucy could not smile at all; she was beginning to look indignant. “I can forgive that poor Fred Kinney,” she said. “He’s just blundering—but George—oh, George behaved outrageously!”

“It’s a difficult age,” her father observed, his calmness somewhat restored. “Girls don’t seem to have to pass through it quite as boys do, or their savoir faire is instinctive—or something!” And he gave away to a return of his convulsion. She came and sat upon the arm of his chair. “Papa, why should George behave like that?”

“He’s sensitive.”

“Rather! But why is he? He does anything he likes to, without any regard for what people think. Then why should he mind so furiously when the least little thing reflects upon him, or on anything or anybody connected with him?” Eugene patted her hand. “That’s one of the greatest puzzles of human vanity, dear; and I don’t pretend to know the answer. In all my life, the most arrogant people that I’ve known have been the most sensitive. The people who have done the most in contempt of other people’s opinion, and who consider themselves the highest above it, have been the most furious if it went against them. Arrogant and domineering people can’t stand the least, lightest, faintest breath of criticism. It just kills them.”

“Papa, do you think George is terribly arrogant and domineering?”

“Oh, he’s still only a boy,” said Eugene consolingly. “There’s plenty of fine stuff in him—can’t help but be, because he’s Isabel Amberson’s son.” Lucy stroked his hair, which was still almost as dark as her own. “You liked her pretty well once, I guess, papa.”

“I do still,” he said quietly.

“She’s lovely—lovely! Papa—” she paused, then continued—“I wonder sometimes—” “What?”

“I wonder just how she happened to marry Mr. Minafer.”

“Oh, Minafer’s all right,” said Eugene. “He’s a quiet sort of man, but he’s a good man and a kind man. He always was, and those things count.”

“But in a way—well, I’ve heard people say there wasn’t anything to him at all except business and saving money. Miss Fanny Minafer herself told me that everything George and his mother have of their own—that is, just to spend as they like—she says it has always come from Major Amberson.”

“Thrift, Horatio!” said Eugene lightly. “Thrift’s an inheritance, and a common enough one here. The people who settled the country had to save, so making and saving were taught as virtues, and the people, to the third generation, haven’t found out that making and saving are only means to an end. Minafer doesn’t believe in money being spent. He believes God made it to be invested and saved.”

“But George isn’t saving. He’s reckless, and even if he is arrogant and conceited and bad-tempered, he’s awfully generous.”

“Oh, he’s an Amberson,” said her father. “The Ambersons aren’t saving. They’re too much the other way, most of them.”

“I don’t think I should have called George bad-tempered,” Lucy said thoughtfully. “No. I don’t think he is.”

“Only when he’s cross about something?” Morgan suggested, with a semblance of sympathetic gravity.

“Yes,” she said brightly, not perceiving that his intention was humorous. “All the rest of the time he’s really very amiable. Of course, he’s much more a perfect child, the whole time, than he realizes! He certainly behaved awfully to-night.” She jumped up, her indignation returning. “He did, indeed, and it won’t do to encourage him in it. I think he’ll find me pretty cool—for a week or so!” Whereupon her father suffered a renewal of his attack of uproarious laughter.
