It was after eleven when the Gaineses came home from Mrs. Lamborn's card party, and they came home in a silence so complete that the hired man, who had sat up to put away the horse, afterward told the cook he guessed somebody must have died. Nobody had died. Mrs. Gaines had won the second prize, a hand-painted cracker jar, and carried it upon her lap the whole way home with the rigid care of one transporting the ashes of an ancestor. Mr. Gaines drove. Twice he remarked that the roads were dusty for October, and twice he received no answer; whereupon he began to whistle under his breath, a tuneless little hiss of a whistle, until his wife said, "Walter, please!" in a voice that ended the music for the evening.

There is a kind of silence, well known to husbands, that is not an absence of speech at all but a postponement of it. A man may sit beside it for twenty minutes, perceiving it as plainly as he perceives the rump of the horse before him, and he will spend the time, as Walter Gaines spent it, reviewing his recent conduct in the hope of discovering what he has done. Mr. Gaines reviewed. He had not trumped his partner's ace; that had been Mr. Clement Hollis, who always did. He had not told the story about the Irishman and the mule, though he had been tempted. He had taken only one helping of the chicken salad, and that a moderate one, and he had said nothing at all about the tariff. Yet the silence sat there, cool and patient, and he knew that it would keep.

The house, when they reached it, was dark except for the gas in the hall, turned low, and the small red eye of the base-burner glowing through its mica in the sitting room. Mrs. Gaines went upstairs at once without taking off her hat. Mr. Gaines lingered below. He turned out the hall gas, turned it on again because he could not find the newel post, turned it out a second time, and then stood for some moments in the dark, considering the clock on the mantel. It was a black marble clock in the shape of a small Greek temple, a wedding present from his wife's aunt, and he had wound it every night for twenty-two years with a gravity that suggested he believed the turning of the earth to depend upon it. He wound it now, slowly, counting the turns. Then he went up.

His wife was seated before her dressing table, taking down her hair. She did this with an air of having been waiting some time, though she had been in the room scarcely five minutes, and she did not look round when he entered. He saw her face in the glass, and it was the face of a woman who has made up her mind to be very calm.

"Well," he said cheerfully, unbuttoning his waistcoat, "I thought it was a right pleasant evening, didn't you? Mrs. Lamborn certainly sets a good table."

"Yes," said Mrs. Gaines. "She does."

"That cracker jar's mighty pretty, too. You'll want to put it on the sideboard, I expect."

"I expect I shall."

He hung his coat over a chair, thought better of it, and took it to the wardrobe, where he spent an unusual time arranging it upon a hanger. When he turned, she had set down her brush and was looking at him in the glass, and he discovered that he had nowhere further to go.

"Walter," she said, "Mrs. Lamborn told me something to-night."

"Did she?" said Mr. Gaines. "Well, she generally does. That woman could talk the ears off a—"

"She told me," his wife went on, exactly as if he had not spoken, "that the Judge saw you at the Merchants' National on Tuesday, in Mr. Bassett's office, with the door shut. She said she supposed you were arranging about Florence's tuition. She said it in front of Mrs. Hollis and Mrs. Doctor Stroud, and I said, 'Yes, I suppose he was,' and I smiled. I smiled, Walter. I didn't know what else to do."

Mr. Gaines sat down upon the edge of the bed and began to unlace his shoes. It is a curious thing that a man in difficulty will nearly always find something to do with his hands, and that the thing he finds is nearly always beneath him. He untied one lace with great deliberation and drew it entirely out of the shoe, which he had never done before in his life.

"Well, I did go in to see Bassett," he admitted. "There's nothing so remarkable about a man going in to see his banker, Emmeline."

"There is when the man never goes in to see his banker except on the first of January, and then only to wish him a Happy New Year. There is when the door is shut. There is when his wife has to hear about it over Mrs. Lamborn's chicken salad." She turned round upon the bench now and faced him directly, and the hairpins in her lap slid to the floor with a little scattering sound, like the beginning of rain. "Walter, what were you seeing Mr. Bassett about?"

"Business," said Mr. Gaines.

"What business?"

"Just—business. A little matter. I don't know why you have to go worrying yourself about every little matter that comes up downtown."

"I am not worrying myself," said Mrs. Gaines. "I am asking you a question."

He drew the lace back into the shoe, missed an eyelet, and had to begin again. The clock in the hall below, which he had just wound, struck the half hour with a sound like a small silver hammer upon a bell, and both of them listened to it as though it might have something to contribute.

"Emmeline," he said at last, not looking up, "you remember that fellow Sackett?"

She did not answer at once. When she did, her voice had dropped, and he liked the low voice even less than the other.

"The one with the yellow gloves," she said. "The one who came to supper in August and talked about Mexico."

"Well, now, he didn't only talk about Mexico. He talked about a mighty sound proposition. You heard him yourself. Rubber, Emmeline. The whole world's crying out for rubber—bicycle tires, automobile tires, hose, every kind of thing. And here's a plantation down there in Tabasco, seven thousand acres, trees already planted and coming along, and the land bought for next to nothing, and all it needed was a little capital to see it through till the first tapping. Why, he showed me the photographs. He showed me letters from men in Indianapolis that had gone into it—"

"How much?" said Mrs. Gaines.

"What?"

"How much, Walter?"

He set the shoe down upon the carpet beside its fellow, and arranged the two of them side by side, toes even, with the care of a man laying out a pair of pistols for a duel he had no wish to fight.

"Three thousand," he said.

There was a long pause. Mrs. Gaines did not cry out, and she did not rise. She sat perfectly still upon the bench, with the lamplight behind her making a sort of brown halo of her loosened hair, and he understood, as he had understood perhaps a dozen times in twenty-two years, that he would rather she had thrown the cracker jar.

"Three thousand," she repeated. "That's Florence's money."

"It's not exactly Florence's money—"

"It's the money we put by for Florence to go East. It's the money from my mother's lots on Pratt Street. It's the money you and I sat at that very table downstairs and figured over, four winters running, and said we wouldn't touch, not if the roof fell in. That's whose money it is."

"I know it, I know it." He spread his hands. "But don't you see, that's just why I did it? It was going to be six thousand, Emmeline. It was going to be nine, maybe, by the time she was ready. Sackett said the first dividend alone would be eighteen per cent, and then when the trees came into full bearing—why, she could have gone to Vassar and Europe both, and you could have gone with her. I meant it to be a surprise."

"It has been," said Mrs. Gaines.

He winced. He had never been a man of quick tongue, and he had always known that she was quicker; it was one of the things he had admired in her, long ago, when she was Emmeline Pruitt and sat in the choir at Second Presbyterian with a white rose in her hat, and every young man in the town had been a little afraid of her. He found now that he was still a little afraid of her, and that being afraid made him stubborn.

"Well, there's no use taking that tone," he said. "Things haven't gone just the way they were expected to, that's all. There's been some delay. Sackett wrote me there's been trouble down there with the government, some kind of a revolution or other—those Mexicans are always having a revolution—and the stockholders have got to wait a while. It doesn't mean the money's gone. It only means we've got to be patient."

"Have you heard from Mr. Sackett lately?"

Mr. Gaines rubbed his chin. "Not since the middle of September."

"Have you written him?"

"Three times."

"And?"

"The last one came back," said Mr. Gaines, with a dignity that was almost touching. "They said there wasn't any such person at that address."

His wife looked at him a moment longer; then she bent down and began to pick up the hairpins from the carpet, one by one, dropping them into a little china tray shaped like a swan. It took her a long while, for some of them had rolled under the bench and one had gone beneath the edge of the rug, and he watched her the whole time without speaking, feeling the minutes go by like the slow drip from an eave. When she had found the last of them she set the tray down and folded her hands upon her knee.

"And Mr. Bassett?" she said.

"I went to see if he'd carry a note for me. Just till spring. Just so as Florence could go in January the way we planned, and nobody need be the wiser."

"Will he?"

"He said he'd think it over." Mr. Gaines looked at the floor. "He said it in a kind of a way."

"I know the way," said Mrs. Gaines.

It may be set down here, for the benefit of the unmarried, that the most dangerous moment in such a conversation is not the moment of discovery but the moment after, when the injured party has learned the worst and has not yet decided what to feel about it. The air of the room grows thin. The furniture seems to listen. A husband in this interval would give a year of his life to know which way the wind will set, and he will very often, out of pure nervousness, say the one thing that settles it against him. Walter Gaines said it.

"I don't see that you need to look at me like that," he said. "It was my money as much as yours. I earned it, didn't I? I've stood behind that counter at Gaines and Whitcomb's for twenty-six years, selling stovepipe and carpet tacks to every farmer in the county, and I guess I've got a right to try and better myself once in a while without having to ask permission."

He knew at once that it was the wrong thing. He knew it by the faint lift of her chin, and by the colour that came into her cheeks, not suddenly but slowly, the way the sky colours before a storm out on the prairie.

"Permission!" she said. "Is that what you think I'd have made you do? Ask permission?" She stood up. She was not a tall woman, but she had a way of standing up that added several inches. "Walter Gaines, I have never in my life told you what you might or might not do with a dollar. Not once. When you bought that horse from the Ridley boy and it turned out to have the heaves, did I say one word? When you lent your cousin Asa two hundred dollars to start a chicken farm, and he went off to Oklahoma with the chickens, did I say one word?"

"You said a few," said Mr. Gaines.

"I said one, and it was 'Well!' That's all I said, and you know it." She took a step toward him. "It isn't the money. Can't you see that? I don't care so much about the money. Money goes; Mother always said so. It's that you sat across the table from me every night since August, and passed me the butter, and asked me how my day had been, and talked about the weather and the Democrats and whether the Hollises were going to paint their porch, and all that time you had this—this thing in your mind, and you never told me. You let me go on sewing name tapes into Florence's things. You let me write to Cousin Ada in Poughkeepsie about a room. You let me go to Mrs. Lamborn's to-night and smile like a fool in front of the whole town. Twenty-two years, Walter, and you didn't think I was fit to be told."

"It wasn't that." He had risen, too, in his stocking feet, and he found that he could not quite meet her eyes. "It wasn't that at all."

"Then what was it?"

He opened his mouth and closed it again. Below them, in the hall, the clock ticked with a kind of smug regularity, as if it alone in that house had nothing to reproach itself for. Outside a dog barked somewhere over on Locust Street, and another answered it, and then both were still.

"I guess," said Mr. Gaines slowly, "I guess I wanted to do something you'd think was smart."

She stared at him.

"You always were the smart one," he went on, looking at the bedpost, "ever since we were young. You were the one that figured the accounts, and you were the one that knew what to say to people, and you were the one the minister's wife always asked to head the committees. And I was just—well, I was Walter, that sold tacks. And I got to thinking, here I am fifty-one years old, and I never once in my life did a thing that'd make anybody say, 'Well, that Walter Gaines, he's got a head on him.' And then Sackett came along, and I thought, by George, here's my chance. I'll walk in some evening and lay a dividend check on the table in front of Emmeline, and I'll just say, 'There!' and that's all I'll say. Just 'There!' The way you said 'Well!'" He laughed, a short laugh without any amusement in it. "That was the whole of it. I didn't tell you because I wanted to see your face when it came out right. And then it didn't come out right, and after that I couldn't tell you, because I'd have had to see your face anyhow."

Mrs. Gaines did not answer. She stood quite still in the middle of the room, her hands at her sides, and the colour went slowly out of her cheeks again, and something else came into her face that he could not read. It was not forgiveness, precisely; it was more nearly a kind of bewilderment, as of one who has lived for years in a house and comes suddenly upon a door she had never noticed.

"You thought I didn't think you were smart," she said at last.

"Well—"

"Walter, I married you."

"I know it," he said humbly. "I never could understand that, either."

For a moment it seemed that she would laugh, and for a moment it seemed that she would cry, and in the end she did neither, but sat down again upon the bench before the dressing table, rather suddenly, as if her knees had decided the matter for her. She looked at her own reflection in the glass, and then at his, standing behind her in his shirt sleeves and his gray socks, with his hair on end where he had run his hand through it, and his face, in the lamplight, looking older than she had let herself see it look in a long while.

"You haven't been sleeping," she said. "I've heard you. I thought it was your stomach."

"It's been my stomach, too," said Mr. Gaines.

She picked up her brush again and drew it once or twice through her hair, absently, not looking at what she was doing. When she spoke, her voice had changed again, and he recognized it now with a rush of relief that was almost painful: it was the voice in which she ordered coal, and dealt with the paper hanger, and settled the yearly disputes of the Ladies' Aid.

"Florence will have to wait a year," she said. "That's all. It won't kill her. She's only seventeen, and she's a good deal too fond of that Pemberton boy to go East with any good grace this winter, anyhow. We'll tell people she's decided to stay home with us another year, and that will be true by the time we've told her. You'll go see Mr. Bassett to-morrow and tell him you've thought better of the note. And you'll write to Judge Lamborn's nephew, the one that practices law in St. Louis, and ask him to find out what he can about Mr. Sackett and his seven thousand acres, though I expect there's not one tree on them, nor ever was."

"I expect not," said Mr. Gaines.

"And Walter."

"Yes?"

"The next time you want to do something smart," said his wife, "you tell me first, and I'll tell you whether it is."

He came and stood behind her, and after a moment, a little awkwardly, as though it were a thing he had grown out of practice in, he put his hand upon her shoulder. She did not move away. She went on brushing her hair, a long slow stroke and then another, and in the glass he saw that her eyes were wet, though her mouth was firm and set as ever, and he was wise enough, for once, to say nothing about either.

"Come to bed," she said presently. "It's past midnight."

"In a minute," said Mr. Gaines. He went to the door and stood there in his stocking feet, listening. "I believe I forgot to wind the clock."

"You wound it," said Mrs. Gaines. "I heard you."

"Did I?" He looked back at her, puzzled, and then, all at once, rather sheepish. "Well," he said, "I guess I did."

But he went down anyway, in the dark, feeling his way along the banister; and she heard him at the mantel, and heard the small dry click of the key going round and meeting nothing, round and meeting nothing, as if he could not quite bring himself to believe that anything in the house was really wound up and safe until he had tried it with his own hand.

You know my theory of life because I explained it to you on our first drive together, when I told you I would not talk to everybody about things I feel like the way I spoke to you of my theory of life. I believe those who are able should have a true theory of life, and I developed my theory of life long, long ago. Well, here I sit smoking my faithful briar pipe, indulging in the fragrance of my tobacco as I look out on the campus from my many-paned window, and things are different with me from the way they were way back in Freshman year. I can see now how boyish in many ways I was then. I believe what has changed me as much as anything was my visit home at the time I met you. So I sit here with my faithful briar and dream the old dreams over as it were, dreaming of the waltzes we waltzed together and of that last night before we parted, and you told me the good news you were going to live there, and I would find my friend waiting for me, when I get home next summer. I will be glad my friend will be waiting for me. I am not capable of friendship except for the very few, and, looking back over my life, I remember there were times when I doubted if I could feel a great friendship for anybody—especially girls. I do not take a great interest in many people, as you know, for I find most of them shallow. Here in the old place I do not believe in being hail-fellow-well-met with every Tom, Dick, and Harry just because he happens to be a classmate, any more than I do at home, where I have always been careful who I was seen with, largely on account of the family, but also because my disposition ever since my boyhood has been to encourage real intimacy from but the few. My theory of literature is an author who does not indulge in trashiness—writes about people you could introduce into your own home. I agree with my Uncle Sydney, as I once heard him say he did not care to read a book or go to a play about people he would not care to meet at his own dinner table. I believe we should live by certain standards and ideals, as you know from my telling you my theory of life. Well, a letter is no place for deep discussions, so I will not go into the subject. From several letters from my mother, and one from Aunt Fanny, I hear you are seeing a good deal of the family since I left. I hope sometimes you think of the member who is absent. I got a silver frame for your photograph in New York, and I keep it on my desk. When I look at your photograph, I say to myself, “At last, at last here is one that will not prove shallow.” My faithful briar has gone out. Friend, this is from your friend, G.A.M. George’s anticipations were not disappointed. When he came home in June his friend was awaiting him; at least, she was so pleased to see him again that for a few minutes after their first encounter she was a little breathless, and a great deal glowing, and quiet withal. Their sentimental friendship continued, though sometimes he was irritated by her making it less sentimental than he did, and sometimes by what he called her “air of superiority.” Her air was usually, in truth, that of a fond but amused older sister; and George did not believe such an attitude was warranted by her eight months of seniority. But the Major, declining to hear him out, interrupted querulously, saying that he had enough to bother him without any advice from George; and retired to his library, going so far as to lock the door audibly.

“Second childhood!” George muttered, shaking his head; and he thought sadly that the Major had not long to live. However, this surmise depressed him for only a moment or so. Of course, people couldn’t be expected to live forever, and it would be a good thing to have someone in charge of the Estate who wouldn’t let it get to looking so rusty that riffraff dared to make fun of it. For George had lately undergone the annoyance of calling upon the Morgans, in the rather stuffy red velours and gilt parlour of their apartment at the hotel, one evening when Mr. Frederick Kinney also was a caller, and Mr. Kinney had not been tactful. In fact, though he adopted a humorous tone of voice, in expressing his sympathy for people who, through the city’s poverty in hotels, were obliged to stay at the Amberson, Mr. Kinney’s intention was interpreted by the other visitor as not at all humorous, but, on the contrary, personal and offensive. George rose abruptly, his face the colour of wrath. “Good-night, Miss Morgan. Good-night, Mr. Morgan,” he said. “I shall take pleasure in calling at some other time when a more courteous sort of people may be present.”

“Look here!” the hot-headed Fred burst out. “Don’t you try to make me out a boor, George Minafer! I wasn’t hinting anything at you; I simply forgot all about your grandfather owning this old building. Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor! I won’t—” But George walked out in the very course of this vehement protest, and it was necessarily left unfinished. Mr. Kinney remained only a few moments after George’s departure; and as the door closed upon him, the distressed Lucy turned to her father. She was plaintively surprised to find him in a condition of immoderate laughter.

“I didn’t—I didn’t think I could hold out!” he gasped, and, after choking until tears came to his eyes, felt blindly for the chair from which he had risen to wish Mr. Kinney an indistinct good-night. His hand found the arm of the chair; he collapsed feebly, and sat uttering incoherent sounds.

“Papa!”

“It brings things back so!” he managed to explain, “This very Fred Kinney’s father and young George’s father, Wilbur Minafer, used to do just such things when they were at that age—and, for that matter, so did George Amberson and I, and all the rest of us!” And, in spite of his exhaustion, he began to imitate: “Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor!” “I shall take pleasure in calling at some time when a more courteous sort of people—” He was unable to go on. There is a mirth for every age, and Lucy failed to comprehend her father’s, but tolerated it a little ruefully.

“Papa, I think they were shocking. Weren’t they awful!”

“Just—just boys!” he moaned, wiping his eyes. But Lucy could not smile at all; she was beginning to look indignant. “I can forgive that poor Fred Kinney,” she said. “He’s just blundering—but George—oh, George behaved outrageously!”

“It’s a difficult age,” her father observed, his calmness somewhat restored. “Girls don’t seem to have to pass through it quite as boys do, or their savoir faire is instinctive—or something!” And he gave away to a return of his convulsion. She came and sat upon the arm of his chair. “Papa, why should George behave like that?”

“He’s sensitive.”

“Rather! But why is he? He does anything he likes to, without any regard for what people think. Then why should he mind so furiously when the least little thing reflects upon him, or on anything or anybody connected with him?” Eugene patted her hand. “That’s one of the greatest puzzles of human vanity, dear; and I don’t pretend to know the answer. In all my life, the most arrogant people that I’ve known have been the most sensitive. The people who have done the most in contempt of other people’s opinion, and who consider themselves the highest above it, have been the most furious if it went against them. Arrogant and domineering people can’t stand the least, lightest, faintest breath of criticism. It just kills them.”

“Papa, do you think George is terribly arrogant and domineering?”

“Oh, he’s still only a boy,” said Eugene consolingly. “There’s plenty of fine stuff in him—can’t help but be, because he’s Isabel Amberson’s son.” Lucy stroked his hair, which was still almost as dark as her own. “You liked her pretty well once, I guess, papa.”

“I do still,” he said quietly.

“She’s lovely—lovely! Papa—” she paused, then continued—“I wonder sometimes—” “What?”

“I wonder just how she happened to marry Mr. Minafer.”

“Oh, Minafer’s all right,” said Eugene. “He’s a quiet sort of man, but he’s a good man and a kind man. He always was, and those things count.”

“But in a way—well, I’ve heard people say there wasn’t anything to him at all except business and saving money. Miss Fanny Minafer herself told me that everything George and his mother have of their own—that is, just to spend as they like—she says it has always come from Major Amberson.”

“Thrift, Horatio!” said Eugene lightly. “Thrift’s an inheritance, and a common enough one here. The people who settled the country had to save, so making and saving were taught as virtues, and the people, to the third generation, haven’t found out that making and saving are only means to an end. Minafer doesn’t believe in money being spent. He believes God made it to be invested and saved.”

“But George isn’t saving. He’s reckless, and even if he is arrogant and conceited and bad-tempered, he’s awfully generous.”

“Oh, he’s an Amberson,” said her father. “The Ambersons aren’t saving. They’re too much the other way, most of them.”

“I don’t think I should have called George bad-tempered,” Lucy said thoughtfully. “No. I don’t think he is.”

“Only when he’s cross about something?” Morgan suggested, with a semblance of sympathetic gravity.

“Yes,” she said brightly, not perceiving that his intention was humorous. “All the rest of the time he’s really very amiable. Of course, he’s much more a perfect child, the whole time, than he realizes! He certainly behaved awfully to-night.” She jumped up, her indignation returning. “He did, indeed, and it won’t do to encourage him in it. I think he’ll find me pretty cool—for a week or so!” Whereupon her father suffered a renewal of his attack of uproarious laughter.

Julian Tewksbury came home on the afternoon train from the East, having been eight years away, and he came home with a pointed brown beard, a soft black hat of a shape never before seen upon National Avenue, and a cane of some pale and knotted wood which he carried not as a support but as a kind of punctuation. He had been in Paris. He had studied there, at first under a master whose name meant a great deal in the Rue Notre-Dame-des-Champs and nothing whatever in the town of his birth, and afterward under no master at all, having arrived at the conclusion, somewhere in his fifth year, that masters were for the timid. He had sold two pictures. One of them hung in a café near the Luxembourg, in payment for a number of dinners; the other had been bought by an American lady from Ohio, who had mistaken it for something else and had been too polite to say so.

His mother met him at the station in the family surrey, and wept upon the beard, and said she supposed she would get used to it. She talked all the way up National Avenue, telling him who was dead and who had married and who had built where; and Julian, looking out from beneath the soft black hat, perceived that the town had grown both larger and uglier in his absence. There were new factories down by the river, sending up a smoke that lay over everything like a dingy shawl; there were rows of narrow frame houses, all alike, where there had been the Pettigrew pasture; and the old Mansfield place, which he remembered as a stately brick dwelling with a cupola, had become a boarding-house, with a sign in the window advertising "Table Board, Reasonable." He sighed, and his mother asked him if he was tired, and he said no, not tired; he was only thinking.

"Your cousin Ned's coming over after supper," she said. "He wanted to come to the train, but he couldn't get away from the store. He's doing just splendidly, Julian. His father's turned the whole business over to him, practically, and they've put in a plate-glass front, and they've got a young man now just to do nothing but keep the books. And you ought to see the baby! You never saw such a baby. Everybody says so."

"I'll be very glad to see Ned," said Julian; and he said it with the gentle, faintly melancholy kindness of a man who expects to find an old acquaintance much diminished.

For he remembered Ned. He remembered him perfectly. They had been born within three months of each other, in houses not two squares apart, and for eighteen years they had been, as their grandmother used to say, "as thick as thieves and twice as troublesome." Together they had run away to join a circus, getting as far as the Pennsylvania freight yards before supper-time recalled them; together they had smoked corn-silk behind the Methodist church, and been sick together, and lied together, without much skill, about the cause of it; together they had loved the same girl in the seventh grade, and together, when she preferred a boy named Orville Pease who owned a goat-cart, they had sworn off the sex forever. But all that was childhood, and Julian had long since put away childish things, including, he would have told you, most of the illusions under which the inhabitants of his native town continued to labour. Ned, he had no doubt, had remained. Ned had stayed at home and gone into his father's hardware store, and married—his mother had written him of it—a Miss Hattie Bolander, whom Julian remembered dimly as a plump little girl with a lisp and a great many hair-ribbons. It was all, he felt, very natural and very sad. He resolved to be kind to Ned.

He was the more resolved upon it because he suspected Ned would be shy of him. A man returning from the capital of the arts to a town of hardware and table board must expect a certain awkwardness in his old associates; they would feel the distance between them, poor fellows, and he must do what he could to bridge it without seeming to condescend. He thought about this a good deal during supper, and his mother, observing his abstraction, pressed upon him a second helping of chicken and a third of hot biscuit, which he accepted absently, and with more enjoyment than he would have cared to confess. They had nothing like those biscuits in the Rue Notre-Dame-des-Champs.

Ned arrived at about half-past seven, while the long June twilight was still lingering, and Julian, who had arranged himself upon the front porch in a wicker chair, with the knotted cane across his knees and an expression of tolerant reverie upon his face, heard him before he saw him. He heard a heavy, cheerful step on the brick walk, and a voice that called out, "Where is he? Where's the Frenchman?" and then Ned came up the porch steps two at a time, in a manner which caused the boards to complain, and seized him by both hands.

It must be admitted that Julian was somewhat taken aback. He had prepared himself for a Ned diminished; he was confronted with a Ned considerably enlarged. His cousin had grown stout—not fat, precisely, but solid and wide and ruddy, like a well-nourished young oak—and he wore a gray suit of an extremely new and confident cut, a straw hat with a striped band, and a gold watch-chain across a waistcoat which already displayed the first promise of what would one day be a fine, prosperous curve. He was beaming. He did not seem shy at all.

"Well, I'll be switched!" he said, holding Julian off at arm's length and examining him with frank delight. "Look at the whiskers on him! Julian, you look like the Czar of Russia—no, you don't, either—you look like that fellow on the cough-drop box! Doesn't he, Aunt Mary? Doesn't he look exactly like the fellow on the cough-drop box?"

Julian's mother, who had come to the screen door, said she didn't know but what he did, a little; and laughed in a way that Julian thought unnecessary.

"It is the fashion, among men of my profession, in Paris," Julian said, with dignity, and resumed his chair.

"Oh, I don't doubt it!" said Ned heartily, taking another, which creaked under him. "I don't doubt it a minute. I expect it's the very thing over there. I only meant it gives a fellow a start, first off. You went away with nothing on your face but a couple of pimples, and here you come back looking like an Old Master. Well, sir, it's good to see you, I tell you that. I don't care what you've got on your face." He produced a cigar case, much engraved, and offered it. "Have a smoke? These are pretty fair. I get 'em from a man in Cincinnati."

Julian declined, and drew from his pocket a small packet of French cigarettes, of a rank, black tobacco, one of which he lit with a slow and thoughtful gesture. He had found this tobacco intolerable for the first two years and had persevered in it ever since.

"Phew!" said Ned, sniffing. "What's that you're burning? Smells like the time the Odd Fellows' Hall caught fire."

"It is the tobacco of the people, in France," said Julian. "One acquires the taste."

"I'll bet one does!" said Ned, with admiration. "I'll bet it takes some acquiring, too."

There followed a pause, during which Julian considered how best to put his cousin at his ease. It was clear to him that Ned's noisy cordiality was the cover for an inner embarrassment—that the poor fellow, feeling the gulf between a hardware store and the ateliers of the Left Bank, was talking loudly in order not to feel it. He decided to lead the conversation, kindly, toward subjects within Ned's range.

"And how is business, Ned?" he asked, in the tone a gentle visitor might use to inquire after a cottager's pig.

"Business?" said Ned. "Business is fine! Never better. You heard about the plate-glass front? Well, that's only the beginning. I've been figuring, and I tell you, Julian, this town's going to be a city. It's going to be a big city. You see those factories down by the river? Five years ago there was just the one, the old Gilbert Wagon Works. Now there's seven, and two more coming, and every man that works in 'em has got to have a house, and every house has got to have nails and hinges and a cook-stove and a lawn-mower. You know what I sold last month? Forty-one lawn-mowers. Forty-one! When we were boys I don't suppose there were forty-one lawn-mowers in the county."

"I noticed the factories," said Julian, gazing with melancholy toward the river, where the smoke was turning a dull violet in the dusk. "I confess I thought them rather a pity. The town used to be beautiful in its way—quiet, I mean, and green. Now it seems to me to be losing its soul."

"Losing its what?"

"Its soul," Julian repeated, a little less firmly.

Ned considered this. He was not a man who rejected ideas merely because they were unfamiliar; he turned them over, like a customer examining a new kind of padlock, and gave them every fair chance. "Well," he said at last, "I don't know about that. Maybe it is. But I'll tell you one thing—it's getting its sidewalks. You remember how the mud used to be on Plum Street, every spring? You remember the time Orville Pease's goat got stuck in it up to the belly, and the whole fire company had to come and pull him out? Well, it's all paved now, clear out to the cemetery. I guess a town can do without a little soul if it gets pavements."

Julian smiled the smile of a man who has crossed the ocean and need not argue with those who have not. But at the mention of Orville Pease's goat, something odd happened to him: he felt a twitch at the corner of his mouth that was not at all the smile he intended, and he was obliged to draw rather hard upon the black cigarette to suppress it.

"And you're married, I hear," he said, recovering. "My mother wrote me. I remember Hattie Bolander—a little thing, wasn't she, with ribbons?"

At this a change came over Ned. His heartiness did not abate, but it took on a quality almost reverent, and he lowered his voice as men do in speaking of a cathedral or a bank president.

"She's—well, she's the finest woman in this town, Julian, and I don't care who hears me say so. She'd have come over with me to-night, only the baby's cutting a tooth, and she won't leave him with the girl. You'll come to supper Sunday, of course. She told me to make you promise. And you'll see the baby." He paused, and then added, with an air of making a confession that cost him something but which honesty required: "I don't want to brag on him. People that brag on their own babies are a nuisance; I always said so before I had one. But you'll see him, and you can judge for yourself."

"I shall be delighted," said Julian, a trifle coolly; for he perceived that Ned, so far from envying him, pitied him for having no baby; and this was not at all the direction in which he had meant the conversation to run.

He resolved to bring it back. He began, therefore, to speak of Paris—not boastfully, for he was too well-bred for that, but in a tone of quiet reminiscence which let fall, here and there, the names of streets and cafés and painters, as a rich man might let fall, here and there, the names of his estates. He spoke of the light on the Seine at evening; of long nights at a little table outside the Closerie des Lilas, where one argued until dawn about the true nature of beauty; of a friend of his, a Pole, who painted only in shades of green and had been expelled from three salons; of his own theory of art, which was that the painter must paint not what he saw but what he felt, and that most painters, having felt nothing, had better stop. He was conscious, as he talked, of speaking rather well. The twilight deepened; the lightning-bugs came out over the lawn; and Ned sat listening with his cigar gone cold in his fingers and an expression upon his broad face which Julian took, with satisfaction, for awe.

"And so," said Julian, concluding, "one comes back to a place like this, after all that, and one feels—I won't say superior—but one feels a certain loneliness. One has been so far, you understand. One has seen so much."

Ned was silent for a moment. Then he leaned forward and laid a large hand on his cousin's knee, and when he spoke his voice was full of a deep and simple sympathy.

"Julian," he said, "I've been listening to you, and I want to tell you something. I think it's just fine, what you've done—going over there and learning all that, and arguing all night about beauty and everything. I couldn't have done it. I haven't got the brains for it. But I've been sitting here thinking, and I'm afraid you've had it pretty hard."

"Hard?" said Julian, startled.

"Well, yes. Sitting up all night with a lot of foreigners, and nobody to cook for you, and that Polish fellow getting thrown out of places—and smoking that tobacco." Ned shook his head slowly. "It doesn't sound to me like you've had much of a home, old man. I expect it'll be a real rest to you, being back where folks know you."

There are moments in the life of every young man when he discovers that the person he has been condescending to has, all the while, been condescending to him; and the discovery is seldom agreeable, and is usually salutary. Julian opened his mouth to reply, and found that he had nothing ready. He looked at his cousin's kind, ruddy, troubled face, glimmering in the dusk, and in it he saw, with a disconcerting clearness, not pity for a failure, which he could have resented, but pity for a lost boy, which he could not.

And then—it was the lightning-bugs that did it, perhaps, or the smell of his mother's honeysuckle on the trellis, or the remembered goat—the soft black hat and the pointed beard and the theory of art fell away from him all together, like a costume dropped on the floor at the end of a masquerade, and he was eighteen again, and fourteen, and nine, and he heard himself laugh. It was not the laugh he had cultivated in the Rue Notre-Dame-des-Champs. It was a loud, undignified, explosive laugh that he had not used since he was a boy; and Ned, astonished for an instant, joined it with a roar that brought Julian's mother to the screen door again to ask what on earth.

"Nothing, mother," Julian gasped. "Nothing. Ned—Ned, do you remember the circus?"

"Do I remember it!" cried Ned, slapping his knee. "Do I remember it! You had two doughnuts and a jackknife, and you said that was all a man needed to start life on, and we got as far as the freight yards and you ate both the doughnuts before we'd been gone an hour!"

"I did not! You ate one of them!"

"I did not! You ate 'em both and then cried because you were hungry!"

"I never cried in my life!"

"You cried like a calf," said Ned, with relish. "And then a brakeman chased us, and you lost the jackknife, and when we got home your father—"

"Never mind what my father did," said Julian, and they laughed again, until the wicker chairs creaked in protest and a neighbour across the way, sitting on his own porch, called over to ask if that was Julian Tewksbury back from France, and to say he'd have known that laugh anywhere.

They talked for two hours more, and it is to be recorded that in all that time the Closerie des Lilas was not mentioned once. They talked of Orville Pease, who was now, it appeared, a deacon and a dealer in coal, and very stout; of the girl in the seventh grade, who had married a dentist in Terre Haute; of old Mr. Gilbert of the wagon works, who used to chase them out of his cherry tree with a buggy-whip; of the swimming-hole above the mill-dam, which had been filled in to make way for the new railroad spur. Ned grew solemn over the swimming-hole, and Julian, a little to his own surprise, grew solemn with him, and said it was a shame, a downright shame; and for a moment the two young men sat together in the dark, mourning, as men have mourned in every generation, for the particular piece of creek bank upon which they had once been happy and which progress had covered over with cinders.

At last Ned rose, stretching, and said he must be getting home; Hattie would be wondering, and the baby might be awake.

"Sunday, then," he said, at the top of the steps. "Half-past twelve. And Julian—"

"Yes?"

Ned hesitated, with the delicacy of a man approaching a subject upon which a friend might be sensitive. "You don't have to, of course. But Hattie's mother is going to be there, and she's kind of old-fashioned, and I thought maybe—well, just for Sunday—you might sort of trim those whiskers down a little? Not take 'em off, you understand. Just trim 'em."

Julian drew himself up. He felt the dignity of the Left Bank, of the Polish painter, of his two sold pictures, rising within him; he felt the soft black hat, which lay on the porch floor beside his chair, crying out to him to be true to it.

"I'll think about it," he said.

"That's all I ask," said Ned comfortably; and went off down the brick walk, whistling a tune that had been popular in the year they were twelve.

Julian sat on alone for some time, watching the lightning-bugs and listening to the distant, rhythmic thump of a factory by the river, which apparently worked at night. He was conscious of a curious mixture of feelings, in which humiliation and contentment were so oddly blended that he could not tell where one left off and the other began. He had come home to be kind to his cousin, and his cousin had been kind to him; he had come home to be lonely and misunderstood, and he had laughed more in one evening than in a year of Paris. It was not at all what he had planned, and he resented it a little, and he would not have had it otherwise for the world.

When he went up to bed, his mother, who was turning down the lamp in the hall, observed that he looked happier than when he came.

"Mother," he said, pausing on the stair, "have we still got Father's old razor?"

She said she believed it was in the bureau drawer, and asked why.

"Oh, no particular reason," said Julian carelessly. "I was only thinking I might trim things up a little. One doesn't want to frighten Hattie Bolander's mother."

And he went on up the stairs with the knotted cane under his arm, quite forgetting to lean upon it.

At least she told me she had told you the night before you left that her father had decided to return here to live. It was appropriate that your mother, herself an old friend, should assemble a representative selection of Mr. Morgan’s old friends around him at such a time. He was in great spirits and most entertaining. As your time was so charmingly taken up during your visit home with a younger member of his family, you probably overlooked opportunities of hearing him talk, and do not know what an interesting man he can be. He will soon begin to build his factory here for the manufacture of automobiles, which he says is a term he prefers to “horseless carriages.” Your Uncle George told me he would like to invest in this factory, as George thinks there is a future for automobiles; perhaps not for general use, but as an interesting novelty, which people with sufficient means would like to own for their amusement and the sake of variety. However, he said Mr. Morgan laughingly declined his offer, as Mr. M. was fully able to finance this venture, though not starting in a very large way. Your uncle said other people are manufacturing automobiles in different parts of the country with success. Your father is not very well, though he is not actually ill, and the doctor tells him he ought not to be so much at his office, as the long years of application indoors with no exercise are beginning to affect him unfavourably, but I believe your father would die if he had to give up his work, which is all that has ever interested him outside of his family. I never could understand it. Mr. Morgan took your mother and me with Lucy to see Modjeska in “Twelfth Night” yesterday evening, and Lucy said she thought the Duke looked rather like you, only much more democratic in his manner. I suppose you will think I have written a great deal about the Morgans in this letter, but thought you would be interested because of your interest in a younger member of his family. Hoping that you are finding college still as attractive as ever, Affectionately, Aunt Fanny. George read one sentence in this letter several times. Then he dropped the missive in his wastebasket to join the clipping, and strolled down the corridor of his dormitory to borrow a copy of “Twelfth Night.” Having secured one, he returned to his study and refreshed his memory of the play—but received no enlightenment that enabled him to comprehend Lucy’s strange remark. However, he found himself impelled in the direction of correspondence, and presently wrote a letter—not a reply to his Aunt Fanny. Dear Lucy: No doubt you will be surprised at hearing from me so soon again, especially as this makes two in answer to the one received from you since getting back to the old place. I hear you have been making comments about me at the theatre, that some actor was more democratic in his manners than I am, which I do not understand. You know my theory of life because I explained it to you on our first drive together, when I told you I would not talk to everybody about things I feel like the way I spoke to you of my theory of life. I believe those who are able should have a true theory of life, and I developed my theory of life long, long ago. Well, here I sit smoking my faithful briar pipe, indulging in the fragrance of my tobacco as I look out on the campus from my many-paned window, and things are different with me from the way they were way back in Freshman year. I can see now how boyish in many ways I was then. I believe what has changed me as much as anything was my visit home at the time I met you. So I sit here with my faithful briar and dream the old dreams over as it were, dreaming of the waltzes we waltzed together and of that last night before we parted, and you told me the good news you were going to live there, and I would find my friend waiting for me, when I get home next summer. I will be glad my friend will be waiting for me. I am not capable of friendship except for the very few, and, looking back over my life, I remember there were times when I doubted if I could feel a great friendship for anybody—especially girls. I do not take a great interest in many people, as you know, for I find most of them shallow. Here in the old place I do not believe in being hail-fellow-well-met with every Tom, Dick, and Harry just because he happens to be a classmate, any more than I do at home, where I have always been careful who I was seen with, largely on account of the family, but also because my disposition ever since my boyhood has been to encourage real intimacy from but the few. What are you reading now? I have finished both “Henry Esmond” and “The Virginians.” I like Thackeray because he is not trashy, and because he writes principally of nice people. My theory of literature is an author who does not indulge in trashiness—writes about people you could introduce into your own home. I agree with my Uncle Sydney, as I once heard him say he did not care to read a book or go to a play about people he would not care to meet at his own dinner table. I believe we should live by certain standards and ideals, as you know from my telling you my theory of life. Well, a letter is no place for deep discussions, so I will not go into the subject. From several letters from my mother, and one from Aunt Fanny, I hear you are seeing a good deal of the family since I left. I hope sometimes you think of the member who is absent. I got a silver frame for your photograph in New York, and I keep it on my desk. When I look at your photograph, I say to myself, “At last, at last here is one that will not prove shallow.” My faithful briar has gone out. Friend, this is from your friend, G.A.M. George’s anticipations were not disappointed. When he came home in June his friend was awaiting him; at least, she was so pleased to see him again that for a few minutes after their first encounter she was a little breathless, and a great deal glowing, and quiet withal. Their sentimental friendship continued, though sometimes he was irritated by her making it less sentimental than he did, and sometimes by what he called her “air of superiority.” Her air was usually, in truth, that of a fond but amused older sister; and George did not believe such an attitude was warranted by her eight months of seniority. But the Major, declining to hear him out, interrupted querulously, saying that he had enough to bother him without any advice from George; and retired to his library, going so far as to lock the door audibly.

“Second childhood!” George muttered, shaking his head; and he thought sadly that the Major had not long to live. However, this surmise depressed him for only a moment or so. Of course, people couldn’t be expected to live forever, and it would be a good thing to have someone in charge of the Estate who wouldn’t let it get to looking so rusty that riffraff dared to make fun of it. For George had lately undergone the annoyance of calling upon the Morgans, in the rather stuffy red velours and gilt parlour of their apartment at the hotel, one evening when Mr. Frederick Kinney also was a caller, and Mr. Kinney had not been tactful. In fact, though he adopted a humorous tone of voice, in expressing his sympathy for people who, through the city’s poverty in hotels, were obliged to stay at the Amberson, Mr. Kinney’s intention was interpreted by the other visitor as not at all humorous, but, on the contrary, personal and offensive. George rose abruptly, his face the colour of wrath. “Good-night, Miss Morgan. Good-night, Mr. Morgan,” he said. “I shall take pleasure in calling at some other time when a more courteous sort of people may be present.”

“Look here!” the hot-headed Fred burst out. “Don’t you try to make me out a boor, George Minafer! I wasn’t hinting anything at you; I simply forgot all about your grandfather owning this old building. Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor! I won’t—” But George walked out in the very course of this vehement protest, and it was necessarily left unfinished. Mr. Kinney remained only a few moments after George’s departure; and as the door closed upon him, the distressed Lucy turned to her father. She was plaintively surprised to find him in a condition of immoderate laughter.

“I didn’t—I didn’t think I could hold out!” he gasped, and, after choking until tears came to his eyes, felt blindly for the chair from which he had risen to wish Mr. Kinney an indistinct good-night. His hand found the arm of the chair; he collapsed feebly, and sat uttering incoherent sounds.

“Papa!”

“It brings things back so!” he managed to explain, “This very Fred Kinney’s father and young George’s father, Wilbur Minafer, used to do just such things when they were at that age—and, for that matter, so did George Amberson and I, and all the rest of us!” And, in spite of his exhaustion, he began to imitate: “Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor!” “I shall take pleasure in calling at some time when a more courteous sort of people—” He was unable to go on. There is a mirth for every age, and Lucy failed to comprehend her father’s, but tolerated it a little ruefully.

“Papa, I think they were shocking. Weren’t they awful!”

“Just—just boys!” he moaned, wiping his eyes. But Lucy could not smile at all; she was beginning to look indignant. “I can forgive that poor Fred Kinney,” she said. “He’s just blundering—but George—oh, George behaved outrageously!”

“It’s a difficult age,” her father observed, his calmness somewhat restored. “Girls don’t seem to have to pass through it quite as boys do, or their savoir faire is instinctive—or something!” And he gave away to a return of his convulsion. She came and sat upon the arm of his chair. “Papa, why should George behave like that?”

“He’s sensitive.”

“Rather! But why is he? He does anything he likes to, without any regard for what people think. Then why should he mind so furiously when the least little thing reflects upon him, or on anything or anybody connected with him?” Eugene patted her hand. “That’s one of the greatest puzzles of human vanity, dear; and I don’t pretend to know the answer. In all my life, the most arrogant people that I’ve known have been the most sensitive. The people who have done the most in contempt of other people’s opinion, and who consider themselves the highest above it, have been the most furious if it went against them. Arrogant and domineering people can’t stand the least, lightest, faintest breath of criticism. It just kills them.”

“Papa, do you think George is terribly arrogant and domineering?”

“Oh, he’s still only a boy,” said Eugene consolingly. “There’s plenty of fine stuff in him—can’t help but be, because he’s Isabel Amberson’s son.” Lucy stroked his hair, which was still almost as dark as her own. “You liked her pretty well once, I guess, papa.”

“I do still,” he said quietly.

“She’s lovely—lovely! Papa—” she paused, then continued—“I wonder sometimes—” “What?”

“I wonder just how she happened to marry Mr. Minafer.”

“Oh, Minafer’s all right,” said Eugene. “He’s a quiet sort of man, but he’s a good man and a kind man. He always was, and those things count.”

“But in a way—well, I’ve heard people say there wasn’t anything to him at all except business and saving money. Miss Fanny Minafer herself told me that everything George and his mother have of their own—that is, just to spend as they like—she says it has always come from Major Amberson.”

“Thrift, Horatio!” said Eugene lightly. “Thrift’s an inheritance, and a common enough one here. The people who settled the country had to save, so making and saving were taught as virtues, and the people, to the third generation, haven’t found out that making and saving are only means to an end. Minafer doesn’t believe in money being spent. He believes God made it to be invested and saved.”

“But George isn’t saving. He’s reckless, and even if he is arrogant and conceited and bad-tempered, he’s awfully generous.”

“Oh, he’s an Amberson,” said her father. “The Ambersons aren’t saving. They’re too much the other way, most of them.”

“I don’t think I should have called George bad-tempered,” Lucy said thoughtfully. “No. I don’t think he is.”

“Only when he’s cross about something?” Morgan suggested, with a semblance of sympathetic gravity.

“Yes,” she said brightly, not perceiving that his intention was humorous. “All the rest of the time he’s really very amiable. Of course, he’s much more a perfect child, the whole time, than he realizes! He certainly behaved awfully to-night.” She jumped up, her indignation returning. “He did, indeed, and it won’t do to encourage him in it. I think he’ll find me pretty cool—for a week or so!” Whereupon her father suffered a renewal of his attack of uproarious laughter.

Mr. Henry Pilcher came home from the bank at a quarter past six, as he had done every evening for eleven years except Sundays and the Fourth of July, and he knew before he had fairly closed the front door behind him that something was wrong. A man who has been married long enough learns to read the atmosphere of his own hall as a farmer reads the western sky; and there was in the hall that evening a kind of ominous stillness, a hush with a quality of waiting in it, which Mr. Pilcher had encountered before and had never once enjoyed. He hung his overcoat upon the walnut rack with unusual care, as if the act might propitiate the powers, and he cleared his throat in a tentative manner.

"Henry?" said Mrs. Pilcher's voice from the sitting room. It was a quiet voice, and that was the worst of it.

"Yes, my dear," he answered, and went in.

His wife was seated by the window with her sewing in her lap, but she was not sewing. Her needle was thrust through the cloth and left there, abandoned, like a sword planted in the earth after a battle; and her face wore that look of patient endurance which mothers have worn since the world began, and which fathers have learned, through long and bitter experience, to dread more than any open tempest.

"Sit down, Henry," she said.

He sat down. He had been about to ask whether supper was ready, but he perceived that this was not a time for supper.

"I suppose," said Mrs. Pilcher, "you will want to know where your silk hat is."

Mr. Pilcher had not wanted to know anything of the kind; in fact, he had not thought of his silk hat since the Sunday previous, when he had worn it to church and to the Methodist dinner afterward, and had suffered under it as he always suffered. But he saw that he was expected to want to know, and so he said, "Why—where is it?"

"It is gone," said Mrs. Pilcher.

"Gone?"

"Gone. Your son traded it to the rag-man this afternoon."

Mr. Pilcher's mouth opened, and for a moment no sound came out of it. Then he said, "Traded it? For what?"

His wife regarded him steadily. "For a horned toad," she said.

There followed a silence of some duration, during which Mr. Pilcher looked at the carpet, and then at the ceiling, and then at the gas fixture, which was of brass and had been a wedding present from his Aunt Lavinia. It must be recorded, in fairness to him, that the first emotion of which he was conscious was not indignation. It was something quite different, something which rose in him from deep places and threatened, for an alarming instant, to come to the surface in the form of a sound. He suppressed it heroically. He knew that if it came to the surface now, in the presence of his wife, he would hear of it at intervals for the remainder of his natural life.

"A horned toad," he repeated, and his voice was admirably grave.

"It is in a cigar box in the woodshed," said Mrs. Pilcher. "He has put holes in the lid with an ice pick. He has also put in some grass and a piece of my good sponge cake, which I was saving for the Thursday Club. The toad has not eaten the cake. I do not blame it."

"Where is Roderick?"

"He is in his room. I sent him there at four o'clock, and I told him that his father would attend to him when he came home." She took up her sewing again, and drew the needle through with a decisive little jerk. "I have attended to him enough for one day, Henry. It is your turn."

Mr. Pilcher rose. He was a man of medium height and medium girth, with a mild, pinkish face and a mustache which he had cultivated in his youth under the impression that it gave him an air of authority; it had never done anything of the sort. He was, in short, one of those men who are constitutionally incapable of sternness, and who know it, and who are forced nevertheless, by the terrible necessities of fatherhood, to assume from time to time a sternness which fits them as badly as a borrowed coat. He went up the stairs slowly. On the landing he paused and arranged his features. He drew down the corners of his mouth and contracted his brows, and he tried to remember how his own father had looked upon similar occasions, thirty years before, in a house in Indiana that had long since been torn down. It came back to him with a surprising vividness: the heavy tread upon the stair, the knob of the door turning, the dreadful pause; and the recollection did not help him in the least, for it brought with it a sympathy for the culprit which was wholly out of place in a man about to administer justice.

He knocked upon the door, which was an absurd thing to do, since it was his own house and the room within was his own son's; but there was something in the situation which seemed to call for ceremony.

"Come in," said a small voice, in which resignation and defiance were mingled in about equal parts.

Mr. Pilcher went in.

Roderick was seated upon the edge of his bed, his hands folded in his lap and his feet, which did not reach the floor, hanging motionless. He was seven years and some months old, and he had arrived at that period of life when a boy has discovered that the world is full of interesting objects and has not yet discovered that most of them belong to somebody else. He was a sturdy child, freckled across the nose, with hair that no brush had ever permanently subdued; and at the present moment his face wore an expression of such profound and saintly innocence that a stranger, coming upon him unawares, might have supposed him to be meditating upon the Sunday School lesson. His father was not a stranger. He had seen that expression before, and he knew that it was the most dangerous of all the expressions in his son's repertory.

"Well, sir," said Mr. Pilcher, and closed the door behind him.

Roderick said nothing. He looked at his father with large, clear eyes, and waited.

Mr. Pilcher took the single chair, which was small and painted white, and which creaked alarmingly under him; he sat upon it with his knees rather higher than was consistent with dignity, and he folded his arms.

"Roderick," he said, "your mother tells me that you have disposed of my silk hat."

"Yes, sir."

"To the rag-man."

"Yes, sir. He gave me a horned toad for it." The boy's face brightened, in spite of himself, as he said this; the light of a collector illumined it for a moment, and then, recollecting the gravity of the occasion, he extinguished it. "It's a real one," he added, in a lower tone. "From Texas."

"I don't doubt it," said Mr. Pilcher. "Do you know what that hat cost, Roderick?"

Roderick did not know. He shook his head.

"It cost," said his father impressively, "eight dollars and a half."

The effect of this announcement was not what he had intended. Roderick's eyes widened, but not with remorse; they widened with a kind of awed respect, as if he had been told that he had unwittingly conducted a transaction of enormous magnitude, comparable to the dealings of Mr. Vanderbilt or Mr. Gould.

"Eight dollars and a half!" he breathed.

"Eight dollars and a half," Mr. Pilcher repeated, and was immediately aware that he had taken a wrong turning. He hastened to correct his course. "That is a great deal of money, Roderick. It is more money than you have ever seen at one time in your life. And you gave that hat away—a hat that did not belong to you—for a toad."

"It's not just a toad," Roderick said, with a touch of earnestness. "It's a horned toad. It's got horns. It can squirt blood out of its eyes when it's mad. The rag-man said so."

"I don't care," said Mr. Pilcher, "whether it can squirt blood out of its eyes or recite the Declaration of Independence. The point is—"

He stopped. The point, for the moment, had escaped him; for the image of a toad reciting the Declaration of Independence had risen in his mind with a dreadful completeness, and the thing that had threatened him downstairs threatened him again. He coughed, and looked severely at the wallpaper, which was ornamented with a pattern of small blue sailboats, all sailing in the same direction, apparently toward the window.

"The point is," he resumed, when he had recovered himself, "that the hat was not yours. It was mine. And a person has no right to dispose of what does not belong to him. Do you understand that?"

Roderick appeared to consider. He considered for some time, his brow furrowed and his lower lip thrust slightly forward; and his father, watching him, felt a faint stirring of hope. It is one of the most touching illusions of parenthood that a child, presented with a moral principle in plain language, will examine it, acknowledge its justice, and resolve to amend his ways. Mr. Pilcher had cherished this illusion for seven years, and it had never once been borne out by events, but he cherished it still.

"But you didn't want it," said Roderick at last.

Mr. Pilcher blinked. "What?"

"You didn't want it," the boy repeated, with the air of one who has found firm ground beneath his feet and means to stand upon it. "You said so."

"I said nothing of the kind."

"Yes, you did. Last Sunday. When we came home from church. You took it off in the hall and you said—" Roderick paused, and an expression of scrupulous accuracy came over his face, as if he were determined to quote his authority without the slightest deviation—"you said, 'I'd give anything on earth to be shut of that confounded stovepipe.' You said that. And Mamma said, 'Henry, not before the child.' And you said, 'Well, I would, though.'"

Mr. Pilcher opened his mouth and closed it again.

It was true. He remembered it now with perfect distinctness: the heat of that Sunday, the tightness of the band across his forehead, the red mark it had left, and the fervent words that had escaped him in the hall. He remembered, too, his wife's reproving glance toward the small figure on the stairs, which had appeared at the time to be wholly absorbed in the business of sliding down the banister. Evidently it had not been wholly absorbed. It is a mistake commonly made by grown persons to suppose that a child who seems to be occupied with his own affairs is not listening; the truth is that a child is always listening, particularly to those remarks which are not intended for him, and that he lays them away in some secret storehouse of his mind, to be brought forth at the moment when they will be most inconvenient.

"And so," Roderick continued, warming to his argument, "when the rag-man came by, and he said did we have any old things, I thought about what you said. And I thought, Papa would give anything on earth to be shut of it. And the rag-man didn't want to give anything on earth for it—he only wanted to give a nickel, and I said that wasn't enough, and then he said how about a horned toad, and I said all right." He looked up at his father with an expression of the most transparent candour. "I thought you'd be glad."

There was a long pause.

Mr. Pilcher found that his arms, which had been folded across his chest in a posture of judicial severity, had somehow come unfolded, and that his hands were resting upon his knees. He looked at his son. His son looked at him. And Mr. Pilcher understood, with the clarity that sometimes visits a man at the most unwelcome moments, that he was face to face with a logic which he could not refute—not because it was sound, for it was not, but because it was built upon his own words, and a man cannot very well knock down a house of which he himself has laid the cornerstone.

He was aware, also, that he must not let this appear. There are moments in the life of a father when the whole edifice of parental authority, so laboriously constructed, trembles upon its foundations; and a wise father, in such a moment, does not pause to inquire whether the foundations are sound. He simply leans against the wall and hopes that nobody notices.

"Roderick," he said, and he was pleased to find that his voice was still steady, "when a person says he would give anything on earth for a thing, he does not mean it—literally. It is what is called a figure of speech."

"What's a figure of speech?"

"It is—" Mr. Pilcher hesitated. He had not anticipated being called upon to deliver a lecture on rhetoric. "It is when a person says a thing that he doesn't mean exactly, in order to show how strongly he feels."

Roderick pondered this. "Then why does he say it?"

"Because—" Mr. Pilcher stopped again. It occurred to him that he had never seriously considered why people said things they did not mean, and that this was perhaps not the best occasion on which to begin. "Because that is the way people talk," he said, somewhat lamely.

"Grown people?"

"Yes. Grown people."

Roderick nodded slowly, as if a great many things had been made clear to him at once, none of them entirely to the credit of grown people. "Then how is a person supposed to know," he asked, "when they mean it and when they don't?"

It was a question which philosophers have debated since the time of Socrates without arriving at any satisfactory answer, and Mr. Pilcher, who was not a philosopher but a cashier, did not feel equal to it. He took refuge, as fathers have always taken refuge when argument fails, in the simple assertion of power.

"That will do," he said. "The question is not what I said or did not say. The question is that you took a thing which was not yours and gave it away without asking anybody. You should have asked your mother. You know perfectly well that you should have asked your mother."

Roderick's eyes dropped. Here, at last, was a charge to which he had no answer, and he knew it; and the knowledge was written upon his face so plainly that his father, who had been feeling for some minutes like a man struggling in deep water, felt solid ground beneath his feet once more.

"Didn't you?" Mr. Pilcher pressed.

"Yes, sir," said Roderick, very low.

"Why didn't you?"

The boy was silent a moment. Then he said, with a candour that was the more disarming for being entirely unconscious, "'Cause I knew she'd say no."

Mr. Pilcher rose abruptly from the little white chair, which uttered a sharp cry of relief, and went to the window. He stood there with his back to the room, looking out at the darkening yard and the woodshed, where somewhere in a cigar box a horned toad from Texas sat contemplating a piece of Thursday Club sponge cake; and his shoulders, for a few seconds, were not altogether steady. When he turned around, his face was composed, though rather redder than before.

"Roderick," he said, "you will go without your dessert tonight. And tomorrow, you will go to your mother and tell her that you are sorry. And you will tell her that you will never again give away anything that belongs to anybody else without asking first. Do you understand?"

"Yes, sir."

"And—" He hesitated. The matter of the toad remained. Justice, strictly construed, demanded that the toad be surrendered; but justice, Mr. Pilcher reflected, would not bring back the hat, for the rag-man's wagon was by this time doubtless miles away, and the hat with it, rolling toward some unknown destiny in a heap of old boots and broken lamps. And there was another consideration, which he did not examine too closely, but which had to do with that Sunday in the hall and the band across his forehead and the red mark it had left. "And you may keep the toad," he finished, "provided you keep it in the woodshed and do not bring it into the house. If your mother finds it in the house, it goes. Is that clear?"

Roderick's face underwent a transformation. The saintly innocence fell away from it like a mask, and beneath it appeared a radiance of such pure and uncomplicated joy that his father was obliged to look at the sailboats on the wallpaper again.

"Yes, sir!" said Roderick. "Thank you, Papa! Did you know it can live without water for a whole month? The rag-man said so. And it eats ants. I'm going to catch it some ants tomorrow, first thing. And Papa—"

"Well?"

"Can I name it after you?"

Mr. Pilcher went out and closed the door rather quickly behind him.

He descended the stairs with the measured tread of a man who has done his duty, and he paused upon the landing, as he had paused on the way up, to arrange his features. This time the arrangement was more difficult. When he entered the sitting room his wife looked up from her sewing with an expression of inquiry.

"Well?" she said.

"I have attended to him," said Mr. Pilcher.

"What did you do?"

"He is to go without dessert. And he is to apologize to you in the morning. I spoke to him very seriously, my dear—very seriously indeed. I don't think we shall have any more trouble of this kind."

Mrs. Pilcher regarded him for a long moment. She had been married to him for eleven years, and she had never once in all that time been deceived by any arrangement of his features, however careful.

"Henry," she said, "what did he say?"

"Say? Oh, nothing to speak of. The usual thing. He was sorry. He—" Mr. Pilcher's voice wavered. "He seemed to think," he said, with an effort, "that I wanted to be rid of the hat."

"And where," said his wife, in a tone of the most perfect calm, "would he get an idea like that?"

Mr. Pilcher did not answer. He crossed to the mantelpiece, and stood there examining a china shepherdess with an absorbed attention which the shepherdess, a rather vacant young person in a pink bodice, had never before received from him. Mrs. Pilcher watched his back. Presently she observed that the back was shaking; and a moment later a sound escaped from the region of the mantelpiece—a sound which might, by a charitable listener, have been mistaken for a cough.

"Henry Pilcher!" said his wife.

But it was no use. A hot dislike struck him at the sight of Eugene; and a vague revulsion, like a strange, unpleasant taste in his mouth, came over him as he looked at his mother: her manner was eloquent of so much thought about her companion and of such reliance upon him. And the picture the two thus made was a vivid one indeed, to George, whose angry eyes, for some reason, fixed themselves most intently upon Isabel’s lifted hand, upon the white ruffle at her wrist, bordering the graceful black sleeve, and upon the little indentations in her cheek where the tips of her fingers rested. She should not have worn white at her wrist, or at the throat either, George felt; and then, strangely, his resentment concentrated upon those tiny indentations at the tips of her fingers—actual changes, however slight and fleeting, in his mother’s face, made because of Mr. Eugene Morgan. For the moment, it seemed to George that Morgan might have claimed the ownership of a face that changed for him. It was as if he owned Isabel. The two began to walk on toward the gate, where they stopped again, turning to face each other, and Isabel’s glance, passing Eugene, fell upon George. Instantly she smiled and waved her hand to him; while Eugene turned and nodded; but George, standing as in some rigid trance, and staring straight at them, gave these signals of greeting no sign of recognition whatever. “Georgie!” she called, laughing. “Wake up, dear! Georgie, hello!” George turned away as if he had neither seen nor heard, and stalked into the house by the side door.
