She came and sat upon the arm of his chair. “Papa, why should George behave like that?”

“He’s sensitive.”

“Rather! But why is he? He does anything he likes to, without any regard for what people think. Then why should he mind so furiously when the least little thing reflects upon him, or on anything or anybody connected with him?” Eugene patted her hand. “That’s one of the greatest puzzles of human vanity, dear; and I don’t pretend to know the answer. In all my life, the most arrogant people that I’ve known have been the most sensitive. The people who have done the most in contempt of other people’s opinion, and who consider themselves the highest above it, have been the most furious if it went against them. Arrogant and domineering people can’t stand the least, lightest, faintest breath of criticism. It just kills them.”

“Papa, do you think George is terribly arrogant and domineering?”

“Oh, he’s still only a boy,” said Eugene consolingly. “There’s plenty of fine stuff in him—can’t help but be, because he’s Isabel Amberson’s son.” Lucy stroked his hair, which was still almost as dark as her own. “You liked her pretty well once, I guess, papa.”

“I do still,” he said quietly.

“She’s lovely—lovely! Papa—” she paused, then continued—“I wonder sometimes—” “What?”

“I wonder just how she happened to marry Mr. Minafer.”

“Oh, Minafer’s all right,” said Eugene. “He’s a quiet sort of man, but he’s a good man and a kind man. He always was, and those things count.”

“But in a way—well, I’ve heard people say there wasn’t anything to him at all except business and saving money. Miss Fanny Minafer herself told me that everything George and his mother have of their own—that is, just to spend as they like—she says it has always come from Major Amberson.”

“Thrift, Horatio!” said Eugene lightly. “Thrift’s an inheritance, and a common enough one here. The people who settled the country had to save, so making and saving were taught as virtues, and the people, to the third generation, haven’t found out that making and saving are only means to an end. Minafer doesn’t believe in money being spent. He believes God made it to be invested and saved.”

“But George isn’t saving. He’s reckless, and even if he is arrogant and conceited and bad-tempered, he’s awfully generous.”

“Oh, he’s an Amberson,” said her father. “The Ambersons aren’t saving. They’re too much the other way, most of them.”

“I don’t think I should have called George bad-tempered,” Lucy said thoughtfully. “No. I don’t think he is.”

“Only when he’s cross about something?” Morgan suggested, with a semblance of sympathetic gravity.

“Yes,” she said brightly, not perceiving that his intention was humorous. “All the rest of the time he’s really very amiable. Of course, he’s much more a perfect child, the whole time, than he realizes! He certainly behaved awfully to-night.” She jumped up, her indignation returning. “He did, indeed, and it won’t do to encourage him in it. I think he’ll find me pretty cool—for a week or so!” Whereupon her father suffered a renewal of his attack of uproarious laughter.

Mr. and Mrs. Walter Dunbar drove home from the Ridgelys' dinner in a silence which Mr. Dunbar, at the wheel of his new touring-car, at first mistook for contentment. It was a fine October night, the kind that the local papers would describe on the following morning as "crisp," and the leaves along Pennsylvania Street lay in drifts that rustled pleasantly under the tires. Mr. Dunbar was in excellent spirits. He had eaten a great deal of terrapin, which he did not like, and a great deal of Mrs. Ridgely's famous caramel ice, which he did. He had told his story about the Indianapolis lawyer and the mule, and it had gone off better than ever, old Judge Fairbanks laughing until he coughed and had to be patted upon the back by the lady at his left. Altogether, Mr. Dunbar felt that he had been something of a figure at the table, and he hummed a little as he drove, a tune he believed to be from "The Merry Widow," though persons more musical than he would have been unable to identify it.

It was not until they had passed the Methodist church at the corner of Twelfth Street that he became aware of anything unusual in his wife's demeanour. He glanced at her sidewise. She sat very straight, her gloved hands folded in her lap, and she was looking directly ahead of her through the wind-shield with an expression of such complete and serene composure that a less experienced husband might have been deceived by it. But Walter Dunbar had been married eleven years, and he had learned, by a process of instruction which had not always been gentle, that when Cora looked serene she was seldom so.

"Pretty good dinner," he said tentatively.

"Yes," said Mrs. Dunbar.

"Ridgely's getting fat, though. He'll have to look out." There was no response to this, and he tried again. "Judge Fairbanks seemed to enjoy himself."

"Yes," said Mrs. Dunbar.

Mr. Dunbar ceased to hum. He drove the remaining four blocks in a growing uneasiness, searching his memory of the evening for some offence he might have committed; but he could find none. He had not spilled anything; he had not contradicted Mrs. Ridgely about the Chautauqua lecturer; he had not, so far as he could recall, said anything whatever to the youngest Miss Ridgely, who was understood to be "sensitive" since her return from boarding-school. He turned the car into his own driveway with a clash of gears that made him wince, for he was still uneasy with the new machine and privately believed that it had a malicious temperament; and he brought it to a stop before the carriage-house with a jerk that threw them both forward.

"Sorry," he said.

"It doesn't matter," said Mrs. Dunbar, and got out before he could come round to help her.

He followed her up the side path and into the house, where the coloured girl had left a single gas-jet burning in the hall. Mrs. Dunbar removed her hat before the mirror, slowly, drawing out the long pins one at a time and laying them in a row upon the little marble shelf beneath the glass, and her husband, standing behind her with his overcoat half off, perceived in the mirror that her face was entirely without expression. This alarmed him more than anything yet.

"Look here, Cora," he said, "what's the matter?"

"Nothing's the matter."

"Well, something is. You haven't said six words since we left the Ridgelys'."

"I didn't suppose you'd noticed," she said. "You seemed to have so much to say yourself, this evening, I didn't think you'd miss anything I might have said."

Mr. Dunbar hung his coat upon the rack with care, as if the operation required all his attention. He had a feeling, familiar to husbands, that he was standing at the edge of something, and that the next step he took would determine whether he fell into it. He decided to be jovial.

"Oh, come now!" he said, laughing. "You don't mean that story about the mule? Why, everybody laughed at that. The Judge nearly choked."

"I'm not speaking of the mule."

"Well, what then?"

Mrs. Dunbar laid the last of her hatpins upon the shelf, beside the others, and turned to face him. She was a handsome woman, a little past thirty, with fair hair that she wore rather high, in the fashion, and with a pair of gray eyes which, in the opinion of the ladies of the Wednesday Afternoon Club, were "her best feature, though she's got a temper behind them, if you ask me." These eyes were now fixed upon her husband with a look of quiet inquiry, as though she were curious to discover how much he would be able to remember without assistance.

"You told them," she said, "that you'd decided not to take the Chicago offer."

"Well?" said Mr. Dunbar.

"That's all. You told them."

"Well, but I have decided not to. What's the harm in saying so?"

"You told them," Mrs. Dunbar repeated, with a precision that made each word seem to have been separately chosen and examined before it was spoken, "before you told me."

Mr. Dunbar opened his mouth, and then closed it again. The truth was that he had made up his mind that very afternoon, in his office, while looking out of his window at the court-house square, where an old man was feeding the pigeons; and the decision had seemed to him so plainly right, so evidently the only sensible course, that it had not occurred to him that there was anything left to discuss. He had meant to mention it at supper, but they had dined out, and Cora had been dressing, and then there had been the drive to the Ridgelys', and somehow it had slipped out over the terrapin, when Ridgely asked him whether it was true that the Chicago people were after him. It had slipped out, and Ridgely had said, "Well, I'm glad of it, Walter; this town can't afford to lose men like you," and the Judge had said, "Hear, hear!" and Mr. Dunbar, warmed by these tributes, had enlarged a little upon the subject, explaining to the table his views upon the superiority of a moderate-sized city as a place for an American to bring up his family, and upon the folly of exchanging a position of respect in a community where one was known for a mere salary in a place where one was nobody. He remembered now, with an uncomfortable clearness, that he had used the phrase "a mere salary" more than once, and that it had been very well received.

"Why, Cora," he said, "I didn't think—I mean, you knew how I felt about it. We talked it all over last week."

"We talked it over," she agreed. "That is, you talked and I listened. And then you said you'd think about it. And I supposed—I suppose I was foolish to suppose it—that when you'd finished thinking about it you'd tell me what you'd thought. I didn't expect to hear it from Mrs. Ridgely's end of the table, along with the rest of the company."

"Well, but hang it, it's the same thing, isn't it? You heard it."

"Yes," said Mrs. Dunbar. "I heard it. So did Mrs. Ridgely. So did Mrs. Judge Fairbanks, who will have it all over the Wednesday Club by Thursday that I didn't know a thing about it. You might have seen her look at me, Walter, if you'd been looking at anything except the Judge."

"Oh, Mrs. Fairbanks!" Mr. Dunbar said, with a large gesture intended to dispose of that lady entirely. "Who cares what she says?"

"I do," said his wife.

There was a pause. Mr. Dunbar walked into the parlour, turned up the gas, and stood before the cold grate with his hands in his pockets, rocking a little upon his heels, which was a habit of his when he wished to appear at ease. Mrs. Dunbar followed him as far as the doorway and stood there, one hand resting upon the portière, which was of green plush with a ball fringe and had been a wedding present from her Aunt Mattie. She did not come farther into the room. Her husband, glancing at her, had the impression that she was prepared to leave at any moment, and that this was in some way a disadvantage to him.

"Well, I'm sorry if it annoyed you," he said, in the tone of a man making a generous concession. "I didn't mean anything by it. It just came out. Ridgely asked me straight, and I couldn't very well lie to him, could I?"

"Nobody asked you to lie."

"Then what do you want? I've said I'm sorry."

"You haven't said you're sorry you decided it," she said. "You've only said you're sorry I was annoyed."

Mr. Dunbar stopped rocking upon his heels. This was a distinction which seemed to him both subtle and unfair, a kind of thing women were always bringing up; and he felt, as men commonly do in such moments, that he was being drawn onto ground where the footing was uncertain and the rules had been written by the other side.

"Well, I'm not sorry I decided it," he said. "Why should I be? It was the right thing. You know it was the right thing."

"Do I?"

"Why, of course you do! Look here, Cora, be reasonable. What on earth would we do in Chicago? I'd be one of a hundred men in that office. Here I'm—well, I don't want to brag, but here I'm somebody. People know me. When I walk down Washington Street, half the men I pass speak to me. In Chicago I wouldn't know a soul, and nobody'd know me, and nobody'd care."

"I'd know you," said Mrs. Dunbar.

"You know what I mean."

"Yes," she said slowly, "I think I do. I think I know exactly what you mean. You mean you like walking down Washington Street and having half the men you pass speak to you."

"Well, what's wrong with that?"

"Nothing. Nothing in the world. Only you've never once asked me what I like."

Mr. Dunbar stared at her. It was so plainly absurd, the idea that she could prefer Chicago—Chicago, with its smoke and its stockyards and its dreadful flat-buildings, where people lived stacked up one on top of another like goods in a warehouse—that he could not at first believe she was serious. Then, looking at her face, he saw that she was; and the discovery gave him a curious, unpleasant sensation, as if a piece of furniture he had been leaning against for years had suddenly moved.

"You don't mean you wanted to go?" he said.

"Did you ever think I might?"

"Why—why, no. I never thought—Why, Cora, you were born here! Your people are all here. Your mother—"

"My mother," said Mrs. Dunbar, "lives three blocks away and comes to see me every afternoon of my life, and tells me how to manage my house, and how to manage Dorothy, and how to manage you; and I've been listening to her for eleven years. Do you know, Walter, I've lived in this town thirty-two years, and I've never been anywhere except to Cincinnati twice and to the World's Fair when I was a little girl? I've never been to a real theatre, except when the companies come through on the road. I've never heard a real orchestra. I've never seen anything. I've never done anything. I've just been to the Wednesday Club and to the Ridgelys' and to church and back again, and I'll go on doing it till I'm as old as Mrs. Fairbanks, and then I'll sit at somebody else's dinner and look at some other woman the way she looked at me to-night."

She said all this without raising her voice, and without moving from the doorway; but her hand had tightened upon the green plush of Aunt Mattie's portière, and Mr. Dunbar, who had never in his life heard her speak at such length upon a subject not connected with the household, was so astonished that for a moment he could think of nothing to say at all. When at last he spoke, it was in the injured tone of a man who has been wronged by circumstances.

"Well, why didn't you say so?"

"I'm saying so now."

"But it's too late now! I've told Ridgely. I've told the Judge. I've told the whole table. You don't expect me to go back on it, do you, and have them all laughing at me?"

"No," said Mrs. Dunbar. "I don't expect you to do that."

There was something in the way she said this that he did not like, a kind of finality, as though she had been expecting precisely this answer and was neither surprised nor much disappointed by it. He felt that he was being judged and found wanting, and the sensation was so novel to him, and so disagreeable, that it made him angry.

"Now see here," he said, taking his hands out of his pockets, "I don't think that's fair. I don't think that's fair at all. Here I've been working like a dog for eleven years to give you a good home and a good position in the town, and the first time I make a decision without consulting you about every little—"

"It wasn't a little thing, Walter."

"Well, it was my business, wasn't it? It's my profession. I'm the one that has to make the living. I suppose I've got a right to decide where I'm going to make it."

"Yes," she said. "I suppose you have."

"Well, then!"

"Well, then," Mrs. Dunbar agreed, and turned as if to go upstairs.

But Mr. Dunbar was not satisfied. He had won the argument—he was sure he had won it, for she had agreed with every word he said—and yet he had the distinct and uncomfortable feeling that he had somehow lost it, and that she was going upstairs in possession of the field. This was intolerable. He took two quick steps after her.

"Cora!"

She stopped, her foot upon the lowest stair, and looked back at him over her shoulder. The light from the single gas-jet in the hall fell upon her face, and he saw, with a shock, that her eyes were wet. Mrs. Dunbar was not a weeping woman; he had seen her cry perhaps three times in their married life, once when Dorothy had the croup, once when her father died, and once, inexplicably, at a performance of "Way Down East"; and the sight of those wet gray eyes now went through him like a cold draught from an open window.

"Oh, see here," he said, in an altered voice, "you're not—you don't—"

"I'm tired, Walter," she said. "That's all. It's late, and I'm tired. Good-night."

"But, Cora—"

"Good-night."

"But look here, I didn't know you felt like this! How could I know? You never said a word."

Meanwhile, Lucy sat silent, and the two Sharon girls leaned forward, staring at him with strained eyes, their lips tightly compressed; and both were but too easily diagnosed as subject to an agitation which threatened their self-control. He began again.

“I er—I hope you have had a—a pleasant time. I er—I hope you are well. I hope you are extremely—I hope extremely—extremely—” And again he stopped in the midst of his floundering, not knowing how to progress beyond “extremely,” and unable to understand why the infernal word kept getting into his mouth.

“I beg your pardon?” Lucy said. George was never more furious; he felt that he was “making a spectacle of himself”; and no young gentleman in the world was more loath than George Amberson Minafer to look a figure of fun. And while he stood there, undeniably such a figure, with Janie and Mary Sharon threatening to burst at any moment, if laughter were longer denied them, Lucy sat looking at him with her eyebrows delicately lifted in casual, polite inquiry. Her own complete composure was what most galled him.

“Nothing of the slightest importance!” he managed to say. “I was just leaving. Good afternoon!” And with long strides he reached the door and hastened through the hall; but before he closed the front door he heard from Janie and Mary Sharon the outburst of wild, irrepressible emotion which his performance had inspired. He drove home in a tumultuous mood, and almost ran down two ladies who were engaged in absorbing conversation at a crossing. They were his Aunt Fanny and the stout Mrs. Johnson; a jerk of the reins at the last instant saved them by a few inches; but their conversation was so interesting that they were unaware of their danger, and did not notice the runabout, nor how close it came to them. George was so furious with himself and with the girl whose unexpected coming into a room could make him look such a fool, that it might have soothed him a little if he had actually run over the two absorbed ladies without injuring them beyond repair. At least, he said to himself that he wished he had; it might have taken his mind off of himself for a few minutes. For, in truth, to be ridiculous (and know it) was one of several things that George was unable to endure. He was savage. He drove into the Major’s stable too fast, the sagacious Pendennis saving himself from going through a partition by a swerve which splintered a shaft of the runabout and almost threw the driver to the floor. George swore, and then swore again at the fat old darkey, Tom, for giggling at his swearing.

“Hoopee!” said old Tom. “Mus’ been some white lady use Mist’ Jawge mighty bad! White lady say, ‘No, suh, I ain’ go’n out ridin’ ’ith Mist’ Jawge no mo’!’ Mist’ Jawge drive in. ‘Dam de dam worl’! Dam de dam hoss! Dam de dam nigga’! Dam de dam dam!’ Hoopee!”

“That’ll do!” George said sternly.

“Yessuh!” George strode from the stable, crossed the Major’s back yard, then passed behind the new houses, on his way home. These structures were now approaching completion, but still in a state of rawness hideous to George—though, for that matter, they were never to be anything except hideous to him. Behind them, stray planks, bricks, refuse of plaster and lath, shingles, straw, empty barrels, strips of twisted tin and broken tiles were strewn everywhere over the dried and pitted gray mud where once the suave lawn had lain like a green lake around those stately islands, the two Amberson houses. And George’s state of mind was not improved by his present view of this repulsive area, nor by his sensations when he kicked an uptilted shingle only to discover that what uptilted it was a brickbat on the other side of it. After that, the whole world seemed to be one solid conspiracy of malevolence. In this temper he emerged from behind the house nearest to his own, and, glancing toward the street, saw his mother standing with Eugene Morgan upon the cement path that led to the front gate. She was bareheaded, and Eugene held his hat and stick in his hand; evidently he had been calling upon her, and she had come from the house with him, continuing their conversation and delaying their parting. They had paused in their slow walk from the front door to the gate, yet still stood side by side, their shoulders almost touching, as though neither Isabel nor Eugene quite realized that their feet had ceased to bear them forward; and they were not looking at each other, but at some indefinite point before them, as people do who consider together thoughtfully and in harmony. The conversation was evidently serious; his head was bent, and Isabel’s lifted left hand rested against her cheek; but all the significances of their thoughtful attitude denoted companionableness and a shared understanding. Yet, a stranger, passing, would not have thought them married: somewhere about Eugene, not quite to be located, there was a romantic gravity; and Isabel, tall and graceful, with high colour and absorbed eyes, was visibly no wife walking down to the gate with her husband. George stared at them. A hot dislike struck him at the sight of Eugene; and a vague revulsion, like a strange, unpleasant taste in his mouth, came over him as he looked at his mother: her manner was eloquent of so much thought about her companion and of such reliance upon him. And the picture the two thus made was a vivid one indeed, to George, whose angry eyes, for some reason, fixed themselves most intently upon Isabel’s lifted hand, upon the white ruffle at her wrist, bordering the graceful black sleeve, and upon the little indentations in her cheek where the tips of her fingers rested. She should not have worn white at her wrist, or at the throat either, George felt; and then, strangely, his resentment concentrated upon those tiny indentations at the tips of her fingers—actual changes, however slight and fleeting, in his mother’s face, made because of Mr. Eugene Morgan. For the moment, it seemed to George that Morgan might have claimed the ownership of a face that changed for him. It was as if he owned Isabel. The two began to walk on toward the gate, where they stopped again, turning to face each other, and Isabel’s glance, passing Eugene, fell upon George. Instantly she smiled and waved her hand to him; while Eugene turned and nodded; but George, standing as in some rigid trance, and staring straight at them, gave these signals of greeting no sign of recognition whatever. Upon this, Isabel called to him, waving her hand again.

“Georgie!” she called, laughing. “Wake up, dear! Georgie, hello!” George turned away as if he had neither seen nor heard, and stalked into the house by the side door.

Friend, this is from your friend, G.A.M. George’s anticipations were not disappointed. Their sentimental friendship continued, though sometimes he was irritated by her making it less sentimental than he did, and sometimes by what he called her “air of superiority.” Her air was usually, in truth, that of a fond but amused older sister; and George did not believe such an attitude was warranted by her eight months of seniority. “Papa, I think they were shocking. Weren’t they awful!”

“Just—just boys!” he moaned, wiping his eyes. But Lucy could not smile at all; she was beginning to look indignant. “I can forgive that poor Fred Kinney,” she said. “He’s just blundering—but George—oh, George behaved outrageously!”

“It’s a difficult age,” her father observed, his calmness somewhat restored. “Girls don’t seem to have to pass through it quite as boys do, or their savoir faire is instinctive—or something!” And he gave away to a return of his convulsion. She came and sat upon the arm of his chair. “Papa, why should George behave like that?”

“He’s sensitive.”

“Rather! But why is he? He does anything he likes to, without any regard for what people think. Then why should he mind so furiously when the least little thing reflects upon him, or on anything or anybody connected with him?” Eugene patted her hand. “That’s one of the greatest puzzles of human vanity, dear; and I don’t pretend to know the answer. In all my life, the most arrogant people that I’ve known have been the most sensitive. The people who have done the most in contempt of other people’s opinion, and who consider themselves the highest above it, have been the most furious if it went against them. Arrogant and domineering people can’t stand the least, lightest, faintest breath of criticism. It just kills them.”

“Papa, do you think George is terribly arrogant and domineering?”

“Oh, he’s still only a boy,” said Eugene consolingly. “There’s plenty of fine stuff in him—can’t help but be, because he’s Isabel Amberson’s son.” Lucy stroked his hair, which was still almost as dark as her own. “You liked her pretty well once, I guess, papa.”

“I do still,” he said quietly.

“She’s lovely—lovely! Papa—” she paused, then continued—“I wonder sometimes—” “What?”

“I wonder just how she happened to marry Mr. Minafer.”

“Oh, Minafer’s all right,” said Eugene. “He’s a quiet sort of man, but he’s a good man and a kind man. He always was, and those things count.”

“But in a way—well, I’ve heard people say there wasn’t anything to him at all except business and saving money. Miss Fanny Minafer herself told me that everything George and his mother have of their own—that is, just to spend as they like—she says it has always come from Major Amberson.”

“Thrift, Horatio!” said Eugene lightly. “Thrift’s an inheritance, and a common enough one here. The people who settled the country had to save, so making and saving were taught as virtues, and the people, to the third generation, haven’t found out that making and saving are only means to an end. Minafer doesn’t believe in money being spent. He believes God made it to be invested and saved.”

“But George isn’t saving. He’s reckless, and even if he is arrogant and conceited and bad-tempered, he’s awfully generous.”

“Oh, he’s an Amberson,” said her father. “The Ambersons aren’t saving. They’re too much the other way, most of them.”

“I don’t think I should have called George bad-tempered,” Lucy said thoughtfully. “No. I don’t think he is.”

“Only when he’s cross about something?” Morgan suggested, with a semblance of sympathetic gravity.

“Yes,” she said brightly, not perceiving that his intention was humorous. “All the rest of the time he’s really very amiable. Of course, he’s much more a perfect child, the whole time, than he realizes! He certainly behaved awfully to-night.” She jumped up, her indignation returning. “He did, indeed, and it won’t do to encourage him in it. I think he’ll find me pretty cool—for a week or so!” Whereupon her father suffered a renewal of his attack of uproarious laughter.

Mr. Lucius Hollister arrived at the Union Station forty minutes before the eastern train was due, which was precisely thirty-five minutes earlier than he had told his wife he would arrive, and fully half an hour earlier than any reasonable man would think necessary. He was aware of this himself, and he explained it, to a baggageman who had not inquired, by remarking that "you never could tell about those eastern trains"; though in truth the eastern train had come in upon its schedule every afternoon for eleven years, and Mr. Hollister could have told about it very accurately if he had cared to. He was a stout man of forty-six, with a stout gold watch-chain stretched across a stout waistcoat. He had been to the barber's at noon, which he did not do upon weekdays, and his son Herbert, who accompanied him, had been to the barber's under protest at one, and still bore upon his neck the faint powdery evidences of the outrage.

Herbert was fifteen, and of that age at which a boy suffers acutely from the public appearance of his parents. He kept a distance of four or five feet from his father on the platform, so that strangers might suppose them unconnected, and he looked at the locomotives with an air of hardened worldliness, as one who had seen a great many locomotives in his time and found them, upon the whole, overrated. Nevertheless, he was in a state of considerable inward excitement, for the person whose arrival they awaited was his father's cousin, Fenwick Hollister, and around the name of Cousin Fen there had gathered, in Herbert's mind, a mist of legend not unlike that which surrounds the name of Robin Hood.

It was known in the family (it was known, indeed, to most of the older residents of the town, who still mentioned it when the conversation flagged) that Fen Hollister, at the age of nineteen, had borrowed the fire department's best team from the engine-house on Pratt Street, without consulting the fire department, and had driven it four times around the Court House square at midnight, standing up, with a young lady beside him who was never identified; that he had subsequently fought a professional pugilist at the County Fair for a purse of five dollars, and won it; that he had been engaged to three girls in a single winter, one of them twice; and that, upon the death of his father, he had sold out his share of the old Hollister grocery business to his cousin Lucius, and had gone East "to make a big thing of it," leaving behind him a debt at the livery stable which he had afterward paid by mail, with a letter so humorous that the liveryman had it framed. He had not been home since. That was twenty-two years ago. He had written perhaps once a year—breezy, brief letters on the stationery of hotels in New York, Philadelphia, Chicago, and places further off, with mentions of "a deal I have on" and "some people I am seeing"—and from these Herbert had built a figure of dazzling vagueness, a sort of composite of a railway magnate and a soldier of fortune, wearing a silk hat.

"Pa," said Herbert, edging two feet nearer, for the platform was momentarily deserted and there was no one to see, "what's he do, anyway? Cousin Fen. What's his business?"

"Well, sir," said Mr. Hollister, "it's hard to say, exactly. He's been in a good many things. Promoting, mostly, I guess. Fen always was a promoter. Why, when we were boys he promoted a circus in our barn, and charged admission, and the only animal in it was our cow, and he billed her as the 'Sacred White Buffalo of the Sioux,' and got eleven cents out of the Kittredge boys before their mother found out." Mr. Hollister laughed so heartily at this recollection that he was obliged to wipe his eyes; and Herbert, perceiving a stranger approaching, withdrew instantly to his former distance.

There is a peculiar anxiety which attends the meeting of kinsmen long separated, and Mr. Hollister, as the train time drew near, became subject to it. He found himself buttoning his coat and then unbuttoning it again, upon the theory that a buttoned coat made a stout man look stouter, and an unbuttoned one made him look careless; and he could not decide which was worse. For the truth is that Lucius Hollister, who had stayed at home and minded the business, and enlarged it until "Hollister Wholesale Groceries" was painted across the whole side of a five-story building near the freight yards, and who was a director of a bank and a deacon of a church and had been mentioned, though not seriously, for the City Council—Lucius Hollister had, all those twenty-two years, felt himself in some obscure way a dull dog beside his cousin Fen. He would never have admitted this to anyone, and had scarcely admitted it to himself; but it was there, and it rose up in him now like a schoolboy's dread of a recitation.

The train came in with a great deal of hissing and clanging, and an important Pullman porter got down and set a little step upon the platform, and people began to emerge. Mr. Hollister searched the faces eagerly. A young woman with a canary in a cage came first; then two drummers with sample cases; then a very old lady assisted by the porter; then a lean, grey gentleman in a somewhat narrow-brimmed hat and an overcoat with a velvet collar, carrying a single valise of the kind that has been a good valise once. This gentleman paused upon the step and surveyed the station with an expression of amused tolerance, as if he had been asked to pass judgment upon it and was inclined to be lenient. Then his eye fell upon Mr. Hollister, and he raised his hand in a broad gesture that seemed to include the station, the train, the town, and the afternoon.

"Lucius!" he cried. "Lucius, by all that's holy! Don't tell me! I'd have known you in the dark—in a coal mine—at the bottom of the sea!"

"Fen!" said Mr. Hollister; and the two cousins advanced upon each other and shook hands with a violence which caused the old lady to look back at them in alarm. They shook hands for a long time, neither of them able to think how to stop; and then Mr. Hollister, with an inspiration, clapped his cousin upon the shoulder, and Fen clapped him upon the shoulder, and that brought it to a conclusion.

"Well, well, well!" said Mr. Hollister.

"Well, sir!" said Fen. "Well, sir, well, sir!"

"Well, well!" said Mr. Hollister again; and there seemed nothing to add to this, for a moment, so he turned and beckoned. "Herbert! Come here. This is my boy, Fen. This is Herbert."

Herbert came forward, scarlet, and gave his hand. He had been examining his legendary kinsman with the frank and terrible eye of youth, and he had already observed several things: that the velvet collar was worn shiny at the back; that the narrow-brimmed hat was not a silk hat; and that the gentleman's shoes, though highly polished, had been half-soled. But Cousin Fen, gripping his hand, looked down at him with an eye so bright and a smile so knowing that Herbert's observations became, for the moment, of no account.

"So this is the heir," said Fen. "This is the young man that's going to inherit the Hollister groceries and run the whole state. Well, sir, I'm glad to know you. I hear you're quite a rounder."

"Sir?" said Herbert.

"I say I hear you're quite a rounder. Stay out late. Break hearts. Your father wrote me." Fen winked tremendously; and Herbert, who had never been out later than half-past ten in his life, and whose father had certainly written nothing of the sort, felt a warm and grateful glow suffuse him. He perceived that here was a man who understood.

They went out to the automobile, which Mr. Hollister had bought only that spring, and of which he was so proud that he had been unable to sleep the first night he owned it. He watched his cousin from the corner of his eye as they approached it, and was rewarded; for Fen stopped short upon the pavement and whistled.

"Lucius! Is that yours?"

"Oh, it's just a little runabout kind of thing," said Mr. Hollister carelessly. "Five-passenger. Forty horse-power. They tell me it'll do fifty miles an hour, but I never tried it." He said this in a tone of indifference so elaborate that Herbert, climbing into the tonneau, was obliged to look the other way.

"Well, sir, you've come up in the world," said Fen, settling himself in the front seat with his valise between his feet; and then, as if he feared he had conceded too much, he added: "Of course, in New York you hardly notice 'em any more. Fifth Avenue's just one solid stream. A man gets so he doesn't see 'em."

"I suppose so," said Mr. Hollister, a little dashed.

They drove up from the station through streets which the returning cousin had last seen as a boy, and the experience was evidently a strange one to him. He kept turning his head this way and that, and making exclamations, and asking "Where's this?" and "What's that?" in a voice which had lost some of its breeziness. For the town had done what all the Midland towns were doing in those years: it had grown, and it had not grown handsomely. Where there had been elms there were telegraph poles; where there had been big brick houses with cupolas and iron deer upon the lawns, there were boarding-houses with placards in the windows, or new apartment buildings of yellow brick with names like "The Alhambra" and "The Ivanhoe"; and over all of it hung the soft-coal smoke, so that the October sun came through like a lamp behind a dirty shade.

"Why, where's the Mayberry place?" Fen demanded. "Used to be right along here—big place with the conservatory?"

"That's it," said Mr. Hollister, pointing to a building in which, upon the ground floor, there was a plumbing supply company, and upon the upper floors a business college.

Mrs. Hollister was waiting for them in the front hall, in her second-best silk, which was the one she liked best. Only Mrs. Hollister, listening with her pleasant smile, observed that Cousin Fen ate as if he had not had a good dinner in some time, and accepted a third helping of chicken with an alacrity which his anecdotes did not explain.

"And what are you in now, Fenwick?" she asked him gently, when the ice cream came.

"Now?" said Fen. He laid down his spoon. "Well, Nettie, I'm just looking around. Just looking around. I've got two or three things on the string. Big things. I thought I'd run out and see the old place while I'm making up my mind." He took up his spoon again. "Of course," he added, with a laugh, "I don't suppose there's anything in this town for a man like me."

"I don't suppose there is," said Mrs. Hollister, still gently; and she looked across the table at her husband, who did not see her.

After dinner the two cousins went out to sit upon the front porch, for the evening was warm with that last warmth of October which seems, in the Midland country, to be a kind of farewell. Herbert, who had been told that it was time for him to do his lessons, did not do them; he went up to his room, which was directly over the porch, and sat upon the floor beside the open window, in the darkness, with his chin upon the sill. He did not consider this eavesdropping. He considered it research.

For some time the cousins smoked in silence. Mr. Hollister had brought out a box of his best cigars, which he kept for the visits of the bank president, and Fen had taken three, putting two of them in his waistcoat pocket with the remark that he would "try 'em later." Down the street an arc-light sputtered and hissed; somewhere a mother was calling a boy named Willie, and Willie was declining to hear her; a street car went by on the next block with a long dwindling whine. Herbert, at the window above, began to fear that nothing more was going to happen.

"Lucius," said Fen at last, and his voice was different. It was lower, and had lost its flourish. "Lucius, that's a fine boy you've got."

"Oh, Herbert's all right," said Mr. Hollister. "He's at a kind of a funny age."

"He's a fine boy," Fen repeated. "And that's a fine wife. And that's a fine house, and a fine automobile, and I guess it's a fine business, too, from what I saw of the sign. You've done well, Lucius. You've done mighty well."

"Oh, I don't know," said Mr. Hollister uncomfortably. "I just kept on with what father left. Anybody could have done it. It's not like—well, it's not like what you've done, Fen. Getting around. Seeing things. I've never been further east than Pittsburgh in my life, except the once we went to Niagara Falls. Sometimes I've thought—" He paused, and the cigar glowed and faded in the darkness. "Sometimes I've thought I'd missed a good deal, Fen. Sitting here. I used to read your letters and think, 'There's Fen, out in the world, doing things, and here I am, figuring the price of canned tomatoes.' I guess I always kind of envied you, if you want to know the truth."

There was a long silence upon the porch. Above, at the window, Herbert held his breath.

"You envied me," said Fen slowly. "You envied me!" And then, to Herbert's consternation, his cousin began to laugh—not the loud laugh of the dinner table, but a queer, low, shaking laugh, that went on for some time and did not sound altogether like laughter. "Lucius," he said, when he could speak, "do you know what I've got in that valise? Two shirts and a razor. Do you know what I'm in, now? I'm not in anything. I've been selling a kind of encyclopædia, on commission, in the small towns of Pennsylvania, and the company went bankrupt last month, and owes me sixty dollars I'll never see. That's what I'm in. That's the big thing I've got on the string."

"Fen!"

"That's right. And the mine was a hole in the ground, and the theatrical company stranded in Ogden, Utah, and I walked a good part of the way to Salt Lake. And the fly-trap didn't catch flies. I've been thinking about this house, Lucius—about this porch—on and off for twenty-two years. When things were bad, I used to think, 'Well, there's Lucius, sitting on his porch, safe and solid, with Nettie inside, and nobody can touch him.' Envied me!" He laughed again, more quietly. "I guess I'm the one that did the envying."

Mr. Hollister did not answer for a while. When he did, it was in a voice which Herbert had never heard him use, and which made the boy feel suddenly that his father was a stranger, and a rather fine one.

"Fen," he said, "there's a place down at the store. I've been needing a man to go out on the road and handle the new accounts in the southern part of the state—a man that can talk to people and make them like him. I never could do it myself. It's not a big thing. But it's a salary, and there's a room upstairs here that nobody uses—"

"Now, Lucius, I didn't come out here to—"

"I know you didn't," said Mr. Hollister. "That's why I'm asking."

What Cousin Fen replied, Herbert never knew; for at that moment a firm hand descended upon his shoulder from behind, and he found his mother standing over him in the darkness. She did not scold him. She merely drew him away from the window, and closed it, and stood for a moment looking down through the glass at the two glowing points of the cigars upon the porch below.

"Mamma," Herbert whispered, in a kind of grief, "he isn't anything! He hasn't got anything! He just—he just sold books!"

"I know it," said Mrs. Hollister. "I knew it at the station, from the way your father described him on the telephone. I knew it twenty-three years ago, if it comes to that." She smiled a little, in the dark. "But he drove those horses four times around the square, Herbert, and nobody else in this town ever did. You go do your lessons."

Herbert went; but he did not do his lessons. He sat at his desk for a long time, with his geometry open before him, considering the strange case of a man who had nothing, and was glorious, and of another who had everything, and envied him; and he arrived at no conclusion whatever, which, considering his age, was perhaps the soundest conclusion available. The next morning, at breakfast, Cousin Fen was magnificent again, and told a story about a duel in New Orleans that had certainly never happened; and Herbert, who now knew better, listened to every word of it with his mouth open, and believed it all.

He was generous, poor, well-dressed, and his amazing persuasiveness was one reason why he was always in debt. One of Miss Amberson’s brothers was among the serenaders, and, when the party had dispersed, remained propped against the front door in a state of helpless liveliness; the Major going down in a dressing-gown and slippers to bring him in, and scolding mildly, while imperfectly concealing strong impulses to laughter. Miss Amberson also laughed at this brother, the next day, but for the suitor it was a different matter: she refused to see him when he called to apologize. “You seem to care a great deal about bass viols!” he wrote her. “I promise never to break another.” She made no response to the note, unless it was an answer, two weeks later, when her engagement was announced. She took the persistent one, Wilbur Minafer, no breaker of bass viols or of hearts, no serenader at all. A few people, who always foresaw everything, claimed that they were not surprised, because though Wilbur Minafer “might not be an Apollo, as it were,” he was “a steady young business man, and a good church-goer,” and Isabel Amberson was “pretty sensible—for such a showy girl.” But the engagement astounded the young people, and most of their fathers and mothers, too; and as a topic it supplanted literature at the next meeting of the “Women’s Tennyson Club.”

“Wilbur Minafer!” a member cried, her inflection seeming to imply that Wilbur’s crime was explained by his surname. “Wilbur Minafer! It’s the queerest thing I ever heard! To think of her taking Wilbur Minafer, just because a man any woman would like a thousand times better was a little wild one night at a serenade!”

“No,” said Mrs. Henry Franklin Foster. “It isn’t that. It isn’t even because she’s afraid he’d be a dissipated husband and she wants to be safe. It isn’t because she’s religious or hates wildness; it isn’t even because she hates wildness in him.”

“No, that wasn’t her reason,” said the wise Mrs. Henry Franklin Foster. “If men only knew it—and it’s a good thing they don’t—a woman doesn’t really care much about whether a man’s wild or not, if it doesn’t affect herself, and Isabel Amberson doesn’t care a thing!”

“No, she doesn’t. What she minds is his making a clown of himself in her front yard! It made her think he didn’t care much about her. She’s probably mistaken, but that’s what she thinks, and it’s too late for her to think anything else now, because she’s going to be married right away—the invitations will be out next week. It’ll be a big Amberson-style thing, raw oysters floating in scooped-out blocks of ice and a band from out-of-town—champagne, showy presents; a colossal present from the Major. The wedding was of Ambersonian magnificence, even to the floating oysters; and the Major’s colossal present was a set of architect’s designs for a house almost as elaborate and impressive as the Mansion, the house to be built in Amberson Addition by the Major. I can’t quite promise to like people I don’t care about one way or another, but you can be sure I’ll be careful, after this, not to let them see it. It’s all right, and you’d better toddle along to bed, because I want to undress.”

“But, George,” she said earnestly, “you would like him, if you’d just let yourself. You say you don’t dislike him. Why don’t you like him? I can’t understand at all. What is it that you don’t—” “There, there!” he said. “It’s all right, and you toddle along.”

“But, George, dear—” “Now, now! I really do want to get into bed. Good-night, old lady.”

“Good-night, dear. But—” “Let’s not talk of it any more,” he said. “It’s all right, and nothing in the world to worry about. So good-night, old lady. I’ll be polite enough to him, never fear—if we happen to be thrown together. So good-night!”

“But, George, dear—” “I’m going to bed, old lady; so good-night.” Thus the interview closed perforce. She kissed him again before going slowly to her own room, her perplexity evidently not dispersed; but the subject was not renewed between them the next day or subsequently. Nor did Fanny make any allusion to the cryptic approbation she had bestowed upon her nephew after the Major’s “not very successful little dinner”; though she annoyed George by looking at him oftener and longer than he cared to be looked at by an aunt. He could not glance her way, it seemed, without finding her red-rimmed eyes fixed upon him eagerly, with an alert and hopeful calculation in them which he declared would send a nervous man into fits. For thus, one day, he broke out, in protest: “It would!” he repeated vehemently. “Given time it would—straight into fits! What do you find the matter with me? Is my tie always slipping up behind? Can’t you look at something else? My Lord! We’d better buy a cat for you to stare at, Aunt Fanny! A cat could stand it, maybe. What in the name of goodness do you expect to see?” But Fanny laughed good-naturedly, and was not offended. “It’s more as if I expected you to see something, isn’t it?” she said quietly, still laughing.

“Now, what do you mean by that?”

“Never mind!”

“All right, I don’t. But for heaven’s sake stare at somebody else awhile. Try it on the house-maid!”

“Well, well,” Fanny said indulgently, and then chose to be more obscure in her meaning than ever, for she adopted a tone of deep sympathy for her final remark, as she left him: “I don’t wonder you’re nervous these days, poor boy!” And George indignantly supposed that she referred to the ordeal of Lucy’s continued absence. During this period he successfully avoided contact with Lucy’s father, though Eugene came frequently to the house, and spent several evenings with Isabel and Fanny; and sometimes persuaded them and the Major to go for an afternoon’s motoring. He did not, however, come again to the Major’s Sunday evening dinner, even when George Amberson returned. Sunday evening was the time, he explained, for going over the week’s work with his factory managers. When Lucy came home the autumn was far enough advanced to smell of burning leaves, and for the annual editorials, in the papers, on the purple haze, the golden branches, the ruddy fruit, and the pleasure of long tramps in the brown forest. George had not heard of her arrival, and he met her, on the afternoon following that event, at the Sharons’, where he had gone in the secret hope that he might hear something about her. Janie Sharon had just begun to tell him that she heard Lucy was expected home soon, after having “a perfectly gorgeous time”—information which George received with no responsive enthusiasm—when Lucy came demurely in, a proper little autumn figure in green and brown. Her cheeks were flushed, and her dark eyes were bright indeed; evidences, as George supposed, of the excitement incidental to the perfectly gorgeous time just concluded; though Janie and Mary Sharon both thought they were the effect of Lucy’s having seen George’s runabout in front of the house as she came in. George took on colour, himself, as, he rose and nodded indifferently; and the hot suffusion to which he became subject extended its area to include his neck and ears. Nothing could have made him much more indignant than his consciousness of these symptoms of the icy indifference which it was his purpose not only to show but to feel. She kissed her cousins, gave George her hand, said “How d’you do,” and took a chair beside Janie with a composure which augmented George’s indignation.

“How d’you do,” he said. “I trust that ah—I trust—I do trust—” He stopped, for it seemed to him that the word “trust” sounded idiotic. Then, to cover his awkwardness, he coughed, and even to his own rosy ears his cough was ostentatiously a false one. Whereupon, seeking to be plausible, he coughed again, and instantly hated himself: the sound he made was an atrocity. Meanwhile, Lucy sat silent, and the two Sharon girls leaned forward, staring at him with strained eyes, their lips tightly compressed; and both were but too easily diagnosed as subject to an agitation which threatened their self-control. He began again.

“I er—I hope you have had a—a pleasant time. I er—I hope you are well. I hope you are extremely—I hope extremely—extremely—” And again he stopped in the midst of his floundering, not knowing how to progress beyond “extremely,” and unable to understand why the infernal word kept getting into his mouth.

“I beg your pardon?” Lucy said. George was never more furious; he felt that he was “making a spectacle of himself”; and no young gentleman in the world was more loath than George Amberson Minafer to look a figure of fun. And while he stood there, undeniably such a figure, with Janie and Mary Sharon threatening to burst at any moment, if laughter were longer denied them, Lucy sat looking at him with her eyebrows delicately lifted in casual, polite inquiry. Her own complete composure was what most galled him.

“Nothing of the slightest importance!” he managed to say. “I was just leaving. Good afternoon!” And with long strides he reached the door and hastened through the hall; but before he closed the front door he heard from Janie and Mary Sharon the outburst of wild, irrepressible emotion which his performance had inspired. He drove home in a tumultuous mood, and almost ran down two ladies who were engaged in absorbing conversation at a crossing. They were his Aunt Fanny and the stout Mrs. Johnson; a jerk of the reins at the last instant saved them by a few inches; but their conversation was so interesting that they were unaware of their danger, and did not notice the runabout, nor how close it came to them. George was so furious with himself and with the girl whose unexpected coming into a room could make him look such a fool, that it might have soothed him a little if he had actually run over the two absorbed ladies without injuring them beyond repair. At least, he said to himself that he wished he had; it might have taken his mind off of himself for a few minutes. For, in truth, to be ridiculous (and know it) was one of several things that George was unable to endure. He was savage. He drove into the Major’s stable too fast, the sagacious Pendennis saving himself from going through a partition by a swerve which splintered a shaft of the runabout and almost threw the driver to the floor. George swore, and then swore again at the fat old darkey, Tom, for giggling at his swearing.

“Hoopee!” said old Tom. “Mus’ been some white lady use Mist’ Jawge mighty bad! White lady say, ‘No, suh, I ain’ go’n out ridin’ ’ith Mist’ Jawge no mo’!’ Mist’ Jawge drive in. ‘Dam de dam worl’! Dam de dam hoss! Dam de dam nigga’! Dam de dam dam!’ Hoopee!”

“That’ll do!” George said sternly.

“Yessuh!” George strode from the stable, crossed the Major’s back yard, then passed behind the new houses, on his way home. These structures were now approaching completion, but still in a state of rawness hideous to George—though, for that matter, they were never to be anything except hideous to him. Behind them, stray planks, bricks, refuse of plaster and lath, shingles, straw, empty barrels, strips of twisted tin and broken tiles were strewn everywhere over the dried and pitted gray mud where once the suave lawn had lain like a green lake around those stately islands, the two Amberson houses. And George’s state of mind was not improved by his present view of this repulsive area, nor by his sensations when he kicked an uptilted shingle only to discover that what uptilted it was a brickbat on the other side of it. After that, the whole world seemed to be one solid conspiracy of malevolence. In this temper he emerged from behind the house nearest to his own, and, glancing toward the street, saw his mother standing with Eugene Morgan upon the cement path that led to the front gate. She was bareheaded, and Eugene held his hat and stick in his hand; evidently he had been calling upon her, and she had come from the house with him, continuing their conversation and delaying their parting. They had paused in their slow walk from the front door to the gate, yet still stood side by side, their shoulders almost touching, as though neither Isabel nor Eugene quite realized that their feet had ceased to bear them forward; and they were not looking at each other, but at some indefinite point before them, as people do who consider together thoughtfully and in harmony. The conversation was evidently serious; his head was bent, and Isabel’s lifted left hand rested against her cheek; but all the significances of their thoughtful attitude denoted companionableness and a shared understanding. Yet, a stranger, passing, would not have thought them married: somewhere about Eugene, not quite to be located, there was a romantic gravity; and Isabel, tall and graceful, with high colour and absorbed eyes, was visibly no wife walking down to the gate with her husband. George stared at them. A hot dislike struck him at the sight of Eugene; and a vague revulsion, like a strange, unpleasant taste in his mouth, came over him as he looked at his mother: her manner was eloquent of so much thought about her companion and of such reliance upon him. And the picture the two thus made was a vivid one indeed, to George, whose angry eyes, for some reason, fixed themselves most intently upon Isabel’s lifted hand, upon the white ruffle at her wrist, bordering the graceful black sleeve, and upon the little indentations in her cheek where the tips of her fingers rested. She should not have worn white at her wrist, or at the throat either, George felt; and then, strangely, his resentment concentrated upon those tiny indentations at the tips of her fingers—actual changes, however slight and fleeting, in his mother’s face, made because of Mr. Eugene Morgan. For the moment, it seemed to George that Morgan might have claimed the ownership of a face that changed for him. It was as if he owned Isabel. The two began to walk on toward the gate, where they stopped again, turning to face each other, and Isabel’s glance, passing Eugene, fell upon George. Instantly she smiled and waved her hand to him; while Eugene turned and nodded; but George, standing as in some rigid trance, and staring straight at them, gave these signals of greeting no sign of recognition whatever. Upon this, Isabel called to him, waving her hand again.

“Georgie!” she called, laughing. “Wake up, dear! Georgie, hello!” George turned away as if he had neither seen nor heard, and stalked into the house by the side door.

Dear Lucy: No doubt you will be surprised at hearing from me so soon again, especially as this makes two in answer to the one received from you since getting back to the old place. I hear you have been making comments about me at the theatre, that some actor was more democratic in his manners than I am, which I do not understand. You know my theory of life because I explained it to you on our first drive together, when I told you I would not talk to everybody about things I feel like the way I spoke to you of my theory of life. I believe those who are able should have a true theory of life, and I developed my theory of life long, long ago. I will be glad my friend will be waiting for me. I am not capable of friendship except for the very few, and, looking back over my life, I remember there were times when I doubted if I could feel a great friendship for anybody—especially girls. I do not take a great interest in many people, as you know, for I find most of them shallow. Here in the old place I do not believe in being hail-fellow-well-met with every Tom, Dick, and Harry just because he happens to be a classmate, any more than I do at home, where I have always been careful who I was seen with, largely on account of the family, but also because my disposition ever since my boyhood has been to encourage real intimacy from but the few. My theory of literature is an author who does not indulge in trashiness—writes about people you could introduce into your own home. I agree with my Uncle Sydney, as I once heard him say he did not care to read a book or go to a play about people he would not care to meet at his own dinner table. I got a silver frame for your photograph in New York, and I keep it on my desk. It is the only girl’s photograph I ever took the trouble to have framed, though, as I told you frankly, I have had any number of other girls’ photographs, yet all were only passing fancies, and oftentimes I have questioned in years past if I was capable of much friendship toward the feminine sex, which I usually found shallow until our own friendship began. When I look at your photograph, I say to myself, “At last, at last here is one that will not prove shallow.” My faithful briar has gone out. I will have to rise and fill it, then once more in the fragrance of My Lady Nicotine, I will sit and dream the old dreams over, and think, too, of the true friend at home awaiting my return in June for the summer vacation. Friend, this is from your friend, G.A.M. George’s anticipations were not disappointed. When he came home in June his friend was awaiting him; at least, she was so pleased to see him again that for a few minutes after their first encounter she was a little breathless, and a great deal glowing, and quiet withal. Their sentimental friendship continued, though sometimes he was irritated by her making it less sentimental than he did, and sometimes by what he called her “air of superiority.” Her air was usually, in truth, that of a fond but amused older sister; and George did not believe such an attitude was warranted by her eight months of seniority. But the Major, declining to hear him out, interrupted querulously, saying that he had enough to bother him without any advice from George; and retired to his library, going so far as to lock the door audibly.

“Second childhood!” George muttered, shaking his head; and he thought sadly that the Major had not long to live. However, this surmise depressed him for only a moment or so. Of course, people couldn’t be expected to live forever, and it would be a good thing to have someone in charge of the Estate who wouldn’t let it get to looking so rusty that riffraff dared to make fun of it. For George had lately undergone the annoyance of calling upon the Morgans, in the rather stuffy red velours and gilt parlour of their apartment at the hotel, one evening when Mr. Frederick Kinney also was a caller, and Mr. Kinney had not been tactful. In fact, though he adopted a humorous tone of voice, in expressing his sympathy for people who, through the city’s poverty in hotels, were obliged to stay at the Amberson, Mr. Kinney’s intention was interpreted by the other visitor as not at all humorous, but, on the contrary, personal and offensive. George rose abruptly, his face the colour of wrath. “Good-night, Miss Morgan. Good-night, Mr. Morgan,” he said. “I shall take pleasure in calling at some other time when a more courteous sort of people may be present.”

“Look here!” the hot-headed Fred burst out. “Don’t you try to make me out a boor, George Minafer! I wasn’t hinting anything at you; I simply forgot all about your grandfather owning this old building. Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor! I won’t—” But George walked out in the very course of this vehement protest, and it was necessarily left unfinished. Mr. Kinney remained only a few moments after George’s departure; and as the door closed upon him, the distressed Lucy turned to her father. She was plaintively surprised to find him in a condition of immoderate laughter.

“I didn’t—I didn’t think I could hold out!” he gasped, and, after choking until tears came to his eyes, felt blindly for the chair from which he had risen to wish Mr. Kinney an indistinct good-night. His hand found the arm of the chair; he collapsed feebly, and sat uttering incoherent sounds.

“Papa!”

“It brings things back so!” he managed to explain, “This very Fred Kinney’s father and young George’s father, Wilbur Minafer, used to do just such things when they were at that age—and, for that matter, so did George Amberson and I, and all the rest of us!” And, in spite of his exhaustion, he began to imitate: “Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor!” “I shall take pleasure in calling at some time when a more courteous sort of people—” He was unable to go on. There is a mirth for every age, and Lucy failed to comprehend her father’s, but tolerated it a little ruefully.

“Papa, I think they were shocking. Weren’t they awful!”

“Just—just boys!” he moaned, wiping his eyes. But Lucy could not smile at all; she was beginning to look indignant. “I can forgive that poor Fred Kinney,” she said. “He’s just blundering—but George—oh, George behaved outrageously!”

“It’s a difficult age,” her father observed, his calmness somewhat restored. “Girls don’t seem to have to pass through it quite as boys do, or their savoir faire is instinctive—or something!” And he gave away to a return of his convulsion. She came and sat upon the arm of his chair. “Papa, why should George behave like that?”

“He’s sensitive.”

“Rather! But why is he? He does anything he likes to, without any regard for what people think. Then why should he mind so furiously when the least little thing reflects upon him, or on anything or anybody connected with him?” Eugene patted her hand. “That’s one of the greatest puzzles of human vanity, dear; and I don’t pretend to know the answer. In all my life, the most arrogant people that I’ve known have been the most sensitive. The people who have done the most in contempt of other people’s opinion, and who consider themselves the highest above it, have been the most furious if it went against them. Arrogant and domineering people can’t stand the least, lightest, faintest breath of criticism. It just kills them.”

“Papa, do you think George is terribly arrogant and domineering?”

“Oh, he’s still only a boy,” said Eugene consolingly. “There’s plenty of fine stuff in him—can’t help but be, because he’s Isabel Amberson’s son.” Lucy stroked his hair, which was still almost as dark as her own. “You liked her pretty well once, I guess, papa.”

“I do still,” he said quietly.

“She’s lovely—lovely! Papa—” she paused, then continued—“I wonder sometimes—” “What?”

“I wonder just how she happened to marry Mr. Minafer.”

“Oh, Minafer’s all right,” said Eugene. “He’s a quiet sort of man, but he’s a good man and a kind man. He always was, and those things count.”

“But in a way—well, I’ve heard people say there wasn’t anything to him at all except business and saving money. Miss Fanny Minafer herself told me that everything George and his mother have of their own—that is, just to spend as they like—she says it has always come from Major Amberson.”

“Thrift, Horatio!” said Eugene lightly. “Thrift’s an inheritance, and a common enough one here. The people who settled the country had to save, so making and saving were taught as virtues, and the people, to the third generation, haven’t found out that making and saving are only means to an end. Minafer doesn’t believe in money being spent. He believes God made it to be invested and saved.”

“But George isn’t saving. He’s reckless, and even if he is arrogant and conceited and bad-tempered, he’s awfully generous.”

“Oh, he’s an Amberson,” said her father. “The Ambersons aren’t saving. They’re too much the other way, most of them.”

“I don’t think I should have called George bad-tempered,” Lucy said thoughtfully. “No. I don’t think he is.”

“Only when he’s cross about something?” Morgan suggested, with a semblance of sympathetic gravity.

“Yes,” she said brightly, not perceiving that his intention was humorous. “All the rest of the time he’s really very amiable. Of course, he’s much more a perfect child, the whole time, than he realizes! He certainly behaved awfully to-night.” She jumped up, her indignation returning. “He did, indeed, and it won’t do to encourage him in it. I think he’ll find me pretty cool—for a week or so!” Whereupon her father suffered a renewal of his attack of uproarious laughter.
