Mr. Harlan Pettibone was a man of fixed habits and an unfixed temper, and of the two it was the habits that his household relied upon. He came home from his office in the Second National Bank building at a quarter before six. He hung his hat upon the third peg of the walnut rack in the hall, never the second, which belonged to the umbrella. He kissed his wife upon the left temple, inquired whether the evening paper had come, and was told that it had. He then went into the library, sat in the leather chair that had taken his shape so faithfully over twelve years that it seemed to resent visitors, and read the paper until Delia rang the bell for supper. In all this he had the deep satisfaction of a man who believes he governs his own life, and the world was kind enough, as a rule, not to contradict him.

Upon a certain Thursday in the late spring, however, the world contradicted him at the very threshold. His wife did not wait to be kissed upon the temple; she met him in the vestibule, closed the inner door behind her with the air of one shutting a prisoner away from his rescuers, and said in a low voice:

"Harlan, before you go in, you must hear about Roscoe."

Mr. Pettibone held his hat in mid-air, the third peg forgotten. "What's he done now?"

"I want you to promise first that you won't be too severe with him."

This was not encouraging. Long experience had taught Mr. Pettibone that his wife asked him not to be too severe only when the case was one in which she would have been severe herself, if she could have managed it. Mrs. Pettibone's severity, like a lady's revolver, was something she owned but had never been able to fire.

"I'll promise nothing of the kind," he said. "What is it?"

"Well, you know Mrs. Corliss's dog?"

"I know it," Mr. Pettibone admitted gloomily. Everybody on Meridian Street knew it. It was a white bull-terrier of great age and settled melancholy, named Prince Albert, and it slept upon the Corliss front steps in a manner that suggested it had been placed there by an undertaker.

"It's blue," said Mrs. Pettibone.

"It's what?"

"Blue. All over. Roscoe and the Tinker boy and that little Heffelfinger got it into our stable this afternoon and put it in the wash-tub with a whole bottle of Delia's bluing, and then they kept it there and charged the children in the neighbourhood to come and look at it. They called it 'The Sacred Blue Hound of India.' Roscoe painted a sign. It's on the stable door now. Mrs. Corliss has been here twice. The second time she cried."

Mr. Pettibone's face underwent a change that his wife watched anxiously, for she had never been sure, in eleven years of married life, whether this particular change preceded wrath or laughter; and indeed it was possible that Mr. Pettibone himself did not know. There was an interval, during which a muscle in his cheek moved and was sternly mastered.

"Charged them?" he said. "Charged them what?"

"Pins, mostly. And some marbles. And a cent from the Willoughby child, and an agate. And—Harlan, this is the worst of it—when Mrs. Corliss came over the first time and asked him what he meant by it, he told her—" Mrs. Pettibone lowered her voice still further, as though Mrs. Corliss might be crouching in the shrubbery. "He told her she ought to be glad, because you'd said yourself that Prince Albert was the dullest-looking dog in the state, and now at least he'd be interesting."

"I never said any such thing!"

"You said it at supper on Sunday. 'Dullest-looking dog in the whole commonwealth' were the words. Roscoe was right there."

Mr. Pettibone was silent. It is one of the profounder sorrows of parenthood that the child, who will not remember for five minutes where he left his cap, retains with the fidelity of a court stenographer every incautious word let fall at the dinner table; and he will produce these words, not at home where they might be safely discussed, but in the presence of precisely the person they concern. Mr. Pettibone felt himself, for the moment, more the defendant than the judge, and the sensation did not soften him toward his son. On the contrary, it hardened him. A man will forgive a great deal in a child before he will forgive being quoted.

"Where is he?"

"Upstairs in his room. I sent him there as soon as Mrs. Corliss left. He's been very quiet."

"I should hope so," said Mr. Pettibone, and hung up his hat, upon the second peg, with the umbrella.

He did not go upstairs at once. He went into the library and sat in the leather chair and held the evening paper before him for perhaps ten minutes without reading a word of it; for he was composing what he intended to say. Mr. Pettibone had a great belief in the efficacy of a well-ordered speech. He had been, in his youth, a member of the Philo-Rhetorian Society at Wabash, and he still thought of most of the difficulties of life as things that could be met by the proper arrangement of three points and a peroration. His points, upon this occasion, were to be: first, the wickedness of tormenting dumb animals; second, the dishonesty of taking pins and marbles from smaller children upon a false pretense; and third, the grave disrespect of repeating to a neighbour words spoken in the privacy of one's own home. He was a little uneasy about the third point, which seemed to him to lead somewhere he did not wish to go; but he decided that if he spoke of it firmly enough it would not lead anywhere at all.

Having thus prepared himself, he folded the paper, rose, and went to the foot of the stairs.

"Roscoe!"

There was no answer, though there was a sound overhead that might have been made by a boy of nine getting quickly off a window-sill.

"Roscoe! Come down here to the library. I want to speak to you."

The door of the room above opened, very slowly, as doors do when they are opened by people who have a strong preference for remaining behind them; and Master Roscoe Pettibone descended the stairs. He descended them one at a time, with a hand upon the rail, and his eyes fixed upon each step as though it were new to him and might not bear his weight. He was a small, compact boy with a round head of cropped yellow hair, freckles distributed over him with great liberality, and that expression of limpid, heavenly innocence which nature, in her unfathomable humour, bestows most generously upon those boys who least deserve it. His mother had once been told by a visiting cousin that he looked like a cherub by Correggio, and she had believed it ever since, in the face of evidence that would have convinced a jury.

He arrived at the bottom step, and paused there, as at a frontier.

"In here," said his father, and led the way.

Mr. Pettibone resumed the leather chair, which gave him an advantage of position, and Roscoe stood upon the hearth-rug before him, with his hands behind his back. There was blue upon them, to the wrists, and a long streak of blue upon one cheek, and his stockings, which had been tan in the morning, were now of an indeterminate shade not found in nature. Mrs. Pettibone had followed them as far as the doorway, where she stood with one hand at her throat, in the attitude of a woman who has delivered someone to the authorities and immediately regretted it.

"Well, sir," said Mr. Pettibone.

Roscoe said nothing. He had learned, by the age of nine, that "Well, sir" was not a question, and that to treat it as one was only to hasten matters.

"I have been hearing," said Mr. Pettibone, "some very remarkable things about you."

"Yes, sir."

"Very remarkable and very disgraceful things."

Roscoe's gaze travelled slowly from his father's face to the clock on the mantel, as though he wished to fix the hour of the proceedings for future reference, and then returned.

"Do you know what you've done?"

"Yes, sir," said Roscoe. Then, upon reflection, he added cautiously, "Well—which?"

Mr. Pettibone was momentarily disconcerted by the implication that the list was a long one, and that his son was not sure how much of it had come to light. He chose to ignore it, and proceeded to his first point.

"You took a poor, harmless old dog," he said, "a dog that never did you any harm in its life, and you dragged it into our stable, and you—"

"We didn't drag him."

"What?"

"We didn't haf to drag him," Roscoe explained earnestly. "He came. Willie Tinker had a piece of liver. He came right along. He liked it."

"He liked having bluing poured all over him, I suppose!"

"Well, he didn't mind it any," said Roscoe. "He just stood there. He never even wiggled. Prince Albert never does wiggle, papa. He's too old to wiggle. Mr. Heffelfinger's hired man says he's been dead three years and nobody's told him."

This was so exactly the sort of remark that Mr. Pettibone might have made himself, at the Thursday Club, that he was obliged to pause and look severely at the fire-irons. When he looked back at his son his face was stern again, and he passed hastily on to his second point.

"And then," he said, "you charged other children to come and look at this poor animal. You took their pins and their marbles—you took a cent from little Effie Willoughby, who can't be more than five years old—and you told them it was a—what was it?"

"The Sacred Blue Hound of India," said Roscoe, not without a certain quiet pride.

"And it was not a sacred blue hound of India! It was Mrs. Corliss's dog! You knew perfectly well it was Mrs. Corliss's dog! That was obtaining money under false pretenses, sir! Do you know what they do to grown men who do that?"

Roscoe's eyes widened with a lively interest that was not altogether what his father had intended. "What do they do?"

"They put them in jail!"

"For how long?"

"For years!" said Mr. Pettibone, with feeling. "For years and years!"

Roscoe considered this, and his brow cleared. "Well, but anyway Effie Willoughby knew it was Prince Albert. Everybody knew it. Effie said, 'Why, that's ole Prince Albert!' the minute she came in, and she paid her cent just the same. She said she'd rather see him blue than white any day. She said it was worth it."

"That has nothing to do with it."

"Well, but papa, if everybody knew it was Prince Albert, then it wasn't any false pretenses, was it? It was only a show. Like the Wild Man of Borneo at the County Fair, that Mr. Heffelfinger's hired man says is a colored fellow from Terre Haute. Everybody knows that, too, and they all pay a dime."

It is a curious thing that a man who can conduct himself with perfect competence before a board of directors, and who has more than once silenced the president of a rival bank in open meeting, may find himself wholly at a loss before a child of nine standing upon a hearth-rug in blue stockings. Mr. Pettibone was aware that his second point had somehow been taken from him and was lying in fragments upon the rug; and he was aware, too, of a faint sound from the doorway that he preferred to believe was his wife clearing her throat. He did not look toward it. He gathered himself, and advanced upon his third point with the determination of a general who has lost two redoubts and means at any cost to hold the citadel.

"Roscoe," he said, in his deepest voice, "when Mrs. Corliss came to ask you what you meant by this conduct, what did you say to her?"

For the first time, the cherub by Correggio looked uneasy. His glance went to the doorway, found no ally there, and came reluctantly back.

"I don't remember exactly."

"Then I will remind you. You told her that I had said her dog was—that I had made a certain remark about her dog."

"Well, you did, papa."

"That is not the point!"

"You said it Sunday," Roscoe insisted, with the doggedness of a witness who perceives that the truth is his only friend. "You said, 'That Corliss dog is the dullest-looking dog in the whole commonwealth,' and mamma said, 'Harlan, the child,' and you said, 'Well, it is,' and then you had some more chicken."

There was a silence in the library. Mr. Pettibone, who had not expected to hear himself reproduced with such terrible accuracy, even to the chicken, sat very still. The doorway was silent too.

"What I say at my own table," he said at last, rather slowly, "is said in private, to my own family. It is not intended to be carried to the neighbours. A gentleman does not repeat what he hears in his own home. He does not go out and tell people things that will hurt their feelings. Mrs. Corliss is an old lady, Roscoe. She is a widow. That dog is all she has. She cried, Roscoe. She sat in our parlour and cried. Do you understand that? You made an old lady cry."

He had not prepared this; it came of itself, and it was better than anything he had prepared. Roscoe's lower lip, which had been firm throughout the cross-examination upon pins and marbles, now showed signs of instability. He looked at the rug, and at his blue hands, and swallowed.

"I didn't mean to make her cry."

"What did you mean, then?"

"I meant—" Roscoe struggled. It was evident that he was trying to recover, for his father's benefit, the precise logic that had seemed so luminous at three o'clock in the afternoon, and that it was not coming back to him in its original shape. "I meant she oughtn't to be so mad, because he wasn't hurt any, and he was a whole lot more interesting blue, and you said yourself he was dull, so I thought—I thought she'd be kind of glad, if she knew you thought so, too. Because now he isn't. Now everybody looks at him. Before, nobody ever looked at him at all."

Mr. Pettibone opened his mouth and closed it again. He was conscious that somewhere in this answer there lay a principle—a perverse, upside-down principle, but a principle nevertheless—and that a boy who could find it at nine would very likely end either in the legislature or in the penitentiary, and that it was the duty of a father to steer him firmly toward the former. He took refuge in authority, which is the last resort of a man who has run out of arguments, and the first resort of a man who never had any.

"That will do," he said. "I have heard enough. You have behaved very badly indeed, and you are going to be punished. In the first place, every pin and every marble and every cent you took from those children is going back to them to-morrow morning, and you are going to take them yourself."

"Yes, sir," said Roscoe, in a small voice; then, with sudden anxiety, "The agate, too?"

"Certainly the agate, too!"

"But papa, Sammy Heffelfinger only gave me that agate because he owed it to me anyway, from last week, and he—"

"The agate goes back."

Roscoe was silent, though the silence was eloquent of a deep sense of injustice in the matter of the agate.

"In the second place," his father went on, "you are going over to Mrs. Corliss's house to-morrow, and you are going to tell her you are sorry, and you are going to help wash that dog until he is white again."

"It won't come out," Roscoe said simply. "We tried. Willie Tinker said it would come out, but it won't. Delia says it'll have to wear off."

Mr. Pettibone had a sudden, distinct vision of Prince Albert reclining upon the Corliss steps through the remainder of the season, an enduring azure monument visible from the car-line, and of the remarks that would be made concerning it by the Thursday Club, and by the president of the rival bank, who lived three doors down. The muscle in his cheek moved again, and this time it was only with an effort that resembled pain that he compelled it to be still.

"Then you will help wash him every day until it does wear off," he said. "And in the third place, you will go up to your room now, and you will have your supper there—bread and milk—and you will not come down again to-night. Do you understand?"

"Yes, sir."

"And I want you to think, Roscoe. I want you to think about Mrs. Corliss, and about how you would feel if somebody did such a thing to a dog of yours."

"I haven't got a dog," said Roscoe, in a tone that suggested this was a grievance of long standing and that his father had at last stumbled upon the root of the whole matter.

"Go upstairs!"

Roscoe went. He went more briskly than he had come down, as one whose ordeal is over and whose sentence, though harsh, is at least known; and his mother, as he passed her in the doorway, put out a hand and touched the blue streak upon his cheek, and then, recollecting herself, withdrew it and looked stern. Roscoe, who understood perfectly well the value of that touch, did not presume upon it. He mounted the stairs, and they heard his door close.

Mrs. Pettibone came into the library, and Mr. Pettibone, without looking at her, unfolded the evening paper and held it before him.

"Harlan," she said, "you were very fine with him. At the end, about Mrs. Corliss crying. I think he really felt it."

"I hope so," said Mr. Pettibone, from behind the paper.

"Only—you won't say things like that at the table any more, will you? About the neighbours?"

"I don't intend to discuss it."

"Of course, dear." She lingered a moment. "Harlan—the dog really is very blue. I saw it from the side window. It's the bluest thing I ever saw in my life. It's bluer than the sky."

The paper trembled slightly.

"I'll go and see about the bread and milk," said Mrs. Pettibone hastily, and went out.

Mr. Pettibone remained alone in the library. He read, or appeared to read, the same column three times; it concerned the tariff, and he could not afterward have said which side of it he had been on. Presently, with the air of a man performing an act of purely civic duty, he rose and walked to the side window, which commanded, across the lilac hedge, a partial view of the Corliss front steps. The light of the long spring evening still lay over Meridian Street, and in that light, upon the top step, unmoving and serene and incomparably blue, lay Prince Albert. A small group of children had gathered upon the sidewalk before him, keeping a respectful distance and gazing upward in silence, as pilgrims gaze upon a shrine; and Mr. Pettibone observed that one of them, a very small girl in a sunbonnet, was attempting to pass something between the palings of the Corliss fence, and that the something glinted like a pin.

He stood there for some time. Then he went back to the leather chair, and those in the kitchen, Delia afterward reported, heard a sound from the library that she could not account for, unless the master had swallowed something the wrong way; for it went on a good while, and stopped, and then began again worse than before.

Upstairs, Master Roscoe Pettibone, eating his bread and milk upon the window-sill, heard it too, and was much puzzled by it. But he was a philosopher in his way, and after a little consideration he concluded that it was probably something about the bank, and that it was none of his business; and he returned to the more pressing question of how, if the agate must go back to Sammy Heffelfinger, it might be got back again from Sammy Heffelfinger by Saturday.

The cold had come down upon the land in the night, and it lay now upon the cabin like a great hand pressing. It was a cold that had weight and substance, that crept in at the chinks where the moss had shrunk from the logs, and that made the stove, red-hot though it was, seem a feeble and futile thing, a little spark of warmth adrift in an infinite sea of frost. On the shelf above the bunk the spirit thermometer had given up its office at sixty-five below, the red thread drawn down into the bulb and sulking there, refusing further testimony. Outside, the spruce trees stood rigid and white, and once in a while one of them split with a report like a rifle-shot as the sap froze in its heart.

Lars Hendricks sat on an upturned box by the stove, greasing his moccasins with the last of the bacon fat. He was a big man, with shoulders that had been built for heavy work and a jaw that had been built for heavier, and the lamplight caught in the coarse red hair of his beard and made it glow like copper wire. His hands moved over the moose-hide with a slow, deliberate patience, but his eyes did not follow them. His eyes were on the door, and through the door, and beyond the door, to the frozen sweep of the Stewart and the white hills behind it, and to a creek he had never seen.

His wife watched him from the table. She did not speak, for she had learned in two winters in the North that speech was a thing to be spent carefully, like flour and matches and the strength of dogs. She was a slender woman, but there was nothing frail in her slenderness. It was the leanness of a creature that has been worn down to bone and sinew by hard living and has found, at the bottom of itself, something that would not wear further. Her name was Anna, and she had come into the country over the Chilkoot with a pack on her back that would have shamed many a man, and she had never once asked to be carried.

"You'll be going, then," she said at last.

He did not look up. "I'll be going."

"Tomorrow?"

"Before light. Pelletier says the whole of Sixtymile will be on the trail by the day after. A man has to be first, Anna. There's no gold for the second man. There's only claims staked to the rim and a long walk home."

She rose and went to the stove and lifted the lid of the coffee pot and looked into it, though she knew well enough what was there. It was the third boiling of the same grounds, and the stuff had the color of weak tea and the taste of nothing at all. She set the lid back with care.

"Pelletier," she said. "Pelletier came down the river with frost on his face and a story in his mouth, and he ate two of our biscuits and a slab of our beans, and he went on in the morning to tell his story somewhere else. I have seen Pelletier's kind before, Lars. The country is full of them. They walk from cabin to cabin on their stories, and the stories feed them better than any pick and pan."

"He saw it with his own eyes. Coarse gold, he said, in nuggets like melon seeds, right at the grass roots. Two Indians from the Pelly brought it in."

"Did he see the Indians?"

Lars paused in his work. The moccasin hung from his fingers. "He talked with a man who saw them."

"Ah," she said, and there was a world in the word.

He threw the moccasin down upon the floor. It struck with a dull slap, and the dog that lay curled against the wall by the woodpile lifted its head and watched them with yellow, unwinking eyes. It was a big husky, wolf-gray and wolf-shouldered, and it had the wolf's way of seeing everything and saying nothing.

"You'd have me sit here," Lars said, and his voice was low, but it was the lowness of a thing held in. "You'd have me sit here by this stove and eat our grub down to the last bean and come out in the spring as poor as I went in. Two years, Anna. Two years of muck and frozen gravel and burning down to bedrock by the inch, and what have we got? Wages. Not even wages. A man could make more swamping on a scow at Dyea. And now there's a chance, a real chance, a straight shot at it, and you'd have me let it go by because a man named Pelletier eats biscuits."

"I would have you live," she said simply.

He laughed, a short, hard laugh with no mirth in it. "Live! Is this living? Look at it." He swept his arm about the cabin, at the low roof black with smoke, at the bunk with its robes of rabbit-skin, at the cache of grub stacked in the corner, at the frost thick as a man's thumb on the inside of the single window. "This is a hole in the snow. A wolf has as good. A wolf has better, for a wolf can hunt."

"And a wolf can starve," she answered. "I have seen them, Lars, at the end of the winter, coming down to the river with their ribs like the staves of a barrel. The wolf goes out to hunt when there is no hunting, and he does not come back. That is the way of the wolf. You need not make it yours."

She went to the corner where the grub was stacked and stood looking down at it. There were two sacks of flour, one of them nearly empty. There was a half-sack of beans, a slab of bacon no longer than a man's forearm, a little tin of baking powder, a smaller tin of salt, a lump of sugar wrapped in a rag. It was not much. She had counted it a hundred times in the long darkness, lying awake while he slept, counting and dividing and counting again, the way a miser counts his coins, but with a deeper and more desperate need.

"Come here," she said.

He did not move.

"Come here, Lars, and look at it with me. Look at it the way I look at it every night."

Something in her voice drew him, and he got up from the box and came and stood beside her, his great bulk towering over her, and the two of them looked down at the little heap of food that stood between them and the spring.

"There is enough here," she said slowly, "for the two of us to the break-up, if we are careful. If we eat one meal a day when the days are short, and two when they grow long. If nothing goes wrong. If no cache is robbed and no flour spoils. It is enough, and not one pound more. I know. I have counted it."

"I'll take only what I need."

"And how much will you need? It is a hundred miles to the Pelly by the river, and the river is not frozen smooth. You know what it is. Jams and ice-ridges and open water under the snow where the springs come up. You will be ten days going, if you are lucky. You will be ten days coming back. And you will be working all the while, breaking trail, and a man breaking trail at sixty below burns food the way that stove burns wood. You will need two pounds a day, Lars. Two pounds of grub every day, or you will be weak, and if you are weak you will make a mistake, and in this cold you need make only one."

She stooped and laid her hand flat upon the full sack of flour.

"Take forty pounds out of this," she said, "and what is left for me?"

He was silent. The stove ticked and muttered. Outside, another tree split, and the sound went rolling away among the hills and died.

"I'd be back," he said at last, but the words had lost their edge. "I'd be back before you ran short. And I'd bring grub. A man with a claim on a rich creek can get credit at any post on the river."

"If there is a rich creek. If you find it. If you stake it before the others. If the post has grub to sell, which no post on this river has had since November. If you come back at all." She straightened and faced him, and her eyes, which were gray as the winter sky, met his and held them. "There are a great many ifs, Lars, and every one of them is a hole in the ice."

He turned from her abruptly and went back to the stove and stood with his hands spread over it, and she saw the muscles bunch and work along his jaw beneath the beard. She knew the look. It was the look of a man fighting something in himself, and losing, and angry at the losing. She had seen it on him the night he first spoke of coming North, sitting in the little kitchen in Minnesota with the newspaper spread before him and the word *Klondike* printed across it in letters an inch high. It was the look of a man who had smelled gold, and in whom the smell had wakened something old and ravenous that would not lie down again.

"You don't understand," he said, without turning. "A woman can't understand. It isn't only the gold."

"Then what is it?"

He was a long time answering. When he spoke, it was slowly, groping, like a man feeling for a trail in the dark.

"It's the—the sitting. The waiting. Day after day in this hole, and the dark coming down at two in the afternoon, and nothing to do but chop wood and thaw gravel and lie in the bunk and listen to the frost. It gets into a man. It eats at him. And then a chance comes, a chance to *do* something, to go out and take hold of a thing with both hands, and—" He broke off and struck his fist against his palm. "A man's got to move, Anna. A man's made to move. If he doesn't, he rots. I can feel myself rotting."

She came to him then and stood at his side, not touching him, but near.

"I know," she said, and her voice was gentler now. "Do you think I do not feel it too? Do you think I do not lie awake and listen to the frost and feel the walls closing in? I am not made of wood, Lars. But this is what the North is. It is waiting. It is enduring. The country does not care about a man's wanting to move. It does not care about anything. It will let you go out on the trail, and it will let you walk a hundred miles, and then some night it will reach out and close its hand on you, and it will not even notice that it has done it. I have seen the men who went out because they could not bear to wait. You have seen them too. You helped to bury one of them."

He remembered. It had been the Swede, Johanssen, in their first winter, who had gone out alone after moose in the cold snap of January because he could not abide his cabin another day. They had found him in March, sitting with his back against a spruce, his rifle across his knees and his face turned up toward the sky, and the snow had drifted over him to the shoulders. There had been no mark upon him. The cold had simply come and taken him, as it took the sap in the trees.

"That was different," Lars said. "Johanssen was a fool. He went out without matches."

"Every man who dies out there was a fool," she said, "after he is dead. Before, he was only a man who thought he knew better."

The dog by the woodpile stirred, and rose, and stretched, and came across the floor to them, its claws clicking on the frozen boards. It thrust its great head against Lars's thigh and stood so, looking up at him, and he dropped a hand absently upon its skull and worked his fingers into the thick fur behind its ears.

"You'd take Brute," Anna said.

"I'd take Brute. I'd take all four of them. A man alone can't break trail and haul a sled too."

"And the dogs must eat. Have you counted the fish?"

He had not, and she saw that he had not, and she saw the knowledge of it come into his face like a shadow. There were perhaps sixty dried salmon in the cache outside. Four dogs on hard trail would eat two a day apiece. He could figure that as well as she.

"So," she said quietly. "You see. It is not only my flour you would take. It is the dogs, and the fish, and with them any chance I would have of getting out to Sixtymile if the grub ran short, or if I fell sick, or if—" She stopped.

He looked down at her sharply. "If what?"

She did not answer at once. She turned from him and went back to the table and sat down, folding her hands before her on the rough planks, and she looked at her hands for a long moment as though she were reading something written there. The lamp flickered, and in its unsteady light her face was very pale, and very still, and he saw something in it that he had not seen before, or had seen and not marked.

"I had not meant to tell you," she said. "Not yet. Not until I was sure. And then I thought, if I tell him, he will stay because of it, and I do not want him to stay because of it. I want him to stay because he sees with his own eyes that he should."

The big man stood motionless by the stove. The dog, feeling the change in him, looked up into his face and whined once, very low.

"Anna," he said.

"In the summer," she said. "July, I think. Perhaps August."

The silence came down upon the cabin then, and it was not like any silence that had been there before. It was the silence of the North itself, the White Silence, vast and patient and indifferent, and it seemed to Lars Hendricks in that moment that it had come in through the walls and was standing in the room with them, looking on. He felt it as a physical thing. He felt his own smallness in it, and the smallness of the woman at the table, and the smallness of the unborn thing she carried, a spark of warmth even feebler than the stove's, adrift in a world of frost.

He crossed the floor in two strides and dropped upon his knees beside her and took her hands in his, and his hands were so great that hers vanished in them.

"Why didn't you say?" His voice was hoarse. "Why in God's name didn't you say before?"

"Because I wanted you to choose," she said. "Not to be driven. You are a man who is driven by so many things, Lars. By the gold, and the waiting, and the need to move. I did not want to be one more thing that drove you. I wanted to be the thing you chose."

He bowed his head over their joined hands, and for a long time he did not speak. She could feel the struggle in him, the old hunger and the new knowledge locked together like two bull moose in the rutting season, antlers clashed and hooves braced in the snow, neither yielding. She did not help him. She had said all that she had to say. The rest was his.

Outside, very far off, a wolf began to howl. It was a long, quavering, mournful cry, rising and rising until it seemed it must break, and then sinking away into a sobbing that was almost human. It was the cry of the hunger that is in all living things, the cry of the Wild that is never fed, and it went up into the frozen sky and was swallowed there, and there was no answer.

Lars lifted his head and listened. The dog listened too, its ears pricked and its hackles half risen, and something stirred in its yellow eyes, something ancient that remembered the pack and the long chase under the moon. Then the howling ceased, and the dog sighed and lay down at the man's feet and put its muzzle upon its paws.

"That's a lean wolf," Lars said slowly. "That's a wolf that went out to hunt when there was no hunting."

"Yes," said Anna.

He got up off his knees. He went to the corner and stood once more over the little heap of grub, and he looked at it for a long while, and she saw his lips moving as he counted, the way she had counted it so many nights in the dark. Then he went to the stove and picked up the moccasin from where he had thrown it, and he turned it over in his hands, and he looked at it as though he had never seen it before.

"Pelletier will be sorry," he said, "when he comes back up the river and finds us still here to feed him."

It was not much of a jest, but she smiled at it, and the smile was the first warmth that had been in the cabin that night.

He sat down again upon the upturned box and went on greasing the moccasin, slowly, carefully, working the fat into the seams. But his eyes were not on the door now. They were on the woman at the table, and they stayed there, and from time to time he shook his head a little, as a man does who has come up out of deep water and is not yet sure of the ground beneath him.

Anna rose and put a stick of wood into the stove, and the fire took it and roared, and for a moment the cabin was bright. Then the roar died down to a steady muttering, and the cold pressed in again upon the logs, patient and immense. The thermometer on the shelf still sulked at sixty-five below. The spruce trees still split in the night. The White Silence still stood waiting beyond the walls, as it had stood since the beginning of the world, and as it would stand when the cabin was a heap of moss-grown logs and the two who sheltered in it were less than a memory.

But for this night, at least, it waited in vain. The little spark of warmth held. And the man sat by the fire and did not go.

The cold had come down upon the Stewart River country like a hand that closes and does not open again. For a week the spirit thermometer at the Mayo cabin had stood below sixty, and on the eighth day the spirit had shrunk into the bulb and lay there, a little dead bead of red, and Lon Brayton had ceased to look at it. There was no need. A man who had wintered seven times in the Yukon basin did not require glass and alcohol to tell him what the frost was doing. He knew it by the way his spittle crackled in the air before it struck the snow, by the way the dogs lay curled with their tails across their noses and would not rise for the whip, by the way the very logs of his cabin talked in the night, splitting and groaning as the sap in them went to iron.

He was a big man, Lon Brayton, with a big man's slowness of movement that was not slowness at all but economy, the economy that the North beats into those it does not kill. His beard was black and grew close to his eyes, and his eyes were gray and very quiet, and when he looked at a thing he looked at it as though he were measuring how much it would cost him. Everything in that land had its cost. Fire cost wood, and wood cost the labor of the axe, and the labor of the axe cost meat, and meat cost the long hunt in the snow, and the long hunt cost something of a man that he did not get back. Lon Brayton had paid out a great deal in seven years, and he had received gold for it, a fair amount of gold, sewn into moosehide pokes and buried beneath the floor of his cache. But he did not think often of the gold. He had learned that the gold was the least of what the land gave and the least of what it took.

On this night he sat before his stove, mending a dog harness by the light of a slush lamp, when the huskies outside broke into clamor. It was not the long wolf howl they lifted to the stars at midnight, the old song of their kind, full of the sorrow of existence. It was a sharp and savage outcry, the challenge of the pack to strange dogs. Lon laid down his awl and listened. Through the clamor came another sound, faint and cracked, the voice of a man calling to his team, and the voice was weak and it broke in the middle of a word.

He drew on his parka and his mittens and went out. The cold struck him in the face like a flung handful of needles. Overhead the aurora was writhing, great pale streamers of green and rose that flared and faded and flared again across the zenith, and by that unearthly light he saw a sled coming up from the river ice, and five dogs before it, crawling, their bellies in the snow, and behind the sled a man who walked as a drunken man walks, holding to the handlebar and stumbling and holding again.

Lon went down to him. He beat his own dogs back with his fists and took the stranger by the arm. The man's beard was a solid mass of ice, so that his mouth was sealed in a muzzle of his own frozen breath, and his eyelashes were beaded white, and his cheekbones showed the dead yellowish patches that Lon knew too well.

"Inside," Lon said. "Leave the dogs. I'll tend 'em."

The man made a sound behind his ice muzzle that might have been a word. Lon did not wait to make it out. He half carried him up the slope and through the door and set him on the bunk, and then he went back out into the frost and unharnessed the stranger's team, and threw them each a dried salmon, and stood a moment with his own dogs snarling about his legs, looking at the sled.

It was a poor outfit. The sled was too heavy and too long, the kind the outfitters at Skaguay sold to men who did not know better. The lashings were tied with knots that would not hold and had not held, for the load had shifted and been retied by fingers too stiff to do the work properly. There was a rifle, a good one, and an axe with a handle too short. A cheechako's outfit. Lon grunted and went back in.

The stranger had not moved from where he had been set. He sat with his mittened hands lying open on his knees and stared at the stove. Lon knelt before him and with his own bare hands began to break the ice from his beard, cracking it off in chunks and flinging it into the woodbox. It came away with hair in it. The man did not flinch. He was past flinching. Lon pulled off the stranger's mittens and looked at the fingers. They were white but not hard, and he grunted again, satisfied. Then he went to the door and scooped a pan of snow and came back and began to rub the dead patches on the cheekbones.

It was then, with the ice gone from the face and the lamplight falling full upon it, that Lon Brayton stopped rubbing and sat back on his heels.

"Clem," he said.

The man's eyes came slowly away from the stove and found his. They were blue eyes, pale and watery from the cold, and they looked at Lon a long time before anything moved behind them.

"I was looking for you," the man said. His voice was a whisper. "They told me at Stewart Crossing you were up this way. I been three days."

"Three days from the Crossing? It's a day and a half."

"I got off the trail. Went up a slough."

Lon Brayton said nothing. He took up the snow again and went on rubbing, and the man's face, under his hard palms, began to burn red and then purple, and the man groaned as the blood came back. It is a cruel thing, the return of blood to frozen flesh. Lon went on rubbing until he was satisfied and then got up and put coffee on and cut bacon into the pan.

Clem Ashby was his cousin, the son of his mother's sister, and they had been raised together under one roof on a rocky hill farm in the Sonoma country when they were boys, after Lon's own father had gone down with his schooner off Point Reyes and left a widow with nothing but a boy and a debt. Lon remembered the farm. He remembered the fog that came in over the hills from the sea in the summer mornings, and the smell of the wet oaks, and the long sullen labor of clearing the stones from the fields, stones that came up fresh every spring as though the earth bred them. He remembered Clem as a slim, quick, laughing boy, a year younger than himself and a head shorter, who could talk his way out of any whipping and who had a way with the girls at the Grange dances that Lon, big and slow and silent, had watched with a dull envy he had never put into words.

That had been fourteen years ago. Seven of them Lon had spent in the North, and the seven before that in the forecastles of lumber schooners and sealers and on the wheat ranches of the San Joaquin, drifting, always drifting, with something gnawing at him that he did not understand and did not try to. And in all that time he had not seen his cousin's face. He had had letters, three or four of them, at long intervals, which had come in over the ice to Forty Mile and Dawson, and he had read them once and put them away.

He looked now at the man on the bunk. The slim quick boy was gone. The man was thin, but it was not the thinness of youth; it was the thinness of a body that has been worn down, and the face, now that the frost was out of it, showed lines about the mouth that had not come from laughing. The hair at the temples was gray. Clem Ashby was thirty-three years old, and he looked forty-five.

They ate in silence. Clem ate as a starving man eats, wolfishly, without looking up, and Lon watched him and filled his plate again and said nothing until the second plate was empty and the man had pushed it back and sat holding his tin cup of coffee in both hands, as though the warmth of it were a living thing he was afraid would get away.

"Well," Lon said. "You came a long way."

"I came a long way."

"How's my mother?"

Clem looked into his cup. "She's well enough. She's old, Lon. She keeps the place. Hires the Petersen boy to do the plowing. She asked me to tell you she reads your letters every Sunday after meeting."

Lon nodded slowly. He had written his mother twice a year, and twice a year he had sent her a draft on the Canadian bank, and she had written back in her careful cramped hand that she did not need the money and was putting it by for him. He thought of her now sitting in the kitchen of the old house with the lamp lit and his letters spread before her, and something moved in his chest that he did not care to look at.

"And Aunt Martha?"

"Dead. Four years back. The pneumonia."

"I didn't hear."

"I wrote. Maybe it didn't come through."

"Maybe it didn't." Lon was silent a while. He remembered his Aunt Martha, a tall, bony, hard-handed woman who had taken in her widowed sister and her sister's boy without a word of complaint and had worked them all, herself hardest of all, from dark to dark. She had whipped him once for letting the calves into the corn, and he had hated her for a week, and then she had given him a jackknife on his birthday, the first thing he had ever owned that was his alone. He found that he could not remember her face clearly. It had worn smooth in his mind, like a coin.

"She was a good woman," he said.

"She was."

The stove roared. Outside the dogs had quieted, and the great silence of the land came in through the chinks of the cabin and sat with them, the silence that is not an absence of sound but a presence, heavy and patient and indifferent, the silence that waits.

"You're married," Lon said. "You wrote that."

Clem's hands tightened on the cup.

"Nell," Lon said. "Nell Sorensen."

"Yes."

Lon Brayton looked at the stove. Fourteen years. He could see her, if he let himself, standing by the creek below the Sorensen place with her yellow hair down her back and her skirt kilted up, laughing at something, and he could see himself on the far bank, big and red-faced and dumb, unable to find one word to say to her, and he could see Clem crossing the creek on the stepping stones as light as a cat and sitting down beside her as though he had every right in the world. He had left the farm that autumn. He had told himself and told his mother that he was going to sea because there was no money on the farm and never would be. It had been true, as far as it went.

He had thought the North had burned that out of him, as it burned out so much. He found now that it had not. It had only frozen it, as the frost freezes a dead thing in the ice and keeps it whole and perfect through the long months, so that when the thaw comes it is there exactly as it was.

"How is she?" he asked, and his voice was steady.

Clem set his cup down on the table, very carefully, as though it were full to the brim, though it was empty.

"She's dead, Lon."

The fire talked in the stove. A log in the wall cracked like a pistol shot in the frost, and neither man started.

"Last spring," Clem said. "There was a baby. It didn't live and she didn't either. The doctor was drunk. I rode for him eleven miles and he was drunk when I found him, and by the time I'd sobered him and got him back—" He stopped. He looked at his hands. They were burned and blistered from the frost, and they shook. "It was raining. I remember that. It rained the whole night."

Lon Brayton sat very still. He had seen many men die in the North. He had seen them die of scurvy, slowly, their gums rotting and their old wounds opening; he had seen them go through the ice; he had helped dig, with fire and pick through the frozen muck, the grave of a man who had been crushed by a falling spruce. He had come to think of death as a plain fact of the land, like the frost and the long dark, a thing that the strong survived for a while and the weak did not, and that in the end took strong and weak alike. He had thought he had made his peace with it. But this was another thing. This was a girl with yellow hair laughing by a creek in the Sonoma hills, and she was dead, and she had been dead nine months, and he had been out on his claim on Haggerty Creek all that while, burning down to bedrock and thinking of nothing, nothing at all.

"I'm sorry, Clem," he said at last. The words were heavy and clumsy and of no use, and he knew it.

"I sold the place," Clem went on, as though he had not heard. "I couldn't stay. Every board in it—" He made a small gesture with his ruined hand. "I put the money in the bank at Santa Rosa and the bank broke in August. I had enough left for the steamer to Skaguay and the outfit. They told me there was gold up here. They told me a man could start fresh." He laughed, and it was a terrible little sound, dry as a stick breaking. "Start fresh. I near died in a slough three miles from your door, Lon, because I didn't know the difference between a slough and a river. I've been near dying all the way from the Pass. I don't know anything. I don't know how to do anything here."

"No," Lon said. "You don't."

Clem looked up at him then, quick and stung, and for a moment Lon saw the boy again, the quick proud boy who could not bear to be beaten at anything. Then it went out of his face and he only looked tired.

"No," he agreed. "I don't. I came because you're all the blood I've got left, Lon. Your mother's old. There's nobody else. I came because I had to go somewhere."

Lon Brayton got up from the table and went to the door and opened it and stood in it, and the frost poured in past him in a white smoke along the floor. He looked out at the night. The aurora had faded and the stars were out, hard and many and very near, and below them the snow ran away in every direction, pale and endless, to the black line of the spruce, and beyond the spruce to the white hills, and beyond the hills to other hills, and so on to the edge of the world. It was a land that did not care. It did not care whether a man came to it for gold or for grief, whether he was strong or weak, whether he had loved a woman or lost her. It asked only one thing, and asked it without pity: Can you endure? And to those who could not, it gave the long sleep in the snow, and to those who could, it gave nothing but the chance to go on enduring.

He thought of the years. He thought of the forecastles and the wheat fields and the long trail over the Chilkoot with a hundred pounds on his back and the ice of the Yukon breaking up in the spring with a roar like the end of the world. He thought of all the miles he had put between himself and a creek in the Sonoma hills, and he saw now that he had been running, all those years, and that the thing he had been running from had not followed him, had not cared, had simply gone on and lived its life and died its death without him. There was a bitterness in that, and a strange relief, and a great emptiness, and he stood in the door with the frost eating at his face and let all of it pass through him until it was gone.

He shut the door and came back.

"You'll stay the winter," he said.

Clem shook his head. "I didn't come to be carried, Lon."

"You'll be carried till you can walk. Then you'll walk." Lon sat down heavily and looked at his cousin across the table. "Listen to me. This is a hard country. It's harder than you know and harder than I can tell you. It's killed better men than you and it's killed worse, and it don't care which. You came in with a cheechako's outfit and a cheechako's head, and if I hadn't been here you'd be lying in that slough with your dogs eating the harness off you. That's the truth, and I ain't saying it to shame you."

"I know it."

"I've got ground on Haggerty Creek. It's good ground. There's more of it than one man can work. I've been working it alone four years because I never found a man I wanted for a partner." He paused. "I didn't want one. I'll tell you that straight. I didn't want anybody."

Clem was watching him.

"In the spring," Lon said, "when you've learned how to cut wood so it'll burn and how to make a fire that won't go out and how to know a slough from a river, you'll go up to Haggerty with me. Half shares."

"Lon—"

"Half shares. I don't need it. I've got more in the cache than I'll ever spend. And there's nothing to spend it on." He looked down at his own hands, big and scarred and black-nailed, lying on the table. "I've got nobody to spend it on."

They sat a long while without speaking. The stove ticked as it cooled, and Lon got up and fed it, and the flames roared up again. Clem's head had begun to nod, and his eyes kept falling shut, and each time he jerked them open, as a man does who has been fighting sleep in the cold for three days and knows that sleep is death.

"Lie down," Lon said. "It's safe here. You can sleep."

Clem looked at him, and something broke in his face, something that had been held hard for a long time, and he put his head down on his arms on the table and his shoulders shook. He made no sound. Lon Brayton sat across from him and did not touch him and did not speak. He let him be. It was not a thing that words could mend, and he had learned, in the North, that there are hurts a man must be let alone to bear, as a wounded dog crawls off into the brush to lick itself. After a time the shaking stopped, and Clem's breathing grew long and even, and he was asleep where he sat.

Then Lon rose and lifted him, as easily as he would have lifted a child, and laid him in the bunk and drew the rabbit-skin robe over him. He stood looking down at the gray-templed head and the scarred, frost-blackened cheeks. He thought of two boys picking stones from a hill field in the fog, cursing the stones and the fog and the old woman who had set them to it, and laughing, and racing each other to the end of the row. They had been very young. The world had seemed very large and very easy.

He turned down the slush lamp and sat before the stove with his hands on his knees. He did not sleep. Outside, one of the dogs lifted its muzzle to the stars and began the long howl, and the others took it up, one after another, until the whole pack was singing, the old song, wild and sorrowful and without hope, the song of all living things that are born and struggle and die beneath an indifferent sky. Lon Brayton listened to it. He had heard it a thousand times, and he had always thought it a lonely sound. Tonight, for the first time in seven years, it did not seem so lonely, and he sat with it until the long night wore toward a morning that would bring no sun, and the man in the bunk behind him slept on.

The short day had already burned itself out when Jim Haughton swung down the last bend of the trail and came in sight of the cabin. Behind him, across the wide flat of the Stewart, the sun had made its brief, half-hearted circuit above the southern rim of the world and gone down again, leaving a cold and bloodless light that lingered without warmth upon the snow. The spirit thermometer on the cache-post had stood at fifty-three below when he started out that morning to run his line of traps, and he knew by the bite in his nostrils and the brittle crackle of his own breath that it had dropped lower since. It was the kind of cold that did not tolerate mistakes. A man in such cold lived by small things: by dry socks, by the angle of his mitten upon the gee-pole, by the matches in the oilskin at his breast. Neglect any of them for the space of a quarter of an hour, and the cold came in and took him.

He was a big man, heavy in the shoulder and long in the arm, with a face that the wind and frost of six winters had weathered to the colour and texture of saddle leather. A rime of frozen breath sheathed his beard and moustache, and he had to break the ice from his lashes with his mittened thumb before he could see clearly. What he saw brought him up short in his tracks.

There was no smoke above the cabin.

For a moment he stood quite still, and the dogs, sensing the change in him, ceased their whining and stood still too. Then he was running, the snowshoes clacking and slithering beneath him, the sled forgotten, the dogs bunching and tangling in their traces behind. He knew before he flung open the door what he would find, and he found it. The stove was dead. The kettle on it had frozen solid and split its seam. The bunk where the boy slept was empty, and the small fur parka that should have hung upon its peg was gone.

"Davy!" he roared, and the walls of the cabin flung the name back at him, small and foolish. He went out again into the deepening gloom and shouted it once more across the frozen land, and the land gave him back nothing, not even an echo. It was a vast land and an indifferent one, and it had swallowed bigger things than a six-year-old boy without so much as a ripple upon its white face.

It was then that the fear came upon him, and it was not the fear he had known in other places, on the Chilkoot in the avalanche or on the rotten ice of Lake Le Barge when the team had gone through. That had been a clean fear, a fear for his own hide, and it had sharpened him and made him quick. This was another thing. It came up from somewhere deep and old in him, from the dim places where the race had crouched about its fires in the long night and listened for the padding of beasts beyond the circle of the light. It was the fear of the creature for its young, and it turned his bowels to water and his heart to a hammering fist against his ribs.

But he was a man of the North, and the North had taught him that fear which does not work is so much wasted heat. He found the tracks easily enough. They were small tracks, the round, toed-in prints of little moccasins, and they led away from the cabin past the woodpile and on beyond the blazed spruce at the edge of the clearing. Haughton's jaw set hard at sight of that spruce. He had blazed it himself in the fall, chopping the white wound deep into the trunk at the height of the boy's eyes, and he had stood the boy before it and told him, as plain as a man could tell anything, that the world ended there. Beyond the spruce was the river, and the woods, and the cold, and all the things that ate small boys. Inside the spruce was the cabin, and the fire, and safety. The boy had nodded his solemn little nod and said that he understood.

The tracks went past the spruce without a waver.

They led down the bank and out upon the river, and Haughton followed them at a lope, his eyes on the snow, his breath sawing in his throat. They wandered, those tracks. Here they had stopped, and the snow was trampled as though the boy had stood a long while looking at something. Here, a little further, was the dainty, mincing trail of a fox, crossing the river from the far bank, and the moccasin prints turned and followed it. Haughton understood then. The boy had seen the fox, or seen its tracks, and the hunting thing that lies in every man-child had awakened and drawn him on, as it had drawn the boy's father and his father's fathers, back and back into the dark of time. It was a good thing, that hunting instinct. It had made the race what it was. But in a child of six, at fifty-three below, it was a thing that killed.

He found the boy a mile down the river, under the lee of a cutbank where the fox trail went up and over and lost itself in the timber. The boy had tried to climb after it and failed, and he had sat down in the snow at the foot of the bank, and he was sitting there still. He was not crying. He was past crying. He sat with his small mittened hands in his lap and his head drooping forward, and when his father came up he lifted his face slowly, like one who wakes from a deep sleep, and smiled.

"I most got him, Daddy," he said. His voice was thick and slurred. "He was a red one."

Haughton saw that his cheeks were white. Not the pink white of a child's skin, but the dead, waxen white of frozen flesh, two hard patches the size of dollar pieces, and the tip of his nose the same. He saw, too, the drowsy droop of the eyelids and the slowness of the smile, and he knew what they meant. He had seen that slowness before, in grown men, and he had seen what followed it. The cold had got inside the boy. It had crept in through the clothing and the skin, and it was moving now upon the small, stubborn engine of the heart, and in a little while longer the boy would have lain down in the snow, very comfortably and very peacefully, and gone to sleep, and in the spring, when the ice went out, the river would have taken what was left.

He did not speak. There was no time for speech. He tore off his own mitten and scooped up snow and fell to rubbing the white cheeks, hard, with the brutal, rasping strength of a man who has learned that gentleness is a luxury the cold does not permit. The boy cried out at that, and twisted, and Haughton was glad of the cry, for it meant there was fight in him yet. He rubbed until the white went red and angry, and the boy wailed and struck at him with small fists. Then he stripped off his own parka and bundled the child inside it, and caught him up against his chest, and set off back up the river at a dogtrot, the cold driving in through his shirt like the thrust of a knife and his bare hand already gone numb and senseless.

It was full dark when he reached the cabin. The dogs had dragged the sled up to the door and lay curled in the snow beside it, tails over noses, and they lifted their heads and watched him go in. He laid the boy upon the bunk and built up the fire with shaking fingers, splitting kindling with his knife and coaxing the flame until it roared up red in the stovepipe and the iron began to tick and crackle with the heat. Then he turned to the boy, and for the better part of an hour he worked over him, chafing his hands and feet, rubbing the life back into the small limbs, watching the colour come and the drowsiness go, until at last the child sat up of his own accord and began to cry in earnest, a hearty, howling, outraged crying that was the sweetest sound Jim Haughton had heard in all his years upon the Yukon.

And then, the work being done and the danger past, the anger came.

It rose in him slowly, the way the river rises in the spring when the ice begins to groan and buckle. It was made of the fear, and of the long run down the river, and of the white patches on the boy's cheeks, and of the blazed spruce that the boy had walked past without a glance. It was made, too, of other things, of a grave at Sheep Camp under the shoulder of the pass, where the boy's mother lay with the rocks heaped over her against the wolves, and of the promise he had made above that grave with the snow driving into his face. He had promised to bring the boy through. He had promised it to her and to himself and to whatever God there was that looked down upon the trail of the Ninety-Eight, and today, because of a fox and a child's heedlessness, he had come within a hair of breaking that promise.

He stood up from beside the bunk, and he was very tall in the low cabin, so that his head nearly brushed the ridgepole, and his shadow, flung by the open door of the stove, went up the log wall and across the ceiling and hung over the boy like a great dark wing. The boy stopped crying. He looked up at his father, and something in his father's face made him draw back against the wall.

"Davy," said Haughton, and his voice was low and hard. "You get up off that bunk and stand there in front of me."

The boy got up. He stood in his little stockinged feet upon the rough puncheon floor, and his chin trembled, but he held it up. He was a Haughton, and there was that much in him.

"Where's the spruce?" said Haughton.

The boy did not answer.

"I asked you a question. Where's the spruce I blazed?"

"By—by the woodpile," the boy whispered.

"And what did I tell you about that spruce?"

"That I wasn't to go past it."

"And why weren't you to go past it?"

The boy's eyes slid away to the fire. "'Cause of the cold," he said. "And the river. And things."

"'Cause of the cold," Haughton repeated. "'Cause of the cold." He said it twice more under his breath, and his great hands opened and closed at his sides, and the boy watched those hands. For a long moment Haughton himself did not know what those hands would do.

He had been raised hard. His own father had been a Michigan lumberjack, a man with a fist like a maul and a temper like a crown fire, and Jim Haughton had learned his lessons under the strap and the open hand. He had learned them well, too. They had made him tough, and the toughness had carried him through the passes and down the rivers and through six winters of the Northland when softer men had died like flies around him. There was a voice in him now that said: Thrash the boy. Thrash him till he remembers. Thrash him till the memory of it is burned into his hide, and the next time he looks past that spruce he will feel the strap across his legs and turn back. It was an old voice, as old as the fear, and it had the authority of all the generations behind it.

But there was another thing in him, too, and he did not have a name for it. It was a thing that the North had taught him, in the long nights when a man has nothing to do but lie in his blankets and listen to the cold cracking in the timber and think. The North did not thrash a man. The North did not raise its voice. It simply waited, with an infinite and passionless patience, for the man to make his mistake, and when he made it, it killed him. It killed him without anger and without malice, as a man might brush a mosquito from his wrist. There was no learning in that. A dead man learned nothing. And Jim Haughton saw, standing there with his shadow over his son, that a strap would teach the boy to fear his father, but it would not teach him to fear the cold, and it was the cold that would be waiting for him when his father was not there.

So he did not strike. He knelt instead, slowly, so that his eyes were on a level with the boy's, and he took the small hands in his own great scarred ones, and he spoke.

"Davy," he said, "you listen to me, and you listen good, for I'm only going to say this the once. You see these hands?"

The boy nodded.

"Count the fingers on 'em."

The boy counted, his lips moving. He came to the end of the left hand and stopped, puzzled. There were only three fingers there, and a thumb, and a smooth, shiny stub of scar where the fourth should have been.

"That's the cold," said Haughton. "That's the cold on the Pelly, three winters back. I was a grown man, and I knew the country, and I'd been told. And I got careless for ten minutes, just ten minutes, fixing a harness without my mitts on, and the cold came in and took that finger, and I had to cut it off myself with a knife by the light of the fire. I was lucky. It could have been the hand. It could have been the whole of me." He paused, and his grip tightened. "You remember Swede Anderson, that come by here in the fall and give you the sugar lump?"

"Yes," whispered the boy.

"Swede's dead. They found him a month back on the Sixty Mile, sitting up against a tree with his matches in his lap. He'd got his feet wet in an overflow and tried to build a fire, and his hands was too far gone to strike a light. He was a strong man, Swede. Stronger than me. He could carry two hundred pound up the Chilkoot without stopping to blow. But the cold didn't care how strong he was. The cold don't care about nothing."

The boy's eyes had grown very wide. The firelight glistened in them.

"Now you listen," said Haughton, and his voice dropped lower still, so that the boy had to lean toward him to hear. "This country ain't like a town. In a town, if you're bad, a man takes a switch to you and that's the end of it. Here it ain't like that. Here, if you're careless, if you forget, if you go chasing a fox past where you've been told, the country don't switch you. It kills you. It don't get mad. It don't give you a second chance. It just kills you, quiet and easy, and you sit down in the snow and go to sleep, and you never wake up. You were going to sleep today, Davy. Down under that cutbank. Another half hour and you'd have been gone, and I'd have found you stiff as a stick of stovewood." His voice cracked on the last word, and he stopped, and looked at the floor a moment, and when he went on it was steadier. "And then I'd be all alone up here. I'd have nobody. Your ma's gone, and you'd be gone, and there'd be nobody but me and the dogs and the cold. You understand what I'm telling you?"

The boy's chin had begun to tremble again, but it was a different trembling now. "I didn't mean to, Daddy," he said. "The fox was so red. And I thought I'd catch him and bring him home and you'd be glad."

Haughton closed his eyes. It was the oldest excuse in the world, and the truest, and he had used it himself in his time. The fox was always red. There was always a fox, glimmering just beyond the line where a man had been told to stop, and the man who would live in the North must learn to let it go. Not because the fox was not beautiful, nor because the hunting was not good, but because the North set a price on everything, and some prices were too high to pay.

"I know you didn't mean to," he said. "Nobody means to. Swede didn't mean to. But meaning ain't worth a thing up here. It's doing that counts. You hear me? It's doing." He let go of the boy's hands and stood up again, slowly, and his shadow went back up the wall. "So here's what's going to happen. Tomorrow you ain't leaving this cabin. Not to the woodpile, not to the cache, not to the door. And the day after, and the day after that. You're going to sit right here by the stove and think on what I told you, and every morning I'm going to ask you about that spruce, and you're going to tell me. And when I figure you've learned it, and not a minute before, you can go out as far as the woodpile again. That's all. That's the whole of it."

It was not a hard punishment, as punishments went in that country, and Haughton knew it. But he saw by the boy's face that the boy did not think so, for there is no prison like four log walls to a child who has once smelled the free air of the river, and he was satisfied.

"Now get back in them blankets," he said, "and I'll warm you some beans."

The boy crept back into the bunk and lay there, very small and very quiet, watching his father move about the cabin. Haughton chipped ice from the water-barrel and set it to melt, and sliced bacon into the frying pan, and went out to unharness and feed the dogs, flinging each of them its frozen salmon and standing for a while in the dark while they wolfed it down. The cold struck at him through his clothing, and above his head the sky was bare and black and hard, sown thick with stars that burned with a fierce white light. Along the northern rim the aurora had begun to stir, great pale curtains of green and rose that rippled and folded upon themselves in utter silence, and he stood with his back against the cabin wall and watched them, and felt the vastness of the land pressing in upon him from every side.

It was a cruel land. There was no getting around that. It had no love in it, nor hate either, but only an endless, grinding indifference, and against that indifference a man had nothing but his wits and his strength and his small, stubborn will to live. He had brought the boy into it, because there had been nowhere else to bring him, and some nights he lay awake and cursed himself for it. But tonight, standing under the cold fire of the sky, he found himself thinking that perhaps it was not so bad a school. A boy raised in a town might grow up never knowing that the world could kill him. A boy raised here would know it in his bones before he was ten, and the knowing would make him wary, and the wariness would make him strong, and some day, when Jim Haughton was old and slow and the cold had at last come in and taken him, the boy would stand where he stood now and look up at the lights and not be afraid.

That was what a father could give. Not safety; there was no safety under that sky. Only the knowledge of the danger, passed down hand to hand, as the race had passed it down since the first man crouched shivering at the mouth of the first cave and taught his son to fear the dark.

When he went back in, the boy had fallen asleep. He lay curled upon his side, one small fist against his mouth, and the frostbitten patches stood out red and raw upon his cheeks. In a few days they would scab and peel, and in a few weeks they would be gone, and only the memory would remain. Haughton hoped it would remain. He sat down upon the edge of the bunk and looked at his son for a long time, while the bacon spat and smoked in the pan behind him and the fire roared in the iron belly of the stove, and once, very lightly, so as not to wake him, he laid his maimed hand upon the boy's tousled head.

Outside, in the darkness, one of the dogs lifted its muzzle to the stars and gave tongue, a long, quavering, wolfish howl, and the others took it up, one by one, until the whole of the night was full of their ancient sorrow. But the boy did not stir, and the man did not take away his hand.
