Not but that I was afloat in a safe craft, for the Martinez was a new ferry-steamer, making her fourth or fifth trip on the run between Sausalito and San Francisco. The danger lay in the heavy fog which blanketed the bay, and of which, as a landsman, I had little apprehension. In fact, I remember the placid exaltation with which I took up my position on the forward upper deck, directly beneath the pilot-house, and allowed the mystery of the fog to lay hold of my imagination. A fresh breeze was blowing, and for a time I was alone in the moist obscurity—yet not alone, for I was dimly conscious of the presence of the pilot, and of what I took to be the captain, in the glass house above my head. I remember thinking how comfortable it was, this division of labour which made it unnecessary for me to study fogs, winds, tides, and navigation, in order to visit my friend who lived across an arm of the sea. It was good that men should be specialists, I mused. The peculiar knowledge of the pilot and captain sufficed for many thousands of people who knew no more of the sea and navigation than I knew. On the other hand, instead of having to devote my energy to the learning of a multitude of things, I concentrated it upon a few particular things, such as, for instance, the analysis of Poe’s place in American literature—an essay of mine, by the way, in the current Atlantic. Coming aboard, as I passed through the cabin, I had noticed with greedy eyes a stout gentleman reading the Atlantic, which was open at my very essay. And there it was again, the division of labour, the special knowledge of the pilot and captain which permitted the stout gentleman to read my special knowledge on Poe while they carried him safely from Sausalito to San Francisco. A red-faced man, slamming the cabin door behind him and stumping out on the deck, interrupted my reflections, though I made a mental note of the topic for use in a projected essay which I had thought of calling “The Necessity for Freedom: A Plea for the Artist.” The red-faced man shot a glance up at the pilot-house, gazed around at the fog, stumped across the deck and back (he evidently had artificial legs), and stood still by my side, legs wide apart, and with an expression of keen enjoyment on his face. I was not wrong when I decided that his days had been spent on the sea.

“It’s nasty weather like this here that turns heads grey before their time,” he said, with a nod toward the pilot-house.

“I had not thought there was any particular strain,” I answered. “It seems as simple as A, B, C. They know the direction by compass, the distance, and the speed. I should not call it anything more than mathematical certainty.”

“Strain!” he snorted. “Simple as A, B, C! Mathematical certainty!” He seemed to brace himself up and lean backward against the air as he stared at me. “How about this here tide that’s rushin’ out through the Golden Gate?” he demanded, or bellowed, rather. “How fast is she ebbin’? What’s the drift, eh? Listen to that, will you? A bell-buoy, and we’re a-top of it! See ’em alterin’ the course!” From out of the fog came the mournful tolling of a bell, and I could see the pilot turning the wheel with great rapidity. The bell, which had seemed straight ahead, was now sounding from the side. Our own whistle was blowing hoarsely, and from time to time the sound of other whistles came to us from out of the fog.

“That’s a ferry-boat of some sort,” the new-comer said, indicating a whistle off to the right. “And there! D’ye hear that? Blown by mouth. Some scow schooner, most likely. Better watch out, Mr. Schooner-man. Ah, I thought so. Now hell’s a poppin’ for somebody!” The unseen ferry-boat was blowing blast after blast, and the mouth-blown horn was tooting in terror-stricken fashion.

“And now they’re payin’ their respects to each other and tryin’ to get clear,” the red-faced man went on, as the hurried whistling ceased. His face was shining, his eyes flashing with excitement as he translated into articulate language the speech of the horns and sirens. “That’s a steam-siren a-goin’ it over there to the left. And you hear that fellow with a frog in his throat—a steam schooner as near as I can judge, crawlin’ in from the Heads against the tide.” A shrill little whistle, piping as if gone mad, came from directly ahead and from very near at hand. Gongs sounded on the Martinez. Our paddle-wheels stopped, their pulsing beat died away, and then they started again. The shrill little whistle, like the chirping of a cricket amid the cries of great beasts, shot through the fog from more to the side and swiftly grew faint and fainter. I looked to my companion for enlightenment.

“One of them dare-devil launches,” he said. “I almost wish we’d sunk him, the little rip! They’re the cause of more trouble. And what good are they? Any jackass gets aboard one and runs it from hell to breakfast, blowin’ his whistle to beat the band and tellin’ the rest of the world to look out for him, because he’s comin’ and can’t look out for himself! Because he’s comin’! And you’ve got to look out, too! Right of way! Common decency! They don’t know the meanin’ of it!” I felt quite amused at his unwarranted choler, and while he stumped indignantly up and down I fell to dwelling upon the romance of the fog. And romantic it certainly was—the fog, like the grey shadow of infinite mystery, brooding over the whirling speck of earth; and men, mere motes of light and sparkle, cursed with an insane relish for work, riding their steeds of wood and steel through the heart of the mystery, groping their way blindly through the Unseen, and clamouring and clanging in confident speech the while their hearts are heavy with incertitude and fear. The voice of my companion brought me back to myself with a laugh. I too had been groping and floundering, the while I thought I rode clear-eyed through the mystery.

“Hello! somebody comin’ our way,” he was saying. “And d’ye hear that? He’s comin’ fast. Walking right along. Guess he don’t hear us yet. Wind’s in wrong direction.” The fresh breeze was blowing right down upon us, and I could hear the whistle plainly, off to one side and a little ahead.

“Ferry-boat?” I asked. He nodded, then added, “Or he wouldn’t be keepin’ up such a clip.” He gave a short chuckle. “They’re gettin’ anxious up there.” I glanced up. The captain had thrust his head and shoulders out of the pilot-house, and was staring intently into the fog as though by sheer force of will he could penetrate it. His face was anxious, as was the face of my companion, who had stumped over to the rail and was gazing with a like intentness in the direction of the invisible danger. Then everything happened, and with inconceivable rapidity. The fog seemed to break away as though split by a wedge, and the bow of a steamboat emerged, trailing fog-wreaths on either side like seaweed on the snout of Leviathan. I could see the pilot-house and a white-bearded man leaning partly out of it, on his elbows. He was clad in a blue uniform, and I remember noting how trim and quiet he was. His quietness, under the circumstances, was terrible. He accepted Destiny, marched hand in hand with it, and coolly measured the stroke. As he leaned there, he ran a calm and speculative eye over us, as though to determine the precise point of the collision, and took no notice whatever when our pilot, white with rage, shouted, “Now you’ve done it!” On looking back, I realize that the remark was too obvious to make rejoinder necessary.

“Grab hold of something and hang on,” the red-faced man said to me. All his bluster had gone, and he seemed to have caught the contagion of preternatural calm. “And listen to the women scream,” he said grimly—almost bitterly, I thought, as though he had been through the experience before. The vessels came together before I could follow his advice. We must have been struck squarely amidships, for I saw nothing, the strange steamboat having passed beyond my line of vision. The Martinez heeled over, sharply, and there was a crashing and rending of timber. I was thrown flat on the wet deck, and before I could scramble to my feet I heard the scream of the women. This it was, I am certain,—the most indescribable of blood-curdling sounds,—that threw me into a panic. I remembered the life-preservers stored in the cabin, but was met at the door and swept backward by a wild rush of men and women. What happened in the next few minutes I do not recollect, though I have a clear remembrance of pulling down life-preservers from the overhead racks, while the red-faced man fastened them about the bodies of an hysterical group of women. This memory is as distinct and sharp as that of any picture I have seen. It is a picture, and I can see it now,—the jagged edges of the hole in the side of the cabin, through which the grey fog swirled and eddied; the empty upholstered seats, littered with all the evidences of sudden flight, such as packages, hand satchels, umbrellas, and wraps; the stout gentleman who had been reading my essay, encased in cork and canvas, the magazine still in his hand, and asking me with monotonous insistence if I thought there was any danger; the red-faced man, stumping gallantly around on his artificial legs and buckling life-preservers on all comers; and finally, the screaming bedlam of women. This it was, the screaming of the women, that most tried my nerves. It must have tried, too, the nerves of the red-faced man, for I have another picture which will never fade from my mind. The stout gentleman is stuffing the magazine into his overcoat pocket and looking on curiously. A tangled mass of women, with drawn, white faces and open mouths, is shrieking like a chorus of lost souls; and the red-faced man, his face now purplish with wrath, and with arms extended overhead as in the act of hurling thunderbolts, is shouting, “Shut up! Oh, shut up!” I remember the scene impelled me to sudden laughter, and in the next instant I realized I was becoming hysterical myself; for these were women of my own kind, like my mother and sisters, with the fear of death upon them and unwilling to die. And I remember that the sounds they made reminded me of the squealing of pigs under the knife of the butcher, and I was struck with horror at the vividness of the analogy. These women, capable of the most sublime emotions, of the tenderest sympathies, were open-mouthed and screaming. They wanted to live, they were helpless, like rats in a trap, and they screamed. The horror of it drove me out on deck. I was feeling sick and squeamish, and sat down on a bench. In a hazy way I saw and heard men rushing and shouting as they strove to lower the boats. It was just as I had read descriptions of such scenes in books. The tackles jammed. Nothing worked. One boat lowered away with the plugs out, filled with women and children and then with water, and capsized. Another boat had been lowered by one end, and still hung in the tackle by the other end, where it had been abandoned. Nothing was to be seen of the strange steamboat which had caused the disaster, though I heard men saying that she would undoubtedly send boats to our assistance. I descended to the lower deck. The Martinez was sinking fast, for the water was very near. Numbers of the passengers were leaping overboard. Others, in the water, were clamouring to be taken aboard again. No one heeded them. A cry arose that we were sinking. I was seized by the consequent panic, and went over the side in a surge of bodies. How I went over I do not know, though I did know, and instantly, why those in the water were so desirous of getting back on the steamer. The water was cold—so cold that it was painful. The pang, as I plunged into it, was as quick and sharp as that of fire. It bit to the marrow. It was like the grip of death. I gasped with the anguish and shock of it, filling my lungs before the life-preserver popped me to the surface. The taste of the salt was strong in my mouth, and I was strangling with the acrid stuff in my throat and lungs. But it was the cold that was most distressing. I felt that I could survive but a few minutes. People were struggling and floundering in the water about me. I could hear them crying out to one another. And I heard, also, the sound of oars. Evidently the strange steamboat had lowered its boats. As the time went by I marvelled that I was still alive. I had no sensation whatever in my lower limbs, while a chilling numbness was wrapping about my heart and creeping into it. Small waves, with spiteful foaming crests, continually broke over me and into my mouth, sending me off into more strangling paroxysms. The noises grew indistinct, though I heard a final and despairing chorus of screams in the distance, and knew that the Martinez had gone down. Later,—how much later I have no knowledge,—I came to myself with a start of fear. I was alone. I could hear no calls or cries—only the sound of the waves, made weirdly hollow and reverberant by the fog. A panic in a crowd, which partakes of a sort of community of interest, is not so terrible as a panic when one is by oneself; and such a panic I now suffered. Whither was I drifting? The red-faced man had said that the tide was ebbing through the Golden Gate. Was I, then, being carried out to sea? And the life-preserver in which I floated? Was it not liable to go to pieces at any moment? I had heard of such things being made of paper and hollow rushes which quickly became saturated and lost all buoyancy. And I could not swim a stroke. And I was alone, floating, apparently, in the midst of a grey primordial vastness. I confess that a madness seized me, that I shrieked aloud as the women had shrieked, and beat the water with my numb hands. How long this lasted I have no conception, for a blankness intervened, of which I remember no more than one remembers of troubled and painful sleep. When I aroused, it was as after centuries of time; and I saw, almost above me and emerging from the fog, the bow of a vessel, and three triangular sails, each shrewdly lapping the other and filled with wind. Where the bow cut the water there was a great foaming and gurgling, and I seemed directly in its path. I tried to cry out, but was too exhausted. The bow plunged down, just missing me and sending a swash of water clear over my head. Then the long, black side of the vessel began slipping past, so near that I could have touched it with my hands. I tried to reach it, in a mad resolve to claw into the wood with my nails, but my arms were heavy and lifeless. Again I strove to call out, but made no sound. The stern of the vessel shot by, dropping, as it did so, into a hollow between the waves; and I caught a glimpse of a man standing at the wheel, and of another man who seemed to be doing little else than smoke a cigar. I saw the smoke issuing from his lips as he slowly turned his head and glanced out over the water in my direction. It was a careless, unpremeditated glance, one of those haphazard things men do when they have no immediate call to do anything in particular, but act because they are alive and must do something.

The cold had come down upon the Stewart River country in the night, and by morning it had settled into that deep and abiding grip which the old-timers knew and feared, and which the new-comers, the men of the soft lands, did not know enough to fear until it had taken toll of them. The spirit thermometer nailed to the logs outside the cabin door stood at sixty-two below. It had stood there for three days. Within, the little sheet-iron stove roared and reddened, and the frost on the inner walls retreated a hand's breadth before it, only to creep back, white and patient, the instant the fire died down.

Martha Haskell sat on the edge of the bunk with her hands in her lap. They were large hands, brown and capable, the knuckles swollen and cracked from the axe and the frozen dish-water, and she looked at them now as though they belonged to some other woman. Her husband stood by the stove, his back to her, feeding it with split spruce, one stick at a time, and with a deliberation that was out of all proportion to the task. She knew that he was afraid to turn around. She had known it for a full ten minutes, ever since she had come in from the cache with the empty sack in her hand and laid it, without a word, upon the table.

It lay there still, a limp and greasy thing of burlap, and it was more eloquent than speech. It had held bacon, a full side of it, when they had freighted their outfit in over the ice in November. There had been a third of it remaining a week ago. She had measured it with her eye and with her mind, as she measured everything now—the flour, the beans, the dried apples, the tea, the little tin of baking-powder—measured it against the days and weeks that lay between them and the break-up of the river, when the first steamers would come up from St. Michael and men would eat again as men were meant to eat. And this morning the sack was empty.

"Well, John," she said at last.

He dropped another stick into the stove and closed the door upon it with the toe of his moccasin. Then he straightened and turned, and she saw his face, and she was sorry for him, and despised herself for being sorry, and despised him for making her so.

He was a slender man, and he had been a handsome one. In Oakland, behind the counter of the Bay Mercantile Company, in a starched collar and with his hair parted in the middle and slicked with bay rum, he had been very handsome indeed, and she had thought, when he courted her, that she had never seen a man with such clean hands. That was four years gone. The North had laid hold of him since, and it had not been kind. His cheeks had fallen in beneath the cheek-bones, and the frost had bitten them and left them scarred and black at the peaks. His beard grew thin and ragged. His eyes, which she had once thought gentle, had acquired a shifting, sidelong quality, like the eyes of a dog that has been whipped and expects to be whipped again.

"Well, what?" he said. He tried to make his voice hard, and it cracked in the middle.

"You know what."

"I don't know anything of the kind. If you've got something to say, Martha, say it, and be done with it. I won't be talked at in riddles."

She did not answer at once. She was a slow woman, slow of speech and slow of anger, bred on a ranch in the San Joaquin among men who said little and did much, and she had learned there that a word spoken in heat could not be called back, any more than a bullet could. So she sat and looked at him, and the silence of the cabin pressed in upon them both—a silence made the more terrible by the vaster silence without, the White Silence of the North, which lay upon the frozen river and the frozen hills and the frozen stars like the hand of God upon the face of the deep.

"There was eleven pounds of bacon in that sack a week ago Tuesday," she said. "I weighed it on the gold-scales. I weighed it because I had to know. I've been feeding you, and I've been feeding myself, and I've been feeding the dogs on what we could spare, and I know to the ounce what went into the pot. And there was eleven pounds a week ago Tuesday, John, and this morning there's none."

"The wolverine—" he began.

"There's been no wolverine. The cache is tight. I looked. And there's no tracks but yours on the ladder."

He opened his mouth, and shut it again. A dull red crept up from his beard and spread over the black frost-scars, and for a moment she thought he would strike her. She almost wished that he would. It would have been a thing a man might do; it would have been something, at least, to set against the other. But the red faded, and he sat down heavily on the box that served them for a chair, and put his face in his hands.

"I was hungry," he said, his voice muffled. "God help me, Martha, I was hungry. You don't know what it's like."

"I don't know what it's like," she repeated slowly, and she laughed—a short, hard laugh, without any mirth in it, that startled her as much as it startled him. "I don't know what it's like. I've had two spoons of beans a day since Christmas, and a bit of bannock the size of my palm. I've given you the bigger share, and you've taken it, and never asked if I'd had my own. And I don't know what it's like."

"You're stronger than I am," he said. "You always were. You were raised to it. I wasn't. I was raised in a house with a furnace in it, and a cook, and a hired girl to bring hot water up the stairs of a morning. I never knew what cold was till I came into this cursed country. I never knew what hunger was. It eats at you, Martha. It gets into your head. You lie awake at night and you can't think of anything else. I'd lie there and think of that bacon, and think of it, and think of it, till I'd get up and go out to the cache in the dark, and I'd tell myself I'd only take a little—a little strip, a mouthful, just enough to stop the gnawing—and then I couldn't stop. I couldn't stop."

She looked at him, bowed upon the box, and something cold went through her that was colder than the frost. For she saw, as in a flash of lightning across a dark landscape, the truth of the thing, and it was a truth that she had not wanted to see. It was not the bacon. Eleven pounds of bacon, more or less, would neither save them nor kill them. It was what the bacon meant. It meant that the man she had married was a man who would rob his own wife in the night to fill his belly; and more than that, it meant that the North had found him out. It had stripped him as the wind strips the leaves from the birches in the fall, and left him naked, and there was nothing underneath.

She had heard the old-timers talk of it, around the stoves at Dawson and at the Forks, when the whiskey was going round and men grew philosophic. The North, they said, did not care about a man's family, or his schooling, or the cut of his coat, or the money he had in the bank at home. It cared about one thing only, and that was whether he could stand up under it. It took the soft men and broke them, and it took the hard men and made them harder, and it took the men who were neither soft nor hard and showed them, past all argument, which they were. There was no hiding from it. A man might lie to his neighbours and to his wife and to his own soul in the cities of the South, where there was food in the shops and fire in the grates and a policeman on every corner to keep the wolf from the door. But in the North the wolf came to the door in very truth, and sat down upon the step, and waited. And when it came, there was no more lying.

"Get up, John," she said.

He lifted his head and looked at her dully.

"Get up," she said again. "I want to talk to you, and I'll not talk to the top of your head."

He got up. He stood before her, swaying a little, and she saw for the first time how thin his legs were in the heavy German socks, and how his hands trembled. Pity rose in her again, and she put it down, firmly, as she would have put down a dog that tried to steal from the table.

"Here's how it stands," she said. "There's eighteen pounds of flour, near as I can figure, and twelve of beans, and a little tea, and some of the dried apples, and that's all. There's six dogs. It's ninety miles to the Forks by the river trail, and the trail's not broke past the mouth of the McQuesten, for Lacey's outfit came through a fortnight back and said so. The break-up won't come before the middle of May, and it's the twentieth of February now. You can count as well as I can."

"We'll make it," he said. "We'll stretch it. We'll kill the dogs—"

"We'll kill the dogs, and then what? Then nobody goes anywhere. Then we sit here and wait, and starve slow instead of fast, and the last one alive digs a hole for the other in the snow, if he's got the strength for it, which he won't." She paused. "No. Somebody's got to go out to the Forks for grub. Somebody's got to take the dogs and the light sled and go now, while the dogs are fit to pull, and fetch back enough to see us through. There's flour at the Forks. Harper's got flour. He'll trust us till the clean-up."

"In this cold?" His voice rose. "In sixty below? Martha, you're crazy. It'd be death. It's sixty-two this morning; I looked. A man's lungs freeze in cold like that. His spit crackles before it hits the snow. You've seen it. You've heard it. Nobody travels in cold like this—nobody but a fool."

"Then a fool has got to go," she said quietly. "And I'm asking you, John. I'm asking you as your wife. Will you go?"

It was a long time before he answered. The stove ticked and snapped as the iron cooled. Outside, one of the dogs began to howl, a long, quavering wail that rose and rose until it seemed it must break, and then dropped and died away into the silence; and the other dogs took it up, one after another, until the whole team was singing, their muzzles pointed at the cold stars, in that ancient and mournful song which their wild forebears had sung before ever man came into the land, and which their descendants would sing when man had gone out of it. It was a song of hunger and of the long dark, and of the pitilessness of all things, and John Haskell, listening, shivered where he stood.

"I can't," he said at last. "Martha, I can't. You know I can't. I'd never get as far as the McQuesten. I'd go through the ice in some airhole, or I'd freeze my feet and lie down, and that'd be the end of it. I'm not built for it. I'm not like Lacey, or Harper, or those other fellows. I can't do it."

"No," she said. "You can't."

She said it without heat, as one might state a fact about the weather, and perhaps that was the cruellest thing of all. He flinched as though she had struck him with her open hand.

"What would you have me do?" he cried. "Go out and die, to prove I'm a man? Is that what you want? You'd sooner have a dead husband than a live one, is that it? You'd sooner—"

"I'd sooner have a husband," she said.

The words fell between them like a stone into a deep well, and they both stood waiting, as it were, to hear it strike bottom. It did not strike. It went on falling, down and down into a darkness that had no floor.

Then Martha Haskell stood up. She stood up slowly, as a woman will who has been sitting a long while in the cold, and she went to the nail beside the door where her parka hung, and took it down, and began to put it on.

"What are you doing?" he said.

"I'm going to look at the dogs' feet. Old Buck was favouring his near fore yesterday. If it's a split pad, I'll have to boot him."

"Why? What for? Martha—"

She drew the hood of the parka up over her head and turned to face him, and her eyes were very steady.

"Because I'm going, John," she said. "I'm going out to the Forks for grub, and I'm starting at first light tomorrow. You'll stay here and keep the fire going and eat what's left, and if I'm not back in three weeks you'll know I'm not coming, and you can do as you like."

He stared at her as though she had gone mad. Then he laughed, a high, cracked, unnatural laugh that frightened her more than anything he had yet said or done.

"You?" he said. "You'll go? A woman, alone, in sixty below, ninety miles over an unbroken trail? You'll be dead in two days. They'll find you in the spring, sitting up against a tree, with the dogs eaten down to the harness. Is that what you want? To shame me? To make me out a coward before the whole country, so that every sourdough from here to Circle will say, 'There goes Haskell, that let his wife go out and die for his grub'?"

"I don't care what they say," she answered. "And I'm not going out to die. I'm going out to fetch flour. There's a difference, John, though I don't expect you to see it."

"I forbid it," he said. "Do you hear me? I'm your husband, and I forbid it."

She regarded him for a long moment, and there was something in her face—something old and weary and very wise—that he had never seen there before, and that he never afterward forgot.

"You forbid it," she said. "And what will you do to stop me? Will you take the dogs yourself? Will you tie me in the bunk? You can't stop me, John. You haven't the strength. That's the whole of it, and we may as well have it out in plain words, for there's no one here to hear us but the dogs. You haven't the strength. The North has found you out, and it's found me out too, and it's no use either of us pretending any longer. You can't go, and I can. So I'll go."

"And if you die?"

"Then I'll die," she said simply. "Folks do. But I'd sooner die on the trail, going somewhere, than sit here in this cabin and watch you creep out to the cache in the dark."

She went out, then, and the door closed behind her, and the cold that had rushed in with its opening rolled across the floor in a white vapour and curled about his feet and was slowly vanquished by the stove. He stood looking at the door. He heard her moccasins squeaking on the hard-packed snow, and he heard the dogs leap up whining to greet her, and he heard her voice speaking to them, low and even, as she spoke to all dumb things. It was the voice she had used to him once, in the early days, before the North.

He sat down again on the box. The greasy bacon sack lay on the table before him, and he looked at it, and after a while he reached out and took it up in his hands. A faint smell of salt and smoke still clung to the burlap. His mouth filled with water at the smell of it, and he hated himself, and his mouth filled with water nonetheless; for hunger is older than shame, and stronger, and it does not listen when a man reproaches it.

In that moment John Haskell came near to understanding something. He came near to understanding that the world was not built as he had been taught to believe it was built, with men set over women by the ordinance of God and the custom of nations, and the strong arm of the law to keep each in his place. He came near to seeing that all such ordinances and customs were but a thin crust laid over a deeper and more ancient order, as the snow lay over the river; and that the deeper order had one law only, and that law was strength. Not the strength of the arm alone, though that was a part of it, but the strength of the will that drives the arm, the stubborn, unreasoning, invincible strength that rises up in the face of death and says, I will not lie down. Some had it and some did not. It came not by sex, nor by breeding, nor by schooling. It came as it chose. And where it came, there was the master, and where it did not come, there was the slave, and all the starched collars and all the marriage lines in Christendom could not alter it by a hair.

He came near to understanding this, but he did not quite understand it, for to understand it fully would have been to look into the bottom of his own soul, and that he had not the strength to do.

The door opened again and Martha came in, beating the frost from her mittens. She did not look at him. She went to the shelf where the flour was kept, and took down the sack, and began to measure out, with a tin cup, the portion that she would carry with her on the trail. He watched her hands moving, steady and sure. She measured very little. When she had done, she looked at the remainder, and then she looked at him, for the first time since she had come in.

"There's enough left there for you to eat a cup a day for three weeks," she said. "Not more. If you eat more, it won't last. I'm leaving it to you, John."

He understood what she was saying. She was not leaving him the flour. She was leaving him the choice. And he knew, as surely as he knew the cold was waiting beyond the door, that she did not believe he would make it rightly.

"Martha," he said hoarsely. "Martha, I—"

But she had turned away, and was mending a dog-harness by the light of the stove, her big, cracked, capable fingers working the stiff walrus-hide; and whatever it was that he had meant to say, he did not say it. Outside, the dogs had ceased their howling. The silence came down again, vast and white and patient, upon the cabin and the river and the frozen hills, as it had come down upon a thousand other cabins and a thousand other men and women in that land, and weighed them, and found them what they were.

Not but that I was afloat in a safe craft, for the Martinez was a new ferry-steamer, making her fourth or fifth trip on the run between Sausalito and San Francisco. The danger lay in the heavy fog which blanketed the bay, and of which, as a landsman, I had little apprehension. In fact, I remember the placid exaltation with which I took up my position on the forward upper deck, directly beneath the pilot-house, and allowed the mystery of the fog to lay hold of my imagination. A fresh breeze was blowing, and for a time I was alone in the moist obscurity—yet not alone, for I was dimly conscious of the presence of the pilot, and of what I took to be the captain, in the glass house above my head. I remember thinking how comfortable it was, this division of labour which made it unnecessary for me to study fogs, winds, tides, and navigation, in order to visit my friend who lived across an arm of the sea. It was good that men should be specialists, I mused. The peculiar knowledge of the pilot and captain sufficed for many thousands of people who knew no more of the sea and navigation than I knew. On the other hand, instead of having to devote my energy to the learning of a multitude of things, I concentrated it upon a few particular things, such as, for instance, the analysis of Poe’s place in American literature—an essay of mine, by the way, in the current Atlantic. Coming aboard, as I passed through the cabin, I had noticed with greedy eyes a stout gentleman reading the Atlantic, which was open at my very essay. And there it was again, the division of labour, the special knowledge of the pilot and captain which permitted the stout gentleman to read my special knowledge on Poe while they carried him safely from Sausalito to San Francisco. A red-faced man, slamming the cabin door behind him and stumping out on the deck, interrupted my reflections, though I made a mental note of the topic for use in a projected essay which I had thought of calling “The Necessity for Freedom: A Plea for the Artist.” The red-faced man shot a glance up at the pilot-house, gazed around at the fog, stumped across the deck and back (he evidently had artificial legs), and stood still by my side, legs wide apart, and with an expression of keen enjoyment on his face. I was not wrong when I decided that his days had been spent on the sea.

“It’s nasty weather like this here that turns heads grey before their time,” he said, with a nod toward the pilot-house.

“I had not thought there was any particular strain,” I answered. “It seems as simple as A, B, C. They know the direction by compass, the distance, and the speed. I should not call it anything more than mathematical certainty.”

“Strain!” he snorted. “Simple as A, B, C! Mathematical certainty!” He seemed to brace himself up and lean backward against the air as he stared at me. “How about this here tide that’s rushin’ out through the Golden Gate?” he demanded, or bellowed, rather. “How fast is she ebbin’? What’s the drift, eh? Listen to that, will you? A bell-buoy, and we’re a-top of it! See ’em alterin’ the course!” From out of the fog came the mournful tolling of a bell, and I could see the pilot turning the wheel with great rapidity. The bell, which had seemed straight ahead, was now sounding from the side. Our own whistle was blowing hoarsely, and from time to time the sound of other whistles came to us from out of the fog.

“That’s a ferry-boat of some sort,” the new-comer said, indicating a whistle off to the right. “And there! D’ye hear that? Blown by mouth. Some scow schooner, most likely. Better watch out, Mr. Schooner-man. Ah, I thought so. Now hell’s a poppin’ for somebody!” The unseen ferry-boat was blowing blast after blast, and the mouth-blown horn was tooting in terror-stricken fashion.

“And now they’re payin’ their respects to each other and tryin’ to get clear,” the red-faced man went on, as the hurried whistling ceased. His face was shining, his eyes flashing with excitement as he translated into articulate language the speech of the horns and sirens. “That’s a steam-siren a-goin’ it over there to the left. And you hear that fellow with a frog in his throat—a steam schooner as near as I can judge, crawlin’ in from the Heads against the tide.” A shrill little whistle, piping as if gone mad, came from directly ahead and from very near at hand. Gongs sounded on the Martinez. Our paddle-wheels stopped, their pulsing beat died away, and then they started again. The shrill little whistle, like the chirping of a cricket amid the cries of great beasts, shot through the fog from more to the side and swiftly grew faint and fainter. I looked to my companion for enlightenment.

“One of them dare-devil launches,” he said. “I almost wish we’d sunk him, the little rip! They’re the cause of more trouble. And what good are they? Any jackass gets aboard one and runs it from hell to breakfast, blowin’ his whistle to beat the band and tellin’ the rest of the world to look out for him, because he’s comin’ and can’t look out for himself! Because he’s comin’! And you’ve got to look out, too! Right of way! Common decency! They don’t know the meanin’ of it!” I felt quite amused at his unwarranted choler, and while he stumped indignantly up and down I fell to dwelling upon the romance of the fog. And romantic it certainly was—the fog, like the grey shadow of infinite mystery, brooding over the whirling speck of earth; and men, mere motes of light and sparkle, cursed with an insane relish for work, riding their steeds of wood and steel through the heart of the mystery, groping their way blindly through the Unseen, and clamouring and clanging in confident speech the while their hearts are heavy with incertitude and fear. The voice of my companion brought me back to myself with a laugh. I too had been groping and floundering, the while I thought I rode clear-eyed through the mystery.

“Hello! somebody comin’ our way,” he was saying. “And d’ye hear that? He’s comin’ fast. Walking right along. Guess he don’t hear us yet. Wind’s in wrong direction.” The fresh breeze was blowing right down upon us, and I could hear the whistle plainly, off to one side and a little ahead.

“Ferry-boat?” I asked. He nodded, then added, “Or he wouldn’t be keepin’ up such a clip.” He gave a short chuckle. “They’re gettin’ anxious up there.” I glanced up. The captain had thrust his head and shoulders out of the pilot-house, and was staring intently into the fog as though by sheer force of will he could penetrate it. His face was anxious, as was the face of my companion, who had stumped over to the rail and was gazing with a like intentness in the direction of the invisible danger. Then everything happened, and with inconceivable rapidity. The fog seemed to break away as though split by a wedge, and the bow of a steamboat emerged, trailing fog-wreaths on either side like seaweed on the snout of Leviathan. I could see the pilot-house and a white-bearded man leaning partly out of it, on his elbows. He was clad in a blue uniform, and I remember noting how trim and quiet he was. His quietness, under the circumstances, was terrible. He accepted Destiny, marched hand in hand with it, and coolly measured the stroke. As he leaned there, he ran a calm and speculative eye over us, as though to determine the precise point of the collision, and took no notice whatever when our pilot, white with rage, shouted, “Now you’ve done it!” On looking back, I realize that the remark was too obvious to make rejoinder necessary.

“Grab hold of something and hang on,” the red-faced man said to me. All his bluster had gone, and he seemed to have caught the contagion of preternatural calm. “And listen to the women scream,” he said grimly—almost bitterly, I thought, as though he had been through the experience before. The vessels came together before I could follow his advice. We must have been struck squarely amidships, for I saw nothing, the strange steamboat having passed beyond my line of vision. The Martinez heeled over, sharply, and there was a crashing and rending of timber. I was thrown flat on the wet deck, and before I could scramble to my feet I heard the scream of the women. This it was, I am certain,—the most indescribable of blood-curdling sounds,—that threw me into a panic. I remembered the life-preservers stored in the cabin, but was met at the door and swept backward by a wild rush of men and women. What happened in the next few minutes I do not recollect, though I have a clear remembrance of pulling down life-preservers from the overhead racks, while the red-faced man fastened them about the bodies of an hysterical group of women. This memory is as distinct and sharp as that of any picture I have seen. It is a picture, and I can see it now,—the jagged edges of the hole in the side of the cabin, through which the grey fog swirled and eddied; the empty upholstered seats, littered with all the evidences of sudden flight, such as packages, hand satchels, umbrellas, and wraps; the stout gentleman who had been reading my essay, encased in cork and canvas, the magazine still in his hand, and asking me with monotonous insistence if I thought there was any danger; the red-faced man, stumping gallantly around on his artificial legs and buckling life-preservers on all comers; and finally, the screaming bedlam of women. This it was, the screaming of the women, that most tried my nerves. It must have tried, too, the nerves of the red-faced man, for I have another picture which will never fade from my mind. The stout gentleman is stuffing the magazine into his overcoat pocket and looking on curiously. A tangled mass of women, with drawn, white faces and open mouths, is shrieking like a chorus of lost souls; and the red-faced man, his face now purplish with wrath, and with arms extended overhead as in the act of hurling thunderbolts, is shouting, “Shut up! Oh, shut up!” I remember the scene impelled me to sudden laughter, and in the next instant I realized I was becoming hysterical myself; for these were women of my own kind, like my mother and sisters, with the fear of death upon them and unwilling to die. And I remember that the sounds they made reminded me of the squealing of pigs under the knife of the butcher, and I was struck with horror at the vividness of the analogy. These women, capable of the most sublime emotions, of the tenderest sympathies, were open-mouthed and screaming. They wanted to live, they were helpless, like rats in a trap, and they screamed. The horror of it drove me out on deck. I was feeling sick and squeamish, and sat down on a bench. In a hazy way I saw and heard men rushing and shouting as they strove to lower the boats. It was just as I had read descriptions of such scenes in books. The tackles jammed. Nothing worked. One boat lowered away with the plugs out, filled with women and children and then with water, and capsized. Another boat had been lowered by one end, and still hung in the tackle by the other end, where it had been abandoned. Nothing was to be seen of the strange steamboat which had caused the disaster, though I heard men saying that she would undoubtedly send boats to our assistance. I descended to the lower deck. The Martinez was sinking fast, for the water was very near. Numbers of the passengers were leaping overboard. Others, in the water, were clamouring to be taken aboard again. No one heeded them. A cry arose that we were sinking. I was seized by the consequent panic, and went over the side in a surge of bodies. How I went over I do not know, though I did know, and instantly, why those in the water were so desirous of getting back on the steamer. The water was cold—so cold that it was painful. The pang, as I plunged into it, was as quick and sharp as that of fire. It bit to the marrow. It was like the grip of death. I gasped with the anguish and shock of it, filling my lungs before the life-preserver popped me to the surface. The taste of the salt was strong in my mouth, and I was strangling with the acrid stuff in my throat and lungs. But it was the cold that was most distressing. I felt that I could survive but a few minutes. People were struggling and floundering in the water about me. I could hear them crying out to one another. And I heard, also, the sound of oars. Evidently the strange steamboat had lowered its boats. As the time went by I marvelled that I was still alive. I had no sensation whatever in my lower limbs, while a chilling numbness was wrapping about my heart and creeping into it. Small waves, with spiteful foaming crests, continually broke over me and into my mouth, sending me off into more strangling paroxysms. The noises grew indistinct, though I heard a final and despairing chorus of screams in the distance, and knew that the Martinez had gone down. Later,—how much later I have no knowledge,—I came to myself with a start of fear. I was alone. I could hear no calls or cries—only the sound of the waves, made weirdly hollow and reverberant by the fog. A panic in a crowd, which partakes of a sort of community of interest, is not so terrible as a panic when one is by oneself; and such a panic I now suffered. Whither was I drifting? The red-faced man had said that the tide was ebbing through the Golden Gate. Was I, then, being carried out to sea? And the life-preserver in which I floated? Was it not liable to go to pieces at any moment? I had heard of such things being made of paper and hollow rushes which quickly became saturated and lost all buoyancy. And I could not swim a stroke. And I was alone, floating, apparently, in the midst of a grey primordial vastness. I confess that a madness seized me, that I shrieked aloud as the women had shrieked, and beat the water with my numb hands. How long this lasted I have no conception, for a blankness intervened, of which I remember no more than one remembers of troubled and painful sleep. When I aroused, it was as after centuries of time; and I saw, almost above me and emerging from the fog, the bow of a vessel, and three triangular sails, each shrewdly lapping the other and filled with wind. Where the bow cut the water there was a great foaming and gurgling, and I seemed directly in its path. I tried to cry out, but was too exhausted. The bow plunged down, just missing me and sending a swash of water clear over my head. Then the long, black side of the vessel began slipping past, so near that I could have touched it with my hands. I tried to reach it, in a mad resolve to claw into the wood with my nails, but my arms were heavy and lifeless. Again I strove to call out, but made no sound. The stern of the vessel shot by, dropping, as it did so, into a hollow between the waves; and I caught a glimpse of a man standing at the wheel, and of another man who seemed to be doing little else than smoke a cigar. I saw the smoke issuing from his lips as he slowly turned his head and glanced out over the water in my direction. It was a careless, unpremeditated glance, one of those haphazard things men do when they have no immediate call to do anything in particular, but act because they are alive and must do something.

The note had come up to Arthur Sutton's desk by the hand of the office boy a little after three, and it lay there among the bills of lading the rest of the afternoon, a soiled and creased square of paper that smelled faintly of tar and tobacco and something else he could not name. He read it a dozen times. The hand was large and laborious, the hand of a man who had learned his letters well enough in boyhood and had since found little use for them. "Arthur," it ran, "I am in town and will be at Hansen's on East Street at six. If you are the same Art I knew you will come. If you are not, no hard feelings. Dan."

That was all. Eleven years, and that was all. Arthur Sutton laid the note under the brass paper-weight that had been given him on the occasion of his fifth year with Morrow, Lacey & Company, ship chandlers and commission merchants, and he bent once more over the ledger. But the figures would not stay in their columns. They swam before his eyes, and in their place he saw a lean, brown boy of seventeen standing on the end of a lumber wharf at Petaluma, a bundle under his arm and a grin on his face, waving his cap as the scow schooner swung out into the creek. That was the last he had seen of his cousin Dan Tierney, and it had seemed to him then, at fourteen, that the whole glory of the world was going out with the tide.

At half after five he closed the ledger, wiped his pen with great care, and put on his hat and coat. Old Lacey, peering over his spectacles from the inner office, remarked that Sutton was leaving early. Sutton said that he was, that he had an engagement, and he went out into the street with a guilty flush upon his face, as though he had been caught at some small theft.

East Street was in its evening uproar. The drays were rumbling home over the cobbles, the great horses steaming and stamping, the drivers bawling at one another and at the world. Sailors were coming ashore in twos and threes, rolling a little in their walk as though the pavement still lifted beneath them, and the saloon doors swung open and shut upon gusts of warmth and light and the clink of glasses. A wind was blowing in off the bay, raw and salt, and it bore with it the creak of rigging and the slap of water against the piles. Arthur Sutton turned up his collar. He was not used to this end of the town after dark. His road home lay by the cable-car to a quiet street on the hill, where his wife would be laying the table and the two little ones would be clamouring to be put to bed by their father and no one else.

Hansen's was a low-ceilinged place with sawdust on the floor and a long counter running down one side, behind which a fat Swede in a dirty apron was cutting chops with a cleaver. The air was thick with the smoke of frying meat and of cheap cigars. Sutton paused in the doorway, blinking, and in that moment a voice boomed out from a table at the rear.

"Art! By the Lord, it's Art!"

A man rose up from the table and came toward him, and Sutton, staring, did not at first know him. He was big—bigger than Sutton had any memory of—with shoulders that seemed to fill the narrow passage between the tables, and he moved with a curious lightness for one of his bulk, the swift, easy, balanced movement of a cat or of a man who has learned to keep his feet on decks that heave and ice that slides away. His face was burned to the colour of old saddle-leather, and seamed and creased about the eyes as though he had spent long years squinting into wind and glare. A scar, white against the brown, ran from the corner of his mouth halfway to his ear. But the eyes were Dan's eyes, blue and laughing, and the grin was the grin of the boy on the lumber wharf.

"Dan," Sutton said, and could say nothing more.

The big man seized his hand and wrung it, and Sutton winced in spite of himself, for the grip was like the closing of a vise. Then Dan Tierney stood back and looked him up and down, frankly, from his polished shoes to his derby hat, and the grin widened.

"Well, well," he said. "Well, well, well. A regular gentleman. Collar and cuffs and a watch-chain across his belly. I'd 'a' passed you on the street, Art, and never known you. Come and sit down. Hey, Hansen! Two of your thickest, and coffee, and none of your bilge-water, neither!"

They sat. Sutton took off his hat and laid it carefully on the bench beside him, and was conscious, as he did so, of his cousin's amused eye upon the operation. He was conscious, too, of his own hands lying upon the oilcloth of the table—white hands, soft hands, with the ink stain on the second finger of the right that no scrubbing would ever quite remove. And across from them lay Dan's hands, and Sutton looked at them and could not look away. They were enormous, knotted and broken-nailed, the backs of them crossed with old cuts and burns. And on the left hand the two smallest fingers were gone, cleanly, at the second joint.

Dan saw where his gaze rested, and held up the hand and turned it in the lamplight as though it were a curiosity belonging to some other man.

"Frost," he said simply. "Up the Stewart River, the winter of 'ninety-eight. Sixty-two below, and my mitten fell off while I was cuttin' the dogs out of a tangle. I didn't notice it for maybe a minute. A minute's long enough, up there. I took 'em off myself, next morning, with a hunting knife, and a fellow named Joe Ladue held the candle. I was lucky. I've seen men lose both feet that way, and die of it after."

He said it without any emotion whatever, as a man might remark upon the weather, and Sutton felt a slight sickness rise in his throat. He had read of such things in the newspapers, during the great rush, and had shuddered pleasantly over them by his own fireside. But this was different. This was a hand he had once held, when they were small boys, crossing the creek on the stepping-stones behind their grandfather's barn.

The chops came, great slabs of meat swimming in their own grease, and Dan fell upon his with a fierce and single-minded appetite that Sutton had never before seen in a human being. He ate as a wolf eats, steadily and without speech, his jaws working, his eyes upon the plate. Sutton, who had dined at noon on a sandwich and a glass of milk, cut at his own chop and found he had no stomach for it.

"You've been north, then," he said at last. "All this time?"

"North, and south, and in between." Dan wiped his mouth with the back of his hand. "Let's see. That schooner you saw me off on—the *Annie Lacey*, you remember her?—she took me down to the city, and I shipped out of here before the mast on a lime-juicer bound round the Horn for Liverpool. A hundred and forty days, and the mate a devil out of hell, and I was the youngest aboard and the butt for every man's boot. I learned things on that voyage, Art. I learned that a man's got just what he can hold and no more, and that nobody's goin' to hand him anything on a plate." He laughed shortly. "I hit the mate with a belaying-pin off the Falklands. He had it comin', and the crew stood by me, and nothing was ever said. But I never went back to a deep-water ship after that one."

He talked on, and as he talked the chop-house fell away from about them and Sutton saw the world his cousin had lived in. He saw the sealing grounds off the Japan coast, the schooners hunting in the fog and the boats going out at dawn, the hunters at the bows with their rifles and the herd sleeping on the long grey swell. He saw a fight in a Yokohama dance-hall and a knife coming out of nowhere—so that was the scar—and a night spent bleeding in a sampan with a Japanese boatman who would not take money for his trouble. He saw the Bering Sea, and the islands where the fur seals bred in their thousands and the air was one long roar of them. He saw Dutch Harbour, and a whaler frozen in at Herschel Island for two winters, and men going mad with the dark and the cold and the scurvy. And he saw, at last, the Klondike—the Chilkoot in the spring of 'ninety-seven, a black line of men toiling up the white face of it like ants on a sugar loaf; the lakes, and the whip-sawing of green timber for boats; the White Horse Rapids roaring between their walls of basalt; and Dawson in the first mad winter, when flour was a dollar a pound and men were glad to pay it.

"Did you strike it?" Sutton asked. He found his voice was hoarse.

"Struck it twice," said Dan. "Lost it twice. The first time it was a bench claim on Bonanza, and I sold it for eleven thousand, and a Swede named Olsen took ninety thousand out of it the next season. The second time I hung on, and I had a hundred and twenty thousand in dust in my cabin, and I sat down to a game of stud with Swiftwater Bill and a gambler out of Circle City." He shrugged, and his great shoulders rose and fell. "That's the way of it. The gold's there, and it's anybody's that can take it and hold it. I could take it. I never could hold it. There's some men are built that way."

He pushed his plate away and leaned back, and his eyes, in their nest of wrinkles, rested on his cousin with a sudden shrewdness.

"But that's enough of me. I've been talkin' like a phonograph. What about you, Art? What've you been doin' with yourself these eleven years?"

And Arthur Sutton opened his mouth to tell him, and found that there was nothing to tell.

It was a strange sensation, and a humiliating one. He was a man of some consequence in his own small world. He had risen from office boy to chief clerk; he had a house with a bay window and a little garden in front where his wife grew roses; he had a membership in a debating society and had once read a paper before it upon the tariff question which had been well received. He sat on Sundays in a pew near the front of the church. All these things he had been proud of, and they had seemed to him solid and substantial, the very stuff and substance of a man's life. Yet now, when he came to lay them out before this brown giant who had fought with knives and frozen his fingers off and gambled away a hundred thousand dollars in a single night, they shrank and dwindled to nothing. They were like the toys of a child, set out upon a nursery floor.

"I'm with Morrow, Lacey & Company," he said lamely. "Chandlers. I keep their books. I've been there twelve years now. I'm married, Dan. Her name is Edith. You never knew her. We have two children, a boy and a girl. The boy's named for grandfather."

"Married!" Dan slapped the table so that the dishes jumped. "Little Art married, with young ones of his own! And a boy named for the old man! Well, if that don't beat all." He shook his head slowly, and for a moment his face wore an expression that Sutton could not read. "The old man," he said. "He's gone, I take it?"

"Six years ago. In the spring. He went out to see to a heifer in the night, and they found him in the morning, by the corral gate. His heart, the doctor said."

Dan was silent. He took a black pipe from his pocket, filled it from a pouch of sealskin, and lighted it, and the smoke curled up about his head.

"I wrote him once," he said finally. "From Unalaska. I wonder if he got it."

"He got it. He kept it in his Bible. I saw it there, after."

Again there was silence between them, and the noise of the chop-house flowed in to fill it—the rattle of dishes, the bawling of Hansen at his cook, the laughter of a knot of longshoremen at the counter. It was Dan who broke the silence, and he broke it with a laugh.

"And the old man come down in the morning with a team and a wagon and hauled us home, and he never said one word the whole way. Not one word. "And which was it?" Sutton asked, smiling.

But Dan did not smile. He took the pipe from his mouth and looked at it.

"Neither," he said. "That's the joke of it, Art. Neither one."

Sutton waited. The big man was silent for a long moment, and when he spoke again his voice had changed. It was lower, and there was something in it that Sutton had not heard before, and it made him uneasy.

"I've been everywhere, pretty near," Dan said. "I've seen more in eleven years than most men see in eleven lifetimes. And I'll tell you what I've learned, for whatever it's worth. It's a hard world. It's a world where the strong man eats and the weak man gets eaten, and there ain't no third way. I've seen it on the ships and I've seen it on the trail. Up on the Chilkoot I seen a man sit down in the snow and cry because he couldn't pack his outfit one more foot, and the rest of us walked round him. Walked round him, Art, like he was a stone in the road. And I walked round him too. You can't stop. You stop, and you're the next one sittin' in the snow." He drew upon his pipe, and the coal glowed red. "I was strong. I'm strong now. There ain't a man on this waterfront I couldn't put on his back. And I've got nothing. Nothing in the world but a sea-bag and forty dollars and a berth on a sealer that sails for the Russian side Thursday week. That's all I've got to show."

"But the things you've done—" Sutton began.

"Done!" Dan laughed again, harshly. "Sure, I've done things. And what've they come to? I'll tell you what they've come to. They've come to me sittin' here talkin' about 'em to a man who'll go home tonight to a wife and a pair of kids and a fire in the grate. I've been the strong man, Art. And I've been thinkin' lately, layin' awake in my bunk, that maybe the strong man's a fool. Maybe there's a kind of strength I never had. The kind that keeps a man at a desk twelve years, addin' up figures for another man's profit, because there's a woman and two kids dependin' on him. I couldn't do it. I couldn't do it to save my soul. I'd bust out inside a month. And I used to think that was because I was the better man." He knocked his pipe out against the table edge. "Now I don't know."

Arthur Sutton did not know what to say. He felt a strange warmth rising in him, and at the same time a strange shame, for even as his cousin spoke he had been sitting there envying him—envying him the frozen fingers and the knife scar and the hundred thousand dollars thrown away upon a card. Envying him the Horn and the Bering Sea and the black line of men on the white face of the Chilkoot. For it had come upon Sutton, as he listened, that he had never once in his life been really cold, or really hungry, or really afraid; that he had never once pitted his body against the elements and won; that the whole of his existence had been lived in a little lighted room, with the shutters drawn against the dark, and that outside that room the great world had been roaring on, savage and splendid and indifferent, and he had never so much as put his head out of the window to look at it.

And here was Dan, who had lived in that roaring world, envying him his little lighted room.

It was a joke, he thought, and the joke was on both of them. It was the joke of life itself, which gives to each man what he does not want and withholds from him what he desires, and sets him forever staring over the fence at his neighbour's field. He thought of a phrase he had read somewhere—in Spencer, perhaps, or in one of those books on evolution that he had laboured through in his evenings, years ago, when he still had ambitions toward self-improvement—a phrase about the individual being sacrificed always to the type. He had not understood it then. He thought he understood it now. Dan was a type, and he was a type, and the world had need of both of them, and cared not a whit for either.

"Come home with me," he said suddenly. "Tonight. Come home and meet Edith and the children. There's a spare room. Stay till your ship sails."

Dan looked at him, and for an instant something softened in the hard brown face. Then he shook his head.

"No," he said. "No, Art. I'd only track mud on her carpets and teach your boy to cuss. And I'd sit at your table and eat your grub and look at your wife and your kids, and the next morning I'd be gone, and I'd have that to carry with me, along with the rest." He reached across the table and gripped his cousin's shoulder, and this time the grip was gentle. "You've done all right, Art. You've done better than all right. Don't let nobody tell you different. Least of all me."

They sat a while longer, and talked of other things—of the ranch, which had been sold; of an aunt in Santa Rosa who had married a second time; of a girl named Molly Brennan whom they had both, at different seasons, adored, and who was now a stout matron with six children in Petaluma. They laughed a good deal, and Hansen brought more coffee, and the longshoremen at the counter went out and others came in to take their places. And at half past eight Arthur Sutton looked at his watch and said that he must go.

They walked together to the corner of Market Street. The wind had freshened, and the fog was beginning to roll in through the Gate, grey and wet, swallowing the lights of the shipping one by one. At the corner they stopped, and the cable-car came clanging up out of the murk, its lamp glowing yellow.

"Thursday week," Sutton said. "I'll come down to see you off."

"Don't," said Dan. "I'll be drunk, most likely. I generally am, sailin' day." He grinned the old grin. "Take care of the old man's namesake. Make a bookkeeper of him. Or a preacher. Anything but a sailor."

They shook hands, and Sutton climbed aboard, and the car jerked forward and went grinding up the hill. When he looked back his cousin was still standing on the corner, a big dark shape against the lighted window of a saloon, his hands in his pockets and his collar turned up against the wind. Then the fog came between them, and he was gone.

Arthur Sutton sat on the slatted bench of the cable-car, swaying with its motion, and looked down at his white hands lying in his lap. He thought of the two missing fingers. He thought of the man who sat down in the snow and cried. He thought of the boy on the lumber wharf, waving his cap. And he thought of Edith, who would be waiting up for him with the lamp turned low, and of the children asleep upstairs, and of the ledger lying closed upon his desk at Morrow, Lacey & Company, which he would open again tomorrow at eight o'clock precisely, as he had opened it every working morning for twelve years.

He did not know, riding up the hill through the fog, which of them had chosen rightly. He suspected, with a dim and troubled wisdom new to him, that neither of them had chosen at all—that the choosing had been done for them, long before, by forces older and blinder than either, working in the blood and the bone. And the cable-car clanged on, and the fog closed in behind it, and somewhere far below, on the black water of the bay, a ship's bell was tolling the hour.

The danger lay in the heavy fog which blanketed the bay, and of which, as a landsman, I had little apprehension. In fact, I remember the placid exaltation with which I took up my position on the forward upper deck, directly beneath the pilot-house, and allowed the mystery of the fog to lay hold of my imagination. A fresh breeze was blowing, and for a time I was alone in the moist obscurity—yet not alone, for I was dimly conscious of the presence of the pilot, and of what I took to be the captain, in the glass house above my head. I remember thinking how comfortable it was, this division of labour which made it unnecessary for me to study fogs, winds, tides, and navigation, in order to visit my friend who lived across an arm of the sea. It was good that men should be specialists, I mused. The peculiar knowledge of the pilot and captain sufficed for many thousands of people who knew no more of the sea and navigation than I knew. On the other hand, instead of having to devote my energy to the learning of a multitude of things, I concentrated it upon a few particular things, such as, for instance, the analysis of Poe’s place in American literature—an essay of mine, by the way, in the current Atlantic. Coming aboard, as I passed through the cabin, I had noticed with greedy eyes a stout gentleman reading the Atlantic, which was open at my very essay. And there it was again, the division of labour, the special knowledge of the pilot and captain which permitted the stout gentleman to read my special knowledge on Poe while they carried him safely from Sausalito to San Francisco. A red-faced man, slamming the cabin door behind him and stumping out on the deck, interrupted my reflections, though I made a mental note of the topic for use in a projected essay which I had thought of calling “The Necessity for Freedom: A Plea for the Artist.” The red-faced man shot a glance up at the pilot-house, gazed around at the fog, stumped across the deck and back (he evidently had artificial legs), and stood still by my side, legs wide apart, and with an expression of keen enjoyment on his face. I was not wrong when I decided that his days had been spent on the sea.

“It’s nasty weather like this here that turns heads grey before their time,” he said, with a nod toward the pilot-house.

“I had not thought there was any particular strain,” I answered. “It seems as simple as A, B, C. They know the direction by compass, the distance, and the speed. I should not call it anything more than mathematical certainty.”

“Strain!” he snorted. “Simple as A, B, C! Mathematical certainty!” He seemed to brace himself up and lean backward against the air as he stared at me. “How about this here tide that’s rushin’ out through the Golden Gate?” he demanded, or bellowed, rather. “How fast is she ebbin’? What’s the drift, eh? Listen to that, will you? A bell-buoy, and we’re a-top of it! See ’em alterin’ the course!” From out of the fog came the mournful tolling of a bell, and I could see the pilot turning the wheel with great rapidity. The bell, which had seemed straight ahead, was now sounding from the side. Our own whistle was blowing hoarsely, and from time to time the sound of other whistles came to us from out of the fog.

“That’s a ferry-boat of some sort,” the new-comer said, indicating a whistle off to the right. “And there! D’ye hear that? Blown by mouth. Some scow schooner, most likely. Better watch out, Mr. Schooner-man. Ah, I thought so. Now hell’s a poppin’ for somebody!” The unseen ferry-boat was blowing blast after blast, and the mouth-blown horn was tooting in terror-stricken fashion.

“And now they’re payin’ their respects to each other and tryin’ to get clear,” the red-faced man went on, as the hurried whistling ceased. His face was shining, his eyes flashing with excitement as he translated into articulate language the speech of the horns and sirens. “That’s a steam-siren a-goin’ it over there to the left. And you hear that fellow with a frog in his throat—a steam schooner as near as I can judge, crawlin’ in from the Heads against the tide.” A shrill little whistle, piping as if gone mad, came from directly ahead and from very near at hand. Gongs sounded on the Martinez. Our paddle-wheels stopped, their pulsing beat died away, and then they started again. The shrill little whistle, like the chirping of a cricket amid the cries of great beasts, shot through the fog from more to the side and swiftly grew faint and fainter. I looked to my companion for enlightenment.

“One of them dare-devil launches,” he said. “I almost wish we’d sunk him, the little rip! They’re the cause of more trouble. And what good are they? And romantic it certainly was—the fog, like the grey shadow of infinite mystery, brooding over the whirling speck of earth; and men, mere motes of light and sparkle, cursed with an insane relish for work, riding their steeds of wood and steel through the heart of the mystery, groping their way blindly through the Unseen, and clamouring and clanging in confident speech the while their hearts are heavy with incertitude and fear. The voice of my companion brought me back to myself with a laugh. I too had been groping and floundering, the while I thought I rode clear-eyed through the mystery.

“Hello! somebody comin’ our way,” he was saying. “And d’ye hear that? He’s comin’ fast. Walking right along. Guess he don’t hear us yet. Wind’s in wrong direction.” The fresh breeze was blowing right down upon us, and I could hear the whistle plainly, off to one side and a little ahead.

“Grab hold of something and hang on,” the red-faced man said to me. The Martinez heeled over, sharply, and there was a crashing and rending of timber. I was thrown flat on the wet deck, and before I could scramble to my feet I heard the scream of the women. This it was, I am certain,—the most indescribable of blood-curdling sounds,—that threw me into a panic. I remembered the life-preservers stored in the cabin, but was met at the door and swept backward by a wild rush of men and women. What happened in the next few minutes I do not recollect, though I have a clear remembrance of pulling down life-preservers from the overhead racks, while the red-faced man fastened them about the bodies of an hysterical group of women. This memory is as distinct and sharp as that of any picture I have seen. It is a picture, and I can see it now,—the jagged edges of the hole in the side of the cabin, through which the grey fog swirled and eddied; the empty upholstered seats, littered with all the evidences of sudden flight, such as packages, hand satchels, umbrellas, and wraps; the stout gentleman who had been reading my essay, encased in cork and canvas, the magazine still in his hand, and asking me with monotonous insistence if I thought there was any danger; the red-faced man, stumping gallantly around on his artificial legs and buckling life-preservers on all comers; and finally, the screaming bedlam of women. This it was, the screaming of the women, that most tried my nerves. It must have tried, too, the nerves of the red-faced man, for I have another picture which will never fade from my mind. The stout gentleman is stuffing the magazine into his overcoat pocket and looking on curiously. A tangled mass of women, with drawn, white faces and open mouths, is shrieking like a chorus of lost souls; and the red-faced man, his face now purplish with wrath, and with arms extended overhead as in the act of hurling thunderbolts, is shouting, “Shut up! Oh, shut up!” I remember the scene impelled me to sudden laughter, and in the next instant I realized I was becoming hysterical myself; for these were women of my own kind, like my mother and sisters, with the fear of death upon them and unwilling to die. And I remember that the sounds they made reminded me of the squealing of pigs under the knife of the butcher, and I was struck with horror at the vividness of the analogy. These women, capable of the most sublime emotions, of the tenderest sympathies, were open-mouthed and screaming. They wanted to live, they were helpless, like rats in a trap, and they screamed. The horror of it drove me out on deck. I was feeling sick and squeamish, and sat down on a bench. In a hazy way I saw and heard men rushing and shouting as they strove to lower the boats. It was just as I had read descriptions of such scenes in books. The tackles jammed. Nothing worked. Another boat had been lowered by one end, and still hung in the tackle by the other end, where it had been abandoned. Nothing was to be seen of the strange steamboat which had caused the disaster, though I heard men saying that she would undoubtedly send boats to our assistance. I descended to the lower deck. The Martinez was sinking fast, for the water was very near. Numbers of the passengers were leaping overboard. Others, in the water, were clamouring to be taken aboard again. No one heeded them. A cry arose that we were sinking. I was seized by the consequent panic, and went over the side in a surge of bodies. How I went over I do not know, though I did know, and instantly, why those in the water were so desirous of getting back on the steamer. The water was cold—so cold that it was painful. The pang, as I plunged into it, was as quick and sharp as that of fire. It bit to the marrow. It was like the grip of death. I gasped with the anguish and shock of it, filling my lungs before the life-preserver popped me to the surface. The taste of the salt was strong in my mouth, and I was strangling with the acrid stuff in my throat and lungs. But it was the cold that was most distressing. I felt that I could survive but a few minutes. People were struggling and floundering in the water about me. I could hear them crying out to one another. And I heard, also, the sound of oars. I had no sensation whatever in my lower limbs, while a chilling numbness was wrapping about my heart and creeping into it. Small waves, with spiteful foaming crests, continually broke over me and into my mouth, sending me off into more strangling paroxysms. The noises grew indistinct, though I heard a final and despairing chorus of screams in the distance, and knew that the Martinez had gone down. I could hear no calls or cries—only the sound of the waves, made weirdly hollow and reverberant by the fog.
