A pack of bloodhounds followed the way of his bleeding feet. And the sleuth-hounds of the law, the paid fighting animals of society, with telephone, and telegraph, and special train, clung to his trail night and day. Sometimes they came upon him, and men faced him like heroes, or stampeded through barbed-wire fences to the delight of the commonwealth reading the account at the breakfast table. It was after such encounters that the dead and wounded were carted back to the towns, and their places filled by men eager for the man-hunt. And then Jim Hall disappeared. The bloodhounds vainly quested on the lost trail. Inoffensive ranchers in remote valleys were held up by armed men and compelled to identify themselves; while the remains of Jim Hall were discovered on a dozen mountain-sides by greedy claimants for blood-money. In the meantime the newspapers were read at Sierra Vista, not so much with interest as with anxiety. The women were afraid. Judge Scott pooh-poohed and laughed, but not with reason, for it was in his last days on the bench that Jim Hall had stood before him and received sentence. And in open court-room, before all men, Jim Hall had proclaimed that the day would come when he would wreak vengeance on the Judge that sentenced him. For once, Jim Hall was right. He was innocent of the crime for which he was sentenced. It was a case, in the parlance of thieves and police, of “rail-roading.” Jim Hall was being “rail-roaded” to prison for a crime he had not committed. Because of the two prior convictions against him, Judge Scott imposed upon him a sentence of fifty years. Judge Scott did not know all things, and he did not know that he was party to a police conspiracy, that the evidence was hatched and perjured, that Jim Hall was guiltless of the crime charged. And Jim Hall, on the other hand, did not know that Judge Scott was merely ignorant. Jim Hall believed that the judge knew all about it and was hand in glove with the police in the perpetration of the monstrous injustice. So it was, when the doom of fifty years of living death was uttered by Judge Scott, that Jim Hall, hating all things in the society that misused him, rose up and raged in the court-room until dragged down by half a dozen of his blue-coated enemies. To him, Judge Scott was the keystone in the arch of injustice, and upon Judge Scott he emptied the vials of his wrath and hurled the threats of his revenge yet to come. Then Jim Hall went to his living death . . . and escaped. Of all this White Fang knew nothing. But between him and Alice, the master’s wife, there existed a secret. Each night, after Sierra Vista had gone to bed, she rose and let in White Fang to sleep in the big hall. Now White Fang was not a house-dog, nor was he permitted to sleep in the house; so each morning, early, she slipped down and let him out before the family was awake. On one such night, while all the house slept, White Fang awoke and lay very quietly. And very quietly he smelled the air and read the message it bore of a strange god’s presence. And to his ears came sounds of the strange god’s movements. White Fang burst into no furious outcry. It was not his way. The strange god walked softly, but more softly walked White Fang, for he had no clothes to rub against the flesh of his body. He followed silently. In the Wild he had hunted live meat that was infinitely timid, and he knew the advantage of surprise. The strange god paused at the foot of the great staircase and listened, and White Fang was as dead, so without movement was he as he watched and waited. Up that staircase the way led to the love-master and to the love-master’s dearest possessions. White Fang bristled, but waited. The strange god’s foot lifted. He was beginning the ascent. Then it was that White Fang struck. He gave no warning, with no snarl anticipated his own action. Into the air he lifted his body in the spring that landed him on the strange god’s back. White Fang clung with his fore-paws to the man’s shoulders, at the same time burying his fangs into the back of the man’s neck. He clung on for a moment, long enough to drag the god over backward. Together they crashed to the floor. White Fang leaped clear, and, as the man struggled to rise, was in again with the slashing fangs. Sierra Vista awoke in alarm. The noise from downstairs was as that of a score of battling fiends. There were revolver shots. A man’s voice screamed once in horror and anguish. There was a great snarling and growling, and over all arose a smashing and crashing of furniture and glass. But almost as quickly as it had arisen, the commotion died away. The struggle had not lasted more than three minutes. The frightened household clustered at the top of the stairway. From below, as from out an abyss of blackness, came up a gurgling sound, as of air bubbling through water. Sometimes this gurgle became sibilant, almost a whistle. But this, too, quickly died down and ceased. Then naught came up out of the blackness save a heavy panting of some creature struggling sorely for air. Weedon Scott pressed a button, and the staircase and downstairs hall were flooded with light. Then he and Judge Scott, revolvers in hand, cautiously descended. There was no need for this caution. White Fang had done his work. In the midst of the wreckage of overthrown and smashed furniture, partly on his side, his face hidden by an arm, lay a man. Weedon Scott bent over, removed the arm and turned the man’s face upward. A gaping throat explained the manner of his death.

“Jim Hall,” said Judge Scott, and father and son looked significantly at each other. Then they turned to White Fang. He, too, was lying on his side. His eyes were closed, but the lids slightly lifted in an effort to look at them as they bent over him, and the tail was perceptibly agitated in a vain effort to wag. Weedon Scott patted him, and his throat rumbled an acknowledging growl. But it was a weak growl at best, and it quickly ceased. His eyelids drooped and went shut, and his whole body seemed to relax and flatten out upon the floor.

“He’s all in, poor devil,” muttered the master.

“We’ll see about that,” asserted the Judge, as he started for the telephone.

“Frankly, he has one chance in a thousand,” announced the surgeon, after he had worked an hour and a half on White Fang. Dawn was breaking through the windows and dimming the electric lights. With the exception of the children, the whole family was gathered about the surgeon to hear his verdict.

“One broken hind-leg,” he went on. “Three broken ribs, one at least of which has pierced the lungs. He has lost nearly all the blood in his body. There is a large likelihood of internal injuries. He must have been jumped upon. To say nothing of three bullet holes clear through him. One chance in a thousand is really optimistic. He hasn’t a chance in ten thousand.”

“But he mustn’t lose any chance that might be of help to him,” Judge Scott exclaimed. “Never mind expense. Put him under the X-ray—anything. Weedon, telegraph at once to San Francisco for Doctor Nichols. No reflection on you, doctor, you understand; but he must have the advantage of every chance.” The surgeon smiled indulgently. “Of course I understand. He deserves all that can be done for him. He must be nursed as you would nurse a human being, a sick child. And don’t forget what I told you about temperature. I’ll be back at ten o’clock again.” White Fang received the nursing. Judge Scott’s suggestion of a trained nurse was indignantly clamoured down by the girls, who themselves undertook the task. And White Fang won out on the one chance in ten thousand denied him by the surgeon. The latter was not to be censured for his misjudgment. All his life he had tended and operated on the soft humans of civilisation, who lived sheltered lives and had descended out of many sheltered generations. Compared with White Fang, they were frail and flabby, and clutched life without any strength in their grip. White Fang had come straight from the Wild, where the weak perish early and shelter is vouchsafed to none. In neither his father nor his mother was there any weakness, nor in the generations before them. A constitution of iron and the vitality of the Wild were White Fang’s inheritance, and he clung to life, the whole of him and every part of him, in spirit and in flesh, with the tenacity that of old belonged to all creatures. Bound down a prisoner, denied even movement by the plaster casts and bandages, White Fang lingered out the weeks. He slept long hours and dreamed much, and through his mind passed an unending pageant of Northland visions. All the ghosts of the past arose and were with him. Once again he lived in the lair with Kiche, crept trembling to the knees of Grey Beaver to tender his allegiance, ran for his life before Lip-lip and all the howling bedlam of the puppy-pack. He ran again through the silence, hunting his living food through the months of famine; and again he ran at the head of the team, the gut-whips of Mit-sah and Grey Beaver snapping behind, their voices crying “Ra! Raa!” when they came to a narrow passage and the team closed together like a fan to go through. He lived again all his days with Beauty Smith and the fights he had fought. At such times he whimpered and snarled in his sleep, and they that looked on said that his dreams were bad. But there was one particular nightmare from which he suffered—the clanking, clanging monsters of electric cars that were to him colossal screaming lynxes. He would lie in a screen of bushes, watching for a squirrel to venture far enough out on the ground from its tree-refuge. Then, when he sprang out upon it, it would transform itself into an electric car, menacing and terrible, towering over him like a mountain, screaming and clanging and spitting fire at him. It was the same when he challenged the hawk down out of the sky. Down out of the blue it would rush, as it dropped upon him changing itself into the ubiquitous electric car. Or again, he would be in the pen of Beauty Smith. Outside the pen, men would be gathering, and he knew that a fight was on. He watched the door for his antagonist to enter. The door would open, and thrust in upon him would come the awful electric car. A thousand times this occurred, and each time the terror it inspired was as vivid and great as ever. Then came the day when the last bandage and the last plaster cast were taken off. It was a gala day. All Sierra Vista was gathered around. The master rubbed his ears, and he crooned his love-growl. The master’s wife called him the “Blessed Wolf,” which name was taken up with acclaim and all the women called him the Blessed Wolf. He tried to rise to his feet, and after several attempts fell down from weakness. He had lain so long that his muscles had lost their cunning, and all the strength had gone out of them. He felt a little shame because of his weakness, as though, forsooth, he were failing the gods in the service he owed them. Because of this he made heroic efforts to arise and at last he stood on his four legs, tottering and swaying back and forth.

“The Blessed Wolf!” chorused the women. Judge Scott surveyed them triumphantly.

“Out of your own mouths be it,” he said. “Just as I contended right along. No mere dog could have done what he did. He’s a wolf.”

“A Blessed Wolf,” amended the Judge’s wife.

“Yes, Blessed Wolf,” agreed the Judge. “And henceforth that shall be my name for him.”

“He’ll have to learn to walk again,” said the surgeon; “so he might as well start in right now. It won’t hurt him. Take him outside.” And outside he went, like a king, with all Sierra Vista about him and tending on him. He was very weak, and when he reached the lawn he lay down and rested for a while. Then the procession started on, little spurts of strength coming into White Fang’s muscles as he used them and the blood began to surge through them. The stables were reached, and there in the doorway, lay Collie, a half-dozen pudgy puppies playing about her in the sun. White Fang looked on with a wondering eye. Collie snarled warningly at him, and he was careful to keep his distance. The master with his toe helped one sprawling puppy toward him. He bristled suspiciously, but the master warned him that all was well. Collie, clasped in the arms of one of the women, watched him jealously and with a snarl warned him that all was not well. The puppy sprawled in front of him. He cocked his ears and watched it curiously. Then their noses touched, and he felt the warm little tongue of the puppy on his jowl. White Fang’s tongue went out, he knew not why, and he licked the puppy’s face. Hand-clapping and pleased cries from the gods greeted the performance. He was surprised, and looked at them in a puzzled way. Then his weakness asserted itself, and he lay down, his ears cocked, his head on one side, as he watched the puppy. The other puppies came sprawling toward him, to Collie’s great disgust; and he gravely permitted them to clamber and tumble over him. At first, amid the applause of the gods, he betrayed a trifle of his old self-consciousness and awkwardness. This passed away as the puppies’ antics and mauling continued, and he lay with half-shut patient eyes, drowsing in the sun.

Excerpt 3: It was wanton slaughter, and all for woman’s sake. No man ate of the seal meat or the oil. After a good day’s killing I have seen our decks covered with hides and bodies, slippery with fat and blood, the scuppers running red; masts, ropes, and rails spattered with the sanguinary colour; and the men, like butchers plying their trade, naked and red of arm and hand, hard at work with ripping and flensing-knives, removing the skins from the pretty sea-creatures they had killed. It was my task to tally the pelts as they came aboard from the boats, to oversee the skinning and afterward the cleansing of the decks and bringing things ship-shape again. It was not pleasant work. My soul and my stomach revolted at it; and yet, in a way, this handling and directing of many men was good for me. It developed what little executive ability I possessed, and I was aware of a toughening or hardening which I was undergoing and which could not be anything but wholesome for “Sissy” Van Weyden. One thing I was beginning to feel, and that was that I could never again be quite the same man I had been. While my hope and faith in human life still survived Wolf Larsen’s destructive criticism, he had nevertheless been a cause of change in minor matters. He had opened up for me the world of the real, of which I had known practically nothing and from which I had always shrunk. I had learned to look more closely at life as it was lived, to recognize that there were such things as facts in the world, to emerge from the realm of mind and idea and to place certain values on the concrete and objective phases of existence. I saw more of Wolf Larsen than ever when we had gained the grounds. For when the weather was fair and we were in the midst of the herd, all hands were away in the boats, and left on board were only he and I, and Thomas Mugridge, who did not count. But there was no play about it. The six boats, spreading out fan-wise from the schooner until the first weather boat and the last lee boat were anywhere from ten to twenty miles apart, cruised along a straight course over the sea till nightfall or bad weather drove them in. It was our duty to sail the Ghost well to leeward of the last lee boat, so that all the boats should have fair wind to run for us in case of squalls or threatening weather. It is no slight matter for two men, particularly when a stiff wind has sprung up, to handle a vessel like the Ghost, steering, keeping look-out for the boats, and setting or taking in sail; so it devolved upon me to learn, and learn quickly. Steering I picked up easily, but running aloft to the crosstrees and swinging my whole weight by my arms when I left the ratlines and climbed still higher, was more difficult. This, too, I learned, and quickly, for I felt somehow a wild desire to vindicate myself in Wolf Larsen’s eyes, to prove my right to live in ways other than of the mind. Nay, the time came when I took joy in the run of the masthead and in the clinging on by my legs at that precarious height while I swept the sea with glasses in search of the boats. I remember one beautiful day, when the boats left early and the reports of the hunters’ guns grew dim and distant and died away as they scattered far and wide over the sea. There was just the faintest wind from the westward; but it breathed its last by the time we managed to get to leeward of the last lee boat. One by one—I was at the masthead and saw—the six boats disappeared over the bulge of the earth as they followed the seal into the west. We lay, scarcely rolling on the placid sea, unable to follow. Wolf Larsen was apprehensive. The barometer was down, and the sky to the east did not please him. He studied it with unceasing vigilance.

“If she comes out of there,” he said, “hard and snappy, putting us to windward of the boats, it’s likely there’ll be empty bunks in steerage and fo’c’sle.” By eleven o’clock the sea had become glass. By midday, though we were well up in the northerly latitudes, the heat was sickening. There was no freshness in the air. It was sultry and oppressive, reminding me of what the old Californians term “earthquake weather.” There was something ominous about it, and in intangible ways one was made to feel that the worst was about to come. Slowly the whole eastern sky filled with clouds that over-towered us like some black sierra of the infernal regions. So clearly could one see cañon, gorge, and precipice, and the shadows that lie therein, that one looked unconsciously for the white surf-line and bellowing caverns where the sea charges on the land. And still we rocked gently, and there was no wind.

“It’s no squall,” Wolf Larsen said. “Old Mother Nature’s going to get up on her hind legs and howl for all that’s in her, and it’ll keep us jumping, Hump, to pull through with half our boats. You’d better run up and loosen the topsails.”

“But if it is going to howl, and there are only two of us?” I asked, a note of protest in my voice.

“Why we’ve got to make the best of the first of it and run down to our boats before our canvas is ripped out of us. After that I don’t give a rap what happens. The sticks ’ll stand it, and you and I will have to, though we’ve plenty cut out for us.” Still the calm continued. We ate dinner, a hurried and anxious meal for me with eighteen men abroad on the sea and beyond the bulge of the earth, and with that heaven-rolling mountain range of clouds moving slowly down upon us. Wolf Larsen did not seem affected, however; though I noticed, when we returned to the deck, a slight twitching of the nostrils, a perceptible quickness of movement. His face was stern, the lines of it had grown hard, and yet in his eyes—blue, clear blue this day—there was a strange brilliancy, a bright scintillating light. It struck me that he was joyous, in a ferocious sort of way; that he was glad there was an impending struggle; that he was thrilled and upborne with knowledge that one of the great moments of living, when the tide of life surges up in flood, was upon him. Once, and unwitting that he did so or that I saw, he laughed aloud, mockingly and defiantly, at the advancing storm. I see him yet standing there like a pigmy out of the Arabian Nights before the huge front of some malignant genie. He was daring destiny, and he was unafraid. He walked to the galley. “Cooky, by the time you’ve finished pots and pans you’ll be wanted on deck. Stand ready for a call.”

“Hump,” he said, becoming cognizant of the fascinated gaze I bent upon him, “this beats whisky and is where your Omar misses. I think he only half lived after all.” The western half of the sky had by now grown murky. The sun had dimmed and faded out of sight. It was two in the afternoon, and a ghostly twilight, shot through by wandering purplish lights, had descended upon us. In this purplish light Wolf Larsen’s face glowed and glowed, and to my excited fancy he appeared encircled by a halo. We lay in the midst of an unearthly quiet, while all about us were signs and omens of oncoming sound and movement. The sultry heat had become unendurable. The sweat was standing on my forehead, and I could feel it trickling down my nose. I felt as though I should faint, and reached out to the rail for support. And then, just then, the faintest possible whisper of air passed by. It was from the east, and like a whisper it came and went. The drooping canvas was not stirred, and yet my face had felt the air and been cooled.

“Cooky,” Wolf Larsen called in a low voice. Thomas Mugridge turned a pitiable scared face. “Let go that foreboom tackle and pass it across, and when she’s willing let go the sheet and come in snug with the tackle. And if you make a mess of it, it will be the last you ever make. Understand?”

“Mr. Van Weyden, stand by to pass the head-sails over. Then jump for the topsails and spread them quick as God’ll let you—the quicker you do it the easier you’ll find it. As for Cooky, if he isn’t lively bat him between the eyes.” I was aware of the compliment and pleased, in that no threat had accompanied my instructions. We were lying head to north-west, and it was his intention to jibe over all with the first puff.

“We’ll have the breeze on our quarter,” he explained to me. “By the last guns the boats were bearing away slightly to the south’ard.” He turned and walked aft to the wheel. I went forward and took my station at the jibs. Another whisper of wind, and another, passed by. The canvas flapped lazily.

“Thank Gawd she’s not comin’ all of a bunch, Mr. Van Weyden,” was the Cockney’s fervent ejaculation. And I was indeed thankful, for I had by this time learned enough to know, with all our canvas spread, what disaster in such event awaited us. The whispers of wind became puffs, the sails filled, the Ghost moved. Wolf Larsen put the wheel hard up, to port, and we began to pay off. The wind was now dead astern, muttering and puffing stronger and stronger, and my head-sails were pounding lustily. I did not see what went on elsewhere, though I felt the sudden surge and heel of the schooner as the wind-pressures changed to the jibing of the fore- and main-sails. My hands were full with the flying-jib, jib, and staysail; and by the time this part of my task was accomplished the Ghost was leaping into the south-west, the wind on her quarter and all her sheets to starboard. Without pausing for breath, though my heart was beating like a trip-hammer from my exertions, I sprang to the topsails, and before the wind had become too strong we had them fairly set and were coiling down. Then I went aft for orders. Wolf Larsen nodded approval and relinquished the wheel to me. The wind was strengthening steadily and the sea rising. For an hour I steered, each moment becoming more difficult. I had not the experience to steer at the gait we were going on a quartering course.

“Now take a run up with the glasses and raise some of the boats. We’ve made at least ten knots, and we’re going twelve or thirteen now. The old girl knows how to walk.” I contested myself with the fore crosstrees, some seventy feet above the deck. As I searched the vacant stretch of water before me, I comprehended thoroughly the need for haste if we were to recover any of our men. Indeed, as I gazed at the heavy sea through which we were running, I doubted that there was a boat afloat. It did not seem possible that such frail craft could survive such stress of wind and water. I could not feel the full force of the wind, for we were running with it; but from my lofty perch I looked down as though outside the Ghost and apart from her, and saw the shape of her outlined sharply against the foaming sea as she tore along instinct with life. Sometimes she would lift and send across some great wave, burying her starboard-rail from view, and covering her deck to the hatches with the boiling ocean. At such moments, starting from a windward roll, I would go flying through the air with dizzying swiftness, as though I clung to the end of a huge, inverted pendulum, the arc of which, between the greater rolls, must have been seventy feet or more. Once, the terror of this giddy sweep overpowered me, and for a while I clung on, hand and foot, weak and trembling, unable to search the sea for the missing boats or to behold aught of the sea but that which roared beneath and strove to overwhelm the Ghost. But the thought of the men in the midst of it steadied me, and in my quest for them I forgot myself. For an hour I saw nothing but the naked, desolate sea. And then, where a vagrant shaft of sunlight struck the ocean and turned its surface to wrathful silver, I caught a small black speck thrust skyward for an instant and swallowed up. I waited patiently. Again the tiny point of black projected itself through the wrathful blaze a couple of points off our port-bow. I did not attempt to shout, but communicated the news to Wolf Larsen by waving my arm. He changed the course, and I signalled affirmation when the speck showed dead ahead. It grew larger, and so swiftly that for the first time I fully appreciated the speed of our flight. Wolf Larsen motioned for me to come down, and when I stood beside him at the wheel gave me instructions for heaving to.

“Expect all hell to break loose,” he cautioned me, “but don’t mind it. Yours is to do your own work and to have Cooky stand by the fore-sheet.” I managed to make my way forward, but there was little choice of sides, for the weather-rail seemed buried as often as the lee. Having instructed Thomas Mugridge as to what he was to do, I clambered into the fore-rigging a few feet. The boat was now very close, and I could make out plainly that it was lying head to wind and sea and dragging on its mast and sail, which had been thrown overboard and made to serve as a sea-anchor. The three men were bailing. Each rolling mountain whelmed them from view, and I would wait with sickening anxiety, fearing that they would never appear again. Then, and with black suddenness, the boat would shoot clear through the foaming crest, bow pointed to the sky, and the whole length of her bottom showing, wet and dark, till she seemed on end. There would be a fleeting glimpse of the three men flinging water in frantic haste, when she would topple over and fall into the yawning valley, bow down and showing her full inside length to the stern upreared almost directly above the bow. Each time that she reappeared was a miracle. The Ghost suddenly changed her course, keeping away, and it came to me with a shock that Wolf Larsen was giving up the rescue as impossible. Then I realized that he was preparing to heave to, and dropped to the deck to be in readiness. We were now dead before the wind, the boat far away and abreast of us. I felt an abrupt easing of the schooner, a loss for the moment of all strain and pressure, coupled with a swift acceleration of speed. She was rushing around on her heel into the wind.

The cabin stood on a bench of land above the Stewart, where the river swung wide around a bluff of spruce and then ran on, white and frozen and dumb, into the north. It was a small cabin, of logs chinked with moss, and its roof was of poles laid over with earth, so that in summer grass grew upon it and in winter the snow lay there in a thick and level blanket. One window it had, of oiled flour-sacking stretched upon a frame, and through this window, on the short days, came a dim and yellowish light that was not so much light as the absence of complete dark. A sheet-iron stove squatted in the corner. There were two bunks against the back wall, one long and one short, and a table made of a split log, and a shelf whereon were ranged the tins of baking-powder and the sack of beans and the precious can of matches, wrapped in oilskin against the damp.

Will Garrity had built that cabin with his own hands in the fall of the year, when the leaves of the birches were yellow and the first skim ice was forming in the eddies. He had built it for three. But the woman had died at Forty Mile in the spring before, of a fever that came up the river with the first steamboat, and so it was a cabin for two, a man and a boy. The boy was seven years old, and his name was Robbie.

On this day Garrity had gone out at dawn, which is to say at nine o'clock, to run the long line of his traps that stretched away up the creek for a dozen miles. It was a hard day's travel, and he would not be back before dark. He had left the boy in charge of the cabin, as he had left him a score of times before, with the fire banked and wood piled high beside the stove, and with instructions which were simple and which had been repeated until the boy could say them over in his sleep. Keep the fire. Stay inside. Do not go down to the river. And above all, do not go into the timber.

The cold had come down upon the land three days before, and it had come to stay. The spirit thermometer which Garrity had carried in from Dawson, and which he valued above any other thing in the cabin save the matches and the rifle, showed fifty-two degrees below zero when he looked at it in the morning. At such a temperature spittle crackles in the air before it strikes the snow. At such a temperature a man does not stop to rest, nor does he wet his feet, nor does he travel alone if he can help it. And at such a temperature the Northland is not a place for mistakes. It does not forgive them. It does not even take notice of them, as a man takes notice of a gnat that he crushes on his wrist; it merely crushes, without heat and without malice, because that is its nature.

Garrity knew this. He had learned it in eleven winters, and he had paid for the learning with the tips of two fingers on his left hand and with the memory of more than one man who had not paid in time. The boy did not know it. He had been told it, which is a different thing. He was seven years old, and he believed, as all young creatures believe, that the world was a warm place and well disposed toward him, and that the things his father said were things that happened to other people.

It was past three o'clock and the dark was settling when Garrity came down the creek-bed to the river. He was weary, and the frost was thick in his beard and on his eyebrows, and the pack upon his back held two marten and a lynx. He looked up toward the bench where the cabin stood, as he always looked, for the thin blue thread of smoke that should be climbing straight into the windless sky.

There was no smoke.

He stood still. For a long moment he stood still, and the breath went out of him in a long plume of vapour, and he did not draw another. Then he began to run. A man does not run at fifty below. It sears the lungs and opens the body to the cold, and he knew this, and he ran nevertheless, up the steep trail to the bench, his snowshoes slapping and his pack thumping upon his back.

The door of the cabin was shut. He flung it open. The stove was black and cold. He laid his bare hand upon it, and it was cold as the outer air. Frost had begun already to form in a white rime upon the inner walls, and the water in the bucket by the door was frozen solid. The short bunk was empty. The cabin was empty.

He went out again into the deepening dark and stood and looked about him, and then he looked down, as a hunter looks, and read the snow. There were the tracks of small moccasins going out from the door. They did not go to the river. They went, instead, along the edge of the bench, and beside them, a little before them, went the tracks of a snowshoe rabbit. Garrity read the whole story in a glance. He saw the boy at the window, bored with the long hours, pressing his face to the greasy sacking. He saw the rabbit, white upon white, hopping in the open. And he saw the boy taking down the little bow he had made for him in the fall, a toy, a plaything, and going out after it, as the man-cub goes out after the first meat of its life, with the old hunting blood singing up in it and all the warnings of its elders forgotten.

The tracks led into the timber.

Garrity followed them. He did not call out. Calling would waste breath, and there would be nothing to hear the call but the trees and the silence and whatever else might be abroad in the dark. The tracks wandered. They doubled and turned, as the tracks of the rabbit doubled and turned, and the boy had followed blindly, his eyes on the quarry, never once looking back to mark his way. Here he had stopped, and the snow was trampled where he had stood and fitted an arrow. Here he had shot, and missed, for the little willow shaft lay half-buried where it had fallen. And here, a long way farther, the tracks of the rabbit vanished into a thicket of alder, and the tracks of the boy went round and round in a circle, and then they went off at random, aimlessly, and Garrity knew that his son had become lost.

He found him in a clump of willows at the edge of a frozen slough, a mile and more from the cabin. The boy was crouched down with his back against the stems, his knees drawn up and his arms wrapped about them, very small and very still. He did not look up when Garrity came crashing through the brush. He did not move. And for a space of time that Garrity was never afterward able to measure, a space that might have been a heartbeat and might have been an hour, the man believed that his son was dead.

Then the boy lifted his head. His eyes were dull and heavy, like the eyes of one who is very sleepy, and he looked at his father without surprise.

"I'm awful tired, Dad," he said. "I was just restin' a spell."

Garrity did not answer. He tore off his mittens and seized the small face between his hands. The cheeks were white, a dead and waxen white, two round patches high upon the bones, and the tip of the nose was white also. He scooped up snow in his bare palms and rubbed, hard and without mercy, until the boy cried out and twisted in his grasp, and he went on rubbing until the white patches flushed and reddened and the boy was weeping with the pain of the blood coming back. Then he pulled off the boy's moccasins and looked at the feet, and they were cold, very cold, but they were not white, and he thrust them inside his own parka against the bare skin of his belly, and held them there, and the cold of them went into him like knives.

It was when he stood up, with the boy in his arms, that he saw the other tracks.

They came out of the timber on the far side of the slough and they crossed the open snow in a line as straight as a stretched cord, without haste and without hesitation. They were large tracks, larger than the tracks of any dog Garrity had ever driven, and they came to within a dozen yards of the willow clump. There they stopped. The snow was pressed down in an oval where something had lain, and watched, and waited. And then the tracks went away again, back into the timber, and Garrity knew that the thing which had made them had gone only because it had heard him coming.

He said nothing of this to the boy. He wrapped him in the lynx skin out of the pack and carried him home.

---

It was a long time before the cabin was warm. Garrity built the fire high, till the sides of the stove glowed a dull and angry red and the frost upon the walls ran down in little rivulets and the steam rose from the boy's clothing where it hung drying on a line. He made tea, very hot and very sweet with the sugar he had been hoarding, and he made the boy drink it, cup after cup. He fried bacon and thawed a lump of sourdough bread. He did all these things without speaking, and the boy watched him from the bunk, wrapped in blankets to the chin, and as the warmth crept back into his body and the life into his limbs, a new feeling crept into him also, which was the feeling of fear.

For he had never seen his father like this. He had seen him angry, often, in the swift and passing way of a man who is tired and who works hard; he had seen him laugh, and seen him grieve, that time at Forty Mile when they put the woman in the frozen ground and the priest said words over her. But he had never seen him silent in this way, moving about the cabin with a face like the face of the bluff above the river, grey and set and with no warmth in it anywhere.

When the meal was eaten and the plates were scoured with sand and stacked upon the shelf, Garrity sat down upon the end of the boy's bunk. He sat for a long time with his elbows upon his knees and his maimed hand and his whole hand clasped together, looking at the floor. The fire roared in the stove. Outside, very far away, a long cry went up, thin and quavering, and climbed and hung and died.

The boy shivered, though he was no longer cold.

"Robbie," said Garrity.

"Yes, Dad."

"What did I tell you this mornin', before I went up the creek?"

The boy's lip trembled. "To keep the fire."

"An' what else?"

"To stay inside."

"An' what else?"

"Not to go to the river." He stopped. His father waited. The boy swallowed, and the words came out very small. "An' not to go in the timber."

"An' where did you go?"

The boy said nothing. There was nothing he could say. He began to cry, quietly, the tears running down his raw red cheeks, and he did not wipe them, because to raise his hand would have been to move, and he was afraid to move.

Garrity did not comfort him. He wanted to. Every fibre of him cried out to reach across the bunk and draw the small body against his own and hold it, and feel the warmth of it, and know that it lived. But he did not. He had thought it all out on the long trail home, with the boy's feet freezing against his belly and the empty dark of the timber pressing in on every side, and he knew that there are times when comfort is the cruellest gift a man can give.

"Listen to me," he said. "Listen good, Robbie, because I ain't goin' to say this but the once. You're old enough to hear it now. Maybe you ain't, but you got to be, because the country don't wait for nobody to get old enough."

He got up and went to the shelf and took down the spirit thermometer, and he held it close to the lamp so the boy could see the little red thread sunk far down in its glass.

"See that? That's fifty-two below. Know what fifty-two below does to a man? It don't hate him. It don't even know he's there. It just takes the heat out of him, the way you'd take the water out of a bucket with a dipper, a little an' a little an' a little, till there ain't none left. An' it don't hurt, Robbie. That's the devil of it. At first it hurts, an' then it stops hurtin', an' a man gets warm an' sleepy, an' he says to himself, I'll just set down an' rest a spell." He paused, and his voice went harsh. "That's what you said to me, out there. You remember? You was restin' a spell. Another half hour of restin' an' you'd 've been restin' for good, an' I'd 've found you settin' there froze stiff as a stick of cordwood, with your eyes open an' snow on your eyelashes. I seen it, Robbie. I seen grown men like that. Big men, strong men, men that could pack two hundred pounds over the Chilcoot. They set down to rest a spell."

The boy was sobbing now, his thin shoulders heaving under the blankets. Garrity put back the thermometer and came and sat down again.

"You let the fire go out," he said, more quietly. "You figure that's a little thing. It ain't. Suppose I'd broke a leg up the creek today. Suppose I'd went through the ice on an overflow an' come home with my feet wet an' my hands too stiff to strike a match. I'd 've come in that door expectin' a fire, an' there'd 've been none, an' I'd 've died on the floor of my own cabin while you was out chasin' rabbits. That's what a fire is in this country. It ain't for comfort. It's life an' death, an' it's the difference between 'em."

He leaned forward. The lamplight fell upon his face, upon the frost-scars on his cheekbones and the deep lines about his eyes, and the boy, looking up through his tears, saw something there he had not seen before, something that was not anger at all.

"There's one thing more," Garrity said, "an' then I'm done. I wasn't goin' to tell you. I been arguin' with myself the whole way home whether to tell you. But I reckon you got to know." He drew a long breath. "You heard that howlin' a minute back?"

The boy nodded, his eyes very wide.

"There was a wolf in that slough, Robbie. A big timber wolf, alone, an' hungry, the way they get hungry in the cold snaps when the moose has gone over the divide an' the rabbits is scarce. I seen his tracks. He come out of the trees an' he come straight across the slough to where you was settin', an' he laid down in the snow not twenty steps off, an' he watched you. He was waitin'. Wolves is patient. They know what the cold does. He was waitin' for you to go to sleep."

The boy made a small sound, a whimper like a puppy's, and drew the blankets up over his mouth.

"I come along an' he heard me an' he went off. That's the only reason. Not because you was smart, nor because you was brave, nor because the Lord was lookin' out for you special. Just because I happened to come home by the creek-trail instead of over the ridge. That's all that stood between you an' that wolf. Just a trail I happened to take." Garrity's voice broke a little, and he stopped, and when he went on it was hard again. "You can't count on luck in this country. Luck's like that wolf. It'll lay off a ways an' watch you, an' it'll leave you be for a time, an' then one day it won't."

For a while neither of them spoke. The fire crackled. The lamp hissed softly. Far away the cry went up again, and was answered by another, farther still.

"You goin' to lick me, Dad?" the boy whispered at last.

Garrity looked at him. He thought of his own father, a hard man in a hard country, back in the Michigan woods, and of the strap that hung behind the kitchen door, and of how little he had learned from it save to hate the hand that held it. He shook his head slowly.

"No," he said. "I ain't goin' to lick you. A lickin' 's over in a minute, an' you'd forget it in a week. I want you to remember this. I want you to remember it every day you live in this country, an' every time you get to thinkin' you know better than the cold."

"What're you goin' to do?"

"Tomorrow mornin'," said Garrity, "you an' me is goin' to walk back out to that slough. You're goin' to walk it on your own two feet, the whole way. An' you're goin' to stand where that wolf laid down an' watched you, an' you're goin' to look at them tracks, close, till you know 'em by heart. An' after that, for a month, you're goin' to keep the fire. Not me. You. You're goin' to split the kindlin' an' pack in the wood an' feed that stove, mornin' an' night, an' if it goes out once, just once, you'll answer to me for it. You understand?"

"Yes, Dad."

"Say it back."

"I'm to keep the fire. For a month. An' if it goes out I answer to you."

"An' the timber?"

"I ain't to go in the timber." The boy's voice cracked. "Not never. Not without you."

"Not without me," Garrity agreed. "Not till you're grown an' know the country. An' maybe not even then." He stood up. "Now go to sleep."

---

The boy slept. He slept the heavy, dreamless sleep of the very young and the very weary, his mouth a little open and one red fist curled against his cheek. But Garrity did not sleep. He sat on the bench by the stove, feeding it from time to time with lengths of spruce, and he watched the boy, and he did not take his eyes off him.

And as he sat there, his hands began to shake. It was a thing he had not let them do all that long day, not on the trail nor in the willows nor in the cabin while he talked, and now that there was no one to see, they shook, and he could not stop them. He held them out before him in the red glow from the stove's draft and looked at them, the whole one and the maimed one, and watched them tremble, as a man might watch the hands of a stranger. He had faced the cold for eleven winters and never feared it as he feared it now. He had gone hungry and been lost and gone through the ice and walked out of it alive, and none of it had shaken him like this. For a man may wager his own life against the Wild and think little of it; it is only when he is made to wager the life of another, one whom he loves, that he comes to know how small he is, and how vast and indifferent the thing that he has set himself against.

Toward midnight he rose and went to the door and opened it a crack. The cold came in upon him like a living thing, and the stars burned overhead, very many and very near, crackling and blazing in the black. The aurora was out, a pale green curtain that rippled and folded across the northern sky. The timber stood dark and silent at the edge of the bench. Somewhere in it, he knew, the wolf was hunting still, patient, unhurried, obedient to the one law it knew, which was the law of meat.

Garrity shut the door and barred it. He went back to the stove and put on another stick. Then he went and stood a long while over the short bunk, looking down at the sleeping boy, and at last, because there was no one to see, he bent and laid his maimed hand very gently upon the small rough head, and kept it there, and felt the warmth of it come up into his palm.

In the morning the boy rose before him and built the fire. It was a poor fire, smoky and slow to catch, and the kindling was split too thick. But it burned. And when Garrity came awake and saw the thin blue thread of it climbing through the stovepipe and out into the windless morning, he lay still in his blankets for a moment and said nothing at all.

It was after eleven o'clock when Andrzej Sobczak came up the hill from the mill, and the lamp was still burning in the kitchen of the little frame house on Furnace Street. He saw it from the corner, a yellow square in the blackness, and his heart sank within him, for he knew what it meant. Kasia had not gone to bed. Kasia was waiting for him, and she had been waiting since nine, when the shift let out and he did not come home.

The house was one of four hundred exactly like it, which the Monongahela Valley Steel Company had built along the slope above the river, and which it rented to its workmen at eleven dollars a month, deducted from their wages before they ever saw them. They were built of boards which had warped in the first summer, so that the wind came through the walls in winter and the soot came through them all the year round. There was no getting away from the soot in that town. It lay upon the window sills and the bed-quilts; it got into the bread and the children's lungs; when the women hung out the washing on Monday it was gray by noon, and they took it in and washed it again, and it was gray again by evening. Over everything, day and night, hung the glare of the furnaces and the roar of the blowing engines, so that a man who had lived there five years no longer heard the sound at all, and would wake up in a fright if it stopped.

Andrzej stood for a minute at the gate, making up his mind. He was a big man, broad in the shoulders, with a heavy, slow face and hands that were cracked and scarred from eleven years of handling hot iron. He had come over from Galicia when he was nineteen, with a cardboard valise and a paper that a cousin had sent him, and he had believed then, as all of them believed, that in America a man who was strong and willing would rise. He had been strong and willing for eleven years, and he was now a second helper on Number Four open hearth, earning nineteen cents an hour for a twelve-hour day, and every other Sunday a twenty-four-hour turn when the shifts changed over. He had not risen; but he had not yet altogether ceased to believe that he might, and that was the thing which he could not explain to his wife.

He went in. Kasia was sitting by the stove, with the baby asleep in her lap and a pile of mending on the table beside her. She did not look up when the door opened, and she did not speak; she went on drawing the needle in and out of a little shirt, and Andrzej stood and watched her, and the silence grew between them until it was like a thing that could be touched.

"Supper is in the oven," she said at last. "It is dried up. You can eat it or not."

"I am not hungry," he said.

"No," she answered. "I suppose they gave you something to eat at the hall."

So she knew. He had thought perhaps she might not know, that he could tell her in his own way; but of course she knew. In that town there was nothing that the women did not know within the hour. Mrs. Kowalczyk next door had a husband on the same turn, and Mrs. Kowalczyk had a tongue that ran like a mill race.

"Who told you?" he asked.

"Does it matter who told me? Half the street saw you go in. Do you think the company has no eyes? Do you think Gallagher does not have a man standing across the road, writing down the names?" She put the mending down and looked at him, and he saw that her face was white and her eyes were red, and that she had been crying a long time and had stopped only because there were no more tears. "Andrzej, Andrzej, what have you done to us?"

He took off his cap and turned it round in his hands. He was not a man of words; it had cost him a great deal of labor to understand the things that had been said in the hall that night, and now he must say them over again, to a woman who did not want to hear them, and he did not know how to begin.

"Kasia," he said, "listen to me. It is not only me. There were three hundred men there. Three hundred! From the open hearth and the blooming mill and the rail mill—Hungarians and Slovaks and Italians, and some Americans too, men who have been in the mill twenty years. They are going to organize. They say if all the men stand together, the company cannot do anything. It cannot fire everybody."

"It can fire you," said Kasia.

He had no answer for that, and she went on, her voice rising. "It can fire you, and it can put us out of this house, which belongs to the company, and it can tell the store to give us no more credit, which also belongs to the company. And then what? Where do we go? To Homestead? To Braddock? It is the same company there. To McKeesport? The same. You know what happened to Wojcik. You know what happened to the Dombrowski family, with five children, and the snow on the ground."

He knew. Everybody knew. The story of Stanislas Wojcik had been told and retold in every kitchen on Furnace Street. Wojcik had been heard to say, in a saloon, that the men ought to have a union; and two days later he had been told at the gate that there was no more work for him. He had gone to the other mills in the valley, and at each of them the employment clerk had looked in a little book, and shaken his head. He had gone to Cleveland, and to Gary, and the little book had gone ahead of him. In the end he had taken a job shovelling coal for a dollar a day on the river barges, and his wife had taken in washing, and their oldest boy, who was twelve, had gone into the glass works, where the boys carried the hot bottles at night; and the boy had coughed for a winter and then died. These things were not secrets. The company did not wish them to be secrets. It wished every man in the valley to know them, and to think of them whenever he heard the word "union."

For the reader who has never lived in a mill town, it may be well to explain how this system worked; for it was a system, and a very perfect one, built up by able men over many years. The Monongahela Valley Steel Company was one of the subsidiaries of a great corporation whose capital ran into the hundreds of millions, and whose shares were held by bankers in New York and by widows and colleges and churches all over the land. These shareholders did not know Andrzej Sobczak, and would have been shocked to hear of Stanislas Wojcik; they knew only that the dividends came in regularly, eight per cent upon the preferred stock and a handsome rate upon the common, which had been issued in the first place for nothing at all. The managers of the corporation knew that these dividends depended upon keeping down the cost of labor, and they knew that the cost of labor could be kept down only so long as the laborers did not combine. They had broken the old Amalgamated Association twenty years before, with Pinkerton detectives and the militia and starvation; and since that time they had seen to it that no union should ever again get a footing in their mills. They kept spies among the men—spies who went to the meetings and sometimes made the most violent speeches there, in order to learn who applauded. They kept a blacklist, which passed from mill to mill and from state to state. They mixed the races in every gang, so that Slovak could not talk to Italian nor Italian to Pole; and they had a regular policy of bringing in a new nationality whenever the old one began to grow restless. And they owned the houses and the stores and the bank, and the mayor and the burgess and the police, and the newspaper which told the people every morning what a beneficent thing the corporation was, and how prosperous the country had become under its rule.

Against all this stood Andrzej Sobczak, with his cracked hands and his slow mind, and three hundred other men like him, who had met that night in a hall over a saloon on Water Street and listened to an organizer from Chicago. And in the kitchen on Furnace Street, against Andrzej, stood his wife.

"Kasia," he said, "you do not understand. Sit down and let me tell you what the man said."

"I am sitting down," said Kasia. "Tell me."

He drew a chair up to the table and sat on the edge of it, leaning forward, and the lamplight fell upon his face and showed the lines in it, which were the lines of an old man, though he was barely thirty.

"He said," began Andrzej, slowly, feeling for the words, "he said that the company made last year a profit of—I do not remember the number, but it was more money than there is in all of Galicia. Millions and millions. He had it written in a paper. And he said that out of every ton of steel that we make, the company keeps so much, and pays us so little, that if they paid us twice as much they would still be rich. He said that we work twelve hours, and men in England work eight, and in some places in this country also. He said that the reason we work twelve hours is because we let them. Because every man is afraid alone. But if every man stands together—"

"And who is this man?" Kasia interrupted. "Does he work in the mill?"

"No. He is an organizer. From the federation."

"So. He does not work in the mill. He makes his speech, and he takes the train back to Chicago, and you lose your job. Does the federation pay the rent?"

"There will be strike benefits," said Andrzej. "He said—"

"How much?"

He hesitated. "Three dollars a week, maybe. For a man with a family."

Kasia laughed; it was a dreadful sound, and the baby stirred in her lap and whimpered, and she rocked it mechanically until it was quiet again. "Three dollars a week," she said. "Andrzej, do you know what we owe at the store? Do you know? I will tell you, because you never ask. Forty-one dollars and sixty cents. Since Christmas, when you had the burn on your arm and lost three weeks. Since the doctor came for Józef, when he had the pneumonia. Forty-one dollars, and every pay-day they take what they please and give us the rest in an envelope, and every pay-day the envelope is thinner. I have not bought a pair of shoes for myself in two years. I wear your old ones, with paper in the toes. Józef has no coat for the winter. And you go to a hall and listen to a man from Chicago, and you come home and tell me three dollars a week!"

Andrzej's face had gone dark, and his big hands closed upon his knees. "You think I do not know these things?" he said, in a low voice. "You think I do not see? I see Józef with no coat. I see you with my shoes. That is why I go to the hall. Because I have worked eleven years and we are poorer than when we came. Because every year the work is harder and the pay is the same, and the prices at the store go up and up. Because they speed up the furnaces so that a heat that took ten hours takes eight now, and we must do the same work in less time, and still twelve hours. Last month Mikula was killed when the ladle broke. You remember Mikula. He was twenty-four years old. The company paid his widow one hundred and fifty dollars and she signed a paper. One hundred and fifty dollars for a man! A horse costs more. And the superintendent said it was Mikula's own carelessness. Mikula was not careless. The ladle was cracked, and everybody knew it was cracked, and the foreman said to use it anyway, because they would not stop the heat. I was there, Kasia. I saw it. I saw what was left of him."

He stopped, and wiped his forehead with the back of his hand, and for a moment neither of them spoke. Through the thin walls they could hear the roar of the mill below, steady and endless, like the breathing of some vast animal; and down the street a dog was barking, and somewhere a man was singing drunkenly in a foreign tongue.

When Kasia spoke again her voice was quieter, but it was harder too. "And if you go into the union," she said, "does that bring Mikula back?"

"No. But maybe it keeps the next man from being Mikula. Maybe it is me next time, Kasia. Did you think of that? Every day I go in there I think, maybe today. Maybe today the roof falls, maybe today the steel splashes. And if it is me, you get a hundred and fifty dollars and a paper to sign, and they put another man on the furnace before I am cold."

She flinched as if he had struck her, and he saw it and was sorry; but he could not stop now. All the bitterness of eleven years was coming up in him, all the things he had swallowed and not said, at the gate and in the store and on the floor of the open hearth, where the foremen cursed the men in a language which most of them did not understand, but the meaning of which was plain enough.

"I am not a dog," he said. "They treat us like dogs. Worse than dogs. A dog, at least, they do not work twelve hours. The man said—the man from Chicago said—that we make all the wealth, that without us there would be no steel, no railroads, no buildings in New York forty stories high. He said that we are not slaves, that in America no man is a slave unless he lets himself be. And I thought, he is right. I have let myself be a slave. Eleven years I have let myself be a slave, because I was afraid. Now I will not be afraid any more."

Kasia looked at him for a long time. She was a small woman, and she had been pretty once—he remembered how pretty, at the wedding in the Polish church on Third Street, with the ribbons in her hair and the fiddles playing until morning. Now she was thin, and her hands were red and swollen from the washing, and there was a gray streak in her hair that had come the winter Józef was sick. She was twenty-seven years old. And looking at her, Andrzej felt suddenly that the man from Chicago had not told the whole truth; that it was not only he who was a slave, but she also, and that her slavery was worse than his, because she had not even the furnace to fight against, but only the soot and the store and the endless arithmetic of hunger.

"You will not be afraid," she said slowly. "That is very fine. You will not be afraid. But I will be afraid, Andrzej. I will be afraid for both of us. When they put us in the street, I will be afraid. When the baby cries because there is no milk, I will be afraid. You can be brave—you are a man, and you have the other men, and you can go to the hall and shout and feel strong. But who is with me? Who stands together with the women? We stay in the kitchen and count the pennies and wait to see what the men have done to us."

"The women can stand together too," he said, but it sounded foolish even to him, and she did not answer it.

"I am not saying the company is good," she went on. "I know what the company is. I am not a fool. I know they cheat at the store, and I know they killed Mikula, and I know they will kill you some day if they can get another man cheaper. I know all that. But Andrzej, they are so big. They have the police. They have the soldiers. You remember what the old men say about Homestead, how the soldiers came. And we are so small. We are nothing. How can nothing fight against everything?"

It was the question which has been asked in every working-class kitchen in the world, since the first master set the first slave to labor; and Andrzej Sobczak, second helper on Number Four, had no better answer to it than any of the millions who had gone before him. He sat with his head bowed, and his hands hanging between his knees, and he thought of the hall, and of the faces there—hundreds of faces, black from the mill, hollow-eyed, hungry—and of the moment when the organizer had cried out, "There are a hundred thousand of you in this valley, and a few hundred of them! Who is small now?" and the whole hall had risen and shouted, Slovaks and Hungarians and Italians together, each in his own tongue. He had felt then, for the first time in eleven years, that he was not nothing; that he was part of something vast, a force like the river or the furnace itself, which no company could stand against. But here in the kitchen, with the lamp smoking and the soot on the sill and his wife's frightened eyes upon him, the feeling had gone out of him, and he did not know how to bring it back.

"I do not know," he said at last. "I do not know how. But the man said, if we do nothing, nothing changes. And then Józef goes into the mill when he is fourteen, and works twelve hours, and gets killed like Mikula, or gets old like me. You want that for Józef?"

"I want Józef to eat," said Kasia.

"So do I. So do I! But I want him to eat when he is a man too, not only now."

The baby woke and began to cry in earnest, and Kasia got up and walked the floor with it, back and forth across the narrow kitchen, hushing it in Polish, the old words her own mother had sung to her in a village by the Vistula, where there had been no furnaces and no soot, only poverty of another kind. Andrzej watched her, and the misery in him was so great that he could not bear it, and he got up and went to the window and stood looking out at the glare in the sky.

"Did you sign the paper?" Kasia asked, from behind him. "The union paper. Did you put your name?"

He was silent a moment. Then he said, "Yes."

He heard her stop walking. He did not turn around. Below him the Bessemer converters were blowing, and the sky over the river was lit up red and gold, as if the whole valley were burning; and for a moment it seemed to him that it was burning, that it had always been burning, and that all the men and women in it were being consumed in that fire, year after year, so that a few people far away in New York might grow richer than any king.

"Then it is done," Kasia said, and her voice was very tired. "It is done, and there is nothing more to say."

"Kasia—"

"No. I am going to bed. Tomorrow I will go to the store and ask Mr. Hagerty for flour, and I will see in his face if he knows. And if he knows, then we will see." She paused at the door of the bedroom, with the baby against her shoulder, and looked back at him; and in her look there was anger still, and fear, and something else that he could not name, and that perhaps she could not have named either—something that was not quite forgiveness, but was akin to it. "You are a fool, Andrzej," she said. "You are a big, stupid fool. But you are my fool."

Then she went in and closed the door, and he stood alone by the window, with the dried-up supper in the oven and the roar of the mill in his ears, and the red glare on his face, until the lamp burned down and went out.
