It was in the month of March, when the snow upon the hillsides above the river had turned to a grey slush, and the slush to a brown and sticky mud, that Edward Thorne came back to the valley of the Monongahela. He had been gone for seven years: four of them at a famous university in the East, where he had learned a great deal of Greek and a little of political economy, and three more in travel and in the reading of law in his father's office in the city. In all that time he had not once set foot in the town of Carrville, though it lay only forty miles from his father's house; and if anyone had asked him why, he would have been hard put to it to give an answer. The truth was that the place had simply dropped out of his mind, as such places drop out of the minds of those who do not have to live in them.

But now a letter had come from his aunt, his mother's younger sister, who had married a man named Malloy and gone to live among the mills; and the letter said that she was ailing, and would like to see her sister's boy once more before she died. So Edward had taken the morning train, and now he stood upon the platform of the little station, with his overcoat buttoned to his chin and his fine leather bag in his hand, and stared about him at a world he had forgotten.

He had remembered Carrville as a boy remembers things, a place of wonder and excitement, of great fires that roared in the night and painted the clouds red, of whistles that shrieked and engines that thundered; he and his cousin Danny had used to sit upon the hill behind the Malloy cottage and watch the slag-cars dump their burden of molten waste down the bank, and it had seemed to them the most glorious spectacle in the world. Now he saw it with the eyes of a man, and what he saw made him catch his breath. The whole length of the valley, as far as the eye could reach, was one vast smear of smoke; it poured from a hundred stacks, black and brown and yellow, and it rolled along the river and settled upon the town like a blanket, so that at eleven o'clock in the morning the sun was a dull copper disk that one could look at without blinking. The air had a taste to it, a taste of sulphur and of iron, and it caught in the throat and made one cough. The buildings along the street were of wood, unpainted, or of brick that had once been red and was now the color of soot; and everything—the walls, the fences, the windows, the very faces of the people who passed—was coated with the same fine grey grime.

Edward was still standing there when a hand fell upon his shoulder, and he turned and found himself face to face with his cousin.

He would not have known him. That was the first thought that came to him, and it was a thought that shamed him, so that he flushed and stammered as he took the hand that was held out. Danny Malloy was twenty-six years of age, a year younger than Edward himself; but he might have been forty. He was a big man, broad in the shoulders and deep in the chest, as he had promised to be when he was a boy; but there was a stoop to his shoulders now, and his face was lined and hollow, and there were patches of grey in the hair above his temples. His skin had a curious mottled look, red in some places and pale in others, which Edward learned afterwards was the mark of the furnaces, where a man's face is roasted on one side while his back freezes on the other. And when he held out his hand, Edward saw that two of the fingers were missing from it, and that the others were twisted and scarred.

"Well, Eddie," said Danny, and grinned—and the grin, at least, was the same. "You've come up in the world, I can see that. Look at the coat on him! I'd have to work a month for a coat like that."

Edward laughed, because he did not know what else to do; and then, because the remark had stung him a little, he said, "How is your mother, Danny?"

The grin went away. "She's bad," said the other. "The doctor says it's her lungs. It's the smoke, you know—it gets into everybody, sooner or later. She'll be glad to see you, though. She's talked of nothing else since she wrote."

They set out up the hill together, Danny carrying the leather bag in spite of Edward's protests. The street was unpaved, and the mud was ankle-deep in places, so that Edward's polished shoes were ruined before they had gone a block; he noticed that the people they passed wore heavy boots, or else went with their feet wrapped in rags and sacking, and he noticed also that most of them were foreigners—short, swarthy men with drooping mustaches, and women with shawls over their heads, who stared at his clothes and then looked quickly away. Danny nodded to some of them, and spoke a word or two in a language Edward did not understand.

"Hunkies," he explained. "Slovaks, most of them, and some Croatians. The company brings them in by the trainload. They'll work for anything, and they don't make trouble—or they didn't, anyway, until lately. I've picked up a bit of their talk. You have to, if you're going to get along in the mill."

"I didn't know there were so many," said Edward.

"There's more of them than us, now. The Irish and the Welsh used to run the mills, back when my father started. But they got too uppity, you see—they wanted a union, and a decent wage, and the company wasn't having any of that. So they broke the union, back in ninety-two, and they've been bringing in the Hunkies ever since. A Hunky will work a twelve-hour shift for a dollar sixty, and he'll live in a shack with fifteen others to save the rent, and send the money home to the old country. You can't fight that, Eddie. A white man can't live like that."

Edward had heard of the great strike of ninety-two; he had read about it in his history classes, where it had been presented as a regrettable episode in the progress of American industry, in which misguided workmen, led astray by foreign agitators, had attacked the property of their employers and had been very properly suppressed. He started to say something of this kind, and then thought better of it. Instead he asked, "Is that what you're getting now, Danny? A dollar sixty?"

His cousin laughed—a short, hard laugh, with no mirth in it. "I'm a skilled man," he said. "I'm a second helper on the open hearth. I get two dollars and forty cents."

"A day?"

"A day. A twelve-hour day. Seven days a week."

Edward stopped in the road and stared at him. "Seven days?" he cried. "But surely—surely you don't mean you work on Sundays?"

"The furnaces don't know it's Sunday," said Danny. "You can't let them go cold—it'd cost the company thousands to heat them up again. So the men work. Every day of the year, Eddie, except the Fourth of July and Christmas. And every two weeks, when we change from the day turn to the night turn, we work the long turn—twenty-four hours straight, from six in the morning till six the next morning. That's how they work it, so the other gang can get a day off."

Edward said nothing. He was trying to imagine it—twenty-four hours in front of a furnace, in that heat, with that smoke—and he could not imagine it. It was something outside the range of his experience, like the tortures of the Inquisition, or the sufferings of the damned in hell. He had been tired, often enough; he had sat up all night with his books before an examination, and had thought himself a martyr. But this!

They had come by now to the top of the hill, and to the row of houses where the Malloys lived. They were company houses, all alike, built of boards that had warped and shrunk so that the wind came in through the cracks; each of them had two rooms below and two above, and a little yard behind, in which there was a privy and a pile of ashes and a few sticks of firewood. Danny's own house was next door to his mother's; he had married, it appeared, five years ago, and had three children, and a fourth on the way. He told Edward about it as they stood before the door, and there was a note in his voice that Edward could not quite make out—pride, and tenderness, and something else, that was very like despair.

"Mary's a good girl," he said. "She was a Kearney—you wouldn't remember her. Her father was killed in the Number Three blast furnace, the year before we married. A hang-up, they call it—the stuff sticks in the furnace, and then it slips all at once, and the gas blows out the top. Six men were killed that time. The company gave her mother a hundred and fifty dollars, and they made her sign a paper that she wouldn't sue."

"A hundred and fifty dollars!" Edward exclaimed. "For a man's life!"

"That was generous," said Danny, with the same hard laugh. "Lots of them get nothing. The company lawyer comes round the next morning, before the widow's had time to think, and he's got the paper all ready, and the money in his hand. And she's got children to feed, and the rent's due, and she's never seen a hundred and fifty dollars in one place in her life. So she signs. And if she doesn't sign, then she has to go to court—and who's going to testify for her? Not the men in the mill. They know what happens to a man who testifies against the company. He's out of a job the next day, and his name goes on the list, and he can't get work anywhere in the valley."

Then he opened the door, and they went in to see his mother.

Of that visit Edward never afterwards cared to speak. The sick woman lay in a bed in the front room, propped up on pillows, and she held out her thin arms to him and wept, and called him by the name he had not heard since he was a child. He had remembered her as a plump and rosy woman, who baked pies and scolded the boys for tracking mud upon her floor; now she was a skeleton, and her breath came in gasps, and every few minutes she was shaken by a fit of coughing that left her limp and grey upon the pillows. She asked about his mother, and about his studies, and about the great city where he lived; and he answered her as best he could, and all the time he was looking about the room, at the cracked plaster and the stained ceiling, at the cheap prints of saints upon the walls, at the medicine bottles on the table by the bed, and at the coal-scuttle in the corner, which was empty. He thought of his own mother's bedroom, with its carpet and its satin hangings, and its fire burning in the grate all through the winter; and he felt something rise in his throat that he could not swallow.

When they came out again into the street, it was some time before either of them spoke. At last Danny said, "Come on over to my place. Mary will have something for us. You'll stay the night, won't you? We haven't got much room, but the kids can sleep with us."

Edward said that he would stay; and they went next door, and he met Mary Malloy, who was a thin, tired young woman with large frightened eyes, and the three children, who stared at him from behind their mother's skirts and would not be coaxed out. They sat down at the kitchen table, and Mary set before them a plate of boiled potatoes and cabbage, and a little bacon, and some bread, and a pot of coffee; and Edward, who had dined the night before at his club upon terrapin and champagne, ate it and said that it was very good.

And then, while Mary washed the dishes and put the children to bed, the two cousins sat on by the stove and talked.

They talked of the old days first—of the summers at their grandfather's farm in the hills, where they had fished for sunfish in the creek and stolen apples from the orchard and slept in the hayloft; of the time Danny had fallen out of the big walnut tree and broken his arm, and of the time Edward had been chased by the bull. They laughed over these things, and for a while it was almost as if the seven years had never been, and they were boys again. But always, sooner or later, the talk came back to the mill; it was as if there were nothing else in Danny's life, nothing else in the whole world, but that great roaring monster in the valley below, that swallowed men up and spat them out again, broken and used.

He told Edward about his hand. It had happened three years ago, when he was a third helper; a ladle had tipped, and he had thrown up his hand to save his face, and the steel had splashed upon it. He had been in the company hospital for six weeks, and the company had paid his doctor's bill, but not his wages; and when he came out, they had given him his job back, which was considered a great kindness, since many men in his condition were simply turned off. He had been lucky, he said. He had seen men burned to cinders, men crushed under falling ingots, men caught in the rolls and drawn through them like dough. There was one Hunky, a young fellow, who had fallen into a vat of molten steel; there was nothing left of him at all, not so much as a bone, and the company had buried the steel, so the story went, with a priest to say a prayer over it. "There's a lot of men in that steel, Eddie," said Danny. "When you see a big building going up in the city, with the girders all shining—you think about that. There's men in there."

He told about the speed-up: how the company was always setting new records, and posting them on the bulletin boards, and offering bonuses to the superintendents and the foremen who could get the most tons out of their furnaces; and how the foremen drove the men to get the bonuses, so that each year the work grew harder and faster, while the wages stayed the same, or were cut. He told about the spotters, the company spies who mingled with the men and reported every word that was said, so that a man dared not complain, even to his best friend, for fear that his best friend might be in the pay of the company. He told about the company store, where the prices were higher than anywhere else in town, but where a man had better trade if he wanted to keep his job; and about the company church, and the company school, and the company newspaper, and the company politicians, who were elected every fall by the votes of men who were marched to the polls by their foremen. "They own us, Eddie," he said. "They own the houses we live in and the ground we walk on, and the air we breathe, and they'd own our souls if they could find a way to make a profit on them."

Edward listened, and as he listened a strange feeling came over him. He had been taught, all his life, that America was the land of opportunity, where any man who was willing to work might rise; he had been taught that the great industrialists who had built the mills were benefactors of the race, who had given employment to millions and had made the nation rich and strong. He had read the books of the economists, which explained that wages were fixed by the iron law of supply and demand, and that any attempt to interfere with that law could only result in harm to the workingman himself. And he had believed these things—he had never thought to question them. But now he looked at his cousin's twisted hand, and at the lines in his face, and at the patches of grey in his hair, and he thought of the woman coughing her life away in the next house; and it seemed to him that the books had left something out.

"Danny," he said, slowly, "do you know what my father does?"

"Sure," said Danny. "He's a lawyer. A big one, Ma says."

"Yes. And do you know who his clients are?"

Danny looked at him, and did not answer.

"He's counsel for the Consolidated," said Edward. "He's been counsel for them for fifteen years. And he owns stock in it—a great deal of stock. The money that sent me to college, Danny—the money that bought this coat—" He stopped, because his voice had begun to shake.

There was a long silence. The fire crackled in the stove, and from somewhere outside came the shriek of a whistle, and the far-off thunder of the mills. At last Danny reached over and put his maimed hand upon his cousin's knee.

"I know, Eddie," he said gently. "I've always known. Ma told me, years ago. It's not your fault. You didn't make the world the way it is."

"No," said Edward. "But I've been living on it. I've been living on you." He got up and went to the window and stood looking out. Down below, the valley was a sea of fire; the flames leaped from the tops of the blast furnaces, and the smoke rolled up red and gold against the black sky, and the whole scene was like some vision of the infernal regions out of Dante. As a boy he had thought it beautiful. Now he knew what it was made of. It was made of men—of their sweat and their blood and their broken bodies; of the lungs of old women and the hunger of little children; of seven-day weeks and twenty-four-hour turns and hundred-and-fifty-dollar lives. And all of it was pouring, in a great golden stream, down the valley and over the hills to the city, where it became terrapin and champagne, and satin hangings, and Greek grammars, and fine overcoats for young men who had never done a day's work in their lives.

"What are you going to do?" asked Danny, behind him.

Edward did not know. He stood there for a long time, with his forehead pressed against the cold glass, watching the fires burn; and when at last he turned around, his cousin saw that there were tears upon his face.

"I don't know, Danny," he said. "But I'm not going back the same. I promise you that. I'm not going back the same."

Little Antanas Kovas was six years old that winter, and he had never in his life owned anything so precious as the pair of shoes which his mother had bought for him in October, at the store of Mr. Feldheim on Railroad Avenue, for one dollar and thirty-five cents. They were stout shoes, with copper toes and with laces of rawhide, and they had been chosen with a view, not to their beauty, but to their durability; for it was understood in the family that they must last until the spring, and if possible until the following winter as well, at which time they would go to the baby, Elzbieta, who was not yet able to walk, but who would presumably be able to do so by then, and would need shoes as badly as anyone else. All this had been explained to Antanas many times, in the slow and solemn manner in which such things are explained to children among the poor; and he had listened with wide eyes, and had nodded his head, and had promised; and then he had gone out with the other boys of the alley and forgotten all about it, as children will, whether they are the children of steel-workers or of the men who own the steel.

To understand what happened on that afternoon in January, one must understand something of the place where the Kovas family lived, and of the circumstances which hemmed them in. They lived in Millvale Bottoms, which lay along the river below the great works of the Consolidated Steel Company; and anyone who has seen Millvale Bottoms will not need to be told about it, and anyone who has not seen it will never quite believe what is told. It was a district of perhaps two square miles, laid out upon ground which had been made by dumping slag and cinders into the marshes; and it was crowded with frame houses which had been built by speculators, and sold upon the installment plan to immigrants who could not read the contracts. Over everything there hung, by day and by night, a pall of smoke from the blast-furnaces and the open-hearths, so that the snow, which fell white and clean upon the hills across the river, came down upon Millvale Bottoms the color of an old rag, and lay there in drifts that were streaked with soot and with the yellow stain of the sulphur fumes. Between the houses and the river ran the tracks of the railroad which served the mills, and beyond the tracks were the slag-heaps, where the molten refuse of the furnaces was dumped from great ladle-cars; and these slag-heaps smoked all winter long, and in places they glowed red beneath the crust, and the children of the district went there to warm themselves, and to pick out bits of unburned coke to carry home in their pails.

This last was strictly forbidden by the company, and there were signs posted to that effect, and a watchman with a club; but the watchman was an old man, and he had grandchildren of his own, and he could not be everywhere at once. Also it was forbidden by the parents of the children, and for a better reason than the company's; for every year one or two of the little ones would break through the crust of a slag-heap that had not cooled, and would be burned so dreadfully that it was a mercy when they died. Antanas knew this as well as he knew his prayers. His mother had told him, and his father had told him, and he had seen the funeral of little Stanislovas Petraitis, who had been eight years old, and whose coffin had been closed. Nevertheless, upon that January afternoon, when the cold was so bitter that the water froze in the pails inside the houses, and when there was no coal in the Kovas kitchen except what had to be saved for the evening, Antanas had gone with Jonukas Mazeika and the two Grabowski boys over the railroad tracks and up onto the slag; and he had found there a great treasure of coke, nearly half a pail, and he had been so happy over it that he had not noticed where he was stepping.

He had not broken through; that much the saints had spared him. But he had stood for some minutes upon a place where the crust was hot, and when he came down from the heap there was a smell of scorching leather about him, and when he looked at his feet he saw that the soles of his precious shoes had curled up at the edges like the leaves of a book that has been left in the rain, and that the stitching had parted, and that in one of them there was a hole through which he could see the gray wool of his stocking. He stood and stared at them, and all the joy of his half-pail of coke went out of him, and in its place there came a sick and dreadful fear, such as no child of six years ought ever to have to know.

---

His mother was at home when he came in, for she was always at home in the afternoons now. Until the baby came she had worked in the bottling department of the Schlitz agency on Front Street, washing bottles at four dollars and a half a week; but since the baby she had been obliged to take in washing instead, and also two boarders, who slept in the front room upon mattresses that were laid on the floor at night and stood up against the wall in the daytime. The father, Juozas Kovas, was a helper on the open-hearth furnaces, and that month he was working on the night shift, which meant that he went out at half-past five in the evening and came home at half-past seven in the morning, having worked thirteen hours in a heat that would have killed a horse; and he slept in the back room through the day, behind a curtain made of flour-sacks, and it was the first law of the household that he must not be awakened. For Juozas was paid eighteen cents an hour, and if he did not sleep he could not work, and if he could not work he would be "laid off," and there were a dozen men waiting at the gate of the mill every morning to take his place. So it was that all through the short winter days the mother moved about her kitchen like a ghost, and hushed the baby when it cried, and spoke to Antanas in whispers; and so it was that the scene which follows was played out in whispers also, which made it more terrible than if there had been shouting.

Teofilė Kovas was a woman of twenty-six, but no one who saw her would have guessed it. She had come from a village in the Suwałki district, where she had been a strong, red-cheeked girl who could carry two pails of milk upon a yoke and sing while she did it; and seven years of America had made her into what she was now—a thin, stooped creature with gray in her hair and two front teeth gone, and with hands that were cracked and swollen from the lye in the wash-water, so that she wrapped them in rags at night. She was standing over the tub when Antanas came in, with her sleeves rolled to the elbow and the steam rising about her face; and she did not look up at first, for she had learned that it was best not to look up from work until the work was done. But then she smelled the leather, and she turned.

The child stood just inside the door, with his half-pail of coke in his hand, and his face was white under its smudges of soot. He did not say anything. He did not need to; she saw his feet, and she understood everything at once, as mothers do. She stood there, with the water dripping from her hands upon the floor, and for a long moment she did not move; and Antanas, watching her, saw something come into her face which he had never seen before, and which frightened him far more than anything that had happened upon the slag-heap.

It is necessary to try to understand what was passing in the mind of this woman, because it was not what a comfortable person, reading of it, would suppose. She was not thinking that her son might have been killed; that would come afterwards, in the night, when she lay awake beside her husband's empty place. What she was thinking of, in that first instant, was one dollar and thirty-five cents. She was thinking that the rent of eleven dollars was due upon the first of the month, and that there were but seven dollars in the tin box upon the shelf behind the clock. She was thinking that one of the boarders, the Pole Wojciech, had been laid off at the rail-mill a week ago, and had not paid his board, and would perhaps not pay it at all. She was thinking that the grocer Mikšys had refused her credit on Saturday, and had said, in front of all the women in the store, that she already owed him nine dollars and forty cents. She was thinking that the baby had a cough which would not go away, and that there was no money for a doctor, and that the doctor would only say, as he had said before, that the child needed milk and warm rooms and to be taken out of the smoke. And she was thinking that it was January, and that it would be January and February and March before the ground was fit for a child to walk upon in bare feet; and that Antanas could not go to school without shoes, and that if he did not go to school the truant officer would come, and there would be a fine; and that somewhere in the world there must be a dollar and thirty-five cents, but that she did not know where it was, and there was no one on earth who would give it to her.

All this went through her mind in less time than it takes to tell it; and then something broke inside of her, and she crossed the room in two steps, and seized the boy by the shoulder.

"Where were you?" she whispered. "Where were you? Tell me!"

The child's lips moved, but no sound came from them. He held up the pail, as if it were an explanation, as if it were an offering; and she struck it out of his hand, so that the precious coke went scattering across the floor and rolled under the stove.

"The slag!" she hissed. "You went on the slag! After I told you! After your father told you! After Stasys—after they buried Stasys—you went on the slag!"

"Mama," he began—"Mama, it was cold—"

"Cold!" She shook him, and his head went back and forth upon his thin neck. "Cold! And what will you be now, with no shoes? Will you be warm now? Look at them! Look what you have done! A dollar and thirty-five cents—do you know what that is? Do you know how many shirts I must wash for a dollar and thirty-five cents? Do you know how many hours your father must stand by the furnace? Do you know?"

He did not know; he could not know. He was six years old, and the arithmetic of hunger was a thing beyond his grasp, though he had lived by it all his life. But he knew that his mother was shaking him, and that her face was twisted and strange, and that her eyes were full of tears which did not fall; and he began to cry himself, not loudly, for even in his terror he remembered his father behind the curtain, but with a thin, choking whimper, like a puppy that has been stepped on.

"Be still!" she whispered. "You will wake him! Do you want to wake him too? Do you want him to lose his place, so that we all starve? Be still!"

And then, because he could not be still, because no child could have been still at such a moment, she raised her hand and struck him across the face.

It was not a hard blow, as such things go in Millvale Bottoms. There were men in that district who beat their children with belts and with stove-lifters, and women who did worse; there were children who came to the parish school with marks upon them that the sisters did not ask about. Teofilė Kovas had never struck her son before in his life, except to spank him once or twice when he was very small; and the blow she gave him now was such as would scarcely have left a mark upon the cheek of a child who had been properly fed. But Antanas had not been properly fed for a long time, and the skin of his face was thin, and the print of her fingers showed upon it red and plain; and he did not cry out, but stood perfectly still and looked at her, with his mouth open, as if he could not believe what had happened.

In the back room, behind the curtain of flour-sacks, the sleeping man turned over upon his bed and muttered something; and both mother and child stood frozen, hardly daring to breathe, until his breathing became slow and heavy again.

Then the mother sank down upon the bench by the table, and covered her face with her ruined hands.

---

There are people—and some of them write books upon the subject, and some of them sit upon the boards of charitable societies, and draw up reports upon the "condition of the foreign-born"—who would have had a great deal to say about Teofilė Kovas, if they had witnessed this scene. They would have said that she was ignorant and brutal, as all these peasant people are; that she did not understand the principles of child-training which had been worked out by the experts; that she ought to have reasoned with the boy, and explained to him the consequences of his act, and administered some suitable and moderate punishment, such as sending him to bed without his supper. They would not have reflected that Antanas had had no dinner, and that the supper was to be bread and lard and a little coffee made from grounds that had been boiled twice already; nor that there was no bed to send him to, save a pile of rags in the corner of the kitchen, where he slept with his baby sister for the sake of the warmth of the stove. They would not have reflected that this woman had been up since four o'clock that morning, and had carried eleven pails of water from the hydrant at the end of the alley, and had scrubbed the shirts and the underclothing of four strange men upon a washboard, and had nursed a sick baby, and had cooked two meals, and had not sat down once except to feed the child; and that she had done the same thing the day before, and would do it the day after, and every day until she died. After a while he came over to her, slowly, a step at a time, as one might approach some animal that had been hurt. He did not touch her. He stood beside the bench, and looked at her bowed head, and at the gray in her hair, which he had never noticed before; and then, in a small, cracked whisper, he said, "Mama, I will not go on the slag again."

She did not answer.

"Mama," he said again, "I will go barefoot. I do not need shoes. Jonukas goes barefoot, and he is not cold. I will go barefoot until the spring."

This was not true, and both of them knew that it was not true. Jonukas Mazeika had gone barefoot through the month of December, and his feet had frozen, and two of his toes had turned black, and the company doctor had cut them off with a pair of shears upon the kitchen table, while the women of the alley held him down. Antanas had heard him screaming. But the child said it anyway, because it was the only thing he could think of to offer; and when his mother heard it, she lifted her face from her hands and looked at him, and then she caught him to her breast, and held him so tightly that he could scarcely breathe, and the tears which she had been holding back all this while came pouring down her cheeks at last, and fell upon his hair.

"No, no," she whispered—"no, my little one, my little bird—you will not go barefoot—I will not let you. Mother will find shoes. Mother will find them. Forgive me—forgive me—"

She kissed the red place on his cheek, over and over, as if she could kiss it away; and the boy, who did not know what there was to forgive, nor why his mother should be asking him for it, clung to her and wept also, and the two of them rocked together upon the bench in the gray light of the window, while the steam from the forgotten wash-tub rose up about them, and the baby coughed and whimpered in its box beside the stove.

That night, when Juozas had gone out to the furnaces with his tin pail, and the boarders had eaten their bread and gone to the saloon of Kazimieras Rudis on the corner, which was the only warm place in Millvale Bottoms where a man might sit without paying, Teofilė took down the tin box from behind the clock and counted the money in it again. There were seven dollars and five cents, the same as before; it had not grown in the meantime. She sat looking at it for a long time. Then she took out a dollar and thirty-five cents, and put it into the pocket of her apron, and put the box back upon the shelf.

What she meant to do about the rent she did not know. Perhaps the agent would wait a week; perhaps he would not. Perhaps Wojciech would find work again, and pay what he owed; perhaps he would go away in the night, as boarders sometimes did. Perhaps she could take in another washing, from the family of the foreman Schultz, whose wife had once asked her; she did not know where she would find the hours for it, but she supposed that she would find them somewhere, as she had found them before—in the night, perhaps, when the others were asleep. She would have to give up something; and since there was nothing left to give up but her sleep and her food, she would give up some of those. It did not occur to her that there was anything else she could do. It did not occur to her that she had any right to anything else.

She went over to the corner where Antanas lay asleep upon his rags, with his arm thrown across his baby sister; and she knelt down beside him, and looked at his face in the light of the little lamp. The mark of her fingers had faded, but she thought she could still see it, and she knew that she would always see it. She put out her hand to touch his hair, and then drew it back, for fear of waking him; and she knelt there a long while upon the cold floor, with her lips moving, saying the prayers she had learned as a girl in the village church at home, where there had been fields and a river with clean water in it, and where the snow, when it fell, stayed white.

Down the river the furnaces flared and roared, and the glare of them came in through the frost upon the window-pane and lay red across the floor, so that it seemed as if the whole room were on fire; and upon the slag-heaps beyond the tracks the molten refuse of the Consolidated Steel Company poured down out of the ladle-cars, and lit up the sky for miles, and men in fine houses upon the hills across the water looked out at it from their windows, and said to their guests that it was a magnificent sight, and a symbol of the greatness of American industry.

It was after ten o'clock when Tom Hollister came home that night, and Lucy knew before he opened his mouth that something had happened at the office. You could always tell with Tom; he was a big, slow-moving fellow, with a red face and sandy hair that would not lie down, and when things went well with him he came stamping up the steps of the porch and called out, "Hello, old girl!" in a voice that set the dog to barking three houses away. But tonight he came up the steps as if they were made of eggs, and he hung his hat on the peg behind the door and stood looking at it, as if he had never seen a hat before and was wondering what it was for.

Lucy was sitting at the kitchen table with the mending. The two children were asleep in the little room off the kitchen, and the lamp had a green shade, so the light fell in a circle on the table, and Tom's face was up above it in the shadow. She waited, and he said nothing, and so she said, "There's coffee on the back of the stove, Tom. It's been there since eight, but it'll be hot."

"I don't want any coffee," said Tom. Then, after a while, "Well, maybe I do." He got himself a cup, and poured it, and sat down across from her, and stirred in three spoons of sugar, which was one more than he ever took; and Lucy watched him do it and said nothing about the sugar, which cost eleven cents a pound at the company store, and had cost nine before the strike.

You must understand about the town of Cedar Falls, or you will not understand what was the matter with Tom Hollister. It was a lumber town in the western part of Washington, set down in a valley among hills that had once been covered with Douglas fir, two hundred feet tall and older than the Christian religion; and now the hills were covered with stumps, grey and silver and black where the fires had gone over them, and the trees were in the form of lumber, piled in yards along the railroad siding, waiting to be shipped to Kansas City and Chicago and New York, where people would build houses with them and never think about where they came from. The town belonged to the Western Pacific Timber Company; that is to say, the company owned the mill, and the bunk-houses, and the rows of little frame cottages where the married men lived, and the store, and the hotel, and the moving-picture theatre, and the church, and the minister in the church, and the doctor, and the constable. It did not own the post-office, because that belonged to the government at Washington, D.C.; but the postmaster was the brother-in-law of the mill superintendent, so that came to pretty much the same thing.

Tom Hollister was the timekeeper. He had come up from the woods, where he had been a choker-setter, and then a hook-tender, and then he had hurt his back when a log rolled, and the superintendent, Mr. Gaylord, who liked him because he was steady and didn't drink more than a man ought to, had given him a desk job in the office, at a hundred and forty dollars a month. That was thirty dollars more than he had got in the woods, and it meant a white collar on Sundays, and a cottage on the upper street, with a bay window and a picket fence, instead of one of the shacks down by the creek, where the smell of the wigwam burner came in at the windows night and day. Lucy had put up lace curtains in the bay window, and had planted sweet peas along the fence, and she was the only woman in the upper street who had a phonograph, except the superintendent's wife, who had a piano.

But now there was a strike. The men in the mill wanted the eight-hour day, which the government had promised them during the war, when it needed spruce for its airplanes, and which the company had taken away again as soon as the war was over and the airplanes were no longer needed. Also they wanted clean bedding in the bunk-houses, and they wanted to be paid in money instead of in brass checks that were good only at the company store. These demands did not seem unreasonable to the men; but to the Western Pacific Timber Company they seemed like Bolshevism, and the newspapers in Seattle, which were owned by people who owned lumber companies, said that the strike was the work of the I.W.W., and that the I.W.W. was paid with Russian gold, and that the men who were demanding clean blankets were plotting to blow up the Capitol and nationalize the women.

And there was this further complication, that Lucy's younger brother, Ned Carver, was a sawyer in the mill, and was on the strike committee.

"Well?" said Lucy, at last. "You might as well say it, Tom. Whatever it is, I'd rather have it now than lie awake all night guessing."

Tom drank half his coffee before he answered. "Gaylord called me into the inside office this afternoon," he said. "There was a feller there from Seattle—a feller named Mr. Burke. Tall feller, with spats on, and a pearl in his necktie. He's from the Employers' Association, or some such, I didn't rightly get it."

"A detective," said Lucy.

"Well, I don't know as you'd call him that."

"What would you call him, then?"

Tom did not answer that. He turned his cup around in the saucer, the way he did when he was trying to work out a sum in his head. "They had a list," he said. "The names of the men that's been goin' to the meetin's over at Swede Olsen's barn. Only it ain't complete, and they figger I can complete it, on account of I know every man on the payroll by sight, and most of 'em by their first names. They want me to go over it with 'em, and mark the ones that's the ringleaders, as they call it, so's the company'll know who not to take back when the thing's over."

Lucy laid down the sock she was darning. She did not say anything for a moment; she was thinking how strange it was that a thing could come at you so quietly, in your own kitchen, with the clock ticking on the shelf and the kettle singing a little on the back of the stove. She had known for three weeks that something like this would happen; she had known it the way you know that a tooth is going bad, without wanting to look at it.

"And Ned's name is on the list," she said.

"I didn't say that."

"You didn't have to say it, Tom."

He made a gesture with his big hand, as if he were brushing a fly off the oilcloth. "Ned's name is on every list they got, Lucy. He's been shootin' off his mouth in the bunk-house for a year. There ain't nothin' I could tell 'em about Ned that they don't already know."

"Then what do they want with you?"

"They want the others. The little fellers—the ones that's been keepin' quiet."

"And you'd give them?"

"I ain't said I'd give anybody!" Tom raised his voice, and then remembered the children, and lowered it again. "I ain't said nothin' yet. I told Gaylord I'd think it over. That's what I'm doin'—thinkin' it over. A man's got a right to think, ain't he?"

Lucy looked at him across the circle of lamplight, and it seemed to her that she was seeing him for the first time in eight years of married life; or rather, that she was seeing two men, one laid over the other, like the pictures in the stereoscope that the superintendent's wife had in her parlor. One of them was the Tom she had married, the young choker-setter with the red face who had walked her home from the Grange dance, and had told her that he didn't hold with the way the bosses treated the men in the woods, and that some day, by golly, somebody would do something about it. The other was a man with a white collar and a desk, who said "Mr. Gaylord" when he talked about the superintendent at the supper table, and who had lately taken to reading the editorial page of the Seattle paper aloud, as if it were the Bible.

"What did Mr. Gaylord say," she asked, "if you don't do it?"

Tom shifted in his chair. "He didn't say nothin' about that."

"Tom."

"Well—he said he'd always looked on me as one of the office family, as you might say. He said there was a time comin' when a man had to show which side he was on, and that a man that couldn't show it wasn't much use to anybody. He said Hopkins, down in the shipping office, is due to retire next spring, and they'd be lookin' for somebody to take his place. That's two hundred a month, Lucy."

"And if you don't?"

"He didn't say."

"He didn't have to say that, either," said Lucy.

There was a silence. Outside, the rain had begun again; it rained in Cedar Falls the way the sun shines in California, as a matter of course, not worth remarking upon. The water ran down the tin gutter at the corner of the house and splashed in the barrel, and somewhere off in the dark the wigwam burner at the mill glowed red, though there was no sawdust going into it now, and it was only the old fire dying down.

"I want you to look at it sensible, Lucy," said Tom, and his voice had taken on the reasonable, patient tone which men use when they have made up their minds and want their wives to help them feel good about it. "This here strike ain't goin' to win. You know it, and I know it, and Ned knows it, if he'd only own up. The company's got the courts, and they got the sheriff, and they can bring in men from Portland and Spokane—there's thousands of fellers walkin' the roads lookin' for work, since the war. Mr. Burke says there's a trainload comin' in Monday. In a month the mill'll be runnin' again, and the men that went out'll be on the road themselves, and them that's lucky'll be let back in at the old rate. That's how it's goin' to come out, whatever I do or don't do. Now what good is it goin' to do anybody if I lose my job on top of it?"

It was a good argument; Lucy had to admit that to herself. It was the argument that has been used ever since the beginning of the world, by every man who has ever been asked to do something he didn't like for the people who held the keys to his bread-box. The thing is going to happen anyway; so why should I be the one to suffer? And the beauty of the argument is that it is generally true. The thing does happen anyway. The only trouble is that it happens because every man who is asked tells himself the same thing.

"It'll do this much good," said Lucy. "It'll mean that there's one man in Cedar Falls that didn't sell his friends."

Tom's face got redder, so that it was almost the color of the glow from the burner. "Now that ain't fair! I ain't sellin' nobody. Them men knew what they was gettin' into. They knew the company'd find out—it always does. If it ain't me, it'll be somebody else. It'll be that little rat Spencer, that sweeps out the office; he'd do it for a dollar and be glad of the chance."

"Then let Spencer do it."

"And let Spencer have the shipping office? Gosh, Lucy, you don't understand business!"

She understood that the company store charged eleven cents for sugar and fourteen cents for a can of tomatoes that sold for nine cents in Tacoma, and that the brass checks the men were paid with were worth ninety cents on the dollar if they tried to spend them anywhere else. She understood that the cottage they lived in, with the lace curtains and the bay window, belonged to the company, and that if Tom lost his job they would have thirty days to get out of it, and that there was a clause in the lease which said so, because she had read it, though Tom had signed without reading. She understood that business was a game in which some people made the rules and other people obeyed them, and that the people who made the rules lived in Seattle and San Francisco and never saw a stump.

"I understand that Ned's got a wife and a baby coming," she said. "I understand that Mamie Carver came here Tuesday, crying, because the store had cut off their credit, and I gave her two dollars out of the egg money and didn't tell you. There, now you know that, too."

"Lucy!"

"Well, I did. And I'd do it again. She's my brother's wife, and she's carrying his child, and if the company wants to starve them out it'll have to starve me with them."

Tom got up and walked over to the window. There was nothing to see out of it but the rain, and the dark shape of the next cottage, where the Lindquists lived; Lindquist was a filer in the mill, and he was on strike too, and he hadn't spoken to Tom in two weeks. Tom stood with his back to her, and his shoulders were very broad and very tired.

"You think I like this?" he said, without turning around. "You think I like walkin' down the street and havin' fellers I worked with in the woods look the other way? You think I like hearin' Ned call me a company stiff, right out loud in front of the post-office? I got feelin's, same as anybody. But I got two kids in there, Lucy, and I got a bad back, and I ain't goin' back to the woods. You know what the doctor said. One more log like that last one, and I'm in a wheel-chair for life. What's goin' to happen to you then? Is the union goin' to take care of you? Is Ned?"

Lucy did not answer at once. She was ashamed to find that she had not thought about his back; she had been so busy thinking about Ned, and Mamie, and the men in the shacks down by the creek, that she had forgotten the night they had brought Tom home on a stretcher, with his face grey under the red, and the long months when he could not lift the baby. That was the trouble with being poor, she thought; there was never just one thing to be afraid of, there were a dozen, and every time you set yourself against one of them, another came up behind you.

"I know, Tom," she said, more gently. "I know about your back. But listen to me. If you do this thing, you'll get the shipping office, maybe, and two hundred a month. And then next year there'll be something else, and Mr. Gaylord will call you into the inside office again, and there'll be another man with spats and a pearl in his necktie. And you'll have to do that, too, because by then you'll have more to lose. That's the way it works. They don't buy you all at once; they buy you a piece at a time, and every piece comes cheaper."

Tom turned around. "Where'd you get all that? Out of Ned's papers?"

"I got it out of watching you," said Lucy.

It was the hardest thing she had ever said to him, and she saw it go into him, the way you see a nail go into soft wood. He stood there with his mouth open a little, and for a moment she thought he was going to shout at her, or go out and slam the door and walk down to Spencer's room over the pool hall and get drunk on the bootleg whiskey that everybody knew Spencer kept there, and that the constable never found. But he did none of those things. He came back and sat down at the table, heavily, the way an old man sits down, and he put his elbows on the oilcloth and his face in his hands.

"Gosh, Lucy," he said, through his fingers. "Gosh."

The clock ticked on the shelf. It was a fine clock, with a gilt eagle on top; they had bought it on the installment plan from a mail-order house in Chicago, the first winter after Tom had got the office job, and there were still four payments owing. Lucy found herself thinking about that—about how many things in the house were not paid for yet, the clock and the phonograph and the sewing machine, and how each of them was a little chain, very light and pretty, so that you hardly knew you were wearing it until somebody pulled.

"I ain't said I'd do it," Tom said at last, lifting his head. "I told you that. I said I'd think it over."

"I know you did."

"Gaylord wants an answer tomorrow, by noon."

"Then you'll have to give him one."

"What if I told him I didn't know them men? What if I said I couldn't recollect who was at them meetin's, on account of I never went to none of 'em—which is the God's truth?"

Lucy looked at him, and for the first time that evening something like a smile came onto her face, though it was a tired and doubtful one. It was such a Tom-like idea; he had always been one to look for the door that wasn't quite locked, the trail around the windfall instead of over it. And she knew, and he knew, that Mr. Gaylord would not believe him, and that Mr. Burke with the pearl in his necktie would not believe him, and that it would come to the same thing in the end. But it was something; it was not the whole road, but it was turning the team around and facing the right way.

"You could tell him that," she said.

"He'd fire me, likely."

"Likely he would."

"And then what?"

"Then we'd go somewhere else. My cousin Will has a dairy down by Chehalis, and he's always writing that he can't get help that'll stay. It wouldn't be lifting logs. It'd be milking, and keeping the books, maybe. You're good at books, Tom."

"Milkin' cows," said Tom, and he said it with such disgust that Lucy laughed out loud, and then put her hand over her mouth, for fear of waking the children. And Tom looked at her, and after a moment his red face cracked, and he laughed too, though it was not much of a laugh, and it did not last.

"I'd have to give up the white collar," he said.

"You could wear it Sundays. The cows wouldn't mind."

He was silent for a long time then, and Lucy went back to her darning, because there was nothing more she could say, and she knew that if she said any more she would spoil it. Men were like that; you could lead them up to a thing, but you had to let them take the last step by themselves, and believe that they had thought of it all on their own. That was another kind of business, the kind that wives understood, and that was never taught in any school.

At half past eleven Tom got up and wound the clock, as he did every night, and stood for a moment looking at the gilt eagle. Then he said, "I'm goin' to bed, Lucy," and went into the other room; and she heard him sit down on the edge of the bed and take off his shoes, one and then the other, and drop them on the floor, and then she heard nothing more for a long while, and she knew that he was sitting there in the dark with his hands between his knees, the way he had sat on the night after the log rolled on him, when the doctor had told them about his back.

She did not know what he would say to Mr. Gaylord at noon. She did not believe that he knew himself. She put away the mending, and turned down the lamp, and sat for a while in the dark kitchen, listening to the rain in the barrel, and thinking about all the other kitchens in Cedar Falls, and in all the other company towns up and down the coast, where women were sitting up at this hour, waiting to find out what their men would do; and how the men who owned the towns were asleep in Seattle and San Francisco, in big houses on the hills, and did not have to wait for anything at all.

Soon after this it was time for Bunny to visit his mother. Bunny’s mother did not bear Dad’s name, as other boys’ mothers do; she was called Mrs. Lang, and lived in a bungalow on the outskirts of Angel City. There was an arrangement whereby she had a right to have Bunny with her one week in every six months; Bunny always knew when this time was approaching, and looked forward to it with mixed emotions. His mother was sweet, and gave him the petting which he missed at other times; “pretty little Mamma,” was her name for herself. But in other ways the visit was embarrassing, because there were matters supposed to be kept hidden from Bunny, but which he could not help guessing. Mamma would question him about Dad’s affairs, and Bunny knew that Dad did not wish his affairs talked about. Then too, Mamma complained that she never had enough money; Dad allowed her only two hundred dollars a month, and how could a young and charming grass-widow exist on such a sum? Her garage bill was always unpaid, and she would tell Bunny about it, and expect him to tell Dad—but Dad would evade hearing. And next time, Mamma would cry, and say that Jim was a tyrant and a miser. The situation was especially difficult just now, because Mamma had read about the new well in the papers, and knew just how much money Dad had; she unfolded to Bunny a plan, that he should try to persuade Dad to increase her allowance, but without having Dad suspect that she had suggested it. And this, right after Bunny had renounced the luxury of small lies! Also there was the mystery about Mamma’s friends. There were always gentlemen friends who came to see her while Bunny was there, and who might or might not be agreeable to Bunny. When he came home, Aunt Emma would ask him questions, from which it was evident that she wanted to know about these gentlemen friends, but didn’t want Bunny to know that she wanted to know. Bunny noticed that Dad never referred to such matters; he never asked any questions about Mamma, and Aunt Emma always did her asking out of Dad’s presence. All this had a peculiar effect upon Bunny. Just as Dad kept a safe deposit box at the bank, into which nobody ever looked but himself, so Bunny kept a secret place in his own mind. Outwardly, he was a cheerful and frank little fellow, if somewhat too mature for his years; but all the time he was leading a dual life—picking up ideas here and there, and carrying them off and hiding them, as a squirrel does nuts, so that he may come back at a later season and crack them open and nibble them. Some nuts were good and some were bad, and Bunny learned to judge them, and to throw away the bad ones. One thing was plain: there was something which men and women did, which they were all in a conspiracy to keep you from knowing that they did. It was a dark corner of life, mysterious and rather hateful. In the beginning, Bunny was loyal to his father, not trying to find out what his father didn’t want him to know. But this could not continue indefinitely, for the mind automatically seeks understanding. It was not merely that the birds and the chickens and the dogs in the street gave you hints; it was not merely that every street-boy knew, and was eager to explain; it was that the stupid grown-ups themselves persisted in saying things which you couldn’t help getting. It was Aunt Emma’s fixed conviction that every lady was after Dad; “setting her cap at him,” or “making sheep’s eyes at him”—she had many such phrases. And Dad always showed a queer embarrassment whenever he had been the least bit polite to any lady; he seemed to be concerned lest Bunny should share Aunt Emma’s suspicions. But the truth was, Bunny was irritated by his aunt, and learned to evade her questions, and not tell what Dad had said to the nice lady in the hotel at Lobos River, and whether or not the lady had had dinner with them. These worldly arts Bunny acquired, but all the time he was in secret revolt. Why couldn’t people talk plainly? Why did they have to be pretending, and whispering, and making you uncomfortable? Within a week after bringing in Ross-Bankside No. 1, Dad had a new derrick under way on the lease, and in another week he had it rigged up, and the old string of tools was on its way into the earth again. Also he had two new derricks under way, and two new strings in process of delivery. There would be four wells, standing on the four corners of a diamond-shaped figure, three hundred feet on the side. It was necessary to call house-movers, and take the Bankside homestead to another lot; but that didn’t trouble Mr. Bankside, who had already moved himself to an ocean-front palace near Dad, and bought himself a whole outfit of furniture, and a big new limousine, also a “sport-car,” in which to drive himself to the country club to play golf every afternoon. The Bankside family was accustoming itself to the presence of a butler, and Mrs. Bankside had been proposed at the most exclusive of the ladies’ clubs. Efficiency was the watch-word out here in the West, and when you decided to change your social status, you put the job right through. Dad and Bunny made another trip to Lobos River, and not without some difficulty they conquered the “jinx” in Number Two, and brought in a very good well. There were to be two more derricks here, and more tools to be bought and delivered. That was the way in the oil business, as fast as you got any money, you put it back into new drilling—and, of course, new responsibilities. You were driven to this by the forces inherent in the game. You were racing with other people, who were always threatening to get your oil. As soon as you had one well, you had to have “offset wells” to protect it from the people on every side who would otherwise get your oil. Also, you might have trouble in marketing your oil, and would begin to think, how nice to have your own refinery, and be entirely independent. But independence had its price, for then you would have to provide enough oil to keep the refinery going, and you would want a chain of filling-stations to get rid of your products. It was a hard game for the little fellow; and no matter how big you got, there was always somebody bigger! But Dad had no kick just now; everything was a-comin’ his way a-whoopin’. “They say there’s no end of quail there, Dad.”

“Yes, but we can get quail a lot nearer home.”

“I know, Dad; but I’ve never been there, and I want to see it.”

“But what made you hit on that place?” Bunny was embarrassed, because he knew Dad was going to think he was “queer.” Nevertheless, he persisted. “That’s where the Watkins family live.”

“Watkins family—who are they?”

“Don’t you remember that boy, Paul, that I met one night when you were talking about the lease?”

“Gosh, son! You still a-frettin’ about that boy?”

“I met Mrs. Groarty on the street yesterday, and she told me about the family; they’re in dreadful trouble, they’re going to lose their ranch to the bank because they can’t meet the interest on the mortgage, and Mrs. Groarty says she can’t think what they’ll do. You know Mrs. Groarty didn’t get any money herself—at least, she spent her bonus money for units, and she isn’t getting anything out of them, and has to live on what her husband gets as a night watchman.”

“What you want to do about it?”

“I want you to buy that mortgage, Dad; or anything, so the Watkinses can stay in their home. It’s wicked that people should be turned out like that, when they’re doing the best they can.”

“There’s plenty o’ people bein’ turned out when they don’t meet their obligations, son.”

“But when it’s not their fault, Dad?”

“It would take a lot of bookkeeping to figger jist whose fault it is; and the banks don’t keep books that way.” Then seeing the protest in Bunny’s face, “You’ll find, son there’s a lot o’ harsh things in the world, that ain’t in your power to change. You’ll jist have to make up your mind to that, sooner or later.”

“But Dad, there’s four children there, and three of them are girls, and where are they to go? Paul is away, and they haven’t any way to let him know what’s happened. Mrs. Groarty showed me a picture of them, Dad; they’re good, kind people, you can see they’ve never done anything but work hard. Honest, Dad, I couldn’t be happy if I didn’t help them. You said you’d buy me a car some day, and I’d rather you took the money and bought that mortgage. It’s less than a couple of thousand dollars, and that’s nothing to you.”

“I know, son; but then you’ll get them on your hands—” “No, they’re not like that, they’re proud; Mrs. Groarty says they wouldn’t take money from you, any more than Paul would. But if you bought the mortgage from the bank, they couldn’t help that. Or you might buy the ranch, Dad, and rent it back to them. Paul says there’s oil on that ranch—at least his Uncle Eby had seen it on top of the ground.”

“There’s thousands of ranches jist like that in California, son. Oil on top of the ground don’t mean anything special.”

“Well, Dad, you’ve always said you wanted to try some wild-catting; and you know, that’s the only way you’ll ever get what you talk about—a whole big tract that belongs to you, with no royalties to pay, and nobody to butt in. So let’s take a chance on Paradise, and drive through there and camp out a few days and get some quail, and we’ll see what we think of it, and we’ll help those poor people, and give your kidneys a rest at the same time.” So Dad said all right; and he went away thinking to himself: “Gosh! Funny kid!” The San Elido valley lay on the edge of the desert, and you crossed a corner of the desert to get to it; a bare wilderness of sun-baked sand and rock, with nothing but grey, dusty desert plants. You sped along upon a fine paved road, but the land was haunted by the souls of old-time pioneers who had crossed it in covered wagons or with pack-mules, and had left their bones beside many a trail. Even now, you had to be careful when you went off into side-trails across these wastes; every now and then a car would get stuck with an empty radiator, and the people would be lucky to get out alive. You could get water if you sunk a deep well; and so there were fruit ranches and fields of alfalfa here and there. There came long stretches where the ground was white, like salt; that was alkali, Dad said, and it made this country a regular boob-trap. The stranger from the East would come in and inspect a nice fruit ranch, and would think he was making a good bargain to get the land next door for a hundred dollars an acre; he would set out his fruit-trees and patiently water them, and they wouldn’t grow; nothing would grow but a little alfalfa, and maybe there was too much alkali for that. Tightly clutched in Bunny’s two hands were a couple of repeating shot-guns; he held these for hours, partly because he liked the feel of them, and partly because they had to be carried in the open—if you shut them up in the compartment they would be “concealed weapons,” and that was against the law. The letter came on a Tuesday, in a cheap envelope with a two-cent stamp, and the handwriting sprawled across it as if the pen had been held by a fist that was more accustomed to a pick-handle. Ned Carrow found it on the hall table when he came in from his tennis, and he did not recognize the writing; but when he turned it over and saw "T. Hebley, Gen. Delivery, Copperhill, Ariz.," he gave a whoop that brought the Japanese house-boy out of the pantry to see what was the matter.

It was Tom! Cousin Tom, whom he had not laid eyes on for eight years, not since the summer when Ned was eleven and had spent six glorious weeks on the Hebley ranch in the Verdugo valley, riding bareback on a fat mare named Dolly, and learning to milk a cow, and being initiated into the mysteries of a swimming-hole where the irrigation ditch made a bend under the cottonwoods. Tom had been fourteen then, a lanky, freckled boy with enormous bare feet and a knowledge of the world which seemed to Ned beyond anything a human being could acquire. Tom knew how to catch a gopher, and how to tell when a melon was ripe by thumping it, and he knew what the hired man said when he hit his thumb with a hammer, and what the words meant. He had been Ned's hero for six weeks, and then the summer had ended, and Ned had gone home to Harbor City and the private school with the uniforms; and after that the families had somehow drifted apart.

Ned knew in a general way why that was. His mother and Aunt Martha were sisters, and when they were girls they had been as poor as each other, back in a little town in Iowa. But Ned's mother had married a young man who clerked in a wholesale grocery, and the young man had become a partner, and then the owner, and then the president of the Carrow Mercantile Company, with branches in three cities. Aunt Martha, on the other hand, had married a farmer, and had gone on being a farmer's wife. That is the way it happens in America; two girls start from the same doorstep, and one of them ends up in a house on Buena Vista Heights with a butler, and the other one ends up somewhere you do not talk about at dinner. Nobody intends it; it is just that the money goes one way and not the other, and after a while the sisters find that they have nothing to say in their letters, and the letters come at Christmas only, and then not at all.

There had been trouble on the ranch, Ned remembered; a dry year, and then another dry year, and the water company had raised its rates, and the bank had done what banks do. Ned had heard his father speak of it once at the table, in that tone of mild regret with which a successful man refers to the misfortunes of his relatives: "Too bad about Hebley. Good, hard-working fellow, but no head for business. Ought never to have borrowed on that last crop." And Ned's mother had looked at her plate, and nothing more had been said. Then, later, there had been a rumor that the Hebleys were in Arizona, and that Uncle Will was working in the mines.

Now here was Tom's letter, written on ruled paper torn out of a tablet. "Dear Cousin Ned," it said. "I guess you will be surprised to hear from me after so long. I am coming to Harbor City to look for work, as things are not so good here at present, and I would like to see you if it is convenient. I will be on the Thursday train getting in at 4:10. You do not need to meet me if you are busy. Your cousin, Tom Hebley. P.S. Ma died last spring. I guess maybe you did not hear."

Ned read that postscript twice, and something went cold in his stomach. Aunt Martha dead, and nobody had heard! He remembered her as a big, red-armed woman who laughed all the time and made doughnuts in a kettle of fat, and who had called him "the little city feller" and given him the first doughnut out of every batch. He went to find his mother, and showed her the letter; and his mother sat down suddenly in a chair and put her hand to her throat, and said, "Oh, Ned! Oh, poor Martha!" and began to cry. Afterwards she said that she had written twice, and the letters had come back; and she said that she would write to Will at once, and send some money—and then she stopped, and looked troubled, and said that perhaps Ned had better not mention it to his father just yet; Father had been so worried lately about the strike at the cannery.

So on Thursday Ned drove himself down to the Union Station in his roadster, which was a cream-colored affair with red wire wheels, and which had been his father's present when he entered the university. He got there half an hour early, and walked up and down the platform, and wondered whether he would know Tom, and whether Tom would know him, and what on earth they would find to say to each other. He had a vague idea that he ought to be very tactful, and not seem to notice that Tom was poor; he would take him to a good restaurant, but not too good, so as not to embarrass him. Then the train came in, and the people poured out of the day-coaches, and there was a tall young man in a blue work-shirt and a cheap gray suit-coat, carrying a cardboard suit-case tied with a rope; and Ned knew him at once, because he walked the same way, with long loose strides, as if he were stepping over furrows.

"Tom!"

"Well, I'll be darned! If it ain't the little city feller!"

They shook hands, and then they stood and looked at each other, and grinned, and neither of them could think of anything to say. Tom was taller than Ned by half a head, and his face had gone thin and brown, with lines around the eyes that should not have been there at twenty-two. His hands were the thing that Ned noticed most; they were big and hard and scarred, and there was a crooked finger on the left one, and a white seam across the back of it. When Ned gripped one of those hands, it was like taking hold of a piece of harness leather.

"Gosh, Tom, I'm sorry about Aunt Martha. We never heard a word. Mother's terribly cut up."

"Yeah," said Tom. "Well, it was quick, anyhow. She didn't suffer so much at the end." He shifted his suitcase to the other hand, and looked away down the platform. "It was the dust, mostly. The doctor said she'd ought to go somewheres else, where the air was better. But there wasn't any place to go."

Ned took the suitcase, and they went out to the car; and when Tom saw the cream-colored roadster with the red wire wheels, he stopped and let out a long whistle. "Holy smoke! That yours?"

"Dad gave it to me," said Ned, and felt himself go red, as if he had been caught at something.

"Some boat," said Tom, and walked around it, and looked at the engine, and asked how many cylinders, and what she would do on the open road; and Ned told him, and found that the awkwardness was passing, because a car is a thing that two young men can always talk about, whatever else may lie between them.

They drove along the boulevard by the water-front, and Tom looked at everything—the ships at the wharves, and the cranes swinging cargo, and the warehouses with "Carrow Mercantile Co." painted on them in letters six feet high. "Your old man's, eh?" he said; and Ned said yes, and Tom said nothing more, but kept on looking. Ned had meant to take him straight home, but at the last moment he had a cowardly feeling about his father, and about the butler, and about his sister Evelyn, who was nineteen and had just come back from a finishing-school in the East, and who said "my deah" to people. So instead he turned off and went to a place he knew on the beach, a little fish-restaurant with oil-cloth on the tables, where you could get a plate of fried abalone for forty cents and nobody cared what you had on.

They sat by the window, where they could see the surf coming in long and green and breaking white on the sand, and Tom ate as if he had not eaten since Arizona, which, as it turned out, was very nearly the truth. And between mouthfuls he answered Ned's questions; and so, little by little, the story of eight years came out.

It was not a story that Tom told with any sense of drama; he told it as a man tells about the weather, because it was the weather of his life and he had stopped expecting anything else. After the bank took the ranch, they had loaded what they could into a Ford truck and gone to Arizona, because a man had told Uncle Will there was good money in the copper mines. And there was good money, in a way; four dollars and a half a day, which sounded like a fortune to a farmer. But you had to pay rent to the company for a shack, and you had to buy your groceries at the company store, and the prices at the company store were such that when you came to the end of the month you found that the company had most of the four-fifty back again. Tom had gone into the mine himself at fifteen, lying about his age, the way all the boys did; it was the only way the family could make out.

The men had asked for five dollars a day and a ventilating system in the lower levels, where three men had died of the heat in a single month. The company had said no; and the men had walked out; and then, Tom said, "the fun started." The company had brought in guards from a detective agency in Los Angeles, men with rifles who had never seen a mine in their lives, and the sheriff had sworn them all in as deputies. "But—but that's against the law!" cried Ned. "They can't do that! You can't just put people in cars and ship them off!"

Tom looked at him with an expression which Ned could not quite read; it was partly amusement, and partly something like pity, and partly something harder than either. "Who's going to stop 'em?" he said. "The sheriff? He was the one that done it. The judge? The company put him in. The governor? He's a friend of the people that owns the company. You'd ought to read the newspapers out there; they said we was all Reds and anarchists, and had been paid by the Russians to wreck the country. Pa! It was the strike at his father's cannery, down at the south end of the harbor, which had been going on for three weeks. The women who cut fish there had asked for thirty cents an hour instead of twenty-two, and Ned's father had said at the dinner-table that it was the work of outside agitators, and that he would close the plant before he would let a lot of Bolsheviks tell him how to run his business. He did not say any of this to Tom. He was ashamed, and he did not quite know why; it was not his cannery, after all, and he had never been inside it. "What are you going to do now?" he asked.

Pa's still out at Copperhill with the kids—there's Ella and the two little ones, you never seen them—and they're living in a tent the union put up. I got to send them something soon." He said it quite simply, and then he added, as if it had just occurred to him that Ned might misunderstand: "I didn't come here to ask your folks for nothing, Ned. I want you to know that. I just thought—well, you was the only person I knew in this town, and I'd kind of like to see you, after that summer and all."

"Gosh, Tom," said Ned; and that was all he could say for a while.

They sat and watched the sun go down into the ocean, which it does in a great flare of crimson and gold along that coast, every evening, for the rich and for the poor alike. And presently, because they were young, and because the abalone had been good, they began to talk about the old days; and then it was easier. Did Tom remember the time they had tried to ride the calf, and the calf had gone through the fence? Did Ned remember the hired man, Swede Olaf, who could crack walnuts with his teeth? Did Tom remember the night the coyote got into the chicken-house, and Aunt Martha had gone out after it in her nightgown with a broom? They laughed until the waiter looked around at them; and then Tom stopped laughing, and was quiet, and Ned knew that he was thinking about Aunt Martha, and that the nightgown and the broom were a long way off now, farther off than Iowa.

"She always said you'd be somebody," Tom said, after a while. "She used to read about your old man in the papers, when he give the money for the hospital, and she'd say, 'Some day Ned'll be running all that.' She was right proud of you, Ma was."

Ned turned his face to the window, because something had got into his eyes. He thought of all the things he had meant to say to Tom—tactful things, about how sorry he was, and how he would speak to his father about a job, and how Tom must come up and meet the family. They all seemed foolish now. You could not be tactful with a man who had spent seven years in a hole in the ground and then been shipped into the desert in a cattle-car; it would be like being tactful with a forest fire. What Ned wanted to do, though he could not have put it into words, was to understand; to find out how the world had come to be arranged like this, so that one cousin got a roadster and the other got a crooked finger, and both of them had been the same kind of boy, splashing in the same irrigation ditch under the cottonwoods.

"Tom," he said, "you'll stay with me tonight. No—don't argue. We'll go up to the house, and you'll meet Mother; she wants to see you more than anything. And Dad—" He hesitated, and then he set his jaw in a way that would have surprised his father, had his father been there to see it. "Dad will just have to see you too."

Tom looked at him with that same hard, half-pitying look. "You sure about that, kid? I'm one of them Reds, you know. It was in the papers."

"I don't care what was in the papers," said Ned; and he found, rather to his own astonishment, that he meant it.

So they went out to the roadster, and Tom put his cardboard suitcase with the rope around it into the rumble-seat, where Ned's golf-bag usually rode; and they drove up the winding road to Buena Vista Heights, with the lights of the harbor spread out below them like a jeweled carpet. Somewhere down there among those lights was the cannery, dark now, with the women who cut fish standing in front of it on the picket-line; and somewhere farther off, beyond the mountains and the desert, was a tent in a mining-camp, where an old man who had once been a farmer was sitting with three children and wondering how they would eat next week. Ned did not see these things, of course; you cannot see such things from Buena Vista Heights, which is one of the reasons why people build their houses there. But he knew now that they were there; and that is the beginning of a great deal of trouble, for a young man in his position.
