Jurgis was vexed when the cynical Jokubas translated these signs with sarcastic comments, offering to take them to the secret rooms where the spoiled meats went to be doctored.

Their good luck, they felt, had given them the right to think about a home; and sitting out on the doorstep that summer evening, they held consultation about it, and Jurgis took occasion to broach a weighty subject. Passing down the avenue to work that morning he had seen two boys leaving an advertisement from house to house; and seeing that there were pictures upon it, Jurgis had asked for one, and had rolled it up and tucked it into his shirt. At noontime a man with whom he had been talking had read it to him and told him a little about it, with the result that Jurgis had conceived a wild idea. He brought out the placard, which was quite a work of art. It was nearly two feet long, printed on calendered paper, with a selection of colors so bright that they shone even in the moonlight. The center of the placard was occupied by a house, brilliantly painted, new, and dazzling. The roof of it was of a purple hue, and trimmed with gold; the house itself was silvery, and the doors and windows red. It was a two-story building, with a porch in front, and a very fancy scrollwork around the edges; it was complete in every tiniest detail, even the doorknob, and there was a hammock on the porch and white lace curtains in the windows. Underneath this, in one corner, was a picture of a husband and wife in loving embrace; in the opposite corner was a cradle, with fluffy curtains drawn over it, and a smiling cherub hovering upon silver-colored wings. For fear that the significance of all this should be lost, there was a label, in Polish, Lithuanian, and German—“Dom. Namai. Heim.” “Why pay rent?” the linguistic circular went on to demand. “Why not own your own home? Do you know that you can buy one for less than your rent? We have built thousands of homes which are now occupied by happy families.”—So it became eloquent, picturing the blissfulness of married life in a house with nothing to pay. It even quoted “Home, Sweet Home,” and made bold to translate it into Polish—though for some reason it omitted the Lithuanian of this. Perhaps the translator found it a difficult matter to be sentimental in a language in which a sob is known as a gukcziojimas and a smile as a nusiszypsojimas. Over this document the family pored long, while Ona spelled out its contents. It appeared that this house contained four rooms, besides a basement, and that it might be bought for fifteen hundred dollars, the lot and all. Of this, only three hundred dollars had to be paid down, the balance being paid at the rate of twelve dollars a month. These were frightful sums, but then they were in America, where people talked about such without fear. They had learned that they would have to pay a rent of nine dollars a month for a flat, and there was no way of doing better, unless the family of twelve was to exist in one or two rooms, as at present. If they paid rent, of course, they might pay forever, and be no better off; whereas, if they could only meet the extra expense in the beginning, there would at last come a time when they would not have any rent to pay for the rest of their lives. They figured it up. There was a little left of the money belonging to Teta Elzbieta, and there was a little left to Jurgis. Marija had about fifty dollars pinned up somewhere in her stockings, and Grandfather Anthony had part of the money he had gotten for his farm. If they all combined, they would have enough to make the first payment; and if they had employment, so that they could be sure of the future, it might really prove the best plan. It was, of course, not a thing even to be talked of lightly; it was a thing they would have to sift to the bottom. And yet, on the other hand, if they were going to make the venture, the sooner they did it the better, for were they not paying rent all the time, and living in a most horrible way besides? Jurgis was used to dirt—there was nothing could scare a man who had been with a railroad gang, where one could gather up the fleas off the floor of the sleeping room by the handful. But that sort of thing would not do for Ona. They must have a better place of some sort soon—Jurgis said it with all the assurance of a man who had just made a dollar and fifty-seven cents in a single day. Jurgis was at a loss to understand why, with wages as they were, so many of the people of this district should live the way they did. The next day Marija went to see her “forelady,” and was told to report the first of the week, and learn the business of can-painter. Marija went home, singing out loud all the way, and was just in time to join Ona and her stepmother as they were setting out to go and make inquiry concerning the house. That evening the three made their report to the men—the thing was altogether as represented in the circular, or at any rate so the agent had said. The houses lay to the south, about a mile and a half from the yards; they were wonderful bargains, the gentleman had assured them—personally, and for their own good. He could do this, so he explained to them, for the reason that he had himself no interest in their sale—he was merely the agent for a company that had built them. These were the last, and the company was going out of business, so if any one wished to take advantage of this wonderful no-rent plan, he would have to be very quick. As a matter of fact there was just a little uncertainty as to whether there was a single house left; for the agent had taken so many people to see them, and for all he knew the company might have parted with the last. Seeing Teta Elzbieta’s evident grief at this news, he added, after some hesitation, that if they really intended to make a purchase, he would send a telephone message at his own expense, and have one of the houses kept. So it had finally been arranged—and they were to go and make an inspection the following Sunday morning. That was Thursday; and all the rest of the week the killing gang at Brown’s worked at full pressure, and Jurgis cleared a dollar seventy-five every day. That was at the rate of ten and one-half dollars a week, or forty-five a month. Jurgis was not able to figure, except it was a very simple sum, but Ona was like lightning at such things, and she worked out the problem for the family. Marija and Jonas were each to pay sixteen dollars a month board, and the old man insisted that he could do the same as soon as he got a place—which might be any day now. That would make ninety-three dollars. Then Marija and Jonas were between them to take a third share in the house, which would leave only eight dollars a month for Jurgis to contribute to the payment. So they would have eighty-five dollars a month—or, supposing that Dede Antanas did not get work at once, seventy dollars a month—which ought surely to be sufficient for the support of a family of twelve. An hour before the time on Sunday morning the entire party set out. They had the address written on a piece of paper, which they showed to some one now and then. It proved to be a long mile and a half, but they walked it, and half an hour or so later the agent put in an appearance. He was a smooth and florid personage, elegantly dressed, and he spoke their language freely, which gave him a great advantage in dealing with them. He escorted them to the house, which was one of a long row of the typical frame dwellings of the neighborhood, where architecture is a luxury that is dispensed with. Ona’s heart sank, for the house was not as it was shown in the picture; the color scheme was different, for one thing, and then it did not seem quite so big. Still, it was freshly painted, and made a considerable show. It was all brand-new, so the agent told them, but he talked so incessantly that they were quite confused, and did not have time to ask many questions. There were all sorts of things they had made up their minds to inquire about, but when the time came, they either forgot them or lacked the courage. The other houses in the row did not seem to be new, and few of them seemed to be occupied. When they ventured to hint at this, the agent’s reply was that the purchasers would be moving in shortly. To press the matter would have seemed to be doubting his word, and never in their lives had any one of them ever spoken to a person of the class called “gentleman” except with deference and humility. The house had a basement, about two feet below the street line, and a single story, about six feet above it, reached by a flight of steps. In addition there was an attic, made by the peak of the roof, and having one small window in each end. The street in front of the house was unpaved and unlighted, and the view from it consisted of a few exactly similar houses, scattered here and there upon lots grown up with dingy brown weeds. The house inside contained four rooms, plastered white; the basement was but a frame, the walls being unplastered and the floor not laid. The agent explained that the houses were built that way, as the purchasers generally preferred to finish the basements to suit their own taste. The attic was also unfinished—the family had been figuring that in case of an emergency they could rent this attic, but they found that there was not even a floor, nothing but joists, and beneath them the lath and plaster of the ceiling below. All of this, however, did not chill their ardor as much as might have been expected, because of the volubility of the agent. There was no end to the advantages of the house, as he set them forth, and he was not silent for an instant; he showed them everything, down to the locks on the doors and the catches on the windows, and how to work them. He showed them the sink in the kitchen, with running water and a faucet, something which Teta Elzbieta had never in her wildest dreams hoped to possess. After a discovery such as that it would have seemed ungrateful to find any fault, and so they tried to shut their eyes to other defects.

Excerpt 3: It was four o’clock when the ceremony was over and the carriages began to arrive. There had been a crowd following all the way, owing to the exuberance of Marija Berczynskas. The occasion rested heavily upon Marija’s broad shoulders—it was her task to see that all things went in due form, and after the best home traditions; and, flying wildly hither and thither, bowling every one out of the way, and scolding and exhorting all day with her tremendous voice, Marija was too eager to see that others conformed to the proprieties to consider them herself. She had left the church last of all, and, desiring to arrive first at the hall, had issued orders to the coachman to drive faster. When that personage had developed a will of his own in the matter, Marija had flung up the window of the carriage, and, leaning out, proceeded to tell him her opinion of him, first in Lithuanian, which he did not understand, and then in Polish, which he did. Having the advantage of her in altitude, the driver had stood his ground and even ventured to attempt to speak; and the result had been a furious altercation, which, continuing all the way down Ashland Avenue, had added a new swarm of urchins to the cortege at each side street for half a mile. This was unfortunate, for already there was a throng before the door. The music had started up, and half a block away you could hear the dull “broom, broom” of a cello, with the squeaking of two fiddles which vied with each other in intricate and altitudinous gymnastics. Seeing the throng, Marija abandoned precipitately the debate concerning the ancestors of her coachman, and, springing from the moving carriage, plunged in and proceeded to clear a way to the hall. Once within, she turned and began to push the other way, roaring, meantime, “Eik! Eik! Uzdaryk-duris!” in tones which made the orchestral uproar sound like fairy music.

“Z. Graiczunas, Pasilinksminimams darzas. Vynas. Sznapsas. Wines and Liquors. Union Headquarters”—that was the way the signs ran. The reader, who perhaps has never held much converse in the language of far-off Lithuania, will be glad of the explanation that the place was the rear room of a saloon in that part of Chicago known as “back of the yards.” This information is definite and suited to the matter of fact; but how pitifully inadequate it would have seemed to one who understood that it was also the supreme hour of ecstasy in the life of one of God’s gentlest creatures, the scene of the wedding feast and the joy-transfiguration of little Ona Lukoszaite! She stood in the doorway, shepherded by Cousin Marija, breathless from pushing through the crowd, and in her happiness painful to look upon. There was a light of wonder in her eyes and her lids trembled, and her otherwise wan little face was flushed. She wore a muslin dress, conspicuously white, and a stiff little veil coming to her shoulders. There were five pink paper roses twisted in the veil, and eleven bright green rose leaves. There were new white cotton gloves upon her hands, and as she stood staring about her she twisted them together feverishly. It was almost too much for her—you could see the pain of too great emotion in her face, and all the tremor of her form. She was so young—not quite sixteen—and small for her age, a mere child; and she had just been married—and married to Jurgis, of all men, to Jurgis Rudkus, he with the white flower in the buttonhole of his new black suit, he with the mighty shoulders and the giant hands. Pronounced Yoorghis Ona was blue-eyed and fair, while Jurgis had great black eyes with beetling brows, and thick black hair that curled in waves about his ears—in short, they were one of those incongruous and impossible married couples with which Mother Nature so often wills to confound all prophets, before and after. Jurgis could take up a two-hundred-and-fifty-pound quarter of beef and carry it into a car without a stagger, or even a thought; and now he stood in a far corner, frightened as a hunted animal, and obliged to moisten his lips with his tongue each time before he could answer the congratulations of his friends. Gradually there was effected a separation between the spectators and the guests—a separation at least sufficiently complete for working purposes. There was no time during the festivities which ensued when there were not groups of onlookers in the doorways and the corners; and if any one of these onlookers came sufficiently close, or looked sufficiently hungry, a chair was offered him, and he was invited to the feast. It was one of the laws of the veselija that no one goes hungry; and, while a rule made in the forests of Lithuania is hard to apply in the stockyards district of Chicago, with its quarter of a million inhabitants, still they did their best, and the children who ran in from the street, and even the dogs, went out again happier. A charming informality was one of the characteristics of this celebration. The men wore their hats, or, if they wished, they took them off, and their coats with them; they ate when and where they pleased, and moved as often as they pleased. There were to be speeches and singing, but no one had to listen who did not care to; if he wished, meantime, to speak or sing himself, he was perfectly free. The resulting medley of sound distracted no one, save possibly alone the babies, of which there were present a number equal to the total possessed by all the guests invited. There was no other place for the babies to be, and so part of the preparations for the evening consisted of a collection of cribs and carriages in one corner. In these the babies slept, three or four together, or wakened together, as the case might be. Those who were still older, and could reach the tables, marched about munching contentedly at meat bones and bologna sausages. The room is about thirty feet square, with whitewashed walls, bare save for a calendar, a picture of a race horse, and a family tree in a gilded frame. To the right there is a door from the saloon, with a few loafers in the doorway, and in the corner beyond it a bar, with a presiding genius clad in soiled white, with waxed black mustaches and a carefully oiled curl plastered against one side of his forehead. In the opposite corner are two tables, filling a third of the room and laden with dishes and cold viands, which a few of the hungrier guests are already munching. At the head, where sits the bride, is a snow-white cake, with an Eiffel tower of constructed decoration, with sugar roses and two angels upon it, and a generous sprinkling of pink and green and yellow candies. Beyond opens a door into the kitchen, where there is a glimpse to be had of a range with much steam ascending from it, and many women, old and young, rushing hither and thither. In the corner to the left are the three musicians, upon a little platform, toiling heroically to make some impression upon the hubbub; also the babies, similarly occupied, and an open window whence the populace imbibes the sights and sounds and odors. Suddenly some of the steam begins to advance, and, peering through it, you discern Aunt Elizabeth, Ona’s stepmother—Teta Elzbieta, as they call her—bearing aloft a great platter of stewed duck. Behind her is Kotrina, making her way cautiously, staggering beneath a similar burden; and half a minute later there appears old Grandmother Majauszkiene, with a big yellow bowl of smoking potatoes, nearly as big as herself. So, bit by bit, the feast takes form—there is a ham and a dish of sauerkraut, boiled rice, macaroni, bologna sausages, great piles of penny buns, bowls of milk, and foaming pitchers of beer. There is also, not six feet from your back, the bar, where you may order all you please and do not have to pay for it. “Eiksz! Graicziau!” screams Marija Berczynskas, and falls to work herself—for there is more upon the stove inside that will be spoiled if it be not eaten. So, with laughter and shouts and endless badinage and merriment, the guests take their places. The young men, who for the most part have been huddled near the door, summon their resolution and advance; and the shrinking Jurgis is poked and scolded by the old folks until he consents to seat himself at the right hand of the bride. The two bridesmaids, whose insignia of office are paper wreaths, come next, and after them the rest of the guests, old and young, boys and girls. The spirit of the occasion takes hold of the stately bartender, who condescends to a plate of stewed duck; even the fat policeman—whose duty it will be, later in the evening, to break up the fights—draws up a chair to the foot of the table. And the children shout and the babies yell, and every one laughs and sings and chatters—while above all the deafening clamor Cousin Marija shouts orders to the musicians. The musicians—how shall one begin to describe them? All this time they have been there, playing in a mad frenzy—all of this scene must be read, or said, or sung, to music. It is the music which makes it what it is; it is the music which changes the place from the rear room of a saloon in back of the yards to a fairy place, a wonderland, a little corner of the high mansions of the sky. The little person who leads this trio is an inspired man. His fiddle is out of tune, and there is no rosin on his bow, but still he is an inspired man—the hands of the muses have been laid upon him. He plays like one possessed by a demon, by a whole horde of demons. You can feel them in the air round about him, capering frenetically; with their invisible feet they set the pace, and the hair of the leader of the orchestra rises on end, and his eyeballs start from their sockets, as he toils to keep up with them. Tamoszius Kuszleika is his name, and he has taught himself to play the violin by practicing all night, after working all day on the “killing beds.” He is in his shirt sleeves, with a vest figured with faded gold horseshoes, and a pink-striped shirt, suggestive of peppermint candy. A pair of military trousers, light blue with a yellow stripe, serve to give that suggestion of authority proper to the leader of a band. He is only about five feet high, but even so these trousers are about eight inches short of the ground. You wonder where he can have gotten them or rather you would wonder, if the excitement of being in his presence left you time to think of such things. For he is an inspired man. Every inch of him is inspired—you might almost say inspired separately. He stamps with his feet, he tosses his head, he sways and swings to and fro; he has a wizened-up little face, irresistibly comical; and, when he executes a turn or a flourish, his brows knit and his lips work and his eyelids wink—the very ends of his necktie bristle out. And every now and then he turns upon his companions, nodding, signaling, beckoning frantically—with every inch of him appealing, imploring, in behalf of the muses and their call. For they are hardly worthy of Tamoszius, the other two members of the orchestra. The second violin is a Slovak, a tall, gaunt man with black-rimmed spectacles and the mute and patient look of an overdriven mule; he responds to the whip but feebly, and then always falls back into his old rut. The third man is very fat, with a round, red, sentimental nose, and he plays with his eyes turned up to the sky and a look of infinite yearning. He is playing a bass part upon his cello, and so the excitement is nothing to him; no matter what happens in the treble, it is his task to saw out one long-drawn and lugubrious note after another, from four o’clock in the afternoon until nearly the same hour next morning, for his third of the total income of one dollar per hour. Before the feast has been five minutes under way, Tamoszius Kuszleika has risen in his excitement; a minute or two more and you see that he is beginning to edge over toward the tables. His nostrils are dilated and his breath comes fast—his demons are driving him. He nods and shakes his head at his companions, jerking at them with his violin, until at last the long form of the second violinist also rises up. In the end all three of them begin advancing, step by step, upon the banqueters, Valentinavyczia, the cellist, bumping along with his instrument between notes. Finally all three are gathered at the foot of the tables, and there Tamoszius mounts upon a stool. Now he is in his glory, dominating the scene. Some of the people are eating, some are laughing and talking—but you will make a great mistake if you think there is one of them who does not hear him. His notes are never true, and his fiddle buzzes on the low ones and squeaks and scratches on the high; but these things they heed no more than they heed the dirt and noise and squalor about them—it is out of this material that they have to build their lives, with it that they have to utter their souls. And this is their utterance; merry and boisterous, or mournful and wailing, or passionate and rebellious, this music is their music, music of home. It stretches out its arms to them, they have only to give themselves up. Chicago and its saloons and its slums fade away—there are green meadows and sunlit rivers, mighty forests and snow-clad hills. They behold home landscapes and childhood scenes returning; old loves and friendships begin to waken, old joys and griefs to laugh and weep. Some fall back and close their eyes, some beat upon the table. Now and then one leaps up with a cry and calls for this song or that; and then the fire leaps brighter in Tamoszius’ eyes, and he flings up his fiddle and shouts to his companions, and away they go in mad career. The company takes up the choruses, and men and women cry out like all possessed; some leap to their feet and stamp upon the floor, lifting their glasses and pledging each other. Before long it occurs to some one to demand an old wedding song, which celebrates the beauty of the bride and the joys of love. In the excitement of this masterpiece Tamoszius Kuszleika begins to edge in between the tables, making his way toward the head, where sits the bride. There is not a foot of space between the chairs of the guests, and Tamoszius is so short that he pokes them with his bow whenever he reaches over for the low notes; but still he presses in, and insists relentlessly that his companions must follow. During their progress, needless to say, the sounds of the cello are pretty well extinguished; but at last the three are at the head, and Tamoszius takes his station at the right hand of the bride and begins to pour out his soul in melting strains. Little Ona is too excited to eat. Once in a while she tastes a little something, when Cousin Marija pinches her elbow and reminds her; but, for the most part, she sits gazing with the same fearful eyes of wonder. Teta Elzbieta is all in a flutter, like a hummingbird; her sisters, too, keep running up behind her, whispering, breathless. But Ona seems scarcely to hear them—the music keeps calling, and the far-off look comes back, and she sits with her hands pressed together over her heart. Then the tears begin to come into her eyes; and as she is ashamed to wipe them away, and ashamed to let them run down her cheeks, she turns and shakes her head a little, and then flushes red when she sees that Jurgis is watching her. When in the end Tamoszius Kuszleika has reached her side, and is waving his magic wand above her, Ona’s cheeks are scarlet, and she looks as if she would have to get up and run away.

It was nearly six o'clock when little Wladek came home, and his mother had been watching for him from the window for more than an hour. The window looked out upon an alley, and beyond the alley upon a board fence plastered with circus bills, and beyond the fence upon the long black wall of the rolling mill, from whose stacks there poured, day and night, a smoke so thick that the sun had to fight its way through it like a swimmer through a flood. There was not much to see from that window; but Agnieszka Mrozek had stood at it so long that she knew every crack in the fence and every tatter of the circus bills, and she could have told you how many times in that hour the switch engine had gone puffing by with its string of ore cars, and how many times the whistle had blown at the gate. She had gone down to the street twice, with her shawl over her head, and had stood at the corner and peered both ways; and each time she had come back up the three flights of stairs, holding her side, for she was seven months gone with her fifth child, and the stairs were very steep.

She had sent the boy at four o'clock to Kowalski's on the avenue, with a quarter of a dollar tied up in the corner of a handkerchief. He was to buy a loaf of bread, which was five cents, and a pound of lard, which was twelve, and with what was left he was to get soup bones from the butcher next door. It was a simple errand, and he had done it many times before; he was a bright boy, and he could count up to a hundred in English and in Polish both, and he knew the price of everything in Kowalski's store as well as his mother did. But the quarter of a dollar was the last money in the house. That was a thing which Wladek did not know, and which it would not have occurred to his mother to tell him. One does not tell a child of seven that the rolling mill has been shut down for six weeks for "repairs," and that the father goes out every morning at five to stand in the crowd at the gate of the Harvester works, and comes back every night at dark without having been let in. One does not explain to a child that there are four dollars owing at Kowalski's already, and that the agent has been twice about the rent, and that the last time he had looked about the room at the bed and the stove and the trunk from the old country in a way that had made Agnieszka's heart stand still. These are the affairs of grown persons, and children have no part in them—or so the grown persons believe, until the day comes when the children find out.

It was the shoes which Agnieszka heard first; Wladek wore a pair of shoes which had belonged to a boy in the next building, and which were three sizes too big for him, so that he went clumping up the stairs like a cart horse. She ran to the door and flung it open; and there he stood upon the landing, breathless and rosy-cheeked from the cold, with the loaf of bread under one arm and the package of lard under the other—and with his mouth all smeared about with red, and his two fists clutched tight upon something which he held behind his back.

"Where have you been?" cried his mother. "Do you know what time it is? Where are the bones?"

The boy did not answer, but came in slowly, and laid the bread and the lard upon the table. His mother seized him by the shoulder and turned him about. "What have you got there? Show me!"

He brought his hands around, very reluctantly; and in one of them there was a tin whistle, painted red and blue, with a little bird on the end of it, and in the other there was a stick of candy, striped like a barber's pole, which he had already sucked down to a point. Agnieszka stared at these objects as if they had been two live snakes. It took her a moment to comprehend what they meant; and when she did, the color went out of her face, and she sat down suddenly in a chair.

"Jezus Maria!" she whispered. "The money! What did you do with the money?"

Wladek began to tremble. He had known all the way home that he had done something wrong; he had stood for a long time on the corner of the avenue, feeling of the two pennies and the nickel that were left in the handkerchief, and trying to make up his mind to go back. But he had not known how wrong it was; he had thought that perhaps he would be scolded, and that would be all. Now he saw his mother's face, and he did not understand it, and that frightened him more than any scolding.

"I bought—" he stammered. "There was a store—there was a window—"

There was indeed a store, and there was indeed a window; and if the reader will take the trouble to walk along the avenue he will find it still, a narrow little shop between a saloon and an undertaker's, kept by a Greek with a cast in one eye. It is a place which has been arranged with a great deal of cunning, for it lies directly upon the path which the children of the district must take to the school and to the church and to the grocery; and in its window, which is the only clean window in the block, there is spread out such a display as is calculated to work upon the soul of a child as the sight of a saloon works upon the soul of a drunkard. There are candies of every color in the rainbow, and several which the rainbow has never thought of: red and green and yellow and purple, in sticks and in balls and in the shapes of animals and fishes; there are licorice whips and chocolate mice and little hearts with mottoes printed upon them. There are tin trumpets and tin whistles and jumping jacks and rubber balls, and paper masks with grinning faces, and pistols that shoot caps. And over it all there hangs a great placard, with a picture of a fat and happy little boy in a velvet suit, who holds up a stick of candy and smiles at you, and underneath him the words, in letters a foot high, "EVERY BOY LIKES BUSTER'S!"

Now it does not matter to the man who made that placard, nor to the man who made the candy, nor to the man with the cast in his eye who sells it, that the little boys who pass that window have never seen a velvet suit in their lives, and that most of them have never had enough to eat in their lives either. It does not matter that the candy is made of glucose and coal-tar dyes and a little flour, and that it costs perhaps a tenth of a cent to make, and that the whistle is made of tin scraps from a canning factory and will be broken in three days. All that matters is that the little boys shall stop and stare, and that every now and then one of them shall have a penny in his pocket. There are a great many little boys in the district behind the rolling mills—some thirty thousand of them, according to the census—and if each one of them can be made to spend only a penny a week, it comes to fifteen thousand dollars in the course of a year; and that is a sum which will keep a candy manufacturer in a very fine house upon the Lake Shore Drive, with a velvet suit for each of his own little boys, and a governess to see that they do not eat too many sweets and spoil their digestions.

Wladek had stood before that window for a long time—he did not know how long. He had not meant to go in; he had gone into the butcher's first, and found a crowd there, and had come out again to wait until it should thin. And then the little boy in the velvet suit had smiled at him, and the whistle with the bird on the end of it had seemed to call to him; and there had come over him all at once a feeling such as he could not have put into words, a hunger that was not in his stomach but somewhere farther in. He had never owned a toy in his life that had not been somebody else's first; and here was a whistle that nobody had ever blown, painted fresh and shining, and it cost only ten cents. He had told himself that he would ask the price, and no more; and then, somehow, the handkerchief was untied, and the Greek had taken the dime and given him the whistle, and had thrown in a stick of candy for a penny more—because he was such a fine boy, the Greek had said. So there had been only two cents left for the soup bones; and the butcher had laughed at him, and given him nothing.

All of this came out at last, in broken pieces, between sobs; and his mother listened to it, sitting motionless in her chair, with her hands lying in her lap. When he had finished, she said nothing for a while. Then she got up slowly, and went to the nail behind the stove, and took down the strap.

It was a leather strap, about two feet long and two inches wide, which had once been part of a harness; Wladek's father had brought it from the old country, and it had hung on a nail in every place where they had lived, as a sort of household god. It was not often taken down. Agnieszka was not a harsh woman; she had been a merry girl once, in the village of Brzeziny, where she had danced at the harvest festivals with a wreath of cornflowers in her hair, and the young men had come from three villages around to see her. She loved her children with the fierce and anxious love of the poor, which is a different thing from the love of the rich, as different as a wolf is from a lapdog. But there are times when love itself becomes a terror, when it sees the danger so plainly that it can think of nothing but to strike; and this was one of those times.

"Come here," she said.

The boy shrank back against the wall. "Mamo!" he wailed. "I didn't mean—I'll take it back—I'll take the whistle back to the man!"

"You will take nothing back," said his mother. "Do you think he will give you the money? Do you think anybody in this country gives anybody back their money? Come here, I say!"

He came, because there was nothing else for him to do; there is no place to hide in a room twelve feet square, which holds a stove and a table and two beds and a trunk, and in which four children and two grown persons sleep. Agnieszka took her son by the arm and bent him over her knee, and lifted the strap.

"Ty lobuzie!" she cried, and brought it down. "You good-for-nothing! You thief! Do you know what you have done? Do you know?" And at each question the strap came down again.

She did not know what she was beating him for—she only knew that she must beat something. All the misery of the past six weeks rose up in her and came down with that strap: the nights she had lain awake listening to her husband's breathing, and knowing by the sound of it that he was not asleep either; the mornings she had divided the bread into six pieces and then into seven, so that there would be a little for the noon; the face of the rent agent, and the voice of Kowalski when she had asked him for credit the last time, and the way the women at the pump had looked at her when she said that her man would surely be taken on next week. She was beating the mill that had shut down, and the Harvester works that would not open their gates, and the agent and the grocer and the man with the cast in his eye, and the man who had painted the little boy in the velvet suit. She was beating the whole vast and pitiless city, which had lured them across the ocean with its promises and was now squeezing them slowly to death; and since she could not reach any of these things, she beat the only thing within her reach, which was the body of her own child.

"Do you know," she cried, "that your father has had nothing to eat since morning? Do you know there is no more money—none—not a penny? What are we to eat tomorrow? Your whistle? Will you blow your whistle for the agent when he comes to put us in the street? Will you give your candy to the twins when they cry for bread?"

The boy did not answer; he could not have answered if he had tried, for he was screaming so that the people in the next room began to pound upon the wall. He did not understand the words; he understood only that the world, which had seemed to him a fairly safe and comfortable place, in spite of cold and hunger, had turned all at once into a place of horror, where his own mother had become a stranger with a white face and blazing eyes. Many years afterward, when he was a grown man working in the mill himself, Wladek would remember that moment; he would remember the smell of the stove, and the sound of the twins wailing in the corner, and the red-and-blue whistle lying on the floor where it had fallen, with the little tin bird broken off its end. It was the first lesson he had ever had in political economy, and it was a lesson he never forgot—though it was many years more before he learned to read it rightly.

It did not last long—perhaps a minute, perhaps two. Then quite suddenly the strap fell from Agnieszka's hand, and she pushed the boy off her knee, and put both hands over her face, and began to sob. They were not the sobs of a woman who weeps easily; they came up from somewhere deep inside her, harsh and dreadful, shaking her whole body, so that the boy, who had crawled away under the table, stopped his own crying to stare at her in terror. He had never seen his mother cry before, not even when the baby died the winter before last; and it seemed to him somehow far worse than the strap.

"O Matko Boska," she moaned, rocking herself to and fro. "Mother of God, what will become of us? What will become of us?"

There is a picture which the comfortable classes have of the poor, and which they put into their novels and their Sunday sermons: the picture of the honest workingman's home, humble but clean, where the mother sits by the hearth with her knitting and the children say their prayers at her knee, and the father comes home in the evening to his pipe and his slippers. The comfortable classes like this picture very much; they hang it up in their minds, as it were, and look at it whenever they feel uneasy about the wages they are paying. And if they were to come upon such a scene as this in the Mrozek tenement—the woman with her apron over her head, the child cowering under the table, the strap upon the floor—they would turn away with a shudder and say that these foreigners were a brutal and degraded lot, who did not know how to raise their children; and they would go home and write a check to the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children, and feel that they had done their duty. It would not occur to them that the strap had been put into Agnieszka Mrozek's hand by the same men who had shut down the mill to keep up the price of steel rails; and that the blows which fell upon little Wladek had been struck, in the last analysis, by persons who would never in their lives set foot in that alley, and who were at that very hour sitting down to dinners of seven courses in houses upon the Lake Shore Drive.

After a while the sobbing grew quieter; and then Agnieszka lifted her head and looked about her, at the frightened children, and at the bread and the lard upon the table, and at the broken whistle upon the floor. She got up heavily and went over to the table, and got down upon her knees—which was not an easy thing for her to do—and looked under it, where Wladek lay curled up against the wall with his face hidden in his arms.

"Wladziu," she said. "Come out, little one."

He did not move; and so she reached in and took hold of him, gently this time, and drew him out, and gathered him up into her lap, there upon the floor. He was stiff at first, and would not look at her; but she held him close and rocked him, and smoothed his hair, which was yellow like her own had been once, and murmured to him in Polish, the old words that she had learned from her own mother in Brzeziny—words about little birds in the forest, and the Christ child in the manger, and the good God who watches over children while they sleep. And little by little the boy's body loosened, and he turned his face against her breast and began to cry again—but quietly now, as a child cries when the worst is over.

"I'll never do it again, Mamo," he whispered. "Never, never. I'll go and work. I'll sell papers like Stefek Nowak. I'll get the money back."

"Hush," said his mother. "Hush, now. You are too little to work."

But even as she said it she was thinking—for she could not help thinking—that Stefek Nowak was only eight, and brought home thirty cents on a good day; and that there was a glass works over on the river that took boys of ten, if their parents would swear that they were fourteen; and that in three years Wladek would be ten. She put the thought away from her with a shudder; but it came back, as such thoughts always do, and she knew that it would come back again and again, until one day it would not have to come back any more, because it would have become a fact. That is the way such things happen in the district behind the rolling mills. Nobody decides them; nobody wishes them; they simply come, as the smoke comes down from the stacks and settles upon everything, and nobody can say just when it was that the window turned black.

So they sat there upon the floor in the gathering dusk, the mother and the child, while the twins crept up and clung to her skirts and little Hela brought the broken whistle and laid it in her brother's hand. Outside the switch engine went puffing by again, and the circus bills fluttered upon the fence, and the long black wall of the mill stood silent and dark, as it had stood for six weeks now; and upon the avenue, a few blocks away, the window of the little shop between the saloon and the undertaker's was all lit up with gas, so that the candies glowed like jewels, and the little boy in the velvet suit smiled down upon the passing children and told them, in letters a foot high, that every boy liked Buster's.

It was nearly nine o'clock when the father came up the stairs. He came slowly, as he always did now, and he stood for a moment in the doorway, looking at the bread and the lard upon the table, and at his wife's red eyes, and at the strap upon the floor. He asked no questions; he was a man of few words at any time, and these six weeks had taken most of the words out of him. He hung up his cap, and sat down at the table, and cut the loaf into seven pieces, very carefully, with his big knife; and when he came to Wladek's piece he hesitated a moment, and then cut it a little bigger than the rest, and handed it to the boy without a word.

Lyman J. Tuttle came home at six-fourteen, which was one minute earlier than usual, and he came home whistling. He whistled "Smile, Smile, Smile," and then, because the first had gone so well, he whistled it again, with a trill at the end which he believed to be the trill of a professional. He was president of the Tuttle Household Appliance Company, sole agent in Sioux Bend for the Glo-Rite Electric Washer, the Purity Vacuum Sweeper, and the Kold-Kist Ice Box with the Patented Seepless Drain, and he was forty-six years old, and that afternoon he had been elected chairman of the Greater Sioux Bend Week Committee of the Forward Club.

He put his car, a 1922 Comet Six sedan with nickel-plated bumpers and a motometer on the radiator cap, into the garage, which was of the same tapestry brick as the house and which had cost him eleven hundred and forty dollars, not counting the cement drive. He stood for a moment in the drive and looked at his house. It was a good house. Everyone said so. It was a Dutch Colonial with green shutters that could not be shut, a sun-parlor with wicker furniture which no one sat in, and a front door with a brass knocker in the shape of a lion's head which no one knocked, since there was also an electric bell. On the lawn there was a concrete birdbath, and in the birdbath there was a sparrow, and Lyman regarded the sparrow with approval, as a fellow citizen who knew a good residential district when he saw one.

"Some little old shack," he said aloud, and went in.

His wife Hazel was in the living-room. She was not, as a wife should be at six-fourteen, in the kitchen supervising the hired girl, nor upstairs changing into her blue foulard, nor on the telephone talking to Mrs. Doc Haverstraw about the Thursday Bridge Club. She was sitting in the overstuffed davenport, beneath the hand-colored photograph of the Grand Canyon, with her hands folded in her lap, and she was looking at nothing. Lyman did not observe this. He was a man who observed sales charts, weather which might affect the sale of electric fans, and the faces of competitors at Forward Club luncheons; but he had been married for twenty-two years, and he had not looked at his wife with real attention since approximately the Taft administration.

"Well, well, well!" he boomed. "Guess who's the new big noise around this burg! Go on, guess!"

"I'm sure I couldn't, Lyman."

"Old Lyme Tuttle, that's who! Chairman of Greater Sioux Bend Week! Unanimous! Well, practically unanimous. Ed Sorensen voted for Charley Pruitt, but that's just because Charley sold him his furnace. Old Ed, he's a good scout, but he hasn't got any more vision than a—than a bedbug. And say, listen here. Here's the big news. Senator Bloodgood is coming down for the Wednesday banquet, and the committee figured, well, the chairman ought to put him up, and so I said, why, sure, the Senator'll stay with us, and Hazel'll give a little dinner Tuesday night, nothing fancy, just the Haverstraws and the Pruitts and maybe the Reverend and Mrs. Gilchrist, and—what's the matter? Don't you feel good?"

For Hazel had not risen. She had not cried, "Why, Lyman, isn't that splendid!" which was the speech that had been composed for her, in his mind, all the way home from the Hotel Majestic.

"Sit down a minute, Lyman," she said. "I've got something to tell you."

He sat down, warily, on the edge of the Morris chair. He had a quick vision of disasters: the boy, Delbert, had been fired out of the State University for drinking; the girl, Marjorie, had eloped with that pimply young cub from the bond house; the furnace had blown up; Hazel had been to see Doc Haverstraw about that pain in her side and Doc had found—

"It's nothing bad," said Hazel. "At least I don't think it's bad. I've rented the store on Fremont Street. The little one between the shoe repair and the Greek's. I signed the lease this afternoon. I'm going to open a book shop."

Lyman Tuttle looked at her. He looked at the Grand Canyon above her head, as though the Grand Canyon might explain. He looked at the radio cabinet, a Melodia Super-Five, which had brought in Pittsburgh on a clear night, and at the phonograph, and at the bronze lady holding up a lamp with a silk shade, and at the set of Kipling in maroon limp-leather which had been given to him by the Glo-Rite Company as a prize for exceeding his quota in 1921. None of them explained anything.

"You've what?"

"I've rented a store. For a book shop. And a circulating library, two cents a day. I'm going to call it the Hearthside Book Nook. Or maybe not. I haven't decided on the name."

"Now, look here, Hazel. Now, just a minute. You mean to sit there and tell me you went downtown and signed a lease, a legal lease, without so much as asking—without even consulting—"

"I knew what you'd say."

"Well, by golly, I should think you would know what I'd say! What any man would say! I never heard of such a thing! Where's the money coming from? You think I'm made of money? You think a man in the appliance game with the Kold-Kist people raising the dealer's price on him six per cent can just go and throw away—"

"It's Aunt Lottie's money," said Hazel.

That checked him. He had forgotten Aunt Lottie's money. Aunt Lottie, of Red Wing, had died the previous winter and left Hazel three thousand two hundred dollars in Liberty Bonds and a set of hand-painted china depicting the cathedrals of Europe. The china was in the dining-room. The bonds were in the safety deposit box at the Farmers' and Merchants' National, and Lyman had always thought of them, vaguely and comfortably, as his own, as part of the general Tuttle prosperity, like the garage and the motometer and the brass knocker; for it is a principle of American domestic economy that what is the wife's is the husband's, and what is the husband's is his own business.

"Well, Aunt Lottie's money, then. All the more reason. That's—that's capital, that's what that is. You don't go throwing capital into some fool proposition like a—a book shop. My gosh, Hazel, who reads books in Sioux Bend? I ask you. Name me one person."

"I do."

"Oh, well, you."

He said it kindly. He said it with the tolerance of a man who indulges his wife in her small eccentricities, as other men indulge their wives in canaries or the Christian Science. It was true that Hazel read books. She took out three a week from the Carnegie Library, and sometimes she bought one, and once, at dinner with the Pruitts, she had mentioned a novel which had been banned in Boston, and there had been a silence, and Lyman had had to tell the story about the Swede and the mule to make things go again.

"Yes, me," said Hazel, and her voice was not loud, but it was not the voice he knew. "And Mrs. Gilchrist, she reads. And the girls at the high school, the teachers. And there's the young people. And there's lots of women, Lyman, women in this town that sit home all afternoon with the housework done by ten o'clock and nothing on earth to do but play bridge and talk about each other, and they'd read if there was anything to read besides what's in the drugstore rack, and they'd come in and talk about it—"

"Talk!" said Lyman. "That's what I'm afraid of! Talk! Have you thought for one minute what people are going to say? About me? Lyme Tuttle's wife keeping store! Why, they'll say I can't support my own family! They'll say the business is on the rocks! Charley Pruitt'll have it all over the Forward Club by Thursday noon—'Heard about poor old Lyme? Wife had to go to work.' My gosh! The week I get elected chairman! The very week! And Senator Bloodgood coming!"

He stood up. He walked to the window and looked out at the birdbath. The sparrow had gone. He walked back. He took a cigar from his vest pocket, a Corona del Plaza at fifteen cents straight, and bit off the end, and did not light it.

"Lyman," said Hazel, "I'm not going to work. Not the way you mean. I'm going to have a book shop."

"It's the same thing."

"It isn't the same thing. Mrs. Fenstermacher runs the hat shop, and her husband's the cashier at the bank, and nobody says he can't support her."

"Mrs. Fenstermacher," said Lyman with dignity, "is a widow in everything but name, and everybody knows it, and you know it, and anyway that's millinery. That's different. That's a woman's line. Hats. Women understand hats. But books—why, a book store, that's—" He searched for the word; he was not a man accustomed to examining the foundations of his own opinions, any more than he would have examined the foundations of the Farmers' and Merchants' National Bank before depositing his money there. "That's highbrow," he said at last. "People'll think you're getting stuck-up. They'll think you think you're better than they are."

There was a pause, and in the pause the kitchen door swung, and Tillie, the hired girl, put her head in and said, "Supper's on, Mrs. Tuttle," and withdrew, having received the impression that there was trouble, which she would communicate that evening to the Pruitts' hired girl, who would communicate it to Mrs. Pruitt, so that Lyman's fears concerning the Forward Club on Thursday noon were, as it happened, entirely justified, though not for the reason he supposed.

They went in to supper. There was pot roast with brown gravy, and mashed potatoes, and creamed carrots, and a bowl of piccalilli, and bread-and-butter, and lemon meringue pie. The table was mahogany veneer, and the chairs were mahogany veneer, and the sideboard held a silver-plated coffee service which they had received as a wedding present from the Lodge and had used twice. Lyman ate heavily and with resentment. He felt that he was being deprived not only of his rightful triumph but of his digestion as well, and he chewed each mouthful as though it were an argument.

"I suppose," he said, after a time, "you've thought about the lease. What kind of lease is it? What's the rent?"

"Thirty-five a month. One year."

"Thirty-five! For that hole? Hazel, you've been stung. Who owns it? Old man Kratzer? He saw you coming. Thirty-five! I could have got it for you for twenty-eight, twenty-eight-fifty at the outside, if you'd let me handle it. That's what comes of a woman trying to do business. You don't know the first thing about it."

"If I'd let you handle it," said Hazel, "you wouldn't have got it for me at all."

He could not answer that, because it was true, and he did not like her for saying it.

"And what about the house?" he said. "Who's going to run the house? Who's going to see to Tillie? Who's going to be here when I come home? And the Bridge Club, and the Eastern Star, and the Ladies' Aid—you just going to drop all that? And this dinner. Tuesday. For the Senator. You're going to give that dinner, aren't you? You're not going to be down in some store selling—selling poetry—when the Senator comes?"

"I'll give your dinner, Lyman."

"Well. Well, that's something, anyway."

But it did not feel like something. It felt, obscurely, like a concession granted to him, and Lyman Tuttle was not used to having concessions granted to him by his wife. He was used to granting them. He granted her the household allowance on the first of each month, with a little speech about economy. He granted her a new spring coat every second year. He granted her permission to have the Bridge Club in the house, and permission to put up the new curtains in the sun-parlor, and permission to go to Minneapolis to see the Follies with her sister, provided she was back by Thursday. He had always considered himself a generous husband, broad-minded, a regular modern husband, not one of those old-fashioned tyrants you read about, and he felt, eating his lemon meringue pie, that his generosity was being thrown back in his face.

"I don't get it," he said, and there was genuine bewilderment in it now, and a little pain. "I just don't get it, Hazel. What do you want? Haven't you got everything? Haven't I always given you everything? Look at this house. Look at that car. Look at the furniture. You got the best electric washer in the state of Minnesota, I don't care where you go. There isn't a woman in Sioux Bend has got any more than you have. What do you want to go and do a thing like this for?"

Hazel put down her fork. She looked at him across the mahogany veneer, and for a moment he saw her, really saw her, the way he had not seen her in years: a woman of forty-four with gray coming in above her ears, and a mouth that had gotten thinner, and eyes that were the same eyes he remembered from a Methodist strawberry social in 1899, gray-blue and serious and, he now realized with alarm, not entirely friendly.

"Lyman," she said, "do you know what I did today? Before I went down to see Mr. Kratzer?"

Then I dusted the living-room, though Tillie had dusted it yesterday. Then I sat down and looked at the Grand Canyon. Then I telephoned Lou Haverstraw, and she told me about Mrs. Pruitt's new permanent wave, and I told her about the sale at Bjornstad's. Then it was eleven o'clock. Then I went upstairs and lay down. Then it was lunch. And I thought—I thought, I'm forty-four years old. And Delbert's gone, and Marjorie'll be gone in a year, and I'm going to do this, this very same thing, every day, until I die. And then they'll say at the Ladies' Aid, 'She was a fine woman, Hazel Tuttle, she kept a lovely home.' And that'll be all. That'll be the whole of it."

"Nothing's wrong with it," said Hazel. "Nothing at all. Only it isn't enough."

And there it was, the thing that could not be answered, the thing that had no column in the ledger and no line in the Glo-Rite sales manual. Lyman Tuttle knew how to answer an objection about price, or about the reliability of the wringer mechanism, or about whether a family of four really needed the Kold-Kist Model Twelve or could make do with the Model Eight. He had been to the Glo-Rite Dealers' Convention in Chicago, three times, and had heard Dr. J. Harold Speers, the Business Psychologist, lecture on Overcoming Customer Resistance, and he had taken notes in a small leather book which he still carried. But he did not know how to answer "It isn't enough." Nobody had ever told him that a thing could fail to be enough when it was, by every reasonable standard, the best on the market.

He tried, nevertheless.

"Now, look here, Hazel. Let's be sensible about this. Let's look at this thing like two grown-up people. I'll tell you what I'll do. You want something to do, fine. That's fine. I'm for it. Hundred per cent. Now, there's the Women's Auxiliary of the Forward Club. They're putting on a pageant for Greater Sioux Bend Week, 'The Spirit of Progress,' and they need somebody to head up the costumes, and I could speak to Mrs. Pruitt—"

"No, Lyman."

"Or the Red Cross. Or the Library Board! There you are! You like books! I could get you on the Library Board, easy, I know Judge Lindquist, and you could pick out the books, and it'd be a real honor, and nobody'd say a word—"

"No."

"Well, then, I don't know what you want!" He brought his fist down on the table, not hard, but hard enough to rattle the piccalilli. "I'm trying to meet you halfway! I'm doing my darnedest! I come home with the biggest news a man in this town could have, chairman of the whole works, Senator Bloodgood coming to stay in this house, in our house, Hazel, and I can't even tell it. I can't even get it out. And you sit there and spring this on me. On this night, of all nights. I'd think you'd at least have the—the consideration—"

He stopped, because he saw that she was smiling, a small, tired, curious smile, and he could not tell whether she was laughing at him.

"Congratulations on the chairmanship, Lyman," she said. "I mean it. I know how much you wanted it."

"Well," he said, somewhat mollified. "Well, it's a big thing. It's a big thing for the business, too. Gets your name around."

"And I'll give your dinner Tuesday. I'll get a ham, and Tillie can do the scalloped potatoes, and we'll have the Haverstraws and the Pruitts and the Gilchrists. And I'll wear my blue foulard. And when the Senator asks me what I do, I'll tell him I run the Hearthside Book Nook on Fremont Street."

"You wouldn't."

"I would, Lyman. I'd be proud to."

He looked at her a long time. Then he took out the Corona del Plaza again and lighted it, with hands that were not quite steady, and puffed, and looked at the coffee service from the Lodge.

"Yes," said Hazel. "I suppose I have."

"Only don't come crying to me when it goes bust. That's all I ask. Don't come crying to me in six months when you've lost every cent and old Kratzer's after you for the rent. Because I warned you. I want that understood. I warned you."

"It's understood, Lyman."

He read it twice. It was a good advertisement; he had written it himself. Then he sat with the paper in his lap and thought about what he would say to Charley Pruitt.

He would say—he worked it out carefully, the way he worked out a sales talk—he would say, "Well, sir, the Missus has gone and got herself a little hobby. Bound to do it. You know how women are. Wants to run a little book shop. I said, sure, go ahead, Hazel, have your fun, I can afford it." And he would laugh, and Charley would laugh, and it would be all right. It would be, in fact, rather a good thing: a broad-minded man, Lyman Tuttle, a modern man, lets his wife have her little hobby. He could afford it. That was the point. That was the whole point.

By ten o'clock he had very nearly convinced himself that the book shop had been his own idea.

At ten-thirty he wound the clock on the mantel, and locked the front door, and looked in on the furnace, and went upstairs. Hazel was already in bed, in the twin bed nearer the window, with the light off. He undressed in the bathroom, and brushed his teeth with Dento-Glo, and came out in his pajamas, which were striped in lavender, and got into his own bed.

"Hazel?"

"Yes, Lyman."

"I was thinking. About that name. 'Hearthside Book Nook.' That's not bad. That's got a homey ring. But you want something with more pep to it. Something that'll catch the eye. How about 'Tuttle's Better Books'? Then folks'd know right off it was connected with—well, with the family. Kind of a tie-in. Good for both businesses."

There was a long silence from the other bed.

"I'll think about it, Lyman."

"You do that. Night, Hazel."

"Good night."

He was asleep in four minutes, and dreamed that he was introducing Senator Bloodgood to an audience of eleven hundred, and that the Senator, at the end of his speech, turned to him and said, before them all, "And to the man who made this possible, our distinguished chairman—" and that the applause went on and on, like the sound of a Glo-Rite washer on the rinse cycle.
