The train from Chicago was nineteen minutes late, and Walter Ebbing, who sold the Thermo-King Automatic Furnace ("Heat That Thinks for Itself") to the more progressive householders of Vandalia Springs, spent the nineteen minutes walking up and down the platform of the Union Station with the air of a man who personally owned the railroad and was disappointed in it.

He was forty-four. He was a large, pink, scrubbed man, with the scrubbed look of a boy who has been made to wash behind the ears for a party, and he wore a gray suit from Feldheimer & Sons ("Clothes for the Man Who Gets There"), a pearl stickpin in the shape of a horseshoe, and the button of the Benevolent and Protective Order of Moose. Every few minutes he took out his watch, a seventeen-jewel Hamilton presented to him by the Thermo-King Corporation for Outstanding Sales Achievement in the Upper Mississippi District, looked at it with irritation, and then, because it was a very fine watch, looked at it again with pleasure.

He was waiting for his cousin Lester Pruitt, whom he had not seen in twenty-two years.

They had been boys together on adjoining farms outside Kettle Creek, where their mothers were sisters and their fathers were not on speaking terms, owing to a dispute about a line fence which neither could remember the origin of and both could defend with Scripture. They had fished together, stolen melons together, been licked together in the woodshed of Grandfather Haskell, and had together made a solemn vow, at the age of fourteen, beside a dead muskrat, that they would never, never settle down in any town smaller than Minneapolis. Then Lester had gone East to study art, which was considered in Kettle Creek to be a kind of illness, like consumption, only less respectable. And Walter had gone to Vandalia Springs to clerk in a hardware store, which was considered to be the beginning of a career.

The careers had gone their ways. Walter had married Myrtle Bloomquist, the daughter of the man who owned the hardware store; had two children, a bungalow on Fernwood Terrace, a Buick sedan, and a seat on the Program Committee of the Rotary Club. Lester had, so far as Walter could tell from his infrequent letters, gone to New York and then to Paris, and then to New York again, and had been in something called a Salon, and had illustrated books, and had once been mentioned in the Saturday Evening Post, though only in an advertisement.

The train came in. It came in with the snorting self-importance of all trains entering all Midwestern cities, as though it were bringing news of great events from the capitals of the world, though it was actually bringing a drummer in notions, two Lutheran ministers returning from a synod, a lady with a canary, and Lester Pruitt.

Walter would not have known him. He had expected, he did not know why, a slender youth in a flowing tie, with a beret, perhaps, and a sensitive mouth. He saw a thin, stooped, graying man of forty-five in a brown suit that had been good once and was now merely tolerable, with a cane, a cigarette, and a face that seemed to have been folded up and put away in a drawer and taken out again without being pressed.

"Les!" roared Walter. "Lester, you old son of a gun! Well, I'll be a hammered tinker! Well, well, well!"

He pounded his cousin on the back. Lester, who had not been pounded on the back since 1904, coughed and smiled and said, "Hello, Walt. You've gotten—you've gotten prosperous."

"Well, I don't know about that, I don't know about that," said Walter, who did know about it, and who had hoped that it would be noticed. "Can't complain. Mustn't complain. Here, give me that grip. No, no, I insist. Car's right outside. Wait'll you see the old burg, Les. You won't know it. Why, when you left here—well, you never were here, you were back home in Kettle Creek, but when you left, why, Vandalia Springs wasn't anything but a jerkwater whistle-stop with a couple of grain elevators and a saloon. Population eighteen thousand. Know what it is now?"

"I'm afraid I don't."

"Ninety-four thousand, six hundred and twelve. That's by the 1920 census. We figure we'll crowd a hundred and twenty-five by 'thirty. Fastest-growing city of its size between Chicago and the Rockies, bar none. That's a fact. I've seen the figures."

---

The Buick was a dark-blue sedan with nickel trimmings, and it had, Walter explained as he drove, a self-starter, a gasoline gauge on the dash, balloon tires, a cigar lighter, and a rear window with a little curtain that could be pulled down, though he did not know why anyone would want to pull it down. He drove his cousin up Commercial Avenue, past the Second National Bank (eleven stories, the tallest building in the state outside the Twin Cities), past the Orpheum Theatre, past the new Elks Temple with its granite elk, past Hamberger's Department Store, the Mid-Continent Life Insurance Building, the Bon Ton Lunch, the Vandalia Springs Daily Clarion, and a vacant lot on which a sign announced that THIS SITE WILL SOON BE THE HOME OF THE VANDALIA SPRINGS ATHLETIC CLUB—WATCH US GROW!

"Watch us grow," Walter repeated with satisfaction. "That's our slogan. I was on the committee that picked it. We had it narrowed down to that and 'The Springs Spring Ahead,' but some of the boys thought that one was kind of highbrow. Too much like a pun."

"I think you chose wisely," said Lester.

Walter glanced at him sharply, for there had been something in the voice—some dryness, some little curl at the end of it—that he did not quite like. But Lester was gazing out at the Elks Temple with an expression of gentle and apparently sincere interest, and Walter concluded that he had imagined it. Lester had always been a quiet kid. Artistic. Probably he had been brooding about something artistic.

"Now that," said Walter, slowing the car, "is the new Carnegie Library. Cost a hundred and sixty thousand dollars. Got eleven thousand books in it. And over there's the Methodist church. I'm a Presbyterian myself, but you've got to hand it to the Methodists, they put up a dandy building. Organ come all the way from Philadelphia. Say, do you still—I mean, are you a churchgoing man, Les?"

"Not especially."

"Well, I don't know as I'd hold that against a fellow. Lot of fine men aren't. Still, it's good for business. A man's got to belong."

---

The bungalow on Fernwood Terrace was exactly like the bungalows on either side of it, except that it was painted cream instead of gray-green, and had a pergola, which was considered in Fernwood Terrace to be very artistic and slightly daring. It had a living room with a fumed-oak davenport, a Victrola, a reading lamp with a shade of beaded silk, a set of the Book of Knowledge in a glass-fronted case, a framed reproduction of a painting of a stag at sunset, and a radio set, with a loudspeaker shaped like a morning-glory, on which Walter had once received, at two in the morning, a station in Havana.

"Havana, Cuba," he told his cousin. "Clear as a bell. Some fellow talking Spanish. Couldn't understand a word, of course, but think of it! Havana! Right here in my own living room!"

Myrtle Ebbing came in from the kitchen, wiping her hands on her apron and then hastily taking off the apron, as though she had been caught in some indecency. She was a plump, anxious, kind woman who had been pretty at twenty and was still pretty in the dim light of the reading lamp. She shook hands with Lester and said she had heard so much about him and she certainly hoped he liked pot roast, because that was what they were having, and she certainly hoped it wasn't too plain for him after all those fancy foreign places.

"I've eaten a great many meals in Paris," said Lester, "that I'd trade gladly for a good pot roast."

Myrtle flushed with pleasure, and Walter, who had been watching his cousin with the suspicion of a man who has been sold a bad lot of carburetors, relaxed again.

The children were produced. There was Harold, who was sixteen and had a pompadour and a ukulele and a passionate conviction that his parents were the most old-fashioned people in the United States. And there was Dorothy, who was twelve and stared at Lester with frank fascination, because she had been told he was an Artist, and she had expected him to have a mustache that curled up at the ends.

"Do you paint ladies without any clothes on?" she asked.

"Dorothy!" cried her mother.

"Sometimes," said Lester gravely. "But mostly I paint fruit. Fruit is less trouble. It doesn't want to be paid, and it doesn't talk."

Dorothy considered this, decided it was a joke, and laughed. Harold looked at his uncle (for so he had been instructed to call him, though the relation was more remote) with sudden respect. A man who painted ladies without any clothes on, and could say so in front of Mother, was a man of some consequence.

---

At dinner Walter talked. He talked about the Thermo-King Automatic Furnace, which had a thermostat that regulated itself, so that a man did not have to go down cellar in his nightshirt at three o'clock on a January morning and shake down the clinkers, which was, he observed, a real step forward in civilization, a bigger step forward, if you wanted his opinion, than any number of these Bolshevik notions they were always talking about in Europe. He talked about the Rotary Club and the fine bunch of fellows in it, live wires, men who did things. He talked about the Volstead Act, which he supported on principle and violated in practice, and about the price of lots in the new Glenwood Heights addition, and about the Republican party, and about a fellow named Swanson who had cheated him on a deal in 1919 and whom he had nevertheless forgiven, since you couldn't hold a grudge in business.

Lester listened. He listened with his head a little on one side, the way he had listened as a boy to the whippoorwills at dusk, and he ate Myrtle's pot roast with every appearance of enjoyment, and now and then he said "Really?" or "I see," or "That's remarkable," and Walter, warmed by the pot roast and by the sound of his own voice, decided that his cousin was a pretty good scout after all, even if he was a little quiet, and that maybe all those years among foreigners had not ruined him entirely.

It was only toward the end of the meal, over Myrtle's lemon meringue pie, that Walter thought to ask, "Well, Les, and what about you? How's the painting game? Making a good thing out of it?"

There was a pause, and in the pause the clock on the mantel, a Seth Thomas with Westminster chimes, struck the half hour.

"It goes along," said Lester.

"Sell many pictures?"

"Some."

"What do they bring? Ballpark figure. A good picture, I mean. Say a big one. Oil."

"It depends," said Lester. "Sometimes several hundred dollars. Sometimes nothing at all."

"Nothing at all! Well, I'll be darned. How do you figure overhead in a line like that?"

Lester smiled. It was a curious smile, and Walter could not read it, and the not reading it made him obscurely uneasy, as he was uneasy in the presence of the Episcopal rector, and the president of the Second National, and the one Negro physician in Vandalia Springs, who had attended Harvard.

"I don't figure it," said Lester. "That's probably my trouble."

---

After dinner, while Myrtle washed up and refused all help with the cheerful martyrdom of the American housewife, and Harold went off to a dance at the Masonic Hall in a raccoon coat that his father had bought him against his better judgment, and Dorothy was sent protesting to bed, the two cousins sat on the front porch in the dark.

It was a fine night in early October. The elms along Fernwood Terrace were turning, and the smell of burning leaves came up from the gutters, where the householders had raked them in neat, smoldering piles, and somewhere down the block a radio was playing "Valencia," and somewhere farther off a dog was barking with the steady, unhurried conviction of a dog that has nothing else to do. Walter lit a cigar, a Flor de Melba, and offered one to his cousin, who declined and lit one of his own cigarettes instead, from a flat silver case that had a crest on it and that Walter suspected, with a small thrill, had once belonged to a duke.

For a while neither of them said anything. Then Walter, with the air of a man taking a plunge into cold water, said, "Les, I want to ask you something. Man to man."

"Go ahead."

"You remember that time out by Pickerel Slough? With the dead muskrat? When we swore we'd never settle down in a hick town?"

Lester laughed softly in the dark. "I'd forgotten that. Yes. Yes, I remember."

"Well." Walter cleared his throat. "Well, I just wanted to say. I guess you figure I broke that. Settling down here, and all. I guess you figure Vandalia Springs is just a—just a hick town. Like Kettle Creek, only bigger."

"Walt, I didn't—"

"No, now, hold on. Let me say my say. I know how you fellows talk back East. I read the magazines. I know what they say about towns like this. Boosters. Babbling about population and lots and so on. And I'll tell you something, Les, sometimes I lie awake nights and I think, maybe they're right. Maybe I am just a—" He waved the cigar helplessly. "A furnace salesman. Selling furnaces to fellows who'd be just as warm with the old kind. Going to Rotary and singing songs and slapping backs. And I think, there's old Les, over in Paris, France, painting pictures and drinking wine with counts and baronesses and I don't know what all, living the way a man ought to live, free, and here's me, forty-four years old and I've never even been to New York City. Not once. I had a chance in 'twenty-two, the convention was there, but Dorothy had the measles."

He stopped, appalled at himself. He had not meant to say any of this. He had not, so far as he knew, ever thought any of it, not in so many words. It had simply come out of him, the way a cough comes out of a man who did not know he had a cold.

Lester was quiet for so long that Walter began to be afraid he had offended him. Then his cousin said, very low, "Walt, do you know where I live in New York?"

"Why, no. Some studio, I suppose. Greenwich Village, isn't it?"

"I live in one room on West Fourteenth Street. Over a delicatessen. It smells of pickled herring from six in the morning until midnight. The radiator works two days in five. I share a bathroom with a Polish tailor and a man who plays the trombone in a dance hall and comes home at four. I haven't sold a picture in fourteen months. I make my living, such as it is, drawing ladies' corsets for the Sunday supplement of a newspaper. Very lifelike corsets. I'm considered rather good at them."

"Corsets," said Walter faintly.

"And the counts and baronesses—well, there was one baroness. She was from Cleveland. She'd married a Hungarian who turned out to be a waiter. She borrowed three hundred francs from me and I never saw her again." Lester drew on his cigarette, and in the brief glow of it Walter saw his face, and it was a face that Walter would remember a long time, though he could never afterward have said why. "I came out here, Walt, because the man I work for told me to take two weeks off without pay, because business was slow. And I had nowhere else to go. And I thought—I thought I'd like to see somebody who knew me before."

The radio down the block had stopped playing "Valencia" and begun, after a burst of static, to broadcast a lecture on the cultivation of soybeans.

"And I'll tell you something else," said Lester. "I've been sitting at your table tonight and looking at your wife and your kids and your car and your—your radio set, and listening to you talk about your furnaces, and I've been thinking that you're the one who got it right. You've got a place. You belong somewhere. People know your name when you walk down the street."

"Well, sure they know my name. I'm on the Program Committee."

"I've never been on a Program Committee in my life."

Walter considered this. It seemed to him a fact of enormous and terrible significance, like learning that a man had never been baptized.

"Les," he said at last, "I tell you what. You stay here. Stay a while. As long as you want. Myrtle won't mind, she likes you, I can tell. And look here, I've been thinking. We need a fellow to do the art work on the Thermo-King ads in the Clarion. Right now we just use the cuts the company sends out, and they're no good, they show a furnace in a cellar in Massachusetts or someplace, with a fellow in a smoking jacket, and nobody out here wears a smoking jacket. What we need is a local touch. A fellow who knows the people. And you could do portraits, too. Why, old Judge Kittredge has been wanting his portrait done for the courthouse for years. And there's the Rotary—we could get you in the Rotary, easy. They've got a classification open for Fine Arts. Nobody's ever filled it."

He turned to his cousin eagerly, his pink face shining in the light from the parlor window, and for a moment Lester Pruitt looked at him with an expression of the most profound and tender horror.

Then he laughed. He laughed until he coughed, and Walter, after a moment's bewilderment, laughed too, without knowing why, slapping his knee, and the two of them sat there on the porch of the cream-colored bungalow on Fernwood Terrace, two middle-aged men laughing in the dark like boys beside Pickerel Slough, while the smoke of the burning leaves drifted past them and the soybean lecture droned on.

"I'll think about it, Walt," said Lester, wiping his eyes. "I'll honestly think about it."

"You do that. You do that. No hurry. Sleep on it."

---

Later, in the twin bed beside Myrtle's (they had gone over to twin beds in 1923, on the advice of an article in the Ladies' Home Journal, and Walter had never been sure whether he liked it), Walter lay awake and stared at the ceiling, on which the streetlight threw the shadow of an elm branch.

"Myrtle," he said. "You awake?"

"Mm."

"Les is all right. Isn't he? Kind of a sad bird, but all right."

"He's very nice, Walter. Very refined."

"I offered him a job. Doing the ads."

"That was sweet of you."

"He won't take it, I guess." Walter was silent a moment. "Myrtle, you ever think we ought to go to New York? Just for a trip. See the shows. Go up the Woolworth Building."

"Why, Walter Ebbing. Whatever for?"

He did not know whatever for. He lay there and tried to think of a reason, and he could not think of one, except that he had seen his cousin's face for a moment in the glow of a cigarette, and that face had been lonelier than any face he had ever seen, and yet he had envied it. He had envied it terribly. He could not have said what he envied.

"Oh, nothing," he said. "Just a notion."

And presently, because he had a breakfast meeting of the Furnace Dealers' Association at seven-thirty, and because he was to speak on "Thermostatic Control: The Coming Thing," and because a man had to keep up, had to be on his toes, had to belong, he turned over and went to sleep, and dreamed that he was standing at the top of the Woolworth Building, selling furnaces to a crowd of Hungarian waiters, all of whom wore smoking jackets, and none of whom could understand a word he said.

The house of Mr. Lowell T. Pettibone, on Crestmere Drive in the Ridgewood Park section of the city of Monarch, was in every respect what a house ought to be in the year when Monarch passed the two-hundred-and-fifty-thousand mark and the Chamber of Commerce paid for a banner across Grand Avenue to say so. It was of tapestry brick, with a sun-parlor at one end and a sleeping-porch above, and it had a breakfast nook which Mrs. Pettibone had seen in a magazine and which nobody had ever eaten breakfast in. It had a radio cabinet of genuine walnut veneer, a player-piano with forty-one rolls, a vacuum cleaner that sounded like an aeroplane, and in the living room a fireplace in which no fire had been built since the evening of the Pettibones' housewarming, when the damper had been closed and the guests had been smoked out onto the lawn, laughing heartily and saying it was a great joke on Lowell.

It was a house of standardized comfort, and Mr. Pettibone was its standardized master. He was forty-three, a little thick at the belt, a little thin at the crown, and he sold real estate. He did not call it selling real estate. He called it Building Monarch, and at the weekly luncheon of the Monarch Go-Ahead Club he had once said, to considerable applause, that the realtor was the true pioneer of the twentieth century, blazing trails not with the axe but with the plat-map.

On this particular Thursday in October he came home at six-ten, which was eleven minutes later than usual, because he had stopped at the Velox Motor Company to look at the new Velox Eight Sport Sedan, which he did not intend to buy and which he had been looking at for three weeks. He came up the cement walk whistling "Smile, Darn Ya, Smile" and feeling a good deal like a Captain of Industry, for that afternoon he had disposed of the last two lots in the Willowbrook Addition, down by the river flats, to a man named Gus Brunnemeyer, who ran a bakery on the South Side and who wished to rise in the world.

There had been a small matter, in the selling of those lots, of the river. In April the river had a habit of coming up over the flats and remaining there, sullen and brown, until about the middle of May. Mr. Pettibone had not mentioned this to Gus Brunnemeyer. Mr. Brunnemeyer had not asked. Mr. Pettibone had, indeed, spoken a good deal about the Wonderful Opportunity of the South Extension and the New Boulevard which the city council was Practically Certain to put through, and Mr. Brunnemeyer had signed, and Mr. Pettibone had shaken his hand with real warmth and called him Gus, and had felt that he was a fine, simple, honest sort of fellow, the backbone of the country.

So Lowell Pettibone came home whistling.

He hung his hat on the hall-tree, he flung his topcoat over the newel-post because his wife always told him not to, and he called out, "Hello, everybody! The old man's home! Where's the bunch?"

His wife came out of the kitchen. Mrs. Pettibone, whose name was Myrtle and who had been the prettiest girl in the Junior Class at Monarch Central High School, was now plump and anxious and given to sighing. She wore an apron over her blue foulard, and her face had the expression which Mr. Pettibone had learned, through sixteen years of matrimony, to associate with Trouble About the Children.

"Lowell," she said, "you've got to speak to Buddy."

"Huh? What's he done now?"

"He's taken money. Out of your bureau. Out of the little china pig on your bureau."

Mr. Pettibone stood still. His whistle died on his lips. He said, "Taken money? Buddy has?"

"Fifty cents. Two quarters. Mrs. Kneedler telephoned me—she said she saw him at the Rexall store treating the Kneedler twins and that Hoffmeier boy to ice-cream sodas, and buying jawbreakers and licorice whips and one of those little tin cricket things that go *click*, and she said she thought I'd want to know, and of course, oh, of course she would have to be the one that saw it, you know how she is, she'll have it all over the Wednesday Afternoon Bridge Club by next week, and I went up and looked in the pig and it was all gone except a nickel and three pennies, and I asked him and he just stood there and wouldn't say anything, and Lowell, I just don't know what to *do* with that child, he's only seven, and when I think of—"

"All right, all right, all right! Now don't get all worked up. I'll handle it. Where is he?"

"He's up in his room. I sent him up there. He's been crying."

"Well, he darn well ought to be crying," said Mr. Pettibone, and was surprised to hear that his voice had become loud and heavy, the voice of a Father, the voice he had heard his own father use, back in Turnbull Falls, on the occasion when Lowell had shot out the window of the Lutheran church with an air-rifle.

He went into the living room and sat down in his own chair, the big mohair chair with the smoking-stand beside it, and he lit a cigar, and he considered.

It was, he felt, a serious matter. It was the most serious matter that had come up in the family since Junie, who was now fourteen, had been discovered using lipstick. A thief! His own son! The son for whom he had already taken out an endowment policy that would mature at the age of twenty-one and send the boy to the State University, where he would join a good fraternity and make Contacts! There rose in Mr. Pettibone's mind, unbidden, a picture of Buddy at thirty-five, unshaven, in a striped suit, being led into the county jail by Sheriff Haupt, who belonged to the Go-Ahead Club and would be extremely embarrassed. He shook his head to clear it.

The question was: should he lick him?

Mr. Pettibone's own father had believed in licking. Old Amos Pettibone had kept a razor-strop hanging behind the kitchen door, and he had applied it to Lowell's person, by Lowell's later reckoning, something over two hundred times between the ages of five and fourteen, and Lowell had turned out all right. He frequently said so. "I got licked plenty when I was a kid, and it never hurt me any," he would say at the Go-Ahead luncheons, "and these modern parents that let their kids run hog-wild—well, I'm not saying anything, but you look at the jails." And the other Go-Aheaders would nod and say "You said it, Lowell," and "That's the stuff."

But Mrs. Pettibone took a magazine called *The Modern Parent*, and she had left it, open, on the smoking-stand on several occasions, and Mr. Pettibone had read in it, while waiting for dinner, an article by a Professor of Child Psychology at a large Eastern university, who said that corporal punishment produced Inhibitions and Complexes, and that the wise parent would instead Reason with the child, appealing to his Better Nature and Sense of Fair Play. Mr. Pettibone had snorted at the article. He had said that these college professors had never met a payroll. But he had read it twice, and it had remained with him, for he had a profound respect for anything that was printed and that came from the East.

Moreover, he did not, in fact, much like the idea of licking Buddy. Buddy was small for his age, and freckled, and had a way of looking up at you, with his mouth a little open, as though you were the greatest man in the world, which Mr. Pettibone had come to depend upon more than he knew.

He decided he would have a Talk with him. A real man-to-man talk. He would make it clear to the boy, in terms the boy could understand, the importance of Honesty in the modern world. He had, he reflected with satisfaction, a certain gift for that sort of thing. It was he who had given the talk on "Service Before Self" at the Go-Ahead Club's Ladies' Night, and the president of the Monarch Savings and Trust had come up afterward and said, "Lowell, that was a corker."

He knocked the ash off his cigar, rose, pulled down his vest, and called up the stairs, "Buddy! Come down here. I want to see you in the library."

The library was a small room off the living room which contained a desk at which Mr. Pettibone never wrote anything, a leather couch, a framed photograph of the Monarch Go-Ahead Club at the District Convention in Sioux City, and a glass-fronted bookcase holding a set of Dickens in maroon morocco, a set of the World's Great Orations, an Encyclopedia of Business Correspondence, and four novels about the Canadian Northwest. Mr. Pettibone had read two of the novels about the Canadian Northwest.

Buddy came down the stairs one step at a time, holding onto the banister as though it were the rail of a ship in a storm. He was in his blue sailor suit, which was wrinkled, and there were damp tracks down both his cheeks, and he had a licorice stain on his collar, which was evidence. He came into the library and stood by the door, and he did not look up at his father as though his father were the greatest man in the world. He looked at the rug.

"Shut the door, son," said Mr. Pettibone, in the voice.

Buddy shut the door.

Mr. Pettibone sat down at the desk, swiveled the chair around, folded his hands over his stomach, and looked at his son for a long moment in silence, which was a technique he employed with prospects who were hesitating over a down-payment.

"Well, Buddy," he said at last, "I guess you know what I want to talk to you about."

Buddy said nothing.

"Your mother tells me that you took some money out of Daddy's pig. Is that right?"

Buddy said, to the rug, "Yes, sir."

"How much?"

"Two quarters."

"Fifty cents. Fifty cents!" Mr. Pettibone shook his head slowly. "Now, Buddy, I want you to understand something. I'm not mad at you. Daddy's not mad. But Daddy is—well, Daddy is mighty disappointed. Mighty disappointed. You know what it's called, son, when you take money that doesn't belong to you?"

Buddy's lower lip began to move independently of the rest of his face. "Stealing," he said.

"That's right. That's exactly right. Stealing. And you know what happens to people who steal?"

"They go to jail."

"They go to jail," Mr. Pettibone agreed, gravely. He felt that the interview was going very well. The professor in *The Modern Parent* would have had nothing to complain of. "But that's not the main thing, Buddy. That's not the worst of it. The worst of it is, nobody can *trust* 'em. Now, you take a fellow in business. You take your Daddy. What do you suppose is the most important thing a man in business has got? More important than money? More important than a fine house and a big car and all?"

Buddy considered. He was, his teachers at the Ridgewood Park Grammar School said, a thoughtful child. "A Velox Eight?" he offered.

"No! No, no. I said more important than a car. It's his *word*, Buddy. His word. A man's word is his bond. You ever hear that? A man's word is his bond. That means when a man in business says a thing, folks know it's so. They know they can depend on him. You take your Daddy. When your Daddy tells a fellow something, that fellow knows Lowell Pettibone is telling him the straight goods. That's why folks come to Daddy when they want to buy a lot or a house. That's why we can have this nice house and you can have a nice room and a bicycle next summer, maybe, if you're a good boy. Because folks trust Daddy. You see?"

Buddy looked up from the rug for the first time. There was something in his face which Mr. Pettibone took for dawning comprehension.

"Is that a man's word," said Buddy, "what you said on the telephone?"

"Huh? What telephone?"

"On Sunday. When you were telephoning Mr. Brunny—Mr. Brunnymire. In the hall. You said those lots were high and dry as a church steeple. And then you hung up and you said to Mama, 'If that Dutchman ever sees 'em in April he'll think he bought a duck pond,' and Mama said 'Hush, Lowell, the children,' and you laughed."

Twice during the meal he began to say something about Gus Brunnemeyer and the lots in Willowbrook, which he had been looking forward all afternoon to telling, and twice he stopped.

After dinner he read the evening *Monarch Advocate-Times*: an editorial on the menace of radicalism in the colleges, a column of humorous verse about golf, the market report, and an advertisement for the Willowbrook Addition, Monarch's Coming Residential Paradise, Where Your Dollar Grows While You Sleep, which he had written himself and of which he had been proud. He found that he was reading the advertisement for the third time.

At ten o'clock he went upstairs. He paused outside Buddy's door. He did not mean to go in. He went in.

Buddy was asleep, curled up on his side, with one fist under his chin and the tin cricket clutched in the other. His face, in the light from the hall, looked smaller than it did in the daytime, and younger, and there were still marks on it where the tears had dried. He thought, perhaps, that he might call Gus Brunnemeyer in the morning. He might say—well, he might say that the boulevard was not quite so certain after all. That there was some question about drainage. That if Gus wanted to reconsider—

He bent down and very gently took the tin cricket out of his son's hand and put it on the bureau. Then he picked it up again and put it back on the pillow, near the small fist, where it could be found in the morning.

In the morning it was raining. The coffee was strong, and the toast came up out of the electric toaster at precisely the right moment, and Buddy came down to breakfast and said "Good morning, Daddy," in a small voice, and Mr. Pettibone said "Good morning, old-timer," and rumpled his hair, and everything was all right. Gus Brunnemeyer was a grown man. Everybody did it. That was business.

He did not telephone Gus Brunnemeyer.

They had remembrances, and laughter over old times. Once they quarreled, and he raged that she was as “bossy” as his wife and far more whining when he was inattentive. But that passed safely. He was afraid that they would be seen together. In Zenith it is impossible to lunch with a neighbor’s wife without the fact being known, before nightfall, in every house in your circle. His predominant fear—not from any especial fondness for her but from the habit of propriety—was that his wife would learn of the affair. He was certain that she knew nothing specific about Tanis, but he was also certain that she suspected something indefinite. For years she had been bored by anything more affectionate than a farewell kiss, yet she was hurt by any slackening in his irritable periodic interest, and now he had no interest; rather, a revulsion. He was completely faithful—to Tanis. He was distressed by the sight of his wife’s slack plumpness, by her puffs and billows of flesh, by the tattered petticoat which she was always meaning and always forgetting to throw away. Himself, Babbitt slipped away on Christmas afternoon to take his present, a silver cigarette-box, to Tanis. “Well, just about.”

“Uh-huh.”

Clyde Mumford came home from the Thursday luncheon of the Tecumseh City Boosters' League in that condition of exaltation which, among the commercial classes, takes the place of religious ecstasy and is considerably more convenient, since it requires neither fasting nor any belief in the inconvenient doctrine of sin. He had been called upon, without warning, or with no more warning than the three weeks he had spent preparing, to say a few words on "The Spirit That Makes a Town Hum," and he had said them, every one, while Judge Purdy nodded and Ed Thoroughgood of the Thoroughgood Dairy Lunch System had pounded the table so that the water-glasses chimed. He had spoken of Vision. He had spoken of the Man Who Gets There. He had told the story about the Swede and the Ford, which had always gone well, and it had gone well again.

All the afternoon, in his office above the salesroom of the Mumford Motor Accessory Company (Tires, Batteries, Spotlights, Radiator Ornaments, Everything for the Motorist Who Cares), he had hummed. He had been gracious to Miss Klebs, the stenographer, and had dictated a letter to the Akron people that was, he felt, very nearly literature. He had driven home at a quarter to six in his sedan, which was not the most expensive sedan in Maple Crest but was decidedly not the cheapest, and as he came up the cement drive between the two little cedars that Hazel had planted the year they built, he was whistling "Margie," and he was thinking that a man who had pep and stick-to-it-iveness, and who belonged, and kept himself fit, could look anybody in the eye.

He stamped on the porch, as he had stamped for eleven years, though there was no snow, and he flung open the door and bellowed, "Well, well, well! Where's the little woman? Where's the old girl? Say, Hazel, you ought to've heard 'em to-day! Purdy came up afterward and he says to me, 'Clyde,' he says—"

Hazel Mumford was sitting in the living-room, in the large chair upholstered in a mulberry plush which the salesman at Ruttger's had described as "regal," and she was not doing anything. That in itself was ominous. Hazel was a woman who was always doing something: darning, or reading the Ladies' Home Companion, or telephoning Mrs. Ed Thoroughgood about the Methodist Bazaar, or saying that she had a sick headache and must lie down. To see her merely sitting, with her hands in her lap and the lamp unlit, was as disconcerting as it would have been to find the radiator ornament missing from the sedan.

In her lap was a letter.

"Hello," she said.

"Why, hello! What you doing in the dark? Saving on the electric light bill?" He laughed heartily, to show that this was a joke, and he reached for the chain of the bridge lamp, which had a parchment shade painted with galleons. The galleons sprang into light. So did Hazel's face, and he did not care for it.

It was not that she looked angry. He knew all the varieties of her anger, as a farmer knows the varieties of weather: the brisk clatter of dishes that meant he had forgotten to call up about the ice, the long injured silence that meant he had looked too long at Mrs. Sid Pfaff at the Country Club dance, the sudden tears that meant nothing at all and were best handled by a box of Pangborn's chocolates. This was none of them. She looked tired. She looked, he thought with an odd chill, as though she had been sitting there for hours, waiting for him, and had stopped expecting anything from the waiting.

"Something the matter, Hazel? Kids all right?"

"The children are at the movies. I gave them money. I wanted them out of the house."

"Well, say, that's a hot one! Here I come home all set to tell you about—" He stopped. He had seen the envelope. It was long and buff-colored, and in the corner, in raised blue letters, as he could have recited with his eyes shut, were the words LONE STAR PETROLEUM DEVELOPMENT SYNDICATE, Fort Worth, Texas, "Where the Future Flows."

"Oh," said Clyde Mumford. "That."

"Yes. That."

He sat down on the davenport. He did not mean to sit down; he meant to stride about the room, hands in pockets, in the manner of a man who has nothing on his conscience and a good deal on his mind about the trend of the tire market. But his knees had their own views, and he sat, and the davenport sighed under him.

"Well, now, Hazel," he began, in the voice he used for customers who wished to return a battery after the guarantee had expired, "I don't know what you've been reading there, but I want you to understand right at the start that a lot of these fellows down there write letters that don't mean a thing. Just routine. It's the way they do business in Texas. Different from up here. Big-hearted way, you might say. Free and easy."

"It says," Hazel observed, unfolding the letter with a care that was worse than any violence, "that the Syndicate regrets to inform its shareholders that the Number Three well, on the Pettus lease, has been abandoned as a dry hole, and that owing to the unforeseen expenses of drilling, there will be no further dividends and an assessment of eleven dollars a share is being levied, payable on or before the fifteenth. "Now, you're figuring that wrong—"

"I'm figuring it right. I was always better at figures than you. You know I was. I kept your books the first two years, when you had the store on Railroad Avenue and couldn't pay a bookkeeper."

He did know it, and it was not a recollection he enjoyed. It belonged to the prehistoric age before the Boosters' League, before Maple Crest, before the sedan; it belonged to a time when he had been a skinny young man with a cardboard suitcase and a line of patent tire patches, and Hazel had been the girl who sat at the cashier's desk in the Bon Ton Ice Cream Parlor and smiled at him because, she said afterward, he looked so hungry.

"And besides that," Hazel went on, "it says you already paid four thousand dollars for the shares in the first place. At ten dollars apiece. Last April."

"Well, what if I did? Can't a man make an investment? Doggone it, Hazel, a man in my position has got to look ahead. Every live business man in this town has got something in oil. Look at Sid Pfaff. Look at Doc Ballinger. Why, Ed Thoroughgood told me himself—"

"Did Ed Thoroughgood put four thousand dollars in the Lone Star Petroleum Development Syndicate?"

"Well—no. Not in that one, exactly. But in oil. In principle."

"Clyde, where did the four thousand dollars come from?"

It was here that Clyde Mumford, who had that very noon informed sixty-three business men that the Man Who Gets There never dodges a straight question, discovered that he did not care to answer a straight question. He looked at the galleons on the lampshade. He looked at the reproduction of "The Horse Fair" over the mantel, which Hazel had bought because Mrs. Thoroughgood had one. He looked at the radio cabinet, which was walnut veneer and had cost one hundred and eighty-five dollars, and from which, nightly, issued the voices of sopranos in Pittsburgh and the scores of games in Chicago, assuring him that he lived at the very center of civilization.

"I'll tell you where it came from," said Hazel. "It came out of the savings account at the Second National. The one we started when Dorothy was born. The one that was for her to go to college. I went down there this afternoon, Clyde. I asked Mr. Wennerstrom. He didn't want to tell me, but he told me. There's three hundred and twelve dollars in it."

"You went to the bank? You went behind my back to the bank?"

He was on his feet now. It was enormously relieving to be on his feet and to be indignant. Indignation was a thing he understood; it was a solid ground, like cement, and he planted himself on it.

"Well, by golly, that's a fine thing! That's a fine way for a wife to act! Going down and snooping around with Wennerstrom, that's got the biggest mouth in Tecumseh City, and it'll be all over the Athletic Club by to-morrow noon that Clyde Mumford's wife don't trust him! Did you ever stop to think of that? Did you ever stop to think what that does to a man's credit? To a man's standing? Why, I've been building up my position in this town for fifteen years, working my fingers to the bone, and you go and—"

"Behind your back," said Hazel quietly. "You said behind your back."

"Well, wasn't it?"

"Clyde, you took Dorothy's college money and gave it to a man from Texas, and you never said one word to me. For eight months. You sat at that table every night and ate your supper and talked about the Kiwanis and the Boosters and the paving of Sycamore Street, and you never said one word. And you say I went behind your back."

He had a perfectly good answer to this. He knew he had. It was somewhere in him, in the region where he kept his answers to radicals who wanted the government to own the railroads, and to Professor Dunkel at the State Normal who had once, at a dinner, suggested that American business might not be the final flowering of the human spirit. But it did not come. Instead he heard himself saying, in a voice that was not the platform voice at all, but thinner and more querulous:

"It was Hoskins. Elbert Hoskins. You met him. At the Rotary ladies' night. Big fellow with the cowboy hat—not a real cowboy hat, you know, but one of those gray ones, very classy—and the diamond in his tie. He had all the figures, Hazel. He had geological reports. He had a map with the wells all marked in red ink. He showed me letters from a fellow in Tulsa that put in five hundred and took out nine thousand inside of a year. And he said—he said he was only letting in a few of the substantial men, the real leaders, you understand, in each town; he wasn't peddling it around to every Tom, Dick, and Harry. He said he'd picked me out special. He said he could tell I was a man of vision."

He was ashamed of that last; he heard how it sounded; but he could not take it back.

"And I figured," he went on, more rapidly, "I figured, here's Dorothy, she's only fourteen, she don't need the money for four years yet, and if I could just turn it over once, why, we could send her East. To one of those swell colleges. Vassar or something. Instead of just the State University. And we could get the new sleeping-porch, and maybe one of these electric refrigerators, and you wouldn't have to be fussing with the iceman all the time—and I was going to surprise you. That's the truth, Hazel. I was going to walk in here some night and throw a check for twenty thousand dollars down on that table and say, 'There you are, old girl!' I used to lie awake thinking about it. How you'd look."

There was a silence. In the kitchen the alarm clock which the maid, Olga, had left on the shelf over the sink ticked loudly, with the moral insistence of all alarm clocks. Out on Linden Boulevard a motor horn played the first three notes of "How Dry I Am," which was considered, in Maple Crest, the height of wit.

"I believe you," Hazel said at last. "I believe that's what you thought about. That's what makes it so bad, Clyde."

"Huh? What d'you mean, makes it bad? I'm telling you I did it for you! For you and the kids!"

"I know. You always do things for us. You bought the radio for us, and you never asked if I wanted it, and I don't; I'd rather have the quiet in the evenings. You bought the sedan for us, when the old touring car was perfectly good, because Sid Pfaff got a sedan. You joined the Country Club for us, and I sit there at the bridge tables with women who talk about their maids, and I don't know how to talk about maids, Clyde; I was a maid once myself, very near, before the Bon Ton. You do everything for us. And you never once ask us."

He stared at her. It was not the speech of a wife. Wives, in his experience, which was derived partly from his own household and partly from the comic sections of the Sunday Advocate-Times, complained that their husbands did not buy them enough things; they did not complain that their husbands bought them too many. It was unnatural. It was, he felt dimly, almost socialistic.

"Well, I'll be darned," he said. "I'll be darned. I never knew you felt like that. You never said so."

"You never asked."

"There you go again! Asked, asked! A man can't go around asking his wife about every little thing. He's got to take the responsibility. He's got to lead. That's what a man's for. Why, if I'd gone around asking everybody before I did anything, I'd still be peddling tire patches out of a suitcase."

"Maybe," said Hazel, "we'd have four thousand dollars."

That stung. It stung precisely because it was the kind of thing he would have said himself, in a Boosters' speech, about some other man, some poor fish who had been taken in by a slick promoter; he could hear himself saying it, with the hearty contempt of the Man Who Gets There for the Man Who Falls For It. He reddened. His collar, which was a new and very stiff collar recommended by the clerk at Kessler's Men's Shoppe as "the type worn by the younger executive," began to cut him.

"All right," he said heavily. "All right. Rub it in. Go on and rub it in. I'm a sucker. I'm a boob. I'm the champion all-time boob of Tecumseh City. Is that what you want me to say? Well, I've said it. Now are you satisfied?"

"No," said Hazel. "I'm not satisfied. I don't want you to say you're a boob. I want—" She stopped, and for the first time her voice shook, and she looked down at the buff letter as though it might tell her what she wanted. "I want you to have told me. Last April. I want you to have come home and said, 'Hazel, there's a man named Hoskins and he's got a map with red ink on it, what do you think?' That's all. And I'd have said, 'Clyde, he's a crook, anybody can see he's a crook, he wears a diamond in his tie,' and you'd have got mad, and maybe you'd have done it anyway. But at least it'd have been the two of us. At least I wouldn't have found out from a letter."

He wanted, then, to go to her. He was aware of wanting it, as one is aware of a draught in a room, without quite locating it. He stood in the middle of the Axminster rug, between the mulberry chair and the davenport, and he thought of the girl at the Bon Ton who had smiled at him because he looked hungry, and he thought that it was a long time since anyone had looked at him that way, as though he were simply a person who might need something, and not the proprietor of the Mumford Motor Accessory Company, Everything for the Motorist Who Cares.

But between him and the mulberry chair there lay, invisible and very solid, eleven years of not going to her; and the habit of a man's feet is stronger than the yearning of his heart, as every philosopher and every shoe salesman knows.

"Well," he said, and cleared his throat, and found that he had put his hands in his pockets after all. "Well, the thing is now, what are we going to do about it? That's the practical question. No use crying over spilt milk. Now, about this assessment. I been thinking. Of course, I'm not going to pay any eleven dollars a share. I'm not that big a fool. Let 'em sue. But the thing is—" he lowered his voice, though there was no one to hear but Olga's clock—"the thing is, nobody's got to know about this. Not a soul. You haven't told anybody, have you? You haven't said anything to Mrs. Thoroughgood?"

Hazel looked at him for a long moment. He was never afterward able to describe that look, even to himself. It was not contempt; he could have stood contempt; he had a whole vocabulary for contempt, compiled in the course of many arguments with the Democratic minority on the Board of the Chamber of Commerce. It was something more like pity, and pity, in Maple Crest, was not a thing one bestowed upon a successful man.

"No, Clyde," she said. "I haven't told anybody."

"That's the girl! That's the stuff! Because you see, if it got around—especially just now, with me getting up and talking at the Boosters about vision and all—why, they'd simply kid the life out of me. Ed Thoroughgood would never let up. And it might hurt business, too; you never know; people get funny ideas. A man in my position's got to keep up a front. You understand that, don't you, honey?"

"Yes," said Hazel. "I understand that."

"And about Dorothy's college—don't you worry about that. I'll make it up. Business is going to be fine this spring. Never better. Those balloon tires are going to sell like hot cakes, and I've got the exclusive on the Silver Arrow radiator cap for the whole county. I'll have that four thousand back in the bank by Christmas. You see if I don't. And then—say, I'll tell you what: we'll forget all about this, and next summer, we'll drive out to Yellowstone, the whole family. How'd that be? Wouldn't you like that, Hazel?"

She folded the letter. She folded it along its original creases, very neatly, and slid it back into the buff envelope with LONE STAR PETROLEUM DEVELOPMENT SYNDICATE on the corner, and laid it on the little smoking-stand beside her chair, beside the bronze ash-tray in the shape of a horseshoe that he had won at the Boosters' golf tournament.

"I'll see about supper," she said. "Olga left the pot roast."

She went out. He heard the kitchen door swing, and the clank of the stove-lid, and then nothing.

Clyde Mumford stood alone under the galleons. After a while he went to the radio and turned the dials, and presently, out of the walnut veneer, there came a male quartet in Davenport, Iowa, singing "Love's Old Sweet Song" with a great deal of feeling and some static. He listened to the end of it. Then he turned it off, because it made him feel queer.

He went to the front window and looked out at Linden Boulevard, at the row of houses exactly like his own, Dutch Colonial and Spanish Mission and California Bungalow, each with its cement drive and its little cedars and its lighted living-room, and he wondered, for one disquieting instant, how many of the men in those living-rooms had also bought something from a man with a diamond in his tie, and had also stood alone in front of a window afterward, and had also not gone into the kitchen.

But it was not a thought that could be indulged for long by a member in good standing of the Boosters' League. He shook it off. He straightened his shoulders. He reflected that, after all, he had handled the thing pretty well, considering; that Hazel had taken it better than he could have expected; that women always made a fuss at first and then got over it; and that, by golly, nobody in town need ever know.

By the time the children came home from the movies, chattering about Rudolph Valentino, he was in the mulberry chair himself, the evening Advocate-Times spread before him, explaining to young Myron, who had not asked, that the trouble with the country was that there were too many people who didn't have any vision; and Hazel, carrying in the pot roast, said nothing at all.

The assurance of Tanis Judique’s friendship fortified Babbitt’s self-approval. At the Athletic Club he became experimental. Though Vergil Gunch was silent, the others at the Roughnecks’ Table came to accept Babbitt as having, for no visible reason, “turned crank.” They argued windily with him, and he was cocky, and enjoyed the spectacle of his interesting martyrdom. He even praised Seneca Doane. Professor Pumphrey said that was carrying a joke too far; but Babbitt argued, “No! Fact! I tell you he’s got one of the keenest intellects in the country. Why, Lord Wycombe said that—” “Oh, who the hell is Lord Wycombe? What you always lugging him in for? You been touting him for the last six weeks!” protested Orville Jones.

“George ordered him from Sears-Roebuck. You can get those English high-muckamucks by mail for two bucks apiece,” suggested Sidney Finkelstein.

“That’s all right now! Lord Wycombe, he’s one of the biggest intellects in English political life. As I was saying: Of course I’m conservative myself, but I appreciate a guy like Senny Doane because—” Vergil Gunch interrupted harshly, “I wonder if you are so conservative? I find I can manage to run my own business without any skunks and reds like Doane in it!” The grimness of Gunch’s voice, the hardness of his jaw, disconcerted Babbitt, but he recovered and went on till they looked bored, then irritated, then as doubtful as Gunch. He thought of Tanis always. With a stir he remembered her every aspect. His arms yearned for her. “I’ve found her! I’ve dreamed of her all these years and now I’ve found her!” he exulted. He met her at the movies in the morning; he drove out to her flat in the late afternoon or on evenings when he was believed to be at the Elks. He knew her financial affairs and advised her about them, while she lamented her feminine ignorance, and praised his masterfulness, and proved to know much more about bonds than he did. They had remembrances, and laughter over old times. Once they quarreled, and he raged that she was as “bossy” as his wife and far more whining when he was inattentive. But that passed safely. Their high hour was a tramp on a ringing December afternoon, through snow-drifted meadows down to the icy Chaloosa River. She was exotic in an astrachan cap and a short beaver coat; she slid on the ice and shouted, and he panted after her, rotund with laughter.... Myra Babbitt never slid on the ice. He was afraid that they would be seen together. In Zenith it is impossible to lunch with a neighbor’s wife without the fact being known, before nightfall, in every house in your circle. But Tanis was beautifully discreet. However appealingly she might turn to him when they were alone, she was gravely detached when they were abroad, and he hoped that she would be taken for a client. Orville Jones once saw them emerging from a movie theater, and Babbitt bumbled, “Let me make you ’quainted with Mrs. Judique. Now here’s a lady who knows the right broker to come to, Orvy!” Mr. Jones, though he was a man censorious of morals and of laundry machinery, seemed satisfied. His predominant fear—not from any especial fondness for her but from the habit of propriety—was that his wife would learn of the affair. He was certain that she knew nothing specific about Tanis, but he was also certain that she suspected something indefinite. For years she had been bored by anything more affectionate than a farewell kiss, yet she was hurt by any slackening in his irritable periodic interest, and now he had no interest; rather, a revulsion. He was completely faithful—to Tanis. He was distressed by the sight of his wife’s slack plumpness, by her puffs and billows of flesh, by the tattered petticoat which she was always meaning and always forgetting to throw away. But he was aware that she, so long attuned to him, caught all his repulsions. He elaborately, heavily, jocularly tried to check them. He couldn’t. They had a tolerable Christmas. Kenneth Escott was there, admittedly engaged to Verona. Mrs. Babbitt was tearful and called Kenneth her new son. Babbitt was worried about Ted, because he had ceased complaining of the State University and become suspiciously acquiescent. He wondered what the boy was planning, and was too shy to ask. Himself, Babbitt slipped away on Christmas afternoon to take his present, a silver cigarette-box, to Tanis. When he returned Mrs. Babbitt asked, much too innocently, “Did you go out for a little fresh air?”

“Yes, just lil drive,” he mumbled. After New Year’s his wife proposed, “I heard from my sister to-day, George. She isn’t well. I think perhaps I ought to go stay with her for a few weeks.” Now, Mrs. Babbitt was not accustomed to leave home during the winter except on violently demanding occasions, and only the summer before, she had been gone for weeks. Nor was Babbitt one of the detachable husbands who take separations casually. He liked to have her there; she looked after his clothes; she knew how his steak ought to be cooked; and her clucking made him feel secure. But he could not drum up even a dutiful “Oh, she doesn’t really need you, does she?” While he tried to look regretful, while he felt that his wife was watching him, he was filled with exultant visions of Tanis.

“Do you think I’d better go?” she said sharply.

“You’ve got to decide, honey; I can’t.” She turned away, sighing, and his forehead was damp. Till she went, four days later, she was curiously still, he cumbrously affectionate. Her train left at noon. As he saw it grow small beyond the train-shed he longed to hurry to Tanis.

“No, by golly, I won’t do that!” he vowed. “I won’t go near her for a week!” But he was at her flat at four. He who had once controlled or seemed to control his life in a progress unimpassioned but diligent and sane was for that fortnight borne on a current of desire and very bad whisky and all the complications of new acquaintances, those furious new intimates who demand so much more attention than old friends. Each morning he gloomily recognized his idiocies of the evening before. With his head throbbing, his tongue and lips stinging from cigarettes, he incredulously counted the number of drinks he had taken, and groaned, “I got to quit!” He had ceased saying, “I will quit!” for however resolute he might be at dawn, he could not, for a single evening, check his drift. He had met Tanis’s friends; he had, with the ardent haste of the Midnight People, who drink and dance and rattle and are ever afraid to be silent, been adopted as a member of her group, which they called “The Bunch.” He first met them after a day when he had worked particularly hard and when he hoped to be quiet with Tanis and slowly sip her admiration. From down the hall he could hear shrieks and the grind of a phonograph. As Tanis opened the door he saw fantastic figures dancing in a haze of cigarette smoke. The tables and chairs were against the wall.

“Oh, isn’t this dandy!” she gabbled at him. “Carrie Nork had the loveliest idea. She decided it was time for a party, and she ’phoned the Bunch and told ’em to gather round.... George, this is Carrie.”

“Carrie” was, in the less desirable aspects of both, at once matronly and spinsterish. She was perhaps forty; her hair was an unconvincing ash-blond; and if her chest was flat, her hips were ponderous. She greeted Babbitt with a giggling “Welcome to our little midst! Tanis says you’re a real sport.” He was apparently expected to dance, to be boyish and gay with Carrie, and he did his unforgiving best. He towed her about the room, bumping into other couples, into the radiator, into chair-legs cunningly ambushed. As he danced he surveyed the rest of the Bunch: A thin young woman who looked capable, conceited, and sarcastic. Another woman whom he could never quite remember. Three overdressed and slightly effeminate young men—soda-fountain clerks, or at least born for that profession. A man of his own age, immovable, self-satisfied, resentful of Babbitt’s presence. When he had finished his dutiful dance Tanis took him aside and begged, “Dear, wouldn’t you like to do something for me? I’m all out of booze, and the Bunch want to celebrate. Couldn’t you just skip down to Healey Hanson’s and get some?”

“Sure,” he said, trying not to sound sullen.

“I’ll tell you: I’ll get Minnie Sonntag to drive down with you.” Tanis was pointing to the thin, sarcastic young woman. Miss Sonntag greeted him with an astringent “How d’you do, Mr. Babbitt. Tanis tells me you’re a very prominent man, and I’m honored by being allowed to drive with you. Of course I’m not accustomed to associating with society people like you, so I don’t know how to act in such exalted circles!” Thus Miss Sonntag talked all the way down to Healey Hanson’s. To her jibes he wanted to reply “Oh, go to the devil!” but he never quite nerved himself to that reasonable comment. He was resenting the existence of the whole Bunch. He had heard Tanis speak of “darling Carrie” and “Min Sonntag—she’s so clever—you’ll adore her,” but they had never been real to him. He had pictured Tanis as living in a rose-tinted vacuum, waiting for him, free of all the complications of a Floral Heights. When they returned he had to endure the patronage of the young soda-clerks. They were as damply friendly as Miss Sonntag was dryly hostile. They called him “Old Georgie” and shouted, “Come on now, sport; shake a leg” ... boys in belted coats, pimply boys, as young as Ted and as flabby as chorus-men, but powerful to dance and to mind the phonograph and smoke cigarettes and patronize Tanis. He tried to be one of them; he cried “Good work, Pete!” but his voice creaked. Tanis apparently enjoyed the companionship of the dancing darlings; she bridled to their bland flirtation and casually kissed them at the end of each dance. Babbitt hated her, for the moment. He saw her as middle-aged. He studied the wrinkles in the softness of her throat, the slack flesh beneath her chin. The taut muscles of her youth were loose and drooping. Between dances she sat in the largest chair, waving her cigarette, summoning her callow admirers to come and talk to her. (“She thinks she’s a blooming queen!” growled Babbitt.) She chanted to Miss Sonntag, “Isn’t my little studio sweet?” (“Studio, rats! It’s a plain old-maid-and-chow-dog flat! Oh, God, I wish I was home! I wonder if I can’t make a getaway now?”) His vision grew blurred, however, as he applied himself to Healey Hanson’s raw but vigorous whisky. He blended with the Bunch. He began to rejoice that Carrie Nork and Pete, the most nearly intelligent of the nimble youths, seemed to like him; and it was enormously important to win over the surly older man, who proved to be a railway clerk named Fulton Bemis. The conversation of the Bunch was exclamatory, high-colored, full of references to people whom Babbitt did not know. Apparently they thought very comfortably of themselves. They were the Bunch, wise and beautiful and amusing; they were Bohemians and urbanites, accustomed to all the luxuries of Zenith: dance-halls, movie-theaters, and roadhouses; and in a cynical superiority to people who were “slow” or “tightwad” they cackled: “Oh, Pete, did I tell you what that dub of a cashier said when I came in late yesterday? Oh, it was per-fect-ly priceless!”

“Oh, but wasn’t T. D. stewed! Say, he was simply ossified! What did Gladys say to him?”

“Think of the nerve of Bob Bickerstaff trying to get us to come to his house! Say, the nerve of him! Can you beat it for nerve? Some nerve I call it!”

“Did you notice how Dotty was dancing? Gee, wasn’t she the limit!” Babbitt was to be heard sonorously agreeing with the once-hated Miss Minnie Sonntag that persons who let a night go by without dancing to jazz music were crabs, pikers, and poor fish; and he roared “You bet!” when Mrs. Carrie Nork gurgled, “Don’t you love to sit on the floor? It’s so Bohemian!” He began to think extremely well of the Bunch. When he mentioned his friends Sir Gerald Doak, Lord Wycombe, William Washington Eathorne, and Chum Frink, he was proud of their condescending interest. He got so thoroughly into the jocund spirit that he didn’t much mind seeing Tanis drooping against the shoulder of the youngest and milkiest of the young men, and he himself desired to hold Carrie Nork’s pulpy hand, and dropped it only because Tanis looked angry. When he went home, at two, he was fully a member of the Bunch, and all the week thereafter he was bound by the exceedingly straitened conventions, the exceedingly wearing demands, of their life of pleasure and freedom. He had to go to their parties; he was involved in the agitation when everybody telephoned to everybody else that she hadn’t meant what she’d said when she’d said that, and anyway, why was Pete going around saying she’d said it? Never was a Family more insistent on learning one another’s movements than were the Bunch. All of them volubly knew, or indignantly desired to know, where all the others had been every minute of the week. Babbitt found himself explaining to Carrie or Fulton Bemis just what he had been doing that he should not have joined them till ten o’clock, and apologizing for having gone to dinner with a business acquaintance. Every member of the Bunch was expected to telephone to every other member at least once a week. “Why haven’t you called me up?” Babbitt was asked accusingly, not only by Tanis and Carrie but presently by new ancient friends, Jennie and Capitolina and Toots. If for a moment he had seen Tanis as withering and sentimental, he lost that impression at Carrie Nork’s dance. Mrs. Nork had a large house and a small husband. To her party came all of the Bunch, perhaps thirty-five of them when they were completely mobilized. Babbitt, under the name of “Old Georgie,” was now a pioneer of the Bunch, since each month it changed half its membership and he who could recall the prehistoric days of a fortnight ago, before Mrs. Absolom, the food-demonstrator, had gone to Indianapolis, and Mac had “got sore at” Minnie, was a venerable leader and able to condescend to new Petes and Minnies and Gladyses. At Carrie’s, Tanis did not have to work at being hostess. She was dignified and sure, a clear fine figure in the black chiffon frock he had always loved; and in the wider spaces of that ugly house Babbitt was able to sit quietly with her. He repented of his first revulsion, mooned at her feet, andhappily drove her home. Next day he bought a violent yellow tie, to make himself young for her. He knew, a little sadly, that he could not make himself beautiful; he beheld himself as heavy, hinting of fatness, but he danced, he dressed, he chattered, to be as young as she was... as young as she seemed to be. As all converts, whether to a religion, love, or gardening, find as by magic that though hitherto these hobbies have not seemed to exist, now the whole world is filled with their fury, so, once he was converted to dissipation, Babbitt discovered agreeable opportunities for it everywhere. He had a new view of his sporting neighbor, Sam Doppelbrau. The Doppelbraus were respectable people, industrious people, prosperous people, whose ideal of happiness was an eternal cabaret. Their life was dominated by suburban bacchanalia of alcohol, nicotine, gasoline, and kisses. They and their set worked capably all the week, and all week looked forward to Saturday night, when they would, as they expressed it, “throw a party;” and the thrown party grew noisier and noisier up to Sunday dawn, and usually included an extremely rapid motor expedition to nowhere in particular. One evening when Tanis was at the theater, Babbitt found himself being lively with the Doppelbraus, pledging friendship with men whom he had for years privily denounced to Mrs. Babbitt as a “rotten bunch of tin-horns that I wouldn’t go out with, not if they were the last people on earth.” That evening he had sulkily come home and poked about in front of the house, chipping off the walk the ice-clots, like fossil footprints, made by the steps of passers-by during the recent snow. Howard Littlefield came up snuffling.

“Still a widower, George?”

“Yump. Cold again to-night.”

“What do you hear from the wife?”

“She’s feeling fine, but her sister is still pretty sick.”

“Say, better come in and have dinner with us to-night, George.”

“Oh—oh, thanks. Have to go out.” Suddenly he could not endure Littlefield’s recitals of the more interesting statistics about totally uninteresting problems. He scraped at the walk and grunted. Sam Doppelbrau appeared.

“Evenin’, Babbitt. Working hard?”

“Yuh, lil exercise.”

“Cold enough for you to-night?”

“Well, just about.”

“Still a widower?”

“Uh-huh.”
