When Lyman Pettibone, president of the Pettibone Tire & Vulcanizing Company and second vice-president of the Vanderburg Boosters' League, learned that his cousin Walter was coming through on the Overland Limited and would stop over for two days, he was so moved that he telephoned his wife three times before noon.

"Say, Edna, I been thinking. We better have the pot-roast. Walt always was crazy about pot-roast. Or no, maybe a fellow that's been living in New York all these years, maybe he'd sort of expect a fowl. What do you think? Well, you decide. I can't. Only make it something real nice."

He had not seen Walter for twenty-two years. They had been boys together in Hollister Junction, Iowa. They had stolen Baldwin apples together from the Methodist parsonage, and smoked corn-silk behind the creamery, and, on one memorable Fourth, blown the left eyebrow entirely off the face of Lyman's brother Ferd. Then Walter had gone to Chicago to study at an art school, which in Hollister Junction was regarded as only a little more respectable than going on the stage, and from Chicago he had gone to New York. In New York, so far as the family could learn from his rare letters, he "did illustrating for the magazines." Lyman had once found a drawing signed W. Pettibone in a back number of a periodical, a picture of a young woman in a canoe holding a parasol, and he had carried it in his wallet for a month and shown it to everybody at the Elks.

"That's my cousin did that. Draws for all the big magazines back East. Gets a hundred, maybe two hundred bucks a crack, I wouldn't wonder. Say, it's a gift, that's what it is. You either got it or you haven't."

Now, as he drove his sedan down to the Union Station, he was a little anxious. He was a solid man, Lyman Pettibone, solid in the shoulders and solid in the jowls and solid in his conviction that Vanderburg, with its two hundred and eighteen thousand people (the Chamber of Commerce figure; the government census, out of its mere bureaucratic spite, said a hundred and ninety-one), was the coming city of the Middle West. But he was nervous about Walter. He had a dim fear that a New York artist would look down on him; that Walter would wear a flowing tie and say things about Art in a tone that made a man feel he ought to apologize for selling tires. He had prepared for this. He had read, the evening before, nearly eleven pages of a book about the Italian painters which Edna had bought from a canvasser in 1919 and which had never since been moved from the library table except to be dusted.

The train was twelve minutes late. Lyman spent the time explaining to a redcap, who had not asked, that the new station had cost two million three hundred thousand dollars and had more square feet of marble than the one at Kansas City.

Then the train was in, steaming and hissing, and the passengers were coming down the platform, and Lyman stood on tiptoe, peering. He saw a large man with a yellow suitcase and thought, "No, that's not Walt, he was a skinny little runt." He saw a thin man with spectacles and a black overcoat, and thought, "That might be him," and then, with a queer drop, "Gosh, he looks old."

It was Walter. He came up slowly and stopped and looked at Lyman, and Lyman looked at him, and for a moment neither of them said anything at all. The thin man had gray hair over the ears, and a face lined about the mouth, and his overcoat, though it was a good overcoat, was frayed at the cuffs. Then Walter smiled, and in the smile Lyman saw, quite clearly, a freckled boy of eleven lying on his stomach on the bank of Skunk Creek and saying, "Bet you a nickel I can hold my breath longer'n you."

"Well, well, well!" roared Lyman. "Well, I'll be darned! Well, if it isn't old Walt! Well, sir!"

He pumped Walter's hand. He slapped Walter's shoulder. He seized Walter's suitcase, over Walter's protests, and he said "Well, well!" four times more, because he could not think of anything else to say, and because there was a curious tightness in his throat which he did not care to examine.

"Hello, Lyme," said Walter. "You've—you've filled out some."

"Ha! I'll say I have! Edna feeds me too darn well, that's the trouble. Well, sir, this is great. Come on. Got the car right outside. Say, you're looking fine, Walt. Fine!"

He did not think Walter was looking fine. He thought Walter was looking tired. But it is the first article of the creed of the Lyman Pettibones that everybody is looking fine, that business is looking fine, that the weather, considering the season, is looking fine; and to say anything else is not only discourteous but faintly radical.

The sedan was a new one, a Royal Eight, maroon with nickel trim, and Lyman watched Walter's face as they approached it. Walter said, "That's a handsome car," and Lyman said, carelessly, "Oh, it gets me around. Traded in the old one in March. They give you a good allowance if you know how to talk to 'em." He held the door open with a flourish he would not have admitted to.

He drove Walter through the business district by a route which was not the shortest but which led past the new Second National Bank building ("eighteen stories—tallest between here and Minneapolis"), the Hotel Thornbury ("five hundred rooms, every one with bath"), the site of the proposed Civic Auditorium ("going to seat six thousand, if we can ever get those bone-heads on the council to vote the bonds"), and the Pettibone Tire & Vulcanizing Company, which occupied a one-story brick building with a large sign and a small display window full of inner tubes.

"That's my shop," said Lyman, and slowed the car to nine miles an hour. "Course it don't look like much from outside. But we do more business than any tire house in the city except Kimmel's, and Kimmel's got a chain. Eleven men on the payroll. I started in that place with one helper and a second-hand vulcanizer I bought off a fellow that was going bust. Fifteen years ago."

"It's a fine thing, Lyme, to have built up something of your own," Walter said. He said it gravely, and Lyman glanced at him, suspecting irony, the hidden smile of the city man, and found none. Walter was looking at the inner tubes in the window as though they were, in their limp and rubbery way, quite beautiful.

"Well," said Lyman, oddly embarrassed, "it's a living."

The Pettibone house was on Woodland Heights, in that section of Vanderburg where the streets curve because the realtor who laid them out had once visited a suburb of Philadelphia. It was a Dutch Colonial house, white, with green shutters which could not be closed, a sun-parlor, a sleeping-porch, and a garage with the same green shutters, also unclosable. Edna Pettibone met them at the door. She was a comfortable, anxious woman who had put on her second-best silk, the brown one, because the best one, the blue, seemed to her to say too plainly that she had dressed up for New York.

"Well, I declare, this is Walter," she said. "Lyman's talked of nothing else since Tuesday. You must be just worn out with that long trip. Come right in. Lyman, take his things up. I've put you in the front room, Walter; it gets the morning sun, though I don't suppose you'll care for that, artists always sleep late, don't they? I read somewhere they do."

"I generally get up about seven," said Walter.

"Oh!" Edna was disconcerted, as though a guest had appeared without one of the parts listed in the catalogue.

Dinner was the pot-roast after all, with mashed potatoes and brown gravy, and a fruit salad with marshmallows and whipped cream, and lemon meringue pie. The Pettibone children were present: Harold, who was sixteen and was to be a civil engineer, and who had been told by his father that Cousin Walt was a famous artist, and who therefore regarded him with the uneasy respect a healthy boy feels for a man who might at any moment say something about Beauty; and Marjorie, who was thirteen and who asked, before the gravy had been passed, whether Cousin Walt knew any movie actresses.

"Not one," said Walter.

"Oh," said Marjorie, and lost interest in him permanently.

Lyman carried the conversation. He was aware that he was carrying it, and he could not stop. He told Walter about the Boosters' League and its campaign to bring the national convention of the Brotherhood of Retail Druggists to Vanderburg in 1927. He told him about the new radio set, which could get Pittsburgh on a clear night, and twice had got Havana, Cuba, or something that a man down at the shop swore was Havana, Cuba. He told him what he had paid for the house and what he had been offered for it last spring, and by how many dollars the second figure exceeded the first, and he waited, with the air of a man who has laid down four aces, for Walter to be impressed.

"That's a good deal of money," said Walter. He ate his pie slowly. He said that he had not had a lemon pie like that since he had left home, and Edna glowed, and Lyman, for no reason he could name, felt a small sting of disappointment, as if he had shown a man his car and the man had admired only the ash-tray.

He was waiting all through dinner for Walter to talk about New York. He wanted to hear about it. He had been there once, in 1921, with Edna, for six days, and they had stayed at a hotel near the Grand Central, and seen two shows and the Aquarium and the Woolworth Building, and Lyman had come home and told everybody at the Elks that New York was all right to visit but he wouldn't live there if you gave him the place, a lot of foreigners and no real friendliness, everybody out for the almighty dollar. He had said it so often that he believed it. Yet underneath he wanted Walter to tell him about studios and famous editors and parties where people talked about books, so that he could disapprove of them in detail.

But Walter did not talk about New York. He asked questions about Hollister Junction. He asked whether old Doc Brainard was still alive, and whether the creamery had burned, and what had become of the Swanson girls. He asked about Aunt Hattie, Lyman's mother, who had been dead nine years, and when Lyman told him, he put down his fork and was quiet for a while.

"She used to give me cookies," he said. "Molasses cookies, with a raisin in the middle. She'd say, 'Now don't tell Lyman, he's had his.'"

"Why, the old—!" Lyman laughed, very loud. "She said the same thing to me! She'd say, 'Don't tell Walter!'"

They looked at each other across the table, two middle-aged men, one fat and one thin, and they both laughed, and Edna smiled vaguely, and Harold looked at his plate, and Marjorie asked if she could be excused.

After dinner Edna said that she was sure the men had a lot to talk about and she would just do the dishes, no, Walter, she wouldn't hear of it, and the cousins went into what Lyman called the den. It was a small room with a leather couch, a bookcase containing a set of Dickens bought by the yard, a set of the Encyclopædia Americana bought on the installment plan, and seventeen copies of The Boosters' Bulletin; a humidor shaped like a Scotch terrier; and, framed on the wall, Lyman's certificate of membership in the Benevolent and Protective Order of Elks and a photograph of the 1922 Boosters' League picnic, in which Lyman, in the front row, was holding a watermelon.

Lyman brought out cigars and, after a moment of rather elaborate hesitation, a bottle.

"Course I don't approve of breaking the law," he said. "Prohibition's a fine thing, for the working classes. But a man's got a right to a little something in his own home, with his own folks. This is real stuff. Fellow I know gets it straight from Canada."

It was not real stuff. It had been made, about a week before, by a man named Gus in a garage on the south side, and it tasted faintly of varnish. But they drank it, and Lyman lit a cigar and leaned back in the leather chair and said, with the generous expansiveness of a host who has fed his guest well and shown him the house and the car and the Chamber of Commerce figures:

"Well, Walt, tell me about yourself. Must be great, living back there in the big town. Drawing for all those magazines. I bet you know all the big bugs."

Walter turned his glass round and round in his fingers. The lamp, which had a shade of parchment with a ship painted on it, threw a yellow light on the lines of his face.

"I haven't done much magazine work for a while, Lyme," he said. "The style changed. They want a different kind of thing now. Younger fellows. Lots of white space and slanting lines. I couldn't seem to get the hang of it."

"Oh." Lyman puffed at his cigar. "Well, what're you doing now?"

"I letter show-cards for a department store. Fourteenth Street. It isn't bad. Steady."

Lyman did not say anything for a moment. He had a sense of the floor of the room shifting a little under his chair, as when you step on a stair that isn't there. All his careful anxieties, the eleven pages on the Italian painters, the brown silk dress, his half-resentful, half-eager readiness to be patronized, went sliding away, and he did not know what to put in their place.

"Well, say," he said at last, heartily, too heartily, "that's a darn good line. Show-cards. Every business needs 'em. Why, I been paying a fellow here three dollars apiece for the cards in my window, and they look like the dickens. Steady, that's the main thing."

"That's right," said Walter.

"You married, Walt? You never wrote anything about it."

"I was. She died in 'eighteen. The flu."

"Gosh. I'm sorry, old man. I never knew."

"No. I didn't write much to anybody, those years."

The Scotch-terrier humidor gazed at them with its glass eyes. Out in the kitchen they could hear Edna running water and the clink of dishes, and from upstairs the radio, where Harold was trying for Pittsburgh and getting mostly a noise like frying.

Lyman cleared his throat. He felt that he should say something wise and comforting, something with a moral in it, like the inspirational talks at the Boosters' luncheons. He said, "Well, life's a funny thing," and was ashamed of it, and drank some of Gus's whisky to cover his shame.

Then Walter, quite unexpectedly, smiled, the old smile from the creek bank.

"You know what I used to think about, Lyme? In the city? When things weren't going right? I used to think about that time we built the raft. Remember? Out of the old chicken-house boards. And we were going to float clear down Skunk Creek to the Iowa River, and down the Iowa to the Mississippi, and down the Mississippi to New Orleans."

"And she sank!" Lyman sat up, slapping his knee. "By golly, she sank right in front of the Halvorsens' pasture! Twenty feet from where we launched her! And old Halvorsen's bull come down to the bank and looked at us, and we had to stay in the water till he got tired of it, and you were blue as a—as a—"

"And Aunt Hattie licked us both."

"She licked me twice. Said I was the oldest and ought to've known better. I was eight months older than you, Walt! Eight months!"

They laughed till the tears came. Lyman laughed so hard that he coughed, and his cigar went out, and he did not relight it. He forgot, for a quarter of an hour, that he was the president of the Pettibone Tire & Vulcanizing Company and the second vice-president of the Boosters' League; he forgot what his house had cost and what he had been offered for it. He was a boy in wet overalls on the bank of Skunk Creek, with a bull glowering and the sun going down red over the Halvorsens' corn, and his cousin Walt beside him, shivering and giggling and swearing, in the shocking, inexpert way of boys of ten, that next time they would go clear to New Orleans.

And then, as the laughter wore off, a stranger thing happened to Lyman Pettibone. He looked at his den, at the Dickens bought by the yard and the Elks certificate and the photograph of himself with the watermelon, and for one moment, one disloyal and appalling moment, all of it looked to him small and shabby and a little foolish, like the raft.

"Walt," he said slowly, "you ever think—I mean—I never did get to go anywhere much. You went. You got out. I always kind of figured—"

He stopped. He did not know what he had always kind of figured. It was something about a door that had been open once and that he had not gone through, and he had not known there was a door until this moment, and he did not want to know it now.

Walter was looking at him with an odd gentleness.

"I got out, all right," he said. "And I'd give a good deal, some nights, to have a house like this, Lyme, and a boy who's going to be an engineer, and folks who'd know if I died. You did the sensible thing. You always were the sensible one."

Lyman did not know whether this pleased him or not. He considered it for some time. Then he reached for the bottle and poured them both another drink, and said, with a resumption of his ordinary voice which cost him some effort:

"Well, I don't know about sensible. But I'll tell you one thing. If you ever want to come out here, Walt, I can find a place for a man that can letter. Vanderburg's growing. Biggest little city in the state. There's opportunity here for a fellow with get-up-and-go. I mean it."

"Thanks, Lyme," said Walter. "I'll think about it."

They both knew he would not think about it, and they were both relieved.

Walter left on Thursday, on the noon train. Lyman took him down to the station and bought him a box of cigars and three magazines and a bag of salted peanuts, and stood on the platform waving long after he could no longer see whether Walter was waving back. Then he went to the Boosters' League luncheon at the Hotel Thornbury, where he was late, and where Charley Eckhart, of Eckhart Plumbing Supplies, called down the table:

"Hey, Lyme! How's the famous cousin? Get him to draw you a picture?"

Lyman sat down and unfolded his napkin with dignity.

"Walt's a great fellow," he said. "Great fellow. Course, he's got a big position back there. Does all the art work for one of the biggest department stores in New York. Right on Fourteenth Street. Hundreds of people see his work every day. Thousands, maybe. But you'd never know it to talk to him. No side to him at all. Just as common as you or me. That's the kind of fellow he is."

And as he said it he believed it, quite sincerely; and he ate his chicken croquettes with a satisfaction that was only a little troubled, now and then, by a recollection of brown water and a sinking raft and a red sun going down over a pasture in Iowa, where, a long time ago, two boys had very nearly set out for New Orleans.

The assurance of Tanis Judique’s friendship fortified Babbitt’s self-approval. At the Athletic Club he became experimental. Though Vergil Gunch was silent, the others at the Roughnecks’ Table came to accept Babbitt as having, for no visible reason, “turned crank.” They argued windily with him, and he was cocky, and enjoyed the spectacle of his interesting martyrdom. He even praised Seneca Doane. Professor Pumphrey said that was carrying a joke too far; but Babbitt argued, “No! Fact! I tell you he’s got one of the keenest intellects in the country. Why, Lord Wycombe said that—” “Oh, who the hell is Lord Wycombe? What you always lugging him in for? You been touting him for the last six weeks!” protested Orville Jones.

“George ordered him from Sears-Roebuck. You can get those English high-muckamucks by mail for two bucks apiece,” suggested Sidney Finkelstein.

“That’s all right now! Lord Wycombe, he’s one of the biggest intellects in English political life. As I was saying: Of course I’m conservative myself, but I appreciate a guy like Senny Doane because—” Vergil Gunch interrupted harshly, “I wonder if you are so conservative? I find I can manage to run my own business without any skunks and reds like Doane in it!” The grimness of Gunch’s voice, the hardness of his jaw, disconcerted Babbitt, but he recovered and went on till they looked bored, then irritated, then as doubtful as Gunch. He thought of Tanis always. With a stir he remembered her every aspect. His arms yearned for her. “I’ve found her! I’ve dreamed of her all these years and now I’ve found her!” he exulted. He met her at the movies in the morning; he drove out to her flat in the late afternoon or on evenings when he was believed to be at the Elks. He knew her financial affairs and advised her about them, while she lamented her feminine ignorance, and praised his masterfulness, and proved to know much more about bonds than he did. They had remembrances, and laughter over old times. Once they quarreled, and he raged that she was as “bossy” as his wife and far more whining when he was inattentive. But that passed safely. Their high hour was a tramp on a ringing December afternoon, through snow-drifted meadows down to the icy Chaloosa River. She was exotic in an astrachan cap and a short beaver coat; she slid on the ice and shouted, and he panted after her, rotund with laughter.... Myra Babbitt never slid on the ice. He was afraid that they would be seen together. In Zenith it is impossible to lunch with a neighbor’s wife without the fact being known, before nightfall, in every house in your circle. But Tanis was beautifully discreet. However appealingly she might turn to him when they were alone, she was gravely detached when they were abroad, and he hoped that she would be taken for a client. Orville Jones once saw them emerging from a movie theater, and Babbitt bumbled, “Let me make you ’quainted with Mrs. Judique. Now here’s a lady who knows the right broker to come to, Orvy!” Mr. Jones, though he was a man censorious of morals and of laundry machinery, seemed satisfied. His predominant fear—not from any especial fondness for her but from the habit of propriety—was that his wife would learn of the affair. He was certain that she knew nothing specific about Tanis, but he was also certain that she suspected something indefinite. For years she had been bored by anything more affectionate than a farewell kiss, yet she was hurt by any slackening in his irritable periodic interest, and now he had no interest; rather, a revulsion. He was completely faithful—to Tanis. He was distressed by the sight of his wife’s slack plumpness, by her puffs and billows of flesh, by the tattered petticoat which she was always meaning and always forgetting to throw away. But he was aware that she, so long attuned to him, caught all his repulsions. He elaborately, heavily, jocularly tried to check them. He couldn’t. They had a tolerable Christmas. Kenneth Escott was there, admittedly engaged to Verona. Mrs. Babbitt was tearful and called Kenneth her new son. Babbitt was worried about Ted, because he had ceased complaining of the State University and become suspiciously acquiescent. He wondered what the boy was planning, and was too shy to ask. Himself, Babbitt slipped away on Christmas afternoon to take his present, a silver cigarette-box, to Tanis. When he returned Mrs. Babbitt asked, much too innocently, “Did you go out for a little fresh air?”

“Yes, just lil drive,” he mumbled. After New Year’s his wife proposed, “I heard from my sister to-day, George. She isn’t well. I think perhaps I ought to go stay with her for a few weeks.” Now, Mrs. Babbitt was not accustomed to leave home during the winter except on violently demanding occasions, and only the summer before, she had been gone for weeks. Nor was Babbitt one of the detachable husbands who take separations casually. He liked to have her there; she looked after his clothes; she knew how his steak ought to be cooked; and her clucking made him feel secure. But he could not drum up even a dutiful “Oh, she doesn’t really need you, does she?” While he tried to look regretful, while he felt that his wife was watching him, he was filled with exultant visions of Tanis.

“Do you think I’d better go?” she said sharply.

“You’ve got to decide, honey; I can’t.” She turned away, sighing, and his forehead was damp. Till she went, four days later, she was curiously still, he cumbrously affectionate. Her train left at noon. As he saw it grow small beyond the train-shed he longed to hurry to Tanis.

“No, by golly, I won’t do that!” he vowed. “I won’t go near her for a week!” But he was at her flat at four. He who had once controlled or seemed to control his life in a progress unimpassioned but diligent and sane was for that fortnight borne on a current of desire and very bad whisky and all the complications of new acquaintances, those furious new intimates who demand so much more attention than old friends. Each morning he gloomily recognized his idiocies of the evening before. With his head throbbing, his tongue and lips stinging from cigarettes, he incredulously counted the number of drinks he had taken, and groaned, “I got to quit!” He had ceased saying, “I will quit!” for however resolute he might be at dawn, he could not, for a single evening, check his drift. He had met Tanis’s friends; he had, with the ardent haste of the Midnight People, who drink and dance and rattle and are ever afraid to be silent, been adopted as a member of her group, which they called “The Bunch.” He first met them after a day when he had worked particularly hard and when he hoped to be quiet with Tanis and slowly sip her admiration. From down the hall he could hear shrieks and the grind of a phonograph. As Tanis opened the door he saw fantastic figures dancing in a haze of cigarette smoke. The tables and chairs were against the wall.

“Oh, isn’t this dandy!” she gabbled at him. “Carrie Nork had the loveliest idea. She decided it was time for a party, and she ’phoned the Bunch and told ’em to gather round.... George, this is Carrie.”

“Carrie” was, in the less desirable aspects of both, at once matronly and spinsterish. She was perhaps forty; her hair was an unconvincing ash-blond; and if her chest was flat, her hips were ponderous. She greeted Babbitt with a giggling “Welcome to our little midst! Tanis says you’re a real sport.” He was apparently expected to dance, to be boyish and gay with Carrie, and he did his unforgiving best. He towed her about the room, bumping into other couples, into the radiator, into chair-legs cunningly ambushed. As he danced he surveyed the rest of the Bunch: A thin young woman who looked capable, conceited, and sarcastic. Another woman whom he could never quite remember. Three overdressed and slightly effeminate young men—soda-fountain clerks, or at least born for that profession. A man of his own age, immovable, self-satisfied, resentful of Babbitt’s presence. When he had finished his dutiful dance Tanis took him aside and begged, “Dear, wouldn’t you like to do something for me? I’m all out of booze, and the Bunch want to celebrate. Couldn’t you just skip down to Healey Hanson’s and get some?”

“Sure,” he said, trying not to sound sullen.

“I’ll tell you: I’ll get Minnie Sonntag to drive down with you.” Tanis was pointing to the thin, sarcastic young woman. Miss Sonntag greeted him with an astringent “How d’you do, Mr. Babbitt. Tanis tells me you’re a very prominent man, and I’m honored by being allowed to drive with you. Of course I’m not accustomed to associating with society people like you, so I don’t know how to act in such exalted circles!” Thus Miss Sonntag talked all the way down to Healey Hanson’s. To her jibes he wanted to reply “Oh, go to the devil!” but he never quite nerved himself to that reasonable comment. He was resenting the existence of the whole Bunch. He had heard Tanis speak of “darling Carrie” and “Min Sonntag—she’s so clever—you’ll adore her,” but they had never been real to him. He had pictured Tanis as living in a rose-tinted vacuum, waiting for him, free of all the complications of a Floral Heights. When they returned he had to endure the patronage of the young soda-clerks. They were as damply friendly as Miss Sonntag was dryly hostile. They called him “Old Georgie” and shouted, “Come on now, sport; shake a leg” ... boys in belted coats, pimply boys, as young as Ted and as flabby as chorus-men, but powerful to dance and to mind the phonograph and smoke cigarettes and patronize Tanis. He tried to be one of them; he cried “Good work, Pete!” but his voice creaked. Tanis apparently enjoyed the companionship of the dancing darlings; she bridled to their bland flirtation and casually kissed them at the end of each dance. Babbitt hated her, for the moment. He saw her as middle-aged. He studied the wrinkles in the softness of her throat, the slack flesh beneath her chin. The taut muscles of her youth were loose and drooping. Between dances she sat in the largest chair, waving her cigarette, summoning her callow admirers to come and talk to her. (“She thinks she’s a blooming queen!” growled Babbitt.) She chanted to Miss Sonntag, “Isn’t my little studio sweet?” (“Studio, rats! It’s a plain old-maid-and-chow-dog flat! Oh, God, I wish I was home! I wonder if I can’t make a getaway now?”) His vision grew blurred, however, as he applied himself to Healey Hanson’s raw but vigorous whisky. He blended with the Bunch. He began to rejoice that Carrie Nork and Pete, the most nearly intelligent of the nimble youths, seemed to like him; and it was enormously important to win over the surly older man, who proved to be a railway clerk named Fulton Bemis. The conversation of the Bunch was exclamatory, high-colored, full of references to people whom Babbitt did not know. Apparently they thought very comfortably of themselves. They were the Bunch, wise and beautiful and amusing; they were Bohemians and urbanites, accustomed to all the luxuries of Zenith: dance-halls, movie-theaters, and roadhouses; and in a cynical superiority to people who were “slow” or “tightwad” they cackled: “Oh, Pete, did I tell you what that dub of a cashier said when I came in late yesterday? Oh, it was per-fect-ly priceless!”

“Oh, but wasn’t T. D. stewed! Say, he was simply ossified! What did Gladys say to him?”

“Think of the nerve of Bob Bickerstaff trying to get us to come to his house! Say, the nerve of him! Can you beat it for nerve? Some nerve I call it!”

“Did you notice how Dotty was dancing? Gee, wasn’t she the limit!” Babbitt was to be heard sonorously agreeing with the once-hated Miss Minnie Sonntag that persons who let a night go by without dancing to jazz music were crabs, pikers, and poor fish; and he roared “You bet!” when Mrs. Carrie Nork gurgled, “Don’t you love to sit on the floor? It’s so Bohemian!” He began to think extremely well of the Bunch. When he mentioned his friends Sir Gerald Doak, Lord Wycombe, William Washington Eathorne, and Chum Frink, he was proud of their condescending interest. He got so thoroughly into the jocund spirit that he didn’t much mind seeing Tanis drooping against the shoulder of the youngest and milkiest of the young men, and he himself desired to hold Carrie Nork’s pulpy hand, and dropped it only because Tanis looked angry. When he went home, at two, he was fully a member of the Bunch, and all the week thereafter he was bound by the exceedingly straitened conventions, the exceedingly wearing demands, of their life of pleasure and freedom. He had to go to their parties; he was involved in the agitation when everybody telephoned to everybody else that she hadn’t meant what she’d said when she’d said that, and anyway, why was Pete going around saying she’d said it? Never was a Family more insistent on learning one another’s movements than were the Bunch. All of them volubly knew, or indignantly desired to know, where all the others had been every minute of the week. Elwood Truax was not, in his own considered estimate, a hard man. He was a Father. He had been told so by the Reverend Dr. Ottinger in a sermon titled "The Hearthstone and the Hustler," and by the Ladies' Home Journal, and by a booklet on Child Training that came free with the second payment on the Encyclopædia of Wholesome Knowledge. He believed in Discipline, Firmness, Fair Play, and the Square Deal. He also believed in Not Being Bothered. When these two sets of beliefs met, which was about once a week, he became irritable and eloquent.

On this Thursday evening in October they met in the front hall of his Dutch Colonial house on Linnaeus Avenue in Sioux Wells. The hall had a mahogany-veneer table, a mirror framed in fumed oak, a brass umbrella-stand shaped like an elephant's foot, and a framed motto, burnt into leather by Mrs. Truax during her pyrography period, which said: A SMILE COSTS NOTHING. In the middle of the hall, at the precise spot where the Wilton rug was beginning to go threadbare from the traffic of a prosperous family, stood Elwood Truax, Junior, aged seven. He was called Sonny. Over him stood Elwood Truax, Senior, aged forty-four, president of the Truax Tire & Vulcanizing Company ("We Put the Go in Your Getaway"), Past Exalted Chief of the Loyal Order of Buffaloes, and member of the Sioux Wells Boosters' Club, the Commercial Men's Bowling League, and the Republican party.

Mr. Truax had come home with his collar wilted and his face the color of a boiled ham.

"Hazel!" he bellowed, before he had got his overcoat off. "Hazel! Where's that boy?"

Mrs. Truax came out of the kitchen drying her hands on her apron. She was a plump, anxious woman who had been pretty in the days when she had been Hazel Dorrance, the best soprano in the Methodist choir, and who had since devoted herself to her husband's digestion, her son's tonsils, and the Wednesday Afternoon Literary Circle, which was then studying Lithuania. "Why, Elwood, what on earth? You'll wake the neighbors."

"Wake 'em? It's six o'clock! They're not asleep, they're eating supper, which is what I'd be doing if I had a home where a man could have a little peace and respect! Sonny! You come here this minute!"

Sonny came. He came slowly, from behind the portière of the living-room, where he had been lying on his stomach reading a Big-Little Book about a cowboy named Tex Larrabee who never told a lie and shot nine rustlers before lunch. He was a thin, freckled, round-eyed child, with a cowlick that his mother wetted every morning and that sprang up again by nine. He wore knickerbockers with one stocking down, and an expression of such entire innocence that his father, who had seen the same expression on the faces of tire salesmen explaining their expense accounts, was not for one instant deceived.

"Hello, Papa," said Sonny.

"Don't you hello-Papa me! Stand up straight. Take your hands out of your pockets. Look me in the eye. Now. Now then." Mr. Truax stopped, partly for effect and partly because he had no clear notion of how to proceed. He had been rehearsing the scene all the way home in the Buick, but in the Buick it had gone more smoothly, with the boy bursting into penitent tears at the third sentence. "Now then, young man. I suppose you know what I want to talk to you about."

"No, Papa."

"No, Papa! No, Papa! Well, I'll just tell you, then. I'll just tell you." He hung his overcoat on the elephant's foot, discovered that it was the umbrella-stand, and hung it on the hook, grunting. "Mr. Delbert Gurney came into my place of business this afternoon. Mr. Delbert Gurney. You know who Mr. Gurney is?"

"He's Wilbur Gurney's papa. Wilbur's got an air-rifle."

"He is the president," said Mr. Truax with terrible slowness, "of the Gurney Sanitary Creamery Company. He operates fourteen trucks. Fourteen! Every one of 'em on Truax tires, every one of 'em vulcanized and retreaded in my shop, and that account, young man, that account is worth more to this family than—than—well, it's worth plenty, and it's what buys your shoes, and it's what buys that bicycle you keep pestering me about, and it's what pays for your mother's Literary Circle and all the rest of it."

"Elwood!" said Mrs. Truax.

"Well, it does. Now then. Mr. Gurney came in, and he was not smiling. When Del Gurney comes into a place and doesn't smile, you can figure there's something wrong. He came up to the counter, and I said, 'Well, well, if it isn't the Butter-and-Egg King himself! What can we do you for to-day, Del?' Kind of jolly, you understand, the way you've got to be with a customer. And he looked at me—he looked at me like I was something the cat drug in—and he said, 'Truax, I understand you think I'm a tightwad four-flusher that would skin a flea for its hide and tallow.'"

Mrs. Truax put her hand to her mouth.

"And I said," Mr. Truax went on, his voice rising with the anguish of recollection, "I said, 'Why, Del, whoever told you a thing like that?' And he said—he said, 'My boy Wilbur told me. And your boy told my boy. And your boy said he heard it from you, at your own dinner-table, last Sunday, right after church.'"

There was a silence in the hall. From the kitchen came the smell of pot roast slowly scorching. From the living-room came the tick of the mission clock that had been a wedding present from Hazel's Aunt Minnie in Ottumwa. Sonny considered the threadbare spot on the rug.

"Well?" said his father. "Well? What've you got to say for yourself?"

Sonny thought about it. He was an honest child, which was the root of the trouble. "You did say it, Papa," he observed. "You said it when Mama passed the gravy. You said Mr. Gurney was a tightwad four-flusher that would skin a flea for its hide and tallow, and you said if he wasn't such a good account you'd tell him where to get off."

"That," said Mr. Truax, "is neither here nor there."

It was a phrase he used at the Boosters' Club whenever a speaker brought up figures, and it had always served. It did not serve now. Sonny looked up at him with wide, interested eyes, as though waiting to learn where, then, it was.

"The point is," said Mr. Truax, gathering himself, "the point is—Hazel, will you go see about that roast? I can smell it from here—the point is that what is said in the bosom of a man's own family is private. It is con-fi-den-tial. Do you know what that means?"

"No, Papa."

"It means it's a secret. It means you don't go blabbing it all over town to every Tom, Dick, and Harry, and especially not to the son of a man that's got fourteen trucks. A man has a right to say what he thinks in his own home, doesn't he? A man's home is his castle. That's in the Constitution. Or anyway it's in—well, it's a well-known saying. A man has a right to express his honest opinion in his own castle, and when his own flesh and blood goes and spreads that opinion around, why, that's—that's disloyalty, that's what that is, and if there's one thing I can't stand, it's a fellow that isn't loyal."

Mrs. Truax, who had not gone to see about the roast, said timidly, "Maybe he didn't understand, Elwood. He's only seven."

"Seven! When I was seven I was carrying papers in Cedar Rapids at five o'clock in the morning! In the snow! When I was seven I knew enough to keep my mouth shut!"

This was not precisely accurate. When Elwood Truax was seven he had lived on a comfortable farm outside Marengo and had been chiefly notable for having put a toad in the Sunday-school superintendent's hat. But in the twenty years since he had come to Sioux Wells he had told so many young men at the Boosters' Club how he had carried papers in the snow that he had come to believe it, and the snow had grown deeper with every telling.

Sonny was fumbling with a button of his blouse. He was thinking, with the slow and terrible logic of the very young, about the Constitution and castles and secrets.

"Papa," he said at last.

"Well? Speak up."

"Is it a lie that Mr. Gurney is a tightwad?"

Mr. Truax opened his mouth and shut it again.

"Because," Sonny explained, "you told me never to tell a lie. You said George Washington never told a lie, and Tex Larrabee never tells a lie, and Reverend Ottinger said Ananias got struck dead. So if it isn't a lie, then I wasn't lying when I told Wilbur. And if it is a lie, then—" He stopped, appalled at where his reasoning had led him, and stared at his father as at a man on whom a bolt from Heaven might at any moment descend in the front hall, among the elephant's foot and the fumed oak.

"Now, you look here," said Mr. Truax, and his neck grew redder. "You look here. That's what I call being a smart-aleck. That's what I call sass, and I won't have it in this house. It's got nothing to do with lying, see? There's a difference—there's a big difference between telling a lie and—and using a little tact. You know what tact is?"

"No, Papa."

"Tact is—" Mr. Truax searched his mind. He had, in fact, an excellent working knowledge of tact; he practiced it daily, upon his customers, his bankers, his lodge brothers, his minister, and the Republican county chairman. But he had never been required to define it, and it now appeared to him a slippery and evasive thing, like a wet inner tube. "Tact is when you—when a fellow has the sense to—well, it's being diplomatic. You know. Being a regular fellow. Getting along with people. Not going out of your way to hurt their feelings. That's all. That's tact."

"But you hurt Mr. Gurney's feelings," said Sonny, "when you said he was a tightwad."

"I did not! He wasn't there! How could I hurt his feelings when he wasn't even there?"

"Then I hurt them," said Sonny thoughtfully, "because I told Wilbur, and Wilbur told him."

"Exactly!" cried Mr. Truax, seizing upon this with the relief of a man who has been floundering in the Missouri River and touches a sand-bar. "Exactly! Now you've got it! You're the one that hurt his feelings! Not me! You!"

"But you said it first."

"That," said Mr. Truax, "is neither here nor there!"

Mrs. Truax, perceiving that the conference had arrived at a deadlock not unlike those which occurred at meetings of the Sioux Wells Board of Education, judged it time to intervene with the domestic authority of the female. "Sonny, dear," she said, "Papa only means that we must always try to be kind. Even about people that aren't—that maybe aren't as generous as they might be. Now you tell Papa you're sorry."

"I'm sorry," said Sonny promptly.

"Sorry!" said Mr. Truax. "Sorry doesn't vulcanize any tires! Being sorry isn't going to bring back fourteen trucks! Do you know what Del Gurney said to me before he went out? He said he'd been thinking for some time of giving the Firestone people a trial. A trial! Fourteen trucks! And it took me—it took me forty minutes and two cigars, the good ones, the Havana Perfectos I keep for the bank examiner, to bring him round. Forty minutes! I had to tell him—"

He paused.

"What did you have to tell him, Papa?" asked Sonny, who was genuinely interested.

Mr. Truax cleared his throat. What he had told Mr. Delbert Gurney, standing by the cash-register with an expression of hearty sorrow, was that children made up the darnedest things, that Sonny had been running with a bad crowd at school lately, that the boy had a regular imagination like this Jules Verne, that Elwood Truax had never in his life said one word against a man he regarded as just about the most public-spirited citizen in Sioux Wells, and the best judge of a cigar to boot. Recalling this now, under the round and expectant gaze of his son, Mr. Truax was visited by an emotion which he did not recognize as shame, since he had not felt it in many years, but which he took to be indigestion due to the scorching roast.

"Never mind what I told him," he said. "That's business. That's between grown men. When you're older you'll understand these things."

"Will I understand about tact?"

"Yes. Probably. If you've got any sense." He was conscious that the scene had somehow got away from him, as a sales talk sometimes did when the customer turned out to be a retired schoolteacher, and he made a large effort to recapture it. He planted his feet. He thrust out his jaw in the manner of the portrait of Theodore Roosevelt that hung in the Buffaloes' lodge-room. He lowered his voice, as he did when he was about to describe to the Commercial Men's Bowling League the Spirit of Service.

"Sonny," he said, "I want you to listen to me, and listen good. In this world, a man has got to get along. He's got to be a Mixer. He's got to make friends, and he's got to hang onto 'em. Now, a man may think a lot of things. He may think, say, that a certain party is a little close with his money. That's his privilege. That's what we call free speech, and it's what this country was founded on, and any time a bunch of these foreign agitators come over here and try to tell us different—well, that's another matter. But there's a time to say things and a time not to say 'em. You understand? There's a time and a place. And the dinner-table is the place, and Wilbur Gurney is not the place. You get me?"

Sonny frowned. "Then why did you say the bad word about Mr. Hapgood at Lodge, Papa? Mama said you oughtn't to say it at Lodge, and you said a man ought to say what he thinks right out in meeting, like a man, and not go sneaking around behind people's backs."

Mrs. Truax made a small sound which might have been a cough.

"That," said Mr. Truax, "was different. Hapgood is a Democrat."

He felt that this answer was conclusive. It had been conclusive with every adult in Sioux Wells to whom he had offered it. But Sonny, who did not yet know what a Democrat was, and suspected it to be some sort of beetle, merely waited for more; and when no more came, he looked down again at the threadbare spot on the rug with the courteous patience of a child who has learned that grown-ups frequently stop in the middle of things.

It was this patience, more than any argument, that maddened Mr. Truax. He was accustomed to being answered; he was not accustomed to being waited for. He felt, obscurely, that he was being judged, and that the judge was a person of four feet two inches, with a cowlick and one stocking down, who did not even understand the importance of a fourteen-truck account. It was intolerable. It was un-American.

"All right," he said loudly. "All right. That's enough back-talk. You go up to your room. No supper. No funny papers Sunday. And no—no air-rifle, and don't you ask me again, not for a year."

"I wasn't asking for an air-rifle," said Sonny. "Wilbur has one. I was asking for a bicycle."

"No bicycle, then! Go on! Get!"

Sonny went. He went up the stairs with his hand on the banister, one step at a time, his stocking slipping lower at each step, and at the landing he paused and looked down. His face was not tearful. It was only puzzled, the puzzled face of an explorer who has been handed a map of an unknown country by a native guide and has discovered that the rivers on it run uphill.

"Papa," he said, "is it a secret that I'm being punished? Or can I tell Wilbur?"

"Go to bed!"

The door of the small back bedroom closed, not slammed, which would have been a comfort, but closed with a gentle and reproachful click.

Mr. Truax stood in the hall. Mrs. Truax stood in the doorway of the dining-room. The mission clock ticked. From the kitchen the smell of the roast had changed from scorching to burning, and Mrs. Truax, with a little cry, fled to rescue it.

Mr. Truax went into the living-room and sat down in his own chair, the large leather one with the smoking-stand beside it and the bridge-lamp behind it, and the Sioux Wells Evening Clarion folded on the arm. He picked up the Clarion. He read that the Boosters' Club would hold its annual Father-and-Son banquet on the twenty-third, with an address by the Hon. Purcell D. Blodgett on "Character: The Biggest Asset in the Bank of Life." He put the Clarion down.

He thought of Sonny lying upstairs without supper, and he was irritated, because he had meant to be firm and was now being made uncomfortable by his firmness, which seemed unfair. He thought of Del Gurney and was irritated again, because Del Gurney was a tightwad four-flusher, a man who argued for a nickel off on every retread and kept his own drivers waiting six weeks for their wages, and a fellow ought to be able to say so in his own house. He thought of Hapgood, the Democrat, and felt better for a moment, and then felt worse.

"Doggone it," he said aloud, to the bridge-lamp, "a man tries to raise a kid right—"

He did not finish. It occurred to him, as it occurs to most fathers at least once, and to most of them only once, that he did not entirely know what raising a kid right might consist of, and that the Ladies' Home Journal and the free booklet from the Encyclopædia of Wholesome Knowledge, though full of sound advice about cod-liver oil and the dangers of the moving-pictures, said nothing whatever about how to explain to a boy of seven that honesty was the best policy except when it cost you fourteen trucks.

He was not a philosophical man. He disliked philosophy as he disliked pacifists, poets, and the Firestone Company. He struck the arm of the chair with his fist, said "Well, I've got to be firm, that's all," and went in to supper.

The roast was burned on one side. Mrs. Truax said nothing about it, nor about anything else. She passed the gravy in a silence so complete that Mr. Truax, who had never in twenty years heard his wife be silent at supper, found it more disquieting than any reproach. He ate largely, to show that he was undisturbed, and talked about the price of crude rubber.

At half past eight, when Mrs. Truax had gone to the kitchen to do the dishes, he went quietly up the stairs. He told himself he was going to get his slippers. He did get his slippers. But on the way back he stopped outside the door of the small back bedroom, and stood there, a stout man in his shirt-sleeves holding a pair of carpet slippers, listening.

There was no sound of weeping. There was, very faintly, the rustle of a page. Sonny was reading Tex Larrabee by the light from the street-lamp, Tex Larrabee who never told a lie and never had to explain why.

Mr. Truax went down to the kitchen. He took from the ice-box a glass of milk and two slices of bread and butter, and, after deliberation, a piece of the chocolate cake that was being saved for the Literary Circle. Mrs. Truax watched him and did not say a word, and he did not look at her.

"Kid's got to eat," he muttered. "Can't build character on an empty stomach. Says so in that book."

He carried the tray upstairs and opened the door. Sonny looked up from the bed.

"Here," said Mr. Truax gruffly. "Don't tell your mother."

Then, hearing what he had said, he stood very still in the doorway, with his slippers under one arm and the tray in his two hands. Sonny looked at the cake, and then at his father, and with the solemn, conspiratorial courtesy of a child who has at last grasped a principle, he nodded.

"I won't, Papa," he said. "That's tact."

The chair was hard and mean and creaky. People went through the office and, he thought, stared at him. He felt a belligerent defiance which broke into a wincing fear of this machine which was grinding Paul—Paul— Exactly at half-past three he sent in his name. The attendant returned with “Riesling says he don’t want to see you.”

“You’re crazy! You didn’t give him my name! Tell him it’s George wants to see him, George Babbitt.”

“Yuh, I told him, all right, all right! He said he didn’t want to see you.”

“Then take me in anyway.”

“Nothing doing. If you ain’t his lawyer, if he don’t want to see you, that’s all there is to it.”

“But, my God— Say, let me see the warden.”

“He’s busy. Come on, now, you—” Babbitt reared over him. The attendant hastily changed to a coaxing “You can come back and try to-morrow. Mr. Lucas Prout, the mayor. He bribed the mayor’s doorman with a dollar; he was instantly inside, demanding, “You remember me, Mr. Prout? Babbitt—vice-president of the Boosters—campaigned for you? Say, have you heard about poor Riesling? Well, I want an order on the warden or whatever you call um of the City Prison to take me back and see him. Good. Thanks.” In fifteen minutes he was pounding down the prison corridor to a cage where Paul Riesling sat on a cot, twisted like an old beggar, legs crossed, arms in a knot, biting at his clenched fist. Paul looked up blankly as the keeper unlocked the cell, admitted Babbitt, and left them together. He spoke slowly: “Go on! Be moral!” Babbitt plumped on the couch beside him. “I’m not going to be moral! I don’t care what happened! I just want to do anything I can. I’m glad Zilla got what was coming to her.” Paul said argumentatively, “Now, don’t go jumping on Zilla. I’ve been thinking; maybe she hasn’t had any too easy a time. Just after I shot her— I didn’t hardly mean to, but she got to deviling me so I went crazy, just for a second, and pulled out that old revolver you and I used to shoot rabbits with, and took a crack at her. Didn’t hardly mean to— After that, when I was trying to stop the blood— It was terrible what it did to her shoulder, and she had beautiful skin— Maybe she won’t die. I hope it won’t leave her skin all scarred. But just afterward, when I was hunting through the bathroom for some cotton to stop the blood, I ran onto a little fuzzy yellow duck we hung on the tree one Christmas, and I remembered she and I’d been awfully happy then— Hell. I can’t hardly believe it’s me here.” As Babbitt’s arm tightened about his shoulder, Paul sighed, “I’m glad you came. But I thought maybe you’d lecture me, and when you’ve committed a murder, and been brought here and everything—there was a big crowd outside the apartment house, all staring, and the cops took me through it— Oh, I’m not going to talk about it any more.” But he went on, in a monotonous, terrified insane mumble. To divert him Babbitt said, “Why, you got a scar on your cheek.”

“Yes. That’s where the cop hit me. I suppose cops get a lot of fun out of lecturing murderers, too. He was a big fellow. And they wouldn’t let me help carry Zilla down to the ambulance.”

Good woman, by golly. And afterwards I’ll see that you get started in business out West somewhere, maybe Seattle—they say that’s a lovely city.” Paul was half smiling. It was Babbitt who rambled now. He could not tell whether Paul was heeding, but he droned on till the coming of Paul’s lawyer, P. J. Maxwell, a thin, busy, unfriendly man who nodded at Babbitt and hinted, “If Riesling and I could be alone for a moment—” Babbitt wrung Paul’s hands, and waited in the office till Maxwell came pattering out. “Look, old man, what can I do?” he begged.

“Nothing. Not a thing. Not just now,” said Maxwell. “Sorry. Got to hurry. And don’t try to see him. I’ve had the doctor give him a shot of morphine, so he’ll sleep.” It seemed somehow wicked to return to the office. Babbitt felt as though he had just come from a funeral. He drifted out to the City Hospital to inquire about Zilla. She was not likely to die, he learned. The bullet from Paul’s huge old .44 army revolver had smashed her shoulder and torn upward and out. He wandered home and found his wife radiant with the horrified interest we have in the tragedies of our friends. “Of course Paul isn’t altogether to blame, but this is what comes of his chasing after other women instead of bearing his cross in a Christian way,” she exulted. He was too languid to respond as he desired. He said what was to be said about the Christian bearing of crosses, and went out to clean the car. Dully, patiently, he scraped linty grease from the drip-pan, gouged at the mud caked on the wheels. He used up many minutes in washing his hands; scoured them with gritty kitchen soap; rejoiced in hurting his plump knuckles. “Damn soft hands—like a woman’s. Aah!” At dinner, when his wife began the inevitable, he bellowed, “I forbid any of you to say a word about Paul! I’ll ’tend to all the talking about this that’s necessary, hear me? There’s going to be one house in this scandal-mongering town to-night that isn’t going to spring the holier-than-thou. And throw those filthy evening papers out of the house!” But he himself read the papers, after dinner. Before nine he set out for the house of Lawyer Maxwell. He was received without cordiality. “Well?” said Maxwell.
