It was a little after four o'clock on a Saturday afternoon in the latter part of October when Ambrose Tull, bookkeeper's assistant in the commission house of Gaylord & Wenck, Front Street, came down to the ferry slip at the foot of Market Street to meet his cousin, whom he had not seen in eleven years.

He had been there since half-past three. He had left the office early, by special permission of the head bookkeeper, a dry, yellowish man who had given his consent without lifting his eyes from the ledger. Ambrose had hurried down Front Street in a fever of anticipation, threading his way among the drays and trucks, the hand-carts heaped with crates of onions, the enormous wagons of the produce merchants backed against the sidewalks, and had arrived breathless, his collar wilted, a little cough catching at his throat. Now he stood by one of the iron pillars of the waiting-room, his hat pushed back from his forehead, watching the gates.

The place was thronged. The air was thick with the odours of the bay, of tar, of oakum, of wet planking, and with the smell of the crowd itself, of sweat and of cheap tobacco and of oranges. Newsboys shrilled the evening editions. A peanut-roaster in a corner shrieked continually upon a single exasperating note. Every now and then the floor trembled as a ferry-boat ground against the piles of the slip, and there came a vast clanking of chains and a rumbling of the gangway let down, and then the crowd poured through the gates in a solid mass, a torrent of men and women, hurrying, jostling, crowding one another, their feet making a prodigious shuffling noise upon the boards.

Ambrose was a small man, narrow in the shoulders, with a thin, peaked face and pale eyes, eyes that blinked continually as though the light of day were too much for them. His mustache was sparse and of no particular colour. He wore a suit of black, shiny at the elbows, and on the second finger of his right hand, where the pen rested, was a small ink stain, ineradicable, a mark that no scrubbing removed, so that it had come to be a part of the hand itself. He was thirty-four years old. For eleven years he had sat upon a high stool in the counting-room of Gaylord & Wenck, adding columns of figures relating to hay, barley, potatoes, and wheat, wheat above all, the wheat of the great valleys, which he had never seen growing.

The four-thirty boat came in. The gates opened. The crowd surged forward, and Ambrose, standing on his toes, craned his neck, searching the faces.

All at once he saw him. There was no mistaking him. He towered above the crowd by half a head. He came through the gate like an ox through a flock of sheep, the people falling back from him on either side, and he bore upon his shoulder a carpet-bag that in his grasp seemed no larger than a lunch-pail.

"Ezra!" cried Ambrose. "Ezra! Here! This way!"

The giant turned his head slowly, looking about him, and caught sight of the little bookkeeper waving his hat. A slow grin overspread his face.

"Well, I'll be durned," he said. "Ambrose. Well, I'll be durned."

He came up, dropped the carpet-bag, and put out his hand. It was an enormous hand, red and hairy, hard as a wooden mallet, the knuckles cracked and seamed with dirt that was not dirt but the very soil of the valley ground into the skin. Ambrose's hand disappeared in it. The grip was terrible. Ambrose winced, and laughed to cover his wincing.

"Ezra, I'd have known you anywhere. Anywhere. You haven't changed a particle. Not a particle. Only bigger, I guess."

"I guess I've filled out some," said Ezra.

He had filled out. At twenty-two he had been a raw-boned, gangling youth, all wrists and shanks. Now at thirty-three he was colossal. His shoulders were immense, his neck a column of brick-red muscle that ran down without a break into the vast barrel of his chest. His face was burned almost black by the sun, the skin about his eyes crinkled into a myriad of fine white lines from much squinting across the glare of open country. His hair was yellow, coarse as rope. He wore a suit of brown cheviot, new, bought evidently for the journey, which strained across his back and was too short in the sleeves, and a celluloid collar, and a necktie of brilliant green. He smelled of the train, of coal-smoke and of the dust of the San Joaquin.

"And you," he said, looking down at his cousin. "Why, you ain't hardly growed at all, Ambrose."

"Oh, I keep about the same," said Ambrose, and coughed.

They stood a moment looking at each other, not knowing what to say, smiling foolishly. Then Ambrose caught up the carpet-bag, or tried to, staggered under its weight, and Ezra took it from him gently, as one takes a burden from a child, and swung it to his shoulder again.

"Let's get something to eat," said Ambrose. "I know a place. You must be about starved."

"I could eat some," Ezra admitted.

They went up Market Street together, the little bookkeeper trotting to keep pace with the long, heavy, deliberate stride of the rancher. The street was in the full roar of its Saturday traffic. The cable-cars went clanging by, their grip-men leaning upon the levers; the cables hummed in their slots; there was a never-ending thunder of iron-shod wheels upon the cobbles. The sidewalks were packed. Clerks released from their offices, shop-girls with their arms linked, sailors, Chinamen, messenger boys, women with market baskets, all pushed and elbowed one another in a dense, hurrying, interminable procession. Ezra looked about him with a slow, unwinking stare, like an animal brought suddenly into strange surroundings. He said nothing. Once, when a cable-car shot past within a yard of him, he started violently and put out his free hand as though to fend it off.

"You get used to it," said Ambrose, with a little air of pride.

"I guess you do," said Ezra.

The place Ambrose knew was a German restaurant on Kearny Street, two steps down from the sidewalk, called the Schweizerhalle. It was low-ceilinged and warm, the walls hung with chromos of Swiss lakes and of the Kaiser, and it was full of the smell of sauerkraut, of frying onions, of hot grease, and of beer. There was a long bar at one side, and behind it a fat proprietor in a white apron, polishing glasses. Ambrose came here every Sunday of his life. He was known. The proprietor nodded to him.

They took a table in a corner. Ezra lowered himself upon a bentwood chair, which creaked alarmingly beneath him, and planted his enormous elbows upon the oil-cloth. Ambrose ordered. He ordered lavishly, recklessly, with the prodigality of the poor man playing host: a pot roast with potato pancakes, red cabbage, pickled herring, a dish of sausages, rye bread with caraway seeds, a great wedge of cheese, and two schooners of steam beer. When the food came Ezra ate as he had done everything else, slowly, enormously, steadily, bending his face down over his plate, shovelling in the cabbage with his knife, crushing the bread in his huge fist, his jaws working with the regularity of a machine. Ambrose picked at his herring and watched him, delighted.

"Well," he said at length, "and how's everybody? How's Aunt Sarah?"

Ezra put down his knife.

"Why, didn't you hear? Mother died. Two years ago come February."

Ambrose was dismayed.

"No! I never heard. Nobody ever wrote me. Ezra, I never heard a word."

"Well," said Ezra, "she died. It was her heart. She was out feeding the chickens, and she just set down on the step, and that was all." He took up his knife again. "She used to speak of you. She used to say, 'Ambrose was always the bright one.'"

He saw the little farm in Placer County, the unpainted house, the woodpile, the lean hens scratching in the dooryard, and his aunt, a gaunt, flat-chested woman in a sunbonnet, calling them in to supper across the stubble. "And the old place?" he said.

"Eleven hundred acres!"

"Leased," explained Ezra. "Leased, mostly. Three hundred is mine, clear. The rest I lease off the Tolliver estate." He drank half his schooner at a single draught and wiped his mouth with the back of his hand. "I got married," he added.

"Married! Ezra!"

"Four years ago. Her name's Minnie. Minnie Haas. Her folks are Dutch, from over Hanford way. We got two kids. Boys, both of 'em." He fumbled in an inside pocket and brought out a tintype, which he passed across the table with a certain awkward pride. It showed a broad, fair woman with heavy braids wound about her head, seated rigidly, a baby in her lap, and beside her, scowling at the camera, a fat child in a dress.

"That's Elkanah," said Ezra, pointing with his enormous forefinger. "We named him after Grandpa."

Ambrose looked at the picture a long time. Then he handed it back.

"Grandpa," he repeated. "Elkanah. I'd almost forgot."

"You remember Grandpa?"

"I remember him," said Ambrose.

He remembered him well enough. Old Elkanah Doane, who had come out from Maine in '50 and had dug for gold on the American River and had found a little, and had drunk it, and had dug for more. He remembered him sitting on the porch of the Placer County house in the long summer afternoons, an old man with a tangled white beard stained yellow about the mouth, his eyes red and swimming, and the brown jug always beside his chair. He remembered how the old man would fall into terrible, sudden rages, roaring and smashing things, and how Aunt Sarah would take the two boys out to the barn and keep them there until it was over. Ambrose's hand went out to his schooner. It was empty. He signalled the waiter.

"Another," he said. "Ezra, you'll have another?"

"I guess one's my limit," said Ezra. He was watching his cousin. "I don't hardly touch it, generally. Minnie don't like it."

"Oh, well, one more," said Ambrose. "Just one. It isn't every day."

The beer came. Ambrose drank. A little colour came into his thin cheeks. He began to talk, to talk rapidly, volubly, as he had not talked in years. Ezra considered this gravely.

"I sell to Bodkin, at Hanford," he said.

"Well, but Bodkin sells to somebody, and they sell to us. It all comes through Front Street in the end. It all comes through here." Ambrose struck the table with his small fist. "That's the city for you. Everything comes through here."

He coughed, a dry, hacking little cough that bent him over the table. Ezra watched him, his heavy brows drawn together.

"That's a bad cough you got, Ambrose."

"Oh, that? That's nothing. It's the fog. Everybody has it. You get it in the winter and it goes away in the summer."

"It's October," said Ezra.

"Well, it's a little early this year," said Ambrose, and laughed.

It was dark when they came out of the Schweizerhalle. The street lamps were lit. Ambrose, who was a little unsteady, proposed that they should walk; he wanted Ezra to see the city at night. Below them the city spread out on every side, a vast, glittering confusion of lights, row upon row, tier upon tier, climbing the hills and plunging into the hollows, pricking out the lines of the streets, clustering thick about the water-front, thinning away toward the dark spaces of the west. From below there rose a dull, unceasing murmur, the voice of the city, made up of a thousand thousand sounds, the rumble of wheels, the hum of the cables, the shouts, the whistles, the footsteps, blended together into a single prolonged note, deep and sombre as the sound of the sea. "That's all right," said Ezra.

They stood a while longer. Below them a steamer at the water-front let off a long, hoarse blast, and the sound rolled out over the bay and died away. Then Ezra took out a great silver watch, as thick as a biscuit, and held it close to his eyes.

The gong sounded for the boat. The gates swung open.

"Well," said Ezra. He put out his hand. Again the little hand disappeared in that tremendous grip. "Well, so long, Ambrose."

"Sure," said Ezra. "In the summer."

It was a Saturday, toward six o'clock in the evening, and Anders Hallgren was coming home from his work. All the week long he had been hauling for the Pacific Coast Lumber and Mill Company, driving a great four-horse truck between the wharves at the foot of Third Street and the yards out beyond Brannan, and now the week was finished, his wages were in his pocket, and he was going home to his supper. He walked heavily, with the slow, lurching gait of a man who has stood all day upon the swaying seat of a dray. His boots were enormous. His hands, thrust into the pockets of his canvas coat, were enormous. He was a huge, blond Swede, six feet two in his socks, with a red, square face, a straw-colored mustache that hung down over his mouth, and a jaw like the jaw of one of his own horses: massive, angular, grinding slowly upon a quid of tobacco. His mind was slow and his temper was slow, but when it came it came like the bursting of a dam, and the men at the lumber yards had learned to let him be.

He lived on Tehama Street, between Fourth and Fifth, in the second flat of a narrow wooden house that had once been painted yellow. The street was full of the noise of Saturday evening. Children swarmed upon the sidewalks, shrieking, quarrelling, playing at hop-scotch and leap-frog. A German band was playing in front of a corner saloon, the cornet bellowing, the trombone groaning out its long, rasping notes. There was a smell of frying onions in the air, the smell of coal smoke, of stale beer, of horses, of the tide flats along the bay. A Chinese vegetable peddler went by with his baskets swinging from the pole across his shoulders. Over all, the fog was coming in from the ocean, gray and cold, blotting out the tops of the houses, and the electric lights along Fourth Street were already beginning to show, each with its little halo of mist.

Hallgren climbed the outside stairs. They creaked under his weight. He was thinking of his supper. He was thinking of the pork chops and the boiled potatoes and the coffee that would be waiting for him, and of the pipe he would smoke afterward in the bay window, in his stocking feet, with his coat off, while Lottie washed the dishes and the cuckoo clock that he had brought with him from Göteborg fourteen years before ticked upon the wall. It was his week's end. It was the one hour of the week that he looked forward to. He was content. His content was the content of the ox that has been unyoked and turned into the stall.

But at the head of the stairs his wife met him, and at once he saw that something was wrong.

Lottie Hallgren was a little woman, thin and nervous, with a sharp nose and pale eyes, and hair the color of dead grass, twisted up into a tight knot at the back of her head. She was wiping her hands upon her apron, over and over again, though they were quite dry. She had been crying.

"Oh, Anders," she said, "oh, Anders, I'm glad you've come. I didn't know what to do. I didn't know what to do."

"What is it?" he said. "Hey? What's the matter, then?"

"It's Nils. Oh, it's Nils again. He's hurt the Fennessy girl. He's hurt her bad. He hit her with a rock, a great big rock as big as your fist, and her head was all bleeding, and Mrs. Fennessy came up here and screamed at me. Oh, she screamed at me something terrible, Anders, right out on the landing where everybody could hear. She said she'd have the police. She said she'd have him took up and put in the Reform School. She said he was a little devil, and that he'd end on the gallows. Oh, I didn't know what to do. I didn't know what to do."

Hallgren stood still in the doorway, his hat on his head, his hands still in his pockets. He did not understand at first. His mind moved slowly, like one of his own loaded trucks starting up a grade, and it was some time before it was fairly under way. Then little by little he understood. Nils had hurt somebody. Nils had struck a little girl with a rock. There had been blood. There had been a scene, a scandal, a screaming woman on the landing. The police had been spoken of.

"Where is he?" he said.

"He's in the back room. He's hiding under the bed. He's been there ever since. I couldn't get him out. Oh, Anders, don't be too hard on him. He's only a baby. He didn't know. He didn't mean it."

Hallgren took his hands out of his pockets.

"Get supper," he said.

He went down the narrow, dark entry toward the back room. The floor shook under him. The dishes rattled upon the shelf in the kitchen. Lottie, standing by the stove, the frying pan in her hand, listened to his steps, her lips parted, her pale eyes very wide.

The back room was small and close, and smelled of soap and of damp plaster. It had one window that gave upon the back yards, upon a wilderness of clothes-lines and board fences and tin cans and ash barrels, and beyond, upon the blank wall of a cigar factory. The light was failing. In one corner was the bed, a great iron bed painted white, with brass knobs at the corners, and a patchwork quilt; and under the bed, far back against the wall, in the dust and the darkness, crouched a little boy.

"Come out," said Hallgren.

There was no answer.

"Come out. You hear me? Come out of there."

Nothing stirred. Only, from under the bed, there came a sound of breathing, short and quick, like the breathing of some small animal that has been run to earth.

Hallgren stooped, and putting one enormous hand beneath the bed, took hold of whatever he could find. It was an ankle. He pulled, and the boy came out, sliding over the floor upon his stomach, clutching at the legs of the bed, at the edge of the rag carpet, at the floor itself, kicking, struggling, silent. His father set him upon his feet in the middle of the room and stood looking down at him.

Nils Hallgren was seven years old. He was large for his age, broad in the shoulders, solid in the legs, with a round head covered with tow-colored hair that stood up in a tuft at the crown. His face was smeared with dust and with the dried marks of tears. His blouse was torn at the neck. He did not cry now. He stood with his feet planted wide apart, his hands clenched at his sides, his head lowered, looking up at his father from under his eyebrows. And his jaw was set. That was what one noticed first and last about him: his jaw, square and heavy, too heavy for a child's face, thrust forward, the lower lip pushed out, the teeth shut tight.

"Did you hit the Fennessy girl with a rock?" said Hallgren.

The boy said nothing.

"You hear me? Did you do it? Hey? Answer me when I talk to you."

"Yes," said Nils.

"What for?"

The boy was silent a moment, then, all at once, the words came out of him in a rush, thick and choked:

"She took my top. She took my new top what Uncle Sven gave me, and she wouldn't give it back, and she laughed at me. She laughed. And she said I talked like a Swede. And I told her to give it back, and she wouldn't, and she held it up high so I couldn't reach, and laughed, and all the other kids laughed. And so I hit her. I hit her with a rock. And I'm glad. I'm glad I hit her. I'd do it again."

"Ha!" said Hallgren.

He felt the blood come up into his face. He felt it beat in his neck, in his temples, behind his eyes. It was not so much what the boy had done; it was the defiance of him, the stubbornness, the little set jaw thrust up at him, the fists clenched, the voice that said, "I'd do it again." This was his son. This was his own boy, and he stood there and talked back to him, to him, Anders Hallgren, who had been driving four horses all day long through the mud and the dray-traffic of Townsend Street, who had come home tired and wanted his supper and his pipe, and who must stand here in the dusk and be defied by a child that did not come up to his belt.

"You'd do it again, would you?" he said. His voice was rising. "You'd do it again? You hit a little girl with a rock, so the blood come, and her mother come up here and yell at your mother, and say the police come, and you'd do it again? By God, I show you. I show you something."

He looked about him. Upon a nail behind the door there hung a strap, an old leather strap that had once been part of a set of harness, black and supple and cracked with use. He took it down. The boy's eyes followed it. They grew suddenly very wide. But he did not move, and his jaw did not relax.

Then a strange thing happened to Anders Hallgren.

He had the strap in his hand, and he had taken a step toward the boy, and his arm was lifted; and all at once he was no longer in the back room on Tehama Street. He was in a low, dark kitchen in a farmhouse in Småland, with a peat fire smoldering on the hearth and snow lying deep outside, and he was seven years old himself; and over him there stood a man, a great, gaunt, silent man with a beard, his father, Olaf Hallgren, and in his father's hand there was a strap. He remembered it all, suddenly, with an extraordinary vividness, as one remembers things in dreams. He remembered the smell of the peat smoke and of wet wool. He remembered the sound of the strap. He remembered how his father's face had looked, not angry, but quite still and white, and his eyes, how they had gone small and bright and fixed, like the eyes of a dog that has caught the scent of blood. And he remembered that his father had not been able to stop. That was the thing he remembered best of all. His father had begun, and then he had not been able to stop. Something had got hold of him, something that was not Olaf Hallgren at all, but older than he, deeper, a thing that had come up out of some black pit inside him and taken possession of him, so that he struck, and struck, and struck, long after the boy had ceased to cry, until the mother had come running in from the barn and flung herself between them. And afterward, the father had gone out of the house without a word and had not come back until the next day. And Anders had lain on the straw in the loft for a week, and had not been able to sit down.

And his father's father, they said, had been the same. A great man in his parish, a hard man, a man who drank and fought and, in a rage once, had killed a horse with an axe. It was in the blood. It came down from father to son, the vicious taint, the evil heritage, like a dark stream running underground, never seen, never heard, but always there; flowing on beneath the surface of things, beneath the decent, sober, hard-working life of honest men, waiting, waiting, ready at any moment to burst up into the daylight. It was the brute in them. It was the beast.

Anders Hallgren stood still in the middle of the room with the strap in his hand, and he felt it stirring in him now. He felt it plainly. It was like a hot, thick liquid rising slowly in his throat. He felt his fingers tighten upon the strap. He felt a kind of tingling in his arm, an itching, an eagerness, a desire to strike and to go on striking. His breath came short. His eyes, he knew, were growing small. And there before him stood the boy, the little stubborn boy with the square jaw, looking up at him, waiting.

The jaw. It was his own jaw. It was Olaf Hallgren's jaw. Hallgren saw it suddenly, and he saw it with a kind of terror. It was the same, it was the very same; the heavy, protruding, salient jaw, the jaw of the carnivora, the jaw that the Hallgrens had carried with them out of Småland, generation after generation, as they carried their blond hair and their great hands and their slow, terrible tempers. The boy had it. It was in him already. He was seven years old, and already he had hit a girl with a rock so that the blood came, and was glad. Already it was rising in him, the dark stream, the foul heritage. And here was he, the father, with the strap in his hand, ready to beat it into him, to beat it in deeper, as it had been beaten into himself in the kitchen in Småland thirty years ago.

"Ah," said Hallgren, aloud. "Ah, no. No."

He dropped the strap. It fell upon the floor between them, and lay there in a black coil like a dead snake.

The boy stared at it, and then at his father. He did not understand. His lower lip began to tremble. All at once, now that the blow was not coming, he began to cry, not as a child cries, loudly, but silently, his face working, the big tears running down through the dust on his cheeks. He did not unclench his fists.

Hallgren sat down upon the edge of the iron bed. It creaked and sagged beneath him. He was breathing hard, as though he had been lifting heavy timbers. He took off his hat and turned it round and round between his knees, looking at it. For a long time he did not say anything. Out in the kitchen they could hear the pork chops sizzling in the pan, and the clatter of dishes, and Lottie moving about. From the street there came the sound of the German band, and of the children shrieking, and of a car-bell on Fourth Street, clang, clang, clang. In the front room the cuckoo clock struck the half-hour, and the little wooden bird came out of its door and said "Cuckoo" once, and went back again.

"Come here," said Hallgren at last.

The boy came slowly, dragging his feet, and stood in front of him. Hallgren put one huge hand upon his shoulder. The hand covered it entirely, and part of his arm besides.

"Listen," he said. "You listen to me now. I don't lick you. Not this time. But you listen to what I say. You understand me?"

The boy nodded, sniffling.

"You got a bad temper. Hey? You know that. You got a bad temper, like I got, like your grandfather got. It's in you. It's in all of us Hallgrens. Something gets hold of you, and you don't know what you do. You get mad, and you see red, and you hit. You hit with a rock. Bimeby when you get big you hit with something else, maybe, a knife, maybe a club, and then you kill somebody. Then they hang you. That's what Mrs. Fennessy say, and by God she's right. You understand that?"

He shook the boy a little, not roughly, but heavily, as he might have shaken a sack to settle the grain in it.

"She took my top," said Nils, in a whisper.

"Sure she took your top. And she laugh at you. And she say you talk like a Swede. All right. You *are* a Swede. I'm a Swede. That's nothing. You don't hit girls with a rock for that. You don't hit nobody with a rock for that. Listen. When I was a little feller like you, my father licked me. He licked me so I couldn't sit down for a week. He licked me because I was mad, and he was mad, too, and so he licked me. And it don't do no good. It make me madder. It make me worse. I fight every boy in the parish after that. And when I come over here I fight on the boats, and I fight on the docks, and once I near kill a man in a saloon on Pacific Street. Ya, I near kill him. I don't tell your mother that. I'm telling you. And I don't want you should be like that. You hear? I don't want you should be like me."

He had never said so much at one time in his life. The words came hard. He was not used to them. He stumbled over them and repeated himself, and his great red face grew redder; but he kept on, doggedly, the way he drove his horses up the hill on Second Street with a load of redwood behind them, a step at a time.

"When you feel it come, that mad feeling, you know what you do? You put your hands in your pockets. Like this. See? You put them in your pockets and you hold on tight, and you count, one, two, three, four, all the way up to twenty. And you don't take them out. Not till it go away. And it go away. Bimeby it always go away. You hear me?"

"Yes," said Nils.

"You promise me that?"

"Yes."

"All right."

Hallgren got up. He picked the strap off the floor, looked at it a moment, and then, instead of hanging it upon the nail behind the door, he opened the window and flung it out into the back yard among the ash barrels and the tin cans. Then he put on his hat.

"Now," he said, "you come along with me."

The boy hung back. "Where we going?"

"We go down to the Fennessys'. You tell Mrs. Fennessy you're sorry. You tell the little girl you're sorry. Then we see."

"I don't want to."

Hallgren looked down at him. The jaw had come out again, the lower lip, the scowl. For an instant, a bare instant, the hot thing stirred once more in Hallgren's throat. He felt it, and set his teeth upon it, and thrust his hands deep into the pockets of his canvas coat. He stood there, a huge, motionless figure in the dusk, and his lips moved. He was counting.

The boy watched him. Something in the sight seemed to impress him enormously. He stood very still, staring at his father's hands buried in the pockets, at his father's lips moving; and slowly, slowly, his own jaw went back into its place.

"All right," he said. "I'll go."

They went out through the kitchen. Lottie turned from the stove, the fork in her hand, and looked at them, at the boy's face, at her husband's; and seeing that the boy had not been beaten, she gave a little gasp, and put her hand to her throat.

"We go down to Fennessys'," said Hallgren. "Keep supper hot."

They went down the outside stairs together, the father first, the boy after him, and out upon the sidewalk. The fog had shut down thick and wet over the whole city. The street lamps were blurred and yellow. The German band had moved on to the next corner, and the cornet sounded far off and melancholy through the mist. The children had mostly gone in to their suppers. A drunken man went by, singing. Somewhere a dog was barking, over and over again, monotonously.

Halfway down the block the boy put out his hand, and his father took it. It was a small, hard, dirty hand, and it disappeared entirely within the other. They went on in silence, the great slow Swede and the little stubborn one, side by side, through the fog. Hallgren did not speak. He was thinking. He was thinking, in his dull, laborious way, of the dark stream that ran underground, of the thing that came up out of the pit, of his father, and his father's father, and the horse that had been killed with an axe. He did not know whether he had done right. He did not know whether a man could fight against a thing like that, a thing that was in the blood, older than himself, stronger than himself, and win. He did not know. He only knew that he had dropped the strap, and that the boy's hand was in his, and that the boy had not cried out when he was afraid.

Behind them, in the flat on Tehama Street, the cuckoo clock that had come from Göteborg struck the hour, and the little wooden bird came out of its door and called out into the empty room, seven times, and went back again.

When she had gone, Lyman rose, stretching himself putting up three fingers to hide his yawn. To further loosen his muscles, he took a couple of turns the length of he room, noting with satisfaction its fine appointments, the padded red carpet, the dull olive green tint of the walls, the few choice engravings—portraits of Marshall, Taney, Field, and a coloured lithograph—excellently done—of the Grand Canyon of the Colorado—the deep-seated leather chairs, the large and crowded bookcase (topped with a bust of James Lick, and a huge greenish globe), the waste basket of woven coloured grass, made by Navajo Indians, the massive silver inkstand on the desk, the elaborate filing cabinet, complete in every particular, and the shelves of tin boxes, padlocked, impressive, grave, bearing the names of clients, cases and estates. Unlike Harran, he resembled his mother, but he was much darker than Annie Derrick and his eyes were much fuller, the eyeball protruding, giving him a pop-eyed, foreign expression, quite unusual and unexpected. His hair was black, and he wore a small, tight, pointed mustache, which he was in the habit of pushing delicately upward from the corners of his lips with the ball of his thumb, the little finger extended. As often as he made this gesture, he prefaced it with a little twisting gesture of the forearm in order to bring his cuff into view, and, in fact, this movement by itself was habitual. He was dressed carefully, his trousers creased, a pink rose in his lapel. His office was on the tenth floor of the EXCHANGE BUILDING, a beautiful, tower-like affair of white stone, that stood on the corner of Market Street near its intersection with Kearney, the most imposing office building of the city. The lamp had been lit early that evening in the kitchen of the Kettering place, for the fog had come in from the bay at four o'clock, rolling over the Santa Cruz hills in great, sluggish billows, grey, wet, impenetrable, blotting out the orchard rows one after another, the nearest trees standing up in it like the masts of drowned ships. By six it was dark. The drying-yard behind the house, the long trays of split apricots, the sulphur-house, the packing shed with its stencilled boxes piled to the rafters, all were gone, swallowed up, and only the drip, drip, drip from the eaves of the porch told that the world outside still existed at all.

Hilda Kettering sat at the kitchen table, under the lamp, with the account book open before her. It was a long, narrow book, bound in mottled boards, the corners worn round and greasy from much handling, and she had ruled its pages herself in red and black ink, very neat, very exact, the columns of figures marching down them in close, upright files like soldiers. She wrote with a steel pen, holding it near the nib, her lips moving a little as she added, her forehead creased. Every now and then she paused, wiped the pen upon a bit of flannel she kept for that purpose, and looked across the room toward the door that gave upon the porch, listening.

She was a big woman, Swedish on her mother's side, with heavy, smooth, yellow hair drawn tight back from a broad forehead and twisted into a knot at the nape of her neck. Her arms, bare to the elbow, were large and white and very strong, the arms of a woman who had kneaded bread and turned the drying trays and carried the slop-buckets to the pigs every day of her married life. Her face was calm, even placid; but there was a certain set to the jaw, a certain hardness about the corners of the mouth, that the lamp, striking upward from below, brought out with singular distinctness. She was thirty-four years old. She had been married eleven years.

Around her the kitchen was in perfect order. The range had been blacked that afternoon and shone like a new boot. The tin dish-pan hung upon its nail; the dish-towels, washed and wrung, were spread upon the rack above the stove. On the shelves stood the jars of preserves of her own putting up, apricot, peach, plum, quince, ranged according to their kinds, with labels written in her square, careful hand. The floor was scrubbed white. The clock upon the bracket over the woodbox, a cheap clock with a picture of a steamboat painted on the glass of its door, ticked loudly, insistently, with a little wheezing catch at every fourth stroke, as though it laboured.

At a quarter past eight she heard the wagon.

It came up out of the fog along the lane, the wheels grinding in the wet gravel, the horses blowing, and she heard her husband's voice, thick, a little hoarse, swearing at the off-horse as he backed the wagon under the shed. Then for a long time nothing. Then his step upon the porch, heavy, deliberate, the step of a man who weighed two hundred pounds and was not ashamed of it, and the door opened and Ben Kettering came in, bringing the fog with him in a cold, wet breath that made the lamp flare and smoke.

He was a huge fellow, bigger even than his wife, with enormous shoulders that stooped a little, and great red hands that hung at his sides as if he did not quite know what to do with them. His face was red, too, wind-burned, the skin cracked across the cheekbones, and his small blue eyes were set close together under a thatch of sandy brows. His mustache, sandy also, drooped over his mouth and was beaded now with the wet. He wore a canvas coat lined with blanket, and corduroy trousers tucked into boots that were caked to the ankle with the red mud of the lane.

"Hello," he said.

"Shut the door, Ben. You're letting in the fog."

He shut it, and stood a moment by it, unbuttoning his coat with slow, clumsy fingers. He did not look at her. He looked at the stove, at the clock, at the jars upon the shelves, anywhere but at the table where she sat with the account book open beneath the lamp.

"Supper's in the oven," she said. "I kept it warm."

"I ain't hungry. I had something in town."

"Where'd you have it?"

"At Schmitt's."

She said nothing to this, but dipped her pen and made a figure in the margin of the book, a small figure, very neat. Schmitt's was a saloon, by the depot, where the teamsters and the cannery men drank steam beer and played pedro in the back room, and where, as she knew very well, there was always to be found a free lunch of pickled herring, rye bread, and cold sausage for any man who bought two glasses. Ben hung his coat upon the nail behind the door. Then, as though he had come to a resolution, he dragged a chair from the wall and sat down across the table from her, his elbows upon the oilcloth, his great hands clasped together.

"Well," he said, "I seen Lessing."

"I know you did."

He looked up quickly, startled. "How'd you know?"

"Mrs. Dutra was by this afternoon. Her husband seen you go into the Association office at two o'clock. She said you was in there an hour."

"Well, what if I was? Ain't I got a right to go into the Association office? Ain't I a grower?"

"You got a right," she said quietly. "What did Lessing say?"

Ben did not at once reply. He unclasped his hands and laid them flat upon the oilcloth, palms down, spreading the thick fingers wide, and looked at them. The clock ticked; the fog dripped from the eaves; somewhere out in the orchard a night-bird called once, a long, wavering note, and was silent.

"He says," began Ben at last, "he says the Packers' Combine has fixed it. Four cents. Four cents a pound for the dried, delivered at the warehouse in San José. That's the figure. That's all they'll pay. Every packer in the county has signed with them. There ain't a buyer anywheres, Hilda, not one, that'll go a fraction over. Lessing says they've got it sewed up tight, the whole valley, from Gilroy clean to Alviso."

"Four cents," she repeated.

"Four cents."

"Last year it was seven and a half."

"I know what it was last year."

She bent over the book again. Her pen moved swiftly down the column, then stopped. She drew a line, very straight, with the edge of a blotter for a rule, and wrote a figure beneath it, and looked at the figure for a long moment without speaking. Then she turned the book about upon the table so that it faced him, and pushed it toward him with the end of her pen.

"There," she said. "Look at that."

"I don't want to look at it."

"Look at it, Ben."

He looked at it, frowning, his lips moving as hers had moved, his heavy forefinger following the column down. He was slow with figures; he had never been able to carry them in his head as she could; and she watched him, her hands folded in her lap, while he toiled down the page, item by item: the interest on the note at the bank, the price of the sulphur, the trays, the wages of the Portuguese and the Japs who had cut the 'cots in July, the hauling, the boxes, the feed for the horses, the payment due in October upon the forty acres they had bought of the Delmas estate four years before. At the bottom was the figure she had written, and beside it, in red ink, a second figure, smaller.

"What's the red?" he asked.

"The red's what we lose. At four cents."

He stared at it. The blood came up slowly into his face, darkening the wind-burn to a dull brick colour, mounting to his forehead, to the roots of his sandy hair. He pushed the book away from him.

"Well, then, we lose it," he exclaimed. "What can I do? Can I make 'em pay seven? Can I go down to San José and take the Combine by the neck? It ain't me that fixed the price. It's them. It's the Combine. You talk like it was my fault."

"I ain't said it was your fault."

"You look it."

"I ain't said it was your fault," she repeated, in exactly the same tone, level, unhurried, without emphasis. "I'm asking what you done about it. What did you tell Lessing?"

She knew him so well. She had watched him for eleven years; she knew every turn of his slow mind, every trick of his great body: the way his eyes slid away from hers when he had been drinking, the way he cleared his throat before a lie, the way his hands, those enormous red hands, went flat upon the table when he was afraid. They were flat upon the table now.

"Ben," she said, "what did you sign?"

"I didn't sign nothing."

"Ben."

"I didn't sign nothing, I tell you!" he shouted, and struck the table with his fist so that the lamp chimney rattled and the pen leaped from the inkwell to the floor. "I didn't sign! I just—I told him he could have it. I told him to put me down. The whole crop, the 'cots and the prunes both. What else was I to do? He says if I don't come in now, before the first, they won't take it at all. Not at four cents, not at three. Not at any price. He says they'll leave it lay in the shed and rot. He says it's that or nothing, and the ones that hold out will get nothing, and serve 'em right. He showed me the list. Lockhart's on it. Pellegrini's on it. Old Mattos is on it. Every man on the road. I wasn't going to be the only one, was I? Was I going to hold out alone, me, against the whole Combine?"

Hilda stooped, picked up the pen, wiped it carefully upon the bit of flannel, and laid it in the groove of the inkstand. She did all this slowly, without haste, and when she had done she sat back in her chair and looked at her husband steadily across the lamp.

"You give your word," she said.

"Yes, I give my word."

"Before you come home. Before you asked me."

"Was I to ask you? Ain't I the one that runs this ranch? Do I got to come to you like a kid every time I want to—"

"The forty acres is in my name, Ben."

He stopped short. His mouth remained open a little under the drooping mustache, and he stared at her, and she saw in his small blue eyes a kind of bewilderment, the dull, uncomprehending anger of an ox that has been struck from an unexpected quarter.

"What's that got to do with it?"

"It's got this to do with it. The Delmas forty is in my name. Pa's money paid for it. The note at the bank is in my name. The prunes off that forty is mine, Ben. Every pound. You didn't have no right to give 'em to Lessing, and you know it. You knew it when you done it. That's why you went to Schmitt's first. That's why you didn't come home to supper."

It was true; and because it was true, because she had seen through him so easily, so contemptuously, without even raising her voice, a sudden fury seized upon the man. It came up in him from somewhere deep down, blind, unreasoning, elemental, the anger of the male who finds himself checked, thwarted, held in by a woman's hand. He got up, and his chair went over behind him with a crash upon the scrubbed floor, and he stood there, swaying a little, enormous, looming over the table, over the lamp, over her, his shadow flung up gigantic against the wall and the ceiling, filling the little kitchen.

"Your name!" he cried. "Your money! Your pa! Always your pa! I'm sick of hearing it. Who planted them trees? Who grafted 'em? Who dug the ditch and set the flume and got up at three in the morning in the frost to light the smudge-pots? Was it your pa? Your pa was in the cemetery. It was me! It was me done it, with these hands. Look at 'em!" He thrust them out at her across the table, the great red hands, the fingers knotted, the nails broken, the palms seamed and cracked and calloused, the knuckles scarred. "Look at 'em! Them's what made the Delmas forty. Not your pa's money. Not your name on a piece of paper at the bank."

She did not shrink. She did not even look at the hands. She looked at his face, and her own face did not change.

"Pick up your chair, Ben," she said.

For a moment it seemed as though he would strike her. His fist closed, and the muscles of his forearm stood out in ridges under the skin, and his breath came short and loud through his nose. The clock wheezed and caught and ticked on. Then, quite suddenly, the fury went out of him, as it always did, as she had known it would, draining away and leaving him slack, heavy, bewildered, a little ashamed. He turned about, fumbled for the chair, set it upright, and sat down in it again. He put his elbows on the table and his head in his hands.

"I didn't mean nothing," he muttered.

"I know you didn't."

"It's just—I don't know what to do, Hilda. I swear to God I don't. It's like—it's like being in a fog. You can't see where you're going. You can't see nothing. You just go along."

And then, for the first time that evening, something moved in the woman's face, something that was not hardness. It was gone again almost at once. She drew the account book back to her side of the table and sat looking at it.

For she, too, saw it, though more clearly than he. She saw the thing that he could only feel, dimly, as a pressure, as a weight. She saw the Combine: not Lessing, not the little bald-headed man in the Association office with his gold eyeglasses and his list of names, but the thing behind Lessing, the thing that had no face and no name, that sat in offices in San José and in San Francisco, and, beyond these, in Chicago, in New York, in places she had never seen and could not imagine. She saw it reaching down, reaching out, into every valley of the State, into every orchard, every drying-yard, every packing shed, setting its price, four cents, three cents, any cents it chose, and the growers, the little men, the Kettering and the Mattos and the Pellegrini, scrambling to come in under it, signing, giving their word, glad to be let in at all. She saw it as a vast, slow, insensate force, like the fog itself, rolling in over the hills, blotting out landmark after landmark, enveloping everything, indifferent, cold, without malice and without mercy. It did not hate them. It did not even know their names. It simply went forward, as the tide goes forward, as the seasons go forward, and whatever lay in its path was covered over and submerged.

And against this, what had she? A book of accounts, ruled in red and black. A piece of paper at the bank with her name upon it. Forty acres of prune trees, eleven years old, just coming into their full bearing. A husband who could not add.

"Ben," she said at length, "look at me."

He raised his head.

"Lessing told you if you didn't come in now they'd leave the crop lay. He told you that?"

"Yes."

"Did he tell you about the Eastern buyers?"

"What Eastern buyers?"

"Mrs. Dutra says there's a man stopping at the Vendome, from Philadelphia. A buyer for some grocery house back there. He's been out to Campbell and to Los Gatos. He's been buying direct from the growers, the ones that ain't signed. Five cents. Five and a quarter for the big prunes, forties to fifties. Paying cash, and shipping by the carload, and the Combine can't touch him because he don't go through the packers at all."

Ben stared at her. "Who told Mrs. Dutra that?"

"Her brother-in-law sold him two hundred boxes Tuesday."

"Lessing never said nothing about that."

"No," said Hilda. "He wouldn't."

Ben was silent a long while, his heavy brows drawn together, laboriously turning the thing over and over in his mind. She could all but see the idea entering, slowly, painfully, finding its way among the confusion there, the beer and the shame and the anger and the fear.

"But I give my word," he said at last.

"You give your word for your crop. You didn't have no crop to give but the old orchard. The Delmas forty ain't yours to give. I never give mine."

"Lessing won't see it that way."

"Lessing can see it any way he likes. It's in my name. It's on paper. He's a lawyer's clerk; he knows what paper means. Let him come and talk to me."

"He'll say I lied to him."

"Then you'll have to stand it, Ben."

He looked at her helplessly. "And if the Philadelphia man's gone? If he's bought all he wants? If he don't want ours?"

"Then we've lost nothing but a day. And if Lessing won't take it after, then I'll take it to San José myself, in the wagon, and stand on the sidewalk in front of the Combine's office and sell it by the pound to whoever comes by. I ain't going to give it away, Ben. Not my pa's forty. Not for four cents. Not to nobody."

She said it without heat, without raising her voice, without any gesture at all, her big white hands lying folded upon the open book; and something in the very quietness of it, the dead, flat, immovable obstinacy of it, impressed the man more than any outcry could have done. He knew that tone. He had heard it at her father's funeral, when the Delmas heirs had tried to cheat her of the water-right; he had heard it the winter the bank had wanted to foreclose. It meant that she would not move. It meant that she would go on, and on, and on, like the tide, like the fog, like the Combine itself, and that nothing he could say, nothing anybody could say, would turn her by so much as a hair's breadth.

"All right," he said at length, heavily. "All right, Hilda. I'll go into town in the morning and find this feller."

"No," she answered. "I'll go. You stay and see to the sulphuring. The trays in the south yard want turning."

He did not protest. He sat there a while longer, his big shoulders sagging, staring at the lamp. Then he rose, slowly, and went to the stove and opened the oven door, and took out the plate she had kept warm for him, the boiled beef and the potatoes and the cabbage, dried and shrunken now with the long waiting, and brought it back to the table, and sat down, and began to eat, mechanically, without appetite, because it was there and because he did not know what else to do.

Hilda watched him a moment. Then she drew the account book toward her, dipped her pen, and, very carefully, very neatly, with the blotter for a rule, drew a single straight line through the figure in red ink. Beneath it she wrote nothing at all. She wiped the pen upon the bit of flannel and laid it in its groove.

Outside, the fog pressed close against the windows, grey, thick, motionless, and the drip from the eaves went on, steadily, monotonously, as though it would never stop; and in the kitchen there was no sound but the scrape of the man's fork upon his plate, and the loud, laborious ticking of the clock, wheezing, catching, and going on.

“That's all for the present,” he said at length. Without reply, the typewriter rose and withdrew, thrusting her pencil into the coil of her hair, closing the door behind her, softly, discreetly. When she had gone, Lyman rose, stretching himself putting up three fingers to hide his yawn. To further loosen his muscles, he took a couple of turns the length of he room, noting with satisfaction its fine appointments, the padded red carpet, the dull olive green tint of the walls, the few choice engravings—portraits of Marshall, Taney, Field, and a coloured lithograph—excellently done—of the Grand Canyon of the Colorado—the deep-seated leather chairs, the large and crowded bookcase (topped with a bust of James Lick, and a huge greenish globe), the waste basket of woven coloured grass, made by Navajo Indians, the massive silver inkstand on the desk, the elaborate filing cabinet, complete in every particular, and the shelves of tin boxes, padlocked, impressive, grave, bearing the names of clients, cases and estates. He was between thirty-one and thirty-five years of age. Unlike Harran, he resembled his mother, but he was much darker than Annie Derrick and his eyes were much fuller, the eyeball protruding, giving him a pop-eyed, foreign expression, quite unusual and unexpected. His hair was black, and he wore a small, tight, pointed mustache, which he was in the habit of pushing delicately upward from the corners of his lips with the ball of his thumb, the little finger extended. As often as he made this gesture, he prefaced it with a little twisting gesture of the forearm in order to bring his cuff into view, and, in fact, this movement by itself was habitual. He was dressed carefully, his trousers creased, a pink rose in his lapel. His shoes were of patent leather, his cutaway coat was of very rough black cheviot, his double-breasted waistcoat of tan covered cloth with buttons of smoked pearl. Below him the city swarmed tumultuous through its grooves, the cable-cars starting and stopping with a gay jangling of bells and a strident whirring of jostled glass windows. It was a continuous interest in small things, a people ever willing to be amused at trifles, refusing to consider serious matters—good-natured, allowing themselves to be imposed upon, taking life easily—generous, companionable, enthusiastic; living, as it were, from day to day, in a place where the luxuries of life were had without effort; in a city that offered to consideration the restlessness of a New York, without its earnestness; the serenity of a Naples, without its languor; the romance of a Seville, without its picturesqueness. The train from Sacramento was late, and Otto Riemer, who had been waiting upon the platform of the Sixteenth Street station since a quarter past four, had walked its length perhaps a hundred times. He walked slowly, heavily, his hands clasped behind him beneath the tails of his best coat, his chin sunk upon the knot of his cravat, pausing at either end to look up the long double line of the rails that converged far off in the haze of the marshes and were lost there. Twice he consulted the great clock that hung over the ticket window. Twice he drew out his own watch, a fat silver affair with a hunting case, and compared the two, frowning at the discrepancy. Once he bought a cigar of the man in the news-stand, and having bought it, put it away in his waistcoat pocket without lighting it, as if he had forgotten why he wanted it.

He was a large man of thirty-eight or thereabouts, built square, thick through the chest and shoulders, with the short neck and the red, close-shaven jowl of his people. His hair was yellow, cropped very close, so that the scalp showed pink beneath it. His hands were enormous, the fingers blunt and seamed, the nails broken, and in the creases of the knuckles there was a fine grey dust that no soap could ever quite remove, the dust of the planing mill where for eleven years he had been first hand and for four years foreman. He was dressed with a painful care: a suit of black diagonal, a celluloid collar, a cravat of purple satin, and shoes that were new and that hurt him.

It was eight years since he had seen his cousin August, eight years since Gus had gone away to the copper country in Arizona, swearing that he would come back rich or not at all. In that time there had been perhaps a dozen letters, ill-spelled and brief, written in pencil upon the ruled paper of mining-camp stores; then nothing for two years; then, the week before, a telegram from Sacramento: "Coming down Thursday on the 4.20. Gus."

At length the train came. It came in with a vast deliberation, the locomotive grinding upon the curve, the bell clanging, the steam spreading out in great white rolls along the platform, and the cars, one after another, sliding past, dusty, cinder-stained, the windows streaked with the alkali of the desert. The platform swarmed. There was a jostling and a confusion, a shouting of hackmen, a trundling of baggage trucks, a running to and fro of porters in white jackets. Otto planted himself near the steps of the smoking car, his head thrust forward, his eyes moving from face to face.

He did not know his cousin at first. A man had swung down from the car behind, a tall man, lean, burned black by the sun, wearing a suit of light checked stuff, very new and very loud, a soft hat of grey felt, and a heavy watch chain of nuggets strung across his waistcoat. He carried a valise of yellow leather. He stood a moment looking about him, and Otto's glance passed over him and went on. Then the man laughed, a short, harsh laugh, and Otto turned back.

"Say, don't you know me? Don't you know your own folks any more?"

"Gus!"

"Well, I guess yes."

They shook hands, gripping hard, each trying, after the old fashion of their boyhood, to crush the other's fingers, and neither giving way. Then they stood off and looked at each other, grinning, at a loss, while the crowd flowed around them.

"Well, well, well," said Otto. "Well, well, well."

"You got fat," declared Gus. "You got fat as a hog, Otto. You got a belly on you like a brewer."

"And you," returned the other, "you got so thin a man could see daylight through you. What they been feeding you down there? Cactus?"

"Beans," said Gus, "and bacon, and canned tomatoes. Eight years of beans and bacon and canned tomatoes. I tell you, I ain't going to look a bean in the face again as long as I live."

They went out of the station together, Otto insisting upon carrying the valise and Gus refusing, so that in the end they carried it between them, each holding one handle, like two schoolboys. Outside, Otto would have taken the street-car, but Gus would not hear of it. He hailed a hack, a great lumbering vehicle with a team of bays, and climbed in, throwing himself back upon the cushions with an air, and when they arrived before the flat on Castro Street where Otto lived, he gave the driver a dollar and would not take the change.

Otto watched this with a certain uneasiness, his little blue eyes blinking. A dollar for the hack! It was a day's wage for a man at the mill.

The flat was on the second floor of a narrow frame house, painted drab, with a bay window that looked down upon the street. There were four rooms: the parlour, the dining-room, the bedroom, the kitchen. Minna, Otto's wife, had been at work upon them since early morning. Everything shone. The cook-stove had been blackened, the windows washed, the lace curtains done up fresh and starched until they stood out stiff as paper. In the parlour, upon the centre table with its cover of red plush, stood the family Bible, the album of photographs bound in imitation ivory, and a glass dome beneath which was a wreath of wax immortelles. Upon the walls hung a steel engraving of the Kaiser, a chromo of Lake Lucerne, and the marriage certificate of Otto Riemer and Minna Schell, framed in gilt, with doves and cupids in the corners.

Minna met them at the head of the stairs. She was a little woman, plump, fair, with very pink cheeks and a quantity of straw-coloured hair, done high upon her head and fastened with a comb of tortoise shell. She wore her black silk, and there was a smell of cooking about her, a warm, savoury smell of onions and of roasting meat. She held out her hand, then drew it back to wipe it upon her apron, then held it out again.

"Why, Gus," she said. "Why, it's Gus. How do you do, Gus?"

"How do, Minna," he answered.

For an instant the two looked at each other. Otto, coming up behind with the valise, saw nothing. He was breathing hard from the stairs. But Gus's glance went over her, from the tortoise-shell comb to the hem of the black silk, slowly, deliberately, as a man looks at a house he once lived in; and the colour in Minna's cheeks deepened, and she turned away, saying that the dinner was spoiling, that they must all sit down at once, at once.

The dinner was enormous. There was soup with dumplings; there was a roast of pork with crackling, and red cabbage cooked with vinegar and apples, and potatoes boiled in their skins; there was a dish of pickled beets, and a dish of sliced cucumbers swimming in cream, and a great loaf of rye bread with caraway seed; and at the end there was a Kuchen, heavy with plums, that Minna had baked the night before. Otto had brought up from the corner saloon a pail of steam beer, and this stood beside his chair, sweating upon the oilcloth, and he filled the glasses from it again and again.

They ate in silence for a long time, steadily, enormously, their heads lowered, their elbows wide, the knives travelling to their mouths. It was the old way of the family, the way of their fathers and grandfathers before them, the peasant way, that holds eating to be a serious business, not to be interrupted by talk. Gus ate like a starved man. He tore at the crackling with his teeth, he sopped up the gravy with his bread, he called for more cabbage, and yet more, and Minna watched him, her hands in her lap, a little frightened, a little pleased.

At last the men pushed back their chairs. Otto unbuttoned the lower buttons of his waistcoat and drew a long breath. Gus took from his pocket a leather case and offered cigars, fat, black cigars with gold bands, and when Otto had lit his, he turned it over in his fingers and looked at the band and read the name upon it, his lips moving.

"Two bits apiece," said Gus carelessly. "Got 'em in Sacramento."

"Two bits!"

"Sure. Why not? What's money for?"

Otto did not answer. He sat smoking, his eyes half shut, his great hands folded upon his stomach, and the smoke went up in long, slow coils toward the gas fixture over the table.

Then, little by little, they began to talk. They talked of the old times. They talked of the ranch at Two Rock, beyond Petaluma, where they had been boys together, where their grandfather, old Heinrich Riemer, had kept his cows and made his butter and sat of a Sunday upon the porch in his carpet slippers reading the Staats-Zeitung that came a week late from San Francisco. They remembered the creek where they had fished for trout, and the hill behind the barn where they had fought, and the time Gus had fallen through the hay-chute and broken his arm, and the time Otto had driven the buggy into the ditch on the way home from the dance at the Turnverein. They laughed enormously at these things, thumping the table, wiping their eyes, repeating the same stories over and over again.

"And the old man," cried Gus. "Say, Otto, you remember the old man, when he found us in the smokehouse with his pipe? You remember what he done?"

"I guess I remember. I couldn't set down for a week."

"You couldn't set down! What about me? He licked me first. He always licked me first. He said I was the one that started things."

"Well, you was."

"Sure I was. Sure I was." And Gus laughed again, his head thrown back, his lean throat working.

But the laugh broke off short. It ended in a cough, a dry, hacking cough that seemed to come from somewhere deep down in his chest, that shook him, that bent him forward over the table. It went on for a long time. Minna half rose from her chair. Otto took the cigar from his mouth and looked at his cousin, puzzled. When it was over, Gus sat back, wiping his lips with his handkerchief, and the handkerchief he thrust quickly into his pocket again.

"Smoke went the wrong way," he said.

"You want some water?"

"No, I don't want no water. Give me some beer."

There was a silence. Down in the street a wagon went by, the wheels grinding upon the cobbles; a dog barked; from somewhere in the next block came the jangling of a piano and a woman's voice singing, flat and shrill. Minna began to clear away the dishes, moving softly, quickly, the plates clinking.

"The ranch is sold," said Otto at length. "You heard that? After the old man died. Uncle Fritz sold it to a Portugee from the Azores. Eighteen hundred dollars, and the cows thrown in. I got two hundred and fifty out of it. I put it in the savings bank. It's there now, drawing interest."

"I heard," said Gus.

"Your share's waiting for you. Fritz has got it. You got a right to it."

Gus made a gesture with his cigar, sweeping the thing away. "Let him keep it," he said. "What do I want with it? Two hundred and fifty dollars. Say, Otto, I've seen the time I dropped two hundred and fifty dollars at faro in one night in Bisbee and never turned a hair."

Otto stared at him. Minna, at the kitchen door, stopped with the platter in her hands.

"Dropped it?" said Otto slowly. "You mean you lost it? Gambling?"

"Sure. And won it back the next night, and twice over. That's the way it goes down there. Easy come, easy go. You're rich to-day and you're broke to-morrow and you're rich again the day after. I've been rich, I tell you. I've been rich three times. I had a quarter interest in the Copper Queen extension, and I sold out for eleven thousand dollars, cash. Eleven thousand dollars!"

He leaned across the table, his eyes shining, and his voice grew loud and rapid. He began to talk of the copper country, of Bisbee and Globe and Clifton, of the camps strung out along the gulches, of the smelters roaring day and night, of the saloons that never closed, of the dance halls, of the Mexican towns across the line, of the stage hold-ups and the Apache scares and the shooting in the streets. He talked of fortunes made in a day; of men who had come into camp with a burro and a pick and had gone out in a private car; of claims jumped, of lawsuits, of mines salted and sold to Eastern capitalists for a hundred times their worth. The words poured from him, a torrent, a flood, disordered, extravagant, full of oaths and boastings and strange names, and through it all there ran a fever, a restlessness, a hunger, as of a man who has looked upon great things and has been lifted up by them and flung down again and cannot forget.

Otto listened, his cigar gone out between his fingers, his heavy face expressionless. It was all strange to him, strange and a little terrible. He thought of the mill: the long sheds, the whine of the saws, the shriek of the planers, the smell of fresh-cut pine, the whistle at seven and at twelve and at six; the same faces, the same work, day in and day out, year in and year out; the pay envelope on Saturday night, nine dollars and fifty cents when he began, eighteen dollars now; the savings bank book in the bureau drawer, the entries made in a small, neat hand, a dollar, two dollars, five dollars, never more than five; the interest added twice a year. Eleven thousand dollars! He tried to imagine it and could not. It was too large. It overwhelmed him.

"And where is it now?" he asked suddenly. "The eleven thousand. Where is it?"

Gus stopped short. For a moment he did not answer. Then he laughed, and shrugged his shoulders.

"Gone," he said. "Where it all goes. I put it into a mine over at Tombstone, and the water came in on the lower levels and they couldn't pump it out, and the company busted. That's all. That's the way it goes."

"All of it?"

"Every cent."

Otto drew a long breath through his nose. He put the dead cigar carefully upon the edge of his plate. He looked at the gold chain of nuggets across his cousin's waistcoat, at the loud checked suit, at the soft grey hat hung upon the chair-back, and an idea came into his slow mind and lodged there.

"But you got some left," he said. "You got the clothes. You come in a hack."

"I got some," said Gus. "I made a little stake at Globe, the last six months. Enough to come home on. Enough to see the folks. I wanted to see the folks, Otto." He turned his glass round and round upon the oilcloth. "I wanted to see the old places. Two Rock and the creek and all. I been thinking about 'em, nights."

Minna had come back from the kitchen. She stood behind Otto's chair, her hands upon its back, and her eyes were upon Gus. There was something in them that Otto, had he turned, would not have understood: pity, and a remembrance, and a little fear. For she, too, was thinking of the old places, of the creek at Two Rock, and of a certain evening in May, nine years gone, when a boy with burned cheeks and big hands had walked with her along the bank among the willows and had told her that he was going away, going to make his fortune, and that when he came back—— But he had not come back. The letters had grown fewer and then had stopped, and Otto had been there, steady, slow, kind, with his place at the mill and his account at the savings bank, and she had married Otto. That was all. It was a long time ago. It was nothing. And yet she looked at the lean, burned face across the table, the hollow temples, the eyes too bright, and she remembered.

Gus looked up and met her glance, and for a second held it. Then he turned away to the window.

"You done well, Otto," he said. "You done well for yourself. A good job, and a home, and a—and everything. You always was the steady one. The old man always said so. 'Otto,' he says, 'Otto will have a house and a cow when you're sleeping in a ditch.' That's what he says to me. I guess he was right."

"Ach, no," said Otto, embarrassed, pleased. "It's nothing so much. It's a living."

"It's more'n I got."

The gas was lit. Outside, the twilight had come on, grey, full of a fine wet fog blown in from the bay, and the street lamps were blurred and yellow in it. The singing woman in the next block had stopped. The house was very quiet.

Gus got up. He moved about the parlour, looking at things: at the engraving of the Kaiser, at the chromo of Lake Lucerne, at the wax immortelles beneath their glass. He picked up the album and turned its stiff leaves, looking at the photographs: Otto and Minna on their wedding day, rigid, staring, side by side before a painted balustrade; the old grandfather in his Sunday coat, his hand upon a book; Uncle Fritz and Aunt Lena; and one, at the very back, of two boys in their first long trousers, standing with their arms about each other's necks, scowling into the camera.

"That's us," he said. "That's you and me, Otto. You remember when that was took? At the fair in Santa Rosa."

Otto came and looked over his shoulder, breathing heavily.

"Sure. Sure I remember. You wanted to make faces, and the man wouldn't let you."

They stood there together, the two big men, bent over the little faded picture under the gaslight, and for a long time neither of them spoke. Something had come between them and the boys in the photograph, something vast, impersonal, inexorable, that neither of them could have named: the years, the slow grinding of circumstance, the mill and the mine, the city and the desert, the forces that take men as the wind takes seed and scatter them, this one upon good ground and that one upon stony places, without choice, without reason, without pity. The one had stayed and grown thick and slow and content; the other had gone and been burned and wasted and was come back with nothing in his hands but a nugget chain and a cough. It was not either's doing. It was the way things went.

Gus shut the album and laid it down.

"I got to go," he said.

"Go? Go where? You're going to stay here. Minna's fixed up the sofa. You're going to stay a week, two weeks."

"No," said Gus. "No, I got to go. I'm taking the night boat up to Petaluma. I'm going out to Two Rock in the morning and look around. I want to see the creek. Then I guess I'll go over to Fritz's a while."

They could not persuade him. He took his grey hat from the chair and his valise from the hall. At the head of the stairs he shook hands again with Otto, gripping hard, and this time it was Gus whose fingers gave way first. Then he turned to Minna.

"So long, Minna."

"Good-bye, Gus. You—you take care of yourself, Gus."

"Sure," he said. "Sure I will."

He went down the stairs, and they heard the street door close behind him, and his step going away upon the wet pavement, and then, from a little distance, muffled by the fog, the sound of the cough, the dry, hacking cough, going on and on, and dying away at last among the other noises of the street.

Otto went back into the parlour and sat down heavily in the rocking chair beside the centre table. He took the cigar with the gold band from the edge of his plate, looked at it, and put it into his waistcoat pocket beside the other one, the one he had bought at the station and forgotten to light. Minna stood a long while at the window, holding back the lace curtain, looking down into the street, where there was nothing now to see but the fog and the blurred yellow lamps.

"Two bits apiece," said Otto, half aloud, to himself. "Two bits apiece, and he drops two hundred and fifty dollars in one night." He shook his head slowly, ponderously, from side to side. "Eleven thousand dollars. And now he ain't got nothing. Ach, that Gus. That Gus."

And Minna said nothing at all.

In his office at San Francisco, seated before a massive desk of polished redwood, very ornate, Lyman Derrick sat dictating letters to his typewriter, on a certain morning early in the spring of the year. The subdued monotone of his voice proceeded evenly from sentence to sentence, regular, precise, businesslike.

“I have the honour to acknowledge herewith your favour of the 14th instant, and in reply would state——” “Please find enclosed draft upon New Orleans to be applied as per our understanding——” “In answer to your favour No. 1107, referring to the case of the City and County of San Francisco against Excelsior Warehouse & Storage Co., I would say——” His voice continued, expressionless, measured, distinct. While he spoke, he swung slowly back and forth in his leather swivel chair, his elbows resting on the arms, his pop eyes fixed vaguely upon the calendar on the opposite wall, winking at intervals when he paused, searching for a word.

“That's all for the present,” he said at length. Without reply, the typewriter rose and withdrew, thrusting her pencil into the coil of her hair, closing the door behind her, softly, discreetly. When she had gone, Lyman rose, stretching himself putting up three fingers to hide his yawn. To further loosen his muscles, he took a couple of turns the length of he room, noting with satisfaction its fine appointments, the padded red carpet, the dull olive green tint of the walls, the few choice engravings—portraits of Marshall, Taney, Field, and a coloured lithograph—excellently done—of the Grand Canyon of the Colorado—the deep-seated leather chairs, the large and crowded bookcase (topped with a bust of James Lick, and a huge greenish globe), the waste basket of woven coloured grass, made by Navajo Indians, the massive silver inkstand on the desk, the elaborate filing cabinet, complete in every particular, and the shelves of tin boxes, padlocked, impressive, grave, bearing the names of clients, cases and estates. He was between thirty-one and thirty-five years of age. Unlike Harran, he resembled his mother, but he was much darker than Annie Derrick and his eyes were much fuller, the eyeball protruding, giving him a pop-eyed, foreign expression, quite unusual and unexpected. His hair was black, and he wore a small, tight, pointed mustache, which he was in the habit of pushing delicately upward from the corners of his lips with the ball of his thumb, the little finger extended. As often as he made this gesture, he prefaced it with a little twisting gesture of the forearm in order to bring his cuff into view, and, in fact, this movement by itself was habitual. He was dressed carefully, his trousers creased, a pink rose in his lapel. His shoes were of patent leather, his cutaway coat was of very rough black cheviot, his double-breasted waistcoat of tan covered cloth with buttons of smoked pearl. An Ascot scarf—a great puff of heavy black silk—was at his neck, the knot transfixed by a tiny golden pin set off with an opal and four small diamonds. At one end of the room were two great windows of plate glass, and pausing at length before one of these, Lyman selected a cigarette from his curved box of oxydized silver, lit it and stood looking down and out, willing to be idle for a moment, amused and interested in the view. His office was on the tenth floor of the EXCHANGE BUILDING, a beautiful, tower-like affair of white stone, that stood on the corner of Market Street near its intersection with Kearney, the most imposing office building of the city. Below him the city swarmed tumultuous through its grooves, the cable-cars starting and stopping with a gay jangling of bells and a strident whirring of jostled glass windows. Drays and carts clattered over the cobbles, and an incessant shuffling of thousands of feet rose from the pavement. Around Lotta's fountain the baskets of the flower sellers, crammed with chrysanthemums, violets, pinks, roses, lilies, hyacinths, set a brisk note of colour in the grey of the street. But to Lyman's notion the general impression of this centre of the city's life was not one of strenuous business activity. It was a continuous interest in small things, a people ever willing to be amused at trifles, refusing to consider serious matters—good-natured, allowing themselves to be imposed upon, taking life easily—generous, companionable, enthusiastic; living, as it were, from day to day, in a place where the luxuries of life were had without effort; in a city that offered to consideration the restlessness of a New York, without its earnestness; the serenity of a Naples, without its languor; the romance of a Seville, without its picturesqueness. As Lyman turned from the window, about to resume his work, the office boy appeared at the door.

“The man from the lithograph company, sir,” announced the boy.

“Well, what does he want?” demanded Lyman, adding, however, upon the instant: “Show him in.” A young man entered, carrying a great bundle, which he deposited on a chair, with a gasp of relief, exclaiming, all out of breath: “From the Standard Lithograph Company.”

“Don't know,” replied the other. “Maps, I guess.”

The primaries had to be captured at all costs and by any means, and when the convention assembled it was found necessary to buy outright the votes of certain delegates. There was Darrell and Lyman Derrick, both pledged to the ranches. Good Lord, he was never satisfied. He'd be obstinate till the very last gun was fired. Why, if he got drowned in a river he'd float upstream just to be contrary. In the course of time, the new board was seated. For the first few months of its term, it was occupied in clearing up the business left over by the old board and in the completion of the railway map. But now, the decks were cleared. It was about to address itself to the consideration of a revision of the tariff for the carriage of grain between the San Joaquin Valley and tide-water. Both Lyman and Darrell were pledged to an average ten per cent. cut of the grain rates throughout the entire State. The typewriter returned with the letters for Lyman to sign, and he put away the map and took up his morning's routine of business, wondering, the while, what would become of his practice during the time he was involved in the business of the Ranchers' Railroad Commission. But towards noon, at the moment when Lyman was drawing off a glass of mineral water from the siphon that stood at his elbow, there was an interruption. “Hello, hello!” cried Lyman, jumping up, extending his hands, “why, here's a surprise. I didn't expect you all till to-night. Come in, come in and sit down.
