It was in the latter part of October, at that season when the first cold winds come down off the lake and set the arc-lamps swinging on their wires above the wide, bleak streets of the West Side, that George Hessler, cashier and general factotum to the commission house of Pruett & Lang on South Water Street, came home somewhat later than was his custom and found his wife waiting for him in a mood which he did not at once comprehend. He was a man of forty-one, stout in a solid, not unpleasing way, with a heavy brown mustache, a ruddy complexion, and that air of comfortable assurance which comes to men of a certain type who have risen, by no great effort of intellect but by steadiness and a reasonable shrewdness, to a position of small authority. He made twenty-eight hundred dollars a year. He had a flat of seven rooms on Washington Boulevard, near Ashland, furnished in that solid, gaudy, rather oppressive manner which passed in those days for elegance among people of his class: a parlor done in plush of a dark wine color, with a gilt-framed mirror over the mantel, a piano which no one played, a china closet with curving glass, and a great many lace tidies and painted plates and souvenirs of trips to Milwaukee and the Dells. He belonged to the Elks. He smoked cigars at a dime apiece. He considered himself, and was considered by those who knew him, a substantial man.

His wife, Ada, was a woman of thirty-four, of medium height, with a full figure that was already beginning to lose its firmness, light brown hair which she wore drawn up high in the fashion of the time, and pale, rather shrewd gray eyes which had in them a certain coldness when she was displeased. She had been, at twenty, the daughter of a moderately prosperous dry-goods man in Rockford, and she had married Hessler because he was then a rising young bookkeeper with prospects, and because, truth to tell, there had been no one else of equal promise at hand. She was not without feeling. She had loved him, after a fashion, in the early years, and there had been a child, a boy, who had died at three of the diphtheria, and that loss had drawn them together for a time and then, as such things will, had subtly pushed them apart, each nursing in secret a grief which the other could not reach. Since then there had been nothing but the routine of the household, the card parties, the church socials which she attended and he did not, the summer week at Lake Geneva, the slow accumulation of furniture and silver and linen which, in the minds of such as these, stands for the substance of life itself.

It is a curious thing, and one not sufficiently considered by those who would legislate upon the conduct of men and women, how little of what passes between two people who have lived together for many years is ever said aloud. The mind, in such a union, becomes a kind of sensitive plate upon which the slightest variation in tone or manner registers itself, and is stored away, and is brooded over, long before any word is spoken. So it had been with Ada Hessler. For six weeks now she had observed in her husband a change which she could not at first name. He was more careful of his dress. He had bought two new shirts of a fine striped percale and a cravat of a lighter blue than he had ever worn. He had taken to whistling in the mornings while he shaved, a thing he had not done in years. He came home late on Tuesdays and Fridays, pleading the press of business at the end of the week and the necessity of balancing the accounts of a large shipper from Kankakee. And twice she had found in the pocket of his overcoat, when she went to brush it, a ticket stub from McVicker's Theatre, where he had not taken her.

These things she had gathered up and held, the way a miser holds his coins, counting them over in the long afternoons when the flat was silent and the maid had gone out to market. She did not know what they meant. She feared to know. And yet, by that law of the mind which compels us to probe the very wound that pains us most, she could not leave them alone. And then, on this particular afternoon, there had come to call Mrs. Tilney, the wife of a grain inspector who lived two doors down, a thin, bright-eyed, voluble woman with a gift for conveying unpleasant information in the guise of sympathy, and she had mentioned, among other things, quite casually, that her husband had seen Mr. Hessler at Kinsley's on Adams Street the Friday previous, "having supper with such a nice-looking young lady, all in gray, with a hat with a white wing on it. I suppose she was a relation of yours, Mrs. Hessler? Mr. Tilney said she was quite young."

Ada had said yes, a cousin from Rockford, and had smiled, and had talked of other things, and when Mrs. Tilney was gone she had sat in the dim parlor for a long time with her hands in her lap, looking at nothing.

Now, when Hessler came in, rubbing his hands against the cold and calling out cheerfully, "Well, Ada, it's a raw one tonight. Bet we have snow before the week's out," she was standing by the dining-room table, on which the supper things had long since been laid and allowed to grow cold, and she did not answer him at once.

"Where's Nora?" he asked, looking about for the girl.

"I let her go. It's her evening."

"Oh." He hung up his hat and coat on the hall tree, observing nothing, or pretending to observe nothing, and came into the dining room. "Well, I'm sorry I'm late. That fellow Brandt from Kankakee was in again, and you never saw such a mess as his accounts are in. I told Lang we ought to drop him. More trouble than he's worth."

"Was he?" she said.

There was something in the way she said it, a flatness, a peculiar absence of interest, which made him look at her. He was not a sensitive man, as men go, but he had lived with her eleven years, and the very texture of her voice was known to him as the creak of a familiar stair is known.

"What's the matter?" he asked. "You sick?"

"No, I'm not sick."

"Well, you look it. You look all fagged out." He drew out his chair and sat down, and lifted the cover from the dish of pot roast, which had congealed somewhat in its gravy. "This is cold," he said.

"It's been ready since six."

"Well, I told you I'd be late Fridays."

"Yes," she said. "You told me."

He began to eat, a little uneasily, and she sat down across from him but did not eat. The gas jet over the table hissed faintly. Outside, a streetcar went grinding by on Ashland, its bell clanging, and the window glass hummed in its frame. For a minute or two neither spoke, and in that minute there was gathering between them, like the slow massing of clouds on a summer horizon, that heavy, electric tension which precedes all real conflict between those who have been intimate.

"Mrs. Tilney was here this afternoon," Ada said at last.

"Was she? What did she want?"

"Nothing. She just came to call."

"That woman," said Hessler, cutting his meat, "has got a tongue on her like a bell clapper. I don't see how Tilney stands it."

"She said Mr. Tilney saw you at Kinsley's last Friday."

He did not stop cutting, but there was a perceptible slowing of his knife, the merest hesitation, which was not lost upon her. Then he went on.

"Did he? Well, I guess I was there. I go in there sometimes for a bite when I'm working late."

"She said you were with a young lady."

Now he did stop. He laid down his knife and fork and looked at her, and his ruddy face took on a deeper flush, partly of guilt and partly, it must be said, of a genuine irritation at being thus surprised. For it is one of the peculiarities of the human animal that when he is caught in a thing he knows to be wrong, his first emotion is very often not remorse but anger, as though the discovery and not the act were the offense.

"Well, what of it?" he said. "That was Miss Bremer from the office. She was working late on the Brandt books with me, and I took her over to get a bite to eat. You don't expect a girl to work till nine o'clock on an empty stomach, do you?"

"I don't know what I expect," said Ada coldly. "I didn't know you had a Miss Bremer at the office."

"Well, we have. She's been there since August. She's the new stenographer. Lang hired her."

"You never mentioned her."

"Why should I mention her? I don't mention the office boy either, do I? Or the drayman?"

"No," said Ada. "And I suppose you took the drayman to McVicker's too."

This was a stroke he had not anticipated, and it went home. He sat back in his chair and stared at her, and she saw in his face, as plainly as if it had been written there in letters, the quick, calculating confusion of a man who is searching for a lie and cannot immediately find one to fit. It was this, more than anything he had said, which confirmed her fears, and with that confirmation there came over her a sensation which was not grief, exactly, nor anger, but a kind of sickening cold, as though the floor beneath her had tilted.

"Who told you that?" he demanded.

"Nobody told me. I found the tickets in your coat. Twice."

"You've been going through my pockets?"

"I've been brushing your coat, as I've done for eleven years. I wasn't looking for anything. I didn't want to find anything." Her voice, which had been steady, broke a little on the last words, and she pressed her lips together.

Hessler got up from the table and walked to the window and stood with his back to her, looking out at the dark street where the lamps were flaring in the wind. He was, in truth, in a most uncomfortable position, and one which he had not at all foreseen. For it must be understood that there had been, up to this point, nothing between himself and Miss Lottie Bremer which the most censorious would have called criminal. She was a girl of twenty-two, from Kenosha, slender, dark-eyed, with a quick, warm laugh and a way of looking up at him from her machine when he came by her desk that made him feel, for the first time in years, that he was something more than a stout, middle-aged cashier with a mortgage on a lot in Oak Park. She was poor. She lived in a hall bedroom on Van Buren Street and made eight dollars a week, and the gray dress with which Mrs. Tilney had been so taken was the only good dress she had. He had felt sorry for her. He had taken her to supper because she was hungry, and to the theatre because she had never been, and he had found in her delight at these small luxuries a delight of his own which was out of all proportion to the cost. That was all. Or nearly all. He had held her hand once in the dark of the theatre, and she had let him, and that had been the most exciting thing that had happened to him since his marriage.

What he felt for her he could not have explained, any more than the iron filing can explain the magnet. It was a chemical thing, a thing of the blood, a stirring of some old hunger for youth and novelty and the sense of being admired which lies dormant in the most commonplace of men and which wakes, at forty or thereabouts, with a violence that astonishes its possessor. He did not think of it as wrong, precisely. He did not think of it at all, in any reasoned way. He only knew that the office, which had been a dull and dusty place, was now a place he hurried toward in the mornings, and that the flat on Washington Boulevard, with its plush and its painted plates and its silent, watchful wife, had become in contrast a kind of prison.

"Look here, Ada," he said, turning around. "You're making a mountain out of a molehill. The girl's poor. She hasn't got a soul in this town. I took her to the theatre a couple of times because she never saw a show in her life. There's nothing wrong in that."

"Then why didn't you tell me?"

"Because I knew you'd act just like this."

"Like what?"

"Like this! Suspicious. Picking at things. Going through my pockets."

"I didn't go through your pockets," she cried, and now her face was white and her gray eyes had a hard brilliance in them. "And don't you dare try to turn this around on me, George Hessler. You've been lying to me for six weeks. Brandt from Kankakee! You've been out with that girl every Tuesday and Friday, and you've been buying new shirts and new neckties and whistling like a boy, and you think I'm a fool. You think I don't see anything."

"I never said you were a fool."

"You've acted it. You've treated me like one."

He made a gesture of impatience. "Oh, what's the use of talking to you when you're like this?"

"Like this! And how would you expect me to be? Do you think I'm going to sit here and smile while the whole street talks about you? Mrs. Tilney knows. Mr. Tilney knows. I suppose by tomorrow everybody on the block will know. And what am I to say to them? That she's my cousin from Rockford? That's what I told her. I lied for you. I sat right there in that chair and lied for you."

There was a silence. Hessler stood by the window, his hands in his pockets, his heavy face set in an expression half sullen and half ashamed. He was not a cruel man. He did not like to see her suffer. And yet there was in him, at this moment, a resentment which he could not quell, a sense that she stood between him and something bright and desirable, and that her very suffering was a kind of claim upon him which he did not wish to acknowledge. Such are the contradictions of which we are all composed. We would be kind, and we would be free, and the two desires war within us, and neither ever wholly wins.

"Well, I'm sorry you had to lie," he said at last, heavily. "I didn't ask you to."

"No. You didn't ask me to. You didn't think of me at all."

"Now, that's not so."

"It is so." She had risen and stood by the table, her hand resting on the back of her chair, and she was trembling. "What is she to you? I want to know. I have a right to know."

"She's nothing to me. I told you. She's a girl in the office."

"Then you'll stop seeing her."

He did not answer at once, and that silence was more eloquent than any answer. Ada looked at him, and he looked at the floor, and between them the gas jet hissed and the clock on the sideboard, a heavy marble affair they had received as a wedding present from her father, ticked on with a dull, indifferent regularity.

"I can't very well stop seeing her," he said finally. "She works in the office."

"You know what I mean."

"Well, I don't see why I should be ordered around like a schoolboy. I haven't done anything wrong."

"George," she said, and there was in her voice now something different, something pleading and frightened which had not been there before, "George, look at me."

He looked at her.

"Do you care for her?"

It was the question he had dreaded, the question he had not dared to put even to himself, and now it lay there between them, naked and unavoidable. He could have lied. A cleverer man, or a more callous one, would have lied at once and with conviction. But Hessler was neither very clever nor very callous, and the truth, or some confused portion of it, showed in his face before he could prevent it.

"I don't know," he said. "I don't know what I feel. I like her. She's a nice girl. That's all."

Ada sat down again, slowly, as though her strength had gone out of her. For a long moment she said nothing, and he stood watching her, wishing himself anywhere else in the world. He thought, absurdly, of Miss Bremer's room on Van Buren Street, which he had never seen, and of the little gas ring on which she said she made her tea, and of the way she had laughed at the comedian at McVicker's, throwing back her head. And then he looked at his wife, at her full, slackening figure in the dark merino dress, at her hair with its first threads of gray, at her hands, which were red at the knuckles from the work she would not trust entirely to Nora, and he felt a wave of pity and of something like disgust, and was ashamed of the disgust, and was angry at being ashamed.

"Eleven years," she said, in a low voice, not looking at him. "Eleven years, and Harry, and everything. And you stand there and tell me you don't know."

At the mention of the dead child he winced. It was the one thing she had never used against him, and he felt it now as a blow.

"That's not fair, Ada."

"Fair!" She laughed, a short, harsh sound with no mirth in it. "You talk to me about fair."

"I'm not going to stand here and be badgered," he said, his voice rising. "I've worked like a dog for you. I've given you this flat, and that piano, and everything in it. You've never wanted for a thing. And now because I take a poor girl to a show you act as if I'd committed murder."

"I never asked for the piano."

"You never asked for anything, I suppose. You never wanted the new carpet, or the silver, or the summer at the lake."

"Is that what you think I care about? Things?"

"Well, what else do you care about? You don't care about me. You haven't cared about me in years. You go to your church and your card parties, and you sit here with your plates and your doilies, and when I come home you look at me like I was a boarder."

It was out now, the thing which had lain unspoken between them for so long, and both of them were shocked by it. Ada stared at him, her lips parted. Then her face crumpled, and she put her hands over it and began to cry, not loudly, but with a dreadful, choking quietness that was worse than any outburst.

Hessler stood irresolute. He wanted to go to her, and he wanted to run from her, and he did neither. It is in such moments that the essential helplessness of the human creature is most apparent. Here were two people, neither of them wicked, neither of them very much worse or better than the generality of mankind, bound together by law and custom and the memory of a shared grief, and yet as utterly unable to reach each other across the few feet of carpet that separated them as if they had stood on opposite shores of the sea. What was it that had divided them? Time, perhaps, and the slow attrition of routine, and the death of the boy, and the thousand small disappointments that accumulate in any long association. And beneath all these, the deep, blind, unreasoning pull of desire, which knows nothing of vows or obligations, which seeks only its own fulfillment, and which makes of the most respectable of men a creature driven like a leaf before the wind.

"Ada," he said awkwardly. "Ada, don't. I didn't mean that."

She did not answer. Her shoulders shook.

"I'm going out for a while," he said. "I'll take a walk. We'll talk about it when you're feeling better."

Still she said nothing, and after a moment he went into the hall and took down his hat and coat from the hall tree. He paused at the door, his hand on the knob, and looked back at her through the archway, at her bowed head and her heaving shoulders under the hissing gas, and something in him wavered. But it was only for a moment. Then he opened the door and went out, down the dim stair with its smell of cabbage and floor polish, and into the street.

The wind struck him at once, cold and wet off the lake, and he turned up his collar and walked east toward the river, toward the great, glowing heart of the city, where the lights of the hotels and theatres and restaurants were spread out against the sky like a field of jewels. He did not know where he was going. He told himself he was only walking, only clearing his head. But his feet, of their own accord, it seemed, turned south at Halsted and then east again, toward Van Buren Street.

And behind him, in the flat with the plush parlor and the painted plates and the marble clock, Ada Hessler sat on alone at the cold supper table, and the clock ticked, and the streetcars went grinding by, and the city, vast, indifferent, glittering, went on about its ten thousand affairs, knowing nothing and caring nothing for the small wreck which had just been accomplished within its walls.

prompt:
Write a 2,500–3,000-word prose narrative in the exact literary style and voice of Theodore Dreiser, depicting the following scene: Cousins catching up after a long time apart.
Write in third-person perspective. Match their diction, syntax, tone and voice as closely as you can.  Do not paraphrase or reuse any of the author's content. Output only the piece itself with no title, preamble, or commentary.

It was in the early part of October, at that season when the city, having shaken off the languor of summer, begins once more to hum and glitter with the activities of the coming winter, that Walter Brannock, a young man of twenty-seven, lately of Wapakoneta, Ohio, made his way along Drexel Boulevard in Chicago in search of the residence of his cousin, Mrs. Lucy Ambler. He had in his pocket a slip of paper upon which the number had been written in his mother's laborious hand, and he consulted it more than once, not because he had forgotten it, but because the act of looking gave him a certain sense of purpose amid surroundings which otherwise overawed him. The great houses, set back from the walks behind their iron fences and their little lawns, still green; the carriages which passed with a smart clatter of hoofs, bearing ladies whose faces were turned indifferently away; the trim maids and the occasional liveried man upon a step: all these spoke to him of a world of which he had heard, of which he had read in the Sunday papers that sometimes found their way to Wapakoneta, but which he had never before seen with his own eyes. And they did not speak to him kindly. They spoke rather of distance, of some gulf which separated him, in his brown suit purchased three years before at Hollinger's store for eleven dollars, and his shoes which he had blacked that morning in his boarding-house room on West Madison Street, from those who moved so easily and so assuredly within this order.

It should be said that Walter Brannock was not a man of any marked ability. He was of that large class, so numerous in our American life, who are possessed of a kind of honest, plodding intelligence, sufficient to carry them through the ordinary routine of a small occupation, but not equal to those sudden turns of fortune which require boldness or cunning. He had worked upon his father's farm until the elder Brannock, worn out by debt and a succession of poor seasons, had died and the place had been sold for what it would bring. Thereafter he had clerked for two years in a feed and grain store, and when that business, too, had failed, he had been seized with the notion, so common to the young of his day, that in the city lay opportunity. He had saved forty-two dollars. Of this he had now remaining nineteen, and he had been in Chicago eleven days.

His cousin Lucy he had not seen in nine years. They had been children together, the daughter of his father's sister and himself, running barefoot across the same pastures, wading the same creek in the long, hot afternoons of an Ohio July. She had been a slim, bright, rather wilful girl, with brown hair and a quick way of laughing, and he had, in the dim, unformed manner of boyhood, admired her greatly. Then her father had moved the family to Toledo, and from Toledo, after a time, word had come that Lucy had gone to Chicago, had found employment in a large dry-goods house, and finally that she had married a Mr. Ambler, a man connected in some fashion with the board of trade, who was said to be well-to-do. There had been a photograph sent home one Christmas, of Lucy in a dark dress with a great deal of lace at the throat, and Walter's mother had kept it upon the parlor mantel, where it had seemed to him a kind of emblem of all that was finest and farthest away.

The house, when he found it, was of gray stone, three stories high, with a rounded bay and a heavy door of carved oak in which were set two panes of beveled glass. He stood before it for some moments, considering. It was not that he feared his cousin. Rather it was that he feared the house, and all that it implied, and the possibility that he would be met at the door by some servant who would look him over with that cold, appraising eye which he had already encountered more than once in the offices where he had applied for work. Such is the effect of material magnificence upon the unformed mind. It does not argue; it simply is, and by its being it sets up within the beholder a comparison wholly to his disadvantage. At length, however, he mounted the steps and pulled the bell.

It was a maid who answered, a young Irish girl in a black dress and a white apron, who, when he had given his name and explained, with some stumbling, that he was Mrs. Ambler's cousin from Ohio, bade him wait in the hall. He stood there upon a thick rug of a deep red color, looking about him at the tall mirror with its gilded frame, the hat-rack of polished walnut, the newel-post surmounted by a bronze figure of a woman holding aloft a lamp. A faint perfume hung in the air, compounded, it seemed to him, of furniture polish and flowers and something else which he could not name but which he associated vaguely with wealth. He heard a door open somewhere above, and a quick step, and then a voice which, though it was richer and fuller than he remembered it, he recognized at once.

"Walter! Is it really you? Why, of all things!"

Lucy Ambler came down the stairs with one hand upon the rail and the other gathering her skirt, and she was, he thought, the finest-looking woman he had ever seen. She was now thirty, a little fuller of figure than the girl he had known, but with the same brown hair, dressed high upon her head, and the same quick, bright eyes. She wore a gown of some soft gray material, very close-fitting at the waist, with sleeves that were full at the shoulder and narrowed to the wrist, and at her throat was a brooch of small pearls. She held out both her hands to him, and he took them awkwardly, not knowing whether he ought to kiss her as he had done once, long ago, at a church picnic, when they were children and dared one another.

"I hope I ain't come at a bad time," he said.

"A bad time! As though there could be a bad time for you to come. Mary, take Mr. Brannock's hat. Come in here, Walter, where we can sit down. My, how you've grown! But of course you have. It's been—how long has it been?"

"Nine years, I guess. Nearer ten."

"Ten years," she repeated, and for a moment some shadow passed over her face, as though the figure had touched something in her which she would rather not have touched. But she recovered herself at once and led him into the front parlor, a long room with heavy curtains of green plush at the windows, a piano in one corner, and a great many chairs and small tables upon which were arranged vases and figurines and framed photographs. She seated herself upon a settee and motioned him to a chair opposite, and he sat down upon the edge of it, his hands upon his knees.

"Now tell me everything," she said. "How is Aunt Margaret? And Uncle Ed—oh, Walter, I was so sorry. Mother wrote me. I meant to write you all, I truly did, but somehow—" She made a little gesture which suggested the many claims upon her time and attention, and he nodded as though he understood, though in truth he did not.

"Ma's all right," he said. "She's living with Aunt Hattie in town now. She's got her rheumatism some, but she gets around. Pa—well, he went pretty quick at the end. It was his heart, the doctor said. I guess he'd been worrying a good deal."

"About the farm?"

"About the farm, and everything. Things wasn't going very well." He looked down at the carpet, a rich thing of interwoven blues and reds, and said nothing for a moment. Then: "They sold it. The bank did. It didn't bring hardly anything."

"Oh, Walter."

There was genuine feeling in her voice, and he looked up and saw that her eyes were moist. It moved him strangely, this evidence that she, in all her splendor, could still be touched by the misfortunes of the old life. And yet there was something else in it, too, which he only half perceived, a kind of pity which, however kindly meant, set him down a peg, as it were, below her. For pity, even the most sincere, is a thing which flows from the higher to the lower, and in receiving it a man is made aware of his station.

She asked him then about the others: about old Mrs. Leffingwell, who had kept the post-office; about the Schaefer boys, one of whom had gone to the Dakotas; about Ida Crowe, with whom she had gone to school and who had married a railroad man. He told her what he knew, and as he talked something of the old ease came back to him, and he found himself describing the new brick church which had been built where the old frame one stood, and the fire which had burned out half the business block on Auglaize Street, and the time Henry Schaefer's team had run away with the whole Methodist choir in the wagon behind it. She laughed at this, a full, unaffected laugh, and for a moment she was once more the girl who had waded the creek with him, and the room, with all its plush and its gilding, seemed to fall away.

"Do you remember," she said, "the time we went after the walnuts in Brewer's woods, and you fell out of the tree and I thought you'd killed yourself?"

"I remember. I broke my arm."

"And I ran all the way home for your father, and when we came back you were sitting under the tree eating walnuts with the other hand, as cool as you please." She laughed again, and then, as suddenly, was silent, looking past him toward the window, where the light of the late afternoon fell yellow through a gap in the curtains. "It seems so long ago," she said. "Sometimes I think it must have been somebody else. Not me at all."

He did not know how to answer this, and so he said nothing. He was conscious, in a vague way, that his cousin was not altogether happy, though he could not imagine why this should be so. What was there, in all this abundance, to be unhappy about? He thought of his room on West Madison Street, with its iron bed and its single gas-jet and its window that looked out upon an air-shaft, and of the meals at the boarding-house, at which a dozen men in shirt-sleeves ate in silence and hurried away. He thought of the offices where he had asked for work, and the clerks who had looked at him and shaken their heads. Surely, he thought, if one had this, one would want nothing more.

Yet such is the irony of human desire, that it is never content with what it has but forever reaches toward that which it has not. To Walter Brannock, standing at the bottom of the ladder, the rung upon which his cousin stood seemed the summit of all attainment. To Lucy Ambler, who had climbed to it with no little effort, it seemed merely a landing from which one could see, the more plainly for being nearer, the heights which yet remained unscaled—the houses upon the Lake Shore Drive, the boxes at the opera, the names that appeared in the society columns of the Tribune. And beyond even this, though she could not have put it into words, there was another lack, deeper and more troubling, which had to do not with things at all but with that hunger of the heart which no quantity of things can satisfy.

"And Mr. Ambler," Walter said at length, feeling that some inquiry was expected of him. "Is he well?"

"Oh, Frank is well enough," she said, a little carelessly. "He's in New York just now. He goes a great deal. Business, you know." She smoothed her skirt with one hand. "He's a very busy man."

"I guess he must be, to have all this."

She glanced about the room as though seeing it freshly through his eyes, and something in her expression changed. "Yes," she said. "I suppose it is a good deal. It doesn't seem so much, after a while. You get used to things." She paused. "You get used to everything, Walter. That's the strange part of it. When I first came to Chicago I had a room on Indiana Avenue that I paid two dollars a week for, and I used to walk past these houses on Sunday afternoons and think that if I could ever live in one of them I'd never want anything else as long as I lived. And now—" She did not finish.

"And now?" he prompted, but she only shook her head and smiled.

"Never mind. Tell me about yourself. What are you doing in Chicago? Mother said in her last letter that you'd come up here. Have you found anything?"

He colored, and looked again at the carpet. "Not yet. I been looking. I been to most of the big stores and some of the packing houses. There's a lot of men looking, seems like. More than there's places."

"Yes," she said slowly. "There always are."

"I thought maybe," he went on, and here his voice faltered, for this was the thing he had dreaded saying, the thing which had kept him for some minutes upon the walk outside, "I thought maybe Mr. Ambler might know of something. I don't mean nothing big. I'd take most anything. I can keep books some, and I can figure, and I ain't afraid of work."

He had said it, and now he sat in an agony of shame, waiting for her answer. It was not that he had expected her to refuse him. It was rather that in asking he had made plain, to her and to himself, the full measure of the difference between them. He was no longer her cousin come to call. He was a petitioner, a man in want, come to the house of one who had to ask a favor.

Lucy was silent for a moment. She was, in truth, a kindly woman, more kindly than many in her position, and her heart went out to him. But mingled with this kindliness was another feeling, not so creditable, which she would have been ashamed to acknowledge, and which was nevertheless quite real. It was the feeling of one who has escaped from a certain condition and does not wish to be reminded of it. Walter, sitting there in his brown suit with his red, work-roughened hands upon his knees, was the past made flesh, the past of the farm and the creek and the barefoot summers, but also of the poverty and the narrowness and the small, mean anxieties from which she had fled. She had not seen it in so many years that she had almost persuaded herself it no longer existed. And here it was, in her own parlor.

"I'll speak to Frank when he comes back," she said at last. "He knows a great many people. I'm sure he can find something for you. And Walter—" She hesitated, and then rose and went to a small desk of inlaid wood which stood between the windows, and opened a drawer, and took something out. When she came back to him he saw that she held two bills folded together. "I want you to take this. No, don't say anything. It's only until you find something. You'd do as much for me if things were the other way about."

He took the money because he could not do otherwise; his need was too great, and her manner too insistent. But he took it with a feeling of heaviness, as though he were accepting not merely twenty dollars but a kind of sentence, a fixed and final judgment upon his place in the world. He thanked her in a low voice, and put the bills into his inside pocket, and stood up.

"I guess I better be going," he said.

"Must you? I wish you'd stay to supper. There's no one here but me."

But he would not stay. He could not have sat at her table, with the Irish girl waiting upon him and the silver and the linen spread out before him, and borne it. He said that he had promised to meet a man about a job in the morning and must get back early, which was not true, and she did not press him. She went with him to the door, and there, upon the step, in the fading light, she put her hand upon his arm.

"Come again, Walter," she said. "Come on Sunday. Promise me."

"I'll come," he said.

"It's been so good to see you. You don't know how good." And she looked at him with an expression which he was to remember long afterward and puzzle over, an expression in which there was affection and regret and a kind of loneliness which he could not account for. Then she went in, and the heavy oak door closed behind her, and he was alone upon the walk.

It was dusk now, and the lamps were being lit along the boulevard, one after another, in a long receding line of yellow points. The carriages were more numerous than before, for it was the hour when the people of this quarter returned from their business or set out for their evening's pleasure, and he heard the click of hoofs and the soft roll of rubber tires and now and then a woman's laugh. Through the windows of the great houses he could see the glow of lamps and the gleam of chandeliers and sometimes a figure moving across a lighted room. All of it seemed to him unspeakably desirable and unspeakably remote. He walked slowly westward, toward the cable line, his hands in his pockets, his fingers touching the folded bills.

What were his thoughts? They were confused, as are the thoughts of most men at such moments, a mingling of gratitude and humiliation, of hope and despair. He thought of Lucy as she had been, a laughing girl in a calico dress, and as she was now, in her gray gown with the pearls at her throat, and he could not make the two images agree. He thought of the house, and of the money in his pocket, and of Mr. Ambler, whom he had never seen and of whom he had formed a vague picture as a large, prosperous, impatient man in a silk hat. He thought of his room, and of the morrow, and of the long line of men he would stand among at the gate of some warehouse or factory. And underneath all these, unacknowledged, there stirred a feeling which was neither envy nor resentment but something more obscure: a dim apprehension that the world was not as he had supposed, that the rewards which he had imagined as the certain fruit of honest labor were distributed by some other law, mysterious and indifferent, which took no account of his merit or his need.

Nor was Lucy Ambler, in her parlor behind the green plush curtains, any more at peace. She had gone back to the settee and sat there in the gathering darkness without ringing for the lamps, her hands folded in her lap. She was thinking of Brewer's woods and the walnut tree, of the creek and the long summer afternoons, of a time when the whole of life had seemed to lie ahead of her like an unopened gift. She had got what she wanted, or what she had thought she wanted. She had the house and the gowns and the maid and the carriage, and a husband who provided for her generously and whom she saw perhaps one week in three. And yet, sitting there, she was conscious of a strange ache, a longing for something which she could not name, which the sight of her cousin's honest, bewildered face had awakened in her. It was as though, in looking at him, she had glimpsed for an instant the road she had not taken, and found it, for all its poverty and hardship, not wholly without its charm.

But this, too, was an illusion, as she would have known had she considered it soberly. For the road she had not taken led, in all likelihood, to a frame house in Wapakoneta, and a husband who clerked in a feed store, and a round of cooking and washing and child-bearing which would have worn her out at forty. She knew this; she had seen it in her own mother. And so the longing passed, as such longings do, and she rose and rang for Mary to light the lamps, and went upstairs to dress for the evening, since Mrs. Talbot was giving a musicale and had particularly asked her to come.

Thus do we move, each of us, within the narrow circle of our own desires, looking out upon the lives of others with envy or with pity, and seldom with understanding. The cousin who has risen looks back and sighs for what she has lost; the cousin who has remained below looks up and aches for what he has never had; and neither sees that the thing for which they long is not to be found upon any rung of the ladder, but lies somewhere outside it altogether, in a region which neither money nor the want of it can reach. And the great city, indifferent to them both, goes on with its lamps and its carriages and its endless restless traffic, taking from each what it will and giving, in return, only the promise of something more.

response:
It was in that part of the West Side of Chicago which lies between Halsted Street and the river, and which in the year 1894 was given over almost entirely to the small frame cottages and two-story flats of those who labored for a wage, that Mrs. Clara Hulme, the wife of a motorman on the Blue Island Avenue line, kept house for her husband and her two children upon an income which, at its very best, came to no more than fourteen dollars and a half a week. Out of this, eleven dollars a month went for the rent of the upper floor of a gray clapboard building on Laflin Street, a place of four small rooms, two of which looked out upon a yard of cinders and a leaning fence, and two upon the street, where the wagons of the coal dealers and the ice men passed and repassed throughout the day. The remainder had to be stretched, as such sums are always stretched in such homes, over the coal and the kerosene, the meat and the flour, the shoes which wore out so rapidly upon the children's feet, and that small margin, never more than a few dimes, which Mrs. Hulme liked to set by against the illness or the lay-off that she felt, in the dim, anxious way of her kind, was always waiting for them somewhere in the future.

She was not a woman of any great force or understanding. Born on a farm near Urbana, Ohio, the fourth daughter of a Methodist harness-maker who had failed at farming, she had brought to the city, at nineteen, little more than a certain prim prettiness, now fading, and a set of moral notions which she had never examined and would never have dreamed of examining, since they seemed to her as fixed and as necessary as the rising of the sun. One did not lie. One did not steal. One did not take the name of the Lord in vain, nor play cards on Sunday, nor drink, nor permit one's children to grow up "wild," which last was a word that covered, in her mind, a vast and shadowy region of sin, idleness, and ultimate destruction, of the kind she had seen pictured in the tracts that were handed about at camp-meetings in her girlhood. That these notions were themselves the product of conditions, of a narrow agricultural life in which a stolen hen or an unpaid debt might mean actual want to a neighbor, never occurred to her. They were simply right, and their opposites were simply wrong, and there was an end of it.

Her husband, Asa Hulme, was a large, slow, good-natured man of thirty-four, who had come up from the country somewhat as she had and who, having found employment with the street railway, had held it for nine years without either advancement or complaint. He left the house at half-past five in the morning and returned at seven at night, gray with fatigue, smelling of the oil and the electric dust of his car, and wanting nothing so much as his supper and his pipe. The management of the children he left entirely to her, as did nearly all men of his station, regarding it as a thing outside his province, like the washing or the mending of socks.

Of these children there were two: a girl, Nettie, not yet three, and a boy, Willard, who was in his seventh year and attended the primary grade of the Throop Street school. He was a thin, quick, light-haired child, with his mother's narrow face and something else besides, an eagerness, a responsiveness to color and sound and movement, which she did not possess and did not understand. The street fascinated him. The wagons with their great dappled horses, the hurdy-gurdy man who came on Saturdays, the gaudy posters of the circus pasted upon the fences along Twelfth Street, the windows of the little shops in which were displayed things of a brightness and a desirability that seemed to him beyond anything in the world: all these drew him as a light draws a moth, and he would stand before them, his hands in the pockets of his patched knee-breeches, for long minutes together, lost in a kind of dream. And it is just here that we must pause, for in this matter of desire, of the pull which things exert upon the untutored mind, lies the whole secret of what follows.

For what, after all, is a child but a small bundle of wants, set down in a world which it did not make and whose rules it cannot possibly comprehend? It sees, it desires, it reaches out. That the thing it reaches for belongs to another, that it has been paid for with labor and is guarded by law and custom and the whole elaborate apparatus of property, is a fact as remote from its understanding as the movement of the planets. The notion of mine and thine is not born in us; it is laid upon us, layer by layer, by those who have themselves had it laid upon them, and very often at no small cost of tears.

Now, upon the shelf above the kitchen stove, behind the coffee-mill and a china figure of a shepherdess which had been a wedding present from her sister in Dayton, Mrs. Hulme kept a small tin canister, painted blue and bearing upon its side the faded legend "Arbuckle's," in which she placed, from week to week, such coins as she could spare toward the rent. It was a kind of shrine with her, this canister. She counted its contents on Saturday nights, after Asa had brought home his envelope, and again on Tuesdays, out of a mere nervous habit, and the sight of the small heap of silver and copper upon the oilcloth gave her a feeling of security which nothing else in her life afforded. On this particular Tuesday in early May, then, having put Nettie down for her nap and finished the ironing, she took the canister down, as was her custom, emptied it upon the table, and counted. There should have been, as she well knew, three dollars and eighty-five cents. There were three dollars and sixty.

She counted again, slowly, sliding the coins one by one across the oilcloth with her forefinger, her lips moving. Three dollars and sixty. A quarter was gone.

It is difficult to convey to those who have never known actual want the effect which so small a discovery may produce upon a mind such as hers. A quarter was not, in itself, a great deal of money, even to the Hulmes. It was a pound and a half of round steak, or a peck of potatoes, or a pair of the cheap cotton stockings which Nettie was forever wearing through at the knees. But it was not the quarter alone. It was the sense of violation, of a breach in the frail wall which she had built between her family and the abyss. If a quarter could vanish from the canister, then anything could vanish, and the whole careful structure of her economy, upon which she had spent so many anxious hours, seemed suddenly to tremble. She sat very still, her hands upon the table, and a cold feeling went over her.

Her first thought, naturally enough, was of the woman downstairs, a Mrs. Kubelik, the wife of a cooper, who sometimes came up to borrow a cup of sugar or an iron. But Mrs. Kubelik had not been up in more than a week. Her second thought was of Asa, and this she put away at once, for Asa never touched the canister and would not, she knew, have taken anything without telling her. And then, slowly, unwillingly, as one approaches a thing one does not wish to see, her mind came round to Willard.

She remembered now, as people do remember such things once suspicion has given them a direction, that on Saturday afternoon he had been alone in the kitchen for some little time while she was in the front room with Nettie, who had been fretful with a tooth. She remembered that he had gone out afterward without being told, and had come back nearly an hour later with a flushed face and an air of excitement which she had attributed at the time to some game in the street. And she remembered, too, that on Sunday morning, in brushing his other jacket for Sunday school, she had found in the pocket a small sticky fragment of something black, which she had taken for a bit of tar and had thrown into the stove without a second thought. Licorice. It had been licorice.

She wanted, almost, to take him up in her arms. But she did not. She was afraid for him; and fear, in natures such as hers, has only one outlet.

"Stop that crying," she said. "Stop it this minute. Crying won't help you now. You should have thought of that before." She went to the nail behind the pantry door, where hung a narrow leather strap which Asa had brought home from the car barns and which had hitherto served chiefly as a threat. "Come here."

He backed away from her toward the window, still sobbing. "I won't do it again, Ma. I won't. I won't never do it again."

"Come here, I said."

He came, because there was nothing else to do, because the habit of obedience was stronger in him even than his terror; and she took him by one thin arm and turned him about and struck him three times across the backs of his legs, below the knee-breeches, where the skin was bare above his stockings. They were not, as such punishments went in that day and in that neighborhood, particularly severe blows. Mrs. Kubelik downstairs beat her boys with a stove-lifter, and the Irish family across the street were heard to raise the very roof on Saturday nights. But to Willard, who had been struck only rarely and never with the strap, they seemed the end of the world. He screamed at each one, and when she let go of his arm he fell down upon the floor beside the stove and lay there with his face against the boards, crying as though his heart would break. Mrs. Hulme hung the strap back upon its nail. Her hands were shaking. She stood for a moment looking down at her son, and then she said, in a voice that was not quite steady, "Now you get up and go in your room and stay there till your father comes home. And you get down on your knees and ask God to forgive you, because I don't know as He will." And she went in to quiet the baby.

The rest of that afternoon passed in a kind of gray, heavy silence. The boy lay upon his bed in the back room, sobbing at first and then only catching his breath at long intervals, and finally staring dully at the ceiling, where a water-stain in the plaster made a shape like the map of some unknown country. He did not pray. He did not, in fact, think very clearly about anything. There was in him only a vast, confused sense of having been cast out, of being somehow different from what he had been that morning, of having become, in his mother's eyes and perhaps in the eyes of God, something dark and shameful, a thief. The word went round and round in his mind. It is in such hours, perhaps, more than in any formal instruction, that the moral nature of a child is shaped, and it is shaped not so much by reason as by pain and fear, by the memory of a face turned hard against him and of a voice that had changed. Whether it is shaped for good or ill is a question which those who administer such lessons seldom pause to ask.

As for his mother, she went about the work of getting supper with a tight, preoccupied air, peeling potatoes, slicing bread, setting the table with the heavy white plates, and stopping now and again to stare out of the window at the cinder yard, where a gray cat was picking its way along the top of the fence. She was not satisfied. She had done, as she conceived it, her duty, and yet the doing of it had left her not relieved but strangely heavy and sick at heart. She thought of the marbles, with their twists of color, and of the boy's face when he had first seen them upon the table, and it came to her, dimly and without words, that he had wanted them very badly, in a way that she herself had perhaps once wanted things, ribbons, a hat with a feather, a pair of kid gloves in the window of a store in Springfield, which she had never had and had long since ceased to think about. But this thought was too vague and too disturbing to be followed out, and she put it away, as she put away all such thoughts, and went on slicing the bread.

At a little after seven Asa came heavily up the stairs, hung his cap and his coat upon the hook by the door, and sat down at the table with a long sigh of weariness. She told him, as she set the potatoes and the fried salt pork before him, what had happened. He listened, chewing slowly, his large red hands upon either side of his plate.

"Well," he said at last, "I guess you done right. Can't have him takin' money." And then, after a pause, during which he looked somewhat vaguely at the door of the back room, "He's only a little shaver, though."

"That's just the time to learn him," she said sharply. "If he don't learn now, he never will. You know what happened to Lon."

"I know." He went on eating. He was too tired to argue, and besides, it was not his province. Presently he said, "You call him out to his supper?"

She hesitated, and then went to the door of the back room and opened it. The boy was lying upon the bed with his face to the wall. He had fallen asleep, his cheeks still streaked with the marks of his tears, one hand curled up beneath his chin, his bare legs, with the red welts showing across them, drawn up under him. She stood looking at him in the dim light that came from the kitchen, and something rose in her throat. She did not wake him. She went over, instead, and drew the thin quilt up over his legs, and stood for a moment longer, her hand upon his hair.

Then she came back into the kitchen, gathered up the whistle and the marbles from the table where they still lay, and, after a moment's indecision, put them not into the stove, as she had meant to do, but upon the shelf beside the blue canister, behind the china shepherdess, where they would be out of sight. Why she did this she could not have said. She sat down across from her husband and poured his coffee, and the lamp hissed, and outside, in the soft spring dark, the wagons rolled by upon the cobbles of Laflin Street, and the great city went on about its vast and indifferent business, taking no account whatever of a quarter, or a whistle, or a small boy asleep in a back room, learning, as all of us must learn and at whatever cost, the hard and mysterious laws of the world into which he had been born.

Somewhere a street car ground and clanged its way along. And all the vast, indifferent, teeming life of the place, which he had come to as a youth of nineteen from Racine with such high hopes—what had it given him? This! These four rooms, and the shipping desk, and the sixteen dollars, and a wife who sat and looked at him as though he were a fool.

And was he a fool? The question came to him, there at the window, unbidden and unwelcome. Supposing—supposing Barge were not what he seemed? Supposing there were no streets, no park, no school—only a stretch of sand and scrub oak and marsh, such as he had seen once from the train window, going to Michigan City? Supposing—but no! He would not think of that. Barge had an office in the Monadnock Building. A man did not have an office in the Monadnock Building and go about swindling people. It was not possible. The thing was sound. It must be sound. For if it were not—

Behind him he heard Ada stir, and the faint rustle of the paper as she folded it.

"I'm going to go over there," she said. "Tomorrow. To this Barge."

He turned. "You'll do nothing of the kind!"

"I'm going to go over there and ask him to give it back."

"Give it back! Why, you're crazy, Ada. He can't give it back. It's a sale. It's all signed and recorded and everything. You'd only make a fool of yourself—and of me. What would he think of me, having my wife come down there whining and crying for the money back, like I didn't know my own mind? Do you want to make me a laughingstock?"

"I don't care what he thinks of you," she said, and for the first time her voice trembled a little, not with tears, as he at first thought, but with a kind of suppressed passion which he had rarely heard in her. "I don't care what anybody thinks. Five years, Lewis. Five years I've been putting that by. I've gone without—you don't know what I've gone without. You don't know the half of it. And you go and give it away to a man you met in a saloon—"

"It wasn't a saloon! It was—"

"—to a man you met in a saloon, and never told me, never said one word to me, and hid the paper in your old coat like—like a thief. That's what hurts, Lewis. Not the money so much. That you hid it."

And this, being the exact truth, struck home as nothing else had. For he had hidden it—had gone about for nearly a month now with the knowledge of it lying in him like a stone, unable to bring himself to speak of it, putting it off from day to day, telling himself that he would wait until he had seen the lots, until he could come home some evening with a letter from Barge, perhaps, offering him twice what he had paid, and lay it before her triumphantly and say, "There! What do you think of that? And you wanted to leave it in the bank at two per cent!" That had been the dream. And now instead—this.

"I was going to tell you," he said again, but weakly now, and without conviction.

"When?"

He did not answer. He could not. And she, seeing that he could not, sat a moment longer, very still, her large, work-roughened hands lying folded upon the paper in her lap, and then she got up and went slowly into the little bedroom beyond, and he heard her sit down upon the bed, and then nothing more.

And he, left alone in the front room with the green-shaded lamp and the ticking clock and the basket of mending, stood a long while at the window, looking out at the wet street and the violet arc light and the red glow upon the sky, and turning it over and over in his mind. Was he wrong? Had he been a fool? Barge had seemed so sure, so easy, so prosperous, with his gray waistcoat and his gold watch chain and his large, confident, friendly way of laying a hand on one's shoulder. And all those men he had read about, who had risen from nothing—had they not taken chances too? Had their wives not wept and reproached them? And then afterward, when the money came—what then? Then it was all forgotten, and they were called shrewd and far-seeing, and lived on the Lake Shore Drive. It was only the ones who failed who were called fools. And he would not fail. He would not. Gary was going to be a great city. It had said so in the Tribune.

And yet! And yet! Supposing—

From the bedroom came no sound at all, not even of weeping, and somehow that was worse than any weeping could have been. He thought of going in to her, of sitting down beside her on the bed and putting his arm about her and saying—what? That he was sorry? But he was not sorry—or not entirely. That it would all come out right? But he did not know that it would. And so he did not go, but stood there, a figure of indecision and half-defiance and half-shame, the while the clock ticked on and the rain fell and the great city outside, careless of him and of her and of J. Whitney Barge and of all the little hoards and hopes of all the millions like them, went roaring on its way into the night.

It was on a raw evening in late November, with the wind coming in off the lake in long, cold, searching gusts that rattled the signboards along Cottage Grove Avenue and sent bits of paper and dust whirling about the feet of the homeward-bound, that Walter Pruett, having brushed his one good suit and blacked his shoes twice over and examined himself in the small, wavy mirror of his hall bedroom on Indiana Street with no little dissatisfaction, set out to call upon his cousin Della, whom he had not seen in eleven years. Eleven years! And in that time what had not happened to her, and what, as he could not help reflecting, had not happened to him! For she, as he had learned only a fortnight before through a letter from his mother in Pelham, was now Mrs. Harvey Kinsolving, the wife of a building contractor of some means, and lived (so his mother had written, with an underscoring that conveyed more than any words) on Drexel Boulevard. Whereas he—well, he was a bookkeeper's assistant in the office of the Lake Shore Coal & Coke Company at fourteen dollars a week, and had been for nearly three years, and with no very definite prospect, as he was compelled to admit when he was honest with himself, of being anything much better.

And yet, as he rode southward in the clanging, overheated car, his hands thrust deep into the pockets of an overcoat which had seen two winters too many, he could not keep his mind from going back to the old days in Pelham, when Della Pruett, the daughter of his father's younger brother, had been a thin, freckled, rather tomboyish girl with two long brown braids, who had climbed the Weller apple trees with him and fished for sunfish in Turkey Creek and once (he remembered it now with a sudden warmth) had cried bitterly when he had been whipped by old Professor Haines for a prank that was more hers than his. They had been very close then—as close, almost, as brother and sister. And when her family had moved away to Indianapolis, and later, after her father's death, she had come to Chicago to work in a millinery establishment, he had written to her once or twice, and she to him. But then the letters had stopped, as such letters do, and life, with its endless and impersonal shuffling, had carried them each along their separate ways.

But Drexel Boulevard! The very name, to one who had walked along it on Sunday afternoons and gazed at the great stone and brick houses set back behind their lawns and iron fences, with their bay windows and porte-cocheres and the carriages drawn up before them, held a magic which was not easily to be dispelled. How had she come to that? What chance, what luck, what quality in her had fitted her for such a change? And would she, now that she was a part of all that, care to see him at all? He had written her a note, a stiff and labored thing that had cost him an entire evening, and she had answered promptly enough—a little lavender-scented card in a large, sloping hand: "Dear Walter—of course! Come Thursday at eight. I'm so anxious to see you. Della." Yet even so, he was not sure. People said such things. And she would see at once (he was certain of it) the shine on the elbows of his coat, the frayed edge of his cuff, which he had trimmed with scissors and turned under as best he could.

The house, when at last he found it, after walking two blocks in the wrong direction and being compelled to inquire of a policeman, proved to be a large, square, gray stone affair with a round tower at one corner capped by a pointed slate roof, and with lights glowing warmly behind lace curtains on both floors. A lamp of wrought iron burned at the head of the steps. Walter paused at the foot of these and looked up, conscious of a sinking in the region of his stomach which was not entirely the result of the cold. Here was something—solid, substantial, secure. Here was what money did. And he thought, with a twinge of bitterness which he could not quite suppress, of his own narrow room with its single gas jet and its cracked washbowl and the smell of cabbage that ascended every evening from the kitchen of Mrs. Dorgan below.

He rang. A maid in a black dress and white cap and apron—a stolid Swedish girl with large red hands—opened the door and took his hat and coat with what seemed to him a faint and appraising lift of the eyebrows, and showed him into a front parlor that was so filled with things—a piano draped with a fringed Spanish shawl, gilt chairs, a tall onyx pedestal bearing a bronze of a Greek youth with a discus, palms in brass jardinieres, a cabinet of painted china, heavy curtains of wine-colored plush looped back with silken cords—that for a moment he scarcely knew where to stand. A fire of cannel coal burned brightly in a grate of polished brass. The carpet beneath his feet was thick and soft. He stood very straight, his hands at his sides, and then, deciding that this looked foolish, clasped them behind his back, and then, thinking that this too was not quite right, let them fall again.

And then she came—down the broad staircase, which he could see through the archway, and into the room with a soft rustle of silk, and he scarcely knew her. For this was not the thin, freckled girl of Turkey Creek at all, but a full-figured woman of twenty-eight or nine, handsome in a rather showy way, with her brown hair, now darker than he remembered it, piled high in a pompadour and held by a comb of tortoise shell set with brilliants, and wearing a gown of dove-gray silk with a bodice of cream lace and a high collar, and at her throat a brooch of pearls. Her face had filled out, and the freckles had gone (or had been banished by some art which he did not understand), and yet about the eyes—those same quick, gray-green, half-mocking eyes—there was something which went straight back to the old days and brought them before him with a rush.

"Walter! Walter Pruett! Well, for goodness' sake!" She came toward him with both hands extended, and he took them awkwardly, not knowing whether he was expected to kiss her cheek, as he might have once, or merely to shake hands, as one did with a lady. In his uncertainty he did neither, but stood holding her hands and smiling, a little foolishly, he feared. "Why, you've grown so tall! And a mustache! I'd never have known you on the street—never in this world. Sit down, sit down. Here, by the fire. You must be frozen. Isn't it a perfectly awful night?"

"It is pretty cold," he admitted, seating himself gingerly on the edge of one of the gilt chairs, which seemed to him much too frail for any real use, and wondering whether he ought to have said something about the house first, or about her looks. "But it's not so bad once you get moving. You—you look fine, Della. I mean—you look awful well."

"Do I?" She laughed, pleased, and sank into a deep chair opposite him with a little sigh of comfort, arranging her skirts about her. "Well, I'm getting fat, if you want to know the truth. Harvey says I'm not, but I am. That's what comes of not doing anything. You remember how skinny I used to be? Bean-pole, you used to call me. Bean-pole Della."

"Did I?" he said, and flushed, for he did remember it. "I guess I was a pretty mean kid."

"Oh, no, you weren't. You were the nicest boy in Pelham, and you know it. Don't you remember the time old Haines licked you for putting the garter snake in his desk drawer, and it was really me that put it there? I never forgot that. I cried all night." She laughed again, a warm, throaty laugh that filled the room, and Walter laughed too, feeling for the first time a little of his stiffness go out of him. For whatever else had changed, it was plain that she had not wholly forgotten, and that she was, in some fashion at least, glad to see him.

And then for a time, as is the way with those who have shared a childhood and then been long parted, they talked eagerly and almost at random—of Pelham, and of who had married whom, and of old Mrs. Weller's death, and of the Methodist church that had burned and been rebuilt, and of Hank Shiveley, who had gone to the Klondike and come back with nothing but a frozen foot. And of his mother, and her mother, who had died four years since in Indianapolis (and here Della's face clouded a little and she looked into the fire), and of the creek, which, so he told her, had been dammed up now for a mill and was not what it had been at all. And all the while Walter, even as he talked, was studying her—the rings upon her fingers, three of them, one with a diamond as large as a pea, the soft white hands that had once been brown and scratched with briars, the way she held her head, the faint air of assurance and of being accustomed to service which hung about her like a perfume. How had it come about? What had she done? Was it merely luck—the luck of a pretty face in the right place at the right moment? Or was there something in her, some shrewdness or force, which he himself lacked? For he had always thought himself, in the old days, the quicker of the two.

"But tell me about you, Walter," she said at last, turning to him with renewed interest. "What are you doing here in Chicago? Aunt Mattie wrote that you were with some big company."

And now he was confronted with the very thing which, all the way down in the car, he had dreaded. For what was he to say? That he sat on a high stool in a dingy office on South Water Street, adding columns of figures relating to tons of anthracite and bituminous, under the eye of a sour old Scotchman named McPhail who had been there thirty years and expected to be there thirty more? That he had been passed over twice for a raise? That his whole capital, after three years in the city, came to forty-one dollars in the Hibernian Savings Bank? It was not to be thought of—not here, in this room, with the bronze youth and the onyx pedestal and the diamond the size of a pea. And so, with a readiness which surprised even himself, he heard himself saying:

"Oh, I'm with the Lake Shore Coal and Coke people. In the accounting end. It's a pretty big concern—they do a lot of business with the railroads. I'm—well, I'm in line for something better pretty soon, I think. They've been talking about it." And then, feeling that this was perhaps not sufficient, and being carried along by the very momentum of the lie: "I'm kind of looking around, too. A fellow I know has been after me to go in with him on something—a real estate proposition out in Englewood."

"Why, Walter, that's fine!" she exclaimed, and seemed so genuinely pleased that he felt at once a fresh pang. "I always knew you'd get on. You were always so smart in school. Harvey says there's no end of money in real estate out there, if a person only knows how to go about it."

"That's what they say," he agreed, though he knew nothing whatever about it and was already wishing he had held his tongue. For supposing she should mention it to her husband, and supposing her husband should ask him about it? What then? And he looked down at his shoes, which in the light of the fire showed a crack across the left toe that no blacking could hide, and drew that foot back under the chair.

But just then there was the sound of the front door opening and closing, a heavy step in the hall, and a voice—a large, comfortable, somewhat husky voice—calling: "Del? Where are you, Del?" And Della, with a quick, half-nervous movement of her hand to her hair, rose and said: "In here, Harvey. Walter's here. My cousin, you know, from Pelham." And into the room came a man of perhaps forty-five, broad and heavy and red-faced, with a close-cropped grayish mustache and small, shrewd, pale-blue eyes, wearing a suit of good gray worsted that stretched a little across his middle, and a heavy gold watch chain with an elk's tooth charm depending from it. He had about him that air of large, easy, self-satisfied solidity which Walter had often observed in successful men in the Loop—men who rode in cabs and lunched at the Union League and spoke of thousands as he spoke of dimes.

"Well, well, so this is the cousin," said Mr. Kinsolving, extending a thick, warm hand and gripping Walter's with a force that made him wince. "Glad to know you, young fellow. Del's been talking about you all week. Sit down, sit down. Don't let me break anything up." He lowered himself into the largest chair in the room with a grunt and drew a cigar from his waistcoat pocket, bit off the end and lit it, his small eyes moving over Walter the while in a manner which, though not unfriendly, seemed to Walter to take in everything—the suit, the cuffs, the collar, the very crack in the shoe. "From down in Indiana, eh? I was through there once. Flat country. Good farming, though. What line you in?"

"Coal," said Walter, and then, because it seemed too bald, "the Lake Shore Coal and Coke Company. In the office."

"Lake Shore? That's old Tilden's outfit. I buy from 'em sometimes for the boilers on my jobs. Pretty close-fisted crowd, I hear. Old Tilden'd skin a flea for its hide." He laughed, a short, rumbling laugh, and blew a cloud of smoke toward the ceiling. "Don't pay their help much either, from what I hear."

Walter flushed and said nothing, and Della, catching perhaps something of his discomfiture, put in quickly: "Walter's thinking of going into real estate, Harvey. Out in Englewood. With a friend of his."

"That so?" Mr. Kinsolving turned his pale eyes upon Walter with a new and somewhat sharper interest. "Who with? I know most of the fellows operating out there."

"Oh—it's just a young fellow," Walter stammered. "Nobody you'd know, I guess. It isn't settled yet. It's just—talk, mostly."

"Well, that's mostly what it is," observed Mr. Kinsolving, not unkindly, and, as it seemed to Walter, with a kind of amused knowledge that cut deeper than any rebuke. "Talk. I've seen a lot of young fellows talk themselves into that game and out of their shirts. You want to watch your step. You hang on to your job, young man, till you've got something real. That's my advice." And having delivered himself of this, he turned to his wife and began to speak of a man named Dolan who had failed to deliver a load of brick to a job on Michigan Avenue, and of what he intended to do to Dolan on the morrow, while Walter sat silent, turning his hat in his hands (for he had taken it from the hall stand in anticipation of leaving and then, finding no graceful moment, had been compelled to hold it), and feeling himself smaller and more out of place with every passing minute.

And yet, as he watched them, he became aware of something else—something which he could not at first have named. For Della, as her husband talked, had grown quieter. She sat listening with an expression of polite attention, nodding now and again and saying "Yes, Harvey," and "I should think so," but her eyes, he noticed, wandered more than once to the fire, and once to the window, where the wind was flinging sleet against the panes, and there was in her face a kind of patient, set look which he did not remember from the old days and which did not, somehow, fit with the silks and the diamonds and the bronze youth on his pedestal. Was she happy? It had not occurred to him to wonder. He had supposed, as one does, that with all this—the house, the maid, the rings—she must be. And yet—

Presently Mr. Kinsolving, having finished both his cigar and his account of Dolan, rose heavily and announced that he had some figures to go over in his den and would leave them to their visiting. "Come again, young fellow," he said, again crushing Walter's hand. "Del gets lonesome, I guess, with me out all day. Don't you, Del?" And he patted her shoulder with a large, careless hand and went out, and they heard his step going up the stairs and a door closing somewhere above.

For a moment neither of them spoke. The fire crackled. The sleet ticked against the glass. Then Della, with a little laugh that was not quite the laugh of before, said: "Harvey's awfully good to me, Walter. You mustn't mind the way he talks. He's like that with everybody."

"Oh, I don't mind," said Walter quickly. "He's right, I guess. About the real estate, I mean." And then, moved by something in her face, and by the warmth of the fire, and by the old memories which their talk had stirred, he added, almost before he knew it: "There isn't any real estate, Della. Not really. I just said that. I'm just a clerk down there. Fourteen a week." And he looked at her, half defiantly, half in shame, waiting.

But she did not laugh, or look at him with pity, as he had feared. Instead she gazed at him for a long moment with those gray-green eyes, and then she said, very softly: "Oh, Walter. You didn't have to tell me that. I knew." And then, after a pause: "I was making six dollars a week at Madame Furlong's when I met Harvey. Trimming hats. Six dollars. And living in one room on Wabash Avenue with a girl from Kankakee who stole my stockings. You don't know what that's like for a girl. Or maybe you do." She turned the large diamond on her finger round and round. "I was so tired, Walter. I was so tired of it all."

He did not know what to say. He sat looking at her, and at the room, and at the fire, and for the first time it came to him, dimly and confusedly, that there might be more than one way of paying for things, and that not all of the prices were written on the tags. And yet—and yet! How he envied her, just the same! How gladly, if he could, he would have traded his narrow room and his high stool and his forty-one dollars for all this, whatever it cost! Was that wrong? Was it base? His mother would have said so, no doubt. But his mother had never sat on a stool on South Water Street for three years, adding up other men's coal.

It was after ten when he left, Della going with him to the door herself and pressing his hand and making him promise to come again—to come for Sunday dinner, soon—and he went down the steps into the whirling sleet and turned up his collar and stood a moment looking back at the lighted windows, at the round tower with its pointed slate roof, at the iron lamp. Then he walked toward the car line, his hands deep in his pockets, his head bent against the wind, thinking—of her, of Kinsolving and his cigar and his elk's tooth, of the diamond turning round and round on her finger, and of himself, and of what, in this great, hard, glittering city, a man without money might ever hope to be.
