It was close upon six o'clock of a raw November evening, the sky over the yards of the Erie and the low, smoke-blackened roofs of Sixth Street already gone to a dull slate, when Henry Wertz, a dye-house foreman at the Kimball Woolen Mills, turned in at the gate of the small frame cottage which he rented, at eleven dollars a month, from a German saloonkeeper named Ruppert. The cottage, painted a brownish drab that had long since flaked away at the corners, stood third in a row of five exactly like it, and its narrow porch, sagging a little toward the street, was cluttered with a broken wagon, a coal scuttle and a child's tin pail, all of which, as he mounted the steps, struck him with that peculiar sense of irritation and defeat which the shabby surroundings of the poor so often produce in those who have hoped for better and have not attained it. For Wertz, at thirty-eight, had once thought (and not so very long ago either) that he might rise to be superintendent of the whole dyeing department, or even, by some fortunate turn which he could not quite define, come to own a little mill of his own somewhere, in Akron, say, or Canton, where wool was being bought up cheaply and men with a practical knowledge of colors were in demand. Instead of which, here he was, at the end of eleven hours of steam and indigo and the sour, chemic stench of mordants that clung to his very skin, coming home to this.

And yet it was not of himself that he was thinking as he opened the door, but of what his wife, Hannah, had told him through the telephone at Bodley's drug store that noon. He had been called down from the dye floor to take the message, a thing in itself unusual and disturbing, and had stood there in his stained apron among the clerks and the shelves of patent medicines, hearing her troubled, half-tearful voice explain that Ollie, their boy, seven years old in September, had been brought home that morning by a clerk from Pfeiffer's Dry Goods Emporium on Main Street. The clerk, a tall, pale young man with spectacles, had been very polite but very firm. The boy had been seen to take from a counter near the door a small mechanical toy, a tin monkey that climbed a string when wound, valued at twenty-five cents, and to slip it into the pocket of his coat. Mr. Pfeiffer would not, of course, think of making any trouble over so small a matter, the clerk had said, in view of the child's age and of the respectability of the family. But he thought the parents should know. Yes. He thought they should know.

Respectability! Wertz had hung up the receiver and stood a moment staring at a colored placard advertising Lydia Pinkham's Vegetable Compound, not seeing it at all. A thief. His boy. And Pfeiffer, who was a member of the Elks and of the Second Lutheran, the same church to which Hannah went every Sunday and to which he himself went now and then, at Easter and Christmas, would know of it, and his clerks, and perhaps half the town by now. It was not to be borne. All the afternoon, among the vats, with the bolts of wet flannel steaming upward and the Polish helpers shouting to one another in a tongue he could not understand, he had turned it over and over in his mind. What had he done, or failed to do? What was it in the boy? Was it in the blood, some taint of weakness or of evil that came down from somewhere, from Hannah's people, perhaps, of whom there had been a brother, Gus, who had gone to Toledo and never been heard of again except as one who drank? Or was it merely that the child, seeing other children with things, wanted them, as he himself, Henry Wertz, had wanted and still wanted so very many things that he could not have? He did not know. It was too much for him. But one thing he did know, and that was that it must be stopped, and stopped now, before it went any further. For what else was there to do?

Inside, the small front room, with its worn ingrain carpet, its Morris chair with one broken spring, its oak center table on which stood a lamp with a green glass shade and the family Bible, was dim and chill, for Hannah, in her anxiety, had neglected to feed the base-burner. From the kitchen beyond came the smell of fried potatoes and the sound of a skillet being moved. And then Hannah herself appeared in the doorway, a short, plump, light-haired woman of thirty-four, with an apron over her brown wrapper and an expression of such apprehension and appeal on her round face that he was irritated by it even before she spoke.

"Henry," she began, wiping her hands nervously, "now, Henry, before you say anything—"

"Where is he?" he asked, not unkindly, but with a flatness of tone which told her at once how matters stood with him.

"He's upstairs. I sent him up after dinner. He's been up there all afternoon. He cried and cried, Henry. He knows he did wrong. I talked to him. I think maybe—"

"You think maybe!" He took off his coat and hung it on the hook behind the door with a slowness and deliberation which were not natural to him. "You think maybe. That's always the way with you. You think maybe if you talk to him, and you cry a little, and he cries a little, then it's all over and he's a good boy again. No. This is a time when talking isn't enough. Do you know what Pfeiffer's going to think of us? Do you know what everybody's going to say? 'That's Wertz's boy. The one that steals.'" He brought out the last word with a kind of bitterness, as though it were something that had been done to him personally, and as indeed, in a sense, he felt that it had.

"Oh, Henry, he's only a baby."

"He's seven years old. When I was seven years old I was picking up coal along the tracks in Mansfield and bringing it home in a sack. And if I had ever taken so much as a penny that wasn't mine, my father would have—" He did not finish. He was thinking of his own father, a heavy, silent, bearded man, a cooper, who had beaten him with a barrel stave for lesser things than this, and of whom he had been afraid all his life, even until the old man died. And had he, Henry, been the better for it? He did not know that either. But he thought so. He supposed so. It was what was done.

"Call him down," he said.

Hannah hesitated, her lips trembling, and then went to the foot of the narrow stairs which led up from the kitchen and called, in a voice so soft and so hopeful of mercy that it was almost an apology: "Ollie. Ollie, dear. Come down now. Papa's home."

There was a long pause, during which Wertz, standing beside the center table in his shirt sleeves, his heavy, square hands hanging at his sides, could hear the faint creak of the bed upstairs and then the shuffle of small feet upon the bare boards. And then, slowly, one step at a time, as though each were a thing to be endured separately, the boy came down. He was small for his age, thin and fair like his mother, with large, pale blue eyes that were now red-rimmed and swollen, and a shock of whitish hair that stood up at the back where he had been lying on it. He wore a pair of knee pants of gray cassimere, cut down by Hannah from an old pair of his father's, black ribbed stockings with a darn at one knee, and a blue flannel waist that was too large for him. And as he came into the doorway and stood there, one hand still holding to the jamb, and looked at his father, there was in his face that peculiar mingling of terror and of a dumb, half-defiant wonder which the very young so often show when they find themselves confronted by consequences the meaning of which they cannot fully grasp.

For to Ollie, if the truth were told, the thing had not seemed so very wicked at the time. He had gone with his mother to Pfeiffer's, as he often did, and while she was at the back of the store looking at bolts of outing flannel and talking with Mrs. Schaefer, who lived on Locust Street, he had wandered toward the front where, upon a low counter near the window, were ranged all manner of things that drew him as a candle draws a moth: tin trumpets, jumping jacks, spinning tops painted red and gold, little iron fire engines with horses that had real manes, and this monkey, this wonderful monkey in a red coat and a little red cap, which, when you turned a key in its back, went up a string by itself, hand over hand, as though it were alive. He had watched it, when the clerk showed it to another boy, a boy in a velvet suit whose mother had bought it for him then and there. And he had wanted it so. Oh, so very much. It was the most beautiful thing he had ever seen. And there were three more of them lying there, just the same, and nobody looking. And so he had taken one. That was all. He had not thought about it any further than that. It had seemed, in a way, as though it ought to be his, since he wanted it so much more than anybody else possibly could.

Only, afterward, when the tall clerk with the spectacles had followed them out to the street and taken hold of his arm, and his mother had turned so white, and people had stopped to look, then it had all become something else—a thing dark and dreadful and enormous, which he did not understand at all, but which he knew, from his mother's face and her crying, was very bad indeed.

"Come here," said his father.

The boy let go the doorjamb and came forward, step by step, across the worn carpet, until he stood perhaps three feet away, his hands twisting together before him, his eyes lifted, then lowered, then lifted again.

"Do you know what you did today?"

Ollie's lip began to quiver. "Yes, Papa."

"What did you do?"

"I—I took the monkey."

"You took the monkey," repeated his father, in a heavy, measured way. "You took it. You stole it. That's what it's called. Stealing. Do you know what happens to people who steal?"

The boy did not answer. He stared at the buttons of his father's vest, at the brass watch chain that hung across it, at the stain of blue dye, like a bruise, upon the back of one of his father's hands.

"They go to jail," went on Wertz, and now, in spite of himself, his voice was rising, for the sight of the child's fear and silence, instead of softening him, seemed only to increase his own sense of shame and of injury. "They put them in the reform school, out at Lancaster, with bars on the windows. That's where they put boys who steal. And when they grow up they put them in the penitentiary in Columbus, in stripes, and nobody wants to have anything to do with them ever again. Nobody. Not their own mothers or fathers even. Is that what you want?"

"No, Papa." It was only a whisper.

"Then why did you do it?"

Why? Why indeed? The boy could not have said, any more than his father, standing over him, could have said why it was that he himself, at that very moment, wanted so badly to strike something—not the boy, exactly, but something—the drab walls, the cracked lamp shade, the whole narrow, pinched, eleven-dollar-a-month life of which this was a part. For in the father there was working, though he could scarcely have put a name to it, a sense of the same unsatisfied longing which had moved the child—a longing for the bright, the shining, the unattainable—the things which others had and which he had not, and which, if he were honest with himself, he had more than once been tempted to reach out and take, by some trick or other, had he only the courage or the opportunity. There had been the matter of the dye accounts last spring, when old Kimball's bookkeeper had been sick and he, Wertz, had kept the books for a week, and had seen how easily—how very easily—But no! No! He had not. He was an honest man. He had never taken a cent that was not his. And his boy would not either, not if he had to—

"Answer me!"

"I—I wanted it," faltered Ollie, and burst into tears.

It was the simplest of answers and the truest, and for an instant it struck Wertz with an odd force, as though someone had touched a nerve in him. Wanted it. Yes. Of course. Who did not want things? But was that any excuse? Did that make it right? If everybody took what they wanted, where would the world be? Where would Pfeiffer be, and Kimball, and the Second Lutheran Church, and the whole order of things by which a man went to work at six and came home at six and paid his rent and his grocer and was respected? No. It could not be allowed. The rules were the rules, and they were made by those who had for the protection of what they had, perhaps—a thought which had come to him dimly once or twice before, when listening to a socialist speaker on a soap box on Court Street—but they were the rules just the same, and if you broke them, you were done for. That was the way life was. The sooner the boy knew it the better.

"Wanting isn't any reason," he said harshly. "I want lots of things. Your mother wants lots of things. Do we go and steal them? Do we?"

"N-no, Papa."

"Henry," put in Hannah from the kitchen doorway, her hands clasped against her apron, "he's sorry. Look at him. He's sorry, Henry."

"Sorry! He's sorry because he got caught. That's all he's sorry for." And then, turning again upon the boy, who was now sobbing in great, shaking gulps, his small chest heaving under the blue flannel: "Stop that crying. Stop it, I say! Crying won't help you any."

The child, with a terrible effort, choked back his sobs, so that only a kind of hiccoughing sound came from him, and stood there with the tears running down his cheeks and dripping from his chin onto the front of his waist, his eyes fixed upon his father with an expression which Wertz was to remember afterward, though he did not then understand it—an expression not so much of contrition as of a kind of stunned bewilderment, as though the boy were asking, not in words, but with his whole being: But why is it so terrible? Why? I only wanted it.

"Now listen to me," went on his father, lowering his voice somewhat, though it lost none of its weight. "Tomorrow morning, before I go to work, you and I are going down to Pfeiffer's. And you're going to go in there and walk up to Mr. Pfeiffer, in front of everybody, and you're going to say you're sorry you stole his monkey and that you'll never do it again. Do you hear?"

At this the boy's face went white, whiter even than it had been, and a new terror came into his eyes. To go back there! Into that store, with all the clerks, and the tall one with the spectacles, and perhaps that boy in the velvet suit, all looking at him! It was more than he could bear even to think of.

"Oh, no, Papa! Please, Papa! I won't ever do it again. Honest I won't. Please don't make me!"

"You'll do it," said his father. "And that isn't all. Your mother gave back the monkey. But you're going to pay for the trouble you made. You've got thirty-five cents in that bank of yours upstairs, that your grandmother gave you. You're going to take twenty-five cents of that and give it to Mr. Pfeiffer, and you're not going to get the monkey either. You're going to give him the money and get nothing. So you'll know what it costs to steal."

Here Hannah, who had been holding herself in as best she could, came forward a step. "Henry, that's his Christmas money. He was saving it to buy—"

"I don't care what he was saving it for," returned Wertz, with a sharpness which he instantly half regretted, and yet could not retract. "He'll do as I say. And after that, for two weeks, he doesn't go out of this yard except to school and back. No playing on the street. No going to Pfeiffer's or anywhere else with you. Two weeks."

He paused, breathing heavily, and looked down at the small, shaking figure before him. And now, curiously enough, as he looked, a change began to come over him, or at least a doubt. The child seemed so small—so very small and thin and helpless in his cut-down trousers and his darned stockings. And the tears! And those eyes, so like Hannah's when she had been a girl and he had first walked out with her along the canal at Massillon, before any of this—before the mills and the rent and the eleven hours and the endless, endless struggle to keep up. Was he being too hard? Was this the way? His own father had been hard, harder than this, and he had hated him for it, God knew, and had been glad, secretly glad (though he had never admitted it even to Hannah) when the old man died. Would Ollie hate him too, some day? Would he grow up and go away, like Hannah's brother Gus, and never write?

And yet! And yet! If he were not hard now, what then? Let the boy think that it was nothing—a little crying, a little scolding, and then all forgotten? And then, at ten, at fifteen, at twenty, something bigger—a watch, a pocketbook, money from a till—and then the police, the court, the newspapers, the whole shame of it spread out for all to see? No. Better this. Better that he should cry now. It was for his own good. It was what any decent father would do. And he, Henry Wertz, was a decent father, whatever else he might not be.

"Now go upstairs," he said, more quietly. "Go upstairs and get ready for bed. You don't get any supper tonight. And you get down on your knees and ask God to forgive you, like your mother taught you. Go on."

The boy turned without a word and went, walking blindly, one hand outstretched before him as though in the dark, though the kitchen was lit. They heard him stumble once on the stairs, and then the slow creak of the boards overhead, and then the creak of the bed, and then nothing.

For a long moment neither of them spoke. Hannah stood with her apron to her mouth, looking at her husband with an expression in which reproach and a kind of uncomprehending pity were mingled, for she did not know whether it was the child or the man she was sorrier for. And Wertz, conscious of her gaze and not able to meet it, went over to the base-burner and, opening the little door, began to shake down the ashes with a great rattling, as though by this noisy and practical activity he might drown out something within him that would not be still.

"Your supper's getting cold," said Hannah at last, in a low voice.

"I'm not hungry."

"You've got to eat, Henry."

"I said I'm not hungry." He shoveled coal into the stove from the scuttle, too much coal, so that the fire was nearly smothered, and then closed the door and stood up and wiped his hands on his trousers, leaving a long black smear. And then, after a moment, more gently: "All right. I'll eat. I'll eat something."

He went into the kitchen and sat down at the oilcloth-covered table, under the bracket lamp, and Hannah put before him a plate of fried potatoes and a slice of boiled ham and a cup of coffee, and he ate, slowly and without tasting anything, while she sat opposite with her hands in her lap and did not eat at all. Outside the wind had risen and was rattling the loose pane in the window over the sink, and from the Erie yards came the long, mournful wail of a freight engine pulling out for Cleveland, a sound that he had heard ten thousand times and that tonight seemed somehow to be calling to him of places far off and lives different from this one—lives in which there were no dye vats and no Pfeiffers and no little boys standing white-faced and weeping on worn carpets because they had wanted a tin monkey that climbed a string.

Later, when Hannah had washed the dishes and gone up, he sat on alone in the front room in the broken Morris chair, the lamp turned low, with the Mansfield *Courier* open on his knees, not reading it. Once he thought he heard, through the thin ceiling, a small sound, a whimper or a sob, and he half rose, as though he would go up. But he did not go. Instead he sat down again and stared at the red glow showing through the mica windows of the base-burner, thinking—thinking of his father with the barrel stave, of Kimball's books, of the mill he would never own, of the superintendency that had gone last year to a younger man named Haight who had been to the technical school at Columbus. Of all the things that he too had wanted, and still wanted, and would never have. And of the boy upstairs, who had wanted only a monkey, and had taken it, and been made to cry for it. Was there, after all, so very great a difference? He could not tell. It was a puzzle—life was a puzzle—and the rules were the rules, and a man did what he had to do. That was all. That was all there was to it.

And yet he did not go up to bed until long after the fire had died down and the room had grown cold, and the last freight had gone wailing out of the yards into the dark.

Excerpt 1: Once across the river and into the wholesale district, she glanced about her for some likely door at which to apply. As she contemplated the wide windows and imposing signs, she became conscious of being gazed upon and understood for what she was—a wage-seeker. She had never done this thing before, and lacked courage. To avoid a certain indefinable shame she felt at being caught spying about for a position, she quickened her steps and assumed an air of indifference supposedly common to one upon an errand. In this way she passed many manufacturing and wholesale houses without once glancing in. At last, after several blocks of walking, she felt that this would not do, and began to look about again, though without relaxing her pace. A little way on she saw a great door which, for some reason, attracted her attention. It was ornamented by a small brass sign, and seemed to be the entrance to a vast hive of six or seven floors. “Perhaps,” she thought, “they may want some one,” and crossed over to enter. When she came within a score of feet of the desired goal, she saw through the window a young man in a grey checked suit. That he had anything to do with the concern, she could not tell, but because he happened to be looking in her direction her weakening heart misgave her and she hurried by, too overcome with shame to enter. Over the way stood a great six-story structure, labelled Storm and King, which she viewed with rising hope. It was a wholesale dry goods concern and employed women. She could see them moving about now and then upon the upper floors. This place she decided to enter, no matter what. She crossed over and walked directly toward the entrance. As she did so, two men came out and paused in the door. A telegraph messenger in blue dashed past her and up the few steps that led to the entrance and disappeared. Several pedestrians out of the hurrying throng which filled the sidewalks passed about her as she paused, hesitating. She looked helplessly around, and then, seeing herself observed, retreated. It was too difficult a task. She could not go past them. So severe a defeat told sadly upon her nerves. Her feet carried her mechanically forward, every foot of her progress being a satisfactory portion of a flight which she gladly made. Block after block passed by. Upon streetlamps at the various corners she read names such as Madison, Monroe, La Salle, Clark, Dearborn, State, and still she went, her feet beginning to tire upon the broad stone flagging. She was pleased in part that the streets were bright and clean. The morning sun, shining down with steadily increasing warmth, made the shady side of the streets pleasantly cool. She looked at the blue sky overhead with more realisation of its charm than had ever come to her before. Her cowardice began to trouble her in a way. She turned back, resolving to hunt up Storm and King and enter. On the way, she encountered a great wholesale shoe company, through the broad plate windows of which she saw an enclosed executive department, hidden by frosted glass. Without this enclosure, but just within the street entrance, sat a grey-haired gentleman at a small table, with a large open ledger before him. She walked by this institution several times hesitating, but, finding herself unobserved, faltered past the screen door and stood humbly waiting.

“Well, young lady,” observed the old gentleman, looking at her somewhat kindly, “what is it you wish?”

“I am, that is, do you—I mean, do you need any help?” she stammered.

“Not just at present,” he answered smiling. “Not just at present. Come in some time next week. Occasionally we need some one.” She received the answer in silence and backed awkwardly out. The pleasant nature of her reception rather astonished her. She had expected that it would be more difficult, that something cold and harsh would be said—she knew not what. That she had not been put to shame and made to feel her unfortunate position, seemed remarkable. Somewhat encouraged, she ventured into another large structure. It was a clothing company, and more people were in evidence—well-dressed men of forty and more, surrounded by brass railings. An office boy approached her.

“Who is it you wish to see?” he asked.

“I want to see the manager,” she said. He ran away and spoke to one of a group of three men who were conferring together. One of these came towards her.

“Well?” he said coldly. The greeting drove all courage from her at once.

“Do you need any help?” she stammered.

“No,” he replied abruptly, and turned upon his heel. She went foolishly out, the office boy deferentially swinging the door for her, and gladly sank into the obscuring crowd. It was a severe setback to her recently pleased mental state. Now she walked quite aimlessly for a time, turning here and there, seeing one great company after another, but finding no courage to prosecute her single inquiry. High noon came, and with it hunger. She hunted out an unassuming restaurant and entered, but was disturbed to find that the prices were exorbitant for the size of her purse. A bowl of soup was all that she could afford, and, with this quickly eaten, she went out again. It restored her strength somewhat and made her moderately bold to pursue the search. In walking a few blocks to fix upon some probable place, she again encountered the firm of Storm and King, and this time managed to get in. Some gentlemen were conferring close at hand, but took no notice of her. She was left standing, gazing nervously upon the floor. When the limit of her distress had been nearly reached, she was beckoned to by a man at one of the many desks within the near-by railing.

“Who is it you wish to see?” he required.

“Why, any one, if you please,” she answered. “I am looking for something to do.”

“Oh, you want to see Mr. McManus,” he returned. “Sit down,” and he pointed to a chair against the neighbouring wall. He went on leisurely writing, until after a time a short, stout gentleman came in from the street.

“Mr. McManus,” called the man at the desk, “this young woman wants to see you.” The short gentleman turned about towards Carrie, and she arose and came forward.

“What can I do for you, miss?” he inquired, surveying her curiously.

“I want to know if I can get a position,” she inquired.

“As what?” he asked.

“Not as anything in particular,” she faltered.

“Have you ever had any experience in the wholesale dry goods business?” he questioned.

“No, sir,” she replied.

“Are you a stenographer or typewriter?”

“No, sir.”

“No, sir,” she said.

The words of Mr. McManus had somehow managed to restore her courage, which had fallen low, and she dared to hope that this new line would offer her something. They were along the line of the most effective retail organisation, with hundreds of stores coordinated into one and laid out upon the most imposing and economic basis. There was nothing there which she could not have used—nothing which she did not long to own. She was a work-seeker, an outcast without employment, one whom the average employee could tell at a glance was poor and in need of a situation. It must not be thought that any one could have mistaken her for a nervous, sensitive, high-strung nature, cast unduly upon a cold, calculating, and unpoetic world. Such certainly she was not. But women are peculiarly sensitive to their adornment. Carrie was not familiar with the appearance of her more fortunate sisters of the city. Neither had she before known the nature and appearance of the shop girls with whom she now compared poorly. They were pretty in the main, some even handsome, with an air of independence and indifference which added, in the case of the more favoured, a certain piquancy. Their clothes were neat, in many instances fine, and wherever she encountered the eye of one it was only to recognise in it a keen analysis of her own position—her individual shortcomings of dress and that shadow of manner which she thought must hang about her and make clear to all who and what she was. On the second floor were the managerial offices, to which, after some inquiry, she was now directed. There she found other girls ahead of her, applicants like herself, but with more of that self-satisfied and independent air which experience of the city lends; girls who scrutinised her in a painful manner. After a wait of perhaps three-quarters of an hour, she was called in turn.

“Now,” said a sharp, quick-mannered Jew, who was sitting at a roll-top desk near the window, “have you ever worked in any other store?”

“No, sir,” said Carrie.

“Oh, you haven’t,” he said, eyeing her keenly.

“No, sir,” she replied.

“Well, we prefer young women just now with some experience. I guess we can’t use you.” Carrie stood waiting a moment, hardly certain whether the interview had terminated.

“Don’t wait!” he exclaimed. “Remember we are very busy here.” Carrie began to move quickly to the door.

“Hold on,” he said, calling her back. “Give me your name and address. We want girls occasionally.” When she had gotten safely into the street, she could scarcely restrain the tears. It was not so much the particular rebuff which she had just experienced, but the whole abashing trend of the day. She was tired and nervous. She abandoned the thought of appealing to the other department stores and now wandered on, feeling a certain safety and relief in mingling with the crowd. In her indifferent wandering she turned into Jackson Street, not far from the river, and was keeping her way along the south side of that imposing thoroughfare, when a piece of wrapping paper, written on with marking ink and tacked up on the door, attracted her attention. It read, “Girls wanted—wrappers & stitchers.” She hesitated a moment, then entered. The firm of Speigelheim & Co., makers of boys’ caps, occupied one floor of the building, fifty feet in width and some eighty feet in depth. It was a place rather dingily lighted, the darkest portions having incandescent lights, filled with machines and work benches. At the latter laboured quite a company of girls and some men. The former were drabby-looking creatures, stained in face with oil and dust, clad in thin, shapeless, cotton dresses and shod with more or less worn shoes. Many of them had their sleeves rolled up, revealing bare arms, and in some cases, owing to the heat, their dresses were open at the neck. They were a fair type of nearly the lowest order of shop-girls—careless, slouchy, and more or less pale from confinement. They were not timid, however; were rich in curiosity, and strong in daring and slang. Carrie looked about her, very much disturbed and quite sure that she did not want to work here. Aside from making her uncomfortable by sidelong glances, no one paid her the least attention. She waited until the whole department was aware of her presence. Then some word was sent around, and a foreman, in an apron and shirt sleeves, the latter rolled up to his shoulders, approached.

“Do you want to see me?” he asked.

“Do you need any help?” said Carrie, already learning directness of address.

“Do you know how to stitch caps?” he returned.

“No, sir,” she replied.

“Have you ever had any experience at this kind of work?” he inquired. She answered that she had not.

“Well,” said the foreman, scratching his ear meditatively, “we do need a stitcher. We like experienced help, though. We’ve hardly got time to break people in.” He paused and looked away out of the window. “We might, though, put you at finishing,” he concluded reflectively.

“How much do you pay a week?” ventured Carrie, emboldened by a certain softness in the man’s manner and his simplicity of address.

“Three and a half,” he answered.

“Oh,” she was about to exclaim, but checked herself and allowed her thoughts to die without expression.

“We’re not exactly in need of anybody,” he went on vaguely, looking her over as one would a package. “You can come on Monday morning, though,” he added, “and I’ll put you to work.”

“Thank you,” said Carrie weakly.

“If you come, bring an apron,” he added. He walked away and left her standing by the elevator, never so much as inquiring her name. While the appearance of the shop and the announcement of the price paid per week operated very much as a blow to Carrie’s fancy, the fact that work of any kind was offered after so rude a round of experience was gratifying. She could not begin to believe that she would take the place, modest as her aspirations were. She had been used to better than that. Her mere experience and the free out-of-door life of the country caused her nature to revolt at such confinement. Dirt had never been her share. Her sister’s flat was clean. This place was grimy and low, the girls were careless and hardened. They must be bad-minded and hearted, she imagined. Still, a place had been offered her. Surely Chicago was not so bad if she could find one place in one day. She might find another and better later. Her subsequent experiences were not of a reassuring nature, however. From all the more pleasing or imposing places she was turned away abruptly with the most chilling formality. In others where she applied only the experienced were required. She met with painful rebuffs, the most trying of which had been in a manufacturing cloak house, where she had gone to the fourth floor to inquire.

“No, no,” said the foreman, a rough, heavily built individual, who looked after a miserably lighted workshop, “we don’t want any one. Don’t come here.”

The more circumscribed became her state, the more entrancing seemed this other. So, too, the ideal brought into her life by Ames remained. He had gone, but here was his word that riches were not everything; that there was a great deal more in the world than she knew; that the stage was good, and the literature she read poor. During the last three months of the Warren Street connection, Hurstwood took parts of days off and hunted, tracking the business advertisements. Everything he discovered in his line advertised as an opportunity, was either too expensive or too wretched for him. “Eighty thousand!” he thought. “What an awful thing that is.” This was new reasoning for Hurstwood. In the old days the world had seemed to be getting along well enough. He had been wont to see similar things in the “Daily News,” in Chicago, but they did not hold his attention. Now, these things were like grey clouds hovering along the horizon of a clear day. They threatened to cover and obscure his life with chilly greyness. He tried to shake them off, to forget and brace up. Sometimes he said to himself, mentally: “What’s the use worrying? It was such a cheap looking place he felt that he could not abide it. Another was on the Bowery, which he knew contained many showy resorts. “Cash?” he said.

“Oh, dat iss all over,” said the German. “I vill not sell now.”

The sun shone, the temperature was pleasant. He felt, as he came to the breakfast table, that it wasn’t so terrible, after all.

“Well,” he said to Carrie, “to-day’s my last day on earth.” Carrie smiled in answer to his humour. Hurstwood glanced over his paper rather gayly. He seemed to have lost a load.

He thought about going to some brewery, which, as he knew, frequently controlled saloons which they leased, and get them to help him. Then he remembered that he would have to pay out several hundred any way for fixtures and that he would have nothing left for his monthly expenses. It was costing him nearly eighty dollars a month to live.

“No,” he said, in his sanest moments, “I can’t do it. I’ll get something else and save up.” This getting-something proposition complicated itself the moment he began to think of what it was he wanted to do. Manage a place? Into a place important enough to need such a manager he had not money enough to buy. Nevertheless, he started out. His clothes were very good and his appearance still excellent, but it involved the trouble of deluding. People, looking at him, imagined instantly that a man of his age, stout and well dressed, must be well off. He appeared a comfortable owner of something, a man from whom the common run of mortals could well expect gratuities. Being now forty-three years of age, and comfortably built, walking was not easy. He had not been used to exercise for many years. His legs tired, his shoulders ached, and his feet pained him at the close of the day, even when he took street cars in almost every direction. The mere getting up and down, if long continued, produced this result. The fact that people took him to be better off than he was, he well understood. It was so painfully clear to him that it retarded his search. Not that he wished to be less well-appearing, but that he was ashamed to belie his appearance by incongruous appeals. So he hesitated, wondering what to do. He thought of the hotels, but instantly he remembered that he had had no experience as a clerk, and, what was more important, no acquaintances or friends in that line to whom he could go. He did know some hotel owners in several cities, including New York, but they knew of his dealings with Fitzgerald and Moy. He could not apply to them. He thought of other lines suggested by large buildings or businesses which he knew of—wholesale groceries, hardware, insurance concerns, and the like—but he had had no experience. How to go about getting anything was a bitter thought. Would he have to go personally and ask; wait outside an office door, and, then, distinguished and affluent looking, announce that he was looking for something to do? He strained painfully at the thought. No, he could not do that. He really strolled about, thinking, and then, the weather being cold, stepped into a hotel. He knew hotels well enough to know that any decent individual was welcome to a chair in the lobby. This was in the Broadway Central, which was then one of the most important hotels in the city. Taking a chair here was a painful thing to him. To think he should come to this! He had heard loungers about hotels called chairwarmers. He had called them that himself in his day. But here he was, despite the possibility of meeting some one who knew him, shielding himself from cold and the weariness of the streets in a hotel lobby.

“I can’t do this way,” he said to himself. “There’s no use of my starting out mornings without first thinking up some place to go. I’ll think of some places and then look them up.” It occurred to him that the positions of bartenders were sometimes open, but he put this out of his mind. Bartender—he, the ex-manager! It grew awfully dull sitting in the hotel lobby, and so at four he went home. He tried to put on a business air as he went in, but it was a feeble imitation. The rocking chair in the dining-room was comfortable. He sank into it gladly, with several papers he had bought, and began to read. As she was going through the room to begin preparing dinner, Carrie said:
“The man was here for the rent to-day.”

The Lawlor flat was on the third floor of a narrow brick building in Ridge Avenue, one of those structures thrown up in the eighties by a speculating contractor who had expected the neighbourhood to improve and had been disappointed. It contained four rooms, of which the front one, by virtue of a carpet of red and green figure and a plush-covered settee bought upon the instalment plan, was called the parlour. The others were a bedroom, a kitchen, and a small dining-room which received its light from an air-shaft. Here, of an evening, Henry Lawlor was accustomed to sit after his supper, his shoes unlaced, his newspaper spread upon his knees, reviewing the doings of a world in which he had small part and of which he understood little more than the headlines conveyed.

He was a man of thirty-four, a shipping clerk in the employ of Battle & Kress, wholesale hardware, at a salary of fourteen dollars a week. He was not a man of large imagination. He had come up out of a family of mill-hands in Allegheny, and the fact that he wore a white collar to his work and sat at a high desk with a ledger before him seemed to him in the main a satisfactory ascent. He had a certain pride in it. He liked to think of himself as one who had "got along," and he was given, when in company, to speaking of the firm as "we," as though he had some voice in its councils. In reality he had none, and he knew it in a dim way, but the habit gave him pleasure, and he did not examine it.

His wife, Alma, was of another composition entirely. She was twenty-six, and pretty after that soft, fair, slightly full fashion which wears well enough until thirty and then gives way rather suddenly. She had been a shop-girl at Horne's before her marriage, standing behind the glove counter, and there she had acquired, without at all realising it, a whole philosophy of appearances. She had watched the ladies of the East End come in, drawing off their gloves of French kid and laying them upon the counter to be matched, and she had studied, with that keenness which the eye of the excluded possesses, the cut of their jackets, the set of their hats, and the indefinable manner of their speech. Something of this had entered into her and remained. She did not know what it was she wanted. She could not have put it into words. But it was there, a steady drag upon her, like the pull of a current beneath the surface of still water.

It must not be supposed that the marriage had been an unhappy one. For four years it had moved along in that grey, even fashion which passes, among people of small means, for contentment. Henry had been steady. He did not drink beyond a glass of beer at Schlosser's on a Saturday. He brought his envelope home. Alma kept the rooms clean, cooked, and went on Sundays to visit her mother in Lawrenceville. If there were moments when each regarded the other with a faint, unformulated disappointment, these were not spoken of, and so did not seem to exist. Such is the way of most unions. The great body of men and women are held together not so much by love as by the absence of any compelling reason to part.

On this particular evening, a Thursday in late November, Henry had come home in a mood which was not of the best. There had been talk at the office of a reduction. Old Kress, it was said, had been examining the pay-roll, and the word had gone round among the clerks that two of them would be let go before Christmas. Henry did not think that he would be one of them. He had been there six years. But the thought of it had lain upon him all day like a weight, and he had come up the stairs heavily, with his mind full of figures—the rent, which was eighteen dollars a month; the grocer, who had a bill of eleven dollars standing; the coal, which must be bought before the cold set in in earnest.

Alma had his supper ready. She was in good spirits, rather better than usual, and this, in his present state, irritated him slightly without his knowing why. She chattered of her mother, of a neighbour's child who had the croup, of a new milliner who had opened on Penn Avenue. He ate in silence, answering only with a word here and there. When he had finished, he pushed back his chair and went into the parlour, where the lamp was lighted, and sat down.

It was while he was searching in the drawer of the little table beside the settee for a pencil, intending to do some figuring upon the margin of his paper, that he came upon the card. It was a small buff-coloured slip, printed at the top with the name of Rosenbaum & Co., and below this, in a clerk's hand, were written a description and a series of figures. "One sealskin jacket, plush-lined, $38.00. Paid on acct. $4.00. Bal. $34.00. Weekly payments $2.00." There were three such payments entered, each with its date and the initials of the receiving clerk.

He looked at it a long time. At first he did not understand. Then, as the meaning of it came to him, he felt a slow heat rise in his face, and his hand, holding the card, trembled a little. Thirty-eight dollars! It was nearly three weeks of his wages. And she had said nothing—nothing at all. She had been paying it out of the house money, a dollar here and a dollar there, and lying to him, or at least keeping silent, which in his mind came to the same thing.

He did not call her at once. He sat with the card in his hand, turning it over, reading it again, as though the figures might change. A dozen thoughts ran through his mind in no particular order. Where had she got the four dollars to begin with? What had she been leaving off, that she should have two dollars a week to spare? He thought of the grocer's bill. He thought of the talk at the office. He thought of old Kress bent over the pay-roll with his spectacles on his nose. And all of these things gathered themselves together and became one thing, which was anger.

"Alma," he called.

"What is it?" she answered from the kitchen, where she was washing the dishes.

"Come in here a minute."

She came, drying her hands upon her apron, and stood in the doorway. She saw at once that something was wrong. His face had that heavy, set look which she had seen upon it only a few times before, and his eyes did not meet hers but were fixed upon something he held.

"What's the matter?" she asked.

"What's this?" he said, holding out the card.

She did not take it. She did not need to. She knew it the moment she saw its colour, and a wave of something—not so much guilt as a kind of startled resentment at being found out—went over her. She had meant to tell him. She had certainly meant to tell him, when the jacket was paid for and she could wear it, and he could see how well it looked on her, and how much it was worth. She had pictured this many times—his surprise, his grudging admiration, the matter passed off with a laugh. That it should come out this way, in this light, with this look upon his face, was not at all what she had intended.

"Where did you get that?" she said.

"It doesn't matter where I got it. It was in the drawer. What is it?"

"You can read, can't you?" she returned, and immediately regretted it, for she saw his jaw tighten.

"Yes, I can read," he said slowly. "I can read thirty-eight dollars. That's what I can read. Thirty-eight dollars for a jacket. Did you think I wasn't going to find out?"

"I was going to tell you."

"When?"

"When it was paid for."

"Oh, when it was paid for," he repeated, with a heavy sarcasm that sat ill upon him, being a weapon he was unused to handling. "That's fine. That's very fine. And where was the money coming from in the meantime? Out of my pocket, I suppose."

"It came out of the house money," she said, flushing. "I saved it."

"Saved it! How did you save it? Grocer's got a bill of eleven dollars. I saw it myself Saturday. Is that the way you save?"

This was a thrust which she had not anticipated, and for a moment she had no answer. It was true that she had let the grocer's bill run. She had told herself that it was only for a little while, that the man did not mind, that everybody did it. And it was true that everybody did. But to have it brought up in this fashion, as a crime, stung her.

"Well, what of it?" she said, coming a step into the room. "Everybody owes the grocer. Mrs. Dietz owes him more than that. I'll pay it."

"With what?"

"With what I've always paid it with."

"You'll pay it," he said, "and you'll pay this, and you'll pay the rent, and you'll pay the coal, and all on fourteen dollars a week. Maybe you know something I don't. Maybe you've got a rich uncle somewhere." He laid the card down on the table with a little slap, as though it were a thing that defiled his hand. "Do you know what they're talking about down at the place? They're going to let two men go. Two men. Maybe I'm one of them. How do I know? And here you are, buying sealskin."

She had not heard of this, and it gave her a momentary check. She looked at him more closely, noticing for the first time how tired he seemed, how the lines about his mouth had deepened. But the feeling did not last. It was overwhelmed by the larger sense of injury which was rising in her, compounded of many evenings like this one, of many small denials, of a whole life which had seemed, when she looked at it squarely, to promise nothing.

"You're not going to be let go," she said. "You always think the worst."

"I don't think anything. I'm telling you what they say."

"Well, they say a lot of things."

"Never mind what they say," he returned, rising and beginning to walk about. "That isn't the point. The point is you went and did this without saying a word to me. You went behind my back. That's what I don't like. If you'd come to me and said, 'Henry, I want a jacket,' why, we could have talked it over. Maybe we could have managed something. A cloth one. But you didn't. You went and did it on the sly."

"Talked it over!" she exclaimed, and now her voice rose a little, for this touched something deep in her. "Yes, we could have talked it over. I know how we'd have talked it over. You'd have said we couldn't afford it. You'd have said a cloth one was good enough. You always say that. Everything's good enough. This flat's good enough. That old coat I've had for three winters is good enough. I'm sick of good enough."

He stopped in his walking and looked at her. He had never heard her speak in this way before, and it astonished him more than the card had done. It was as though some other woman had come into the room—a woman he did not know, with a hard brightness in her eyes and a colour in her cheeks that was not from the heat of the kitchen.

"What's the matter with you?" he said. "What's got into you lately?"

"Nothing's got into me."

"Something has. You never used to talk like that."

"I never used to have to," she said, which was not quite logical, but expressed in its way a great deal.

There was a silence. From below came the sound of the street, a car grinding along on its rails, the cry of a boy with evening papers. In the flat across the air-shaft some one was playing a mouth-organ, a thin, wandering tune that went on and on without arriving anywhere. Henry stood by the table, his hands in his pockets, looking at the floor. Alma stood near the door. Neither of them moved.

It is one of the curious facts of human relations that in such moments each party is usually right, and each wrong, and neither is able to see the matter except from his own side. Henry saw only that he had been deceived, that money had been taken which he had earned with his own hands and spent upon a thing he considered a vanity, and that this had been done at a time when his own position was not secure. All of this was true. Alma saw only that she was young, and pretty, and shut up in four rooms in Ridge Avenue with a man who did not understand that a woman might want something more than bread and a roof—who did not understand, indeed, that a woman might want anything at all. And this, too, was true. The jacket itself was a small matter. It was a symbol merely, as such things always are, of a hunger which had no name and could not be satisfied by any purchase, however dear. But neither of them knew this, and so they quarrelled over the jacket.

"Where is it?" said Henry at last.

"Where's what?"

"The jacket."

"It's at the store. They keep it till it's paid for."

"Well, you can go down there to-morrow and tell them you don't want it."

She looked at him in dismay. "I can't do that."

"Why can't you?"

"Because I'd lose what I've paid. Ten dollars. They don't give it back."

"Then you'll lose it," he said. "That's better than losing twenty-eight more."

"I won't," she said.

"You won't, eh?"

"No, I won't." She had come forward now, almost to the table, and stood facing him across it. Her hands were clenched in her apron. "It's my money as much as yours. I work in this house all day. I cook and wash and scrub. What do I get for it? Do I ever get anything? You go out every Saturday to Schlosser's. I don't say anything about that."

"A glass of beer!" he exclaimed, outraged. "Ten cents! You're going to put a glass of beer against thirty-eight dollars?"

"It's not just the beer," she said. "It's everything."

"What everything? What do you mean, everything? I don't do anything. I go to work, and I come home. What more do you want?"

She could not tell him what more she wanted, for she did not know. She only knew that when she walked along Fifth Avenue on a winter afternoon and saw the women in their furs stepping down from their carriages before the shops, something in her ached with a longing that was almost physical. She only knew that she had stood before the glass in Rosenbaum's with the jacket on her shoulders, its soft dark fur close about her throat, and had seen herself for a moment as one of those others—as a woman of consequence, a woman to be looked at—and that the moment had been worth more to her than anything in a year. How could she explain this to Henry, who thought a cloth coat was good enough?

"You wouldn't understand," she said.

"No, I guess I wouldn't," he returned bitterly. "I guess I'm too dumb. I'm just good enough to bring home the envelope."

"I didn't say that."

"You didn't have to say it."

He sat down again heavily in the chair and picked up the newspaper, though he did not read it. His anger was beginning to subside, as anger in a man of his nature always does, giving way to a kind of heavy, sullen hurt that was in some ways worse. He felt, without being able to express it, that something had been taken from him tonight more valuable than thirty-eight dollars. He had always supposed that Alma was satisfied. He had supposed that the flat, and the settee, and the Sundays at her mother's, and his steady place at Battle & Kress made up between them a life that she found good. Now he saw that she did not. And this knowledge, coming upon him all at once, left him bewildered and somehow ashamed, as though he had been caught in a falsehood of his own.

Alma, for her part, felt the change in him and was not softened by it. She had gone too far now to retreat. There was in her a hard little core of determination which the quarrel had brought to the surface, and she clung to it.

"I'm going to keep it," she said. "I'll pay for it myself."

"How?"

"I'll take in sewing. Mrs. Dietz does. She makes four and five dollars a week."

He laughed shortly. "Mrs. Dietz! She's got a machine."

"I can get a machine."

"On the instalment plan, I suppose," he said. "That's fine. That's the way to get out of debt—get in deeper."

She did not answer. She turned and went back into the kitchen, and he heard the dishes rattle as she took up her work again, more loudly than was necessary. He sat looking at the card on the table. After a while he picked it up and put it in his pocket, though he could not have said why. Perhaps it was only that he did not wish to see it lying there.

The evening wore on. The mouth-organ across the shaft ceased. The street grew quieter. Alma finished the dishes and did not come back into the parlour but went directly into the bedroom, where he could hear her moving about, taking down her hair. He sat on, the paper open before him, reading the same paragraph over and over—something about a strike in the coke regions, about men who had been turned out of their company houses and were living in tents in the snow. He read it without taking it in. Then, quite suddenly, it came home to him, and he thought, with a cold little shock, of what it would be to be turned out—of the flat gone, the settee taken back, Alma and himself in two rooms somewhere in Soho, or worse.

"By George," he said to himself, "a man's got enough to think about without this."

He got up and went to the bedroom door. Alma was sitting on the edge of the bed in her nightdress, braiding her hair. She did not look up.

"Alma," he said.

"What?"

"I didn't mean to talk so rough."

She went on braiding. "You did, though."

"Well, I was worried. You know that. That talk at the office."

"I know."

He waited, thinking she would say something more—that she was sorry, that she would give up the jacket, that it was all a mistake. She did not. She finished her braid, tied the end of it with a bit of ribbon, and lay down with her face to the wall.

He stood a moment longer in the doorway, then went back into the parlour and turned down the lamp. In the dark he sat by the window, looking out upon the street, where a single gas-lamp threw its yellow circle on the wet pavement. A man went by below, his collar turned up, walking fast. Henry watched him until he was out of sight. Then he sat on, his hands upon his knees, not thinking exactly, but feeling in a dull way the weight of things—of the rent and the grocer and old Kress, and of the woman in the next room who wanted something he could not give her, and whom, for all his anger, he did not wish to lose.

It was nearly midnight when he went to bed. Alma was asleep, or seemed to be. He lay down beside her carefully, so as not to wake her, and stared up at the ceiling, where the light from the street made a faint, shifting pattern. The card was still in his pocket, in the coat that hung over the chair. He had decided nothing. Neither had she. The thing lay between them unresolved, as such things mostly do, to be taken up again or to be quietly let go, according to forces neither of them understood and over which, in the end, neither had very much control.

Excerpt 1: Once across the river and into the wholesale district, she glanced about her for some likely door at which to apply. As she contemplated the wide windows and imposing signs, she became conscious of being gazed upon and understood for what she was—a wage-seeker. She had never done this thing before, and lacked courage. To avoid a certain indefinable shame she felt at being caught spying about for a position, she quickened her steps and assumed an air of indifference supposedly common to one upon an errand. In this way she passed many manufacturing and wholesale houses without once glancing in. At last, after several blocks of walking, she felt that this would not do, and began to look about again, though without relaxing her pace. A little way on she saw a great door which, for some reason, attracted her attention. It was ornamented by a small brass sign, and seemed to be the entrance to a vast hive of six or seven floors. “Perhaps,” she thought, “they may want some one,” and crossed over to enter. When she came within a score of feet of the desired goal, she saw through the window a young man in a grey checked suit. That he had anything to do with the concern, she could not tell, but because he happened to be looking in her direction her weakening heart misgave her and she hurried by, too overcome with shame to enter. Over the way stood a great six-story structure, labelled Storm and King, which she viewed with rising hope. It was a wholesale dry goods concern and employed women. She could see them moving about now and then upon the upper floors. This place she decided to enter, no matter what. She crossed over and walked directly toward the entrance. As she did so, two men came out and paused in the door. A telegraph messenger in blue dashed past her and up the few steps that led to the entrance and disappeared. Several pedestrians out of the hurrying throng which filled the sidewalks passed about her as she paused, hesitating. She looked helplessly around, and then, seeing herself observed, retreated. It was too difficult a task. She could not go past them. So severe a defeat told sadly upon her nerves. Her feet carried her mechanically forward, every foot of her progress being a satisfactory portion of a flight which she gladly made. Block after block passed by. Upon streetlamps at the various corners she read names such as Madison, Monroe, La Salle, Clark, Dearborn, State, and still she went, her feet beginning to tire upon the broad stone flagging. She was pleased in part that the streets were bright and clean. The morning sun, shining down with steadily increasing warmth, made the shady side of the streets pleasantly cool. She looked at the blue sky overhead with more realisation of its charm than had ever come to her before. Her cowardice began to trouble her in a way. She turned back, resolving to hunt up Storm and King and enter. On the way, she encountered a great wholesale shoe company, through the broad plate windows of which she saw an enclosed executive department, hidden by frosted glass. Without this enclosure, but just within the street entrance, sat a grey-haired gentleman at a small table, with a large open ledger before him. She walked by this institution several times hesitating, but, finding herself unobserved, faltered past the screen door and stood humbly waiting.

“Well, young lady,” observed the old gentleman, looking at her somewhat kindly, “what is it you wish?”

“I am, that is, do you—I mean, do you need any help?” she stammered.

“Not just at present,” he answered smiling. “Not just at present. Come in some time next week. Occasionally we need some one.” She received the answer in silence and backed awkwardly out. The pleasant nature of her reception rather astonished her. She had expected that it would be more difficult, that something cold and harsh would be said—she knew not what. That she had not been put to shame and made to feel her unfortunate position, seemed remarkable. Somewhat encouraged, she ventured into another large structure. It was a clothing company, and more people were in evidence—well-dressed men of forty and more, surrounded by brass railings. An office boy approached her.

“Who is it you wish to see?” he asked.

“I want to see the manager,” she said. He ran away and spoke to one of a group of three men who were conferring together. One of these came towards her.

“Well?” he said coldly. The greeting drove all courage from her at once.

“Do you need any help?” she stammered.

“No,” he replied abruptly, and turned upon his heel. She went foolishly out, the office boy deferentially swinging the door for her, and gladly sank into the obscuring crowd. It was a severe setback to her recently pleased mental state. Now she walked quite aimlessly for a time, turning here and there, seeing one great company after another, but finding no courage to prosecute her single inquiry. High noon came, and with it hunger. She hunted out an unassuming restaurant and entered, but was disturbed to find that the prices were exorbitant for the size of her purse. A bowl of soup was all that she could afford, and, with this quickly eaten, she went out again. It restored her strength somewhat and made her moderately bold to pursue the search. In walking a few blocks to fix upon some probable place, she again encountered the firm of Storm and King, and this time managed to get in. Some gentlemen were conferring close at hand, but took no notice of her. She was left standing, gazing nervously upon the floor. When the limit of her distress had been nearly reached, she was beckoned to by a man at one of the many desks within the near-by railing.

“Who is it you wish to see?” he required.

“Why, any one, if you please,” she answered. “I am looking for something to do.”

“Oh, you want to see Mr. McManus,” he returned. “Sit down,” and he pointed to a chair against the neighbouring wall. He went on leisurely writing, until after a time a short, stout gentleman came in from the street.

“Mr. McManus,” called the man at the desk, “this young woman wants to see you.” The short gentleman turned about towards Carrie, and she arose and came forward.

“I want to know if I can get a position,” she inquired.

“As what?” he asked.

“Not as anything in particular,” she faltered.

“Have you ever had any experience in the wholesale dry goods business?” he questioned.

“No, sir,” she replied.

“Are you a stenographer or typewriter?”

“No, sir.”

“No, sir,” she said.

The words of Mr. McManus had somehow managed to restore her courage, which had fallen low, and she dared to hope that this new line would offer her something. Such a flowering out of a modest trade principle the world had never witnessed up to that time. They were along the line of the most effective retail organisation, with hundreds of stores coordinated into one and laid out upon the most imposing and economic basis. They were handsome, bustling, successful affairs, with a host of clerks and a swarm of patrons. There was nothing there which she could not have used—nothing which she did not long to own. The dainty slippers and stockings, the delicately frilled skirts and petticoats, the laces, ribbons, hair-combs, purses, all touched her with individual desire, and she felt keenly the fact that not any of these things were in the range of her purchase. She was a work-seeker, an outcast without employment, one whom the average employee could tell at a glance was poor and in need of a situation. It must not be thought that any one could have mistaken her for a nervous, sensitive, high-strung nature, cast unduly upon a cold, calculating, and unpoetic world. Such certainly she was not. But women are peculiarly sensitive to their adornment. Carrie was not familiar with the appearance of her more fortunate sisters of the city. Neither had she before known the nature and appearance of the shop girls with whom she now compared poorly. They were pretty in the main, some even handsome, with an air of independence and indifference which added, in the case of the more favoured, a certain piquancy. Their clothes were neat, in many instances fine, and wherever she encountered the eye of one it was only to recognise in it a keen analysis of her own position—her individual shortcomings of dress and that shadow of manner which she thought must hang about her and make clear to all who and what she was. On the second floor were the managerial offices, to which, after some inquiry, she was now directed. After a wait of perhaps three-quarters of an hour, she was called in turn.

“Now,” said a sharp, quick-mannered Jew, who was sitting at a roll-top desk near the window, “have you ever worked in any other store?”

“No, sir,” said Carrie.

“Oh, you haven’t,” he said, eyeing her keenly.

“No, sir,” she replied.

“Well, we prefer young women just now with some experience. I guess we can’t use you.” Carrie stood waiting a moment, hardly certain whether the interview had terminated.

“Don’t wait!” he exclaimed. “Remember we are very busy here.” Carrie began to move quickly to the door.

“Hold on,” he said, calling her back. “Give me your name and address. We want girls occasionally.” When she had gotten safely into the street, she could scarcely restrain the tears. In her indifferent wandering she turned into Jackson Street, not far from the river, and was keeping her way along the south side of that imposing thoroughfare, when a piece of wrapping paper, written on with marking ink and tacked up on the door, attracted her attention. It read, “Girls wanted—wrappers & stitchers.” She hesitated a moment, then entered. The firm of Speigelheim & Co., makers of boys’ caps, occupied one floor of the building, fifty feet in width and some eighty feet in depth. It was a place rather dingily lighted, the darkest portions having incandescent lights, filled with machines and work benches. At the latter laboured quite a company of girls and some men. The former were drabby-looking creatures, stained in face with oil and dust, clad in thin, shapeless, cotton dresses and shod with more or less worn shoes. Many of them had their sleeves rolled up, revealing bare arms, and in some cases, owing to the heat, their dresses were open at the neck. They were a fair type of nearly the lowest order of shop-girls—careless, slouchy, and more or less pale from confinement. They were not timid, however; were rich in curiosity, and strong in daring and slang. Carrie looked about her, very much disturbed and quite sure that she did not want to work here. Aside from making her uncomfortable by sidelong glances, no one paid her the least attention. She waited until the whole department was aware of her presence. Then some word was sent around, and a foreman, in an apron and shirt sleeves, the latter rolled up to his shoulders, approached.

“Do you want to see me?” he asked.

“Do you need any help?” said Carrie, already learning directness of address.

“Do you know how to stitch caps?” he returned.

“No, sir,” she replied.

“Have you ever had any experience at this kind of work?” he inquired. She answered that she had not.

“Well,” said the foreman, scratching his ear meditatively, “we do need a stitcher. We like experienced help, though. We’ve hardly got time to break people in.” He paused and looked away out of the window. “We might, though, put you at finishing,” he concluded reflectively.

“How much do you pay a week?” ventured Carrie, emboldened by a certain softness in the man’s manner and his simplicity of address.

“Three and a half,” he answered.

“Oh,” she was about to exclaim, but checked herself and allowed her thoughts to die without expression.

“We’re not exactly in need of anybody,” he went on vaguely, looking her over as one would a package. “You can come on Monday morning, though,” he added, “and I’ll put you to work.”

“Thank you,” said Carrie weakly.

“If you come, bring an apron,” he added. He walked away and left her standing by the elevator, never so much as inquiring her name. While the appearance of the shop and the announcement of the price paid per week operated very much as a blow to Carrie’s fancy, the fact that work of any kind was offered after so rude a round of experience was gratifying. She could not begin to believe that she would take the place, modest as her aspirations were. She had been used to better than that. Her mere experience and the free out-of-door life of the country caused her nature to revolt at such confinement. Dirt had never been her share. Her sister’s flat was clean. This place was grimy and low, the girls were careless and hardened. They must be bad-minded and hearted, she imagined. Still, a place had been offered her. Surely Chicago was not so bad if she could find one place in one day. She might find another and better later. Her subsequent experiences were not of a reassuring nature, however. From all the more pleasing or imposing places she was turned away abruptly with the most chilling formality. In others where she applied only the experienced were required. She met with painful rebuffs, the most trying of which had been in a manufacturing cloak house, where she had gone to the fourth floor to inquire.

“No, no,” said the foreman, a rough, heavily built individual, who looked after a miserably lighted workshop, “we don’t want any one. Don’t come here.”

The glamour of the high life of the city had, in the few experiences afforded her by the former, seized her completely. He had gone, but here was his word that riches were not everything; that there was a great deal more in the world than she knew; that the stage was good, and the literature she read poor. “Three thousand,” said the man. Hurstwood’s jaw fell.

When it actually arrived, Hurstwood, who had got his mind into such a state where a thunderclap and raging storm would have seemed highly appropriate, was rather relieved to find that it was a plain, ordinary day. The sun shone, the temperature was pleasant. He felt, as he came to the breakfast table, that it wasn’t so terrible, after all.

“Well,” he said to Carrie, “to-day’s my last day on earth.” Carrie smiled in answer to his humour. Hurstwood glanced over his paper rather gayly. He seemed to have lost a load.

“I’ll go down for a little while,” he said after breakfast, “and then I’ll look around. To-morrow I’ll spend the whole day looking about. “Well,” he said at five o’clock, “we might as well count the change and divide.” They did so. The fixtures had already been sold and the sum divided.

“Good-night,” said Hurstwood at the final moment, in a last effort to be genial.

“So long,” said Shaughnessy, scarcely deigning a notice. Thus the Warren Street arrangement was permanently concluded. Carrie had prepared a good dinner at the flat, but after his ride up, Hurstwood was in a solemn and reflective mood.

“Well?” said Carrie, inquisitively.

“I’m out of that,” he answered, taking off his coat. As she looked at him, she wondered what his financial state was now. They ate and talked a little.

“Will you have enough to buy in anywhere else?” asked Carrie.

“No,” he said. “I’ll have to get something else and save up.”

“It would be nice if you could get some place,” said Carrie, prompted by anxiety and hope.

“I guess I will,” he said reflectively. For some days thereafter he put on his overcoat regularly in the morning and sallied forth. On these ventures he first consoled himself with the thought that with the seven hundred dollars he had he could still make some advantageous arrangement. He thought about going to some brewery, which, as he knew, frequently controlled saloons which they leased, and get them to help him. Then he remembered that he would have to pay out several hundred any way for fixtures and that he would have nothing left for his monthly expenses. It was costing him nearly eighty dollars a month to live.

“No,” he said, in his sanest moments, “I can’t do it. I’ll get something else and save up.” This getting-something proposition complicated itself the moment he began to think of what it was he wanted to do. Manage a place? Where should he get such a position? The papers contained no requests for managers. Such positions, he knew well enough, were either secured by long years of service or were bought with a half or third interest. Into a place important enough to need such a manager he had not money enough to buy. Nevertheless, he started out. His clothes were very good and his appearance still excellent, but it involved the trouble of deluding. People, looking at him, imagined instantly that a man of his age, stout and well dressed, must be well off. He appeared a comfortable owner of something, a man from whom the common run of mortals could well expect gratuities. Being now forty-three years of age, and comfortably built, walking was not easy. He had not been used to exercise for many years. His legs tired, his shoulders ached, and his feet pained him at the close of the day, even when he took street cars in almost every direction. The mere getting up and down, if long continued, produced this result. The fact that people took him to be better off than he was, he well understood. It was so painfully clear to him that it retarded his search. Not that he wished to be less well-appearing, but that he was ashamed to belie his appearance by incongruous appeals. So he hesitated, wondering what to do. He thought of the hotels, but instantly he remembered that he had had no experience as a clerk, and, what was more important, no acquaintances or friends in that line to whom he could go. He did know some hotel owners in several cities, including New York, but they knew of his dealings with Fitzgerald and Moy. He could not apply to them. He thought of other lines suggested by large buildings or businesses which he knew of—wholesale groceries, hardware, insurance concerns, and the like—but he had had no experience. How to go about getting anything was a bitter thought. Would he have to go personally and ask; wait outside an office door, and, then, distinguished and affluent looking, announce that he was looking for something to do? He strained painfully at the thought. No, he could not do that. He really strolled about, thinking, and then, the weather being cold, stepped into a hotel. He knew hotels well enough to know that any decent individual was welcome to a chair in the lobby. This was in the Broadway Central, which was then one of the most important hotels in the city. Taking a chair here was a painful thing to him. To think he should come to this! He had heard loungers about hotels called chairwarmers. He had called them that himself in his day. But here he was, despite the possibility of meeting some one who knew him, shielding himself from cold and the weariness of the streets in a hotel lobby.

“I can’t do this way,” he said to himself. “There’s no use of my starting out mornings without first thinking up some place to go. I’ll think of some places and then look them up.” It occurred to him that the positions of bartenders were sometimes open, but he put this out of his mind. Bartender—he, the ex-manager! It grew awfully dull sitting in the hotel lobby, and so at four he went home. He tried to put on a business air as he went in, but it was a feeble imitation. The rocking chair in the dining-room was comfortable. He sank into it gladly, with several papers he had bought, and began to read. As she was going through the room to begin preparing dinner, Carrie said:
“The man was here for the rent to-day.”
