The house of Mrs. Lettie Cranshaw stood upon one of those broad and comfortable avenues of Walnut Hills which, in the early nineties, had come to represent for the city of Cincinnati all that was solid, prosperous, and assured. It was of red brick, three stories in height, with a slate roof, a deep veranda supported by turned white pillars, and a lawn which descended in a gentle slope to an iron fence. Here and there along the street stood other houses of a like character, some more pretentious, some less, but all bearing that air of quiet self-satisfaction which money, long held and comfortably spent, lends to the dwellings of men. To one coming up from the lower city, from the smoke and clatter of the river front and the mean tenements of the bottoms, the change was as from one world to another, and it was with this feeling, half of awe and half of a vague resentment which she did not trouble to analyse, that Agnes Moody stepped down from the cable car at the corner and looked about her for the number she had written upon a slip of paper.

She was a woman of thirty-four, rather tall, thin of face, with brown hair drawn back plainly from a forehead which had once been considered handsome. Her dress was of black serge, made over from one she had worn two winters before, and her hat, a small affair with a single grey feather, had been purchased for a dollar and forty cents at a shop in Vevay, Indiana, where she had lived until a month before. She had been a widow for something over a year. Her husband, a clerk in a hardware store, had died of a fever contracted, as it was said, from the bad water of the river towns, leaving her a small insurance of four hundred dollars and a debt to the undertaker which consumed nearly a third of it. The remainder she had husbanded with what care she could, but it had dwindled, as such sums will, under the steady pressure of rent and food and the hundred small necessities which the poor cannot escape. Now she had come to the city to find work, and, having found it after a fashion, at eight dollars a week in the office of a wholesale drug concern on Pearl Street, she had resolved at last to call upon her cousin.

It had cost her something to make this resolution. She and Lettie had been girls together upon their grandfather's farm near Madison, had slept in the same bed under the slanting roof of the upper room, had gone berrying and to the county fair, and had confided to each other those first fancies concerning young men which girls of fifteen hold so dear. That was nearly twenty years ago. Since then their fortunes had diverged as widely as the paths of two streams which, rising in the same meadow, flow the one into a broad river and the other into a marsh. Lettie had married well—a young man named Cranshaw, then a salesman for a furniture house, now one of its partners. Agnes had married Henry Moody. There had been letters at first, then fewer, then only a card at Christmas, and at last, for some five or six years, nothing at all. It was not that either had willed this silence. It had simply come about, as such things do, through the slow, insensible action of circumstance, which separates people more surely than any quarrel.

She found the number and paused before the gate. A boy was raking leaves upon the lawn of the next house, and she fancied that he looked at her curiously. There was a carriage standing at the curb a little farther on, with a coachman in a dark green coat sitting upon the box. She felt, as she lifted the latch, that she did not belong here, that anyone seeing her must know at a glance what she was and whence she had come, and she was half minded to turn back. Then she thought of the long ride down again, of her room in the boarding house on Ninth Street, of the evening which must be got through somehow, and she went up the walk and rang the bell.

The door was opened by a maid in a white cap and apron, a stout, red-cheeked girl of the kind which the German families of the city supplied in such numbers to the households of the well-to-do.

"Is Mrs. Cranshaw at home?" asked Agnes.

"Who shall I say, please?"

"Tell her it's her cousin—Agnes. Agnes Moody. She'll know."

The maid showed her into a front parlour and went away. Agnes sat down upon the edge of a plush chair and looked about her. It was a large room, heavily furnished after the manner of the time, with a carpet of red and gold, lace curtains at the windows, a black marble mantel upon which stood a gilt clock under a glass bell, and on the walls several oil paintings in deep frames—a landscape with cattle, a ship at sea, and a portrait of an elderly man whom she took to be some relative of Cranshaw's. There was a piano in one corner, with music open upon it, and upon a small table a great lamp with a painted globe. Everything was rich, everything was heavy, everything spoke of an ease of living which she had never known and now never expected to know. She could not help comparing it with the three rooms in Vevay where she had kept house for seven years, with their rag carpets and their cheap walnut set purchased upon the instalment plan, and the comparison gave her a dull ache which she could not have put into words.

It must not be supposed that Agnes was of an envious disposition, or that she had come to this house with any thought of gain. She had not. Her nature was rather simple and good, given to small kindnesses and unused to scheming. But the human heart is not proof against the evidence of the senses, and there is nothing which so instantly and so cruelly measures the difference between two lives as the furniture of a room. She had been, in her own town, a respectable woman, a little above the average of her neighbours in taste and bearing. Here she was nothing—a poor relation, an applicant, one who must be received with that particular graciousness which is reserved for those who can confer no benefit in return.

Presently there was a rustle upon the stair, and Lettie came in. She was a plump woman now, fuller of figure than Agnes remembered, with a round, pleasant face, a high colour, and hair done in the latest fashion, with a fringe over the forehead. She wore a house gown of dark blue silk, trimmed with lace at the throat and wrists, and upon one hand were two rings which caught the light from the window. For a moment the two women looked at each other, and in that moment each took in the other completely—the one seeing prosperity, the other seeing its opposite.

"Why, Agnes!" exclaimed Lettie, coming forward with both hands extended. "Of all people! I never was so surprised. Whatever brought you to Cincinnati?"

"I'm living here now," said Agnes, rising and allowing herself to be kissed upon the cheek. "I've been here nearly a month."

"A month! And you never came to see me before this? Sit down, sit down. Why, I can't get over it. Let me look at you." She held her off at arm's length and surveyed her with frank interest. "You're thinner, Agnes. You've grown thin."

"I suppose I have," said Agnes, smiling a little. "I've had a good deal to think about."

"Yes, I heard about Henry," said Lettie, her face taking on that expression of sympathy which is so readily assumed and so honestly felt in the first instant. "Aunt Sarah wrote me. I meant to write you, Agnes, I truly did, but we were going to Atlantic City just then, and one thing and another—you know how it is. I was so sorry."

"Thank you," said Agnes simply.

They sat down, Lettie upon a sofa and Agnes again upon the plush chair, and for a little while the conversation ran upon those matters which are always first to be disposed of between relatives long parted—the health of this one and that, who had married, who had died, who had moved away to Kansas. Aunt Sarah was still living at Madison, though she was crippled with rheumatism. Uncle Will had sold the farm and gone to live with his son in Indianapolis. The old house had been torn down, Lettie had heard, and a new one built in its place.

"Torn down!" said Agnes, with real regret. "I didn't know that."

"Oh, yes. Two years ago. Charlie and I drove over there once when we were visiting at Madison. You wouldn't know the place. They've cut down the orchard, and the spring house is gone."

"The spring house," repeated Agnes. A picture rose before her of a low stone building, cool and dim within, with crocks of milk and butter standing in the running water, and two girls in calico dresses sitting upon the step, their bare feet in the wet grass. "Do you remember how we used to hide in there when Grandpa wanted us to pick up potatoes?"

Lettie laughed heartily. "Don't I! And the time you fell in the trough and spoiled your new dress, and Grandma whipped you. My, but you cried!"

"You cried, too," said Agnes.

"Did I? I suppose I did. I always cried when you did."

For a few minutes they were girls again, and the room and its furnishings were forgotten. They spoke of the old Methodist church at the crossroads, of the camp meetings in the summer, of a young man named Ed Pierce who had walked home with first one and then the other of them, and who, as Lettie now related, had become a dentist in Louisville and grown very fat. There was a warmth in this which neither had anticipated, a renewal of something which both had supposed lost. Yet it could not last. The past is a country to which we may make brief excursions, but we cannot live there, and the present has a way of reasserting itself with a harshness proportionate to the pleasure of the escape.

It was Lettie who first returned to it.

"And what are you doing here, Agnes?" she asked, settling back among the cushions. "Are you staying with someone?"

"No. I have a room on Ninth Street. I'm working."

"Working!" Lettie's face showed a faint surprise, as though the idea of a relative of hers being employed for wages were a novel and not altogether agreeable one. "Where?"

"At Hollister and Bane's, the drug house. I keep books for them—or help to. I learned a little bookkeeping from Henry, and they were willing to take me on."

"Well, now," said Lettie, thoughtfully. "Do they pay you well?"

"Eight dollars," said Agnes. She said it plainly, without apology, but she felt the colour come into her face as she did so.

"Eight dollars a week," repeated Lettie, and there was in her voice the tone of one who hears of some curious condition of life in a far country. She had not, in fifteen years, had occasion to consider what eight dollars a week would buy. Her husband gave her thirty for the house alone, and she frequently complained that it did not go far enough. "Can you live on that?"

"Oh, yes. My room is two and a half, and I get my meals for three. It does very well."

"But your clothes, and everything?"

"I had some things," said Agnes. "I make them do."

Lettie looked at her cousin's dress, at the made-over serge and the small hat with its single feather, and for the first time the full meaning of the matter came home to her. She was not an unkind woman. She had a good heart, as such hearts are measured, and was given to charities of the more visible sort—to the Orphan Asylum fair and the Christmas baskets of her church. But she had lived so long in comfort that comfort had become, for her, the natural condition of mankind, and poverty a thing which happened to other people, chiefly to the improvident and the unlucky. That it should happen to one who had slept beside her under the eaves of her grandfather's house was a thing which disturbed her obscurely, as though it were a reflection upon herself.

"Agnes," she said, after a moment, "why didn't you write to me? Charlie might have done something. He knows ever so many people."

"I didn't like to," said Agnes.

"Didn't like to! Why, we're cousins."

"I know. But it's been so long, Lettie. I didn't know how you'd feel."

"How I'd feel!" Lettie's tone was one of injured affection, and yet beneath it there was something else—a faint relief that the question had not been put to her before, when it might have been less convenient. "You know I'd always be glad to see you. Always."

Agnes said nothing. She was thinking that in all the years since her marriage Lettie had never once asked her to come, though she must have known, through Aunt Sarah, how things went with her. She did not hold it against her cousin. It was only the way of the world, which she was beginning to understand. People who have much are not unkind to those who have little; they simply forget them. The prosperous live in a bright room, and the poor stand outside in the dark, and it is the nature of light that those within it cannot see beyond the windows.

The maid came in presently with tea upon a silver tray, and a plate of small cakes, and Lettie poured. Agnes took her cup and held it carefully, conscious of the thinness of the china and of her own hands, which were reddened at the knuckles from the cold water of her washbasin. Lettie's hands were white and soft, and she handled the pot with an ease which spoke of long habit.

"We have a girl and a woman who comes in to wash," Lettie observed, as though in answer to some question Agnes had not asked. "Charlie wanted me to have a cook as well, but I said no. I like to see to things myself. It's so hard to get good help."

"I suppose it is," said Agnes.

"You've no idea. The last girl we had stole a pair of my gloves and a silver spoon. Charlie wanted to have her arrested, but I said let her go. They're so ignorant, most of them."

Agnes sipped her tea and said nothing. She was thinking of the girls in the office at Hollister and Bane's, who wrapped packages and addressed labels for five dollars a week, and who sometimes, as she had heard them say among themselves, went without lunch to buy a ribbon. She did not think they were ignorant. She thought they were poor, which was a different thing, though she perceived that to Lettie the two words had come to mean very much the same.

They talked on. Lettie spoke of her children—a boy of twelve, who was at a military school in Kentucky, and a girl of nine, who was out just now at her music lesson. She spoke of their summer at Atlantic City, of the great hotels there and the board walk and the bathing, of a trip they had made the year before to New York, where they had stayed at the Fifth Avenue Hotel and seen a play by Mr. Daly. She spoke of these things not boastfully, but as one speaks of the ordinary furniture of one's existence, and it was this very naturalness which made them the more crushing to her listener. Agnes had never seen the ocean. She had never stayed in a hotel. The farthest she had travelled in her life was to Louisville, once, on an excursion boat, with Henry, in the second summer of their marriage.

"You ought to go East sometime, Agnes," said Lettie, with the generous thoughtlessness of the fortunate. "It would do you good."

"Perhaps I will," said Agnes, smiling faintly, "some day."

It was growing dusk now. The light at the windows had turned from grey to a deeper blue, and the maid came in and lighted the gas in the chandelier, which sprang up with a soft hiss and filled the room with a yellow glow. In this light the heavy furnishings took on a richer look, and the portrait of the elderly man upon the wall seemed to gaze down with an air of stern approval upon all that his descendants had accomplished. Agnes felt that she ought to go. She did not wish to stay until the husband should come in, nor to be asked to supper and so placed under an obligation she could not return. Yet she lingered, held by something she could not have named—a reluctance to go back into the cold and the dark, to the boarding house and its smells of cabbage and coal oil, to the narrow bed and the single gas jet and the long, quiet evening.

Before she could rise, however, the front door opened, and a man's step sounded in the hall.

"That's Charlie," said Lettie, brightening. "Now you'll see him. He's grown so stout, Agnes, you won't know him."

Mr. Cranshaw came in, rubbing his hands. He was a man of forty-five, broad and heavy, with a short brown beard and small, shrewd, good-natured eyes. He wore a suit of dark grey cloth, well cut, and a heavy watch-chain across his waistcoat, from which depended a Masonic charm. He had about him that air of genial authority which comes to men who have succeeded in trade and who feel that the world, on the whole, is a very sensible arrangement.

"Well, well," he said, when Lettie had explained. "Lettie's cousin, eh? I remember now. I've heard her speak of you often. Glad to know you, Mrs. Moody. Very glad." He shook her hand heartily and stood before the fire with his hands clasped behind him. "And you're living in town, you say?"

"Yes," said Agnes.

"She's working at Hollister and Bane's, Charlie," said Lettie. "Keeping books. For eight dollars a week."

"Hollister and Bane's," said Cranshaw, reflectively. "I know Bane. Know him well. Sharp man. Close, too." He looked at Agnes with a kind of practical sympathy, as a man might regard a good horse that had been badly placed. "Eight dollars isn't much. Isn't much at all for a woman that can keep books. I'll tell you what, Mrs. Moody. I'll speak to a man I know over at the Gibson House. They need somebody in the office there, I believe. Might be ten or twelve in it. I'll speak to him."

"That's very kind of you," said Agnes.

"Not at all. Not at all. Glad to do it." He was pleased with himself, as men are when they have discovered an opportunity for benevolence which costs them nothing but a word. "You come up to dinner some Sunday, and I'll let you know what he says. Won't she, Lettie?"

"Of course she will," said Lettie warmly. "You must, Agnes. Come next Sunday."

Agnes said that she would, and rose to go. They pressed her to stay to supper, but she would not, giving as her reason that her landlady expected her. This was not true, but it was the kind of untruth which pride invents for its protection. Lettie went with her to the door and kissed her again upon the cheek.

"Now don't you forget," she said. "Sunday. And Agnes—" she hesitated, and then, with a quick movement, pressed something into her cousin's hand—"get yourself something. A pair of gloves or something. Please. For old times."

Agnes looked down. It was a five-dollar gold piece. She felt the blood rush to her face, and for an instant she was on the point of giving it back. Then she thought of her shoes, which were worn through at the sole and which she had been stuffing with paper for a week, and of the coming winter, and of the eight dollars which never quite reached the end of the week. Her fingers closed upon the coin.

"Thank you, Lettie," she said, in a low voice.

"Don't thank me. Goodness! It's nothing." And Lettie, flushed and happy with the consciousness of having done a good thing, stood in the lighted doorway and waved as her cousin went down the walk.

The night had come on clear and cold. Above the roofs of the great houses the stars were out, and the street lamps made little pools of light along the pavement. From the windows on either side came the glow of gas and the sound, here and there, of a piano. Agnes walked slowly toward the corner where the car would pass, holding the gold piece tightly in her hand within her muff. She was not unhappy, exactly. Her cousin had been kind—kinder than she had expected. The husband had promised to speak for her. There would be a dinner on Sunday, with good food and a warm room. And yet there was in her heart a feeling which she could not shake off, a sense of having been weighed and measured and found wanting, of having come as an equal and gone away as a dependent. She did not blame Lettie. She did not blame anyone. It was simply the way things were.

What she did not understand, and could not have understood, was that the force which had divided them was neither virtue nor vice, neither merit nor its lack, but chance—the blind chance which had sent one young man to a furniture house and another to a hardware store in a dying river town, which had given to one a constitution proof against fever and to the other none. Lettie had done nothing to deserve her silk gown and her silver tea service, and Agnes nothing to merit her made-over serge. Yet the world, which is not given to such reflections, would judge them both by these things, and they themselves, in time, would come to judge each other so. That is the chief cruelty of fortune: not that it raises some and lowers others, but that it persuades both the raised and the lowered that the arrangement is just.

The car came clanking up the hill, its single lamp swinging, and she got on and sat in a corner and looked out at the passing houses. Below, as the car descended, the city spread out before her, a great dark mass pricked with innumerable lights, and beyond it the river, black and silent, flowing on toward Vevay and Madison and all the little towns where she had been young. She thought of the spring house, of the cool water running over the stones, of two girls sitting upon the step with their feet in the grass. Then the car swung around a corner, the river was lost to view, and she was among the tenements again, with their smells and their noises and their dim, crowded windows, and she got down at Ninth Street and went up to her room.

In this way she passed many manufacturing and wholesale houses without once glancing in. At last, after several blocks of walking, she felt that this would not do, and began to look about again, though without relaxing her pace. A little way on she saw a great door which, for some reason, attracted her attention. It was ornamented by a small brass sign, and seemed to be the entrance to a vast hive of six or seven floors. “Perhaps,” she thought, “they may want some one,” and crossed over to enter. When she came within a score of feet of the desired goal, she saw through the window a young man in a grey checked suit. That he had anything to do with the concern, she could not tell, but because he happened to be looking in her direction her weakening heart misgave her and she hurried by, too overcome with shame to enter. Over the way stood a great six-story structure, labelled Storm and King, which she viewed with rising hope. It was a wholesale dry goods concern and employed women. She could see them moving about now and then upon the upper floors. This place she decided to enter, no matter what. She crossed over and walked directly toward the entrance. Several pedestrians out of the hurrying throng which filled the sidewalks passed about her as she paused, hesitating. She looked helplessly around, and then, seeing herself observed, retreated. It was too difficult a task. She could not go past them. So severe a defeat told sadly upon her nerves. Her feet carried her mechanically forward, every foot of her progress being a satisfactory portion of a flight which she gladly made. Block after block passed by. Upon streetlamps at the various corners she read names such as Madison, Monroe, La Salle, Clark, Dearborn, State, and still she went, her feet beginning to tire upon the broad stone flagging. She turned back, resolving to hunt up Storm and King and enter. On the way, she encountered a great wholesale shoe company, through the broad plate windows of which she saw an enclosed executive department, hidden by frosted glass. Without this enclosure, but just within the street entrance, sat a grey-haired gentleman at a small table, with a large open ledger before him. She walked by this institution several times hesitating, but, finding herself unobserved, faltered past the screen door and stood humbly waiting.

“Well, young lady,” observed the old gentleman, looking at her somewhat kindly, “what is it you wish?”

“I am, that is, do you—I mean, do you need any help?” she stammered.

“Who is it you wish to see?” he asked.

“I want to see the manager,” she said. He ran away and spoke to one of a group of three men who were conferring together. One of these came towards her.

“Well?” he said coldly. The greeting drove all courage from her at once.

“Do you need any help?” she stammered.

“No,” he replied abruptly, and turned upon his heel. She went foolishly out, the office boy deferentially swinging the door for her, and gladly sank into the obscuring crowd. “Who is it you wish to see?” he required.

“Why, any one, if you please,” she answered. “I am looking for something to do.”

“Oh, you want to see Mr. McManus,” he returned. “Sit down,” and he pointed to a chair against the neighbouring wall. He went on leisurely writing, until after a time a short, stout gentleman came in from the street.

“Mr. McManus,” called the man at the desk, “this young woman wants to see you.” The short gentleman turned about towards Carrie, and she arose and came forward.

“I want to know if I can get a position,” she inquired.

“As what?” he asked.

“Not as anything in particular,” she faltered.

“Have you ever had any experience in the wholesale dry goods business?” he questioned.

“No, sir,” she replied.

“No, sir.”

They were along the line of the most effective retail organisation, with hundreds of stores coordinated into one and laid out upon the most imposing and economic basis. She was a work-seeker, an outcast without employment, one whom the average employee could tell at a glance was poor and in need of a situation. “Now,” said a sharp, quick-mannered Jew, who was sitting at a roll-top desk near the window, “have you ever worked in any other store?”

“No, sir,” said Carrie.

“Oh, you haven’t,” he said, eyeing her keenly.

“No, sir,” she replied.

“Well, we prefer young women just now with some experience. I guess we can’t use you.” Carrie stood waiting a moment, hardly certain whether the interview had terminated.

“Don’t wait!” he exclaimed. “Remember we are very busy here.” Carrie began to move quickly to the door.

“Hold on,” he said, calling her back. “Give me your name and address. We want girls occasionally.” When she had gotten safely into the street, she could scarcely restrain the tears. It was not so much the particular rebuff which she had just experienced, but the whole abashing trend of the day. She was tired and nervous. It read, “Girls wanted—wrappers & stitchers.” She hesitated a moment, then entered. The firm of Speigelheim & Co., makers of boys’ caps, occupied one floor of the building, fifty feet in width and some eighty feet in depth. It was a place rather dingily lighted, the darkest portions having incandescent lights, filled with machines and work benches. At the latter laboured quite a company of girls and some men. The former were drabby-looking creatures, stained in face with oil and dust, clad in thin, shapeless, cotton dresses and shod with more or less worn shoes. Many of them had their sleeves rolled up, revealing bare arms, and in some cases, owing to the heat, their dresses were open at the neck. They were a fair type of nearly the lowest order of shop-girls—careless, slouchy, and more or less pale from confinement. They were not timid, however; were rich in curiosity, and strong in daring and slang. Carrie looked about her, very much disturbed and quite sure that she did not want to work here. Aside from making her uncomfortable by sidelong glances, no one paid her the least attention. She waited until the whole department was aware of her presence. Then some word was sent around, and a foreman, in an apron and shirt sleeves, the latter rolled up to his shoulders, approached.

“Do you want to see me?” he asked.

“Do you need any help?” said Carrie, already learning directness of address.

“Do you know how to stitch caps?” he returned.

“No, sir,” she replied.

“Have you ever had any experience at this kind of work?” he inquired. She answered that she had not.

“Well,” said the foreman, scratching his ear meditatively, “we do need a stitcher. We like experienced help, though. We’ve hardly got time to break people in.” He paused and looked away out of the window. “We might, though, put you at finishing,” he concluded reflectively.

“How much do you pay a week?” ventured Carrie, emboldened by a certain softness in the man’s manner and his simplicity of address.

“Three and a half,” he answered.

“Oh,” she was about to exclaim, but checked herself and allowed her thoughts to die without expression.

“We’re not exactly in need of anybody,” he went on vaguely, looking her over as one would a package. “You can come on Monday morning, though,” he added, “and I’ll put you to work.”

“Thank you,” said Carrie weakly.

“If you come, bring an apron,” he added. He walked away and left her standing by the elevator, never so much as inquiring her name. While the appearance of the shop and the announcement of the price paid per week operated very much as a blow to Carrie’s fancy, the fact that work of any kind was offered after so rude a round of experience was gratifying. She could not begin to believe that she would take the place, modest as her aspirations were. She had been used to better than that. Her mere experience and the free out-of-door life of the country caused her nature to revolt at such confinement. Dirt had never been her share. Her sister’s flat was clean. This place was grimy and low, the girls were careless and hardened. They must be bad-minded and hearted, she imagined. Still, a place had been offered her. Surely Chicago was not so bad if she could find one place in one day. She might find another and better later. Her subsequent experiences were not of a reassuring nature, however. From all the more pleasing or imposing places she was turned away abruptly with the most chilling formality. In others where she applied only the experienced were required. She met with painful rebuffs, the most trying of which had been in a manufacturing cloak house, where she had gone to the fourth floor to inquire.

“No, no,” said the foreman, a rough, heavily built individual, who looked after a miserably lighted workshop, “we don’t want any one. Don’t come here.”

And now poverty threatened to seize her entirely and to remove this other world far upward like a heaven to which any Lazarus might extend, appealingly, his hands. So, too, the ideal brought into her life by Ames remained. He had gone, but here was his word that riches were not everything; that there was a great deal more in the world than she knew; that the stage was good, and the literature she read poor. He was a strong man and clean—how much stronger and better than Hurstwood and Drouet she only half formulated to herself, but the difference was painful. It was something to which she voluntarily closed her eyes. During the last three months of the Warren Street connection, Hurstwood took parts of days off and hunted, tracking the business advertisements. It was a more or less depressing business, wholly because of the thought that he must soon get something or he would begin to live on the few hundred dollars he was saving, and then he would have nothing to invest—he would have to hire out as a clerk. Everything he discovered in his line advertised as an opportunity, was either too expensive or too wretched for him. Besides, winter was coming, the papers were announcing hardships, and there was a general feeling of hard times in the air, or, at least, he thought so. In his worry, other people’s worries became apparent. No item about a firm failing, a family starving, or a man dying upon the streets, supposedly of starvation, but arrested his eye as he scanned the morning papers. Once the “World” came out with a flaring announcement about “80,000 people out of employment in New York this winter,” which struck as a knife at his heart.

“Eighty thousand!” he thought. “What an awful thing that is.” This was new reasoning for Hurstwood. In the old days the world had seemed to be getting along well enough. He had been wont to see similar things in the “Daily News,” in Chicago, but they did not hold his attention. Now, these things were like grey clouds hovering along the horizon of a clear day. They threatened to cover and obscure his life with chilly greyness. He tried to shake them off, to forget and brace up. Sometimes he said to himself, mentally: “What’s the use worrying? I’m not out yet. I’ve got six weeks more. Even if worst comes to worst, I’ve got enough to live on for six months.” Curiously, as he troubled over his future, his thoughts occasionally reverted to his wife and family. He had avoided such thoughts for the first three years as much as possible. He hated her, and he could get along without her. Let her go. He would do well enough. Now, however, when he was not doing well enough, he began to wonder what she was doing, how his children were getting along. He could see them living as nicely as ever, occupying the comfortable house and using his property.

“By George! it’s a shame they should have it all,” he vaguely thought to himself on several occasions. “I didn’t do anything.” As he looked back now and analysed the situation which led up to his taking the money, he began mildly to justify himself. What had he done—what in the world—that should bar him out this way and heap such difficulties upon him? It seemed only yesterday to him since he was comfortable and well-to-do. But now it was all wrested from him.

“She didn’t deserve what she got out of me, that is sure. I didn’t do so much, if everybody could just know.” There was no thought that the facts ought to be advertised. It was only a mental justification he was seeking from himself—something that would enable him to bear his state as a righteous man. One afternoon, five weeks before the Warren Street place closed up, he left the saloon to visit three or four places he saw advertised in the “Herald.” One was down in Gold Street, and he visited that, but did not enter. It was such a cheap looking place he felt that he could not abide it. Another was on the Bowery, which he knew contained many showy resorts. It was near Grand Street, and turned out to be very handsomely fitted up. He talked around about investments for fully three-quarters of an hour with the proprietor, who maintained that his health was poor, and that was the reason he wished a partner.

“Well, now, just how much money would it take to buy a half interest here?” said Hurstwood, who saw seven hundred dollars as his limit.

“Three thousand,” said the man. Hurstwood’s jaw fell.

“Cash?” he said.

“Cash.” He tried to put on an air of deliberation, as one who might really buy; but his eyes showed gloom. He wound up by saying he would think it over, and came away. The man he had been talking to sensed his condition in a vague way.

“I don’t think he wants to buy,” he said to himself. “He doesn’t talk right.” The afternoon was as grey as lead and cold. It was blowing up a disagreeable winter wind. He visited a place far up on the east side, near Sixty-ninth Street, and it was five o’clock, and growing dim, when he reached there. A portly German kept this place.

“How about this ad of yours?” asked Hurstwood, who rather objected to the looks of the place.

“Oh, dat iss all over,” said the German. “I vill not sell now.”

“Oh, is that so?”

“Yes; dere is nothing to dat. It iss all over.”

“Very well,” said Hurstwood, turning around. The German paid no more attention to him, and it made him angry.

“The crazy ass!” he said to himself. “What does he want to advertise for?” Wholly depressed, he started for Thirteenth Street. The flat had only a light in the kitchen, where Carrie was working. He struck a match and, lighting the gas, sat down in the dining-room without even greeting her. She came to the door and looked in.

“It’s you, is it?” she said, and went back.

“Yes,” he said, without even looking up from the evening paper he had bought. Carrie saw things were wrong with him. He was not so handsome when gloomy. The lines at the sides of the eyes were deepened. Naturally dark of skin, gloom made him look slightly sinister. He was quite a disagreeable figure. Carrie set the table and brought in the meal.

“Dinner’s ready,” she said, passing him for something. He did not answer, reading on. She came in and sat down at her place, feeling exceedingly wretched.

“Won’t you eat now?” she asked. He folded his paper and drew near, silence holding for a time, except for the “Pass me’s.”

“It’s been gloomy to-day, hasn’t it?” ventured Carrie, after a time.

“Yes,” he said. He only picked at his food.

“Are you still sure to close up?” said Carrie, venturing to take up the subject which they had discussed often enough.

“Of course we are,” he said, with the slightest modification of sharpness. This retort angered Carrie. She had had a dreary day of it herself.

“You needn’t talk like that,” she said.

“Oh!” he exclaimed, pushing back from the table, as if to say more, but letting it go at that. Then he picked up his paper. Carrie left her seat, containing herself with difficulty. He saw she was hurt.

“Don’t go ’way,” he said, as she started back into the kitchen. “Eat your dinner.” She passed, not answering. He looked at the paper a few moments, and then rose up and put on his coat.

“I’m going downtown, Carrie,” he said, coming out. “I’m out of sorts to-night.” She did not answer.

“Don’t be angry,” he said. “It will be all right to-morrow.” He looked at her, but she paid no attention to him, working at her dishes.

“Good-bye!” he said finally, and went out. This was the first strong result of the situation between them, but with the nearing of the last day of the business the gloom became almost a permanent thing. Hurstwood could not conceal his feelings about the matter. Carrie could not help wondering where she was drifting. It got so that they talked even less than usual, and yet it was not Hurstwood who felt any objection to Carrie. It was Carrie who shied away from him. This he noticed. It aroused an objection to her becoming indifferent to him. He made the possibility of friendly intercourse almost a giant task, and then noticed with discontent that Carrie added to it by her manner and made it more impossible. At last the final day came. When it actually arrived, Hurstwood, who had got his mind into such a state where a thunderclap and raging storm would have seemed highly appropriate, was rather relieved to find that it was a plain, ordinary day. The sun shone, the temperature was pleasant. He felt, as he came to the breakfast table, that it wasn’t so terrible, after all.

“Well,” he said to Carrie, “to-day’s my last day on earth.” Carrie smiled in answer to his humour. Hurstwood glanced over his paper rather gayly. He seemed to have lost a load.

“I’ll go down for a little while,” he said after breakfast, “and then I’ll look around. To-morrow I’ll spend the whole day looking about. I think I can get something, now this thing’s off my hands.” He went out smiling and visited the place. Shaughnessy was there. They had made all arrangements to share according to their interests. When, however, he had been there several hours, gone out three more, and returned, his elation had departed. As much as he had objected to the place, now that it was no longer to exist, he felt sorry. He wished that things were different. Shaughnessy was coolly businesslike.

“Well,” he said at five o’clock, “we might as well count the change and divide.” They did so. The fixtures had already been sold and the sum divided.

“Good-night,” said Hurstwood at the final moment, in a last effort to be genial.

“So long,” said Shaughnessy, scarcely deigning a notice. Thus the Warren Street arrangement was permanently concluded. Carrie had prepared a good dinner at the flat, but after his ride up, Hurstwood was in a solemn and reflective mood.

“Well?” said Carrie, inquisitively.

“I’m out of that,” he answered, taking off his coat. As she looked at him, she wondered what his financial state was now. They ate and talked a little.

“Will you have enough to buy in anywhere else?” asked Carrie.

“No,” he said. “I’ll have to get something else and save up.”

“It would be nice if you could get some place,” said Carrie, prompted by anxiety and hope.

“I guess I will,” he said reflectively. For some days thereafter he put on his overcoat regularly in the morning and sallied forth. On these ventures he first consoled himself with the thought that with the seven hundred dollars he had he could still make some advantageous arrangement. He thought about going to some brewery, which, as he knew, frequently controlled saloons which they leased, and get them to help him. Then he remembered that he would have to pay out several hundred any way for fixtures and that he would have nothing left for his monthly expenses. It was costing him nearly eighty dollars a month to live.

“No,” he said, in his sanest moments, “I can’t do it. I’ll get something else and save up.” This getting-something proposition complicated itself the moment he began to think of what it was he wanted to do. Manage a place? Where should he get such a position? The papers contained no requests for managers. Such positions, he knew well enough, were either secured by long years of service or were bought with a half or third interest. Into a place important enough to need such a manager he had not money enough to buy. Nevertheless, he started out. His clothes were very good and his appearance still excellent, but it involved the trouble of deluding. People, looking at him, imagined instantly that a man of his age, stout and well dressed, must be well off. He appeared a comfortable owner of something, a man from whom the common run of mortals could well expect gratuities. Being now forty-three years of age, and comfortably built, walking was not easy. He had not been used to exercise for many years. His legs tired, his shoulders ached, and his feet pained him at the close of the day, even when he took street cars in almost every direction. The mere getting up and down, if long continued, produced this result. The fact that people took him to be better off than he was, he well understood. It was so painfully clear to him that it retarded his search. Not that he wished to be less well-appearing, but that he was ashamed to belie his appearance by incongruous appeals. So he hesitated, wondering what to do. He thought of the hotels, but instantly he remembered that he had had no experience as a clerk, and, what was more important, no acquaintances or friends in that line to whom he could go. He did know some hotel owners in several cities, including New York, but they knew of his dealings with Fitzgerald and Moy. He could not apply to them. He thought of other lines suggested by large buildings or businesses which he knew of—wholesale groceries, hardware, insurance concerns, and the like—but he had had no experience. How to go about getting anything was a bitter thought. Would he have to go personally and ask; wait outside an office door, and, then, distinguished and affluent looking, announce that he was looking for something to do? He strained painfully at the thought. No, he could not do that. He really strolled about, thinking, and then, the weather being cold, stepped into a hotel. He knew hotels well enough to know that any decent individual was welcome to a chair in the lobby. This was in the Broadway Central, which was then one of the most important hotels in the city. Taking a chair here was a painful thing to him. To think he should come to this! He had heard loungers about hotels called chairwarmers. He had called them that himself in his day. But here he was, despite the possibility of meeting some one who knew him, shielding himself from cold and the weariness of the streets in a hotel lobby.

“I can’t do this way,” he said to himself. “There’s no use of my starting out mornings without first thinking up some place to go. I’ll think of some places and then look them up.” It occurred to him that the positions of bartenders were sometimes open, but he put this out of his mind. Bartender—he, the ex-manager! It grew awfully dull sitting in the hotel lobby, and so at four he went home. He tried to put on a business air as he went in, but it was a feeble imitation. The rocking chair in the dining-room was comfortable. He sank into it gladly, with several papers he had bought, and began to read. As she was going through the room to begin preparing dinner, Carrie said:
“The man was here for the rent to-day.”
