The house of Martin Kessler stood in a row of six of its kind on Lincoln Street, not far from the place where that thoroughfare crosses Twelfth. It was a two-story frame affair, painted a dull drab which had once been grey, with a narrow porch in front and a small yard behind, in which a few stalks of hollyhock struggled against the soot that drifted down continually from the shops along the river. The rent was eleven dollars a month, a sum which Kessler paid promptly upon the first of each month and which he never once handed over without a certain grim satisfaction that he was able to do so. He was a pattern-maker at the Wells foundry, earning fourteen dollars a week, and he had been earning it for six years. It was his ambition, cherished in silence and spoken of only to his wife upon rare evenings, to own a house of his own somewhere farther out, perhaps in the neighbourhood of Humboldt Park, where the lots were still cheap and the air, as he had been told, was clean. Toward this end he saved. He saved as some men pray, regularly, without great joy, and with a feeling that the thing was right and that its neglect would bring a punishment not easily defined.

Men of Kessler's type are not uncommon in the working populations of our great cities. They are the product of a peasant ancestry transplanted, and they carry with them into the clangour of the factory and the street a set of notions concerning thrift, honesty, and the obedience of children which were well enough suited to the village and the field, but which the city, with its thousand lures and its endless display of desirable things, tends constantly to undermine. Kessler did not know this. He knew only that what he had been taught was right, and that his father had taught it to him with a strap. He was not a cruel man. He was, in the main, rather a kindly one, slow of speech, heavy of movement, and given to long silences in which he sat with his pipe upon the back step and looked at nothing. But he had fixed ideas, and when these were crossed he became hard, almost frighteningly so, with that hardness which comes not of malice but of a mind that has never been called upon to examine itself.

His son Willie was seven years of age at the time of which we write. He was a thin, light-haired boy with large grey eyes and a way of standing with one foot upon the other which his mother found endearing and his father found irritating. He went to the Garfield school, three blocks away, and upon his way there and back he passed a little shop kept by a man named Rubel, who sold candy, newspapers, tobacco, and a variety of small toys arranged in a window none too clean. It was this window which had become, for some weeks past, the centre of Willie's world. In it, among the marbles and the jackstraws and the paper masks, lay a top—a red-and-yellow top with a brass point, wound about with a white cord, and marked upon a slip of pasteboard, "10c." He had looked at it in the morning and looked at it again at noon, and upon the way home he had stood before it until the shopman, seeing him, had come to the door and asked him what he wanted. Willie had fled. He did not know what he wanted, except that he wanted the top, and that the wanting of it had become a thing which he carried about with him all day, as one carries an ache.

It must not be supposed that the boy had any clear notion of wrongdoing in what followed. A child's mind does not work upon such lines. Desire, in the young, is a simple and imperious thing, and the barriers which the adult world erects against it are understood only dimly, as so many inexplicable obstacles put there by persons who are larger and who do not see. Willie knew that his mother kept her purse in the drawer of the kitchen table, beneath the folded dish-towels. He had seen her take money from it a hundred times—for the milkman, for the iceman, for the boy who brought the evening paper. He knew that there was much money in it, as it seemed to him, and that ten cents was a very little part of much. On a Tuesday afternoon in October, when his mother had gone up to the second floor to look after the baby, who was ill with a cold, he opened the drawer, found the purse, and took from it a dime. His hand trembled as he did so, and he looked once over his shoulder at the stairway, but he did not stop. He closed the drawer softly and went out into the street.

The purchase of the top was accomplished with an ease which astonished him. Mr. Rubel took the dime without a word, reached into the window, and handed the thing over. Willie went off down the block clutching it, his heart beating with a strange mixture of triumph and dread. He did not dare to spin it in front of the house. He went instead around the corner into Thirteenth Street, where there was a stretch of board sidewalk before a vacant lot, and there, with the cord wound clumsily and his tongue between his teeth, he set it going. It spun beautifully. The red and yellow merged into a kind of orange blur, and the brass point hummed upon the boards. He spun it again and again. Two other boys came up and watched him, and one of them asked to try it, and Willie, with the air of a proprietor, allowed him. For the better part of an hour he was as happy as he had ever been in his life.

It was Mrs. Kessler who discovered the loss. She was a careful woman, careful by necessity rather than by nature, and she knew to the penny what her purse contained. When she went to it at five o'clock to pay the paper boy, she found it short. She counted it twice, standing by the window in the failing light, and then she stood a moment with her hand against her cheek, thinking. She did not want to believe what came into her mind. Willie had come in a little before and gone straight up to his room, which was unusual for him, and he had not asked, as he always did, what there was for supper. She went up the stairs slowly. The boy was sitting on the edge of his bed, and as she came in he thrust something hastily beneath the pillow.

"What have you got there, Willie?" she asked.

"Nothing," said the boy.

"Let me see it."

He did not move, and she went over and lifted the pillow. The top lay there, its cord trailing, a little dirty now from the sidewalk. She picked it up and turned it over in her hands.

"Where did you get this?"

The boy looked at the floor. His foot went up over the other foot. He said nothing.

"Did you take money out of my purse?"

Still he said nothing, but his face reddened slowly from the neck upward, and his lower lip began to tremble. Mrs. Kessler sat down on the bed beside him. Her first feeling was not anger but a kind of sick dismay, compounded of pity for the child and fear for what her husband would say. She knew Martin. She knew that a thing of this kind, which to her seemed sad and small, would seem to him enormous. She thought for a moment of saying nothing—of replacing the dime from the little store she kept separately for emergencies, and of letting the matter go. But she was an honest woman, and she was afraid, too, of what might come if the thing were hidden and afterward found out.

"You stay here," she said. "Your father will be home soon." And she went downstairs with the top in her apron pocket, feeling heavier than when she had come up.

Kessler came in at a quarter past six, as he always did. He took off his coat and hung it upon the nail behind the kitchen door, washed his hands and face at the sink, and sat down at the table. The kitchen was warm, and smelled of boiled cabbage and of the potatoes frying upon the stove. He was tired, as he always was at this hour, and he looked forward, as he always did, to his supper and his pipe. His wife set his plate before him without speaking. He noticed this, for she was ordinarily talkative at this hour, telling him the small news of the street and the house.

"Where's Willie?" he said.

"Upstairs."

"Is he sick, too?"

"No." She hesitated, standing by the stove with the fork in her hand. "Martin, I want to tell you something. I don't want you to be too hard."

He looked at her. "What is it?"

She took the top from her pocket and laid it on the oilcloth beside his plate. "He took ten cents out of my purse this afternoon and bought that."

Kessler looked at the top for a long moment without touching it. His face did not change greatly, but a certain stillness came into it, and his jaw set. He was not thinking of the dime. Ten cents was nothing—or rather, it was something, but it was not the thing. What he was thinking of, though he could not have put it into words, was a vague and terrible picture which the very word stealing called up in him: the jail on Michigan Avenue, the men he had seen led through the streets by policemen, the young loafers who stood about the saloon corners on Halsted Street at night and who, as everybody knew, would come to no good. He thought of his own father, a carter in a village near Hanover, who had whipped him once, when he was eight, for taking an apple from a neighbour's tree, and who had said to him then, in German, words which he had never forgotten: "A thief begins with an apple." It seemed to Kessler, sitting there in his own kitchen with the gas-light falling upon the cheap red-and-yellow toy, that he stood at the edge of some dark place, and that his son was already halfway into it.

"Bring him down," he said.

"Martin——"

"Bring him down."

She went up. Kessler sat motionless, his supper growing cold before him. He heard the creak of the stairs, and then the boy came in ahead of his mother, slowly, with his hands at his sides, and stopped by the door. He did not look at his father. He looked at the top lying upon the table, and his face, which had been pale, flushed again.

"Come here," said Kessler.

The boy came, step by step, and stood beside the table. He was so small, standing there, that his eyes were scarcely higher than the edge of the oilcloth. Kessler looked down at him. Something stirred in him which was not anger, but he put it aside.

"Did you take money from your mother's purse?"

The boy nodded, very slightly.

"Say it. Say yes or no."

"Yes," whispered Willie.

"How much?"

"Ten cents."

"What for?"

The boy's eyes went to the top. He did not answer. He did not know how to answer. How was he to explain the window, and the red and yellow, and the way the thing had seemed to call to him every morning and every noon? There were no words in him for it. He only stood, his foot creeping up over his other foot, his fingers twisting at the seam of his trousers.

"Stand up straight," said Kessler sharply. The foot came down.

"Do you know what you are?" he went on, his voice low and heavy. "You're a thief. That's what a person is that takes what isn't his. A thief. Do you know what they do with thieves?"

The boy shook his head. His eyes had filled now, and the tears stood in them without falling.

"They put them in jail. They lock them up. You've seen the patrol wagon go by on Twelfth Street. That's where thieves go. Do you want to go there?"

"No," said the boy, and now the tears fell.

"Martin," said Mrs. Kessler from the stove, "he's only seven."

"I know how old he is," said Kessler, without turning his head. "That's why I'm telling him now. Now's the time. Not when he's seventeen." He looked again at the boy. "Who works for that money? Tell me that. Who works for it?"

"You do," said Willie, through his sobs.

"I do. Ten hours a day, down there at Wells's, in the heat and the dirt. Six days a week. Do you think I like it? Do you think I go down there because I like it? I go so there's money for the rent, and for something to eat, and for shoes on your feet. And so some day we can get out of this place and have a house of our own. Every penny of it counts. Every penny. And you go and take it and throw it away on a thing like that." He struck the top with the back of his hand, and it rolled across the oilcloth and fell to the floor with a little clatter. The boy flinched as though he had been struck himself.

It is one of the curious facts of human nature that the passion of rebuke, once begun, tends to feed upon itself, and to carry the one who rebukes farther than he had intended to go. Kessler had meant to speak of the dime, and of honesty, and of the jail. But as he spoke he found other things rising in him—his own weariness, the heat of the foundry, the grinding sameness of the years, the house in Humboldt Park which seemed to recede a little further with each winter's coal bill—and these lent a bitterness to his words which had nothing to do with the child before him. He was, without knowing it, scolding the whole order of things which held him where he was, and the boy, who had merely wanted a top, received the full weight of it.

"I never had a top like that," he said. "Not once. When I was your age I was out in the fields picking stones for a farmer, at ten pfennigs a day. Ten pfennigs! And if I'd taken one of them that wasn't mine my father would have broke my back for me. And he'd have been right. You hear me? He'd have been right."

The boy was crying openly now, his shoulders shaking, his face screwed up and wet. He made no sound beyond a kind of catching in his throat. Mrs. Kessler, at the stove, had turned away and was pretending to look after the potatoes, though they were long since done. She could not bear to watch, and yet she could not bear to leave.

"Now you listen to me," said Kessler, lowering his voice somewhat, for the sight of the child's face had begun at last to reach him. "Tomorrow morning you're going to take that thing back to Rubel's. You're going to give it to him and tell him you bought it with money that wasn't yours. And you're going to ask him for the ten cents back, and if he gives it to you, you'll bring it straight here and put it in your mother's hand. And if he don't give it to you, then you'll go without your Sunday penny till it's paid. Ten weeks. Do you understand?"

The boy nodded. The thought of facing Mr. Rubel, of standing in that dim little shop and saying what he had done, filled him with a horror greater than anything his father had yet said. But he nodded.

"Say it."

"Yes, sir."

"And you'll never do a thing like that again."

"No, sir."

"Because if you do," said Kessler, and here he paused, for he had been about to say something about the strap, and something in him held back—"if you do, I don't know what I'll do. I don't know. Now go upstairs. You can go without supper tonight. Go on."

The boy went. They heard his feet upon the stairs, slow and uneven, and then the closing of his door. Mrs. Kessler stooped and picked up the top from the floor and put it on the shelf above the sink, beside the clock. She did not say anything. She brought the frying-pan and put some fresh potatoes upon her husband's plate, and he began to eat, slowly, without appetite.

"You were hard on him," she said at last.

"He needed it."

"Maybe. But he's only a little boy. He didn't know."

"He knew it wasn't his."

She did not answer this. There was nothing to answer. She sat down across from him and poured herself a cup of coffee and held it in both hands without drinking it. The baby, upstairs, had begun to cough, a thin, tight little cough which went on and on. Neither of them moved. Outside, a streetcar went by on Twelfth Street, its bell clanging, and the windows rattled faintly in their frames.

Kessler finished his supper and pushed back his chair. He took his pipe from his pocket and filled it, and then, instead of going out upon the back step, as was his custom, he sat on at the table, looking at the top upon the shelf. It was a cheap thing. Anybody could see it was a cheap thing. The paint was already chipped where it had struck the sidewalk. And yet he could see, too, in a dim way, how it might look to a child—how bright it was, how it would hum and blur. He thought of the window at Rubel's, which he had passed himself a thousand times without seeing, and of all the windows of the city, all the bright things set out in them, and of the people who went by them every day without the money to buy. He had never thought of such matters before. He did not think of them clearly now. They came to him only as a kind of discomfort, a vague unease which he could not name, and which he presently put aside as he had put aside so many things.

"Well," he said, rising, "it's done."

He went out upon the step and smoked his pipe in the dark. The air was chill, and the smoke from the foundries hung low over the roofs. Somewhere a dog was barking. He sat there a long time, longer than usual, and when he came in at last his wife had gone upstairs. He turned out the gas in the kitchen and followed her. At the door of the boy's room he stopped. It was quite dark within, and he could hear the child's breathing, slow and even now, with now and then a small catch in it, the aftermath of crying. He stood listening for some moments. Then, very quietly, he pushed the door open a little way and looked in. The boy lay on his side, one arm flung out over the coverlet, his face turned toward the wall. The light from the street lamp at the corner fell faintly across the bed.

Kessler did not go in. He stood in the doorway, a heavy, tired figure in his stocking feet, and what he felt he could not have said. It was not regret, exactly. He still believed he had done right. But there was mixed with this belief something softer and more troubling—a sense that the world into which his son had been born was larger and harder than the one he himself had known, and that it would take more than a dime returned and a supper missed to see the boy safely through it. He thought of the house in Humboldt Park, and it seemed to him, for the moment, very far away.

"By God," he said under his breath, not knowing just what he meant by it. Then he drew the door to, gently, and went on to bed.

prompt:
Write a 2,500–3,000-word prose narrative in the exact literary style and voice of Henry James, depicting the following scene: A tense conversation between a couple.
Write in third-person perspective. Match their diction, syntax, tone and voice as closely as you can.  Do not paraphrase or reuse any of the author's content. Output only the piece itself with no title, preamble, or commentary.
response:
It was not until the carriage had set them down, and the door had closed behind them on the wet and lamplit emptiness of the street, that Mrs. Ingram allowed herself to recognise how long, all through the latter part of the evening, she had been keeping her husband in view; and she was by then so far from wishing to lose the advantage of the recognition that she went straight up, not to her room but to the small drawing-room at the back, where a fire had been left for her, and there, without so much as loosening her cloak, sat down to wait. She had the sense, as she did so, of performing an act the importance of which she couldn't yet measure. That was precisely the interest of it: that it was an act at all, when the whole beautiful economy of their life together had been, for eleven years, so cunningly arranged as to make acts superfluous. They had lived, she and Edmund, as people live in a house where everything is to hand, where one never has to cross a room for anything, since whatever one wants has been placed, in advance, just there. She was crossing a room now, and she knew it; she knew it by the very quietness with which she settled her skirts and turned her face to the coals.

He was longer in coming than she had reckoned, and the delay was itself, she presently felt, a sort of answer. He had seen the light under the door; he had paused, she could imagine, on the landing with his candle, weighing whether to take the light for an invitation or to treat it, with the fine discretion he could always command, as no business of his. When at last she heard his step she knew he had decided, and she knew too, which was more, that he had decided in her favour, if her favour it was. He came in with the candle still in his hand and looked about for a place to set it down, as if the room, which he had known all these years, had become in the interval rather strange to him.

"You're not tired?" he asked.

"Oh, tired!" She let the word go, as one lets go a thing one has no use for. "I've been sitting here thinking that I've never been less tired in my life."

He put the candle on the edge of the cabinet and stood a moment considering it, as if its flame were the thing in the room most worth attention. "That sounds rather alarming."

"Does it? I meant it, I think, to sound only true."

"Ah, well, the two are not always so far apart." He smiled at her then, the smile she had for so long admired as the most finished thing about him, more finished even than his manners, which were themselves held to be complete. "What is it you've been thinking?"

She took her time; she had earned, she felt, the right to take it. "I've been thinking about Mrs. Brede."

He received the name, she was obliged to own, beautifully. He neither started nor failed to start; he did what was harder and better: he looked at her with an interest so candid, so perfectly unprepared, that for an instant she almost believed in it. "Mrs. Brede? Was she there to-night? I didn't see her."

"No, she wasn't there. That's partly why I've been thinking of her. One thinks most, don't you find, of the people who are not in the room?"

"I find," he said after a little, "that it depends on the room."

"And on the people. Yes." She turned her eyes back to the fire, because she found she could manage better so. "Lady Drumley spoke of her to me. After dinner, when you men were still downstairs. She spoke of her—how shall I put it?—as if I should naturally know all about her. As if I were, in fact, the one person in London who must know most."

"Lady Drumley," said Edmund Ingram, "takes a great deal for granted. It's her form of hospitality."

"It was very hospitable to-night. It made me feel extraordinarily at home." She paused, and then, since there was nothing for it but to go on, went on. "She said it had been so good of us. She said she had always known we should be good, but she hadn't dreamed we should be so *very* good as that."

He had come nearer the fire now, and she was aware of him standing a little behind her chair, aware of the fact that she couldn't see his face and that he had, by this simple disposition of his person, taken that much of an advantage from her. She didn't resent it; she rather admired it, as one admires a move one has not oneself had the wit to make.

"And what did you say to her?" he asked.

"What could I say? I said that we tried to be good. I said it with the most perfect assurance. I think, Edmund, I was rather wonderful."

"I've no doubt you were."

"You have no doubt because you know me. But consider—" and here she did turn, so that she might at least have him in the corner of her eye—"consider what it was I was being wonderful *about*. I hadn't the remotest notion. I was being good, so to speak, in the dark. I was being thanked for a kindness of which I hadn't heard so much as a whisper, and I took the thanks and I kept them, and I came away with them, and here they are." She made a small gesture, as if she held them in her lap. "I haven't known what to do with them. I've been sitting here with them for half an hour."

He was silent long enough for her to wonder whether he would after all take the line of supposing she had merely misunderstood; and she was ready for that line, she had her answer to it; but he didn't take it. He took, instead, the chair on the other side of the hearth, and leaned forward with his elbows on his knees, and looked at the coals as she had looked at them, so that they sat for a moment like two people warming their hands at a common misfortune.

"You'd better give them to me," he said at last. "The thanks. They were meant, I suppose, for me."

"Ah, then there *was* something to be thanked for!"

"There was something. Whether it deserved thanks is another question."

"It deserved, at any rate," she said, "to be mentioned."

He raised his eyes to her, and she saw in them, to her surprise, nothing that she could call guilt. She saw something she liked much less, because she understood it much less: a kind of patience, as if he had been expecting this hour for a long time and had long since made up his mind as to how he should bear it. "To whom," he asked, "should it have been mentioned?"

"Edmund!"

"No, I'm asking. I'm really asking. Should it have been mentioned to Lady Drumley? It appears she found it out for herself. Should it have been mentioned to Mrs. Brede? She is, I'm afraid, only too well aware of it. Should it have been mentioned to you?"

"Should it not?"

"That," he said quietly, "is exactly what I've never been able to decide."

She felt, at this, the ground she had so carefully chosen begin very gently to shift under her, and she was conscious of an impulse to stand, as if standing might restore her footing. But she kept her seat; she had a notion that whoever stood first would have, in some obscure way, given something up.

"You've been trying to decide," she said, "for how long?"

"For about a year."

"A year!" It was more than she had imagined, and it was less, too; for she had imagined, in the long half-hour by the fire, everything and nothing, and now that a figure had been named she found it at once enormous and absurdly small. "You've been helping her for a year?"

"I've been paying her son's debts for a year. And some of her own. Not all. It would be impossible to pay all of them; one would need to be very much richer than we are. But enough, let us say, to keep her in Kensington and to keep the boy out of a place I needn't name."

"And she was—" Mrs. Ingram hesitated, not because she didn't know how to finish but because she knew so exactly. "She was, before I knew you, a friend of yours."

"She was a friend of mine," he assented, "before you knew me."

"A very great friend."

He let a moment pass. "You have every right to say so. I don't deny it, and I never have. You know it; you have always known it. I told you myself."

"You told me," she said, "that it was over."

"It was over. It *is* over. Hester, you don't imagine—?"

"I don't imagine anything. That's precisely my position. I've been left, you see, to imagine nothing at all, and I find it's a great deal harder than imagining something. If you'd given me something to imagine I should have known where to begin."

He looked at her with a kind of wondering tenderness which, at another moment, would have melted her, and which now, she was dismayed to feel, only made things worse; for it was the look of a man who sees that someone he loves is suffering and who is sorry—sincerely, abundantly sorry—but who has no intention whatever of ceasing to do the thing that causes the suffering. "I'll tell you anything you like," he said. "Ask me what you will."

"Ah, but that's not it! You put it so as to make it my affair—as if it were for me to find the questions, and the only fault were in my not having found them sooner. I'm not asking you to tell me things now. I'm asking why you didn't tell me then."

"Then," he repeated, as if trying the word.

"A year ago. When it began. When she came to you—I suppose she did come?"

"She wrote."

"When she wrote, then. Why, when you had her letter in your hand, didn't you bring it to me? We should have read it together. We should have decided together. I'm not a monster, Edmund; I'm not a jealous little shrew who would have stamped her foot and forbidden you to give a poor woman a shilling. I should very likely have told you to give her more. I should very likely have been—" she caught herself on the edge of Lady Drumley's word, and then, with a kind of defiance, used it—"*good*."

"I know you would."

"Then why—?"

"Because I knew you would."

She stared at him. It was, of all answers, the one she had least prepared for, and it had the effect upon her of a door opening on a room she hadn't known to be in the house. "You'll have to explain that."

He got up then; it was he, after all, who stood first, and she noted it, and noted at the same time that it didn't seem to matter as she had supposed it would. He went to the window and drew back the edge of the curtain and looked out, as if the dripping area railings of Brook Street held some clue he had been seeking. When he spoke it was with his back to her.

"If I had brought you the letter," he said, "you would have read it, and you would have been, as you say, magnificent. You would have told me to help her, and you would have helped her yourself—you would have gone to see her, you would have taken an interest in the boy. You would have made it, in short, a thing we did together; you would have made it beautiful. And every time thereafter that her name was spoken in this house you would have been magnificent again; and every time I wrote her a cheque I should have known that you knew, and that you were being magnificent about it; and I should have watched you, year in and year out, carrying it—this thing that wasn't yours, that had never been yours, that belonged to a time when you weren't even in the world for me. I didn't want you to carry it. It was mine. It was the one thing in my life that was entirely mine, and that I'd done badly, and that I had some faint chance of doing a little less badly now. I wanted to do it myself. I wanted—" he let the curtain fall—"I suppose I wanted to spare you."

The room was very still. Somewhere below, a servant, finishing late, shut a door with an unseasonable firmness, and the sound came up through the house like a punctuation that had arrived too soon.

"To spare me," she said at last.

"Yes."

"To spare me the trouble of being good."

He turned and faced her. "If you like to put it so."

"I don't like to put it so. I don't like to put it any way at all. I'm only trying to see it." She rose now in her turn; it had come to seem, after all, the natural thing, and she walked to the little table where his candle burned and stood looking down into its flame, as he had done at first. "Do you know what you've done? You've made me into something. Without asking me, without so much as a word, you've made me into a person who would have been too good—too beautifully, too intolerably good—to be allowed to know the truth about her own husband. You've decided what I am, and having decided it, you've protected yourself against it. That's what it comes to. You haven't been sparing me; you've been sparing yourself the spectacle of me."

"Hester—"

"No, let me have it out; it's the first time in eleven years I've had anything out, and I find it has a sort of horrid interest." She heard her own voice, light and quick, and wondered at it. "You've been keeping a room in this house that I wasn't to go into, and you've furnished it with the one piece of your past that was really alive, and you've gone in and out of it every week—with your cheques and your letters and your little visits to Kensington, I make no doubt—and you've come out each time and shut the door and sat down with me at dinner and talked about the Drumleys. And all the while it wasn't because you were ashamed. I could have forgiven shame; shame I should have understood. It was because you thought me—what? Too fine for it? Too fine to be let into the one place where you were living?"

He came toward her, and stopped, as if some instinct warned him that the distance between them was not one to be closed by walking. "I thought you too fine for it, yes. I still think so. You're mistaken if you suppose that's an insult."

"I don't suppose it's an insult. I suppose it's a sentence."

"A sentence?"

"To being fine. For life. Without appeal." She lifted her eyes to his at last, and what he saw in them she could not have said; but she saw him see it, and she saw him, for the first time that evening, at a loss. "It's very lonely, Edmund, being thought too fine. One has nobody to talk to but oneself."

He was silent; and in the silence she felt the whole question turn over, as a sleeper turns, and lie down again on its other side. For she perceived—it came to her with a dreadful clearness, as things come by candlelight—that he was not, after all, the only one in the room who had kept a door shut. She had herself, all these years, been grateful for the very finish she now reproached him with; she had leaned upon it; she had taken his perfect manners as one takes a perfect climate, without wishing to know what storms might be required elsewhere to produce it. Had she ever once, in eleven years, asked him what he thought of when he stood at the window? She had not. She had been too fine to ask. They had been fine together; that had been their marriage, and its beauty, and now, it seemed, its sentence.

"I'll stop," he said presently. "If you wish it, I'll stop to-morrow. I'll write to her—"

"You'll do nothing of the sort."

"Then what will you have me do?"

She considered it, there by the little table, with the candle-flame leaning a little toward her in the draught from the door he had left ajar. It was the strangest moment of her life, and she knew it even as it passed; for she saw, laid out before her as plainly as the pattern of the carpet, the two roads that lay open. She might ask him for everything—the letters, the visits, the very look of the rooms in Kensington, the boy's face, the woman's voice; she might insist on being let in, and he would let her in, she didn't doubt it, with that terrible patience of his; and she would be, from to-morrow, the wife who knew. Or she might do the other thing.

"I'll have you," she said slowly, "go on exactly as before."

He looked at her as if he had not heard. "As before?"

"Exactly. You'll write your cheques, and you'll go to Kensington when you must, and you'll come home and we'll talk about the Drumleys. And you'll never tell me anything about it, and I shall never ask."

"But you know now."

"Yes," she said, "I know now. That's the difference. Before, you were sparing me. Now I shall be sparing you." She found she could smile, though the smile was a small cold thing that she would not have cared to look at in a glass. "It's my turn, you see, to have a room of my own—a room you'll never come into. I shall keep in it the knowledge that I knew, and that I chose not to know. It isn't much of a room, but it will be mine."

"Hester, that's—" he broke off, and she wondered, with a kind of detached curiosity, what word he had been about to use; whether "dreadful" or "magnificent"; and she reflected that very possibly, for him, they came to the same.

"It's what you wanted," she said gently. "Isn't it? You wanted me to be fine. I'm being fine. I'm being finer than you ever dreamed. I'm being, Edmund, so very, very good."

He stood quite still, and she could see him take it in—take it in as she had taken in, at Lady Drumley's, the thanks she hadn't earned: all at once, without a sign, with the perfect manners that were the last thing either of them would ever give up. Then he came and took her hand, and raised it, and touched it with his lips, as he had done, she remembered, on the evening she had accepted him; and the gesture was so exactly what it had always been, so complete and so beautiful, that she felt her heart contract with something which was not, she was very sure, forgiveness, and was not, she was nearly as sure, its opposite.

"You had better go to bed," she said. "You'll want your candle."

He took it up from the table, and the room, as he did so, shifted its shadows about her, so that for an instant she seemed to herself to be standing somewhere else entirely, in some larger and colder house of which this was only an antechamber. At the door he turned.

"And you?"

"Oh, I," said Mrs. Ingram, sitting down again before the fire, "I shall stay a little. I've so much to think about—and now, you know, I shall have to think of it all alone."

prompt:
Write a 2,500–3,000-word prose narrative in the exact literary style and voice of Henry James, depicting the following scene: Cousins catching up after a long time apart.
Write in third-person perspective. Match their diction, syntax, tone and voice as closely as you can.  Do not paraphrase or reuse any of the author's content. Output only the piece itself with no title, preamble, or commentary.
response:
I

It was not, she afterwards made out, that she had failed to prepare; it was rather that she had prepared too much, and had arrived, by the hour of his coming, at that state of over-readiness in which the mind, having rehearsed every possible turn of the affair, finds itself caught at last by the one turn it had somehow left out. She had seen to the lamps; she had banished from the little drawing-room in Hill Street two or three objects that seemed to her, on reflection, to speak too loudly of her late husband's taste; and she had then, with a scruple of which she was half ashamed, carried one of them back. Laurence would notice, she was sure, whatever she did. It had been, of old, the very essence of him to notice. The only question, which she had turned over until it was worn as smooth as a pebble in a pocket, was whether it would be better for him to notice that she had kept things or that she had put them away.

He had been gone twelve years, which was long enough, she had told herself, for anything to have happened, and yet, as it now struck her, not quite long enough for nothing to have. That was the difficulty. If he had been gone twenty, they might have met as strangers, with a stranger's large allowance. If he had been gone five, they might have taken each other up at the very place where they had let each other drop. Twelve years left them in a middle region, a sort of no-man's-land of acquaintance, where every step had to be felt for and where, worse still, one could never be certain that the other was not feeling for it too. His letters had been few, and those few had been of the kind that tell everything except the thing one wants. There had been, in the first years, mines; there had been, in the later, as the letters vaguely and almost humorously put it, "not mines"; there had been Colorado and then California and then a stretch of silence that she had filled, as one fills an empty room, with whatever furniture came to hand. And now there was this note, three lines on the paper of a hotel in Jermyn Street, to say that he was in London "for a little," and might he come?

He might come; he had come; she heard, while she was still settling the angle of a screen, the door below and then the voice on the stairs, which was the first of her surprises, for it was so exactly the voice she remembered that she felt, absurdly, as if the twelve years had been a trick played on her by the almanac.

"Ah, Nelly," he said from the threshold, and then, as if the name itself required some apology, "I may still call you that?"

"You may call me," she returned, "whatever you find you can."

It was not what she had meant to say, and she saw that he took it, as he had always taken things, a little more seriously than it had been given. He came forward, and she had him for a moment in the full light: browner, greyer, a trifle heavier about the shoulders, with that look about the eyes of men who have been obliged to judge distances in a clear air. But the face was his face, and the way he stood there, his hat still in his hand as if he had forgotten it, the way he seemed to be taking possession of the room by some process that had nothing to do with sitting down in it, was so entirely what she had kept of him that she had, for an instant, nothing to say at all.

"Well," he said at last, "I find I can call you Nelly. It's the least of the things I find."

"And the greatest?"

He looked about him, at the lamps, at the screen, at the small bronze of a Florentine boy that she had carried back from the landing that very afternoon. "The greatest, I think, is that you haven't changed the light."

She had to laugh. "The light? My dear Laurence, it's gas. One doesn't change gas. One merely pays for it."

"Ah, but one changes how one sits in it. You sit just where you used to, at the old place, at Wraxby, by the window in the long room, so that whoever came in had the sun in his eyes and you had him at your mercy."

"I had no idea," she said, "that I had ever had anyone at my mercy."

"That," he answered, "was precisely your mercy."

They sat down then, she in the chair he had described and he opposite, on the small sofa that had been Mr. Thorne's, and that she saw him take with no consciousness whatever of what it had been, a want of consciousness which, she was to reflect, affected her more than any consciousness could have done. It was as if the dead man had simply been tidied out of the room by the living one's ignorance, and she was not sure, she could not at all have said, whether this was an outrage or a relief.

II

They talked for a while of the things that cousins talk of, and she was struck by how much there was of it, and by how little of it mattered. Aunt Hester had died, as he knew, in the spring of the year before last; the house at Wraxby had been sold, as he perhaps didn't know, to people from Manchester who had put in a billiard-room where the old library had been; Cousin Robert's girls had married, the elder well and the younger, it was generally felt, rather better than she deserved. He received these items with an attention that seemed to her at once perfect and peculiar, as if he were less listening to the news than to the manner of her giving it, and she found herself, under the pressure of that attention, giving it with a little more colour than it had, laying on the Manchester people and the billiard-room as one lays on paint where the canvas shows through.

"You're very hard on them," he observed at last.

"On the Manchester people? Oh, they deserve it. They've cut down the cedar."

"The cedar!" It was the first thing that had really reached him; she saw it go home. "The big one on the lower lawn? Where we used to—"

"Where we used to," she agreed, and was glad, on the whole, that neither of them finished it.

There was a pause in which the clock on the chimney-piece made its small, superior remark, and she wondered whether he too was seeing the lower lawn, the long blue shadow of the tree in the late afternoon, the two children and then the two not-quite-children who had sat beneath it and settled, with the terrible competence of youth, the whole order of the universe. It had been there, of all places, that they had made what they had called their compact, though she could not now, for the life of her, have repeated its terms. She remembered only that it had been very solemn and very comprehensive, and that it had borne, in some fashion she had never quite allowed herself to examine, upon the question of whom each of them should marry, or rather, as it had seemed to her then, upon the question of whether either of them should marry anybody at all.

"I've thought of that tree," he said, "in places where there wasn't a tree for forty miles. It's odd what one keeps."

"It's odd what one's allowed to keep," she said. "I've kept nothing, you see, but gas."

"You've kept," he returned, "a good deal more than that. You've kept, if you'll let me say so, your way of pretending you haven't."

She took this in, and something in her rose to meet it, though whether in defence or in welcome she would have been hard put to say. "And you, Laurence? What have you kept? You've been so very far, and for so very long, and you've told us so beautifully little."

"Ah, I've told you what there was."

"You've told us that there were mines, and then that there were not mines. It was, you'll admit, rather a thin diet for a family that lives on gossip."

He smiled at that, a long, slow smile that seemed to have learned its pace in some country where nobody hurried. "Well, there were the mines, and then, as I said, there weren't. In between there was a great deal of riding about, and a certain amount of being cheated, and a little, toward the end, of cheating back. Not, I hasten to say, very successfully. I hadn't the gift. I found I could only ever do it to people I liked, and those were exactly the people who forgave me, which spoiled it."

"So you've come home poor?"

"I've come home," he said, "neither poor nor rich, which is the most embarrassing of all conditions, for it gives one no excuse. If I were poor I might ask you for something. If I were rich I might offer you something. As it is I can only sit on your sofa and look at you."

She wished he had not said "your sofa." She wished, too, that she might know whether he had said it on purpose. The beauty of Laurence, the old beauty and the old torment, had always been that one never could know; he dropped his words like a man dropping coins into a well, and one was left, long after he had moved on, listening for the sound they made at the bottom.

"Then look," she said bravely, "and tell me what you see."

III

He did look, and for so long that she felt the colour come into her face and was annoyed with it, and then annoyed with herself for being annoyed, for what, after all, at forty, had she to blush for? He looked at her as he had looked at the room, with that taking possession which was not a taking but somehow a giving back, and when he spoke it was very quietly.

"I see," he said, "a woman who has been waiting for something, and who has very nearly persuaded herself that it isn't coming."

The words, so simple, so dreadfully exact, fell between them like a glove on a table, and she had for a moment the sense of having been, after all these years and all these preparations, taken from behind.

"You're very bold," she managed.

"I've had to be. One gets out of the way of the other thing. Out there, you know, nobody has the time to wait for the right moment; one says what one sees, and if it's wrong somebody shoots at one, and then one knows."

"And if it's right?"

"Ah, if it's right," he said, "nobody does anything at all. That's how one knows that."

She got up, for she found she could not sit still under it, and went to the window, where there was nothing to be seen but the lamps of Hill Street and the wet shine of a carriage going by. She stood there with her back to him and was aware that he had not moved, that he was letting her have her back to him as one lets a frightened creature have its corner.

"It isn't fair," she said at last to the glass, "to come after twelve years and say a thing like that in the first half-hour."

"Is it the first half-hour? It feels to me like the last of a very long day."

"You know what I mean."

"I know," he said, "that I've had twelve years to think of what I should say, and that I've thrown it all away for the first thing that came. That's my only excuse. It's a poor one, but I've noticed it's the only kind that ever really serves."

She turned then, because she had to see his face, and she found it, to her surprise, not triumphant, not even eager, but grave, almost sad, with the look of a man who has made a long journey to deliver something and who is not at all sure, now that he is at the door, that it will be received.

"What do you suppose," she asked, "that I've been waiting for?"

He considered. "I don't suppose. I wouldn't presume. I only know what I've been waiting for, and I've an idea that it may be the same thing seen from the other side."

"And what is that?"

"Why," he said simply, "to be forgiven."

IV

It was so far from anything she had imagined, it so neatly turned over the whole structure of her twelve years' supposition, that she sat down again, quite suddenly, as one sits down when the floor of a carriage gives a lurch. She had been waiting, if she had been waiting for anything, for exactly that: for his forgiveness. It was she who had broken the compact under the cedar, she who had married Mr. Thorne within the year of that solemn afternoon, she who had stood in the church at Wraxby and felt, through the whole of the service, the absence of one face as a kind of draught upon her neck. She had told herself, in the years since, a hundred stories of how he must have taken it, and in every one of them she had been the culprit and he the injured party, nobly silent, magnificently aloof, making his way across deserts with the wound she had dealt him. And now here he was, sitting on her husband's sofa, asking her pardon.

"Forgiven," she repeated, "for what?"

"For going. For not staying to see it. For leaving you to it without a word, as if it had been something you'd done to me, when I knew, I knew perfectly, that it was only something you'd done to yourself."

She could not speak. He went on, very gently, and she had the impression that he had indeed rehearsed this, though not, perhaps, in any form he had expected to use.

"I was a beast about it, Nelly. A sulky, romantic, self-pitying beast. I thought I'd been robbed. I went off to the other end of the world to show you, and it was a long time, a long time, before it came over me that there had been nothing to show you, and that you'd very likely never even looked. And then, when it did come over me, I was ashamed to write, because I'd have had to write that, and one doesn't, you know, put that on paper. So I wrote about mines."

"And then about not mines."

"And then about not mines. And then, when I heard about Thorne, I didn't write at all, because I was afraid that anything I wrote would look like what it wasn't."

"And what," she asked, very low, "would it have looked like?"

He met her eyes. "Like a man who'd been waiting for a death."

The silence that followed was of a different kind from the others; it was not a pause but a presence, and she felt that they were both, for the first time that evening, looking at the same thing. It was there between them, the thing he had not written and she had not asked, as solid as the little bronze boy on the table, and quite as impossible to pretend away.

"Were you?" she said at last.

"No," he said. "That's the curious part. I wasn't. I'd got past it. I'd got, I think, to the point of being glad for you, if you were happy, and only sorry, if you weren't, that I couldn't be of use. And then, when it happened, I found that I'd been keeping you, all the same, in a sort of private place of my own, where nothing could touch you, not Thorne and not time and not even I. And I've come back, I think, to see whether you're still there, or whether I invented you."

V

She had, as she put it to herself afterwards, two courses open to her, and she saw them both with a lucidity that was almost a pain. She might take him at his word and come out of the private place into the gaslight of Hill Street, a woman of forty with a dead husband and a house too large for her and nothing in the world to recommend her but the fact that he had once, under a cedar that no longer existed, believed her to be the whole of it. Or she might leave herself where he had put her, untouched, unspoiled, the girl by the window with the sun behind her, and let him go back to his deserts with that image intact. She saw that the second was the finer, and she saw, too, with a little rush of something that was very like amusement, that it was precisely the kind of fineness she had always been accused of, and that she had always, at bottom, rather resented.

"Laurence," she said, "do you know what I've been doing for twelve years?"

"I've no idea. I've imagined everything."

"I've been doing exactly what you've been doing. I've been keeping you. In a private place, as you call it. I've had you there all this while, riding about among the mines and the not-mines, being cheated and not quite cheating back, and suffering, my dear, most beautifully, on my account. You can't think what a comfort you've been to me. Whenever things were dull, and they were dull, you know, rather often, I had only to think of you out there with your wound, and I felt that I had at least been the occasion of something."

He stared at her, and then, slowly, he began to laugh, and she laughed too, and it was the first moment of the evening in which she felt that they were cousins, that they had the same blood and the same absurdities and the same old habit of making, out of the plainest materials, the most elaborate of structures.

"Then we've each," he said, "been keeping the other."

"We've each been keeping the other. And the question, as I see it, is whether we let each other out."

He grew grave again. "And what do you think?"

She looked at him, and at the room, and at the little bronze boy, and at the sofa on which he sat with so sublime an ignorance of its history; and she found that she did not, after all, wish to be the finer one. She found that she wished, very simply, to be the one who had been asked.

"I think," she said, "that the private place has grown a little close. I think we might open a window."

He did not move at once. He sat looking at her as he had looked at her when he came in, with that taking that was a giving back; and then he rose and came and stood beside her chair, not touching her, only standing there, as if to make sure that she was solid.

"Then you're not invented," he said.

"Not wholly. A little, perhaps, round the edges. You'll have to make allowances."

"Oh, I'll make them. I've come prepared to make a great many."

"And I," she said, "had prepared for everything but this."

He smiled down at her, the long slow smile of the country where nobody hurried. "Then we're beautifully where we were."

"Ah, no," said Nelly, and she put up her hand at last and let it rest, for a moment only, upon his sleeve. "We're beautifully where we never were. And that, my dear, I begin to think, is a great deal better."

It was not, Mrs. Lomax afterwards reflected, that she had wished the thing to be dealt with at once, in the first heat of it, so much as that she had felt the danger, should she let the hour pass, of finding it, when she came back to it, grown somehow larger in her absence, as such matters, left to themselves in the corners of a house, had a way of doing. She had therefore, the instant the carriage had borne Lady Bellingham down the drive and out of the gates, with that last wave of a grey-gloved hand which might have meant anything, sent word to the schoolroom that Maud was to come down to her. She had sent it by Parkins, who had received it with the beautiful blankness of a servant who knows everything, and she had then gone, not to the drawing-room, where the tea-things still stood about in their attitude of interrupted grace, but to the little morning-room at the back, which had the advantage of looking on nothing more eloquent than the laurels, and in which, she somehow felt, a reckoning would be less of a scene.

She had wanted, above all, not to have a scene. There had been one already, if one chose to call it so, though it had consisted, after all, of no more than a small clear voice, a pause, and Lady Bellingham's eyebrows; and it was precisely the smallness of the elements, their extraordinary economy, that had made the effect, for Mrs. Lomax, so complete. She stood now at the window with her hands lightly clasped before her and went over it, as one goes over the ground of an accident, looking for the stone.

The child had been brought in at five, in her white frock and her blue sash, to be looked at, which was a thing she did, on the whole, very prettily. She had shaken hands; she had answered, with her small grave air, the questions that were put to her about her lessons and her pony; and Lady Bellingham, who had no children and was understood to think them, in the general way, a provision of Providence for other people, had been as gracious as it was in her to be. It was then, it was in the very glow of this success, that the little girl, having been offered a macaroon and having taken it with a promptness that her mother had noted for later correction, had looked up at their visitor with her clear and candid eyes and said, as one who imparts a pleasant piece of news: "Mamma says we're all to be most awfully nice to you, because you're going to be useful."

That was all. Mrs. Lomax had laughed; she had heard herself laugh, which was the dreadful part, and had heard, too, the quality of the sound, which was that of a lady laughing because she must. She had said something—she could not now recall what—about children and their wonderful inventions; and Lady Bellingham had said, "Oh, but I like to be useful," with a smile that had closed over the remark like water over a dropped coin. The visit had gone on for twenty minutes more. Nothing whatever had been said about the committee, or about Ambrose's name, or about the small matter, so long and so carefully prepared, of the house in Hill Street for the season. Nothing whatever, Mrs. Lomax now perceived, need ever be said about any of these things again.

The door opened behind her, and she turned. Maud stood on the threshold, still in the white frock, with Miss Penge, the governess, hovering in the passage beyond her, as if in some doubt whether she were to be included in the proceedings in the character of accomplice or of witness.

"Thank you, Miss Penge. You needn't wait."

Miss Penge, with a look that seemed to commit the child to a higher jurisdiction, withdrew; and the door, under Maud's own hand, was closed with a care that struck her mother as almost too intelligent. The little girl then came forward a few steps into the room and stopped, at a distance which she appeared to have measured, upon the edge of the hearth-rug.

She was eight years old, and small for it, with her father's straight brows and a mouth that was, as people said, all her own; and she had, at this moment, an air which Mrs. Lomax had never quite seen in her before and which she would have been at a loss, had she been pressed, to name. It was not fear, or not wholly; it was not defiance, for there was nothing to defy. It was rather, she thought, the look of a person who has been sent for and who knows that there is a reason, and who is waiting, with great politeness, to be told what the reason is.

"Come here, Maud."

The child came, and stood at her knee, for her mother had sat down, by an instinct of reducing the matter to the scale of a conversation, in the low chair by the fire. The child's hands were behind her back, and her eyes were on her mother's face with the most perfect readiness.

"You know, I think, why I've sent for you."

Maud considered it, as she considered everything, from the front. "Is it about Lady Bellingham?"

"It's about what you said to Lady Bellingham."

"About her being useful?"

"About her being useful." Mrs. Lomax heard the words come back to her, and they sounded, in the quiet of the room, even worse than they had sounded in the drawing-room; they had, as it were, been stripped of the confusion of the teacups and stood up there in their simple nakedness. "You must have known, my dear, that it was a very dreadful thing to say."

The child's eyes widened, not much, but enough. "Was it dreadful?"

"It was most dreadful. It was, I'm afraid, the most dreadful thing you've ever said in your life."

Maud appeared to receive this as a distinction, and to turn it over, without vanity, to see what it was made of. "But, Mamma," she presently brought out, "you said it."

It was the thing, of course, that Mrs. Lomax had known would come, and she had supposed herself prepared for it; she had even, at the window, among the laurels, framed the reply. But the reply, now that the moment had arrived, seemed to have stayed behind at the window, and what she found instead, in its place, was a sort of wonder at the extraordinary directness with which the small creature before her had gone to the root.

"I said it," she admitted, "to your father. At breakfast. I didn't say it to Lady Bellingham."

"No," Maud agreed. "So I did."

She said it without the least impertinence—that was what was so remarkable; she said it as one who supplies a missing piece, who sees a gap in a pattern and, with the purest helpfulness, fills it. Her mother looked at her and for a moment said nothing whatever; and in the silence the clock on the chimney-piece, a small gilt affair that had been a wedding present from Ambrose's aunt, ticked with a kind of officious discretion.

"My darling," Mrs. Lomax at last began, and she felt that she was beginning, as one says, at the beginning, "there are things one says to one's husband, or—well—to one's friends, or even to oneself, that one doesn't say to the person they're about. You understand that?"

"Because it would hurt them?"

"Because it would hurt them, yes. Partly that."

"Did it hurt Lady Bellingham?"

Mrs. Lomax thought of the grey glove, of the eyebrows, of the smile closing over the coin. "I'm not sure," she said, with a candour that surprised her, "that anything hurts Lady Bellingham. But it was very rude, all the same. It was the rudest thing I've known a little girl to do."

"But I thought she'd like to know." Maud had brought one hand from behind her back and was turning, with absent fingers, the button of her mother's cuff. "I thought she'd like to know we were going to be nice to her. She looked as if she didn't know."

There was something in this, Mrs. Lomax felt, that was quite beyond her for the moment to deal with—something in the picture it gave her of Lady Bellingham, seated in the best chair in a house where she was, for the first time, a visitor of consequence, and looking, to the clear eyes of eight years old, like a person who did not know whether she was welcome. It was a view of their great lady that had certainly not occurred to the grown-up members of the party.

"It was the other part," she said, "that was the trouble. Not the part about being nice."

"About being useful?"

"About being useful."

Maud's fingers paused on the button. "Isn't it nice to be useful? Miss Penge says it's the nicest thing there is. She says it's what we're for."

Mrs. Lomax had a moment—she was to remember it afterwards with a kind of rueful amusement—in which she felt she would have given a good deal to have Miss Penge in the room, so that the governess might be made answerable for her own doctrine. But Miss Penge was in the schoolroom, and the doctrine was here, at her knee, looking up at her with its father's brows.

"It's nice to be useful," she conceded, "when one chooses to be. It's not so nice to be told that people are being kind to one *because* one's going to be useful. Do you see the difference?"

The child looked at her for a long moment, during which her mother had the impression, which she could not afterwards shake off, of being examined with a thoroughness that no governess, and no Lady Bellingham, had ever brought to the business.

"You mean," said Maud slowly, "that we weren't really being nice. We were only being nice because."

It was put with such dreadful neatness that Mrs. Lomax very nearly laughed again, and only did not because she saw that the laugh would have been, in its way, a confession, and that the child would have taken it as one. She looked instead at the fire, which was low, and at the laurels beyond the window, which were dark, and she had a vision, brief but extraordinarily distinct, of the many rooms in which, for the many years of her life, she had been nice because; and of how they had all looked, those rooms, very much like the drawing-room an hour since, with the tea-things and the macaroons and the great lady in the good chair, and of how no one, in any of them, had ever said so.

"I mean," she presently returned, choosing each word as if it were something rather breakable she was taking down from a high shelf, "that grown-up people have a great many reasons for what they do, and that some of those reasons are private. Not wicked—only private. And one doesn't take people's private reasons out and show them in the drawing-room, any more than one would take—well, their letters, or their purses. It isn't what's done."

"Like stealing?"

"It's a kind of stealing, perhaps. It's taking something that isn't yours to give away."

This was, she felt, rather good; she felt it had the merit of being both true and intelligible, which was more than could be said of most of what one told children. And Maud seemed to feel the force of it, for she let go of the button and put her hand behind her back again, and stood for a little in silence, with her eyes on the hearth-rug, where there was a pattern of faded roses that she appeared to be counting.

"Then it was your reason," she said at last, "and I gave it away."

"Yes."

"And she has it now."

"Yes," said Mrs. Lomax, "she has it now."

"Can't we get it back?"

The question was asked with such seriousness, such a clear sense of loss and of the possible means of repairing it, that her mother found herself, for the first time in the interview, quite unable to keep the thing at the distance she had intended. She put out her hand and drew the child a little nearer, so that the white frock was against her knee.

"No, my darling. That's the thing about reasons. Once they're given, they stay given."

Maud absorbed this, too. Then, with a brightening, as of one who has found the way out of a wood: "I could write to her. I could say I made it up. Miss Penge says I'm to write a letter every Sunday, and I could write to her instead of Grandmamma."

"And say you made it up?"

"Yes. Then she wouldn't have it anymore. She'd think she never had it."

Mrs. Lomax looked at her daughter and was conscious, all at once, of standing on the edge of something—not a precipice, exactly, for nothing so dramatic was in question, but a sort of gentle slope, grassy and agreeable, that went down a long way into country she knew very well. She had only to say yes. She had only to say that it would be a very proper letter, and that she would help with the spelling, and that Lady Bellingham, who was a woman of the world, would be charmed by it and would believe not a word of it, and would know, moreover, that she was not expected to believe a word, and would think the better of them all for the elegance of the gesture. It was, when one came to look at it, exactly what one would do. It was exactly what Ambrose would advise. It had, even, a sort of beauty.

"But you didn't make it up," she said.

"No. But she wouldn't know."

"You would know."

The child seemed to weigh this, not so much as a moral objection as a practical one, a difficulty in the arrangement. "Would it matter," she asked, "if only I knew?"

And there it was, Mrs. Lomax said to herself; there, in the morning-room, among the faded roses, with the gilt clock ticking and the laurels darkening outside, was the whole of the question, put to her by a person of eight, in a white frock, who was waiting quite politely for an answer. She had sent for the child to reprove her for having told the truth; and she had arrived, by the most natural steps in the world, at the point of having to explain to her when it was that the truth might be told and when it must be kept, and how one knew the difference, and what it cost. She saw that whatever she said now would be, in a sense, the first lesson—not in manners, which Miss Penge could teach, but in the other thing, the thing that had no name and that she had herself learned, she could not have said when, in rooms very like this one, from people very like herself. She saw that it could not be taught without being, in some degree, a loss; and she saw, too, that it could not be left untaught without a loss of another and perhaps a graver kind.

"It would matter a little," she said slowly. "It would matter to you. I think perhaps it's better not to write."

"Then she'll keep it."

"She'll keep it. And we must just—bear it, you know. That's what one does, when one has given something away that one shouldn't. One bears it, and one's more careful next time."

"Careful about what I say?"

"Careful about what you say. And about—" she hesitated, and then, since she had come so far, went on—"about what you hear. One hears a great many things, Maud, in a house, that aren't meant for one. The clever thing is to hear them and let them go by, like the carriages in the road. They're not one's own carriages, you see. One doesn't get into them."

The figure seemed to please the child; something in her face relaxed, and she looked, for a moment, less like a judge and more like a little girl. But it was only for a moment. Then the straight brows drew together again, and she put, with the most perfect gentleness, the last question of all.

"Then am I to know things," she said, "and not say them?"

Her mother looked at her for a long time before she answered. The fire had sunk to a red glow, and the room had grown dim about them, so that the white frock was the brightest thing in it.

"That," she said at last, "is what, when you're older, people will call your being very good."

Maud received it, as she had received everything, with a little nod; and Mrs. Lomax had the sense that it had gone in, and gone deep, and would stay. The child did not ask to go; she waited to be told, which she presently was, and she kissed her mother's cheek, and crossed to the door, and opened it with the same intelligent care with which she had closed it. On the threshold she paused and looked back.

"Mamma."

"Yes, dear?"

"I won't say anything to Papa. About Lady Bellingham, and the reason."

She was gone before her mother could reply; and Mrs. Lomax sat on by the dying fire, with her hands in her lap, and with the curious consciousness, which did not leave her for the rest of the evening, and which she could by no means have explained to Ambrose when he came in to dress, of having been, in that small dim room, the person who was reprimanded. It was not that she regretted what she had said; she would, she supposed, say it all again. It was rather that she had seen, in the eyes that had looked up at her from the hearth-rug, a thing go out—quite quietly, with no fuss at all, like a candle in a room one has just left—and that she knew, with the completest certainty, that it was she who had put it out, and that Lady Bellingham, with all her grey gloves and all her uses, had had nothing whatever to do with it.
