Valentin de Bellegarde died tranquilly, just as the cold faint March dawn began to illumine the faces of the little knot of friends gathered about his bedside. An hour afterwards Newman left the inn and drove to Geneva; he was naturally unwilling to be present at the arrival of Madame de Bellegarde and her first-born. At Geneva, for the moment, he remained. He was like a man who has had a fall and wants to sit still and count his bruises. He instantly wrote to Madame de Cintré, relating to her the circumstances of her brother’s death—with certain exceptions—and asking her what was the earliest moment at which he might hope that she would consent to see him. M. Ledoux had told him that he had reason to know that Valentin’s will—Bellegarde had a great deal of elegant personal property to dispose of—contained a request that he should be buried near his father in the churchyard of Fleurières, and Newman intended that the state of his own relations with the family should not deprive him of the satisfaction of helping to pay the last earthly honors to the best fellow in the world. He reflected that Valentin’s friendship was older than Urbain’s enmity, and that at a funeral it was easy to escape notice. Madame de Cintré’s answer to his letter enabled him to time his arrival at Fleurières. This answer was very brief; it ran as follows:— “I thank you for your letter, and for your being with Valentin. It is a most inexpressible sorrow to me that I was not. To see you will be nothing but a distress to me; there is no need, therefore, to wait for what you call brighter days. It is all one now, and I shall have no brighter days. Come when you please; only notify me first. My brother is to be buried here on Friday, and my family is to remain here. C. de C.” As soon as he received this letter Newman went straight to Paris and to Poitiers. The journey took him far southward, through green Touraine and across the far-shining Loire, into a country where the early spring deepened about him as he went. But he had never made a journey during which he heeded less what he would have called the lay of the land. He obtained lodging at the inn at Poitiers, and the next morning drove in a couple of hours to the village of Fleurières. But here, preoccupied though he was, he could not fail to notice the picturesqueness of the place. It was what the French call a petit bourg; it lay at the base of a sort of huge mound on the summit of which stood the crumbling ruins of a feudal castle, much of whose sturdy material, as well as that of the wall which dropped along the hill to enclose the clustered houses defensively, had been absorbed into the very substance of the village. The church was simply the former chapel of the castle, fronting upon its grass-grown court, which, however, was of generous enough width to have given up its quaintest corner to a little graveyard. Here the very headstones themselves seemed to sleep, as they slanted into the grass; the patient elbow of the rampart held them together on one side, and in front, far beneath their mossy lids, the green plains and blue distances stretched away. The way to church, up the hill, was impracticable to vehicles. It was lined with peasants, two or three rows deep, who stood watching old Madame de Bellegarde slowly ascend it, on the arm of her elder son, behind the pall-bearers of the other. Newman chose to lurk among the common mourners who murmured “Madame la Comtesse” as a tall figure veiled in black passed before them. He stood in the dusky little church while the service was going forward, but at the dismal tomb-side he turned away and walked down the hill. He went back to Poitiers, and spent two days in which patience and impatience were singularly commingled. On the third day he sent Madame de Cintré a note, saying that he would call upon her in the afternoon, and in accordance with this he again took his way to Fleurières. He left his vehicle at the tavern in the village street, and obeyed the simple instructions which were given him for finding the château.

“It is just beyond there,” said the landlord, and pointed to the tree-tops of the park, above the opposite houses. Newman followed the first cross-road to the right—it was bordered with mouldy cottages—and in a few moments saw before him the peaked roofs of the towers. Advancing farther, he found himself before a vast iron gate, rusty and closed; here he paused a moment, looking through the bars. The château was near the road; this was at once its merit and its defect; but its aspect was extremely impressive. Newman learned afterwards, from a guide-book of the province, that it dated from the time of Henry IV. It presented to the wide, paved area which preceded it and which was edged with shabby farm-buildings an immense façade of dark time-stained brick, flanked by two low wings, each of which terminated in a little Dutch-looking pavilion capped with a fantastic roof. Two towers rose behind, and behind the towers was a mass of elms and beeches, now just faintly green. But the great feature was a wide, green river which washed the foundations of the château. The building rose from an island in the circling stream, so that this formed a perfect moat spanned by a two-arched bridge without a parapet. The dull brick walls, which here and there made a grand, straight sweep; the ugly little cupolas of the wings, the deep-set windows, the long, steep pinnacles of mossy slate, all mirrored themselves in the tranquil river. Newman rang at the gate, and was almost frightened at the tone with which a big rusty bell above his head replied to him. An old woman came out from the gate-house and opened the creaking portal just wide enough for him to pass, and he went in, across the dry, bare court and the little cracked white slabs of the causeway on the moat. At the door of the château he waited for some moments, and this gave him a chance to observe that Fleurières was not “kept up,” and to reflect that it was a melancholy place of residence. “It looks,” said Newman to himself—and I give the comparison for what it is worth—“like a Chinese penitentiary.” At last the door was opened by a servant whom he remembered to have seen in the Rue de l’Université. The man’s dull face brightened as he perceived our hero, for Newman, for indefinable reasons, enjoyed the confidence of the liveried gentry. The footman led the way across a great central vestibule, with a pyramid of plants in tubs in the middle of glass doors all around, to what appeared to be the principal drawing-room of the château. Newman crossed the threshold of a room of superb proportions, which made him feel at first like a tourist with a guide-book and a cicerone awaiting a fee. But when his guide had left him alone, with the observation that he would call Madame la Comtesse, Newman perceived that the salon contained little that was remarkable save a dark ceiling with curiously carved rafters, some curtains of elaborate, antiquated tapestry, and a dark oaken floor, polished like a mirror. He waited some minutes, walking up and down; but at length, as he turned at the end of the room, he saw that Madame de Cintré had come in by a distant door. She wore a black dress, and she stood looking at him. As the length of the immense room lay between them he had time to look at her before they met in the middle of it. He was dismayed at the change in her appearance. Pale, heavy-browed, almost haggard with a sort of monastic rigidity in her dress, she had little but her pure features in common with the woman whose radiant good grace he had hitherto admired. She let her eyes rest on his own, and she let him take her hand; but her eyes looked like two rainy autumn moons, and her touch was portentously lifeless.

“I was at your brother’s funeral,” Newman said. “Then I waited three days. But I could wait no longer.”

“Nothing can be lost or gained by waiting,” said Madame de Cintré. “But it was very considerate of you to wait, wronged as you have been.”

“I’m glad you think I have been wronged,” said Newman, with that oddly humorous accent with which he often uttered words of the gravest meaning.

“Do I need to say so?” she asked. “I don’t think I have wronged, seriously, many persons; certainly not consciously. To you, to whom I have done this hard and cruel thing, the only reparation I can make is to say, ‘I know it, I feel it!’ The reparation is pitifully small!”

“Oh, it’s a great step forward!” said Newman, with a gracious smile of encouragement. He pushed a chair towards her and held it, looking at her urgently. She sat down, mechanically, and he seated himself near her; but in a moment he got up, restlessly, and stood before her. She remained seated, like a troubled creature who had passed through the stage of restlessness.

“I say nothing is to be gained by my seeing you,” she went on, “and yet I am very glad you came. Now I can tell you what I feel. It is a selfish pleasure, but it is one of the last I shall have.” And she paused, with her great misty eyes fixed upon him. “I know how I have deceived and injured you; I know how cruel and cowardly I have been. I see it as vividly as you do—I feel it to the ends of my fingers.” And she unclasped her hands, which were locked together in her lap, lifted them, and dropped them at her side. “Anything that you may have said of me in your angriest passion is nothing to what I have said to myself.”

“In my angriest passion,” said Newman, “I have said nothing hard of you. The very worst thing I have said of you yet is that you are the loveliest of women.” And he seated himself before her again abruptly. She flushed a little, but even her flush was pale. “That is because you think I will come back. But I will not come back. It is in that hope you have come here, I know; I am very sorry for you. I would do almost anything for you. To say that, after what I have done, seems simply impudent; but what can I say that will not seem impudent? To wrong you and apologize—that is easy enough. I should not have wronged you.” She stopped a moment, looking at him, and motioned him to let her go on. “I ought never to have listened to you at first; that was the wrong. No good could come of it. “When what?” said Newman.

It was on the fourth day of her visit to Wrayford, and at an hour when the rest of the party had dispersed themselves, according to their various inclinations, over the lawns and among the glass-houses, that Miss Lavinia Thorne found herself alone in the long library with the gentleman to whom, some six weeks before, she had promised her hand. She had chosen the place and she had chosen the hour; she had chosen, indeed, everything but the thing she was about to say, which had been chosen for her, with a promptitude she could only call brutal, by a letter that had reached her that morning from New York. The letter lay folded in the pocket of her dress, and she was conscious of it there as one is conscious of a small, cold stone in one's shoe, a thing of no size at all which nevertheless determines the whole manner of one's walking. She had read it twice at her window, with the green English park spread out beneath her in the mild light, and she had then put it away and gone down to breakfast, and had talked with Lady Wrayford about the comparative merits of Homburg and Carlsbad with a composure that she afterwards remembered with a kind of wonder. It was not, I think, that she was without feeling; it was rather that her feeling had taken the form, in the first instance, of an immense and lucid curiosity. She wished to see what would happen; and the person in whom it was to happen was Mr. Basil Maitland.

He came in from the terrace, where she had sent a servant to find him, with the air of a man who has been interrupted in nothing more serious than a cigarette and who is very willing to be interrupted in that. He was tall and fair, and he carried his good looks as he carried his good name, with a sort of graceful inattention, as if they had been lent him by a relative and he were too well-bred to examine them. Lavinia had liked him for this inattention; she had liked him for a good many things, and she reflected now, as he crossed the shadowy length of the room towards her, that she had perhaps liked him chiefly because he made her feel that the world was a simpler place than her own anxious American conscience had been inclined to suppose.

"You wanted me?" he said, smiling. "I'm so glad. I was beginning to think you never wanted anything."

"I want very little," said Lavinia. "But I want this. I want you to sit down, and I want you to listen to me without saying anything at all until I have done."

He looked at her a moment, and his smile took on a shade of interrogation, though it did not leave his face. "That sounds very solemn. Is it a lecture? I have had a great many lectures, you know, and I have always been very good at them. I listen beautifully; it's the one thing they taught me at school."

"It isn't a lecture," she said. "It's a piece of news."

He sat down, in obedience to her gesture, in one of the deep leather chairs that stood about the fireplace, where a small fire, more ornamental than useful in the June weather, was smouldering on the hearth. She remained standing; she had a feeling that if she sat down she should be at a disadvantage, though she could not have told him, or herself, at a disadvantage with regard to what. She stood with one hand on the back of a chair and looked down at him, and she was aware, even in that moment, of the extreme beauty of the room: the tall cases of brown and gilded books, the long windows with the light coming in green from the lawn, the great dim portrait over the chimney of a Maitland of the last century, who had been, she had been told, a bishop, and who looked as if he had never in his life been obliged to hear a piece of news.

"I have had a letter from Mr. Pettigrew," she said. "He is my father's man of business; you have heard me speak of him. My father, as you know, has been ill all the winter; he has not been able to attend to things. It appears that other people have attended to them for him, and that they have attended to them very badly. I won't trouble you with the particulars; I don't think I understand them myself, and I am sure you would not care to. The substance of it is that there is nothing left. Or so very little that it comes to the same thing. My father will be able to keep the house in Washington Square, Mr. Pettigrew thinks, if he lets the upper floors. That is the news."

She had meant to say it simply, and she had said it simply; but she found that her voice, at the end, had grown a little thin, as if it had travelled a long distance. Mr. Maitland did not move. He sat with his hands on the arms of his chair, and he looked at her with an expression which she was afterwards to spend a good many hours in trying to interpret, and which she was never quite able to name. It was not dismay, exactly; it was not surprise; it was something more deliberate than either, something that resembled, she thought, the look of a man who has been handed a bill in a shop and who is adding up the figures before he will consent to be shocked by the total.

"My dear girl," he said at last, "I'm awfully sorry."

"I don't doubt it," said Lavinia.

"For your father, I mean. It must be a horrible thing for him. Is he—does he know?"

"He knows. Mr. Pettigrew says he has taken it very quietly. He is a quiet man; he has always taken everything quietly. I suppose I take after him." And she gave a little laugh which did not sound to her own ear in the least like a laugh of her father's.

Maitland got up then, and stood before the fire with his back to it, in the attitude which Englishmen of his class adopt, I have observed, when they wish to give themselves the air of being at home in a difficulty. "You take it beautifully," he said. "I don't think I ever saw anything taken so well. But you mustn't—you mustn't feel that it makes any difference."

She looked at him very straight. "To what?"

"Why, to—to anything. To us." He paused, and she saw the colour come up faintly into his fair face. "You surely don't suppose that I——"

"I don't suppose anything," she interrupted. "That is precisely the reason I sent for you. I wished to know, and I could only know by telling you. I might have written to you from my room, you know; I might have gone up to London by the afternoon train and sent you a note from the hotel. I thought of that. It would have been easier, perhaps, for both of us. But it would have been a kind of cowardice, and I have never been very fond of cowardice, even in myself. So I came down, and I told you, and now——" She stopped.

"And now?"

"And now I am watching you," said Lavinia, with a candour which had in it something almost gay.

He received this, it must be said, rather well. He had a fund of good-humour which was, perhaps, the most valuable part of his inheritance, and he drew upon it now with a liberality that did him credit. "Well," he said, "and what do you see?"

"I see a gentleman," she answered, "who is very much embarrassed, and who is too well brought up to show it."

"Embarrassed! I'm not embarrassed in the least. I'm distressed for you; that's quite another thing."

"Is it?" she asked. "I have sometimes thought they were the same thing in England."

He looked at her for a moment with a slight contraction of his handsome brows; then he turned away and walked to one of the windows, where he stood looking out at the great level lawn and the cedars that cast their flat black shadows across it. She watched him, and she was conscious of a strange sharpening of all her faculties, as if the shock of the morning had cleared some film from her eyes, so that she now saw everything—the room, the man, the very motes that turned in the slanting light—with a hard and painful distinctness. She saw that he was thinking; and she saw, what was worse, that he was thinking of something that was not herself. She did not know precisely what it was. It might have been his father, the old Lord Maitland, who had received her at Brede with such elaborate kindness and who had asked her, at dinner, so many questions about the railroads of the West. It might have been his brother, the heir, who was said to be ruinously in debt. It might have been only the long, grey, honourable perspective of his own future, which had seemed, a week ago, so pleasantly gilded at its farther end, and which now stretched away before him in a light that had grown suddenly pale. She did not blame him for thinking of these things; she had too much imagination for that. But she wished, with a passion that surprised her, that he had not thought of them first.

"You are very hard on me," he said presently, without turning round.

"I don't mean to be hard. I only mean to be clear. One of us must be, and I think it had better be me. You see, I know so exactly what you are going to say."

He turned at this, and came back towards her. "Then perhaps you'll be good enough to tell me," he said, "for I'm hanged if I know myself."

"You are going to say," said Lavinia, "that it makes no difference; that you care for me just as much as you did yesterday; that you are not the sort of man to throw a girl over because her father has lost his money. And all of that will be quite true. I believe it absolutely. I have never thought you anything but honourable; I don't think you could be anything else if you tried. That is just the trouble."

"The trouble!" he repeated, staring.

"The trouble is that you will marry me out of honour," she said, "and I shall know it, and you will know that I know it. And we shall go on knowing it, the two of us, for the rest of our lives. You will be very kind to me; you will never say a word. You are not a man who says words. But there will be a little house somewhere, instead of the house you had thought of, and a little income, instead of the income your father had thought of; and every time you look at the little house and count the little income, you will remember this morning, and you will remember that you were honourable. And I shall see you remembering it. I am very quick at seeing things, Mr. Maitland. It is one of the few accomplishments I brought with me from New York."

He had listened to her with a growing gravity, and when she stopped he was silent for some moments. The clock on the chimney-piece, a florid affair of ormolu which had been presented to the bishop by a grateful diocese, ticked loudly into the pause.

"You have made out a very complete case," he said at last. "You haven't left me a great deal to say."

"I have left you everything to say," she answered. "I have only told you what I am afraid of. You have only to tell me that I am wrong."

It was the moment—she felt it, and she believed afterwards that he felt it too—on which everything turned; and she was never afterwards able to recall it without a certain contraction of the heart. If he had spoken then, if he had come to her and taken her hands and told her, with any sort of violence, any sort of foolishness, that she was wrong, she would have believed him. She was ready to believe him; she was, God knew, she said to herself later, eager to believe him. She asked for nothing more than a sign, a word, a single uncalculated movement; and she stood there, with her hand on the back of the chair and her heart beating in her throat, and waited for it.

He did not come to her. He stood where he was, and he put his hand up to his moustache, and he said, in a voice that was perfectly gentle and perfectly reasonable, "I think you are a little overwrought. It's natural enough, after such a shock. I don't think either of us ought to decide anything to-day."

Lavinia drew a long breath. It was not, I think, a sigh; it was rather the breath of a person who has been holding something very heavy and who has at last been permitted to put it down. "Ah," she said, "you are wise."

"I don't pretend to be wise. I only think we ought to wait. You'll want to write to your father; you'll want to hear more from this man of yours—Pettigrew. These things are never so bad as they look at first. Half the men I know have been ruined at one time or another, and they all seem to get on somehow."

"You are very consoling," said Lavinia. "But I don't think I want to wait."

"Why not, in heaven's name?"

"Because I know already," she said simply. "You have told me."

"I have told you nothing!"

"You have told me that you would like time to think. I don't reproach you for it. It is a very reasonable wish, and I daresay it is what any sensible man would feel. But it is not what I wanted you to feel. And since I can't make you feel what I wanted, I would rather not stay to watch you thinking." She took her hand from the chair, and for the first time she moved a few steps away from him, towards the long table in the middle of the room, where the newspapers lay folded in their neat English rows. "I shall go up to London this afternoon," she went on, "and I shall sail on Saturday. Lady Wrayford will be very much surprised, but I shall tell her that my father has sent for me, which will be no more than the truth. You needn't say anything to anybody; I shall write to your mother myself."

He followed her, and for a moment she thought—she could not help it—that the sign was coming after all; that her going had done what her standing still had failed to do. He put out his hand as if to stop her; but when she turned and faced him, the hand dropped to his side.

"You are treating me," he said, and there was now a real note of injury in his voice, "as if I had behaved like a cad. I have done nothing of the kind. I haven't said a word that any decent man mightn't have said. I've told you I'm sorry; I've told you it makes no difference——"

"You told me I mustn't feel that it made any difference," she corrected him gently. "That is not quite the same thing."

He flushed again, more deeply. "You are splitting hairs."

"Very likely. I have nothing else to split now." She smiled a little, and he saw—or she fancied he saw—that the smile cost her something. "Don't think I am angry with you. I am not angry at all. I think I am rather grateful. If you had been a worse man you would have pretended; you would have swept me off my feet, and I should have let myself be swept, and we should have found it out afterwards. You were too honest to pretend. You stood there and thought, and you let me see you thinking. It was the most honest thing you could have done, and I shall always respect you for it."

"Respect!" he cried, with something between a laugh and a groan. "That's a fine word to put me off with."

"It's the best word I have. I had a better one yesterday; but you are a man who understands that one sometimes has to make do with less than one had." And she looked at him with a sort of melancholy humour which he must have found, I think, more difficult to bear than any reproach.

He walked away from her again, and stood for a time by the empty hearth, kicking at the brass fender with the toe of his boot, like a schoolboy who has been unjustly kept in. She watched him, and her heart, which had been so clear and so hard a moment before, began, in spite of her, to soften. He was very handsome, standing there in the dim light; he was very young, younger than she had ever seen him; and she felt, with a pang that was half pity and half something she did not choose to name, that he was suffering, after his fashion, quite as much as she. But his fashion was not hers. That was the whole of it; that was the thing she had not known until this morning, and that she now knew so well that she could never again not know it.

"I suppose," he said at last, without looking up, "you think my people put it into my head. About the money, I mean. You think I was told to marry you for it."

"I don't think you were told anything," said Lavinia. "I don't think anyone ever tells you anything. It is all in the air you breathe; you take it in without knowing it, as you take in the smell of these old books. It isn't your fault. I daresay I have been breathing something too, all my life, that you would find quite as strange. Only it happens that what I have been breathing makes me unable to bear being married for my honour's sake—or for yours."

"And if I tell you," he said, looking up suddenly, "that I would marry you to-morrow, without a penny, and be glad of the chance?"

She was silent for a moment; and the question hung between them in the quiet room, with the clock ticking above it and the green light lying across the floor. It was the thing she had wanted him to say; it was, word for word, very nearly the thing she had imagined. And yet, now that it was said, she found that it came too late, as a letter comes too late that has been lying unopened on the hall-table while one has been looking for it everywhere else.

"I should believe that you meant it," she said slowly. "I should believe that you meant it at this moment, with me standing here, and you feeling that you had been put in the wrong. But I should not be able to forget that it took you ten minutes to mean it. Ten minutes is not very long, Mr. Maitland. But it is long enough to remember for the rest of one's life."

He made no answer to this. Perhaps he had none to make; perhaps he perceived, with that instinct for the finished thing which was, after all, one of the gifts of his race, that there was nothing more to be said with advantage. He stood looking at her, and she at him, across the length of the great table, and neither of them moved. Then, from the terrace outside, there came the sound of voices and of laughter—the rest of the party returning from the glass-houses, Lady Wrayford's high, cheerful tones rising above the others with some remark about the orchids—and the spell, such as it was, was broken.

"They are coming in," said Lavinia. "I think I will go upstairs."

"Lavinia——" he began.

She held up her hand, and he stopped. "Please don't," she said. "You have been very kind, and very honest, and very much a gentleman. Don't spoil it now by being something else." And she went past him to the door, with her head a little high and her step a little quick; and he heard the rustle of her skirts in the corridor, and then nothing more.

He remained for some minutes where she had left him, and when Lady Wrayford came in, a moment later, with her hands full of flowers, she found him standing at the window with his back to the room, looking out at the cedars. She asked him where Miss Thorne was; and he answered, without turning round, that he believed Miss Thorne had gone to her room to write some letters. It was the only lie, I believe, that he told in the whole course of the affair; and it may be counted to him, perhaps, for righteousness that it was told on her behalf rather than his own.

He was like a man who has had a fall and wants to sit still and count his bruises. He instantly wrote to Madame de Cintré, relating to her the circumstances of her brother’s death—with certain exceptions—and asking her what was the earliest moment at which he might hope that she would consent to see him. M. Ledoux had told him that he had reason to know that Valentin’s will—Bellegarde had a great deal of elegant personal property to dispose of—contained a request that he should be buried near his father in the churchyard of Fleurières, and Newman intended that the state of his own relations with the family should not deprive him of the satisfaction of helping to pay the last earthly honors to the best fellow in the world. He reflected that Valentin’s friendship was older than Urbain’s enmity, and that at a funeral it was easy to escape notice. Madame de Cintré’s answer to his letter enabled him to time his arrival at Fleurières. This answer was very brief; it ran as follows:— “I thank you for your letter, and for your being with Valentin. It is a most inexpressible sorrow to me that I was not. To see you will be nothing but a distress to me; there is no need, therefore, to wait for what you call brighter days. It is all one now, and I shall have no brighter days. Come when you please; only notify me first. My brother is to be buried here on Friday, and my family is to remain here. C. de C.” As soon as he received this letter Newman went straight to Paris and to Poitiers. The journey took him far southward, through green Touraine and across the far-shining Loire, into a country where the early spring deepened about him as he went. But he had never made a journey during which he heeded less what he would have called the lay of the land. He obtained lodging at the inn at Poitiers, and the next morning drove in a couple of hours to the village of Fleurières. But here, preoccupied though he was, he could not fail to notice the picturesqueness of the place. It was what the French call a petit bourg; it lay at the base of a sort of huge mound on the summit of which stood the crumbling ruins of a feudal castle, much of whose sturdy material, as well as that of the wall which dropped along the hill to enclose the clustered houses defensively, had been absorbed into the very substance of the village. The church was simply the former chapel of the castle, fronting upon its grass-grown court, which, however, was of generous enough width to have given up its quaintest corner to a little graveyard. Here the very headstones themselves seemed to sleep, as they slanted into the grass; the patient elbow of the rampart held them together on one side, and in front, far beneath their mossy lids, the green plains and blue distances stretched away. The way to church, up the hill, was impracticable to vehicles. It was lined with peasants, two or three rows deep, who stood watching old Madame de Bellegarde slowly ascend it, on the arm of her elder son, behind the pall-bearers of the other. Newman chose to lurk among the common mourners who murmured “Madame la Comtesse” as a tall figure veiled in black passed before them. He stood in the dusky little church while the service was going forward, but at the dismal tomb-side he turned away and walked down the hill. He went back to Poitiers, and spent two days in which patience and impatience were singularly commingled. On the third day he sent Madame de Cintré a note, saying that he would call upon her in the afternoon, and in accordance with this he again took his way to Fleurières. He left his vehicle at the tavern in the village street, and obeyed the simple instructions which were given him for finding the château.

“It is just beyond there,” said the landlord, and pointed to the tree-tops of the park, above the opposite houses. Newman followed the first cross-road to the right—it was bordered with mouldy cottages—and in a few moments saw before him the peaked roofs of the towers. Advancing farther, he found himself before a vast iron gate, rusty and closed; here he paused a moment, looking through the bars. The château was near the road; this was at once its merit and its defect; but its aspect was extremely impressive. Newman learned afterwards, from a guide-book of the province, that it dated from the time of Henry IV. It presented to the wide, paved area which preceded it and which was edged with shabby farm-buildings an immense façade of dark time-stained brick, flanked by two low wings, each of which terminated in a little Dutch-looking pavilion capped with a fantastic roof. Two towers rose behind, and behind the towers was a mass of elms and beeches, now just faintly green. But the great feature was a wide, green river which washed the foundations of the château. The building rose from an island in the circling stream, so that this formed a perfect moat spanned by a two-arched bridge without a parapet. The dull brick walls, which here and there made a grand, straight sweep; the ugly little cupolas of the wings, the deep-set windows, the long, steep pinnacles of mossy slate, all mirrored themselves in the tranquil river. Newman rang at the gate, and was almost frightened at the tone with which a big rusty bell above his head replied to him. An old woman came out from the gate-house and opened the creaking portal just wide enough for him to pass, and he went in, across the dry, bare court and the little cracked white slabs of the causeway on the moat. He waited some minutes, walking up and down; but at length, as he turned at the end of the room, he saw that Madame de Cintré had come in by a distant door. She wore a black dress, and she stood looking at him. As the length of the immense room lay between them he had time to look at her before they met in the middle of it. “Do I need to say so?” she asked. “I don’t think I have wronged, seriously, many persons; certainly not consciously. To you, to whom I have done this hard and cruel thing, the only reparation I can make is to say, ‘I know it, I feel it!’ The reparation is pitifully small!”

I see it as vividly as you do—I feel it to the ends of my fingers.” And she unclasped her hands, which were locked together in her lap, lifted them, and dropped them at her side. “Anything that you may have said of me in your angriest passion is nothing to what I have said to myself.”

“In my angriest passion,” said Newman, “I have said nothing hard of you. The very worst thing I have said of you yet is that you are the loveliest of women.” And he seated himself before her again abruptly. She flushed a little, but even her flush was pale. “That is because you think I will come back. But I will not come back. It is in that hope you have come here, I know; I am very sorry for you. I would do almost anything for you. To say that, after what I have done, seems simply impudent; but what can I say that will not seem impudent? To wrong you and apologize—that is easy enough. I should not have wronged you.” She stopped a moment, looking at him, and motioned him to let her go on. “I ought never to have listened to you at first; that was the wrong. No good could come of it. That will be the simplest way.” Newman got up and walked away with a crushing sense that his cause was lost, and yet with an equal inability to give up fighting. He went to one of the great windows, and looked out at the stiffly embanked river and the formal gardens which lay beyond it. When he turned round, Madame de Cintré had risen; she stood there silent and passive. “You are not frank,” said Newman; “you are not honest. Instead of saying that you are imbecile, you should say that other people are wicked. Your mother and your brother have been false and cruel; they have been so to me, and I am sure they have been so to you. Why do you try to shield them? Why do you sacrifice me to them? I’m not false; I’m not cruel. You don’t know what you give up; I can tell you that—you don’t. They bully you and plot about you; and I—I”—And he paused, holding out his hands. She turned away and began to leave him. “You told me the other day that you were afraid of your mother,” he said, following her. “What did you mean?” Madame de Cintré shook her head. “I remember; I was sorry afterwards.”

“You were sorry when she came down and put on the thumbscrews. In God’s name what is it she does to you?”

“Nothing. Nothing that you can understand. And now that I have given you up, I must not complain of her to you.”

“That’s no reasoning!” cried Newman. “Complain of her, on the contrary. Tell me all about it, frankly and trustfully, as you ought, and we will talk it over so satisfactorily that you won’t give me up.” Madame de Cintré looked down some moments, fixedly; and then, raising her eyes, she said, “One good at least has come of this: I have made you judge me more fairly. You thought of me in a way that did me great honor; I don’t know why you had taken it into your head. But it left me no loophole for escape—no chance to be the common, weak creature I am. It was not my fault; I warned you from the first. But I ought to have warned you more. I ought to have convinced you that I was doomed to disappoint you. But I was, in a way, too proud. You see what my superiority amounts to, I hope!” she went on, raising her voice with a tremor which even then and there Newman thought beautiful. “I am too proud to be honest, I am not too proud to be faithless. I am timid and cold and selfish. I am afraid of being uncomfortable.”

“And you call marrying me uncomfortable!” said Newman staring. Madame de Cintré blushed a little and seemed to say that if begging his pardon in words was impudent, she might at least thus mutely express her perfect comprehension of his finding her conduct odious. “It is not marrying you; it is doing all that would go with it. It’s the rupture, the defiance, the insisting upon being happy in my own way. What right have I to be happy when—when”—And she paused.

“When what?” said Newman.

“When others have been most unhappy!”

“What others?” Newman asked. “What have you to do with any others but me? Besides you said just now that you wanted happiness, and that you should find it by obeying your mother. You contradict yourself.”

“Yes, I contradict myself; that shows you that I am not even intelligent.”

“You are laughing at me!” cried Newman. “You are mocking me!” She looked at him intently, and an observer might have said that she was asking herself whether she might not most quickly end their common pain by confessing that she was mocking him. “No; I am not,” she presently said.

“Granting that you are not intelligent,” he went on, “that you are weak, that you are common, that you are nothing that I have believed you were—what I ask of you is not heroic effort, it is a very common effort. There is a great deal on my side to make it easy. The simple truth is that you don’t care enough about me to make it.”

“I am cold,” said Madame de Cintré, “I am as cold as that flowing river.” Newman gave a great rap on the floor with his stick, and a long, grim laugh. “Good, good!” he cried. “You go altogether too far—you overshoot the mark. There isn’t a woman in the world as bad as you would make yourself out. I see your game; it’s what I said. You are blackening yourself to whiten others. Would you chop off your hand if your mother requested it?”

The train which deposited Hubert Ashby at the little station of Wenham Falls was so leisurely, and the station itself so much smaller than his memory of it, that he stood for a moment on the wooden platform with the sensation of a man who has come upon a portrait of himself as a child, and who is less touched by the likeness than by the inexplicable shrinkage of the frame. It was eighteen years since he had last looked upon that platform, and it had then seemed to him, if not exactly the threshold of the world, at least the door of the vestibule; he had passed through it with a valise in one hand and a letter of credit in the other, and with that sense of having been let off from something which, at twenty-four, is so easily confounded with the sense of having been called to something. He had been called, as it turned out, to a great many things: to Florence, to Rome, to a winter in Seville and a summer at Homburg, to the acquaintance of several princesses and the friendship of one cardinal, and to the slow, agreeable accumulation of a small collection of Sienese pictures, which was spoken of by people who knew about such matters with a certain respectful indulgence. But he had not been called back, and he was not, even now, quite sure that he had been called at all. He had come, he told himself, because his aunt Harriet was dead, because there was a will, and because there was nobody else; and he had a vague, half-humorous apprehension that these reasons, which had appeared in Rome to be perfectly adequate, would look rather thin in the clear October light of Massachusetts.

There was no carriage, for he had sent no word of the hour; and he walked up the long street, under the elms, which had at least not shrunk, with his small portmanteau consigned to the care of a boy who regarded him, he thought, very much as the natives of a southern village had used to regard him when he arrived among them with a sketching-block. He had acquired, he was aware, a certain foreignness of surface; it was a thing he had sometimes been rather pleased with, as one is pleased with the patina on a bronze; but he was not prepared to find it so evidently a matter of public remark in the main street of Wenham Falls. He was not prepared, either, for the extraordinary quietness of the place, which was not the quietness of Italian towns, where the stillness seems always to be the stillness of a people asleep after a feast, but a quietness that had never been anything else, that had been born quiet and had been brought up on principle.

The house stood where it had always stood, at the end of the street, where the road began to think of becoming a country road and had not yet made up its mind. It was a square white house with green shutters and a fanlight over the door, and it had a deep piazza along one side, upon which, as Hubert came up the walk, a lady was sitting with some work in her lap. She did not rise immediately; she let her work fall, and looked at him, and he had time, before she spoke, to feel himself very distinctly looked at. Then she got up and came to the top of the steps.

"I should have known you anywhere," she said; "but I should have wondered, a good deal, where it was that I knew you from."

"That is exactly what I was going to say to you," Hubert answered, "only I should have said it less well."

It was not true; he had been going to say nothing of the sort; but it struck him at once as the kind of thing that it would be pleasant to have said, and he had lived long enough among people who valued pleasant things to be tolerant of his own small mendacities. She gave him her hand, and he held it a moment longer, perhaps, than was quite necessary, by way of gaining time. Lydia Fenn—she had been Lydia Ashby, and he still, in the privacy of his thoughts, found it difficult to call her anything else—was a woman of forty, tall, rather pale, with a great deal of smooth brown hair, in which he detected, with a curious little pang, one or two threads of grey. She wore the black of a mourning which was evidently not new, and which had been worn, he guessed, with a certain conscientious indifference to its becomingness. She was not beautiful; she had never been beautiful; but she had something which he had not remembered, or had not been old enough to perceive—a sort of finished composure, as of a house in which every room has been lived in and nothing has been left to chance.

"You will have come about Aunt Harriet's things," she said, when she had made him sit down in one of the wicker chairs and had sent the boy round to the kitchen door with his portmanteau. "I wrote to you that there was no need. Mr. Pratt could have managed it all. But I knew you would come."

"You knew it better than I did, then," said Hubert. "I didn't know it until I found myself at Naples, buying my ticket. Even then I thought I was going to Sicily."

"You always thought you were going somewhere else," said his cousin, smiling. "It was what Aunt Harriet used to say of you. She said you would take the wrong boat and arrive at the right place, and then be very much surprised and a little annoyed."

"Did she say that? Dear old woman! She didn't approve of me."

"She approved of you a great deal more than she approved of most people. She had all your letters tied up in a ribbon. I found them in her desk, and I didn't know what to do with them. I thought you might like to have them back."

Hubert was silent a moment. He had written to his aunt, he remembered, perhaps twice a year—long letters, full of pictures and princesses, composed with a care which he had not usually bestowed on his correspondence, because he had felt, obscurely, that they would be read aloud. It was rather terrible to think of them tied up in a ribbon; it was like coming upon one's own ghost, carefully preserved in a drawer.

"I think," he said presently, "I would rather you kept them. Unless you have read them, in which case you had better burn them."

"I have read every one of them," said Lydia simply. "I read them when they came. Aunt Harriet used to send for me on purpose."

He looked at her, and she met his look with perfect tranquillity; and he had the odd impression—it was the first of several such impressions that he was to receive in the course of that afternoon—that she had said something of importance in a manner calculated to make it appear of none. It was a manner he had encountered before, in drawing-rooms where a great deal was said and very little was meant; but he had not expected to encounter it here, on a wooden piazza, in a country town, in the person of a cousin whom he had last seen at the age of twenty-two, crying a little, in a muslin dress, at the gate. He was not even certain that she had cried; he had always believed so, but he had perhaps believed it because it was agreeable to believe.

"Then you know all about me," he said, with a laugh which did not sound to his own ears particularly easy. "I am at a disadvantage. I know nothing whatever about you—except what one knows from the newspapers and from Aunt Harriet's postscripts. And Aunt Harriet's postscripts, you know, were not expansive."

"They said that I was married, I suppose, and that Mr. Fenn had died. There was nothing else to say."

"There must have been a great deal else."

"Oh, a great deal," she assented, with that same air of laying the subject down very gently, as one lays down a cup that is too full. "But nothing that would go into a postscript."

She took up her work again, and he watched her for a little while in silence. The afternoon was very still; the light lay level and golden across the grass, and among the maples on the other side of the road there was that first deep flush of crimson which he had forgotten, and which struck him now as something almost indecently vivid, like a sudden confession. He had seen a great many sunsets on the Campagna, and had talked about them a great deal; but he had a suspicion that the maples were not to be talked about, and that this was very much the sort of thing his cousin would have said if she had been asked.

"You are thinking," Lydia said, without looking up, "that we are all very much as you left us."

"I was thinking precisely the contrary. I was thinking that you are not at all as I left you."

"That is a compliment, I suppose—in Rome."

"In Rome," said Hubert, "it would be the beginning of a compliment. Here I'm afraid it's only an observation. You were a girl when I went away, and you are—"

"An old woman," she suggested.

"I was going to say a person. You are a person, Lydia, and you were not, then—or I didn't see that you were. I suppose that is my fault."

She let her needle rest, and looked at him with a sort of mild curiosity, as if he had produced from his pocket some small foreign coin of which she did not know the value.

"I don't think it was anybody's fault," she said. "One isn't a person at twenty-two; at least not in Wenham Falls. One is somebody's daughter, or somebody's cousin, or—" she hesitated for the fraction of a second—"or somebody's intention."

Hubert flushed; he felt himself flush, and was annoyed, for he had long since supposed himself to be past that particular infirmity. It was impossible to pretend that he did not understand her. The intention had been their grandmother's, and their grandmother had been a person of strong intentions; it had been understood in the family, for a number of years, that the two Ashby cousins, who had played together as children and quarrelled together as young people, would presently, in the natural course of things, cease to quarrel and begin to do something else. Nobody had ever said so in so many words; it had not been the habit of the family to say things in so many words; but it had been in the air, like the smell of the lilacs in May, and Hubert had breathed it until it had seemed to him that he must either go away or suffocate. He had gone away. He had told himself at the time—and he had believed it, more or less, for eighteen years—that he had gone away in order to see the world; and it was only now, sitting on the piazza in the long October light, that it occurred to him, with a disagreeable distinctness, that he might have gone away in order not to see his cousin.

"I have sometimes wondered," he said slowly, "whether you knew."

"Knew what?"

"What everybody intended."

Lydia smiled, and the smile, which was very faint, made her look, for an instant, extraordinarily like the girl at the gate.

"My dear Hubert," she said, "everybody intended it so very loudly. One would have had to be deaf. And I was never deaf, you know; it was only that I didn't talk. You used to say that I was the most silent person you had ever known, and that it was very restful. I suppose you meant that it was very dull."

"I meant exactly what I said. I have met a great many talkers since. I have sometimes thought of your silence as one thinks of a cool room in a hot country."

"That is very pretty," said Lydia; "but one doesn't marry a cool room."

He had nothing to say to this, and he was conscious that she had not meant him to have anything to say. She went on sewing, and he sat watching the long shadows of the elms creep across the lawn, and reflecting—with a ruefulness which was not without its element of amusement, for he was a man to whom his own discomfiture was always, in the long run, a little amusing—that he had come four thousand miles to be told, in the gentlest manner possible, that he had been understood all along.

"And Mr. Fenn?" he presently asked. "Was he—was he a talker?"

"He was a very good man," said Lydia. "He talked about the things he knew. He knew a great deal about the law, and something about apples. We had an orchard, out on the Topsfield road, and he used to walk in it on Sunday afternoons and tell me the names of the varieties. I never could remember them. He didn't mind. He used to say that it was enough for one of us to know." She paused, and then added, with a kind of scrupulous fairness, as if she were reading the terms of a document, "He was very kind to me. He was ill for a long time at the end. I was glad to be able to take care of him."

"You were happy, then?"

She considered the question, with her needle in the air, as she might have considered whether a certain color would wash.

"I was occupied," she said at last. "I think that is what most people mean when they say they are happy. You have been happy, I suppose—in that sense?"

"Oh, I have been tremendously occupied," said Hubert. "I have been occupied with the most delightful things in the world. I have bought pictures and sold them and bought them back again. I have quarrelled with a Florentine dealer for three years about the attribution of a predella. I have dined with people whose grandfathers poisoned each other. I have been, I assure you, very busy."

"And you never married."

"I never married." He looked at her, and then he looked away. "There was a lady in Rome," he said, "a widow, like yourself—only not at all like yourself. Everybody intended that too. I seem to inspire intentions."

"And you went away from Rome?"

"I went to Sicily," said Hubert, laughing. "Or rather, I thought I was going to Sicily. And here I am."

There was a silence, of a kind which he was not accustomed to—a silence in which nothing seemed to be expected of him, and in which, for that very reason, he felt that a great deal was going on. He had lived for eighteen years among people who could not let a pause alone; who filled it, as one fills a gap in a dinner-table, with the first comer; and he found it at once soothing and alarming to sit beside a woman who was evidently prepared to let this one stand for as long as it chose. He found, too, that he was looking at her hands, which were long and pale and very quiet, and that he was thinking—though he could not have said precisely why—of a certain little Madonna by Sano di Pietro which hung in his bedroom in the Via Gregoriana, and which he had never been able to make his friends admire.

"You read all my letters," he said at last.

"All of them."

"Did they amuse you?"

"Very much. Aunt Harriet used to read them aloud, and I used to sit by the window and listen. She read them very badly; she always pronounced the Italian names as if they were the names of patent medicines. But I could hear you through it. I could hear you laughing at yourself, and pretending not to. You used to write, sometimes, a whole page about a picture, and then at the end you would say, 'But I bore you, dear Aunt'—and Aunt Harriet would say, 'He does, rather,' and go on to the next page. I used to wish she would read that page again."

"You might have written to me yourself," said Hubert, a little unsteadily.

"I might," she agreed. "But what would I have said? That the maples had turned, and that Mr. Fenn knew the names of the apples? You would have been very kind; you would have answered me with a page about a Madonna. And then I should have had to write again." She drew her thread through and bit it off. "It was much better to listen."

He got up and walked to the end of the piazza, and stood looking out at the road, where a farm wagon was passing slowly, with a man upon it who lifted his whip in a salutation which seemed to include the house, the lady, the visitor, and the whole golden afternoon. Hubert returned it, a little absurdly, with a foreign wave of the hand. He had a sense, which he was afterwards to describe to a friend in Rome as "the most uncomfortable and the most precious of my life"—and I give the phrase, as he gave it, for what it may be worth—of having been all these years the subject of a long, patient, and perfectly unresentful attention, of which he had been as ignorant as a sleeping man is of the person who sits by his bed. It was not that she had loved him; he did not flatter himself so far, or he did not quite dare to; it was something at once less and more than that. She had watched him; she had heard him; she had, in a sense which he could not altogether make out, kept him; and she had done it without asking for anything, or expecting anything, or even, apparently, minding very much that nothing had come of it.

"Lydia," he said, turning round, "I have been a great fool."

"I don't think so," said his cousin gently. "I think you have been a man who wanted to see things. You have seen them. It would be a great pity if you went back now and told everybody that it had been foolish. Nobody would believe you, and they would think that America had been bad for you."

"And you? What have you wanted?"

She folded her work and laid it on the little table beside her, and stood up; and he saw that she was, after all, very nearly as tall as he.

"I wanted," she said, "to know how it turned out. And now I know."

"How has it turned out?"

She looked at him with a smile which he was to think of a great many times, in many places—on the terrace of the Pincio, and in the hot, dim churches of Siena, and once, at Venice, at two o'clock in the morning, when he could not sleep and had gone out on the balcony to watch the lights on the water.

"Very well," she said. "Very well indeed. Much better than if you had stayed."

"You can't mean that."

"I mean it entirely. If you had stayed, you would have married me, I suppose, because everybody intended it; and you would have walked in the orchard on Sunday afternoons, and you would have been very kind, and you would have hated it. And I should have known that you hated it. And I should have had nothing to listen to." She paused. "As it is, I have had eighteen years of Madonnas and princesses. It is more than most women in Wenham Falls can say."

He would have answered her—he did not know with what; with some protest, some gallantry, some phrase out of the drawing-rooms which would have rung falsely in that clear air—but she had already turned towards the door.

"You will stay to supper," she said, in a different tone, the tone of the house, of the family, of the long habit of hospitality. "There is a room ready; I had it aired on Tuesday. And to-morrow we will go over Aunt Harriet's things with Mr. Pratt. There is a highboy that she wished you to have. I don't know how you will get it to Rome."

"I shall take the wrong boat," said Hubert, "and arrive at the right place."

She laughed—it was the first time she had laughed, and it was not at all a silent laugh—and went into the house; and he remained for a few moments on the piazza, in the last of the light, with his hands in his pockets, considering the crimson maples, which no longer seemed to him indecent, but only, like certain things one has waited too long to say, a little too late in the year to be anything but beautiful.

Ledoux had told him that he had reason to know that Valentin’s will—Bellegarde had a great deal of elegant personal property to dispose of—contained a request that he should be buried near his father in the churchyard of Fleurières, and Newman intended that the state of his own relations with the family should not deprive him of the satisfaction of helping to pay the last earthly honors to the best fellow in the world. He reflected that Valentin’s friendship was older than Urbain’s enmity, and that at a funeral it was easy to escape notice. Madame de Cintré’s answer to his letter enabled him to time his arrival at Fleurières. This answer was very brief; it ran as follows:— “I thank you for your letter, and for your being with Valentin. It is a most inexpressible sorrow to me that I was not. To see you will be nothing but a distress to me; there is no need, therefore, to wait for what you call brighter days. It is all one now, and I shall have no brighter days. Come when you please; only notify me first. My brother is to be buried here on Friday, and my family is to remain here. C. de C.” As soon as he received this letter Newman went straight to Paris and to Poitiers. The journey took him far southward, through green Touraine and across the far-shining Loire, into a country where the early spring deepened about him as he went. But he had never made a journey during which he heeded less what he would have called the lay of the land. He obtained lodging at the inn at Poitiers, and the next morning drove in a couple of hours to the village of Fleurières. But here, preoccupied though he was, he could not fail to notice the picturesqueness of the place. It was what the French call a petit bourg; it lay at the base of a sort of huge mound on the summit of which stood the crumbling ruins of a feudal castle, much of whose sturdy material, as well as that of the wall which dropped along the hill to enclose the clustered houses defensively, had been absorbed into the very substance of the village. The church was simply the former chapel of the castle, fronting upon its grass-grown court, which, however, was of generous enough width to have given up its quaintest corner to a little graveyard. Here the very headstones themselves seemed to sleep, as they slanted into the grass; the patient elbow of the rampart held them together on one side, and in front, far beneath their mossy lids, the green plains and blue distances stretched away. The way to church, up the hill, was impracticable to vehicles. It was lined with peasants, two or three rows deep, who stood watching old Madame de Bellegarde slowly ascend it, on the arm of her elder son, behind the pall-bearers of the other. Newman chose to lurk among the common mourners who murmured “Madame la Comtesse” as a tall figure veiled in black passed before them. He stood in the dusky little church while the service was going forward, but at the dismal tomb-side he turned away and walked down the hill. He went back to Poitiers, and spent two days in which patience and impatience were singularly commingled. On the third day he sent Madame de Cintré a note, saying that he would call upon her in the afternoon, and in accordance with this he again took his way to Fleurières. He left his vehicle at the tavern in the village street, and obeyed the simple instructions which were given him for finding the château.

“It is just beyond there,” said the landlord, and pointed to the tree-tops of the park, above the opposite houses. Newman followed the first cross-road to the right—it was bordered with mouldy cottages—and in a few moments saw before him the peaked roofs of the towers. Advancing farther, he found himself before a vast iron gate, rusty and closed; here he paused a moment, looking through the bars. The château was near the road; this was at once its merit and its defect; but its aspect was extremely impressive. Newman learned afterwards, from a guide-book of the province, that it dated from the time of Henry IV. I am timid and cold and selfish. I am afraid of being uncomfortable.”

“And you call marrying me uncomfortable!” said Newman staring. Madame de Cintré blushed a little and seemed to say that if begging his pardon in words was impudent, she might at least thus mutely express her perfect comprehension of his finding her conduct odious. “It is not marrying you; it is doing all that would go with it. It’s the rupture, the defiance, the insisting upon being happy in my own way. What right have I to be happy when—when”—And she paused.

“Yes, I contradict myself; that shows you that I am not even intelligent.”

“You are laughing at me!” cried Newman. “You are mocking me!” She looked at him intently, and an observer might have said that she was asking herself whether she might not most quickly end their common pain by confessing that she was mocking him. “No; I am not,” she presently said.

There is a great deal on my side to make it easy. The simple truth is that you don’t care enough about me to make it.”

“I am cold,” said Madame de Cintré, “I am as cold as that flowing river.” Newman gave a great rap on the floor with his stick, and a long, grim laugh. “Good, good!” he cried. “You go altogether too far—you overshoot the mark.
