The clock on the drawing-room mantelpiece, a gilt affair of nymphs and garlands which had come to Laura Brede from an aunt in Albany and which she had never quite brought herself to banish, was striking half-past twelve when her husband let himself in at the front door. She heard him pause in the hall, heard the small decisive sounds of a man disposing of his hat and stick with more deliberation than the act required, and she knew, before he had crossed the threshold, that he had come home with something to say.

She had not gone up to bed. She had told herself, on returning from the Pellews' dinner an hour earlier, that she was not tired, and had sat down by the fire in her grey brocade with a novel she did not open. The room, under the rose-shaded lamps, had the look of mellowed propriety which she had spent eleven years in giving it. It was a room in which nothing was new and nothing was shabby, a room which said, to anyone versed in its language, that the Bredes were people who had always had enough and had never been so ill-bred as to have too much. Laura had sometimes reflected that the expense of maintaining this impression exceeded, by a comfortable margin, the cost of the more ostentatious interiors she and her friends were accustomed to deplore. But she had never said so to Austin. There were a great many things she had never said to Austin, and she had come to regard their silence as one of the solid pieces of furniture in the house.

He came in and stood for a moment just inside the door, looking at her with an air of faint surprise, as though he had expected the room to be empty and was obliged to readjust some inward arrangement on finding it occupied.

"You're up late," he said.

"I wasn't sleepy. Did you walk from the club?"

"Yes." He came forward and stood with his back to the fire, a posture he had inherited from his father, along with the house in East Thirty-ninth Street and a habit of regarding all departures from established custom as symptoms of moral fatigue. He was a tall man, still slender at forty-four, with the kind of face which in a portrait is called distinguished and in a drawing-room merely well-bred. His evening clothes were perfect, as they always were. It occurred to her, looking at him, that she had never once seen him look anything but perfect, and that this, which had dazzled her at twenty, had lately come to seem less an attribute than a fortification.

"I saw Halsey Bain at the club," he said.

She turned a page of the novel she was not reading. "Did you? I thought he was in Aiken."

"He came back on Tuesday." Austin paused, and she felt the pause settle over the room like a fine dust. "He told me a curious thing."

"Halsey is always telling curious things. It's what people ask him to dinner for."

"Yes." He took a cigarette from the silver box on the mantel, looked at it, and put it back. "He told me that Dwight Kelling had been saying at the Union League that it was through his good offices that I came out whole on the Mohawk and Western business last autumn."

The fire made a small subsiding sound. Laura closed her book with the care of a woman who has been taught that a closed book, like a closed fan, can be made to say a good deal.

"How very odd of Mr. Kelling," she said.

"I thought it odd myself. I told Bain it was nonsense. I had sold out on my own judgment, as I've told you a dozen times, and on Freddy Asher's advice, which is the same thing, since Freddy has never had an opinion I didn't give him." He smiled faintly, but the smile did not reach his eyes, which were fixed upon her with a steadiness she had not seen in them for years. "Bain was very civil. He said of course it was nonsense. And then he said that Kelling had been particularly struck by the charm of the lady who had carried the message."

Laura was conscious of a sensation she had not felt since she was a girl at Miss Lattimer's school, called up before the headmistress for some infraction she had not known to be one: a sudden withdrawal of warmth from the extremities, as if the blood had gone to stand guard at some inner citadel. She looked at the fire, and then, because looking at the fire was precisely what a guilty woman would do, she looked at her husband.

"And you would like to know," she said, "whether I am the lady."

"I should like to know," he said, "what Kelling meant by saying it."

There it was, the Brede manner: never the direct question, which would have been vulgar, but the question turned a quarter of the way round, so that it might be answered without either party being compelled to acknowledge that it had been asked. She had learned the manner as a bride, as she had learned which forks the Brede silver required and which of their cousins were not to be met at luncheon; she had admired it, and imitated it, and come in time to use it better than he did. It was therefore with a curious sense of sacrilege that she heard herself decline it.

"He meant," she said, "that I went to see him."

Austin did not move. Only his hand, which had been resting on the mantel-shelf, closed slightly upon the edge of the marble.

"You went to see Dwight Kelling."

"In October. At his office in Broad Street. You were in Lenox with your mother."

He was silent so long that she thought he would not speak at all; that he would do what his father would have done, which was to bow, say good-night, and carry the subject upstairs with him to be locked away among the other heirlooms of the family. But he only said, in a voice from which every inflection had been carefully removed, "Would you be good enough to tell me why?"

She rose then, because she found she could not say it sitting down, and went to the window, where the heavy curtains of old-rose damask shut out the street. She put her hand on the fold of them as though she might draw them back and find some other prospect than the brownstone fronts opposite, each with its lamp burning discreetly in the vestibule.

"Because you were going to be ruined," she said. "And you would not let anyone tell you so."

"That is not true."

"Austin, it is quite true. You had put everything into Mohawk and Western on Freddy Asher's word, and Freddy had it from someone at the Knickerbocker who had it from someone else, and none of them knew anything. Everyone else knew. Mrs. Kelling told me at the Thurlows' that the Kelling people were going to let it drop to nothing in November, and she told me because she wished me to know that her husband could ruin mine whenever he chose. She said it very prettily. She asked me whether I didn't find Lenox dull in the autumn."

"And you went to Kelling."

"I went to Kelling. I asked him, as a kindness, whether there was not something a woman ought to know about her husband's affairs. He was very kind. He told me that if I happened to suggest to you that it would be wise to sell before the twentieth, I should be doing you a service. I wrote to you in Lenox that I had dreamed the stock was falling and that you must humour me. You laughed at me in your letter. And then you sold."

"I sold," said Austin slowly, "because Freddy came round to the same view."

"Freddy came round because I went to Freddy's wife." She turned from the window. "I'm sorry. I know how it sounds."

He looked at her with an expression she could not read, an expression in which bewilderment seemed to be struggling with something older and harder, as a living face sometimes struggles beneath the marble of a funeral effigy.

"You know how it sounds," he repeated. "I wonder if you do. My wife goes alone to the office of a man whom no one we know receives, a man whose name was mentioned in the Erie business, a man whose wife has been trying for five years to get herself asked to the Assembly, and she asks him for a favour. And he grants it. And then he goes about the Union League telling people that he has grants of that kind in his gift." He drew a breath. "Did it not occur to you what he would want in return?"

"It occurred to me perfectly. He wanted us to dine there."

Austin stared at her.

"He wanted us to dine there," she went on, with a composure that surprised her, "and he wanted his wife to be asked to the Pellews', and to be put on the committee for the Orphans' Fair. That was all. I have dined there twice, when you were away. Mrs. Kelling was at the Pellews' tonight. You must have noticed her. She wore a great deal of yellow."

"I noticed her," said Austin. "I wondered who had been weak enough to bring her."

"I was."

He turned away from her then, and stood looking down into the fire, and she saw in the rigid line of his shoulders that she had wounded him in some place he had not known to be vulnerable. It was not, she understood with a sudden cold lucidity, the danger he had escaped that offended him, nor even the means of his escape; it was the discovery that he had escaped at all, that the solid ground on which he had always believed himself to be standing had been, for a few weeks of autumn, no more than the outstretched hand of a woman he had married for her serenity.

"You should have told me," he said at last.

"Would you have listened?"

"I should have been given the opportunity."

"You would have been given the opportunity to refuse. You would have told me that a gentleman does not take tips from men like Dwight Kelling, and that the Bredes had weathered worse things than Mohawk and Western, and you would have held on out of sheer principle until there was nothing left to hold. And then we should have let this house, and gone to live in Florence on your mother's allowance, and you would have been noble about it for the rest of your life." She heard her own voice rising, and with an effort brought it down again to the level of the room. "I didn't wish to live in Florence, Austin. I didn't wish to watch you being noble."

It was perhaps the cruellest thing she had ever said to him, and she knew it as she said it; but she knew also, with the strange detachment that sometimes descends upon people at moments of crisis, that it was the truest. She had married him, at twenty, for the very qualities she now reproached him with: for the beautiful inflexibility of his standards, for his air of belonging to an order of things which could not be bought, because it had never been for sale. She had come from a family in which money had been spoken of too often and too anxiously, and she had found in Austin's indifference to it something as restful as the shade of an old tree. It was only gradually that she had perceived the tree to be hollow, and that the indifference was a luxury purchased, like the rose-shaded lamps and the Albany clock, out of a capital which no one in the house had ever troubled to count.

Austin had gone very white.

"I see," he said. "You think me a fool."

"I think you are a man who has never been obliged to be anything else than what he is. It isn't the same thing."

"It seems to come to the same thing, in your account of it." He took the cigarette from the box again, and this time lit it, with a hand that was not perfectly steady. "And what am I to say to Halsey Bain? What am I to say at the club, when Kelling chooses to be confidential again? That my wife manages my investments, and pays the commission in dinner invitations?"

"You might say nothing at all. That is what you generally say."

"Laura."

It was the first time he had used her name that evening, and the sound of it, so long worn smooth by habit, struck her with an odd freshness, like a coin one has carried for years and suddenly turns over to find stamped with an unfamiliar face. She looked at him, and for a moment the two of them stood confronting each other across the hearth-rug as though they had just been introduced.

"I don't think," he said carefully, "that you understand what you have done. I don't mean the money. I daresay you were right about the money. I mean that you have put us in Kelling's hands. A man like that does not do a kindness and forget it. He will want the Assembly next, and then the Patriarchs, and then he will want me to put him up at the Knickerbocker, and every time I refuse, he will tell another story at the Union League, and every story will be a little nearer the truth. You have bought us a year of solvency, and you have paid for it with—" He broke off.

"With what?"

"With our being the sort of people," he said, "to whom that sort of thing can happen."

She was silent. She had foreseen anger, and had armed herself against it; she had foreseen, too, the cold withdrawal which in the Brede family did duty for anger and was a good deal more lasting. What she had not foreseen was this, the note of something very like grief in his voice, as though he were mourning not a loss of fortune but a loss of species. And she understood, with a pang that was half pity and half exasperation, that to Austin the distinction was everything; that he would rather have gone to Florence a Brede than remained in Thirty-ninth Street a man who owed Dwight Kelling a dinner.

"I'm sorry," she said again, and this time she meant it, though not perhaps in the sense he would have wished. "But it's done, Austin. You can't undo it by being shocked."

"No," he said. "I suppose one can't."

He threw the cigarette, barely smoked, into the fire, and they both watched it curl and blacken against the coals. Overhead, a board creaked as one of the servants went along the upper passage, and Laura thought with a sudden irrelevant clarity of the housemaid Annie, who had been with them six years and who would certainly have been dismissed if they had gone abroad. She did not say so. She had a feeling that the conversation had reached a point beyond which arguments were merely so much additional furniture, to be pushed about and rearranged without altering the dimensions of the room.

"What will you do?" she asked at length.

He considered the question with the gravity he gave to all questions of conduct, and she saw his mind move, with the slow precision of long practice, along the established channels: what his father would have done, what his grandfather would have done, what was owed to his name, his club, his wife's reputation, which was after all a portion of his name. It was like watching a man consult a very old and very beautiful map in order to cross a country whose roads had all been altered.

"I shall do nothing," he said finally. "There is nothing to be done. If I contradict Kelling, I make a scandal of it; if I confirm him, I make a worse one. I shall tell Bain that you have a great deal of feminine intuition and that I was lucky enough to heed it. People will laugh a little, and then they will forget."

"And the Kellings?"

He was silent for a moment. "We shall have to dine there," he said, "once. I suppose. And you had better ask them here. In March, when half the town is in Washington and the other half at Lakewood."

It was so exactly what she would have proposed herself that she felt, absurdly, like laughing; and something in her face must have betrayed it, for he looked at her with a sharpness that cut the impulse short.

"You find that amusing?"

"No. I find it sensible. I was only surprised to hear you say it."

"You have been surprising me all evening," said Austin. "I daresay I may be allowed to return the compliment."

He moved away from the fire and stood a moment by the door, his hand on the knob, as if there were something further to be said and he were weighing whether it could be said without loss of dignity. She waited. She had a strange, almost physical sense that the next sentence, whatever it was, would settle the shape of the rest of their lives; that if he turned and said something unguarded, something that did not belong to the map, a door might open upon a country neither of them had ever thought to explore.

"I should be obliged," he said, "if in future you would consult me before undertaking anything of the kind."

The door, if there had been one, closed softly.

"Of course," said Laura.

"Good-night, then."

"Good-night, Austin."

He went out, and she heard him mount the stairs with his usual unhurried tread, the tread of a man who has never in his life been late for anything because nothing has ever been permitted to begin without him. She stood for a while where he had left her, listening to the small domestic noises of the house settling itself for the night: the click of his dressing-room door, the creak of the board in the upper passage, the faint persistent ticking of the gilt clock among its nymphs.

Then she sat down again by the fire and took up the novel she had not been reading. It was, she noticed for the first time, a story about a woman who left her husband and went to live in Italy with a painter; and she remembered that Mrs. Pellew had lent it to her with the remark that it was "very clever, and quite impossible." Laura turned over a few of the pages, smiling slightly. She thought it was quite impossible too. But she found herself reflecting that the impossibility was not, as Mrs. Pellew supposed, a matter of morals; it was merely a question of arithmetic. The heroine had evidently never been obliged to calculate what it would cost to be ruined nobly, nor what it would cost, on the other hand, to be saved in a manner that could never be mentioned.

The fire had burned low. She rose, put the book on the table where the maid would find it in the morning, and turned down the lamps one by one, so that the room withdrew by degrees into the shadow from which it had been so carefully composed. At the door she paused, as Austin had paused, and looked back at it: the old-rose curtains, the faded Aubusson, the portrait of Austin's grandmother with her hands folded over a closed fan. It was a room in which nothing was new and nothing was shabby. It would go on looking like that, she supposed, for a good many years yet; and it occurred to her, as she went slowly up the stairs, that she was the only person in the house who knew precisely what it had cost.

Write in third-person perspective. Match their diction, syntax, tone and voice as closely as you can.  Do not paraphrase or reuse any of the author's content. Output only the piece itself with no title, preamble, or commentary.
response:
It was one of Mrs. Gerald Marchbank's settled convictions that a house reveals its mistress more faithfully than her face, and she had therefore given a good deal of thought to the drawing-room in which she now awaited her cousin. The thought had extended over twenty-six years and had been distributed, with a nice sense of proportion, among the curtains, which were of a crimson damask too costly to be changed merely because it had faded; the Florentine cabinet, which her husband had bought on their wedding journey in the belief that it was Cinquecento; and the portrait of her mother above the mantel, in which a lady of uncompromising shoulders was represented in the act of not being surprised by anything. Mrs. Marchbank had herself, on the whole, been surprised by very little; and she was conscious, as she glanced from the clock to the window and back again, that the agitation she felt was not of a kind she could have permitted to appear in a portrait.

Her cousin Laura Ventnor was coming to tea. The fact, so baldly stated, would have meant nothing to the younger women of her acquaintance, who came and went across the Atlantic as carelessly as their grandmothers had driven to Bloomingdale; but to Mrs. Marchbank it had all the weight of a historical event. Laura had sailed for Europe in the autumn of 1879, when they were both nineteen, and she had not set foot in New York since. In the interval there had been letters, at first long and frequent, then brief and dutiful, and at last reduced to the yearly exchange of Christmas greetings in which each cousin assured the other that she thought of her often; and Mrs. Marchbank, who did think of Laura often, had come to suppose that Laura, in her little house above Florence, thought of her not at all.

The departure itself had been managed with the discretion which old New York reserved for its gravest disasters. Laura had gone abroad with her aunt Mrs. Prentice "for her health," and it had been understood, though never said, that her health required a separation of some duration from a young man named Jasper Lowe, who painted portraits without having been asked to, and who had no other visible means of support. Mrs. Marchbank remembered him as a lean, quick-eyed person with an unfortunate habit of laughing at things one was accustomed to take seriously; and she remembered, too, though she had for many years contrived not to dwell on it, that it was she who had first acquainted her aunt with the extent of Laura's attachment.

She had done it, she had always told herself, from the purest motives. Laura had been engaged to him secretly for three months, meeting him in the Academy galleries and on the less frequented paths of the Park; and Clementine, who had been her only confidante, had borne the weight of the secret until it became intolerable to a conscience trained from infancy to regard concealment as the first of the vices. She had gone to her aunt one wet afternoon in October and had come away, an hour later, with the sensation of having been very brave and very wretched; and within a month Laura was at sea. Lowe had married a Philadelphia heiress two years afterward, which was generally held to have justified everybody; and Clementine had married Gerald Marchbank, which was held to have justified her in particular.

The bell sounded, and she heard the measured progress of her parlour-maid across the hall. Mrs. Marchbank rose, became aware that rising suggested eagerness, and sat down again; so that when the door opened she was discovered in the attitude of a woman interrupted in the perusal of a book she had not, in fact, been reading.

"Mrs. Ventnor," said the parlour-maid, who had been told that Miss Ventnor had never married, and who had silently resolved that a lady of her years could be nothing else.

The woman who came in was smaller than Mrs. Marchbank had expected, and the first emotion of which the latter was conscious was a slight and unworthy satisfaction that Laura had grown so grey. The second, following close upon it, was the perception that the greyness did not matter; for the face beneath it had kept, or acquired, a kind of luminous mobility which made the question of colour seem irrelevant. Laura was dressed with a simplicity which Mrs. Marchbank's experienced eye at once pronounced to be either very poor or very expensive, and which she was a little vexed not to be able to assign with confidence to either category.

"Clemmy!" said Laura; and the old name, which no one had used for a quarter of a century, struck the room like a pebble flung through a pane.

They kissed, and drew apart, and looked at each other with the mutual and searching kindness of women who are each privately computing the ravages of time upon the other. Then Mrs. Marchbank, recovering herself, rang for tea and drew her cousin towards the fire.

"You must be frozen. Our Novembers are so trying after the Italian climate."

"Our Novembers in Florence are trying too. It rains for six weeks together, and the Arno comes up the Lung' Arno to see who is at home. But I had forgotten this light—this hard, bright, honest light. It makes everything look as if it had just been paid for."

Mrs. Marchbank, who had a vague sense that her furniture was being alluded to, said that the light was considered very healthful.

"Oh, I'm sure it is. Everything here is healthful, isn't it? It was always the great argument." Laura laughed, and the laugh, light and unresentful as it was, carried Mrs. Marchbank back with a jolt to a certain conversation in the Academy galleries, where another laugh had been raised against the moral pretensions of a Hudson River landscape. She had not known, until that moment, that Laura had caught it from him.

The tea came, and with it the restoring ceremonial of cups and sugar-tongs, beneath which the two women gradually found their footing. They spoke of the voyage, which had been rough; of the hotel, which Laura found astonishing; of the deaths that had thinned their common circle—Aunt Prentice, Cousin Lavinia Burr, old Mr. Ventnor, whose estate had proved so much smaller than anyone had supposed. Mrs. Marchbank, as she enumerated these losses, was aware of a certain melancholy pride in being the custodian of so much mortality; it was she who had attended the funerals, written the letters, and decided what was to be done with Cousin Lavinia's cameos, and she felt that these offices conferred on her a kind of seniority over a relation who had merely been absent.

"And Gerald?" Laura asked. "I was so sorry. Your letter was very beautiful."

"He was ill for only a fortnight. Dr. Cranch said he could not have suffered."

"I remember him at the Lispenards' cotillion—the year before I went. He wore a camellia, and he danced as if he were signing a lease."

Mrs. Marchbank set down her cup. She had loved her husband with the steady and unexamined devotion which is, perhaps, the most durable form the passion takes; and she was not prepared to hear him described, even with affection, in terms that had evidently been kept in readiness for twenty-six years.

"Gerald was the kindest of men," she said.

"I know he was. I didn't mean—Clemmy, forgive me. One gets into the habit, living among foreigners, of saying the thing one sees. It's a dreadful habit, and they all have it, and it's quite the pleasantest thing about them." She leaned forward and laid her hand for a moment on her cousin's. "Tell me about your children. Your Christmas letters were so full of their measles and their examinations, but I never could tell whether you liked them."

The question was so extraordinary that Mrs. Marchbank, for a moment, could only stare. That one loved one's children was an axiom so universally accepted that she had never thought to inquire whether she also liked them; and she found, to her discomfort, that the inquiry was not immediately to be answered. Her elder son was in the bank and had married a Miss Van Alstyne; her younger was in the bank and had not married anybody; her daughter Eleanor had a house at Lenox and four children who were, in Mrs. Marchbank's opinion, insufficiently checked. She recited these facts with a fluency that gave her time to recover, and Laura listened with an attention which seemed, disconcertingly, to be directed less at the facts than at the manner of their recital.

"And you?" said Mrs. Marchbank at length, feeling that the burden of narration should now be shifted. "You have told me so little, all these years. I have often pictured you in your villa—"

"It's not a villa. It's four rooms and a loggia, and a fig tree that does all the work of a garden."

"—and I have so often wished," pursued Mrs. Marchbank, who had prepared this sentence on the stairs, "that things had been different for you. That you had not been so much alone."

She had expected, she hardly knew what—a tremor, a lowering of the eyes, some acknowledgment of the wound which she had always supposed to lie, decently bandaged, beneath the gaiety of Laura's letters. Instead her cousin looked at her with an expression of the liveliest amusement.

"Alone? My dear, I've never been alone for a fortnight together. There's always someone in the loggia. Last spring it was a Russian prince who had been exiled for writing an essay on drains, and before that a little English governess who had run away from a family in Siena and wanted to be a sculptor. She is one now—she does fountains for rich Americans, and they all think she is Florentine. And there are the Morellis below the hill, and old Mr. Hartigan who is writing a life of Savonarola and will never finish it, and the children of my contadino, who steal my figs and bring me violets to make up for it." She paused, and her voice changed. "I have had a great deal of happiness, Clemmy. I don't think I deserved it, but I've had it."

Mrs. Marchbank looked into the fire. Her mind, which had been arranged for a quarter of a century on a certain pattern, was making the painful discovery that the pattern had been woven, all along, on a loom of its own construction. She had pitied Laura; she had, in her more generous moments, forgiven herself on the ground that Laura's loss was the price of Laura's rescue; and she now perceived, with the sudden lucidity which comes to unimaginative people only once or twice in a lifetime, that neither the pity nor the forgiveness had been required.

"You never married," she said, and was immediately ashamed of the remark, which sounded, in that room, like the reading of an indictment.

"No. I had one or two chances—Italians are so obliging about that sort of thing. But I found I didn't want to be married. I had seen so much of it." Laura smiled at the portrait above the mantel, which returned her gaze with unaltered composure. "Your mother would have said that was sour grapes."

"Mamma would have said nothing of the kind," Mrs. Marchbank replied, with the instinctive loyalty of a daughter whose mother would certainly have said exactly that.

There was a pause, in which the clock, an ormolu affair surmounted by a Diana of improbable proportions, ticked with the complacency of an object that has never been required to have an opinion. Mrs. Marchbank had the sense of standing at the edge of something; and she was aware, too, that if she did not step over it now she would never step over it at all, and that Laura would sail in a month and they would go back to their Christmas letters, and she would die—she was quite clear about that—without having said it.

"Laura," she began, and stopped; and then, because the habit of discharging her obligations was stronger in her than the dread of discharging this one, she went on in a lower voice: "There is something I have wanted, for a great many years, to tell you. It was I who told Aunt Prentice. About Mr. Lowe, I mean. You had trusted me, and I went to her, and it was because of me that you were sent away."

She had imagined this confession so often, in the course of so many sleepless nights, that she had come to regard it as a kind of ordeal, to be endured with dignity under the glare of an injured gaze. She now raised her eyes to meet that gaze and found that her cousin was looking at her with nothing more terrible than a gentle and rather tender astonishment.

"But, my dear Clemmy, of course I knew."

"You knew?"

"Aunt Prentice told me herself, on the boat—the second day out, when we were both too sick to be discreet. She thought it would make me feel that the whole family was against me, and that it was useless to struggle." Laura laughed softly. "I think she rather admired you for it. She said you had shown more character than any Ventnor since the Revolution."

Mrs. Marchbank was silent. The tribute, coming at such a distance and from such a source, gave her no pleasure; she was occupied, rather, in readjusting the long perspective of her life to admit the fact that the central drama of her conscience had been, for its supposed victim, a piece of shipboard gossip.

"And you never reproached me," she said at last. "In all those letters."

"Reproach you? Clemmy, I've wanted for twenty years to thank you, only I didn't know how to put it without sounding heartless. You see"—she hesitated, and for the first time her face showed something that was not quite laughter—"I should have married him. I should certainly have married him, if they had let me alone; I was quite determined. And he would have painted portraits of Philadelphia ladies, just as he did, only I should have had to sit in the next room and be grateful for the commissions. I met him once, you know, in Rome, about ten years ago. He had grown stout, and he talked about his clients' pedigrees, and he was very kind to me in the way one is kind to a woman one might have married. I went home and sat under my fig tree and cried for an hour, and then I laughed for another hour; and I have never been quite so happy since, or so certain that I had got the better of everybody." She leaned across and took Mrs. Marchbank's hand again, holding it this time. "You were the instrument of my deliverance, Clemmy. I didn't mean ever to tell you, because I thought you might be offended at having done me so much good by accident."

Mrs. Marchbank did not withdraw her hand; but she sat very upright, and her eyes travelled slowly round the room—over the faded damask, the doubtful cabinet, the portrait of the woman who had never been surprised. It occurred to her that she had chosen these things, or had them chosen for her, with the same anxious rectitude which had sent her through the rain to Aunt Prentice's door; and that they had served her, on the whole, faithfully enough. "It turned out well for both of us, I hope. You have your children and your house and everybody's respect, and I have my four rooms and nobody's. We each got exactly what we were fitted for—which is more, I suppose, than most people can say." Laura rose and began to draw on her gloves. "And now I must go, or the hotel will think I've been abducted. They are so watchful in America; it's like living inside a conscience."

Mrs. Marchbank accompanied her to the door of the drawing-room, and then, by an impulse which she could not afterward explain, down the stairs and into the hall, where the parlour-maid, scandalized, hovered with the visitor's wrap. At the threshold Laura turned and kissed her again.

"You'll come to Florence, Clemmy? In the spring, when the fig is out? I'll put you in the loggia with the Russian prince."

"Then don't tell Eleanor," said Laura, and went down the steps into the hard, bright, honest light.

Mrs. Marchbank stood for some moments looking after her. Then she went slowly back up the stairs and into the drawing-room, where the tea-things still stood upon the table and the fire had sunk to a sullen glow. She did not ring for the maid. Mrs. Archibald Wentworth Lisle had always prided herself on never raising her voice. It was one of the small distinctions she cultivated, as other women cultivated a particular shade of mauve or the reputation of having been painted by Cabanel, and she had brought it to such perfection that her friends, who knew her temper to be quick, admired the more the composure with which she governed it. She was aware of this admiration, and it was perhaps the chief reason why, on the November afternoon on which her daughter disgraced her, she sat for a full quarter of an hour after the last caller had gone, her hands folded upon the grey faille of her lap, before she rang for the nurse.

The drawing-room in which she sat had been decorated, ten years earlier, by a firm whose name was then pronounced in Fifth Avenue with the hushed respect due to a cathedral architect, and it still bore the marks of that consecration: the walls hung with a sage-green damask that had cost what Mrs. Lisle's mother would have spent on a summer at Newport, the mantel heavy with bronzes of a mythological indecency so remote as to be quite respectable, and the windows so muffled in successive layers of lace, silk and velvet that the light of the street reached the room only as a kind of rumour. Mrs. Lisle had never quite liked it. She had married into it, as she had married into the Lisle silver and the Lisle pew at Grace Church, and she had learned to regard it as one regards a relative of whom one is not fond but whom one would never think of disowning. In the lamp-lit dusk of that afternoon, however, it seemed to her for the first time to have taken on a kind of watchfulness, as if the gilt-framed mirrors and the glazed eyes of the bronze nymphs had witnessed the scene and were waiting to see what she would do about it.

What had happened was, in itself, a very small thing; and Mrs. Lisle knew enough of the world to be aware that it was precisely the small things which were never forgiven. Old Mrs. Thaddeus Corlear had called, as she called on the second Thursday of every month, bringing with her the faint odour of camphor and the far more pervasive atmosphere of a woman who has outlived everyone who might have contradicted her. Mrs. Corlear's position in New York was of the kind that is not so much held as inhabited, like an old house to which no one would think of adding a wing; and her visits, though they were dreaded by every hostess on the list, were dreaded in the way one dreads the passing of a royal carriage, with a secret and not unpleasurable flutter. With her had come her daughter-in-law, the younger Mrs. Corlear, a pale and anxious woman who had been a Miss Pruyn of Albany and who had never, in twenty years of marriage, been allowed to forget it; and young Mrs. Bertram Hale, whose recent return from Europe had given her the slightly bewildered air of a person who has been told that the world has gone on without her.

It had been, until the moment of catastrophe, an entirely satisfactory visit. Mrs. Lisle had poured tea with that slight inclination of the head which her friends found so graceful and which she had copied, in her girlhood, from a portrait of the Empress Eugénie; Mrs. Corlear had pronounced the seed-cake "not what it was at your mother's, my dear, but very fair, very fair indeed"; and the conversation had moved, with the stately reluctance of a procession, from the iniquities of the new Opera boxes to the probable engagement of the youngest Van Ness girl, and from there, by a transition no one could afterward have traced, to the question of who was and who was not to be asked to the Patriarchs' Ball.

It was at this point that the door had opened and the nurse, in obedience to an instruction which Mrs. Lisle now bitterly regretted, had brought in little Rosamund to make her curtsey.

Rosamund was seven, and was generally considered a credit to her mother. She had the Lisle colouring, which was fair, and the Lisle forehead, which was high; and she had been trained from her earliest years to enter a room with her hands at her sides and her eyes lowered, and to say "How do you do" in a voice that carried exactly as far as the person addressed. She performed these offices on the present occasion without a fault. She curtsied to old Mrs. Corlear, and to the younger, and to Mrs. Hale; she submitted to being kissed by the first, patted by the second and exclaimed over by the third; and she then took up her station beside her mother's chair, where she was permitted to remain for ten minutes and to eat one macaroon, on the understanding that she would not speak unless she was spoken to.

It was old Mrs. Corlear who had spoken to her. Mrs. Lisle had seen it coming, as one sees a carriage swerve on an icy street, with a perfect foreknowledge and a perfect inability to prevent it.

"And what does this little lady do with herself all day?" the old woman had inquired, in the tone of indulgent condescension with which she addressed children, servants and the wives of men in trade.

Rosamund had considered the question with the gravity she brought to all questions, and had answered that she did her lessons with Miss Prentice, and walked in the Square, and on Thursdays was allowed to come down and see the ladies.

"And do you like to see the ladies?"

"Yes, ma'am," said Rosamund. And then, with the terrible candour of a child who has been told that she must always tell the truth and has not yet been told the exceptions, she had added: "But Mamma doesn't like it when you come, because she says you count the spoons with your eyes and tell Mrs. Van Ness afterward."

There had followed a silence of the kind that Mrs. Lisle had read of in novels and had supposed to be an invention of novelists. It was not long; it could not, by any reasonable measure, have lasted more than a few seconds; but in that interval she was conscious of everything in the room with a hallucinatory distinctness: the tick of the ormolu clock, the faint rasp of the younger Mrs. Corlear's breath, the sudden rigidity of Mrs. Hale's gloved hand upon her cup, and above all the face of old Mrs. Corlear, which did not change in the least, but which seemed to settle, like a house settling upon its foundations, into an expression of profound and permanent repose.

Then Mrs. Corlear had laughed. It was a short, dry sound, not unlike the closing of a reticule, and it was followed by the remark that children said the most extraordinary things, and that she remembered a little cousin of hers in the year 'forty-one who had informed the Bishop that his breath smelt of onions. The younger Mrs. Corlear had laughed too, a moment late; Mrs. Hale had laughed a moment later still; and Mrs. Lisle, who had felt the blood rise to her face in a manner she had not experienced since her first winter out, had heard herself saying, in a voice of admirable steadiness, that Rosamund was a terrible little romancer and that Miss Prentice despaired of her. The nurse had been rung for; Rosamund had been removed; and the conversation had resumed its procession as though nothing had interrupted it. But Mrs. Corlear had risen to go a full twenty minutes before her usual hour, and in the hall, as Mrs. Lisle bent to receive her parting kiss, the old woman had said in her ear, very pleasantly: "You must bring the child to see me, my dear. I should like to know her better. She seems so remarkably well informed."

It was this last sentence which Mrs. Lisle had been turning over for a quarter of an hour, as one turns over a stone in the hope of finding that the underside is less disagreeable than the upper. She knew perfectly well what it portended. By Saturday it would be known in every drawing-room from Washington Square to Murray Hill that Mrs. Archibald Lisle discussed her callers before her nursery; that she accused old Mrs. Corlear, of all people, of counting spoons; that she was, in short, not quite what one had supposed. Nothing would be said to her directly. Nothing ever was. But there would be a slight cooling in certain quarters, a faint hesitation in certain invitations, a perceptible pause before certain greetings; and she, who had spent eleven years in building up for herself a position which the Lisle name had given her the right to occupy but not the means to secure, would find that she had to begin, in some degree, all over again.

She did not, at first, think very much about Rosamund. Her mind was occupied with the larger question of what was to be done; whether she ought to write to Mrs. Corlear that evening, or whether a note would merely give substance to the offence; whether she might enlist the help of her husband's aunt, Mrs. Ludlow Lisle, who was the only woman in New York to whom Mrs. Corlear was known to defer; whether, above all, she could count upon the discretion of Mrs. Hale, whose long residence abroad had made her, it was feared, careless of the distinction between what one saw and what one repeated. It was only when she had arrived, by a series of reflections which did her worldly sense more credit than her heart, at the conclusion that nothing could be done at all, that her thoughts returned to the child; and then they returned with a force that surprised her.

For it had been true. That was what she could not get past. She had said it, not once but several times, and in very nearly those words. She had said it to her husband at breakfast, and to her sister Mrs. Stuyvesant Brock on the stairs at the Assembly, and once, she now recalled with a sensation of physical discomfort, to Miss Prentice herself, who had been waiting in the hall with Rosamund's hand in hers while Mrs. Lisle drew on her gloves. It had been one of those small, sharp, pleasurable things that one says in the security of one's own house, things that are not malicious, precisely, but are rather a kind of private currency, valuable only because they cannot be spent abroad. And the child had picked it up, as she picked up the chestnuts that fell in the Square, and had carried it into the drawing-room and laid it, with a kind of innocent pride, at the feet of the one person on earth before whom it should never have been produced.

Mrs. Lisle rose and rang the bell.

Rosamund was brought down in her nightgown and wrapper, her hair loosened for the night and falling about her shoulders in the fine pale strands that her mother's maid brushed out every evening for a hundred strokes. The nurse, who had evidently been expecting the summons, delivered her at the door with a look in which sympathy and a certain grim satisfaction were nicely blended, and withdrew. The child came forward across the expanse of Aubusson carpet with her hands at her sides and stopped at the proper distance from her mother's chair. She had been crying, Mrs. Lisle saw; but she had washed her face afterward, and she held herself with a composure that her mother, in other circumstances, would have found admirable.

"Come here, Rosamund."

The child came a step nearer.

Mrs. Lisle looked at her for some moments in silence. She had intended to begin at once; she had, in fact, composed the opening sentences of her reprimand during the interval of waiting, and had found them very satisfactory, firm without harshness and grave without excess. But now that the child stood before her, small and upright in her white wrapper, with her hands clasped together so tightly that the knuckles showed, the sentences seemed to have gone out of her head; and she found herself thinking, irrelevantly, of an afternoon in her own childhood, in her mother's house in Waverly Place, when she had been made to stand in exactly this fashion before exactly such a chair, and had been told, in a voice not raised, that a lady never says what she thinks of anyone except to God, and to Him only in moderation.

"Do you know why I have sent for you?" she said at last.

"Yes, Mamma."

"Tell me, then."

Rosamund's lip trembled, but she controlled it. "Because of what I said to the old lady."

"To Mrs. Corlear," said Mrs. Lisle. "You will call her by her name. And what was it you said?"

The child repeated it, word for word, in a low voice. Hearing it again, divested of the shock of its first utterance, Mrs. Lisle was struck by how very exactly the child had reproduced not only her words but something of her tone; and she felt, absurdly, as if she had caught sight of her own reflection in an unexpected glass and had found it less becoming than she had supposed.

"Do you know that you behaved very wrongly?"

"Yes, Mamma." There was a pause. Then, with the scrupulous honesty which Miss Prentice had been at such pains to instil, and which Mrs. Lisle had hitherto regarded as one of the child's chief merits: "But I don't know why."

Mrs. Lisle had not expected this. She had expected tears, or sullenness, or the vague and comprehensive contrition with which children meet reproof they do not understand; and she had been prepared to deal with any of these. She was not prepared to be asked for reasons.

"You don't know why?" she repeated, and was annoyed to hear in her own voice a faint note of uncertainty.

"You said it, Mamma," said Rosamund. "I heard you say it to Papa. And Miss Prentice says that we must always tell the truth, because God hears everything, and that a lie is the worst thing a little girl can do. And the old lady—Mrs. Corlear—asked me if I liked to see the ladies, and I did tell the truth, and then I told her the other part because I thought she would want to know." The small voice faltered, but went on. "I thought it was the truth too."

There was a silence. The ormolu clock, which had been a wedding present from a Lisle cousin who had since been divorced and was never mentioned, ticked on with the indifference of objects that have outlived their associations. Mrs. Lisle was conscious of a sensation she could not at once identify; it was not quite anger, and not quite shame, but something compounded of both and of a third thing which she afterward came to think of as fear, though she could not have said of what.

"It is quite true that you must never tell a lie," she said slowly. "Miss Prentice is perfectly right about that. But there are some things, Rosamund, that are true, and that one must nevertheless never say. You are too young to understand it now, but you will understand it when you are older. The things that are said in one's own house belong to one's own house. They are not to be carried outside it, any more than you would carry the silver out of the dining-room and give it away to people in the street."

"Like Mrs. Corlear counting the spoons," said Rosamund.

Mrs. Lisle drew in her breath. For a moment she suspected impertinence; but the child's face was perfectly grave, and she saw that the remark had been offered in the purest spirit of inquiry, as one offers a sum to be checked.

"That," she said, "was a foolish thing for me to have said, and I was wrong to have said it where you could hear. But it does not make it any less wrong of you to have repeated it. Grown-up people sometimes say foolish things to one another, in private, which they do not mean in the least. It is a kind of—" she searched for a word, and found none that satisfied her, "a kind of game. And it is very unkind, and very ill-bred, to take what is said in a game and make it into something serious. You have hurt Mrs. Corlear's feelings very much. You have made her think that Mamma does not like her, which is not at all the case."

She heard herself say this with a sort of detached astonishment, as one hears a stranger speak in a railway carriage. Rosamund looked at her with eyes that were very wide and very clear.

"Then it wasn't true?" she said.

Mrs. Lisle had a sudden vision of the long perspective of her daughter's life stretching away before her, a life in which this conversation would be the first of a thousand like it; in which the child would learn, by slow and patient degrees, that there were truths that were told and truths that were kept, and that the whole art of living consisted in knowing which was which; in which she would come at last, as her mother had come, to sit in a sage-green drawing-room pouring tea for women she disliked, and saying of them afterward, to the one person she could trust not to repeat it, the sharp and pleasurable things that relieved the tedium of the pouring. She saw it all, in that instant, with the clarity of a lantern-slide; and she saw also that there was nothing else she could possibly teach her, since there was nothing else she herself had ever learned.

"It was not true in the way you meant it," she said. "And that is the same as not being true at all."

Rosamund considered this for a long moment. Mrs. Lisle watched the small face, and saw upon it the dawning of a comprehension which was not quite the one she had intended to convey, but which she knew, with a sinking of the heart she did not examine, to be the one that would serve.

"Then I must say I'm sorry," the child said at last.

"You will write Mrs. Corlear a little letter tomorrow, and Miss Prentice will help you. You will say that you are very sorry for having been rude, and that you did not mean what you said."

"But I did mean it, Mamma. I only didn't know I wasn't to say it."

"You will say," said Mrs. Lisle, with the first and only edge that had entered her voice, "that you did not mean it."

Rosamund looked down at her clasped hands.

"Yes, Mamma," she said.

Mrs. Lisle bent forward and kissed her on the forehead, the high Lisle forehead that was cool and faintly scented with the orris-root powder the nurse used after her bath; and the child received the kiss as she had received old Mrs. Corlear's, without resistance and without response. Then she curtsied, as she had been taught to curtsy on leaving a room in which her elders sat, and went back across the Aubusson carpet toward the door.

At the threshold she paused, and turned.

"Mamma," she said, "when I am in the nursery, and you are down here with Papa, do you play the game about me?"

Mrs. Lisle opened her lips to answer, and found, for the second time that afternoon, that she had nothing ready to say. The nurse, who had been waiting in the hall, appeared silently in the doorway and put a hand on the child's shoulder; and Rosamund, without waiting for the reply which she seemed, with a precocious wisdom, not to have expected, allowed herself to be led away.

Mrs. Lisle sat on in the lamplight. Presently she heard her husband's latchkey in the front door, and the murmur of the butler's voice, and the heavy, comfortable tread of a man returning from his club to a house in which he has never had occasion to be anything but at ease. In a moment he would come in and ask her what kind of day she had had; and she would tell him, of course, about Mrs. Corlear, because it was the kind of thing one told one's husband, and he would laugh and say that the old harridan had had it coming to her for years. And afterward, when they had dressed and gone down to dinner, she would find herself describing the scene to him again, with a lightness and a dexterity of phrase that would make him laugh still more; and she would not, she was quite certain, say anything at all about the question with which the child had left her.

She rose, and went to the mirror over the mantel, and put up a hand to settle a hairpin that had not moved. The bronze nymphs on either side of the glass regarded her with their blank, voluptuous, unwavering eyes; and it seemed to her, as she turned away to meet her husband at the door, that they had understood the matter a good deal better than she had.

Here is an excerpt of Edith Wharton's writing, to show you their style:

There had never been such a June in Eagle County. Usually it was a month of moods, with abrupt alternations of belated frost and mid-summer heat; this year, day followed day in a sequence of temperate beauty. Every morning a breeze blew steadily from the hills. Toward noon it built up great canopies of white cloud that threw a cool shadow over fields and woods; then before sunset the clouds dissolved again, and the western light rained its unobstructed brightness on the valley. On such an afternoon Charity Royall lay on a ridge above a sunlit hollow, her face pressed to the earth and the warm currents of the grass running through her. Directly in her line of vision a blackberry branch laid its frail white flowers and blue-green leaves against the sky. Just beyond, a tuft of sweet-fern uncurled between the beaded shoots of the grass, and a small yellow butterfly vibrated over them like a fleck of sunshine. This was all she saw; but she felt, above her and about her, the strong growth of the beeches clothing the ridge, the rounding of pale green cones on countless spruce-branches, the push of myriads of sweet-fern fronds in the cracks of the stony slope below the wood, and the crowding shoots of meadowsweet and yellow flags in the pasture beyond. All this bubbling of sap and slipping of sheaths and bursting of calyxes was carried to her on mingled currents of fragrance. Every leaf and bud and blade seemed to contribute its exhalation to the pervading sweetness in which the pungency of pine-sap prevailed over the spice of thyme and the subtle perfume of fern, and all were merged in a moist earth-smell that was like the breath of some huge sun-warmed animal. Charity had lain there a long time, passive and sun-warmed as the slope on which she lay, when there came between her eyes and the dancing butterfly the sight of a man's foot in a large worn boot covered with red mud.

“Oh, don't!” she exclaimed, raising herself on her elbow and stretching out a warning hand.

“Don't what?” a hoarse voice asked above her head.

“Don't stamp on those bramble flowers, you dolt!” she retorted, springing to her knees. The foot paused and then descended clumsily on the frail branch, and raising her eyes she saw above her the bewildered face of a slouching man with a thin sunburnt beard, and white arms showing through his ragged shirt.

“Don't you ever SEE anything, Liff Hyatt?” she assailed him, as he stood before her with the look of a man who has stirred up a wasp's nest. He grinned. “I seen you! That's what I come down for.”

“Down from where?” she questioned, stooping to gather up the petals his foot had scattered. He jerked his thumb toward the heights. “Been cutting down trees for Dan Targatt.” Charity sank back on her heels and looked at him musingly. She was not in the least afraid of poor Liff Hyatt, though he “came from the Mountain,” and some of the girls ran when they saw him. Among the more reasonable he passed for a harmless creature, a sort of link between the mountain and civilized folk, who occasionally came down and did a little wood cutting for a farmer when hands were short. Besides, she knew the Mountain people would never hurt her: Liff himself had told her so once when she was a little girl, and had met him one day at the edge of lawyer Royall's pasture. “They won't any of 'em touch you up there, f'ever you was to come up.... But I don't s'pose you will,” he had added philosophically, looking at her new shoes, and at the red ribbon that Mrs. Royall had tied in her hair. Charity had, in truth, never felt any desire to visit her birthplace. She did not care to have it known that she was of the Mountain, and was shy of being seen in talk with Liff Hyatt. But today she was not sorry to have him appear. A great many things had happened to her since the day when young Lucius Harney had entered the doors of the Hatchard Memorial, but none, perhaps, so unforeseen as the fact of her suddenly finding it a convenience to be on good terms with Liff Hyatt. She continued to look up curiously at his freckled weather-beaten face, with feverish hollows below the cheekbones and the pale yellow eyes of a harmless animal. “I wonder if he's related to me?” she thought, with a shiver of disdain.

“Is there any folks living in the brown house by the swamp, up under Porcupine?” she presently asked in an indifferent tone. Liff Hyatt, for a while, considered her with surprise; then he scratched his head and shifted his weight from one tattered sole to the other.

“There's always the same folks in the brown house,” he said with his vague grin.

“They're from up your way, ain't they?”

“Their name's the same as mine,” he rejoined uncertainly. Charity still held him with resolute eyes. “See here, I want to go there some day and take a gentleman with me that's boarding with us. He's up in these parts drawing pictures.” She did not offer to explain this statement. It was too far beyond Liff Hyatt's limitations for the attempt to be worth making. “He wants to see the brown house, and go all over it,” she pursued. Liff was still running his fingers perplexedly through his shock of straw-colored hair. “Is it a fellow from the city?” he asked.

“Yes. He draws pictures of things. He's down there now drawing the Bonner house.” She pointed to a chimney just visible over the dip of the pasture below the wood.

“The Bonner house?” Liff echoed incredulously.

“Yes. You won't understand—and it don't matter. All I say is: he's going to the Hyatts' in a day or two.” Liff looked more and more perplexed. “Bash is ugly sometimes in the afternoons.” She threw her head back, her eyes full on Hyatt's. “I'm coming too: you tell him.”

“They won't none of them trouble you, the Hyatts won't. What d'you want a take a stranger with you though?”

“I've told you, haven't I? You've got to tell Bash Hyatt.” He looked away at the blue mountains on the horizon; then his gaze dropped to the chimney-top below the pasture.

“He's down there now?”

“Yes.” He shifted his weight again, crossed his arms, and continued to survey the distant landscape. “Well, so long,” he said at last, inconclusively; and turning away he shambled up the hillside. From the ledge above her, he paused to call down: “I wouldn't go there a Sunday”; then he clambered on till the trees closed in on him. Presently, from high overhead, Charity heard the ring of his axe. She lay on the warm ridge, thinking of many things that the woodsman's appearance had stirred up in her. She knew nothing of her early life, and had never felt any curiosity about it: only a sullen reluctance to explore the corner of her memory where certain blurred images lingered. But all that had happened to her within the last few weeks had stirred her to the sleeping depths. She had become absorbingly interesting to herself, and everything that had to do with her past was illuminated by this sudden curiosity. She hated more than ever the fact of coming from the Mountain; but it was no longer indifferent to her. Everything that in any way affected her was alive and vivid: even the hateful things had grown interesting because they were a part of herself.

“I wonder if Liff Hyatt knows who my mother was?” she mused; and it filled her with a tremor of surprise to think that some woman who was once young and slight, with quick motions of the blood like hers, had carried her in her breast, and watched her sleeping. She had always thought of her mother as so long dead as to be no more than a nameless pinch of earth; but now it occurred to her that the once-young woman might be alive, and wrinkled and elf-locked like the woman she had sometimes seen in the door of the brown house that Lucius Harney wanted to draw. The thought brought him back to the central point in her mind, and she strayed away from the conjectures roused by Liff Hyatt's presence. Speculations concerning the past could not hold her long when the present was so rich, the future so rosy, and when Lucius Harney, a stone's throw away, was bending over his sketch-book, frowning, calculating, measuring, and then throwing his head back with the sudden smile that had shed its brightness over everything. She scrambled to her feet, but as she did so she saw him coming up the pasture and dropped down on the grass to wait. When he was drawing and measuring one of “his houses,” as she called them, she often strayed away by herself into the woods or up the hillside. It was partly from shyness that she did so: from a sense of inadequacy that came to her most painfully when her companion, absorbed in his job, forgot her ignorance and her inability to follow his least allusion, and plunged into a monologue on art and life. To avoid the awkwardness of listening with a blank face, and also to escape the surprised stare of the inhabitants of the houses before which he would abruptly pull up their horse and open his sketch-book, she slipped away to some spot from which, without being seen, she could watch him at work, or at least look down on the house he was drawing. She had not been displeased, at first, to have it known to North Dormer and the neighborhood that she was driving Miss Hatchard's cousin about the country in the buggy he had hired of lawyer Royall. She had always kept to herself, contemptuously aloof from village love-making, without exactly knowing whether her fierce pride was due to the sense of her tainted origin, or whether she was reserving herself for a more brilliant fate. Sometimes she envied the other girls their sentimental preoccupations, their long hours of inarticulate philandering with one of the few youths who still lingered in the village; but when she pictured herself curling her hair or putting a new ribbon on her hat for Ben Fry or one of the Sollas boys the fever dropped and she relapsed into indifference. Now she knew the meaning of her disdains and reluctances. The rain, which had held off all through the Mortlakes' dinner, began again as the carriage turned into Fifth Avenue, and Kate Durand, leaning back in her corner, watched it streak the glass with long oblique threads that the street-lamps caught and lost again. Her husband sat beside her in the silence he generally kept after an evening out: a silence she had once taken for fatigue, later for indifference, and had lately learned to regard as a kind of tacit accounting, a summing-up of the hours just passed, in which she suspected that her own part was entered on the smaller side of the ledger. She had always admired his capacity for silence. It had seemed to her, in the first years of their marriage, the sign of a mind too well-furnished to need the noise of talk. She knew now that it was merely the sign of a mind that did not care to be overheard.

She had resolved, somewhere between the fish and the entrée, that she would speak to him that night; and the resolution had sustained her through the rest of the dinner, through the long half-hour in Mrs. Mortlake's drawing-room, where the ladies sat in a lustrous semicircle and discussed the new rector's wife, and even through the moment, ten minutes later, when the gentlemen came in and Philip, with his usual unhurried grace, crossed the room to the sofa where Mrs. Verrall sat alone. Kate had watched him go with the detached interest she might have given to a well-rehearsed scene in a play whose ending she already knew. It was not the crossing of the room that mattered; any man might cross a room to speak to a pretty woman sitting alone. It was the fact that Mrs. Verrall, as he approached, had not looked up.

The carriage drew up before their door, and Philip handed her out under the dripping awning with the same attentive courtesy he had shown her for eleven years. She had once thought that courtesy the finest thing about him; she still thought it very fine, as one admires the carving on a door one has ceased to expect will open.

In the hall the servants had left a lamp burning, and the fire in the small sitting-room behind the library had been made up for their return. It was the room Kate liked best in the house, partly because it was the smallest, and partly because it was the only one her mother-in-law had not furnished. Philip followed her in, as he usually did, to glance at the evening paper before going up; and she saw him take it from the table and unfold it, standing with his back to the fire, while she drew off her gloves slowly, finger by finger, as if the operation required all her attention.

"Mrs. Verrall looked extremely well tonight," she said.

He did not lower the paper at once. When he did, it was with a slight lift of the eyebrows that conveyed nothing more than a polite readiness to be interested in whatever she might choose to say.

"Did she? I don't know that I noticed particularly. The Mortlakes' lamps are so abominably shaded that one can never see anybody's face."

"Oh, one could see her face," Kate said. "And her wrists."

She laid the gloves on the table, side by side, and smoothed them with her hand. She had not meant to say it so soon; she had planned a longer approach, a series of small ascending steps, each one of which he might mount without perceiving that he was climbing. But the words had come of themselves, and having come, they hung in the warm air of the room with a kind of insolent distinctness, like a picture suddenly unveiled in a gallery where everyone had been talking of something else.

Philip folded the paper and laid it down. He did this deliberately, creasing it along its original folds, and Kate, watching his long fingers, reflected that she had never in her life seen him do anything in a hurry. Even his courtship had been conducted with a leisurely assurance that her family had taken for the confidence of an honourable man, and that she herself, at nineteen, had found more thrilling than any ardour.

"Her wrists?" he repeated pleasantly.

"She was wearing a very handsome bracelet. Sapphires, set very close, in a kind of chain. I noticed it because I had seen one like it before."

"Had you? Where?"

"In a description," said Kate. "On a bill from Ditmar's. It came here, in October, by mistake. Bassett put it with my letters instead of yours, and I opened it before I saw the name."

She had wondered, many times in the last six weeks, what his face would do when she told him; and now that she was watching it she was conscious of a faint, unreasonable disappointment, as if she had been promised a spectacle and cheated of it. His face did nothing at all. It remained the face she had always known: a little too long, a little too pale, with the fine dry lines about the eyes that the world called distinguished and that she had once traced with her finger in the dark. Only, after a moment, he turned and pushed a log farther back on the andirons with the toe of his shoe, so that she could no longer see his eyes.

"I'm sorry it should have come to you," he said. "That was careless of Ditmar's."

"It was careless of somebody."

He straightened himself and looked at her again; and now she perceived that something had altered after all, though it was not what she had expected. It was not guilt, nor anger, nor even embarrassment; it was a kind of watchful attention, the look of a man who has been playing a game he thought he understood and finds his opponent has introduced a new rule.

"I suppose," he said, "you have been keeping this for some time."

"Since the eleventh of October."

"That is a long while to keep anything."

"I have had a good deal of practice," said Kate.

It had been a wedding present from one of Philip's aunts, and Kate had always disliked it; it seemed to her now to be commenting on the scene with a kind of tinkling irony, as though the shepherdess had witnessed a great many such conversations and found them all rather tiresome.

She had a sudden sharp desire to laugh. "No. That's what puzzles me." He looked at her with what seemed genuine curiosity. "You might have spoken six weeks ago. You might have made a scene. Most women would. "That's all."

"What would be the use?" said Kate. "You would promise very gracefully, and I should have to believe you, and we should both know that I didn't. I'd rather not have the promise. It would only be one more thing in the house that neither of us looked at."

He got up and walked to the window, where the curtains were drawn against the rain, and stood there with his back to her, his hands in his pockets. She could hear the water running in the gutters of the street outside, and the far-off clatter of a cab going toward the Park.

"You realize," he said without turning, "that people will talk. A woman doesn't go off to Europe for a whole winter, alone with a child, in the middle of the season, without people asking why."

"People will say that Nora's chest is delicate, and that Dr. Ransome advised a change. Dr. Ransome did say something of the kind last spring; I have only to remind him of it. And people will say that it's very sad for you to be left alone, and that you bear it beautifully." She paused. "You will bear it beautifully, Philip. You always do."

He swung round at that, and for an instant she saw in his face a flash of something like anger: not the cold, contained displeasure she had known him to show to tradesmen and incompetent servants, but a quicker, warmer, more human emotion, as if her words had touched him in some place he had believed to be safely covered. It was gone almost as soon as she had seen it, and he came back to the fire and stood looking down at her with his usual composure.

"You've thought it all out very carefully," he said.

"I've had six weeks."

"And the expense? You know how things have been this year. The Southern Pacific business hit us harder than I let you know. A winter in Paris, with a governess and a maid, and the apartment, and the clothes you'll be expected to buy..." He spread his hands in a gesture of reasonable regret. "I don't say it's impossible. But it's a great deal of money, Kate."

"I know exactly how much money it is," she said. "I have worked it out. It comes, as nearly as I can reckon, to a little less than the bill from Ditmar's."

Kate did not look at her husband. She looked at the photograph of her daughter, and thought, with a curious remoteness, of the day it had been taken, and of how Nora had cried afterward because the photographer had made her take off her coral beads.

When Philip spoke at last his voice had changed. It was lower, and had lost its edge of easy irony; and she understood that, for the first time in their life together, he was speaking to her without calculating the effect of his words.

"You're very hard, Kate."

"Am I?" She lifted her eyes to his. "I don't think I am. I think I've only stopped being soft. It isn't quite the same thing, though I daresay it looks the same from where you're standing."

"I never meant to hurt you."

"No," she agreed. "You never meant anything about me at all. That was what I minded, when I first understood it, more than the bracelet, more than her. I used to lie awake and think that if you had hated me, or been tired of me, or even been cruel to me, I should at least have been somebody you thought about. But I wasn't. I was simply the person who ordered the dinners and opened the wrong letters." She gave a little laugh that did not sound like her own. "I don't mean to reproach you. I daresay it's what most marriages come to. Only I found I didn't care to spend the winter watching it."

He was silent again; and she saw that he was looking at her as he might have looked at a stranger whom he had passed every day in the street and suddenly heard speak in a foreign language. It occurred to her, with a pang that was half triumph and half something sadder, that she had at last succeeded in making him think about her, and that it had taken a sapphire bracelet to do it.

"And when you come back?" he asked. "In the spring?"

"In the spring," said Kate, "we shall see. Perhaps I shall find that I've been foolish, and that it doesn't matter after all. Women get used to things; I've seen a great many of them do it, and they seem quite comfortable. Or perhaps I shall find that I like Rome." She rose and gathered up her gloves. "In any case, Nora will have had a winter abroad, and Dr. Ransome will be quite satisfied with her chest."

He did not move to stop her. He stood by the mantelpiece, one hand resting near the gilt clock, and she noticed, as she passed him, that the fine dry lines about his eyes had deepened, so that he looked for a moment older than his years, and oddly tired. She felt a sudden impulse, absurd and unbidden, to put her hand on his sleeve, as she would have done once without thinking; and the impulse frightened her more than anything that had happened that evening, so that she walked quickly to the door before it could overtake her.

"Kate."

She turned on the threshold. He had not moved from the fire.

"You'll want the letter of credit by the first, I suppose."

He would manage very well. "The fifteenth will do," she said, "if it's more convenient."

"Oh, the first," he answered. "I shouldn't like you to be put to any inconvenience."

She put her hand on the banister and began to climb; and from the sitting-room behind her, faint and clear, the shepherdess struck the hour.
