Mrs. Lucius Thorley had always held that the management of children, like the management of servants, was chiefly a matter of so arranging things that one need never be called upon to manage them at all. A well-ordered household, in her view, ran upon the invisible rails of habit, and it was only when some careless hand displaced a switch that the mistress was obliged to descend and look into the machinery. The nursery on the third floor of the house in East Thirty-eighth Street had been organized on this principle from the day of her daughter's birth. A succession of nurses, and latterly an English governess of irreproachable antecedents, had stood between Mrs. Thorley and the more fatiguing aspects of maternity. She herself saw Amabel at stated hours: for a kiss after breakfast, when the child was brought down in a fresh pinafore to the dining-room door; and again at five, when, sashed and brushed, she was permitted to sit on a footstool in the drawing-room and be looked at by such of her mother's visitors as cared for that kind of thing. The arrangement had seemed to Mrs. Thorley eminently satisfactory, since it gave her all the credit of a devoted parent and spared her nearly all of its inconveniences. It was therefore with a sense of real grievance that she found herself, on a raw Tuesday morning in early December, obliged to look into the machinery.

The occasion was a note. It had come up on her breakfast-tray, propped against the coffee-pot, and its heavy cream-laid envelope, with the small engraved crest that Mrs. Ogden Pell had lately and somewhat inexplicably acquired, had at first given her a pleasurable flutter, for the Pells were not people who wrote notes to everybody. She read it once, and then, after an interval during which her coffee grew cold, she read it again. The first reading had acquainted her with the facts; the second made her aware of the tone, and it was the tone that brought the colour slowly to her cheek. Mrs. Pell was sure that dear Mrs. Thorley would wish to know; Mrs. Pell would not for the world have attached the least importance to the chatter of children, but little Cornelia had been so distressed; Mrs. Pell was persuaded that there was some foolish misunderstanding, which a word from Mrs. Thorley would doubtless set right. It was, in short, one of those communications which, by their scrupulous avoidance of reproach, contrive to be more reproachful than any open charge; and Mrs. Thorley, who had herself composed several such letters in her time, was able to appreciate its workmanship even while she smarted under it.

What Amabel had said to Cornelia Pell, at Cornelia's birthday party on the previous Saturday, the note did not precisely state. Mrs. Pell had a delicacy in such matters which forbade her to repeat the words; but she conveyed, by a sort of genteel pantomime of the pen, that they had concerned the reasons for which the Thorleys accepted the Pells' invitations, and that these reasons had not been flattering. Mrs. Thorley laid the letter face downward on the tray, as if it might otherwise continue to speak, and sat for some moments looking at the frosted window, beyond which a cart of coal was being discharged with dismal clatter into the area of the house opposite.

She had cultivated the Pells for two winters. It had not been agreeable work. Mrs. Pell was a large, slow, anxiously amiable woman whose conversation consisted chiefly of the prices she had paid for things, and whose drawing-room, with its frescoed ceiling and its gilt-legged furniture tied up in satin bows, seemed to have been designed for the express purpose of making visitors feel underdressed. But Mr. Ogden Pell sat on the board of the Mid-Continental, and Lucius Thorley's affairs had lately become entangled with that railway in a manner which his wife did not pretend to understand, but which she knew to depend in some obscure fashion upon the Pells' goodwill. She had accepted the Pells, therefore, as one accepts a draughty pew in a fashionable church: as the price, not too exorbitant, of a desirable situation. And she had been careful, as she believed, never to let fall in public a word that could betray the transaction. In private, to Lucius, she had perhaps been less guarded; but surely, she reflected, a woman might be allowed to say what she pleased to her own husband, in her own house, on her own staircase.

It was at this point in her reflections that a disagreeable recollection presented itself. She remembered a night, some three weeks earlier, when she and Lucius had been going out to the Opera, and she had paused on the half-landing to settle her cloak, and had said something—she could not now recall the exact words, but she knew their drift—about Mrs. Pell's Thursday teas being the dearest box at any theatre in New York. And she remembered, too, though she had given it no thought at the time, a faint stir above her, at the turn of the nursery stair, and a glimpse of something white that had vanished before she looked up.

She rang the bell and sent word to Miss Crane that she wished to see Amabel in her sitting-room at eleven.

The interval she employed in dressing, a process which in Mrs. Thorley's case had always the soothing effect that religious observances are said to have upon more devout natures. By the time her maid had fastened the last hook of a grey cashmere morning-gown, and she had chosen, after some deliberation, the plain gold brooch rather than the cameo, she had recovered a measure of composure, and had even begun to see the affair in a more reasonable light. Children repeated things; it was one of their recognized defects, like whooping-cough, and no sensible person held their parents to account for it. She would explain to Amabel that it was naughty to repeat what she had overheard; she would require the child to apologize to Cornelia; and she would write Mrs. Pell a note so charming, so lightly rueful, so full of the humorous helplessness of mothers, that the incident would be turned to positive advantage. It was even possible, she thought, that the Pells would feel themselves rather flattered by so much attention.

Punctually at eleven there was a knock at the sitting-room door, and Miss Crane appeared, propelling before her a small figure in a dark-blue merino frock.

Amabel Thorley was at this time seven years old, and was generally considered by her mother's friends to be "not exactly pretty, but so distinguished-looking," a formula which in their circle was reserved for little girls who promised to be plain. She was small for her age, with a narrow pale face, a stiff fair plait that Miss Crane drew back each morning with a severity suggestive of moral discipline, and a pair of grey eyes so steady and so unsmiling in their gaze that strangers sometimes found them disconcerting. They were her father's eyes; and Mrs. Thorley, who had once found that level look in Lucius rather romantic, had since come to regard it, in her daughter, as something very like a reproach.

"You may leave her with me, Miss Crane," she said; and the governess, who had evidently been told nothing and suspected everything, withdrew with the air of a person who washes her hands of a responsibility she has never been permitted to exercise.

Amabel remained standing just inside the door, her hands folded before her as she had been taught. Her mother, from the sofa by the fire, regarded her for a moment in silence, partly because she felt that silence was impressive, and partly because she had suddenly forgotten how she had meant to begin.

"Come here, Amabel," she said at length. "Do you know why I have sent for you?"

The child advanced to the edge of the hearth-rug and considered the question with visible care.

"Is it about the ink, Mamma?"

Mrs. Thorley, who had been prepared for a number of answers, was not prepared for this one.

"The ink? What ink?"

"The ink on the schoolroom table-cloth. I didn't mean it to go over. I was making a map of Asia, and the bottle was standing on Siberia, and when I moved it—" She paused, and added with scrupulous exactness: "Miss Crane said she would have to tell you."

"Miss Crane has told me nothing whatever about any ink," said Mrs. Thorley, with the irritation of a general whose plan of battle has been disordered by an irrelevant skirmish. "That is not what I wish to speak to you about. I wish to know what you said to Cornelia Pell on Saturday afternoon."

A faint change passed over the child's face—not alarm, her mother noted, but a kind of grave attentiveness, as of one who recognizes that the conversation has turned to matters of consequence.

"On Saturday? At the party?"

"At the party. Mrs. Pell has written to me. She says that you were very unkind to Cornelia, and that Cornelia cried."

"She did cry," Amabel agreed. "But it was after the ices, and she had had three. Miss Crane says that too many ices make people cry."

"Amabel, I will not have you evade me. What did you say to her?"

The grey eyes rested on her mother's face with a candour that was almost judicial.

"Cornelia said that her mamma said we were very lucky to be asked to her party, because we weren't anybody in particular. And I said that wasn't the reason. I said we only came because Papa needed Mr. Pell for his railway, and that you said Mrs. Pell's teas were the most expensive box in New York, but that one had to pay for one's seat." She delivered this information in a level, careful voice, as though she were repeating the dates of the English kings; and then, with the air of one adding a needful footnote, she said: "I didn't say it loud. Only Cornelia heard."

Mrs. Thorley felt the colour mount from her throat to her temples. It was one thing to suspect the source of one's humiliation, and quite another to hear one's own epigram returned to one in a child's treble, stripped of the inflexion that had made it witty and left with nothing but its meaning. She was aware, moreover, that the phrase had been one of her happier inventions, and that in the mouth of Mrs. Pell's daughter it would inevitably have travelled, before nightfall, to Mrs. Pell.

"Where did you hear me say such a thing?" she asked, though she knew.

"On the stairs. The night you went to the Opera in your garnets and the cloak with the swansdown. I had come out to see you go, because Miss Crane was at her supper." Amabel paused, and then volunteered, with the same terrible impartiality: "You looked very beautiful, Mamma."

For a moment Mrs. Thorley did not trust herself to speak. She had come to the interview armed against tears, against sulks, against the small transparent falsehoods of which the infant mind is so prolific; and she found herself confronted instead with an accuracy that left her nothing to correct. She took refuge, as persons of her temperament commonly do, in the larger principle.

"It was very wrong of you to listen to what was not meant for you," she said, "and it was still more wrong to repeat it. You have hurt Cornelia's feelings, and you have made her mamma very unhappy. I am extremely displeased."

Amabel received this sentence in silence. Then she asked, not defiantly, but with the genuine perplexity of one who has been set a sum that will not come out:

"But wasn't it true, Mamma?"

It was the question Mrs. Thorley had least anticipated, and she perceived at once that it was the only one that mattered. She had a confused sense, as she looked at the small upright figure on the hearth-rug, that she was being examined; that the steady grey eyes were weighing her, as they might have weighed a doubtful passage in the catechism; and the sensation was so novel, and so unpleasant, that it took her some moments to collect herself.

"It is not a question of whether it is true," she said at last.

"But Miss Crane says we must always tell the truth. She says God sees when we don't."

"Miss Crane is perfectly right. You must never tell a lie." Mrs. Thorley hesitated, conscious that she was advancing upon ground where the footing was uncertain. "But there are a great many things that are true, Amabel, and that are not said. Nice people don't say them."

The child pondered this.

"Then how does one know which things?"

"One knows," said Mrs. Thorley.

She was aware, even as she spoke, that the answer was inadequate; yet she could not, on reflection, have offered a better. For how had she herself come to know? She tried to remember, and could recall no single lesson, no definite rule laid down; only a long, gradual, imperceptible process, like the slow absorption of moisture by a sponge, through which she had learned, in her mother's drawing-room in Waverly Place, which aunts might be laughed at and which must be deferred to, which friends one visited because one liked them and which because one could not afford not to, and above all, that the second kind must never be suffered to suspect that they were not the first. No one had ever told her these things; she had simply found them, one day, established in her mind, as one finds one's own handwriting formed without remembering the copy-books. And it struck her now, with a faint chill of dismay, that she could not hand them on in any other way; that knowledge of this kind was not to be imparted, but only caught, like an accent; and that her daughter, by some perversity of nature or some failure of the household machinery, had somehow escaped the infection.

"You will understand better when you are older," she said, falling back upon that formula which parents have always found so useful for postponing the questions they cannot answer. "In the meanwhile, you will do as you are told. You will write a letter to Cornelia telling her that you are sorry, and you will give it to her yourself when you go to the dancing-class on Thursday."

"Yes, Mamma." Amabel paused. "Shall I not go to the Pells' any more?"

The question touched a nerve that Mrs. Thorley had not known to be exposed. It had been in her mind, as the natural complement of the reprimand, to forbid the child some pleasure; and the Pells' Christmas party, with its celebrated conjuror and its tree lit by electric bulbs, would have been the obvious sacrifice. But she saw instantly that to withdraw Amabel from that festivity would be to confirm, in the most public manner, the very construction she was anxious to dispel; and she perceived, with a sort of bitter amusement, that she was no more free to punish her daughter by keeping her from the Pells than she was free to please herself by keeping away from them.

"Certainly you will go to the Pells'," she said. "You will go, and you will be particularly nice to Cornelia. That is part of your punishment." And, as the child's eyebrows rose a little at this novel definition of penance, she added hastily: "And you will not drive with Papa in the Park on Sunday."

This, at least, produced its effect. The narrow face quivered for an instant, and the grey eyes filled; but Amabel had been brought up by Miss Crane, who held that tears were a form of self-indulgence, and she blinked them back with a resolution her mother could not help admiring.

"Very well," said Mrs. Thorley, more gently. "Sit down at my desk, and you shall write your letter now, and I will see that it is properly done."

The child climbed into the chair before the little rosewood secretary, and Mrs. Thorley, leaning over her shoulder, selected a sheet of the smallest note-paper and dipped the pen herself, as a precaution against further catastrophes in the geography of the table-cloth. Amabel's tongue appeared at the corner of her mouth, and she began to write, in the large uncertain characters of the schoolroom:

*Dear Cornelia, I am sorry I said what I said at your party. It was not nice.*

She looked up for approval. Mrs. Thorley read the lines, and was conscious of an obscure dissatisfaction. They were correct; they were even, in their way, touching; but they did not undo anything. They acknowledged that something had been said, and left Mrs. Pell at liberty to go on believing it. She considered for a moment, and then, laying a finger on the paper, she said in a low voice:

"Put, 'It was not true.'"

The pen stopped. Amabel turned her head slowly and looked up at her mother; and in that look Mrs. Thorley read, with a distinctness that startled her, the whole course of the child's reasoning: the staircase, the garnets, the swansdown cloak, the sentence spoken in that beautiful voice and now to be unspoken by the same. It was the look, she thought afterward, of someone watching a door close that she had not known was open.

"But, Mamma, you said—"

"Write it, Amabel."

There was a pause, during which the coal-cart in the street below gave a final clatter and rumbled off toward Lexington Avenue. Then the child bent her head and wrote, very slowly, forming each letter with an elaborate care that seemed to her mother a kind of protest:

*It was not true. Your loving friend, Amabel Thorley.*

Mrs. Thorley blotted the sheet, folded it, and slipped it into an envelope, which she addressed herself in her own fine slanting hand. The thing was done, and done, she told herself, exactly as it ought to have been; Mrs. Pell would be appeased, Lucius's railway would run on undisturbed, and Amabel would have learned the lesson that every well-bred girl must learn sooner or later, and that it was perhaps kinder to teach early than late. Yet she did not feel the satisfaction she had promised herself, and she was annoyed with herself for not feeling it.

"You may go now," she said. "And Amabel—you need not tell Miss Crane what we have been talking about."

In the town of Ridgely, Ohio, there lived a man named Ed Hanby who worked at the feed mill down by the tracks. He was a large, slow man with sloping shoulders and a habit of rubbing the backs of his hands against his trousers when he was spoken to, as though he had just come from handling something dusty and was ashamed of it. In the mill he lifted sacks all day long, and the white dust of the meal got into the hair of his arms and into the creases of his neck, so that when he walked home in the evening along Buckeye Street the children who played in the yards called him the flour man. He did not mind. He had been called worse things when he was a boy on his father's farm out on the Trunion Pike.

Ed Hanby had been married for eleven years to a woman named Nell, who had been Nell Stoner before she married him. Her father had kept a little store at the crossroads called Stoner's Corners, and she had grown up there, waiting on farmers who came in for tobacco and plug and kerosene for their lamps. She was a thin woman with brown hair that she wore pulled back hard from her forehead, and there was something about her mouth, a kind of tightness at the corners, that made people in town say she was proud. She was not proud. It was only that she had a way of holding herself in, as one holds a cup of water that is too full and walks carefully across a room with it.

They had no children. There had been one, a boy, who lived for four days in the first winter of their marriage and then died. Neither of them ever spoke of it. Ed had made a little box for the child out of pine boards in the shed behind the house, working at night by a lantern, and when it was done he had sat for a long time looking at it with his big hands hanging down between his knees. Afterward he had gone back to the mill and lifted sacks. Nell had cleaned the house. That was the way it was with them.

I want to tell you about one evening in their lives. It was in August, a hot evening, and nothing in particular happened on it. A great many evenings in the lives of people are like that, and it is a mistake to think that because nothing happens nothing has happened.

For some weeks, perhaps for two months, Nell Hanby had been going out of the house after supper. She would wash the dishes and set them in the rack and hang the dish towel on the nail by the stove, and then she would put on her hat, the brown straw one with the faded ribbon, and go out of the house without saying anything. Ed would be sitting on the back step smoking his pipe. He would hear the front door close. He did not get up. He sat smoking and looking at the garden, at the bean poles and the tomato vines tied up with strips of old cloth, and after a while it would get dark and the lightning bugs would come out over the grass, and he would knock the ashes out of his pipe against the step and go in to bed.

He did not know where she went. In a town like Ridgely a man can find out such a thing without trying very hard, and so in the end he did find out. Will Overton, who was the night operator at the depot, told him. Will did not mean any harm by it. He mentioned it the way men mention things at the mill, standing about in the doorway at noon with their dinner pails.

"Your wife sure likes to see the trains," Will Overton said. "She's down there every night for the eight-forty. Sits on the bench at the end of the platform. Don't get on and don't meet nobody. Just sits."

Ed said nothing. He rubbed the backs of his hands on his trousers. Then he went back inside the mill and lifted sacks all afternoon, and the white dust settled on him, and he did not think, or rather he thought of nothing he could have put into words. There was only a kind of heaviness in him, as though he had swallowed one of the sacks.

That evening, when the dishes were done and the towel was hung on its nail, Nell went to get her hat from the hook in the hallway. Ed was not on the back step. He was sitting in the kitchen, in the chair by the window, and when she came back through the kitchen with the hat in her hand he spoke to her.

"Where is it you go?" he said.

She stopped. She stood in the middle of the floor with the hat in her hand and looked at him, and he saw that her fingers had closed hard on the brim of the hat, so that the straw cracked a little. The sound was very small. It seemed to Ed afterward that he had never heard anything so plainly in his life.

"I go for a walk," she said.

"You go down to the depot," he said. "Will Overton told me. You go and sit on the bench and watch the eight-forty come in."

For a long time she did not answer. Outside, in the yard of the house next door, the Wilmot boy was calling his dog. "Here, Prince. Here, Prince." The voice went on and on, rising at the end, and the dog did not come.

"Well, what of it?" Nell said at last. "What of it if I do?"

Ed got up out of his chair. He was a big man and the kitchen was small, and when he stood up he seemed to fill the room. He did not know what to do with himself. He went to the stove and put his hand on the reservoir, where the water was still warm from supper, and took it away again.

"I just want to know," he said. "A man has got a right to know a thing like that."

"A right," she said. She laughed, and the laugh was not a good one. It was short and dry, like the sound of a stick breaking. "You've got a right. All right then. I go and watch the train. That's all. That's all there is to it."

"Why?"

She put the hat down on the table. She put it down very carefully, as though it were something that might break, and then she put both her hands flat on the oilcloth on either side of it and leaned on them. Her head was bent so that he could not see her face.

"I don't know why," she said. "How should I know why?"

Now it is a strange thing, but Ed Hanby, standing there by the stove, began to be afraid. He was not a man who was often afraid. He had once pulled a horse out of the millrace when it had gone through the rotten planking of the bridge, and he had gone into the water up to his chest with the horse screaming and lashing out with its hooves, and he had not been afraid then. But now, looking at his wife's bent back and at her two hands flat on the oilcloth, a fear came into him that made his knees weak. It seemed to him that there was something in the room he had never seen before, though it had been there a long time. It was as though he had lived for years in a house and had one day opened a door he had always thought led to a closet and found that it led out into a great field, dark and without end.

"You going to go away?" he said. "Is that it? You going to get on it some night?"

She raised her head and looked at him. Her face was white. There were two spots of color high up on her cheeks.

"I've thought of it," she said.

He took a step toward her and stopped. His hands came up from his sides and hung in the air in front of him. They were large hands, the knuckles swollen from lifting, and there was meal dust still in the cracks of the skin. He looked at them as though they belonged to someone else.

"Where would you go?" he said, and his voice was hoarse. "You don't know nobody. You ain't got no folks except your sister in Bidwell, and she can't hardly feed her own."

"I don't know where I'd go," Nell said. "Cleveland, maybe. Or further. I used to think, when I was a girl at the store, that I'd go to Chicago. A woman came in once, a drummer's wife, and she had on a gray dress with little buttons all down the front, and she'd been to Chicago. She talked about the lake. She said you could stand on the edge of it and not see the other side. She said it was like the ocean."

"That ain't any reason," Ed said.

"No," she said. "It ain't any reason."

They were both quiet then. The Wilmot boy had stopped calling. Somewhere down toward Main Street a buggy was going by, and they could hear the slow sound of the horse's feet on the hard road, clop, clop, and then fainter, and then not at all. The light in the kitchen was going gray. Neither of them got up to light the lamp.

Ed Hanby sat down again in the chair by the window. He sat with his knees wide apart and his hands hanging down between them, as he had sat in the shed eleven years before, looking at the little pine box. He did not think of that. Or if he thought of it, it was not in any way he could have told.

"I've done the best I could," he said. "I've worked steady. There ain't a man at the mill works steadier than me. I've never took a drink, hardly. I've never laid a hand on you."

"I know it," she said.

"Well then."

"I know it, Ed. That ain't it."

"What is it then?" He almost shouted the words, and then he was ashamed and looked at the floor. "What is it?" he said again, more quietly.

Nell came around the table. She did not come to him. She went to the window on the other side of the room, the one that looked out on the side yard where the lilac bush grew against the fence, and stood there with her back to him.

"When I go down there," she said, "and the train comes in, I sit on the bench and I watch the people. There ain't many. Sometimes nobody gets off at all. Sometimes there's a drummer with his sample case, or a woman with a little girl, coming to visit somebody. And the people on the train, I can see them through the windows. They're sitting there with the lamps lit, and some of them are reading, and some are asleep with their heads against the glass. And I look at them and I think, they're going someplace. Every one of them is going someplace. And then the conductor calls out and the train starts up, and it goes off down the track toward Clyde, and I sit there and listen to it until I can't hear it anymore."

She stopped. Ed waited. He did not know what he was waiting for.

"And then I come home," Nell said. "That's all. I come home and you're asleep."

"I ain't asleep," Ed said. "I hear you come in."

She turned around and looked at him. In the gray light he could hardly see her face, but he could see that she was surprised.

"You hear me?"

"Every night," he said. "I lay there and hear you come up the walk and I hear you take off your shoes in the hall so as not to wake me. I hear you."

"You never said anything."

"No," he said. "I never said anything."

It is in moments like this one that people come nearest to one another, and it is also in moments like this one that they are farthest apart. Ed Hanby, sitting in his kitchen with the dark coming on, felt that he was very close to understanding something. It was there, just beyond him, as a word sometimes is when you are trying to remember it and it will not come. He felt that if he could only say the right thing, if he could only open his mouth and let the right words come out, then everything would be different. His wife would come across the room to him. She would put her hand on his shoulder. He would no longer be afraid.

But he could not find the words. He was a man who had never found them. When he was a boy on the farm out on the Trunion Pike his father had used to say to him, "Ed, you got a tongue in your head, ain't you? Use it," and he had stood there, red in the face, unable to say anything at all. It had always been so. Words were things other men had, like money or good luck.

"I think about it too," he said finally. He said it very low, so that she had to lean forward to hear.

"About what?"

"About going someplace. I think about it at the mill sometimes. When the cars come in on the siding to be loaded, I think about where they come from. Some of them come from way out in Kansas. You can see it chalked on the sides. Kansas. Nebraska. I think about them places. Wheat as far as you can see, they say. Further than the lake you was talking about."

Nell was looking at him now. She had come a step away from the window.

"You never told me that," she said.

"No."

"Eleven years, and you never told me."

"I didn't figure it mattered," Ed said. "A man thinks things. It don't mean nothing. It don't change nothing. I still got to load the cars."

Then a queer thing happened. Nell Hanby began to cry. She did not cry loudly. She stood in the middle of the dark kitchen with her arms hanging down at her sides and the tears ran down her face, and she made no sound at all except once, a little catch in her throat like a hiccup. Ed got up out of his chair. He went toward her and then stopped, as he had stopped before. His big hands came up again and hung in the air.

"Don't," he said. "Nell. Don't."

"I ain't going to go," she said. "I never was going to go. I just go down there and sit. I can't help it. Something gets into me after supper, when the dishes are done, and I can't stay in the house. I got to go out. And there ain't anyplace to go in this town except down to the depot."

"I know it," Ed said.

"You don't know it. How can you know it?"

He did not answer. He could not have said how he knew. He only stood there with his hands in the air, and after a while he let them drop.

She wiped her face with the back of her wrist, the way a child does. Then she went over to the table and picked up her hat. The brim was cracked where she had held it, and she stood turning it around in her fingers and looking at the crack.

"I spoilt it," she said.

"I'll get you another one," Ed said. "There's hats at Winney's. I'll get you a new one Saturday."

"I don't want a new one."

He did not know what to say to that. He went to the shelf over the stove and took down the lamp and the box of matches and lit the lamp, and the yellow light came up in the kitchen and showed the oilcloth on the table and the dish rack and the dish towel hanging on its nail, and the two of them standing there not looking at each other. It seemed to Ed Hanby that the light made everything worse. In the dark it had been possible for something to happen. Now it was only their kitchen again, the same as always, and they were only the same two people.

Nell put the hat back on the hook in the hallway. She came back into the kitchen and stood by the stove.

"It's past eight-forty," she said. "It's already gone through."

"I heard it," Ed said, though he had not heard it, and did not know why he said so.

After a while he went out onto the back step and sat down and took out his pipe. He did not light it. He sat holding it in his hand and looking at the garden, at the bean poles and the tomato vines, which in the light coming from the kitchen window looked like people standing very still in a row. The lightning bugs had come out over the grass. Far off, down beyond the mill and the tracks, a dog was barking, perhaps the Wilmot boy's dog, Prince, that would not come home.

In a little while the screen door opened behind him and Nell came out and sat down on the step beside him. She did not touch him. She sat with her elbows on her knees and her chin in her hands, the way she must have sat when she was a girl on the porch of the store at Stoner's Corners, looking down the road toward town and waiting for something to come along it.

They sat there for a long time. Neither of them said anything. Once Ed opened his mouth, and Nell turned her head a little as if to listen, but he closed it again. There was nothing he could say. The thing that he had almost understood in the dark kitchen was gone now, and he could not have told what it was. Perhaps it had only been that his wife was a person and not merely his wife, that she had been a girl once and had wanted to see the lake, and that the wanting had not gone out of her but had only been packed away somewhere, as one packs away a dress that no longer fits. Perhaps it had been something about himself. He did not know. He sat on the step with the cold pipe in his hand and felt the heaviness in his chest, and it was not quite the same heaviness as before. It had changed in some way. That was all he could have said about it.

At last Nell got up and went into the house. He heard her moving about in the bedroom, heard the creak of the bed as she sat on it to take down her hair. He did not get up at once. He sat on the step and looked out past the garden, past the fence and the Wilmots' woodshed, toward the place where the tracks ran down toward Clyde and on past Clyde to Toledo and on past Toledo to all the places there are in the world. It was dark there. There was nothing to see.

Then Ed Hanby got up, and knocked the pipe against the step, though there were no ashes in it, and went inside. He blew out the lamp in the kitchen. In the dark he stood for a moment by the table, and he put out his hand and laid it flat on the oilcloth where hers had been, as though there might still be something of her left there, some warmth, some sign. The oilcloth was cool and a little sticky from the heat of the day. He took his hand away and went in to bed.

The next evening, after the dishes were done and the towel was hung on its nail, Nell Hanby put on her hat with the cracked brim and went out of the house. Ed was sitting on the back step. He heard the front door close. After a while he got up and went around the side of the house and down the walk and along Buckeye Street toward the depot. He did not hurry. When he got there she was sitting on the bench at the end of the platform, and he went and sat down beside her, and they waited together for the eight-forty to come in.

Will Hanby came back to the town of Harmon, in Ohio, on a day in late October when the corn stood in shocks in the fields along the railroad and the leaves of the maple trees on Turner Street were yellow and falling. He had been away for nineteen years. He had gone to Chicago when he was a young man of twenty and had got a place there in a wholesale house that sold hardware to the stores in small towns, and later he had become a traveling man and had gone about over the country, to Iowa and to Kansas and once as far as Colorado, carrying his sample cases and sleeping in hotels. Now he was thirty-nine years old and he was a little fat about the waist. His hair had begun to go thin on top of his head and he had a habit of putting his hand up to feel of the place, as though he were not sure it was still there.

He had not intended to come back to Harmon. There was a reason for his coming, and the reason was that his Aunt Sarah, his mother's sister, had died and there was some small matter of property to be settled. A lawyer had written him a letter. When he got off the train at the station he stood for a long time on the platform with his bag in his hand, looking up the street toward the town, and he did not know what to do with himself. The station agent, a man he did not know, looked at him out of a little window. A dog came and smelled of his shoes and went away.

It should be understood that Will Hanby was not a man who thought much about things. In the hotels where he stayed he talked to other traveling men about trade and about women and about the prices of things, and at night he went to bed and slept. When he was alone he did not think. He was afraid of thinking. That is a thing that happens to many men who live as he lived. They become afraid of being alone with themselves, and so they fill up their days with talk and their nights with sleep, and the years go by.

But now, standing on the station platform at Harmon, something happened to him. He felt suddenly like a boy. He felt young and afraid and a little ashamed, and he did not know why. He set his bag down on the boards and stood looking at his hands.

His cousin Tom Hanby had a harness shop on Main Street, beside the bank. Will had known that for years. When he was in Chicago he sometimes got a letter from his aunt, and once in a while there was a line in it about Tom. "Tom is well. Tom's wife has had another baby. Tom has bought the Heffner building and moved his shop." Will had read these letters standing up in the hallway of his boarding house and had put them in his pocket and forgotten them.

He picked up his bag and walked up the street.

---

Tom Hanby was sitting on a low bench in the back of his shop when his cousin came in. He had a strip of leather across his knees and he was sewing it with a heavy needle, pushing the needle through with the palm of his hand, which was protected by a piece of leather. He was a large, slow man with big shoulders and a brown mustache that came down over his mouth. When the door opened and the little bell over it rang he did not look up at once. He finished the stitch he was making. Then he looked up and saw Will standing there in his city clothes with his bag in his hand, and he did not know him.

"What can I do for you?" he said.

Will Hanby laughed. It was a nervous, high laugh, not like the laugh of a grown man. "Don't you know me, Tom?" he said. "Why, it's Will. It's your cousin Will."

Tom Hanby put the leather down on the bench. He stood up slowly. For a moment the two men stood looking at each other across the shop, and neither of them spoke. The shop was dim and smelled of leather and of the oil that is used to make leather soft. Harness hung on pegs along the walls and there were horse collars piled in a corner. A fly buzzed against the dirty window at the front.

"Well, I'll be darned," Tom said. He came forward and put out his hand and Will took it. It was a hard hand, thick and cracked across the palm. Will's own hand felt small and soft inside it, and he was ashamed. He drew his hand away quickly.

"I came about Aunt Sarah," he said. "The lawyer wrote me."

"Yes," Tom said. "Yes, I know. Lawyer Bentley. I told him where to write." He stood looking at Will's face. "You've got fat," he said, and then he flushed, as though he had said something he should not have said.

"I guess I have," Will said. He laughed again. "I guess I have, all right."

---

They did not know how to begin. That was the trouble. There were nineteen years between them and the years were like a wall, and neither of them knew how to get over it. Tom went back and sat down on his bench and Will sat on a box near the door, and they talked about Aunt Sarah and how she had died. She had been sick a long time, Tom said. It was something in her stomach. At the end she did not know anyone. She kept calling for someone named Ella, and no one knew who Ella was.

"Maybe it was someone when she was a girl," Will said.

"Maybe so," said Tom. "I don't know. Nobody knew."

They were silent. Tom picked up the strip of leather and turned it over in his hands and put it down again. Outside, on Main Street, a farm wagon went by and the sound of the wheels came in through the door. Will looked at the wagon. He could see the farmer's back, bent forward on the seat, and a boy sitting beside him with his legs hanging down.

"Do you remember," he began, and then he stopped.

"What?" said Tom.

"Nothing," Will said. "I was just thinking."

---

In the evening Will went to Tom's house for supper. It was a white frame house on Locust Street with a porch across the front, and Tom's wife, whose name was Mary, was a thin woman with tired eyes who did not say much. There were four children. They sat at the table and stared at Will, and when he spoke to them they looked down at their plates. Mary had cooked a chicken and there were mashed potatoes and gravy and a pie made of pumpkin. Will ate a great deal. He talked all through the meal. He told about Chicago and about the hotels in Kansas City and about a man he had known who had made a fortune selling barbed wire. He talked loudly and he laughed often, and all the time he was talking he felt that something was wrong. He did not know what it was. The children stared at him and Mary moved back and forth between the table and the stove, and Tom sat at the head of the table and ate slowly and said nothing at all.

After supper the two men went out onto the porch. It was cold and the stars were out. Tom lit his pipe and the smell of the tobacco came to Will in the darkness. Down the street a woman was calling a child to come in. "Harry," she called. "Harry. Harry." Her voice went up at the end of the word, like a question, and then there was no answer and she called again.

"Let's walk," Tom said suddenly. "Let's walk out a ways."

---

They walked out Locust Street to where the sidewalk ended, and then along the dirt road past the cemetery and on toward the country. Neither of them said where they were going. They walked side by side and their feet made a sound on the hard road. There was no moon, but the starlight was enough to see by, and on either side of the road the fields stretched away flat and gray, with the shocks of corn standing in them like people waiting.

It was on this road that the two of them had walked when they were boys. Will remembered it now. He had not thought of it in years, but now it came back to him, and with it came a great many other things, crowding in on him so that he felt dizzy and had to put his hand up to his head.

When they were boys, Will had lived with his mother in a little house at the edge of town, and Tom had lived on a farm two miles out on this road. Will's father was dead. He had been a drinking man and had fallen under a train one night, and after that Will's mother took in sewing, and it was a poor life. Will used to walk out to the farm on Saturdays and stay with Tom, and the two boys slept together in a room under the roof. In the summer it was hot in the room and they lay with no covers and talked. They talked about what they would do when they were men.

Will was going to go away. He was always going to go away. He would go to Chicago or to New York, and then maybe he would go on a ship to some other country. He would see everything. He would do great things. Lying in the hot darkness under the roof, he talked and talked, and his voice trembled with the things he wanted, and Tom lay beside him and listened.

Tom did not talk much, even then. But once, Will remembered now, Tom had said something. It was late at night and Will had stopped talking and they were both lying still, and Tom said, "I'd like to go too." That was all. "I'd like to go too, Will." And then he had turned over on his side with his face to the wall, and Will had not answered him, because he had not known what to say, and after a while they had both gone to sleep.

Will thought about that now, walking along the road in the starlight beside his cousin. He thought about Tom's voice in the darkness, and about how Tom had turned his face to the wall. It seemed to Will a strange thing that he should remember it. He had forgotten so much. He had forgotten the names of the men he had worked with in the wholesale house, and the names of the towns where he had sold hardware, and the faces of the women he had known. But he remembered Tom's voice saying, "I'd like to go too."

---

They came to a place where there was a bridge over a creek, and Tom stopped and leaned on the rail. Will stood beside him. Below them the water made a little sound, running over stones. It was too dark to see the water, but they could hear it.

"This is where we used to fish," Tom said.

"I know it," said Will.

"You caught a big sucker here once. Do you remember? You were so excited you fell in."

Will laughed. It was a different laugh from the one he had used at the supper table. It was quieter. "I remember," he said. "Your father whipped us both for coming home wet."

"He whipped me," Tom said. "He didn't whip you. You weren't his."

"No," said Will. "No, that's so. I'd forgotten that."

They stood for a long time on the bridge. Tom's pipe had gone out and he did not light it again. He held it in his hand and Will could see the shape of his hand on the rail, large and dark against the gray of the wood. Will wanted to say something. There was something in him that wanted to be said, and it rose up into his throat and stuck there, and he could not get it out. He did not know what it was. He only knew that it had to do with the room under the roof and with Tom turning his face to the wall, and with his own life, the hotels and the trains and the talk, the endless talk that went nowhere.

"You've done well, Will," Tom said. "Aunt Sarah always said you'd done well. She was proud of you. She used to tell people about you."

"Did she?" said Will.

"She used to say, 'My nephew Will is in Chicago. He travels for a big firm.' She'd say it to anybody. She'd say it in the stores."

Will did not answer. He looked down at the dark place where the water was. He was thinking that he had not written to his Aunt Sarah in five years. He had not sent her anything at Christmas. Once, when he was passing through Columbus, he had thought of coming on to Harmon to see her, and then he had not come. He had gone instead to a saloon with a man who sold farm implements, and they had got drunk together and he had missed his train.

"I haven't done so well," he said. His voice was low and Tom turned his head to look at him. "I haven't done anything, Tom. I sell hardware. That's all. I sell nails and hinges and stove bolts to men in little towns like this one. I go from one place to another. I sleep in hotels. There isn't anything to it."

Tom said nothing.

"I used to think," Will said, and then he stopped. He put his hand up to the top of his head and felt of the thin place. "I don't know what I used to think," he said.

---

It was then that a queer thing happened between the two men. It was a thing that could not have been told to anyone afterward, because there were no words for it. Tom Hanby, standing on the bridge with his pipe in his hand, began to speak, and what he said was not much, but it was more than he had said to anyone in years.

"I used to want to go," he said. "You remember. I used to want to go too. When you went to Chicago I thought I'd go after you. I thought maybe in a year I'd go. I had some money saved. Then Father got sick and somebody had to run the farm, and then he died and there was Mother, and then I married Mary." He stopped. "I don't know," he said. "I don't know how it was. It was like one thing came after another, and there wasn't any time when I could stop and say, Now I'll go."

"I know," Will said.

"No, you don't," Tom said. He did not say it angrily. He said it slowly, as though he were puzzled. "You don't know. You went. I used to think about you, out there. Mary doesn't know it, but I used to think about you all the time. When I'd be working in the shop I'd think, Now Will is in Kansas City. Now he's on a train. Now he's seeing things. I used to think about you seeing things." He laughed, a short laugh. "It's foolish," he said. "A grown man."

Will Hanby put his hand on his cousin's arm. He did it without thinking, and when his hand was on Tom's arm he did not know what to do next, and so he left it there. Through the cloth of Tom's coat he could feel the arm, hard and thick, and he could feel that Tom was trembling a little.

"I didn't see anything, Tom," he said. "That's what I'm trying to tell you. I went everywhere and I didn't see anything. I don't know how it was either. I'd get to a place and it was just like the place before. I used to lie in the hotels at night and I'd think about this. About the farm. About the room up under the roof. I'd think, Tom's back there. Tom's got a wife and kids and a house. He's got something. I used to think about you too."

They stood there. Neither of them could say any more. The water ran under the bridge, and far off across the fields a dog was barking, and the sound came to them faint and thin through the cold air. Will took his hand off Tom's arm. He felt ashamed, and at the same time he felt something else that he could not have named, something warm and sad, like the feeling that comes over a man sometimes when he hears music in the street at night and does not know where it is coming from.

---

They walked back to town without talking. When they came to Tom's house the lamp was still burning in the front room and they could see Mary through the window, sitting in a chair with some mending in her lap. Her head had fallen forward. She was asleep.

Tom stopped at the gate. "You'll stay with us," he said. "There's a bed made up."

"I'll go to the hotel," Will said. "I don't want to put Mary out."

"You'll stay," Tom said.

Will went in. He slept that night in a little room at the back of the house, under the roof, and the ceiling sloped down over the bed so that when he lay on his back he could have reached up and touched it. He lay a long time awake. He could hear Tom and Mary talking in low voices in the next room, and then the voices stopped and he heard Tom's heavy step cross the floor, and then the bed creaked and there was no more sound.

Will lay in the darkness. He thought about the bridge and about the water running under it, and about Tom's arm trembling under his hand. He thought that tomorrow he would go to see Lawyer Bentley about the property, and the day after he would take the train back to Chicago, and on Monday he would go out again with his sample cases. Nothing would be any different. He knew that. He was not a fool. He knew that he and Tom would not write to each other, or that if they did it would be only a line or two at Christmas, and that in a year it would be as though this night had never happened.

And yet he did not feel sad, lying there. That was the strange thing. He lay with his eyes open in the dark room and he felt, for the first time in a great many years, that he was not alone. It was as though something had passed between himself and his cousin that could not be taken back. It did not matter that they could not say what it was. Perhaps it was better that they could not say it.

Toward morning he fell asleep. When he woke the sun was coming in through the little window and he could hear the children on the stairs and the smell of coffee came up to him from the kitchen. He lay for a moment without moving, and then he got up and went to the window and looked out. Tom was in the yard below, splitting wood. He swung the axe up over his shoulder and brought it down, and the stick of wood fell apart, and he bent and set up another. He did not look up at the window. He worked slowly and steadily, the way he did everything, and Will stood watching him for a long time before he turned away and began to dress.

Ed Hurd was a tall man with stooped shoulders who worked at the stave factory on the river road at the edge of the town of Clayborne, Ohio. He had been working there for eleven years. All day he stood by a machine that cut barrel staves out of white oak, and the machine made a high whining sound that got into his head and stayed there. At night when he lay in bed the whining went on and on in him, and sometimes he got up and went to the window and stood looking out at the dark street. There was nothing to see. A lamp burned in the window of the house where the widow Kessler lived, and beyond that the street ran down a little hill to the tracks of the Wheeling and Lake Erie railroad.

He was a man who did not talk much. In the factory the other men had given up trying to talk with him. "Ed's all right," they said. "He's a queer one but he's all right." When they said that they meant something. They meant that he did his work and did not make trouble and that they did not know what went on inside him. Nobody in Clayborne knew what went on inside Ed Hurd. Perhaps he did not know himself.

He had big hands. That is a thing to remember about him. They were long, knotted hands with black marks across the knuckles where the oak had bruised them, and when he was not working he did not know what to do with them. He put them in his pockets and took them out again. He laid them on the table and looked at them. Once, in the evening, when he was sitting on the steps of his house, a neighbor going by saw him holding his two hands up before his face and turning them over and over, and the neighbor went on down the street and told it in the barber shop. "What do you suppose a man would be doing that for?" he said. Nobody answered. It was a thing not to be understood.

Two years before the time of this story Ed Hurd's wife had gone away. She was a small dark woman named Mary, and she had come to Clayborne from a farm out on the Medina road to marry him when she was nineteen. For a time they had lived together in the little frame house near the tracks and she had kept it clean and had planted hollyhocks along the fence. Then the boy was born. Then one day in the spring, when the boy was five, she went down to the station and got on the afternoon train going east and did not come back. She left no word. Ed Hurd came home from the factory and found the boy sitting alone on the kitchen floor eating a piece of bread, and he understood. He did not go after her. He did not say anything to anyone. He went on going to the factory, and he hired the widow Kessler to keep the boy in the daytime, and in the evening he came home and cooked supper for the two of them and they ate it in silence.

The boy's name was Joe. He was seven now, a thin small boy with his mother's dark hair and a way of standing very still and looking at things. He would stand in the yard looking at a sparrow on the fence or at the smoke going up from a chimney, and he would stand so long that the widow Kessler would come to the door and call to him. "Joe, Joe," she would call, "what are you doing out there?" and he would not answer. It was as though he were listening for something that had not yet come.

On an evening in the late summer Ed Hurd came home and the boy was not there.

The widow Kessler met him at the gate. She was a large woman with a red face, and she was frightened. "I don't know where he went," she said. "I don't know. I looked everywhere. He was in the yard after dinner and then he wasn't." She began to cry, and Ed Hurd stood looking at her. Then he went into his house and sat down at the kitchen table. He did not go out to look for the boy. That was a strange thing, and afterward the widow Kessler told it about the town. "He just went in and sat down," she said. "It was like he knew." But perhaps he did not know. Perhaps it was only that he was a man to whom things happened and who had got into the habit of waiting for them to finish happening.

It grew dark. The widow Kessler went home and lighted her lamp, and Ed Hurd sat in the kitchen without lighting his. A freight train went by, going east, and the dishes on the shelf over the stove rattled. He heard the long whistle at the crossing below the town and then the sound of the train growing fainter and fainter and at last nothing. He sat with his hands on the table before him.

At nine o'clock a man came up the street carrying the boy. He was a brakeman named Will Sutter who lived at the other end of town, and he had found the boy walking along the tracks two miles east, past the water tank, walking in the dark between the rails with his shoes in his hand. "I seen him from the caboose," Will Sutter said, standing in the doorway with the boy in his arms. "We was going slow up the grade and I seen something white. I thought it was a dog. I swung off and went back and there he was. He didn't cry or nothing. He just looked at me." The brakeman set the boy down on the floor. "I guess you'll want to tan him," he said, and laughed a little, uneasily, and went away. He was a young man and had no children of his own, and something in the dark kitchen and in the silent man sitting at the table made him want to be away from there.

Ed Hurd got up and lighted the lamp. Then he stood by the table and looked at his son.

The boy stood just inside the door. His feet were bare and black with cinders and there was a little cut on one of them. He held his shoes, one in each hand, the laces hanging down. His face was dirty and his dark hair stood up on his head, and he looked at his father without fear, or rather with a kind of fear that was not the ordinary fear of a child. It was more like waiting. He stood waiting, as he stood in the yard waiting, to see what would happen.

Now it is a thing that men who do not talk much sometimes find themselves in a place where they must talk. It is like coming to a river and there is no bridge. They stand on the bank and look at the water. They know that they must get across. Ed Hurd stood by the table in the lamplight with this thing before him, and in his head the whining of the stave machine went on, high and thin, and he could not think. He knew what a father was supposed to do. When he was a boy on his own father's farm in Huron County his father had whipped him for less than this. His father had taken him out to the woodshed and whipped him with a harness strap, and afterward had said, "Now you'll remember," and he had remembered. He remembered still. He could see the woodshed and the light coming through the cracks between the boards and the dust floating in the light, and he could feel the strap.

"Put down them shoes," he said.

The boy put the shoes down on the floor beside him, carefully, side by side.

"Come here."

The boy came and stood before him. He was so small. Ed Hurd had not thought before how small he was. He looked down at the top of the boy's head, at the dark hair, and his hands hung at his sides and the fingers opened and closed.

"Where was you going?" he said.

The boy did not answer.

"I asked you where you was going. Down the tracks in the night. You could have got killed. A train could have come along and killed you and nobody would have known. They'd have found you in the morning." His voice was rising. He had not meant it to rise. It went up and up like the whine of the machine. "You hear me? They'd have found you lying there in the morning. What did you think you was doing? Did you think about Mrs. Kessler, how she'd be scared? Did you think about anybody?"

He stopped. The words had come out of him all in a rush and now they were gone and he did not know where they had come from. He stood breathing hard. The boy looked up at him.

"Answer me," Ed Hurd said.

He reached down and took the boy by the arm. His hand went all the way around the thin arm, and he could feel the bone under his fingers, and something in him shrank from it. But he held on. He was thinking of the woodshed and the harness strap. He was thinking, "A man has got to do it. It's for the boy's own good. If you let a boy go, there's no telling." He began to unbuckle his belt with the other hand. The buckle was stiff and his fingers were clumsy. He fumbled at it.

"I was going where she is," the boy said.

Ed Hurd's hand stopped on the buckle.

Now there is something here that must be told and it is hard to tell. It is hard because nothing happened that anyone could see. If the widow Kessler had been looking in at the window she would have seen only a tall man standing by a table with his hand on his belt and a small boy looking up at him. She would have seen the lamp and the shadow of the man on the wall, very large, and the shadow of the boy beside it, very small. That is all. But inside the man something was happening, and it was like a wall falling down.

He had not said his wife's name in two years. He had not let himself think of her. When he lay awake at night with the whining in his head he thought of the factory and the staves and the oak logs piled in the yard, and when she came into his mind he pushed her out again. He had done this so long that it had become like the work at the machine, something his hands did without his thinking. And now the boy had said it. Where she is. As though there were a place. As though a man could walk down the railroad tracks in the night, carrying his shoes, and come to the place where she was.

He let go of the boy's arm. He stood there.

"You don't know where she is," he said. His voice had gone low and harsh. "Nobody knows. You hear? She ain't anywhere. You can't go walking off down the tracks after nobody."

"She went on the train," the boy said. "I seen her go. I was at the fence. She went that way." He pointed, east, toward the wall of the kitchen and beyond it the dark.

"You was five years old. You don't remember."

"I remember," the boy said.

Ed Hurd turned away from him. He went to the window and stood looking out, as he did at night, at the lamp burning in the widow Kessler's window and at the dark beyond it. He wanted to say something to the boy. He wanted to say a great many things. He wanted to say, "I know. I know how it is. I've been walking down them tracks myself every night for two years, only I never got up out of the chair." He wanted to say, "She was a good woman and she went away because something in her was choked and she couldn't breathe in this house, and it was my fault maybe, I don't know, I never could talk to her." He wanted to say, "You're all I've got now and if you go off down the tracks there won't be anything left." But the words would not come. They were down in him somewhere, all crowded together, and they would not come out. He stood with his back to the boy and his big hands pressed flat against the window sill.

Behind him the boy began to cry. He cried quietly, the way a much older person cries, without making much noise. Ed Hurd heard him and did not turn around.

"It ain't right to run off," he said to the window. "You hear? It ain't right. You got to stay here. A person has got to stay where they are." He said it again. "A person has got to stay." It was not a reprimand any more. It was something else. It was as though he were talking to himself or to someone who was not in the room.

Then he did a thing he had not known he was going to do. He went out of the kitchen by the back door and into the yard and stood there in the dark. It was a warm night. The crickets were making their noise in the grass along the fence where the hollyhocks had been, and over the roof of the widow Kessler's house the sky was full of stars. He stood looking up. Far off, toward the east, a dog was barking, and he thought of the boy walking alone down the tracks past the water tank with his shoes in his hands, walking in the dark toward nothing, and something rose up in his throat and he could not swallow it. He put his hand against the trunk of the old apple tree that grew by the back steps and leaned there.

He thought of his own father and of the woodshed. "Now you'll remember," his father had said. Well, he had remembered. He had remembered all his life. But he had remembered the wrong thing. He had remembered the strap and the light coming through the cracks and the dust, and he had not remembered anything his father said to him, because his father had never said anything. His father had been a silent man too, a man who worked in the fields from daylight to dark and came in and ate and went to bed, and when he died Ed Hurd had stood by the grave and had not been able to think of one thing the old man had ever told him. It was as though a long line of silent men stretched back and back behind him, each one standing at a window looking out, each one with his hands pressed flat on the sill. And now there was the boy.

He stayed in the yard a long time. When he went back into the kitchen the boy was asleep on the floor beside his shoes. He had curled up there like a dog, with his knees drawn up and one arm under his head, and the tears had made little clean streaks down through the dirt on his face. The lamp was smoking. Ed Hurd turned it down. Then he stood looking at the boy.

After a while he knelt down on the floor. It was hard for him to do. He was a tall man and stiff from standing all day at the machine, and his knees cracked. He knelt there and looked at the small dirty feet with the cut on one of them and at the hair standing up and at the hand under the cheek. He put out one of his own big hands and held it above the boy's head, not touching him. His hand trembled. It was a strange thing to see, that big knotted hand with the black bruises across the knuckles trembling in the air above the sleeping child. Then he laid it down very lightly on the boy's hair.

"I'll take you," he said, in a whisper. "Sometime. When you're bigger. We'll get on the train and go east and we'll look. I'll take you." He did not know if he meant it. He did not know if it was a thing that could be done. He said it anyway. It was the most he had said to anyone in two years.

The boy did not wake. Ed Hurd picked him up and carried him into the little room off the kitchen and laid him on the bed, and then he got a basin of water and a rag and washed the cinders off his feet. He did it slowly and carefully, holding each small foot in his palm. When he came to the cut he stopped and looked at it a long time, and then he washed it very gently and tore a strip off an old shirt and tied it around. All the time he was doing this his lips moved, but no sound came out. If anyone had been there to see, they would have thought he was praying. Perhaps he was. Or perhaps he was only saying over and over the things he had wanted to say and could not say, saying them now to the sleeping boy who could not hear.

In the morning he went to the factory as usual. The men saw him come in and nodded to him and he nodded back. He went to his machine and started it, and the high whining sound began, and he stood all day feeding the oak into it and watching the white staves come out. At noon one of the men, a fat jolly fellow named Hartzell, came and sat down beside him while they ate their dinners.

"Heard your boy run off last night," Hartzell said. "Will Sutter was telling it. Said he found him clear out past the tank." He laughed. "I bet you warmed him good."

Ed Hurd looked at his hands.

"No," he said.

Hartzell waited for him to say something more, but he did not, and after a while the fat man got up and went back to the other end of the shed. "There's something wrong with that fellow," he said to the men there. "He just sits and looks at his hands."

That is the way it is in towns like Clayborne. Things happen in the houses at night, in the kitchens with the lamps burning, and in the morning nobody knows. A man stands at a machine all day and the other men work beside him for eleven years and do not know him. And perhaps it is just as well. Perhaps if they knew they would not understand. For what is there to understand? A man had meant to whip his son for running away and had not done it. That is all. It is not much of a story. And yet Ed Hurd, standing at his machine that afternoon with the whining in his ears, felt that something had changed in him that would not change back. He could not have said what it was. He felt it the way you feel the weather turning, a kind of looseness in the air.

That evening when he came home the boy was sitting on the back steps waiting for him. He had the strip of shirt still tied around his foot. When he saw his father come in at the gate he got up and stood very still, the way he did, looking.

Ed Hurd stopped in the middle of the yard. For a moment the two of them looked at each other. Then the man went and sat down on the steps, and after a while the boy sat down beside him, and they sat there together in the evening light without saying anything while the freight train went by, going east, and the dishes rattled on the shelf inside the house.

From where they sat they could see the workers of the night shift idling in the sun on Main Street. From the coke ovens a thin line of smoke rose into the sky. A freight train heavily loaded crept round the hill at the end of the valley. It was spring and over even that hive of black industry hung a faint promise of beauty. The boys talked of the life of people in their town and as they talked thought each of himself. Although he had not been out of the valley and had grown strong and big there, Beaut McGregor knew something of the outside world. It isn't a time when men are shut off from their fellows. Newspapers and magazines have done their work too well. They reached even into the miner's cabin and the merchants along Main Street of Coal Creek stood before their stores in the afternoon and talked of the doings of the world. Beaut McGregor knew that life in his town was exceptional, that not everywhere did men toil all day black and grimy underground, that not all women were pale bloodless and bent. As he went about delivering bread he whistled a song. “Take me back to Broadway,” he sang after the soubrette in a show that had once come to Coal Creek. Now as he sat on the hillside he talked earnestly while he gesticulated with his hands. “I hate this town,” he said. “The men here think they are confoundedly funny. They don't care for anything but making foolish jokes and getting drunk. I want to go away.” His voice rose and hatred flamed up in him. “You wait,” he boasted. “I'll make men stop being fools. I'll make children of them. I'll——” Pausing he looked at his two companions. Beaut poked the ground with a stick. The boy sitting beside him laughed. He was a short well—dressed black—haired boy with rings on his fingers who worked in the town poolroom, racking the pool balls. “I'd like to go where there are women with blood in them,” he said. Three women came up the hill toward them, a tall pale brown-haired woman of twenty-seven and two fairer young girls. The black-haired boy straightened his tie and began thinking of a conversation he would start when the women reached him. Beaut and the other boy, a fat fellow, the son of a grocer, looked down the hill to the town over the heads of the newcomers and continued in their minds the thoughts that had made the conversation.

“Hello girls, come and sit here,” shouted the black-haired boy, laughing and looking boldly into the eyes of the tall pale woman. They stopped and the tall woman began stepping over the fallen logs, coming to them. The two young girls followed, laughing. They sat down on the log beside the boys, the tall pale woman at the end beside red-haired McGregor. An embarrassed silence fell over the party. Both Beaut and the fat boy were disconcerted by this turn to their afternoon's outing and wondered how it would turn out. The pale woman began to talk in a low tone. “I want to get away from here,” she said, “I wish I could hear birds sing and see green things grow.” Beaut McGregor had an idea. “You come with me,” he said. He got up and climbed over the logs and the pale woman followed. The fat boy shouted at them, relieving his own embarrassment by trying to embarrass them. “Where're you going—you two?” he shouted. Beaut said nothing. He stepped over the logs to the road and began climbing the hill. The tall woman walked beside him and held her skirts out of the deep dust of the road. Even on this her Sunday gown there was a faint black mark along the seams—the mark of Coal Creek. As McGregor walked his embarrassment left him. He thought it fine that he should be thus alone with a woman. When she had tired from the climb he sat with her on a log beside the road and talked of the black-haired boy. “He has your ring on his finger,” he said, looking at her and laughing. She held her hand pressed tightly against her side and closed her eyes. “The climbing hurts me,” she said. Tenderness took hold of Beaut. When they went on again he walked behind her, his hand upon her back pushing her up the hill. The desire to tease her about the black-haired boy had passed and he wished he had said nothing about the ring. He remembered the story the black-haired boy had told him of his conquest of the woman. “More than likely a mess of lies,” he thought. Over the crest of the hill they stopped and rested, leaning against a worn rail fence by the woods. Below them in a wagon a party of men went down the hill. The men sat upon boards laid across the box of a wagon and sang a song. One of them stood in the seat beside the driver and waved a bottle. He seemed to be making a speech. The others shouted and clapped their hands. The sounds came faint and sharp up the hill. In the woods beside the fence rank grass grew. Hawks floated in the sky over the valley below. A squirrel running along the fence stopped and chattered at them. McGregor thought he had never had so delightful a companion. He got a feeling of complete, good fellowship and friendliness with this woman. Without knowing how the thing had been done he felt a certain pride in it. “Don't mind what I said about the ring,” he urged, “I was only trying to tease you.” The woman beside McGregor was the daughter of an undertaker who lived upstairs over his shop near the bakery.
