When he passed her standing in the stairway he went hurriedly along and looked into the gutter. They went down the hill and sat on the log upon the hillside. A clump of elders had grown about the log since his visits there with Cracked McGregor so that the place was closed and shaded like a room. The woman took off her hat and laid it beside her on the log. A faint colour mounted to her pale cheeks and a flash of anger gleamed in her eyes. “He probably lied to you about me,” she said, “I didn't give him that ring to wear. I don't know why I gave it to him. He wanted it. He asked me for it time and again. He said he wanted to show it to his mother. And now he has shown it to you and I suppose told lies about me.” Beaut was annoyed and wished he had not mentioned the ring. He felt that an unnecessary fuss was being made about it. He did not believe that the black-haired boy had lied but he did not think it mattered. He began talking of his father, boasting of him. His hatred of the town blazed up. “They thought they knew him down there,” he said, “they laughed at him and called him 'Cracked.' They thought his running into the mine just a crazy notion like a horse that runs into a burning stable. He was the best man in town. He was braver than any of them. He went in there and died when he had almost enough money saved to buy a farm over here.” He pointed down the valley. Beaut began to tell her of the visits to the hillside with his father and described the effect of the scene on himself when he was a child. “I thought it was paradise,” he said. She put her hand on his arm and seemed to be soothing him like a careful groom quieting an excitable horse. “Don't mind them,” she said, “you will go away after a time and make a place for yourself out in the world.” He wondered how she knew. A profound respect for her came over him. “She is keen to guess that,” he thought. He began to talk of himself, boasting and throwing out his chest. “I'd like to have the chance to show what I can do,” he declared. A thought that had been in his mind on the winter day when Uncle Charlie Wheeler put the name of Beaut upon him came back and he walked up and down before the woman making grotesque motions with his hands as Cracked McGregor had walked up and down before him.

“I'll tell you what,” he began and his voice was harsh. He had forgotten the presence of the woman and half forgotten what had been in his mind. He sputtered and glared over his shoulder up the hillside as he struggled for words. “Oh to Hell with men!” he burst forth. “They are cattle, stupid cattle.” A fire blazed up in his eyes and a confident ring came into his voice. “I'd like to get them together, all of them,” he said, “I'd like to make them——” Words failed him and again he sat down on the log beside the woman. “Well I'd like to lead them to an old mine shaft and push them in,” he concluded resentfully.

On the eminence Beaut and the tall woman sat and looked down into the valley. “I wonder why we don't go there, mother and I,” he said. “When I see it I'm filled with the notion. I think I want to be a farmer and work in the fields. Instead of that mother and I sit and plan of the city. I'm going to be a lawyer. That's all we talk about. Then I come up here and it seems as though this is the place for me.” The tall woman laughed. “I can see you coming home at night from the fields,” she said. “It might be to that white house there with the windmill, You would be a big man and would have dust in your red hair and perhaps a red beard growing on your chin. And a woman with a baby in her arms would come out of the kitchen door to stand leaning on the fence waiting for you. When you came up she would put her arm around your neck and kiss you on the lips. The beard would tickle her cheek. You should have a beard when you grow older. Your mouth is so big.” A strange new feeling shot through Beaut. He wondered why she had said that and wanted to take hold of her hand and kiss her then and there. He got up and looked at the sun going down behind the hill far away at the other end of the valley. “We'd better be getting along back,” he said. The woman remained seated on the log. “Sit down,” she said, “I'll tell you something—something it's good for you to hear. You're so big and red you tempt a girl to bother you. First though you tell me why you go along the street looking into the gutter when I stand in the stairway in the evening.” Beaut sat down again upon the log, and thought of what the black-haired boy had told him of her. “Then it was true—what he said about you?” he asked.

“No! No!” she cried, jumping up in her turn and beginning to pin on her hat. “Let's be going.” Beaut sat stolidly on the log. “What's the use bothering each other,” he said. “Let's sit here until the sun goes down. We can get home before dark.” They sat down and she began talking, boasting of herself as he had boasted of his father.

“I'm too old for that boy,” she said; “I'm older than you by a good many years. I know what boys talk about and what they say about women. I do pretty well. I don't have any one to talk to except father and he sits all evening reading a paper and going to sleep in his chair. If I let boys come and sit with me in the evening or stand talking with me in the stairway it is because I'm lonesome. There isn't a man in town I'd marry—not one.” The speech sounded discordant and harsh to Beaut. He wished his father were there rubbing his hands together and muttering rather than this pale woman who stirred him up and then talked harshly like the women at the back doors in Coal Creek. He thought again as he had thought before that he preferred the black-faced miners drunk and silent to their pale talking wives. On an impulse he told her that, saying it crudely so that it hurt. Their companionship was spoiled. They got up and began to climb the hill, going toward home. Again she put her hand to her side and again he wished to put his hand at her back and push her up the hill. Instead he walked beside her in silence, again hating the town. Halfway down the hill the tall woman stopped by the road-side. Darkness was coming on and the glow of the coke ovens lighted the sky. “One living up here and never going down there might think it rather grand and big,” he said. Again the hatred came. “They might think the men who live down there knew something instead of being just a lot of cattle.” A smile came into the face of the tall woman and a gentler look stole into her eyes. “We get at one another,” she said, “we can't let one another alone. I wish we hadn't quarrelled. We might be friends if we tried. You have got something in you. You attract women. I've heard others say that. Your father was that way. Most of the women here would rather have been the wife of Cracked McGregor ugly as he was than to have stayed with their own husbands. I heard my mother say that to father when they lay quarrelling in bed at night and I lay listening.” The boy was overcome with the thought of a woman talking to him so frankly. He looked at her and said what was in his mind. “I don't like the women,” he said, “but I liked you, seeing you standing in the stairway and thinking you had been doing as you pleased. I thought maybe you amounted to something. I don't know why you should be bothered by what I think. I don't know why any woman should be bothered by what any man thinks. I should think you would go right on doing what you want to do like mother and me about my being a lawyer.” He sat on a log beside the road near where he had met her and watched her go down the hill. “I'm quite a fellow to have talked to her all afternoon like that,” he thought and pride in his growing manhood crept over him.

It was a Thursday evening in late October and Tom Fry, the carpenter, sat in the kitchen of his house on Duane Street in the town of Hollins, Ohio, and waited for his wife to come home. He had come home himself at six o'clock and had found the stove cold and the table bare. On the oilcloth there was a plate with three cold potatoes on it and a piece of side meat and beside the plate a note in his wife's hand. "I have gone out for a while," the note said. That was all. Tom Fry read the note and put it into his pocket and then took it out again and read it once more. He did not light the stove. He sat by the table in his work clothes with the sawdust still on his sleeves and ate one of the cold potatoes, holding it in his fingers like a boy. When it grew dark he got up and lit the lamp and turned the wick low and sat down again.

It is a thing that happens in houses. A man and a woman live together for a long time, sleeping in one bed and eating at one table, and they think they know each other. Then on some evening when nothing at all has happened a door opens a crack, and one of them looks through and sees a strange country. After that nothing is quite as it was. Neither can forget what was seen and neither can speak of it.

Tom Fry was a tall stooped man of thirty-six with long arms and a thin neck and big hands scarred and brown from his work. In the town he was thought a good workman and a slow talker. When he built a porch or set a window frame he did it well and men came afterward and ran their hands along the joints and nodded. He had married Ellen Shanks when he was twenty-eight and she twenty-four. She had been teaching the country school out on the Pike road and he had been sent out there to put a new floor in the schoolhouse. For three days he worked on his knees in the room while she sat at her desk on the little platform at the front and corrected the papers of the children. It was summer and the school was closed. He did not know why she came every day to sit there and she did not tell him. On the third day she got up and stood over him while he drove the last nails and said, "You do everything so carefully. I like to watch you." He had been so astonished he hit his thumb with the hammer. Afterward when they were married he used to tell the story at the barber shop and the men laughed. "She married me for my hammer," he said, and that seemed to him a fine joke.

They had no children. In the beginning that had troubled Ellen and then it seemed not to trouble her. She kept the house clean and she read books she got from the library over the bank and in the evenings she sat by the lamp with a book in her lap and did not read it. Tom did not notice. He sat across from her and whittled or looked at the Cleveland paper and at nine o'clock he wound the clock on the shelf and went up to bed.

In September she began going out alone in the evening. At first it was only once a week and then it was oftener. She did not say where she went. Tom did not ask. He thought, "She goes to see her sister on Locust Street." Then one day in the barber shop Ike Shuler, the barber, a little round man with a waxed mustache who knew everything that happened in Hollins and a good deal that did not, stood behind him with the razor in his hand and spoke. "Your wife was out walking on the Pike road last night," Ike said. "Ten o'clock it was. Hank Weaver saw her when he came in from his place. Out by the railroad cut she was, all alone." Ike laughed and the men waiting on the bench along the wall laughed. Tom Fry said nothing. He sat in the chair with the hot towel on his face and his hands gripping the arms of the chair. Afterward he went back to the job he was doing on the Methodist parsonage and worked all afternoon without saying a word, and when he went home that night Ellen was sitting by the lamp and he did not speak of it either.

That had been two weeks before. Now he sat in the kitchen and waited and the clock on the shelf ticked and a dog barked somewhere down by the tannery. Once a wagon went past in the street and he got up and went to the window, but it was only old Doc Ralston going out to see somebody sick in the country. Tom stood at the window a long time looking at nothing. He thought of Ellen on the Pike road at night by the railroad cut and his throat grew tight. He began to think of men. He thought of Will Hensel who clerked in the dry goods store and wore yellow shoes and of the young doctor who had come to town in the spring and of a travelling man he had seen once talking to her in front of the post office. His mind ran from one face to another like a dog running from tree to tree. "I'll ask her straight out," he said aloud, and the sound of his own voice in the empty kitchen startled him.

At half past ten he heard her step on the walk at the side of the house. She came in at the kitchen door and stopped when she saw him. She had on her brown coat and a scarf over her head and her cheeks were red from the cold. For a moment she stood in the doorway with her hand on the knob and looked at him. Then she came in and shut the door and took off her scarf and began to fold it.

"You didn't light the fire," she said. "You've been sitting here in the cold."

"I didn't want any fire," Tom said.

She hung her coat on the nail behind the door and went to the stove and opened the firebox and looked in and shut it again. Her hands moved about, touching things. She took the plate with the cold potatoes on it and carried it to the table by the sink and set it down. Tom watched her. He had made up his mind what he would say and now that she was there before him the words had gone out of him. He put his big hands flat on the table before him and looked at them.

"Where've you been?" he said at last.

Ellen did not turn around. "Out," she said. "Walking."

"Where walking?"

"Out on the Pike road. Out past the fairgrounds."

"Alone?"

She turned then and looked at him. She was a small woman with a long face and grey eyes set wide apart and when she looked at a person she seemed to be looking at something a little behind him. Tom had always thought her pretty, though no one else in Hollins had thought so. Now in the low light of the lamp her face seemed to him like the face of someone he had never seen.

"Yes, alone," she said. "Who would I be with?"

Tom got up from the table. He did not know why he got up. He went to the window and stood with his back to her and then came back and stood by the table again. "They're talking about you down town," he said. "In the barber shop. Ike Shuler said Hank Weaver saw you out by the cut at ten o'clock at night. They laughed about it. They laughed right in my face."

A little colour came into Ellen's face and went out again. "Let them laugh," she said. "What do I care what Ike Shuler says?"

"Well I care," Tom said. His voice rose and he heard it rise and could not stop it. "I've got to go in there and get shaved. I've got to work in this town. A man's got to hold up his head." He brought his fist down on the table and the lamp jumped and the flame flared up in the chimney and smoked. "What do you go out there for? What's out there? I've got a right to know."

Ellen came over to the table and turned down the wick of the lamp. She did it carefully, bending her head, and Tom saw the part in her hair and the grey hairs along it that he had not seen before. She sat down in the chair across from him.

"Sit down, Tom," she said. "I'll tell you if you want to know. Sit down and don't shout."

He sat down. He was ashamed of having struck the table and he put his hands under it, between his knees, as he used to do when he was a boy in school.

For a long time she did not say anything. The clock ticked on the shelf. Tom waited. He thought, "Now it's coming. Now she'll tell me who it is." His heart beat heavily and he felt sick, as he had felt once when he fell from a scaffolding and lay on the ground and could not get his breath.

"There isn't anybody," Ellen said. "I know what you're thinking. I've seen you thinking it these two weeks. There isn't anybody at all."

"Then what——"

"I go out to the railroad cut," she said, "and I stand there by the fence and wait for the night train to go through. The ten o'clock to Cleveland. That's all I do."

Tom stared at her. He had been ready for anything but this and it seemed to him she must be lying, making fun of him the way the men did at the barber shop. "The train," he said stupidly. "What do you want with the train?"

Ellen looked down at the oilcloth on the table. There was a burned place on it where once he had set down a hot pan and she put her finger on the burned place and moved it round and round. "I don't know," she said. "I can't tell you. It comes round the bend by the Weaver place and you hear it a long time before you see it and then the light comes, and then it goes by. The cars are all lighted. You can see people sitting in them. A man reading a paper. A woman with a hat on asleep with her head against the glass. Once there was a girl standing up in the aisle laughing at somebody. They go by so fast. They're going to Cleveland and some of them maybe going farther than that, to New York, I don't know where. And then it's gone and it's dark and you can hear it a long time after, getting fainter." She stopped. "That's all," she said. "I stand there and then I walk home."

Tom did not know what to say. He felt relief go through him and then something else, something worse than the jealousy had been. He did not have a name for it. He looked at his wife across the table and it seemed to him that she was farther away than if she had told him she had a lover. A lover he could have understood. He could have gone out and found the man and hit him. Men did that. There was something a man could do.

"You want to go away," he said slowly. "Is that it? You want to go off to Cleveland?"

"No," she said. "No, I don't think so. I don't know." She raised her eyes and looked at him and now she seemed to be looking right at him and not at something behind. "Tom, did you ever feel that you were shut up in something? Like in a box? And you push against the sides and they don't give? I've been in this house eight years. I get up and get your breakfast and you go off to work and I wash the dishes and sweep and go to the store and come back and get your supper. And you sit there and read the paper and at nine o'clock you wind the clock. Every night for eight years you've wound that clock at nine o'clock."

"Well a clock's got to be wound," Tom said. He was hurt and he spoke angrily. "What's wrong with that? I work hard all day. I don't drink like Jim Moore or go off to Toledo and spend my money like some of them. I give you everything I make. What have I done?"

"You haven't done anything," Ellen said. "That's just it. Nobody's done anything. Oh, I don't mean it like that." She put her hands up to her face and held them there a moment and then took them away. "I can't say it. I'm a fool to try. When I was out at the schoolhouse that summer and you came to lay the floor I used to watch you working. You took such care. You'd look at a board a long time before you nailed it down, turning it over, looking along the edge of it with one eye shut. I thought, 'There's a man who cares about things. There's a man who looks at things.' I thought if I married you you'd look at me that way."

Tom sat very still. He remembered the schoolhouse, the smell of the hot dust and the new pine boards and the sound of a mowing machine somewhere out in a field, and her sitting up there on the platform in a white waist with her hair done up high. He had looked at her then. He remembered that he had been afraid to look at her and had looked anyway, out of the corner of his eye, when he thought she was bent over her papers.

"I did look at you," he said. His voice had gone hoarse. "I always——"

He stopped. He wanted to tell her something and did not know what it was. It seemed to him there was something big in his breast that he had always meant to say to her and had put off from day to day thinking there would be time. Now that the time was here it would not come up into words. He opened his mouth and shut it again. He put his hands up on the table and turned them over and looked at the palms as though the thing he wanted to say might be written there among the scars.

"I'm no hand at talking," he said finally. "You know that. You always knew that."

"Yes," Ellen said. "I know."

She got up and went to the stove and opened the firebox again and began to shake down the ashes. She did it hard and the iron rattled. Tom watched her back. He thought, "If I went over now and put my arms around her——" But he did not move. He sat with his hands on the table and he was afraid, as he had been afraid of nothing else in his life. He was afraid that if he went to her she would stand stiff in his arms the way a stranger would stand. He thought that would be more than he could bear.

"I suppose you'll go on doing it," he said. "Going out there nights."

"I suppose I will," she said without turning.

"And let them talk."

"And let them talk."

A kind of anger came up in Tom again and he was glad of it because it was something he understood. "Ike Shuler will make a story out of it," he said. "He'll say you're crazy. He'll say Tom Fry's wife goes out at night and looks at trains. They'll all laugh." He got up from the chair. "By God I won't have it," he said. "I won't have them laughing."

Ellen straightened up from the stove and faced him. Her face was white and her eyes very bright. "Then you tell them," she said. "You go in there tomorrow and tell them it's somebody. Tell them it's a man. They'd understand that. They'd like that better. Tell them your wife's got a man out on the Pike road and you'll see how they stop laughing at you and start being sorry for you. That's what you want, isn't it? You'd rather that than the truth."

Tom stood with his mouth open. He felt as though she had struck him. For a moment he thought he would go out of the house and walk down the street, anywhere, to the station or the tannery, and not come back until morning. He took a step toward the door. Then he stopped and stood in the middle of the kitchen floor, a tall stooped man with sawdust on his sleeves, and did not know where to go.

It was Ellen who moved. She came across the kitchen and stood before him. She did not touch him. "I'm sorry," she said in a low voice. "That was a mean thing to say. I didn't mean it. I don't know what I mean anymore."

"It's all right," Tom said.

They stood there. Outside the wind had come up and a loose shutter somewhere on the house began to bang. Tom thought, "I'll have to fix that shutter." He had been meaning to fix it for a month. The thought of it, of something to be done with his hands, came to him like a comfort, and then he was ashamed of being comforted by it.

"Ellen," he said.

"Yes."

"Next time," he said. "Next time you go out there. I could go along. I could walk out with you. If you didn't mind."

She looked up at him quickly and then down again. He could not tell what was in her face. "You'd be cold," she said. "You'd stand there and you wouldn't see anything. It's only a train."

"Maybe I would see," Tom said. "Maybe I wouldn't. I could try."

She did not answer. She turned away and took the lamp from the table and held it up so that the light fell on the stairway. "It's late," she said. "You've got to be at the parsonage early."

Tom went to the shelf and took down the key and began to wind the clock. Halfway through he stopped with the key in his fingers and looked at it. Then he looked at his wife standing at the foot of the stairs with the lamp in her hand. She was watching him. He did not know whether to go on winding the clock or to stop. It seemed to him a great deal depended on it, more than he could understand. His hand trembled. At last he set the key down on the shelf with the clock half wound and went across the kitchen to her.

They went up the stairs together, she ahead with the lamp and he behind, and neither of them said anything more. In the night Tom lay awake a long time listening to the shutter bang and to the breathing of his wife beside him. He did not know whether she slept. Once he put out his hand in the darkness and let it rest on her shoulder and she did not move away. Toward morning, very faint and far off, he heard a train whistle for the crossing out by the Weaver place, and he lay listening until the sound had quite gone, and it seemed to him that it was the loneliest sound he had ever heard in his life, and he wondered that he had never noticed it before.

One Sunday afternoon three boys sat on a log on the side of the hill that looked down into Coal Creek. From where they sat they could see the workers of the night shift idling in the sun on Main Street. From the coke ovens a thin line of smoke rose into the sky. A freight train heavily loaded crept round the hill at the end of the valley. It was spring and over even that hive of black industry hung a faint promise of beauty. The boys talked of the life of people in their town and as they talked thought each of himself. Although he had not been out of the valley and had grown strong and big there, Beaut McGregor knew something of the outside world. It isn't a time when men are shut off from their fellows. Newspapers and magazines have done their work too well. They reached even into the miner's cabin and the merchants along Main Street of Coal Creek stood before their stores in the afternoon and talked of the doings of the world. Beaut McGregor knew that life in his town was exceptional, that not everywhere did men toil all day black and grimy underground, that not all women were pale bloodless and bent. As he went about delivering bread he whistled a song. “Take me back to Broadway,” he sang after the soubrette in a show that had once come to Coal Creek. Now as he sat on the hillside he talked earnestly while he gesticulated with his hands. “I hate this town,” he said. “The men here think they are confoundedly funny. They don't care for anything but making foolish jokes and getting drunk. I want to go away.” His voice rose and hatred flamed up in him. “You wait,” he boasted. “I'll make men stop being fools. I'll make children of them. I'll——” Pausing he looked at his two companions. Beaut poked the ground with a stick. The boy sitting beside him laughed. He was a short well—dressed black—haired boy with rings on his fingers who worked in the town poolroom, racking the pool balls. “I'd like to go where there are women with blood in them,” he said. Three women came up the hill toward them, a tall pale brown-haired woman of twenty-seven and two fairer young girls. The black-haired boy straightened his tie and began thinking of a conversation he would start when the women reached him. Beaut and the other boy, a fat fellow, the son of a grocer, looked down the hill to the town over the heads of the newcomers and continued in their minds the thoughts that had made the conversation.

“Hello girls, come and sit here,” shouted the black-haired boy, laughing and looking boldly into the eyes of the tall pale woman. They stopped and the tall woman began stepping over the fallen logs, coming to them. The two young girls followed, laughing. They sat down on the log beside the boys, the tall pale woman at the end beside red-haired McGregor. An embarrassed silence fell over the party. Both Beaut and the fat boy were disconcerted by this turn to their afternoon's outing and wondered how it would turn out. The pale woman began to talk in a low tone. “I want to get away from here,” she said, “I wish I could hear birds sing and see green things grow.” Beaut McGregor had an idea. “You come with me,” he said. He got up and climbed over the logs and the pale woman followed. The fat boy shouted at them, relieving his own embarrassment by trying to embarrass them. “Where're you going—you two?” he shouted. Beaut said nothing. He stepped over the logs to the road and began climbing the hill. The tall woman walked beside him and held her skirts out of the deep dust of the road. Even on this her Sunday gown there was a faint black mark along the seams—the mark of Coal Creek. As McGregor walked his embarrassment left him. He thought it fine that he should be thus alone with a woman. When she had tired from the climb he sat with her on a log beside the road and talked of the black-haired boy. “He has your ring on his finger,” he said, looking at her and laughing. She held her hand pressed tightly against her side and closed her eyes. “The climbing hurts me,” she said. Tenderness took hold of Beaut. When they went on again he walked behind her, his hand upon her back pushing her up the hill. The desire to tease her about the black-haired boy had passed and he wished he had said nothing about the ring. He remembered the story the black-haired boy had told him of his conquest of the woman. “More than likely a mess of lies,” he thought. Over the crest of the hill they stopped and rested, leaning against a worn rail fence by the woods. Below them in a wagon a party of men went down the hill. The men sat upon boards laid across the box of a wagon and sang a song. One of them stood in the seat beside the driver and waved a bottle. He seemed to be making a speech. The others shouted and clapped their hands. The sounds came faint and sharp up the hill. In the woods beside the fence rank grass grew. Hawks floated in the sky over the valley below. A squirrel running along the fence stopped and chattered at them. McGregor thought he had never had so delightful a companion. He got a feeling of complete, good fellowship and friendliness with this woman. Without knowing how the thing had been done he felt a certain pride in it. “Don't mind what I said about the ring,” he urged, “I was only trying to tease you.” The woman beside McGregor was the daughter of an undertaker who lived upstairs over his shop near the bakery. He had seen her in the evening standing in the stairway by the shop door. After the story told him by the black-haired boy he had been embarrassed about her. When he passed her standing in the stairway he went hurriedly along and looked into the gutter. They went down the hill and sat on the log upon the hillside. A clump of elders had grown about the log since his visits there with Cracked McGregor so that the place was closed and shaded like a room. The woman took off her hat and laid it beside her on the log. A faint colour mounted to her pale cheeks and a flash of anger gleamed in her eyes. “He probably lied to you about me,” she said, “I didn't give him that ring to wear. I don't know why I gave it to him. He wanted it. He asked me for it time and again. He said he wanted to show it to his mother. And now he has shown it to you and I suppose told lies about me.” Beaut was annoyed and wished he had not mentioned the ring. He felt that an unnecessary fuss was being made about it. He did not believe that the black-haired boy had lied but he did not think it mattered. He began talking of his father, boasting of him. His hatred of the town blazed up. “They thought they knew him down there,” he said, “they laughed at him and called him 'Cracked.' They thought his running into the mine just a crazy notion like a horse that runs into a burning stable. He was the best man in town. He was braver than any of them. He went in there and died when he had almost enough money saved to buy a farm over here.” He pointed down the valley. Beaut began to tell her of the visits to the hillside with his father and described the effect of the scene on himself when he was a child. “I thought it was paradise,” he said. She put her hand on his arm and seemed to be soothing him like a careful groom quieting an excitable horse. “Don't mind them,” she said, “you will go away after a time and make a place for yourself out in the world.” He wondered how she knew. A profound respect for her came over him. “She is keen to guess that,” he thought. He began to talk of himself, boasting and throwing out his chest. “I'd like to have the chance to show what I can do,” he declared. A thought that had been in his mind on the winter day when Uncle Charlie Wheeler put the name of Beaut upon him came back and he walked up and down before the woman making grotesque motions with his hands as Cracked McGregor had walked up and down before him.

“I'll tell you what,” he began and his voice was harsh. He had forgotten the presence of the woman and half forgotten what had been in his mind. He sputtered and glared over his shoulder up the hillside as he struggled for words. “Oh to Hell with men!” he burst forth. “They are cattle, stupid cattle.” A fire blazed up in his eyes and a confident ring came into his voice. “I'd like to get them together, all of them,” he said, “I'd like to make them——” Words failed him and again he sat down on the log beside the woman. “Well I'd like to lead them to an old mine shaft and push them in,” he concluded resentfully.

On the eminence Beaut and the tall woman sat and looked down into the valley. “I wonder why we don't go there, mother and I,” he said. “When I see it I'm filled with the notion. I think I want to be a farmer and work in the fields. Instead of that mother and I sit and plan of the city. I'm going to be a lawyer. That's all we talk about. Then I come up here and it seems as though this is the place for me.” The tall woman laughed. “I can see you coming home at night from the fields,” she said. “It might be to that white house there with the windmill, You would be a big man and would have dust in your red hair and perhaps a red beard growing on your chin. And a woman with a baby in her arms would come out of the kitchen door to stand leaning on the fence waiting for you. When you came up she would put her arm around your neck and kiss you on the lips. The beard would tickle her cheek. You should have a beard when you grow older. Your mouth is so big.” A strange new feeling shot through Beaut. He wondered why she had said that and wanted to take hold of her hand and kiss her then and there. He got up and looked at the sun going down behind the hill far away at the other end of the valley. “We'd better be getting along back,” he said. The woman remained seated on the log. “Sit down,” she said, “I'll tell you something—something it's good for you to hear. You're so big and red you tempt a girl to bother you. First though you tell me why you go along the street looking into the gutter when I stand in the stairway in the evening.” Beaut sat down again upon the log, and thought of what the black-haired boy had told him of her. “Then it was true—what he said about you?” he asked.

“No! No!” she cried, jumping up in her turn and beginning to pin on her hat. “Let's be going.” Beaut sat stolidly on the log. “What's the use bothering each other,” he said. “Let's sit here until the sun goes down. We can get home before dark.” They sat down and she began talking, boasting of herself as he had boasted of his father.

“I'm too old for that boy,” she said; “I'm older than you by a good many years. I know what boys talk about and what they say about women. I do pretty well. I don't have any one to talk to except father and he sits all evening reading a paper and going to sleep in his chair. If I let boys come and sit with me in the evening or stand talking with me in the stairway it is because I'm lonesome. There isn't a man in town I'd marry—not one.” The speech sounded discordant and harsh to Beaut. He wished his father were there rubbing his hands together and muttering rather than this pale woman who stirred him up and then talked harshly like the women at the back doors in Coal Creek. He thought again as he had thought before that he preferred the black-faced miners drunk and silent to their pale talking wives. On an impulse he told her that, saying it crudely so that it hurt. Their companionship was spoiled. They got up and began to climb the hill, going toward home. Again she put her hand to her side and again he wished to put his hand at her back and push her up the hill. Instead he walked beside her in silence, again hating the town. Halfway down the hill the tall woman stopped by the road-side. Darkness was coming on and the glow of the coke ovens lighted the sky. “One living up here and never going down there might think it rather grand and big,” he said. Again the hatred came. “They might think the men who live down there knew something instead of being just a lot of cattle.” A smile came into the face of the tall woman and a gentler look stole into her eyes. “We get at one another,” she said, “we can't let one another alone. I wish we hadn't quarrelled. We might be friends if we tried. You have got something in you. You attract women. I've heard others say that. Your father was that way. Most of the women here would rather have been the wife of Cracked McGregor ugly as he was than to have stayed with their own husbands. I heard my mother say that to father when they lay quarrelling in bed at night and I lay listening.” The boy was overcome with the thought of a woman talking to him so frankly. He looked at her and said what was in his mind. “I don't like the women,” he said, “but I liked you, seeing you standing in the stairway and thinking you had been doing as you pleased. I thought maybe you amounted to something. I don't know why you should be bothered by what I think. I don't know why any woman should be bothered by what any man thinks. I should think you would go right on doing what you want to do like mother and me about my being a lawyer.” He sat on a log beside the road near where he had met her and watched her go down the hill. “I'm quite a fellow to have talked to her all afternoon like that,” he thought and pride in his growing manhood crept over him.

In the fall of the year Tom Kester came back to the town of Orrville, Ohio, after an absence of eleven years. He came on the evening train from Cleveland and got off at the station carrying a yellow leather bag that had cost him eight dollars. On the platform stood his cousin Albert Dorsey, a heavy man with a brown mustache and a coat too tight across the shoulders. The two men had not seen each other since they were boys of seventeen and eighteen. They had grown up together in two houses that stood back to back on Locust Street, and as boys they had slept in the same bed on summer nights when the Dorsey house was full of visiting relatives. Now they shook hands and did not know what to say. Albert took the yellow bag and carried it, although Tom protested. "It's nothing," Albert said, "I'm used to lifting." He worked in the warehouse of the Orrville Implement Company and all day long lifted plow points and the iron wheels of cultivators into wagons.

They walked up the hill from the station along Mill Street. It was growing dark and in the houses lamps had been lighted. Tom looked at the houses and remembered the names of the people who had lived in them. Some of the names he spoke aloud. "Does old Haskins still live there, the one with the wooden leg?" he asked. Albert said that Haskins had been dead six years. "He fell off the porch one winter night," he said, "and froze before anybody found him." The two men laughed and then were ashamed of having laughed. They went on in silence. Tom thought that his cousin had grown old. There was gray in the brown mustache and he walked with his feet turned out like a farmer walking behind a plow. "He has settled down here and has got heavy," Tom thought. A kind of pity mixed with contempt came into his mind. He thought of himself as a man who had gone out into the world and done things. In Cleveland he was a salesman for a wholesale grocery house and wore a gray suit and a stiff hat. He had been in Pittsburgh and Buffalo and once in New York. He walked beside his cousin and straightened his shoulders.

Albert was thinking too. All day in the warehouse he had thought of the coming of his cousin, and as he lifted the iron wheels into the wagons he had talked to himself. "I'll take him out to the creek where we used to swim," he had thought. "We'll sit there and talk like we used to talk." When he was a boy Albert had been the slow one of the two. Tom had been quick and had a sharp tongue and the girls of the town liked him. Albert had followed him about. It had seemed to him then that Tom knew everything, that he could do anything he set out to do. When Tom went away to the city Albert had stood on the station platform and had felt that something in himself had gone away on the train. He had never quite got over the feeling. Now his cousin walked beside him in a gray suit and a stiff hat and Albert did not know how to begin talking.

There is something in men that makes them want to go back to the places where they were boys. They go back and are disappointed. The streets are narrower than they remembered and the people are smaller. They have built up in their minds a picture of the place, and when they come back the picture is not there. A man comes back to his town as a boy comes back to a house where he has been happy, and finds the furniture moved about and strangers sitting in the chairs.

At the Dorsey house Albert's wife Mary stood in the doorway with a lamp in her hand. She was a small dark woman with thin arms, and when Tom saw her he started. He had forgotten that Albert had married Mary Rutledge. When they were boys Tom had walked with her on Sunday evenings out along the Medina road, and once, on a night in June, he had kissed her by the fence at the end of the fairgrounds. He had not thought of it in years. Now it came back to him and he flushed. Mary held the lamp up so that she could see his face. "You've got fat, Tom Kester," she said, and laughed. Her laugh was harsh and there was something in it that hurt. Behind her in the hallway two children stood looking at the visitor with round eyes. Albert put the yellow bag down by the stairs and stood rubbing his hands together.

They ate supper in the kitchen. Mary had fried chicken and there were biscuits and honey. Tom talked about the city. He told of the tall buildings and of the theatres and of a man he knew who had made forty thousand dollars in a year selling coffee. As he talked he grew excited and his voice rose. He had told the same stories before, in hotel rooms to other salesmen, and he knew how to make them sound well. Albert sat at the end of the table and listened. He ate slowly, putting large pieces of chicken into his mouth and chewing them thoughtfully. Now and then he nodded his head. Mary did not listen. She got up and went to the stove and came back, and once she slapped the smaller of the two children for spilling milk on the oilcloth. When Tom had finished a story about a fire in a Pittsburgh hotel she said, "I suppose you think we're dead here. I suppose you think nothing ever happens in Orrville." Tom said that he did not think so at all. He looked at his plate. "Well it don't," Mary said. "Nothing happens here." She took the children upstairs to bed and did not come down again.

After supper the two men went out of the house and walked through the town. It was a warm night for October, and a few people sat on their porches. Albert spoke to them as they passed and they called back to him. "That's my cousin Tom," he said to a man standing by the gate of the Methodist parsonage, "he's come home from Cleveland." The man came to the fence and shook hands, and Tom remembered him. He was Ed Shaw who had been a clerk in the drug store and had played the cornet in the band. "Well, well," Ed Shaw said, "I suppose you're rich now." He laughed loudly and slapped his leg and Tom laughed too. When they had gone on Tom was angry. "They all think a man who goes away must be rich or a fool," he said. Albert did not answer.

They went out along the Medina road past the last of the houses and came to the bridge over Sugar Creek. Below the bridge was the pool where they had swum as boys. The water was low and they could hear it running over the stones. Albert climbed down the bank and sat on a flat rock, and after a moment Tom followed him, holding up the legs of his gray trousers. They sat side by side. The moon had come up over the trees on the farther bank and the water shone. For a long time neither of them spoke.

Albert had wanted to say something to his cousin all evening. He did not know what it was. It was a feeling rather than a thought. He wanted to tell Tom that he was glad he had come home, that he had thought of him often in the warehouse, that the town had been lonely without him. But when he tried to put the feeling into words they would not come. He picked up a stone and threw it into the water. "Do you remember the time you dared me to swim across in March?" he asked. Tom laughed. "And you did it," he said. "You came out blue as a plum and your mother whipped you." Albert laughed too. He felt better. "I did everything you dared me to," he said. "I was a big fool."

Tom took out a cigar and lighted it and offered one to Albert, who shook his head. The smoke of the cigar hung in the still air over the water. He had told about the theatres and the man who made forty thousand dollars. Shame crept over him and he threw the cigar into the creek.

There's a million people and you don't know one of them."

Albert was astonished. He had thought of his cousin all these years as a man who knew everybody. He had pictured Tom in the city walking along crowded streets, stopping to speak to this one and that, going into fine restaurants with other men in gray suits. He did not know what to say. He got up from the rock and stood beside Tom, and after a moment he put his heavy hand on his cousin's shoulder. Tom did not move. They stood so for a long time.

Then Albert began to talk. He had not meant to say what he said. The words came out of him as water comes out of a spring when a stone is pulled away. "You think I've got everything here," he said. "You think I've got a house and a wife and two kids and a job, and that's everything. Well it ain't. You saw her tonight. She hates it here. She hates me. She ain't said a kind word to me in three years." He took his hand from Tom's shoulder and clenched it. "She wanted you," he said. "That's the truth of it. She wanted you and you went away and she took me. I knew it when I married her. I thought it wouldn't matter. I thought I could make it so it wouldn't matter."

Tom turned and looked at his cousin. The moon was on Albert's face and Tom saw that his lips were trembling under the brown mustache. A strange feeling came over Tom. He wanted to laugh and he wanted to cry. He remembered the night by the fence at the end of the fairgrounds, the smell of the clover and the girl's thin arms about his neck, and how afterward he had gone home and lain awake thinking of the city and of all the things he would do there. He had not thought of Mary Rutledge at all, lying awake. He had thought of himself. "It was nothing," he said. "I swear it was nothing, Albert. We were just kids. I don't know that she ever thought of me after I went."

"She thought of you," Albert said stubbornly. "She thinks of you yet. Tonight when you were talking at the table she wouldn't look at you. That's how I knew." He sat down again on the flat rock and put his head in his hands. Tom stood over him. He did not know what to do. In the city when a man got drunk and began to talk of his troubles Tom knew how to slap him on the back and buy him another drink and change the subject. But this was not like that. This was his cousin Albert who had swum across Sugar Creek in March because Tom had dared him.

"Oh, to hell with it," Tom burst out. "To hell with all of it." He sat down beside Albert and the two men sat with their shoulders touching. Across the creek a dog began to bark at a farmhouse and kept on barking. A wagon went over the bridge above them and the planks rattled. The driver was singing. When the wagon had gone the dog stopped barking and it was very still.

"I'll tell you what," Albert said after a while. His voice was quiet now. "I don't hold it against you. I never did. I used to think about you up there in the city and I'd think, 'Tom's doing it for both of us.' That's a crazy notion, I know. But I'd think it. I'd be lifting them iron wheels and I'd think, 'Tom's out there somewhere and he's doing it for both of us.'" He laughed, a short ashamed laugh. "I guess you didn't know you were carrying me along," he said.

Tom did not answer. Something had happened in his throat. He looked at the water running over the stones in the moonlight and thought of the room on Prospect Avenue with the window that looked out on the brick wall. He thought that his cousin had been sitting in this town all these years thinking of him, believing in him, and that all the time he, Tom, had been sitting on a brass bed with his shoes off listening to strangers quarrel through the wall. It seemed to him the strangest thing in the world. He wanted to tell Albert about the room. He wanted to tell him everything, the whole truth of it, so that there would be nothing false left between them. He opened his mouth and could not do it. "We're a pair, ain't we," he said instead. "We're a fine pair of fellows."

They climbed up the bank to the road and walked back toward the town. The lamps were out in most of the houses now. As they went along Albert began to whistle softly, an old tune they had both known as boys, and Tom fell in beside him and walked as Albert walked, with long slow strides. At the corner of Locust Street they stopped under an elm. Tom looked across at the house where he had lived as a boy. Other people lived in it now and there was a new porch on the front, painted white. "I thought I'd feel something, seeing it," he said. "I don't feel anything." Albert said that the Thompsons had it, that old man Thompson had built the porch himself the spring before. They stood looking at the porch.

"You'll stay the week?" Albert asked. Tom said that he had meant to stay the week but that now he did not know. "I think I'd better go Thursday," he said. "There's a man in Akron I've got to see." Albert knew that there was no man in Akron. He did not say anything. He thought that it was better so. He thought of Mary lying upstairs in the dark with her face to the wall, and of himself going up the stairs in his stocking feet so as not to wake her, and of how she would be awake all the same and would say nothing. He thought that if Tom stayed the week it would be harder for all of them.

They went into the house. In the kitchen Albert lighted the lamp and found a piece of pie in the cupboard and cut it in two, and the two men stood by the table eating pie with their fingers. They did not talk. When they had finished Albert took the lamp and led the way up the stairs to the little room at the back where he had made up the bed for his cousin. He set the lamp on the dresser and stood in the doorway. "Well, good night, Tom," he said. Tom said good night. Albert did not go. He stood in the doorway rubbing his big hands together. "I'm glad you come," he said finally, and went out and closed the door.

Tom sat on the edge of the bed. He did not undress. Through the wall he could hear Albert moving about in the next room and then the creak of the bed as he lay down. He heard no voices. He thought of what his cousin had said by the creek, about doing it for both of them, and he thought it was the queerest thing that had ever been said to him. He put out the lamp and sat in the dark. Outside the window the moon had gone behind the elm and the leaves made moving shadows on the floor. "He's the better man," Tom thought. "He's stayed here and he's carried it. I went away and I didn't carry anything." The thought did not make him sad. It made him feel quiet and humble, as he had felt sometimes as a boy in church when the organ played. He lay back on the bed with his clothes on and his hands under his head.

In the morning Albert was gone to the warehouse before Tom woke. Mary was in the kitchen and gave him coffee and did not speak, and he drank it standing by the window. When he had finished he put the cup down on the table and said, "Mary, I didn't know." She turned from the stove and looked at him, and for a moment he saw in her face the girl who had stood by the fence at the end of the fairgrounds. Then the look went away. "Know what?" she said, and turned back to the stove. Tom went out of the house and walked down Mill Street toward the warehouse of the Orrville Implement Company. He thought he would stand in the doorway and watch his cousin lift the iron wheels into the wagons. He did not know why he wanted to do this. It seemed to him the only thing in the town that he wanted to see.

A freight train heavily loaded crept round the hill at the end of the valley. It was spring and over even that hive of black industry hung a faint promise of beauty. The boys talked of the life of people in their town and as they talked thought each of himself. Although he had not been out of the valley and had grown strong and big there, Beaut McGregor knew something of the outside world. It isn't a time when men are shut off from their fellows. Newspapers and magazines have done their work too well. They reached even into the miner's cabin and the merchants along Main Street of Coal Creek stood before their stores in the afternoon and talked of the doings of the world. Beaut McGregor knew that life in his town was exceptional, that not everywhere did men toil all day black and grimy underground, that not all women were pale bloodless and bent. As he went about delivering bread he whistled a song. “Take me back to Broadway,” he sang after the soubrette in a show that had once come to Coal Creek. Now as he sat on the hillside he talked earnestly while he gesticulated with his hands. “I hate this town,” he said. “The men here think they are confoundedly funny. They don't care for anything but making foolish jokes and getting drunk. I want to go away.” His voice rose and hatred flamed up in him. “You wait,” he boasted. “I'll make men stop being fools. I'll make children of them. I'll——” Pausing he looked at his two companions. Beaut poked the ground with a stick. The boy sitting beside him laughed. He was a short well—dressed black—haired boy with rings on his fingers who worked in the town poolroom, racking the pool balls. “I'd like to go where there are women with blood in them,” he said. Three women came up the hill toward them, a tall pale brown-haired woman of twenty-seven and two fairer young girls. The black-haired boy straightened his tie and began thinking of a conversation he would start when the women reached him. Beaut and the other boy, a fat fellow, the son of a grocer, looked down the hill to the town over the heads of the newcomers and continued in their minds the thoughts that had made the conversation.

“Hello girls, come and sit here,” shouted the black-haired boy, laughing and looking boldly into the eyes of the tall pale woman. They stopped and the tall woman began stepping over the fallen logs, coming to them. The two young girls followed, laughing. They sat down on the log beside the boys, the tall pale woman at the end beside red-haired McGregor. An embarrassed silence fell over the party. Both Beaut and the fat boy were disconcerted by this turn to their afternoon's outing and wondered how it would turn out. The pale woman began to talk in a low tone. “I want to get away from here,” she said, “I wish I could hear birds sing and see green things grow.” Beaut McGregor had an idea. “You come with me,” he said. He got up and climbed over the logs and the pale woman followed. The fat boy shouted at them, relieving his own embarrassment by trying to embarrass them. “Where're you going—you two?” he shouted. Beaut said nothing. He stepped over the logs to the road and began climbing the hill. The tall woman walked beside him and held her skirts out of the deep dust of the road. Even on this her Sunday gown there was a faint black mark along the seams—the mark of Coal Creek. As McGregor walked his embarrassment left him. He thought it fine that he should be thus alone with a woman. When she had tired from the climb he sat with her on a log beside the road and talked of the black-haired boy. “He has your ring on his finger,” he said, looking at her and laughing. She held her hand pressed tightly against her side and closed her eyes. “The climbing hurts me,” she said. Tenderness took hold of Beaut. When they went on again he walked behind her, his hand upon her back pushing her up the hill. The desire to tease her about the black-haired boy had passed and he wished he had said nothing about the ring. He remembered the story the black-haired boy had told him of his conquest of the woman. “More than likely a mess of lies,” he thought. Over the crest of the hill they stopped and rested, leaning against a worn rail fence by the woods. Below them in a wagon a party of men went down the hill. The men sat upon boards laid across the box of a wagon and sang a song. One of them stood in the seat beside the driver and waved a bottle. He seemed to be making a speech. The others shouted and clapped their hands. The sounds came faint and sharp up the hill. In the woods beside the fence rank grass grew. Hawks floated in the sky over the valley below. He got a feeling of complete, good fellowship and friendliness with this woman. Without knowing how the thing had been done he felt a certain pride in it. “Don't mind what I said about the ring,” he urged, “I was only trying to tease you.” The woman beside McGregor was the daughter of an undertaker who lived upstairs over his shop near the bakery. A clump of elders had grown about the log since his visits there with Cracked McGregor so that the place was closed and shaded like a room. The woman took off her hat and laid it beside her on the log. A faint colour mounted to her pale cheeks and a flash of anger gleamed in her eyes. “He probably lied to you about me,” she said, “I didn't give him that ring to wear. I don't know why I gave it to him. He wanted it. He asked me for it time and again. He said he wanted to show it to his mother. And now he has shown it to you and I suppose told lies about me.” Beaut was annoyed and wished he had not mentioned the ring. He felt that an unnecessary fuss was being made about it. He did not believe that the black-haired boy had lied but he did not think it mattered. He began talking of his father, boasting of him. His hatred of the town blazed up. “They thought they knew him down there,” he said, “they laughed at him and called him 'Cracked.' They thought his running into the mine just a crazy notion like a horse that runs into a burning stable. He was the best man in town. He was braver than any of them. He went in there and died when he had almost enough money saved to buy a farm over here.” He pointed down the valley. Beaut began to tell her of the visits to the hillside with his father and described the effect of the scene on himself when he was a child. “I thought it was paradise,” he said. She put her hand on his arm and seemed to be soothing him like a careful groom quieting an excitable horse. “Don't mind them,” she said, “you will go away after a time and make a place for yourself out in the world.” He wondered how she knew. A profound respect for her came over him. “She is keen to guess that,” he thought. He began to talk of himself, boasting and throwing out his chest. “I'd like to have the chance to show what I can do,” he declared. A thought that had been in his mind on the winter day when Uncle Charlie Wheeler put the name of Beaut upon him came back and he walked up and down before the woman making grotesque motions with his hands as Cracked McGregor had walked up and down before him.

“I'll tell you what,” he began and his voice was harsh. He had forgotten the presence of the woman and half forgotten what had been in his mind. He sputtered and glared over his shoulder up the hillside as he struggled for words. “Oh to Hell with men!” he burst forth. “They are cattle, stupid cattle.” A fire blazed up in his eyes and a confident ring came into his voice. “I'd like to get them together, all of them,” he said, “I'd like to make them——” Words failed him and again he sat down on the log beside the woman. “Well I'd like to lead them to an old mine shaft and push them in,” he concluded resentfully.

On the eminence Beaut and the tall woman sat and looked down into the valley. “I wonder why we don't go there, mother and I,” he said. “When I see it I'm filled with the notion. I think I want to be a farmer and work in the fields. Instead of that mother and I sit and plan of the city. I'm going to be a lawyer. That's all we talk about. Then I come up here and it seems as though this is the place for me.” The tall woman laughed. “I can see you coming home at night from the fields,” she said. “It might be to that white house there with the windmill, You would be a big man and would have dust in your red hair and perhaps a red beard growing on your chin. And a woman with a baby in her arms would come out of the kitchen door to stand leaning on the fence waiting for you. When you came up she would put her arm around your neck and kiss you on the lips. The beard would tickle her cheek. You should have a beard when you grow older. Your mouth is so big.” A strange new feeling shot through Beaut. He wondered why she had said that and wanted to take hold of her hand and kiss her then and there. He got up and looked at the sun going down behind the hill far away at the other end of the valley. “We'd better be getting along back,” he said. The woman remained seated on the log. “Sit down,” she said, “I'll tell you something—something it's good for you to hear. You're so big and red you tempt a girl to bother you. First though you tell me why you go along the street looking into the gutter when I stand in the stairway in the evening.” Beaut sat down again upon the log, and thought of what the black-haired boy had told him of her. “Then it was true—what he said about you?” he asked.

“No! No!” she cried, jumping up in her turn and beginning to pin on her hat. “Let's be going.” Beaut sat stolidly on the log. “What's the use bothering each other,” he said. “Let's sit here until the sun goes down. We can get home before dark.” They sat down and she began talking, boasting of herself as he had boasted of his father.

“I'm too old for that boy,” she said; “I'm older than you by a good many years. I know what boys talk about and what they say about women. I do pretty well. I don't have any one to talk to except father and he sits all evening reading a paper and going to sleep in his chair. If I let boys come and sit with me in the evening or stand talking with me in the stairway it is because I'm lonesome. There isn't a man in town I'd marry—not one.” The speech sounded discordant and harsh to Beaut. He wished his father were there rubbing his hands together and muttering rather than this pale woman who stirred him up and then talked harshly like the women at the back doors in Coal Creek. He thought again as he had thought before that he preferred the black-faced miners drunk and silent to their pale talking wives. On an impulse he told her that, saying it crudely so that it hurt. Their companionship was spoiled. They got up and began to climb the hill, going toward home. Again she put her hand to her side and again he wished to put his hand at her back and push her up the hill. Instead he walked beside her in silence, again hating the town. Halfway down the hill the tall woman stopped by the road-side. Darkness was coming on and the glow of the coke ovens lighted the sky. “One living up here and never going down there might think it rather grand and big,” he said. Again the hatred came. “They might think the men who live down there knew something instead of being just a lot of cattle.” A smile came into the face of the tall woman and a gentler look stole into her eyes. “We get at one another,” she said, “we can't let one another alone. I wish we hadn't quarrelled. We might be friends if we tried. You have got something in you. You attract women. I've heard others say that. Your father was that way. Most of the women here would rather have been the wife of Cracked McGregor ugly as he was than to have stayed with their own husbands. I heard my mother say that to father when they lay quarrelling in bed at night and I lay listening.” The boy was overcome with the thought of a woman talking to him so frankly. He looked at her and said what was in his mind. “I don't like the women,” he said, “but I liked you, seeing you standing in the stairway and thinking you had been doing as you pleased.
